AI Engineering: From First Principles to Production

A complete, illustrated textbook on building and shipping real AI systems — how large language models work inside, prompting, retrieval (RAG), AI agents, fine-tuning, model serving, evaluation, reliability, security & governance, the cloud platforms, and system design. Every topic runs from the basics to production, taught as a story with a running banking example, diagrams, and runnable code.

LLMs & internals RAG · retrieval AI agents Fine-tuning & serving Eval & production Security & governance Cloud platforms Interview-ready

About this book

Most AI material is either a shallow tour or a pile of disconnected tutorials. This book is neither. It takes you from first principles — what a language model really is and how it picks each word — all the way to production: the retrieval systems, agents, evaluation harnesses, guardrails, and cloud deployments that real products are actually made of. Every idea is explained in plain language, then deepened to the level a working engineer needs, then shown as it behaves under real traffic.

The journey is grounded in one running example — BankAssist, the AI assistant for a fictional bank — so abstract ideas always land in a concrete, high-stakes setting where correctness, cost, and compliance genuinely matter.

🏦 The running example — BankAssist

Throughout the book you are the engineer building BankAssist: a customer-facing assistant that answers questions, moves money, disputes charges, and flags fraud. Banking is a demanding teacher — a wrong answer costs real money, every action needs an audit trail, and "it usually works" is never good enough. Each technique is shown through a concrete BankAssist scenario, so you see not just how it works, but how it survives contact with real customers and real regulators.

Who this book is for

Software engineers, data scientists, and technical leads who want to build and ship language-model-powered products — not just call an API once. If you can read Python and have used a web API before, you are ready. You do not need a machine-learning background: the internals are built up from scratch, in plain words. A working familiarity with the command line, version control, and web APIs is assumed, and briefly recapped in Part 1.

How this book is organized

Eleven parts, ordered so each builds on the one before — foundations first, the most advanced material (fine-tuning) near the end, and an interview bank to close. Related topics are grouped together within each part.

How each topic is taught

Every topic follows the same path: a plain-language introduction, the core idea, how it actually works on the inside, the advanced trade-offs, and finally what it takes to run it in production — cost, latency, failure modes, and compliance — ending with the common pitfalls and when not to use it. Diagrams make the mechanisms visible, and short, fully commented code shows each idea in practice.

A note on the code

Code examples use the OpenAI API by default, with other providers shown where they add real value, and keep to current, non-deprecated interfaces; every meaningful line is commented with the reason it is there. Figures and amounts use a single currency for clarity. This book teaches engineering, not financial or legal practice — regulatory specifics vary by jurisdiction and change over time, so treat them as a starting point and confirm the current rules for your own setting.

Foundations — LLMs, prompting & how agents think

Before we wire up tools, memory, or retrieval, let's get a clear and honest picture of the "brain" every AI feature sits on top of — what it really is, how you steer it, and where it can quietly let you down.

How we got here: a short history of language models

Today's assistants didn't appear from nowhere — they are the latest step in a sixty-year climb, where each idea fixed the thing the one before it got wrong.

If you want to understand how a modern AI assistant thinks, it helps to know the road that led to it. Every strange habit an LLM has — the way it predicts the next word, the way it turns language into numbers, the way it "pays attention" to context — is an inheritance from an earlier era of research. None of it is magic. It is a stack of clever fixes, each one solving a problem the previous approach couldn't. Let's walk that road from the very beginning, in plain language.

The rule-writers and the word-counters

The earliest attempts, from the 1960s onward, tried to teach computers language the way you'd teach a strict grammar class: by hand-written rules. Engineers wrote thousands of if-then patterns and grammar trees — "if the sentence contains balance and what, treat it as a balance query." It worked for tiny, tidy cases and shattered the moment a real person typed something unexpected. Language is too big and too messy to spell out by hand.

By the 1990s the field switched from rules to statistics. Instead of describing grammar, you simply counted. An n-gram model predicts the next word from the last few words: having seen millions of sentences, it knows that after "overdraft" the word "fee" is far more likely than "banana." Search engines leaned on bag-of-words and TF-IDF — scoring a document by which words it contains and how rare those words are. This was a real leap, but it was brittle: an n-gram only remembers the last two or three words, and counting words gives a machine no sense of meaning. To it, "cancel my card" and "card cancellation request" look like unrelated strings.

Meaning becomes geometry: word embeddings

The breakthrough of word2vec (Google, 2013) and GloVe (Stanford, 2014) was to turn every word into a vector — a list of numbers — positioned so that words with similar meanings sit close together in space. Suddenly "card" and "debit" were neighbours, and you could even do arithmetic on meaning: king − man + woman ≈ queen. Meaning had become geometry. The catch: each word got one fixed vector. The word "bank" had a single point in space whether you meant the side of a river or a place that holds money. Context was still missing.

Reading in order: RNNs, LSTMs, and attention

To handle context, researchers built models that read text in order, carrying a memory as they go — recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their stronger cousin the LSTM (long short-term memory). These powered the first good machine translation. But they had two deep problems: they forgot across long distances (by the end of a long paragraph, the start had faded), and they had to read strictly one word at a time, so they were painfully slow to train. Around 2014–15 a clever add-on called the attention mechanism let a translation model look back at any earlier word it needed, instead of relying on a single fading memory. Attention was the spark.

The Transformer: the breakthrough everything sits on

In 2017, a Google paper with the now-famous title "Attention Is All You Need" made a bold move: throw away the slow sequential reading entirely and keep only the attention. The Transformer lets every word look at every other word all at once, in parallel. That one change fixed both old problems — it handles long-range context and trains in parallel on huge hardware, so it scales. Every major model today, without exception, is a Transformer under the hood.

Pretraining and scale: BERT and GPT

With a scalable engine in hand, the next idea was pretraining: let a model read enormous amounts of raw text first, learning language in general, before fine-tuning it for any specific task. In 2018 two families appeared. BERT (Google) was an encoder built to deeply understand text — great for search, classification, and sentiment. The GPT line (OpenAI) was a decoder built to generate text, one word at a time. Researchers then noticed the scaling laws: bigger model + more data + more compute kept making results reliably better, with no wall in sight. So the models grew — GPT-2 in 2019, GPT-3 in 2020 — and their abilities grew with them.

From raw predictor to helpful assistant

A giant next-word predictor is powerful but not naturally helpful — ask it a question and it might continue with more questions. The fix was two-step tuning: instruction tuning (training on examples of following instructions) and RLHF — reinforcement learning from human feedback, where people rank answers and the model learns to prefer the helpful, honest ones. That recipe turned a raw predictor into an assistant, and in late 2022 it was packaged into a simple chat box: ChatGPT launched on 30 November 2022 and reached a hundred million users faster than anything before it. The explosion you're living through started there.

2023 to today: multimodal, long context, reasoning, and agents

Since then the pace has only quickened. Models became multimodal — they read images, audio, and documents, not just text. Context windows grew from a few thousand tokens to a million. Powerful open-weight models arrived that teams can run themselves. A new class of reasoning models learned to "think" step by step before answering. And finally, models were given tools and goals so they could act, not just chat — which is exactly what agents are, and what the rest of this book is about.

🏦 Picture this

Ask BankAssist "my card's gone, what do I do?" and watch each era answer. The rules system needs the exact keyword "block card" or it's lost. The n-gram search returns pages that merely contain "card." word2vec at least knows "card," "debit," and "stolen" are related. The LSTM can follow a sentence but forgets your earlier mention of travel. The Transformer-based assistant reads the whole conversation, understands intent, and — as an agent — actually calls the "freeze card" tool and books a replacement. Same question; sixty years of progress between the answers.

💡 Key idea

Every milestone fixed the flaw of the last one: rules couldn't scale, so we counted (n-grams); counting had no meaning, so we embedded words as vectors; vectors ignored context, so we read in order (RNN/LSTM); order was slow and forgetful, so attention let us read it all at once (Transformer); and scale plus human feedback turned that engine into a helpful, tool-using assistant.

Why does this lineage matter for the chapters ahead? Because the vocabulary of this whole book is the vocabulary of that journey. Tokens, embeddings, attention, pretraining, context windows — none of these are new jargon invented for assistants. They are the hard-won ideas from this history, and they come back on nearly every page. Knowing where they came from means you're never memorising a buzzword; you're recognising an old friend.

🧠 Remember it

Rules → counts → vectors → memory → attention → scale → assistant → agent. Each arrow is one problem getting solved.

Before you start: the Python and setup you'll need

You do not need to be a Python expert to follow this book — you need a handful of everyday building blocks, a key kept safely, and about ten minutes of setup. This page gets you there.

Every code example in this book is written in Python, because that is the language almost the entire AI world speaks. The good news: the pieces you'll actually meet are the gentle, readable ones. If you can store a value, call a function, and loop over a list, you can follow along. Let's take a quick, friendly tour of exactly the Python you'll see — nothing more — then get your machine ready to make a real call to a model.

The Python you'll actually see — a whirlwind tour

Here is almost every language feature this book leans on, each with a one-line taste. Skim it now; it'll feel familiar the moment you see it again in a real example.

# variables — just name = value, no type declarations needed
name = "Ava"                       # a string (text)
balance = 1572.40                  # a float (a decimal number)
is_overdrawn = balance < 0         # a bool: True or False

# lists hold an ordered sequence; dicts map a key to a value
recent = ["coffee", "rent", "salary"]          # a list
account = {"id": "AC-19", "balance": balance}   # a dict (key -> value)
print(account["balance"])                       # look a value up by its key

# functions — a reusable block: def name(inputs): ... return a result
def fee_for(times):                # define a function
    return 35 * times              # hand a value back to the caller

# f-strings — slot values straight into text inside {curly braces}
msg = f"Hi {name}, your balance is ${balance:.2f}"   # "...is $1572.40"

# loops repeat work; conditionals (if) decide what to do
for item in recent:                # do this once per item in the list
    if item == "salary":           # a yes/no test
        print("Salary found")

# imports — borrow code from the standard library or an installed package
import json                        # Python's built-in JSON helper
from openai import OpenAI          # pull one name out of the openai package

# list comprehension — build a new list in one compact line
loud = [x.upper() for x in recent] # ["COFFEE", "RENT", "SALARY"]

# type hints — optional labels saying what goes in and comes out
def greet(user: str) -> str:       # takes a str, returns a str
    return f"Hello {user}"

# JSON text <-> Python dict — the everyday currency of APIs
data = json.loads('{"ok": true}') # JSON text  -> Python dict
text = json.dumps(data)           # Python dict -> JSON text

Three features show up specifically around models, so meet them briefly now — you'll understand them fully when they appear in context:

# Pydantic models — describe the exact shape you want the model to return
from pydantic import BaseModel
class Dispute(BaseModel):          # a typed data shape for structured output
    amount: float                  # each field has a name and a type
    reason: str

# async / await — begin slow work (a network call) without freezing the rest
import asyncio
async def fetch():                 # an "async" function can pause politely
    await asyncio.sleep(1)         # wait here, letting other work run meanwhile

# context managers — "with" opens a resource and always closes it for you
with open("notes.txt") as f:       # the file is auto-closed at the block's end
    contents = f.read()
▶ Output

Nothing is printed by these definitions on their own — they set up shapes and helpers you'll call later. You'll see Pydantic when we ask a model for clean, structured answers, async/await when agents or streaming do several things at once, and with whenever we open files or network connections safely.

Getting your machine ready

You need three things: a recent Python, a tidy place to install packages, and the OpenAI library. Use Python 3.11 or newer. Then make a virtual environment — a private sandbox so this project's packages never collide with another project's. The classic way is the built-in venv; the fast, increasingly popular way is uv, a single tool that creates the environment and installs packages in one go.

# --- Option A: the classic, built-in way ---
python -m venv .venv               # create a sandbox in a .venv folder
source .venv/bin/activate          # turn it on (Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate)
pip install openai python-dotenv   # install the two packages we need

# --- Option B: the fast way with uv ---
uv init bankassist                 # start a project folder
cd bankassist
uv add openai python-dotenv        # creates the sandbox AND installs, in one step
uv run hello.py                    # run your script inside that sandbox
✅ Setup checklist

Tick these once and every example in the book will run:

  • ☐ Python 3.11+ installed (python --version to check).
  • ☐ A virtual environment active — venv or uv.
  • ☐ pip install openai python-dotenv (or uv add) done.
  • ☐ An API key in an environment variable, never in your code.
  • ☐ A tiny project layout: a hello.py, a .env file for secrets, and a .gitignore that lists .env and .venv/.

Your API key — a secret, treated like one

To call a model you need an API key: a long secret string from your provider's dashboard (for OpenAI, create one under API keys in your account). It identifies and bills you, so it is exactly as sensitive as a password. The golden rule: never type the key into your code, and never commit it to git. Instead, keep it in an environment variable. The easiest habit is a file called .env that stays on your machine only:

# .env  — a plain text file, listed in .gitignore so it is never committed
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-your-real-key-goes-here

Then load it in Python. The python-dotenv package reads the .env file into the environment, and os.environ lets you read it back:

import os                          # standard library: access environment variables
from dotenv import load_dotenv     # reads a .env file into the environment

load_dotenv()                      # load the values from .env (no-op if absent)
key = os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"] # read the secret from the environment, not from code
⚠ Watch out

Never hardcode a key like OpenAI(api_key="sk-...") and never commit .env to git. A key pasted into source code or pushed to a repository is, for all practical purposes, public — bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes, and a leaked key can run up a real bill or, in a bank, breach data-handling rules. Add .env to .gitignore on day one, and if a key is ever exposed, revoke it in the dashboard immediately and issue a new one.

Your first call: "hello, LLM"

Everything is now in place for the smallest possible real program. It reads your key from the environment, sends one line to a current, low-cost model (gpt-4.1-mini), and prints the reply.

import os                          # to read the environment variable
from dotenv import load_dotenv     # to pull the key out of the .env file
from openai import OpenAI          # the official OpenAI Python SDK

load_dotenv()                      # load OPENAI_API_KEY from .env into the environment
client = OpenAI()                  # the client finds the key in the environment by itself

resp = client.responses.create(    # the current Responses API: one call, one reply
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",          # a current, fast, inexpensive model — great for learning
    input="In one sentence, what is a bank overdraft?",  # your prompt
)
print(resp.output_text)            # the finished answer, already assembled as plain text
▶ Output

A bank overdraft lets you withdraw more money than your account holds, up to an agreed limit, usually for a fee or interest.

Line by line: load_dotenv() puts your secret into the environment; OpenAI() builds a client that quietly reads OPENAI_API_KEY for you (no key ever appears in the code); client.responses.create(...) sends your prompt to the model and waits for the full reply; and resp.output_text hands you back the plain answer string, ready to print. That is the exact shape of nearly every model call in this book — the later chapters just add tools, memory, and retrieval around this same core.

🏦 Picture this

This very snippet is the seed of BankAssist. Swap the prompt for a customer's real question, wrap it in the safety and data-grounding you'll learn across this book, and the same four lines grow into an assistant that quotes fees, checks balances, and files disputes — all built on the "read the key, call the model, read the reply" loop you just ran.

What you do not need

Let's clear away the fear. To build real, useful AI features you do not need a background in machine learning, you do not need linear algebra or calculus, and you do not need a GPU or any special hardware to begin — the model runs on the provider's servers and you reach it over the internet with the tiny program above. You are an engineer wiring up a powerful service, not a researcher training one. Basic Python and the setup on this page are genuinely enough to follow every example that follows.

(One neighbour to this page: a later topic, "Just enough developer background: APIs and JSON," zooms in on what an API call is and how JSON travels over the wire — the concepts behind the request you just made.)

💡 Key idea

Setup is a one-time, five-step ritual: a recent Python, a virtual environment, pip install openai, a key in an environment variable, and your first call. Do it once and the rest of the book is just building on that first working reply.

🧠 Remember it

Sandbox, secret, send: isolate your packages in a venv, keep the key in .env, and send your first prompt. Keys live in the environment, never in the code.

Developer foundations: the terminal, Git, and how the web talks (HTTP/REST/JSON)

Before any AI, there are four everyday tools every engineer leans on without thinking — a command line, version control, the language the web speaks, and the little data format that rides on top. Meet all four here, from zero.

Every later page in this book quietly assumes you can open a terminal, save your work with Git, and send a request over the internet. If those words feel foreign, relax — none of them are hard, and you only need the everyday 20% that engineers actually use daily. This page is that 20%, taught for a complete beginner, with tiny examples you can try. Think of it as the toolbox you pick up once and then reach for on every job after.

The terminal: talking to your computer in plain commands

The terminal (also called the command line, shell, or console) is a text window where you type a command and the computer does it — no mouse, no clicking. It feels old-fashioned, but engineers live here because it is fast, exact, and easy to automate: a command you can type is a command you can save, share, and repeat. The two commands you'll use most are moving around and listing what's there.

# "where am I?" — print the current folder
pwd                                 # e.g. /home/ava/bankassist
# "cd" = change directory: step into a folder
cd bankassist                       # move into the bankassist folder
# "ls" = list: show the files and folders here
ls                                  # hello.py   .env   data/
# run a Python script — hand the file to the python program
python hello.py                     # prints whatever hello.py says to print
# install a package so you can import it in your code
pip install requests                # classic installer; "uv add requests" is the fast modern way
# an environment variable: a named value the whole session can read
export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-xxxx       # set a secret once (Windows PowerShell: $env:OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-xxxx")
echo $OPENAI_API_KEY                # read it back; your code reads the same value via os.environ
▶ Output

/home/ava/bankassist, then a file listing, then your script's output. The key mental model: you navigate with cd/ls, you run with python x.py, you install with pip or uv, and you pass secrets in through environment variables so they never sit in your code.

Git & GitHub: a save button with a full history

Version control is a time machine for your code. Instead of folders named final, final2, final_REALLY, you take labelled snapshots as you go, and you can always see what changed, when, by whom — and roll back if you break something. Git is the tool that does this on your machine; GitHub is a website that hosts a shared copy so a team can work together. The everyday rhythm is a short loop of a handful of commands.

# get a copy of an existing project from GitHub onto your machine
git clone https://github.com/bank/bankassist.git
# see what you've changed since the last snapshot
git status                          # lists modified / new files
# stage the files you want in the next snapshot
git add hello.py                    # "add" = mark this file to be saved
# take the snapshot, with a short message saying what & why
git commit -m "Add first LLM call"  # a commit is one saved checkpoint
# send your commits up to the shared copy on GitHub
git push                            # upload; teammates can now see your work
# pull down everyone else's latest commits
git pull                            # download & merge their changes into yours
# work on a feature safely, apart from the main code
git branch fix-fees                 # create a separate line of work
git checkout fix-fees              # switch onto it; commit here without touching main
▶ Output

git status shows your changed files; git commit replies with a short id like [fix-fees a1b9c2f] Add first LLM call. That id is a permanent handle on exactly this version.

The teamwork layer is the pull request (PR). You push your branch (your private line of work) to GitHub and open a PR, which says "please review my changes and merge them into the main code." Teammates read the diff, leave comments, you fix things, and once approved it's merged. In plain words: branch to work in private, PR to ask for review, merge to make it official. Keep that shape in mind — later in the book, prompt libraries and model registries borrow the very same idea of versioned, reviewed, promotable changes.

How the web talks: HTTP and REST

When your program needs something from another computer — a weather service, a payments system, a language model — it sends an HTTP request over the internet and gets a response back. That's the whole conversation, and it has just four parts.

A request is: a method (the verb — GET to fetch, POST to send/create, plus PUT, PATCH, DELETE), a URL (the address of the thing), headers (extra info like Content-Type: application/json and your Authorization key), and an optional body (the data you're sending, usually JSON). The response carries a status code — 200 means OK, 4xx means you got something wrong (401 not authorised, 404 not found, 429 too many requests), 5xx means the server failed — plus a body with the answer. An API (application programming interface) is just a published menu of URLs a server promises to answer, and REST is the common, tidy style of designing them around those verbs and addresses. The punchline that matters for this whole book: calling a language model is nothing more than an HTTPS POST with a JSON body.

import requests                      # the most popular Python library for HTTP

resp = requests.post(               # send a POST request (we are sending data)
    "https://httpbin.org/post",     # a free test URL that echoes back what it got
    headers={"Authorization": "Bearer sk-demo"},  # auth header: who you are
    json={"account": "AC-19", "action": "balance"},  # the JSON body; requests sets Content-Type for you
    timeout=10,                     # give up after 10s instead of hanging forever
)
print(resp.status_code)             # 200 means the server handled it
print(resp.json()["json"])          # .json() parses the reply body into a Python dict
▶ Output

200
{'account': 'AC-19', 'action': 'balance'} — the server received our JSON and echoed it back. The exact same pattern (POST + auth header + JSON body) is what every LLM SDK does for you under the hood.

JSON: the data format that rides on top

Notice the json= above. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the plain-text format almost every API uses to carry data, because it's readable by both humans and machines. It has just a few building blocks: objects in curly braces mapping keys to values ({"name": "Ava"}), arrays in square brackets for ordered lists ([1, 2, 3]), and simple types — strings, numbers, true/false, and null. In Python a JSON object maps cleanly to a dict, and two functions move between them.

import json                          # Python's built-in JSON helper (no install needed)

text = '{"account": "AC-19", "balance": 1572.4, "flags": ["new"]}'  # JSON as a string
data = json.loads(text)             # loads = "load string": JSON text -> Python dict
print(data["balance"])              # look values up by key, like any dict

back = json.dumps(data)             # dumps = "dump string": Python dict -> JSON text
print(back)                         # ready to send over the wire again
▶ Output

1572.4
{"account": "AC-19", "balance": 1572.4, "flags": ["new"]} — loads turns text into a dict you can read; dumps turns it back into text to send. You'll meet this pair on nearly every page.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist engineer clones the repo (git clone), makes a branch to add a "check balance" feature, and tests it from the terminal with python check.py. Inside, the code sends an HTTPS POST to the core-banking API with the customer's account id in a JSON body and the team's key in an Authorization header; the server replies 200 with {"balance": 1572.40}. The engineer opens a pull request, a colleague reviews the diff, and it's merged. Four foundations — terminal, Git, HTTP, JSON — in one everyday task.

⚠ Watch out

Never commit secrets. API keys, passwords, and tokens must never be typed into code or saved in a file that Git tracks — add them to .gitignore (list your .env there) and pass them in through environment variables instead. A key pushed to GitHub is effectively public the moment it lands: bots scan repositories within minutes, and a leaked bank key can mean a real bill or a data-handling breach. If one ever slips out, revoke it immediately and issue a new one — deleting the commit is not enough, because the history keeps it.

💡 Key idea

The terminal runs and installs things, Git saves versioned snapshots and shares them via pull requests, HTTP/REST is the request-response conversation between programs, and JSON is the text format the data travels in. Calling an LLM is simply an HTTPS POST carrying a JSON body — once you see that, the rest of the book stops looking like magic.

🧠 Remember it

Navigate, save, send, shape: the terminal navigates, Git saves, HTTP sends, JSON shapes the data. An API call is a verb + an address + a key + a little JSON.

Working with data in Python: files, JSON, CSV, and a little Pandas

AI runs on data — transactions, documents, test cases, logs. Before you can feed data to a model or measure one, you need to open it, read it, clean it, and look at it. Here's the gentle, beginner's version of exactly that.

Almost every real AI task starts with a humble step that has nothing to do with AI: getting your data in from a file and into a shape you can work with. The data usually arrives as a file — a block of text, a JSON export, or a spreadsheet-like CSV — and your first job is always the same: open it, read it, tidy it, inspect it. Learn this once and you'll do it at the start of nearly every project, from building a set of test questions to checking a month of transactions.

Reading and writing files

A file is just bytes saved on disk. Python opens one with open(...), and the safe habit is the with block, which always closes the file for you even if something goes wrong. Files come in two kinds: text (human-readable characters — .txt, .csv, .json) and binary (raw bytes — images, PDFs). For text you should always say the encoding, the rulebook that maps characters to bytes; UTF-8 is the universal modern default and handles every language and symbol, so name it explicitly and avoid garbled accents or emoji.

# write some text to a file; "w" = write (overwrites), encoding is explicit
with open("note.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:  # with = auto-close when done
    f.write("Overdraft fee refunded ✓\n")           # UTF-8 keeps the ✓ intact

# read it back; "r" = read (the default)
with open("note.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    print(f.read())                                 # prints the whole file as one string
▶ Output

Overdraft fee refunded ✓ — written and read back cleanly because both ends agreed on UTF-8.

JSON files and CSV files — the two formats data arrives in

Data most often lands in one of two shapes. JSON files hold nested, structured records (an API export, a config, a saved result); you load a whole file into a Python object and dump one back out. CSV (comma-separated values) is the plain-text cousin of a spreadsheet: one row per line, columns split by commas — exactly what a bank's "export transactions" button gives you. Python's built-in csv module reads each row, and DictReader hands you each row as a dict keyed by the column headers.

import json, csv                     # both are built in — no install

# JSON file: load the whole file into a Python object, and dump one back
with open("result.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump({"passed": 18, "failed": 2}, f)  # dump = write a dict as JSON to the file
with open("result.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    report = json.load(f)           # load = read JSON from the file into a dict
print(report["passed"])             # 18

# CSV file: read each row as a dict keyed by the header row
with open("txns.csv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in csv.DictReader(f):    # DictReader uses row 1 as column names
        print(row["amount"], row["category"])  # access a cell by its column name
▶ Output

18, then one line per transaction like -4.50 coffee. For a few rows, the built-in modules are perfect. When the file gets big or you want to slice and summarise it, reach for Pandas.

A gentle intro to Pandas

Pandas is the go-to Python library for working with table-shaped data. Its star is the DataFrame — think of it as a spreadsheet living in memory: named columns, numbered rows, and a big toolbox for slicing and summarising. You read_csv a file straight into a DataFrame, then select columns, filter rows, and group to aggregate. Here's the whole everyday loop on a transactions export: load it, keep only debits, then total the spend per category.

import pandas as pd                  # the near-universal nickname for pandas

df = pd.read_csv("txns.csv")        # read the CSV into a DataFrame (a table)
df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])  # parse text dates into real dates (sortable, filterable)

print(df.head(2))                   # peek at the first 2 rows to see the shape

debits = df[df["amount"] < 0]       # filter: keep only rows where amount is negative (money out)

by_cat = (debits                    # group the debits...
    .groupby("category")["amount"]  # ...by category, looking at the amount column
    .sum()                          # ...and sum each group
    .sort_values())                 # biggest spend (most negative) first
print(by_cat)
▶ Output
categoryamount (sum)
rent-1200.00
groceries-310.45
coffee-18.50

From a raw CSV to "where did the money go, by category" in six lines. That load → filter → group → sum loop is the backbone of inspecting almost any dataset.

Missing values are the other everyday reality: real exports have blank cells, which Pandas shows as NaN ("not a number"). Two quick moves cover most cases — df.dropna() throws away rows with gaps, and df["category"].fillna("uncategorised") fills them with a sensible default. Decide on purpose which one fits; silently dropping rows can quietly change your totals.

When to reach for which tool

One line to keep it simple: use plain Python (the csv/json modules) for a handful of rows or a quick one-off; use Pandas when you want to filter, group, join, and summarise tables that fit in memory; and reach for a database when the data is too big for memory, is shared by many users, or must be queried and updated continuously.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist engineer is building a test set to measure the assistant. They export a month of real (anonymised) transactions as txns.csv, load it with read_csv, and in a few lines spot the categories, the odd blank cell, and a few suspicious large debits. They turn 50 of those rows into question-and-answer pairs ("How much did I spend on groceries?" → "$310.45") saved as a JSON eval file. Same tiny toolkit — files, CSV, JSON, Pandas — both inspects the data and builds the dataset that will grade the model.

⚠ Watch out

Three traps bite everyone. Dtypes: Pandas may read an account number like 00123 as the integer 123, dropping the leading zero — load ID columns as strings (dtype={"account": str}). Dates: text like "03/04" is ambiguous (March 4th or April 3rd?) and silently mis-sorts — always parse with pd.to_datetime and know your format. PII: a transactions file is full of personal data — names, account numbers, balances. In a bank, never paste it into a public tool, never commit it to Git, and anonymise or mask it before it goes anywhere near a test set or a log.

💡 Key idea

Data work is always the same shape: open a file, parse it into a Python object, then inspect and reshape it. JSON and CSV are the two formats it arrives in; the built-in json/csv modules handle small jobs, and Pandas' DataFrame handles real tables with a load → filter → group → aggregate loop — minding dtypes, dates, missing values, and PII along the way.

🧠 Remember it

Open, parse, inspect, prep. Small data → plain Python; a table to slice → Pandas; too big or shared → a database.

🐼 pandas 📊 data 🏭 production

The big picture: how all the pieces fit together

Before we dive into any single technique, here is the whole forest in one glance — a plain-language map of every layer, what it does, and which part of this book teaches it.

This is a big field, and it is easy to drown in acronyms before you've seen how they connect. So let's step back and look at the whole machine first. Everything you'll build — including BankAssist, our running example — is the same handful of layers stacked in the same order. Learn the shape once here, and every later chapter becomes "oh, that's the retrieval box, I remember where that sits." Think of this page as the map you keep folded in your pocket for the rest of the journey.

Now walk the same map in words. Each line is one layer: what it is, why it matters, and where in the book you'll learn it.

  • The LLM core (Part 1 — Foundations). A large language model is a next-word predictor; a prompt is how you steer it. It matters because it's the brain every other layer sits on. This part — the one you're reading — covers what the model is, tokens, prompting, and its honest limits.
  • Give it your private knowledge — RAG (Part 2 — the Knowledge Layer). Retrieval-augmented generation searches your own documents and pastes the relevant passages into the prompt. It matters because the model doesn't know your fees, policies, or a customer's balance — you have to hand it those facts so it stops guessing.
  • Let it take actions — the agent (Part 3 — Agents). An agent is a loop: the model thinks, calls a tool, reads the result, and repeats, keeping memory across turns. It matters because answering is not enough — a real assistant must do things, like freeze a card or file a dispute.
  • Build it faster — frameworks (Part 4 — Frameworks & orchestration). Libraries that wire the loop, tools, and memory together so you don't hand-roll everything. They matter because they turn weeks of plumbing into days.
  • Coordinate many agents and connect systems (Part 5 — Multi-agent & protocols). Several specialist agents working together, plus open protocols — MCP to plug in tools and data, A2A for agents to talk to each other. It matters once one agent isn't enough and you must integrate with real bank systems.
  • Make it trustworthy — evaluation, reliability, security & governance (Parts 6–8). Measuring quality, handling failure gracefully, and keeping data safe and compliant. This matters most of all in a bank: an impressive demo that can't be measured or governed never ships.
  • Run it — serving, platforms, cost, latency, scaling (Parts 9–10). How the model is actually hosted and served to thousands of users affordably and quickly. It matters because production traffic breaks things a demo never does.
  • Adapt it when needed — fine-tuning (Part 11). Nudging the model's own weights for a narrow task or house style. It matters occasionally — and the honest truth is that good prompting plus RAG solves most problems first, so this is the last resort, not the first move.
🏦 Picture this

One BankAssist chat touches every layer. A customer asks "why was I charged a fee?" The LLM core reads it; RAG pulls the exact fee policy and the customer's recent transactions; the agent loop calls a "get transactions" tool and remembers the thread in memory; if it's complex, a second agent handles the refund via an MCP connection to the core banking system; the whole thing is evaluated for accuracy, secured so no account number leaks, served fast enough to feel instant, and — only if plain prompting ever fell short — backed by a lightly fine-tuned model. Same chat; the entire stack.

✅ How to read this book

You don't have to read all eleven parts the same way. Pick the path that fits you:

  • Beginner — read straight through, Part 1 → 11. Each part builds gently on the one before, so the order is the lesson.
  • Practitioner building a product — Foundations basics → RAG → Agents → Frameworks → Evaluation/Production → Security → Platforms. Treat the deep model internals (chapter 11) and low-level serving (chapter 12) as optional-deep — reach for them when you hit a wall, not before.
  • Interview prep — skim each part for the shape of it, then focus on chapter 96 (the interview chapter) and chapter 92. Use the diagrams as recall hooks.

One reassurance: the deep internals and serving chapters are not hard prerequisites for building. You can ship a real, grounded, governed assistant knowing that these layers exist and where they sit — the map on this page — long before you know every gear inside them.

💡 Key idea

The entire field is one stack read top to bottom: a model you steer with a prompt, grounded with your knowledge (RAG), driven by an agent loop with tools and memory, scaled up to many agents and connected systems, wrapped in trust (eval, security, governance), and finally run on a platform — with fine-tuning as an optional last tweak. Every chapter is one box on that map.

🧠 Remember it

Predict → Ground → Act → Coordinate → Trust → Run → Adapt. Seven words, eleven parts, one whole field.

Just enough machine learning (the 10-minute version)

You do not need the maths, a GPU, or an ML degree to build with LLMs — but a ten-minute mental model of how machines "learn" makes every later page click into place.

Let's clear the air first. This page is not a machine-learning course, and you will never be asked to do calculus or train a model yourself to follow this book. You are going to be an engineer wiring up a powerful pre-built model, not a researcher who builds one from scratch. But a model behaves the way it does because of how it was taught, so a short, honest mental picture of "learning from examples" will make prompting, hallucinations, fine-tuning, and evaluation all make far more sense. Ten minutes now saves confusion on every chapter ahead.

What "machine learning" even means

In traditional programming, a human writes the rules: if the balance is below zero, charge a fee. You spell out every step. Machine learning flips that around. Instead of writing the rules, you show the machine thousands of examples and let it discover the rules itself. One-line intuition: traditional code is rules in, answers out; machine learning is examples in, rules out. You don't tell it how to spot fraud — you show it a pile of past transactions marked "fraud" or "fine," and it figures out the pattern.

The three flavours of learning

  • Supervised learning — learning from labelled examples. Each example comes with the right answer attached. Show it transactions each tagged fraud or legit, and it learns to predict the tag on new ones. Intuition: a flashcard with the answer on the back.
  • Unsupervised learning — finding structure with no labels. You hand it raw data and ask "what groups naturally fall out?" Clustering customers into spending segments is the classic case. Intuition: sorting a messy drawer without being told the categories.
  • Self-supervised learning — predict a hidden part of the data. The data labels itself: hide a word in a sentence and ask the model to guess it. No human tagging needed, so it can learn from oceans of raw text. Intuition: fill in the blank. This is the big one — self-supervised next-word prediction is exactly how an LLM is trained.

The training loop: how a model actually learns

Underneath all three flavours is one repeating loop. A model is just a big box of adjustable numbers called parameters (or weights). Training tunes those numbers until the box makes good predictions:

Read it as a sentence: data flows into a model whose weights start out random; the model makes a prediction; a loss number measures how wrong that guess was; an algorithm called gradient descent nudges every weight a tiny step in the direction that would have made the loss smaller; then it does it all again — millions of times — until the guesses stop improving. That patient downhill roll, from a random box of numbers to a useful one, is learning.

Train, validation, test — and the memorising trap

A model that aces the examples it studied may still be useless, because it might have simply memorised them. So you split your data three ways: a training set it learns from, a validation set to tune choices as you go, and a held-out test set it has never seen, used once to judge real performance. The two failure shapes: overfitting is memorising the training data and flopping on anything new; underfitting is being too simple to catch the pattern at all. The goal between them is generalising — doing well on data it has never met.

⚠ Watch out

A model scoring 99% on its training data but 70% on new data hasn't learned — it has memorised. That gap is overfitting, and it is why a number measured on data the model has already seen is almost meaningless. Always judge a model on held-out data it never trained on. "It worked great in the demo" often just means "it memorised the demo."

Neural networks and backpropagation, in one breath

The "model" in most of this is a neural network: stacked layers, where each layer takes the numbers below it, computes a bunch of weighted sums, and passes them through a small non-linearity (a simple bend, so the network can learn curved, complex patterns rather than only straight lines). Stack enough layers and it can represent remarkably rich behaviour. And backpropagation? That's just the bookkeeping that makes the loop above work: after measuring the loss, the error is traced backwards through the layers to work out how much each weight contributed, so gradient descent knows exactly which way to nudge each one. No calculus needed here — the intuition is "the error flows back and assigns blame."

Features, embeddings, and the two phases

A model only eats numbers, so raw data must first become numbers. Older systems used hand-picked features (e.g. "transaction amount," "hour of day"). Modern models learn their own richer numeric representation called an embedding — a list of numbers that captures meaning, so that "overdraft" and "insufficient funds" land close together. Finally, keep two phases separate: training is the expensive, one-time learning; inference is using the finished model to answer live requests. You learn once, then serve — every time BankAssist replies to a customer, that's inference, not learning.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist runs two very different learners side by side. Its fraud detector is supervised: it trained on millions of past transactions each labelled "fraud" or "fine," so it predicts a risk score on new ones. The language model behind the chat is self-supervised: nobody labelled anything — it simply read mountains of text and learned by repeatedly predicting the next word. Same training loop underneath; completely different kind of examples.

How this becomes an LLM

Now the payoff. Take that exact training loop, feed it self-supervised next-token prediction (guess the next word, measure the loss, nudge the weights), and run it at massive scale — trillions of words and billions of weights — on top of a particular neural-network design called the transformer, and you get a large language model. The transformer's internals are a story of their own in a later part of this book; for now, the one-line version is enough: an LLM is the training loop you just learned, pointed at "predict the next word," scaled up enormously.

💡 Key idea

Machine learning is examples in, rules out. A model is a box of adjustable weights; training is a loop — predict, measure the loss, nudge the weights, repeat — that slowly turns random numbers into useful ones. An LLM is that same loop aimed at predicting the next word, at enormous scale.

🧠 Remember it

Guess, grade, nudge, repeat. That four-beat loop is all of training — an LLM just plays it on "predict the next word," a billion times over.

🎯 interview 🧠 mental model 📚 ML basics

What a large language model really is

Strip away the mystery and an LLM is a very good guesser of the next word — trained on so much text that its guesses sound like understanding.

Imagine a brand-new teller at BankAssist who has never met a customer, but who has read almost everything ever written about banking — every policy page, every FAQ, every forum thread, millions of chat transcripts. You start a sentence, "To dispute a charge, the first thing you should…" and they can finish it smoothly: "…do is open your transactions and find the charge." They are not looking anything up. They just have an extremely strong sense of what words usually come next.

A large language model (LLM) is exactly that, turned into math. It is a huge program that was shown oceans of text and trained to do one deceptively small task: predict the next chunk of text, over and over. That's the whole trick. Everything else — answering questions, writing emails, summarising a statement — is that one skill applied again and again.

In plain terms

Give the model some text (the "prompt"). It looks at everything so far and produces a probability for every possible next chunk. "The customer's account is over…" → maybe 71% drawn, 12% due, 4% limit, and a long tail of unlikely options. It picks one, glues it on, and repeats. Word by word, a full answer appears.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist customer types, "Is my salary in yet?" The model has never seen this customer, but it has seen the shape of millions of banking chats, so it continues the conversation in a natural, helpful way: "Let me check your most recent deposits." It sounds like it knows your account. It does not — on its own it only knows how banking conversations tend to go. Giving it the real deposit data is a separate job we do on purpose.

Going deeper

Why does next-word guessing produce such smart-looking behaviour? Because to predict the next word well across billions of sentences, the model is quietly forced to learn patterns about grammar, facts, tone, code, and reasoning steps. These abilities emerge as a side effect of getting really, really good at the guessing game. The engine under the hood is called a transformer — a design whose key idea is attention: for each word it is writing, the model weighs how much every earlier word should influence this choice. "Fee" earlier in the chat makes "waiver" more likely later. You don't need the equations; you need the intuition: the model is constantly re-reading the whole conversation to decide what fits next.

⚠ Watch out

Because it is predicting plausible text, an LLM will happily produce a confident, well-worded answer that is simply wrong — a made-up fee, a non-existent policy clause, a fabricated reference number. This is called a hallucination. In a bank that is dangerous. The fix is never "trust the model more"; it is to feed it real data and check its output. Treat fluency and truth as two different things.

⚙️ In production

Running an LLM as a real BankAssist feature is not just "call the model and show the text". Cost & latency: every request is billed per token and takes from a few hundred milliseconds to several seconds, so you choose the smallest model that clears the quality bar and cache stable instructions. Scale: providers enforce rate limits (requests and tokens per minute); busy traffic needs queuing, retries with backoff, and sometimes a fallback model when the primary is overloaded. Failure modes: the two that bite banks are hallucination (a confident wrong fact) and unavailability (the API is down or slow) — so you ground answers in real data and always have a graceful "let me get a human" path. Monitoring: log every prompt and response (with secrets redacted), watch latency, error rate, token spend, and sample outputs for quality drift when the provider silently updates the model. Security & compliance: customer data in a prompt leaves your walls unless you use a zero-retention or private endpoint; mask PII before sending, keep audit logs, and get the provider's data-handling terms past your risk team. The model is one component in a governed pipeline, never the whole system.

When to lean on it, and when not to

Lean on an LLM for language-shaped work: explaining, rephrasing, drafting, classifying, pulling structure out of messy text. Do not lean on its memory for anything that must be exact and current — your balance, today's interest rate, a specific transaction. Those come from your own systems; the model's job is to talk about them well.

🧠 Remember it

An LLM is autocomplete that went to university: brilliant at sounding right, so you must give it the facts and check its work.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Tokens, the context window, and why you pay per token

Models don't read letters or whole words — they read "tokens", and almost every limit and bill in this world is measured in them.

When that tireless BankAssist teller reads text, they don't see smooth words. They see text chopped into small pieces called tokens. A token is often a whole short word ("fee", "the"), sometimes a word-piece ("over" + "draft"), sometimes just a few characters or a punctuation mark. A rough rule of thumb for English: 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of a word. So "BankAssist refunded the overdraft fee" is around 7–8 tokens.

The step that does this chopping is called tokenization. Every model has a fixed vocabulary of tokens it learned during training, and it converts your text into a list of ID numbers from that vocabulary before doing anything else.

✅ A little history

Before transformers, making text ready for a computer meant a whole cleaning pipeline. Teams would strip out common "stopwords" (the, is, at), chop words down to a crude root by stemming (refunding → refund) or a smarter dictionary form by lemmatization, then count what was left as a bag-of-words (a tally of which words appeared, order thrown away). Later, word2vec gave each word a single fixed vector so similar words sat near each other — a big step, but "bank" got the same vector whether you meant a riverbank or a savings account. Modern LLMs quietly made most of that unnecessary: they learn their own sub-word tokens straight from raw text (so nothing is thrown away, and even typos and rare terms survive), and they build contextual embeddings where the same word gets a different vector depending on the sentence around it. You no longer pre-clean the text — you hand the model the raw words and let it figure out the rest.

The context window: the model's desk

Everything you send plus everything the model writes back has to fit inside one workspace called the context window, measured in tokens. Think of it as the size of the teller's desk: only so much paper fits at once. If a window is 200,000 tokens, then your system instructions, the conversation history, any documents you paste in, and the model's reply must together stay under that. Modern models in 2026 range from roughly 128K tokens up to 1,000,000-token windows for the big families (Claude, Gemini, gpt-4.1, and others).

⚙️ Under the hood

A bigger desk is not a free lunch. Two production realities bite: cost and latency grow with how full the window is (more tokens = more compute per request), and models suffer from "lost in the middle" — facts buried in the center of a very long prompt get less reliable attention than facts near the start or end. So stuffing a 300-page policy manual into the window is often worse than retrieving the three relevant paragraphs. Put the most important instructions and the freshest facts near the top or bottom.

Why tokens are money

You are billed per token, and almost always at two different rates: input tokens (what you send) are cheaper, output tokens (what the model generates) are pricier. Illustrative 2026 API prices per million tokens look roughly like this (they change often, so always check current pricing):

Model tier (example)Input / 1M tokensOutput / 1M tokens
Small / fast (e.g. Claude Haiku class)~$1~$5
Mid (e.g. Claude Sonnet / gpt-4.1 mid)~$3~$15
Flagship (e.g. Claude Opus class)~$5~$25
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist answers 50,000 chat messages a day. Each one quietly prepends a 1,500-token system prompt full of bank policy. That prefix alone is 75 million input tokens per day. At flagship prices that's real money for text the model re-reads every single time. Two fixes dominate: pick a cheaper model for simple intents, and turn on prompt caching — the provider stores that stable policy prefix so repeated requests are billed at a steep discount instead of full price.

The number-and-currency trap

Tokenization is tuned for ordinary English, which causes two pitfalls that matter enormously in banking. First, numbers tokenize awkwardly — "$123,456.78" can shatter into many odd pieces, which is part of why models fumble arithmetic and misread amounts. Second, non-English and symbol-heavy text uses far more tokens per sentence, so a Hindi or Arabic prompt can cost two to three times as much as the same meaning in English. Budget for that.

✅ Tip

Never guess token counts from character length for anything that must fit or must be budgeted. Use the provider's own token counter (for example, an endpoint like count_tokens) so your estimate matches exactly what you'll be charged for.

⚠ Watch out

The silent killer in long chats is the context window filling up. Because you resend the whole conversation on every turn, a long BankAssist session (history + a pasted statement + the policy prompt) can creep toward the limit — and when it overflows, the request either errors out or the provider quietly drops the oldest messages, so the model suddenly "forgets" what the customer said ten minutes ago. Never assume the window is infinite: track token usage per conversation and trim or summarise old turns before you hit the wall, not after a customer complains.

⚙️ In production

Cost: tokens are the line item on your bill, so the biggest levers are a cheaper model for simple intents, prompt caching for the stable policy prefix, and trimming history — a BankAssist deployment can cut spend by 50%+ with those three alone. Latency: both a longer input and a longer output take more time; output tokens dominate, so capping reply length keeps response times tight. Scale: providers rate-limit on tokens per minute, not just requests, so a few customers pasting huge documents can throttle everyone — enforce input size limits. Failure modes: context overflow (above) and surprise bills from non-English or number-heavy traffic. Monitoring: alert on average tokens per conversation, cache hit rate, and cost per intent so a regression shows up as a graph, not a month-end invoice shock. Compliance: every token you send may be logged by the provider — mask account numbers and PII before they ever enter the prompt.

👉 When to count tokens carefully: any time something must fit (long documents, long chats) or must be budgeted (high-volume features, per-customer cost caps). For a quick one-off prompt you can ignore the exact count; for a feature that runs 50,000 times a day, token accounting is the difference between a profitable product and a runaway bill.

🧠 Remember it

Tokens are the model's currency and its memory: you pay in tokens and you run out of desk space in tokens.

🎯 interview 💸 cost

How a model actually picks each word

A language model never writes a sentence in one go — it plays a very fast guessing game, one word at a time, and everything else (temperature, top-p, streaming, cost) is a consequence of that one loop.

Before you can tune how a model chooses its words, it helps to see what it is actually doing under the hood. It is simpler than it looks: predict the next token, add it to the text, and do it again. That repeated guess is the whole engine.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist customer types "What is my current". The model doesn't "understand the question and compose a reply." It asks itself one tiny question — given everything so far, what single token comes next? — guesses "balance", appends it, then asks again, and again, until it decides to stop. The fluent answer is thousands of these micro-guesses in a row.

The loop: one token at a time (autoregression)

The model reads the whole text so far (your prompt plus whatever it has written), predicts the next token (a word or word-piece), appends it, and repeats. This "read everything, predict one, append, repeat" cycle is called autoregressive generation. It stops when it generates a special end token or hits your length cap.

Step 1 — the model scores every possible token (logits)

Your text goes through the network and, for the next position, out comes one raw number — a logit — for every token in the model's vocabulary (often 100,000+ tokens). A logit is just a score: higher means "this token fits better here." Logits are not probabilities yet — they can be negative, and they don't add up to anything tidy.

Step 2 — softmax turns scores into a probability list

To turn those raw scores into probabilities that add up to 100%, the model applies softmax: exponentiate each logit, then divide by the total. Exponentiating is what makes a small lead in score become a big lead in probability. Here is the whole thing on four candidate tokens after "Your account balance is":

# raw logits the model produced for the next token
"$"         3.0
"currently" 2.0
"low"       1.0
"fine"      0.0

# softmax: p(token) = exp(logit) / sum(exp of all logits)
exp(3.0)=20.1   exp(2.0)=7.39   exp(1.0)=2.72   exp(0.0)=1.0      # exponentiate each
total = 20.1 + 7.39 + 2.72 + 1.0 = 31.2                            # add them up

p("$")         = 20.1 / 31.2 = 0.64     # 64%
p("currently") = 7.39 / 31.2 = 0.24     # 24%
p("low")       = 2.72 / 31.2 = 0.09     # 9%
p("fine")      = 1.00 / 31.2 = 0.03     # 3%
▶ Output

A tidy probability list: 64% "$", 24% "currently", 9% "low", 3% "fine" — adds up to 100%. Notice the score gap of 1.0 between "$" and "currently" became a probability gap of 64% vs 24%: softmax exaggerates leads.

Step 3 — pick one (sampling)

Now the model chooses a token from that list. Two styles:

  • Greedy: always take the highest-probability token ("$"). Deterministic and safe, but can get repetitive or bland.
  • Sampling: roll a weighted dice — "$" comes up 64% of the time, "currently" 24%, and so on. More natural and varied, but occasionally picks a lower-ranked token.

That is the entire pick. The chosen token is appended, and the loop runs again for the next word. The settings you'll tune — temperature, top-p, penalties — all work by reshaping this probability list before the dice roll.

💡 Key idea

A model doesn't "know" the answer and type it out. At every single position it produces a probability for every possible next token and samples one. Fluent paragraphs are just thousands of these loaded-dice rolls, each one conditioned on all the words before it.

Going deeper

A few consequences fall straight out of this loop, and they explain a lot of LLM behaviour:

  • Why it can hallucinate: there is always a probability for every token, even a wrong account number. The model samples the most plausible-sounding continuation, not a verified fact. Nothing in the loop checks truth.
  • Why output streams word by word: each token is produced in its own lap, so the API can send them to you as they're generated.
  • Why you pay per token: each lap is one forward pass through the network — generating 500 tokens is literally 500 sequential steps, which is also why long answers are slower.
  • Why the same prompt can vary: if the model is sampling (not greedy), the dice roll lands differently on different runs.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost & latency scale with generated tokens — the loop is sequential, so a 600-token answer takes roughly 6× as long to generate as a 100-token one. Cap length and keep answers tight.
  • Determinism is a choice — for a compliance summary a bank wants greedy / temperature 0 so the same input gives the same output; for marketing copy it wants sampling for variety.
  • Truth lives outside the loop — because sampling never checks facts, grounding (retrieval), validation, and human review are what make a BankAssist answer trustworthy, not the model alone.
  • Monitoring — track tokens-per-answer (cost), and watch for repetition loops (a sign greedy decoding got stuck).
⚠ Watch out

"The model is confident" is a trap. A token can be sampled at 64% probability and still be factually wrong — the probability measures "how well this fits the pattern of the text", not "how true this is." Never treat a fluent, high-probability answer as a verified one for money, balances, or policy. Use greedy/low-temperature for exact facts; use sampling only where variety is genuinely wanted — and never to decide something that must be correct.

🧠 Remember it

The model never writes a sentence — it rolls a loaded dice for the next word, then does it again. Logits are the raw scores, softmax turns them into the dice, and sampling rolls it.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

The dials that steer a model: temperature, top-p, max tokens & friends

The same model can be a cautious compliance officer or a chatty copywriter — the difference is a handful of generation settings you control on every request.

Remember that at each step the model has a whole table of possible next tokens with probabilities. How it picks from that table is up to you. These knobs are called generation (or sampling) parameters, and getting them right is the difference between a reliable banking answer and a creative fiction.

⚙️ Under the hood — what each dial changes in the math

Every dial here edits the same probability list before the pick. Recall the mechanism: the model gives each possible next token a raw score (a logit), then softmax — exponentiate each score and divide by the total — turns those into probabilities that sum to 100%. Using four candidates after "Your account balance is" (logits: "$"=3.0, "currently"=2.0, "low"=1.0, "fine"=0.0, which softmax turns into 64% / 24% / 9% / 3%):

  • Temperature divides every logit by T before softmax. Smaller T stretches the gaps (peakier, more confident); larger T shrinks them (flatter, more random): 
    T=0.5: logits become 6, 4, 2, 0   -> 87% / 12% / 1.6% / 0.2%   # sharper: the top choice dominates
T=1.0: logits stay   3, 2, 1, 0   -> 64% / 24% / 9%   / 3%     # the baseline, unchanged
T=2.0: logits become 1.5,1,0.5,0  -> 46% / 28% / 17%  / 10%    # flatter: long shots get a real chance
    As T approaches 0 the top token's share approaches 100% — that is greedy decoding.
  • top_p works after softmax: sort tokens high→low, add up their probabilities, and keep only the smallest group that reaches p, then renormalise and sample from just those. On the T=1 list, top_p=0.9 keeps "$" (0.64), "currently" (running total 0.88) and "low" (0.97, which passes 0.9) and drops "fine". It trims the unlikely tail so a rare, odd token can't slip through.
  • top_k (where a provider exposes it) is the blunt cousin: keep only the k highest-probability tokens, drop the rest, sample from those.
  • frequency / presence penalties subtract a number from a token's logit based on how often (frequency) or whether at all (presence) it has already appeared — nudging the curve away from repeats before softmax runs.

So "set temperature to 0 for a balance" really means "stretch the gaps until the correct token wins every time," and "top_p = 0.9" means "ignore the unlikely tail." It is the same dice every time — you are just reshaping it before the roll.

There are six dials you set on almost every request. For each one, here is what it actually does, a safe starting value, and — the part that matters most — what you use it for.

Temperature — the "boring ↔ bold" slider

What it does: controls how adventurous the pick is, usually on a 0–2 scale. At 0 the model almost always grabs the single most likely token, so the same prompt gives the same steady answer. Raise it and the probability table is flattened, so less-likely (more surprising) tokens start to win — the output gets more varied and creative, but also less predictable and more prone to mistakes.

👉 Use it for: set it to 0 whenever the answer has one correct form — balances, fees, policy quotes, pulling fields out of a document. Raise it to 0.7–1.0 when you actually want variety — three ways to word a reminder, campaign-name ideas. Default: ~0.7 for open chat, 0 for facts. BankAssist: quoting an overdraft fee → 0; drafting three friendly nudge messages → 0.9.

Top-p — keep only the likeliest slice

What it does: "nucleus sampling." Rather than reshaping every probability the way temperature does, it cuts off the long tail: it keeps only the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to p, then picks from just those. top_p=0.1 means "only ever consider the most likely 10% of the probability mass"; top_p=1.0 means "consider everything."

👉 Use it for: the same goal as temperature — tightening or loosening the output — through a different mechanism. Choose one lever (temperature or top-p) and leave the other at its default; tuning both at once makes the behaviour hard to predict. In practice most teams just use temperature. Default: 1.0 (effectively off).

Max tokens — the length cap and cost belt

What it does: a hard ceiling on how many tokens the model may generate in its reply (it does not touch your input). Hit the ceiling and the answer is cut off mid-sentence — the model isn't asked to wrap up, it is simply stopped.

👉 Use it for: keeping cost and latency predictable and stopping runaway output. Set it comfortably above the longest real answer you expect, but not so high it invites rambling. BankAssist: a one-line balance reply might cap at 80; a full dispute explanation at 600.

Stop sequences — "when you produce this, halt"

What it does: one or more strings that, the instant the model generates them, end the response immediately (the stop text itself is left out of the reply).

👉 Use it for: ending output cleanly at a known marker, or stopping the model from running past its turn. BankAssist: in a scripted dialogue you set a stop of "\nCustomer:" so the model writes only the agent's line and never invents the customer's reply; or stop at "---" to end after one section.

Frequency & presence penalties — anti-repetition nudges

What they do: gentle pressure (roughly −2 to 2) against repeating yourself. Frequency penalty lowers a token's odds the more times it has already appeared — it kills "the fee, the fee, the fee" loops. Presence penalty discourages a token once it has appeared at all, nudging the model to cover new ground.

👉 Use it for: long generated text that tends to loop or get samey — a multi-paragraph summary, a list of genuinely distinct suggestions. Leave both at 0 for short factual answers, where you actually want the model to reuse the correct term. Default: 0.

Verbosity — how long the answer is (newer models)

What it does: some of the newest OpenAI models expose a verbosity control (low / medium / high) that shapes how much the model says, without you having to beg "be brief" in the prompt. Unlike max tokens (a hard guillotine that can chop a sentence in half), verbosity lets the model still finish its thought — just more tersely or more fully.

👉 Use it for: matching answer length to the channel. low for a terse "Yes, your salary arrived." in a chat bubble; high for a full explained walkthrough in an email. It is model-dependent — not every model supports it (the gpt-4.1 family, for instance, does not), so check before relying on it.

Here's a real, current request using OpenAI's Responses API, tuned for a BankAssist factual answer:

from openai import OpenAI            # official OpenAI Python SDK
client = OpenAI()                    # reads your API key from the environment

resp = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",                   # a current gpt-4.1-family model
    input="State the customer's current overdraft fee in one sentence.",
    temperature=0,                   # 0 = steady, repeatable — right for money facts
    max_output_tokens=120,           # cap the length so cost & latency stay predictable
    stop=["\n"],                     # one sentence only — halt at the first line break
)
print(resp.output_text)             # the finished text, already assembled for you
▶ Output

Your current overdraft fee is $35 per occurrence.

Line by line: we create a client that quietly picks up the API key; we call the Responses API (the newer, agent-friendly OpenAI endpoint) with our prompt as input; temperature=0 makes the answer stable so the same question gives the same figure; max_output_tokens prevents a runaway bill; and stop=["\n"] keeps it to a single line. resp.output_text hands back the plain string.

⚠ Watch out

Two gotchas on the newest models. (1) Some reasoning models ignore or reject temperature and top_p — they manage their own internal sampling, so don't rely on those dials there. (2) temperature=0 reduces randomness but does not guarantee identical output every time; other sources of variation remain. For true "same answer every time" you need more than a zero temperature; a fixed seed and a stable system version help pin it down.

A quick cheat-sheet — match the dials to the job in front of you:

Tasktemperaturemax tokenspenaltiesverbosity
Quote a balance / fee / policy0tight (~80)0low
Extract fields into JSON0enough for the schema0low
Summarise a long document0–0.3generoussmall +frequencymedium
Draft customer-message variants0.8–1.0medium+presencemedium/high
Brainstorm names / ideas1.0+medium+presencehigh
💡 Key idea

Match the dials to the risk of the task. Money, balances, policy quotes → temperature 0, tight max tokens, low verbosity. Marketing copy or suggested phrasings → higher temperature, higher verbosity. The model is the same; your settings decide whether it behaves like a vault or a poet.

⚙️ In production

Don't scatter these settings across your code — store them as a named, versioned profile per task ("fee-quote" → temp 0, max 80; "message-draft" → temp 0.9, max 300). That way you can audit exactly how a money answer was generated, roll a change back, and keep behaviour identical across environments. Cost & latency: max_tokens is your single best guard against a runaway bill and a slow reply — set it to the shortest length that fits the real answer. Failure modes: a too-tight max_tokens chops answers mid-sentence (customers see a cut-off reply), while a high temperature on a factual route produces different numbers on repeated asks — both show up as support tickets, so test the dials against real traffic, not just one happy-path example. Monitoring: watch truncation rate (answers that hit the ceiling) and, on factual intents, variance across identical inputs — a jump means someone nudged temperature. Compliance: for any regulated output (quotes, disclosures) pin temperature to 0 and record the exact settings alongside the response in your audit log, so you can later show why the model said what it said.

👉 When to tune, when to leave defaults: deliberately set temperature and max_tokens on every production route — those two always matter. Reach for top-p, the penalties, verbosity, or a seed only when you have a specific symptom to fix (repetition, over-long answers, non-reproducibility). Do not fiddle with top-p and temperature together, and do not raise temperature on anything that touches money — there is no upside and real downside.

🧠 Remember it

Temperature is the "boring ↔ bold" slider. For a bank, keep it boring.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Reasoning models vs standard models, and streaming vs waiting

Some models answer instantly from instinct; others deliberately "think" first. Knowing which to reach for — and whether to stream the reply — shapes both your costs and your customer's experience.

Picture two BankAssist colleagues. One is a quick front-desk clerk who fires back an answer the instant you finish your sentence. The other is a careful analyst who, before answering a tricky dispute, scribbles working notes, checks a few steps, then gives you a considered reply. Both are valuable — for different questions.

Standard model

Answers in one quick pass. Fast, cheap, great for chit-chat, classification, rephrasing, simple lookups. Can stumble on multi-step logic or careful math.

Reasoning model

Spends extra hidden "thinking" tokens working through the problem before replying. Slower and pricier, but far stronger on multi-step logic, math, careful policy application, and tricky tool use.

A reasoning model (for example OpenAI's dedicated reasoning models, or Claude and Gemini with their "thinking" settings) generates a private chain of working before the visible answer. You usually don't pay to see that chain, but you do pay for those thinking tokens, and they add latency. Most providers let you dial the depth — an effort or reasoning level like low / medium / high. Higher effort = more careful, more expensive, slower.

resp = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",                       # a model that supports reasoning effort
    input="A customer paid twice by mistake, once on the 3rd ($1,200) "
          "and again on the 5th ($1,200). Only one was valid. "
          "What refund is owed, and what should we check first?",
    reasoning={"effort": "high"},        # think harder — this needs careful, correct steps
)
print(resp.output_text)                  # only the final answer; the private reasoning isn't returned
▶ Output

A refund of $1,200 is owed for the duplicate payment on the 5th. First confirm both charges hit the same account and merchant, and that neither was already reversed, before issuing the refund.

✅ Tip

Don't pay for deep reasoning you don't need. Route simple intents ("What's my balance?") to a fast standard model and reserve reasoning (and high effort) for genuinely multi-step work (dispute logic, reconciliation, eligibility rules). This "use the cheap brain until you need the expensive one" routing is one of the biggest cost levers you have.

Streaming vs non-streaming: how the answer is delivered

Separately from which model you pick, you choose how the answer is delivered back to you. There are two modes, and the difference is entirely about timing, not about the words themselves.

In non-streaming mode (the default) you make one request and then wait. The model generates the entire reply on its servers — token after token after token — and only when it has finished the last token does it send the whole thing back to you in a single lump. From your code's point of view it's one blocking call: ask, wait, receive. If the answer takes four seconds to generate, your customer stares at a spinner for four seconds and then the full paragraph pops in at once.

In streaming mode you ask the model to push each piece of the answer to you the instant it is produced, instead of holding it all back.
