For BankAssist, don't assume a "1M-token" model reads page 900 as carefully as page 2. Test retrieval at the depth you'll actually use, and prefer fetching the right few paragraphs over dumping a whole manual.

When it matters: document summarisation, long chat histories, and anything where the important text sits deep in a big prompt. When you can ignore it: short prompts that live comfortably inside the model's native, un-stretched length never touch these weak edges.

🧠 Remember it

Attention is order-blind, so we add position. Old way: add a wave. Modern way: rotate (RoPE), which bakes in distance. Stretch it later with YaRN — but the stretched edges are thinner.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

The KV cache: why chat is fast, and what it costs in memory

Generating the 500th word shouldn't re-read the first 499 from scratch — the KV cache is the model's short-term memory that stops it repeating all that work.

A transformer emits one token per full pass, then runs again with the text one token longer. Naively, step 500 would recompute attention over all 500 tokens — and step 501 over all 501 — doing almost the same enormous calculation again and again. That would make long replies crawl. The fix is the KV cache.

The simple idea

In attention, each past token produces a Key and a Value. Crucially, a token's K and V never change once it's in the sentence — "the" at position 3 has the same K and V whether the sentence is 4 tokens long or 400. So why recompute them? The KV cache simply stores every token's K and V the first time and reuses them forever after. Each new step then only has to: compute the K, V, Q for the one new token, append its K and V to the cache, and attend against the stored set. One token's worth of fresh work per step instead of the whole history.

Going deeper: the cache is why memory, not maths, is the bottleneck

The KV cache turns generation from "slow and compute-bound" into "fast but memory-hungry". And it can get big. Its size is roughly:

cache ≈ layers × 2 × (num KV heads × head size) × tokens × bytes_per_number
# layers            : one cache per transformer layer, all stacked
# 2                 : we store a Key AND a Value for each token
# num KV heads × size: how wide each stored vector is (the lever we attack below)
# tokens            : grows with every token in the conversation → linear blow-up
# bytes_per_number  : 2 for fp16/bf16; less if the cache is quantised

The sting is the × tokens: the cache grows with every word of the conversation, per layer. For a big model, a long chat can need tens of gigabytes of GPU memory just for the cache — often more than the model's weights. And since each decode step must read the whole cache from memory, it's usually memory-bandwidth, not arithmetic, that caps how fast tokens come out.

The fix: GQA and MQA (share the Keys and Values)

Look back at the formula — the knob we can turn without hurting the model much is num KV heads. Multi-head attention gives every query head its own K/V head, which is lavish. Two cheaper designs cut that:

MQA (multi-query)

All query heads share a single Key/Value head. Shrinks the cache the most (and speeds decoding), but squeezing everything through one K/V can dent quality, especially on long inputs.

GQA (grouped-query)

The middle ground, and today's default. Query heads are split into a few groups, each sharing one K/V head. Nearly MHA quality at nearly MQA cost.

Concretely: Llama 3 70B uses 64 query heads but only 8 KV heads — an 8× smaller KV cache than full multi-head attention, for almost no quality loss. Mistral 7B does the same (32 query heads, 8 KV heads). MQA is just the extreme of GQA with a single group; full multi-head attention is the other extreme with one group per head.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist runs a busy chat line. Every open conversation holds its own KV cache on the GPU, so the real limit on "how many customers can we serve at once" is often cache memory, not raw speed. Switching to a GQA model with 8 KV heads instead of 64 cuts each conversation's cache ~8×, so the same GPU box holds far more simultaneous chats — a direct serving-cost win. This is why "how big is the KV cache?" is a production question, not a trivia one.

⚙️ In production

The KV cache is usually the real ceiling on how many customers BankAssist serves per GPU, so it drives concrete sizing. Put numbers into the formula: Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, 8 KV heads of size 128, in fp16 (2 bytes). That's 80 × 2 × (8 × 128) × 2 ≈ 320 KB of cache per token. A single 8,000-token conversation therefore needs ~2.6 GB just for its cache, on top of the ~140 GB of weights. On an 80 GB GPU, after weights there is barely room for a handful of long concurrent chats — which is exactly why serving stacks obsess over this number. The levers you actually pull, cheapest first: (1) GQA — those 8 KV heads instead of 64 already shrank this 8×; (2) KV-cache quantisation to 8-bit roughly halves it again; (3) paged attention (the vLLM approach) stops each session reserving its worst-case block and packs far more chats onto a box; (4) prefix caching reuses the cache for a shared system prompt across requests. For a bank the decision is usually "pick a GQA model and turn on paged + prefix caching" long before "buy more GPUs" — it is the cheapest throughput you will ever find.

✅ Tip

Two more cache levers you'll meet in serving: KV-cache quantisation (store K/V in 8-bit or 4-bit to shrink memory, at a small accuracy risk) and prefix/cache reuse (keep the cache for a shared system-prompt prefix so repeated requests skip re-encoding it). Pair a GQA model with prefix caching and a long, stable BankAssist policy prompt becomes cheap to reuse.

⚠ Watch out

The KV cache is why "just use a 1M-token window" isn't free even when the model allows it: memory grows linearly with every token held, so a few very long concurrent sessions can exhaust a GPU and stall the whole service. Treat context length as a budget you spend, with the cache as the meter.

When it matters: high-concurrency serving and long sessions — here the cache, not the model's raw speed, caps how many chats a box can hold at once. When you can ignore it: calling a hosted API for a few short requests, where the provider hides all of this behind a flat per-token price.

🧠 Remember it

KV cache = the model's sticky notes: write each word's Key/Value once, reread them free. It makes chat fast but eats memory per token — GQA/MQA shrink it by sharing the notes.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Mixture-of-Experts: the big models that only switch on a sliver of themselves

The trick behind 2026's giant models isn't using more brain per word — it's owning a huge brain but waking only a small, relevant part of it for each token.

Imagine BankAssist hires one impossibly overqualified generalist who personally handles every question — mortgages, fraud, foreign exchange, tax. That's a dense model: for every token, all of its parameters fire. It works, but scaling it means every single word gets more expensive. Now imagine instead a panel of specialists plus a sharp receptionist who, for each question, quietly routes it to just the two most relevant experts. The bank employs hundreds of specialists, but each question only pays for two. That's Mixture-of-Experts (MoE).

Dense vs sparse, in one picture

How it actually works

An MoE model replaces the feed-forward block inside some layers with many parallel expert blocks plus a small router (a gating network). For each token, the router scores all the experts, picks the top-k (often just 2), sends the token only to those, and blends their outputs weighted by the router's scores. The attention parts of the layer stay shared; it's the "think per word" step that becomes a choose-your-specialist step.

This splits a model's size into two very different numbers, and the gap is the whole point:

  • Total parameters — everything the model owns across all experts. Sets how much it can know.
  • Active parameters — what actually runs for a single token (the shared parts + the chosen experts). Sets the cost and speed per token.
Model (2025–26)Total paramsActive / tokenExperts (active)
DeepSeek-V3671B~37B256 (8 + 1 shared)
Llama 4 Maverick400B17B128 routed
Llama 4 Scout109B17B16
Mixtral 8×7B (earlier)~47B~13B8 (2)

Read DeepSeek-V3's row slowly: it owns 671 billion parameters but only spends about 37 billion per token. You get the knowledge of a giant with roughly the per-token cost of a mid-size model. That bargain — big brain, small bill per word — is why nearly every frontier model in 2026 is a sparse MoE rather than a dense one.

⚙️ Under the hood

MoE isn't free lunch, it's a different bill. Load balancing: if the router falls in love with a few experts, the rest never learn, so training adds an auxiliary "spread the tokens out" loss. Shared experts: some designs (DeepSeek) always run one or two common experts for general skill, and route the rest. Memory: you must hold all experts in GPU memory even though each token uses two — so MoE saves compute, not memory. And experts get sharded across GPUs, so tokens are shipped across the network to their expert and back ("expert parallelism"), which makes serving MoE an infrastructure project.

⚙️ In production

MoE changes the shape of the bill in a way a bank must plan for: compute is cheap, memory is not. DeepSeek-V3 spends ~37B active parameters per token, so it runs about as cheaply as a 37B dense model — but you must still hold all 671B parameters in GPU memory to host it, roughly 350–700 GB depending on precision, i.e. a multi-GPU box before you serve a single user. That split forces the classic make-or-buy decision: for most banks a frontier MoE is an API call, not a self-host, precisely because the memory footprint (not the per-token compute) is the barrier. Two more serving realities: (1) latency can be lumpier than a dense model's, because tokens are routed to experts sharded across GPUs and shipped over the network ("expert parallelism"), so tail latency needs watching; (2) quality-per-dollar is excellent — you get frontier answers at a mid-size per-token cost, which is why a hosted MoE often gives BankAssist the best value on hard tasks like dispute reasoning. Rule of thumb: judge cost and speed by active parameters, but judge what hardware or vendor you need by total parameters.

⚠ Watch out

Don't confuse MoE "experts" with human-style domain experts — an expert is not "the mortgage one". The router learns opaque, token-level specialisations that rarely map to tidy topics, so you can't inspect or route to "the fraud expert". Also, because experts hold most of the parameters, a frontier MoE needs lots of GPU memory to host even if it's cheap to run — which shapes whether you self-host or call an API.

When it matters: any self-hosting or capacity decision — total parameters set your hardware bill even though active parameters set your speed, so a model that "runs like a 37B" can still demand a 700 GB box. When you can ignore it: if you only ever call a hosted model through an API, the provider absorbs the memory problem and you simply see a per-token price.

🧠 Remember it

Dense = pay for the whole brain every word. MoE = own a huge brain, wake a slice. "Total params = what it knows; active params = what you pay."

🎯 interview 🏭 production

How a model is made: pretraining, instruction tuning, alignment

A chat model isn't born helpful — it's raised in three stages, and knowing them explains both why it's smart and why it still needs guardrails.

We've seen the machinery; where does the skill come from? A usable assistant like the one behind BankAssist is built in three passes, each teaching a different thing. You won't run these yourself for most projects, but they explain a great deal — why fine-tuning and retrieval (feeding the model fresh facts at answer time) do what they do, and why a model behaves the way it does.

  1. Pretraining — read almost everything. The model is shown an ocean of text and trained on the one task we've met throughout: predict the next token. There are no "right answers" labelled by humans; the text is the answer. This is where grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and code soak in. It's by far the most expensive stage (months of compute on huge GPU clusters). The result is a base model: fluent, knowledgeable, but not yet a helpful assistant — ask it a question and it might just continue it with more questions, because it only knows how text tends to flow.
  2. Instruction tuning — learn to be helpful. Next, the base model is fine-tuned on a curated set of instruction → good response examples (also called supervised fine-tuning, SFT). "Summarise this statement." → a clean summary. "List the steps to dispute a charge." → the steps. After this, the model understands that a prompt is a request to fulfil, not just text to extend. This is what turns a base model into something that acts like an assistant.
  3. Alignment — learn taste and safety. Finally, humans (and other models) rank competing answers — this one is more helpful, that one is rude or unsafe — and the model is nudged toward the preferred style. The classic recipe is RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback); newer, simpler variants like DPO (direct preference optimisation) and Constitutional AI (align against a written set of principles) do similar work. This stage sets the polite, cautious, "I can't help with that" character you feel in a production chatbot.
🏦 Picture this

Why does this framing matter for BankAssist? Because each stage leaves a fingerprint you must manage. Pretraining gave the model broad banking language but also a fixed knowledge cutoff and no clue about your policies — that gap is exactly what retrieval fills. Alignment made it refuse obviously harmful requests, but it was trained on the world's values, not your compliance rulebook — so your own guardrails still sit on top. The model arrives helpful and polite; making it correct for your bank is the job of the extra layers you add on top — retrieval for fresh, private facts and your own guardrails for the rules.

⚙️ Under the hood

Where does your work plug in? Three options, cheapest first. Prompting / RAG changes nothing in the model — you feed it better context at answer time (great for facts that change). Fine-tuning runs a small extra instruction-tuning pass on your examples to bake in a style, format, or narrow skill (not fresh facts). Reasoning models add a further training stage that rewards good step-by-step working. For most banking features you'll reach for prompting and RAG long before you fine-tune — training stages are the vendor's problem; grounding and guardrails are yours.

⚙️ In production

Knowing the three stages tells BankAssist where to spend and what each option costs. The eye-watering stage — pretraining, months on thousands of GPUs — is the vendor's bill, not yours; you rent its result per token. Your money goes to the thin layers on top, cheapest first. Prompting + RAG changes no weights and is the default: you pay only for the extra context tokens at answer time, facts update instantly, and there is no training run to manage. Fine-tuning is a small supervised pass (hours, not months) that bakes in a house style or output format — a modest one-off cost plus a slightly pricier or self-managed model to serve afterward; worth it for high-volume, narrow, stable tasks, rarely worth it for knowledge that changes. Reasoning models add a training stage that rewards step-by-step working; you buy them as-is and pay for the extra "thinking" tokens they emit, so they cost and lag more per answer — reserve them for genuinely hard problems like multi-step dispute adjudication, not balance lookups. The production instinct: climb this ladder only as far as the task forces you, because each rung up costs more to build and more to run.

⚠ Watch out

The biggest trap is treating the model's training as if it were your knowledge base. Pretraining baked in a fixed knowledge cutoff and the public web's version of facts — it does not know today's interest rates, your fee schedule, or a customer's balance, and it will confidently fill those gaps with plausible-sounding fiction. Alignment teaches tone and broad safety, not your compliance rules, so "it was trained to be safe" is never a substitute for your own guardrails. And fine-tuning is for style and format, not for injecting fresh facts — people routinely reach for a fine-tune when what they actually needed was retrieval. When it matters: any feature that depends on current, private, or bank-specific facts — balances, policies, rates — which must come from retrieval and tools at answer time. When you can ignore it: tasks that only need the general language skill the base model already has, like rewriting a message more politely or classifying sentiment.

🧠 Remember it

Pretrain = knows language. Instruction-tune = does what you ask. Align = behaves nicely. Read, then obey, then mind its manners — and your facts and rules still go on top.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

How multimodal models actually see and hear

A picture becomes tokens, and then the same transformer that reads words reads the image too.

A text model turns words into tokens — little numbered pieces — and predicts the next one. A multimodal model does something quietly clever: it turns a picture (or audio) into tokens in the same shared space, so the exact same transformer can attend to pixels and words together, in one stream. Once an image is "tokens," the model treats it like more of the sentence.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist customer photographs a cheque and asks, "Is this filled in correctly?" The model doesn't run a separate OCR program and paste text in — it ingests the image directly as tokens alongside the question, and reasons about the payee line, the amount box, and the signature in one pass.

From pixels to tokens

The pipeline for the "vision" half of a vision-language model:

  1. Patchify. The image is sliced into a grid of small squares (patches) — think of cutting a photo into postage stamps.
  2. Vision encoder. A vision transformer (ViT-style) turns each patch into an embedding — a vector capturing what's in that patch.
  3. Projection / connector. A small learned layer maps those patch embeddings into the same vector space the language model uses for word tokens. Now an image patch and a word live in the same "language."
  4. Joint attention. The transformer attends over the combined sequence of image tokens + text tokens, so "the amount box" in your question can attend directly to the patch showing the amount.
⚙️ Under the hood — how images learn to match words

The reason a model can connect the word "cheque" to a picture of one comes from contrastive pretraining, the idea behind CLIP: train on millions of (image, caption) pairs so that a matching image and caption land close together in embedding space, and mismatched ones land far apart. That alignment is also exactly what powers image↔text search: embed a photo, embed a query, compare. The same trick extends to audio (speech is turned into acoustic features, then into tokens) and to documents (a page is read as an image, so the model can understand layout without a separate OCR step).

Calling a vision-capable model is almost the same as a text call — you just add an image part to the message:

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

resp = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                              # a current vision-capable model
    input=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "input_text",  "text": "Is this cheque filled in correctly?"},  # the question (text tokens)
            {"type": "input_image", "image_url": "https://bank.example/cheque.jpg"},  # the image → becomes image tokens
        ],
    }],
)
print(resp.output_text)                                # the model reasons over image + text together
▶ Output

The payee and amount match, but the signature line is blank — it needs a signature before deposit.

⚙️ In production

Vision is billed in tokens, so an image is a variable-size cost you must manage like any other prompt text. Providers convert an image into tokens based on its resolution — a single high-res photo can become anywhere from a few hundred to a couple of thousand tokens, and that count lands in both your bill and your context budget. Three decisions follow for BankAssist. (1) Set the detail/resolution deliberately — a "low-detail" mode that costs a fixed small number of tokens is plenty for "is there a signature in this box?", while a full cheque-fraud check may justify high detail; don't pay high-res prices by default. (2) Downscale and crop before sending — clipping to the region that matters (the amount box, the signature line) cuts tokens and often improves accuracy. (3) Pick the cheapest tool that answers the question — for extracting typed text at volume, OCR plus a small text model is usually far cheaper and faster than sending full-page images to a vision model; reserve vision for when layout, handwriting, or "does this look right?" genuinely need the pixels. Latency scales with image tokens too, so a batch of full-resolution document images can quietly blow a per-request SLA.

⚠ Watch out

Image tokens are not free. A high-resolution image can turn into hundreds or thousands of tokens, inflating cost and latency and eating your context window just like long text. Use the API's detail/resolution setting deliberately, downscale when you can, and for pure text-from-documents ask whether plain OCR + a text model is cheaper than sending full page images.

When it matters: high-volume or high-resolution image workloads — document pipelines, batch cheque processing — where token counts multiply fast across every request. When you can ignore it: the occasional single screenshot dropped into an interactive chat barely moves the bill.

When to use a vision model vs OCR + text

Vision model

When layout, handwriting, stamps, or "does this look right?" matter — it understands the page as a whole. More tokens, higher cost.

OCR → text model

When you just need the words out of a clean, typed document at volume. Cheaper and faster, but blind to layout and visual cues.

🧠 Remember it

A picture is just more tokens. Patch it, encode it, project it into word-space — then the same transformer reads your image and your question in one breath. (And those image tokens show up on the bill.)

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🖼️ multimodal

Foundations — Running the Model Yourself: Serving & Inference

So far the model has lived somewhere else — you sent a request over the internet and an answer came back. This chapter is about the day a bank decides to run the model inside its own walls: why you'd do that, which tools actually serve a model, and the handful of ideas (KV cache, batching, quantization) that decide whether it's fast, affordable, and fits on the GPU you have.

Self-host or call an API? The banking fork in the road

Calling a hosted API is like ordering takeaway; self-hosting is running your own kitchen. Both feed people — the question is who's allowed in the kitchen.

When BankAssist needs a language model, there are two honest ways to get one. The first is to call an API: you send the customer's question to a provider like OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google — or to a specialist ultra-low-latency provider like Groq, which runs open-weight models on its own custom LPU (Language Processing Unit) chips instead of GPUs — and their servers run the model and send the answer back. You maintain nothing. The second is to self-host: you download an open-weight model (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, and friends), put it on your own GPUs — in your data centre or your private cloud — and run it yourself. Same idea as cooking at home instead of ordering in: more control, more work.

For most teams the API is the right first move, and it stays right for a long time. So why would a bank ever take on the kitchen? Three reasons, and in banking they are big ones.

1. Data residency and privacy

This is the one that actually forces the decision. A regulator may require that customer data never leaves the country, the bank's network, or an approved boundary. If every question to a hosted API sends account details across the internet to someone else's servers, that can simply be not allowed — full stop. Self-hosting keeps the data inside your walls: the prompt, the retrieved documents, and the answer never cross the fence. For a bank handling account numbers, balances, and KYC records, "the data never leaves" is often the whole reason.

2. Cost at scale

Hosted APIs charge per token. At low volume that's wonderfully cheap — you pay for exactly what you use and nothing when you're idle. But imagine BankAssist handles ten million chats a month, each reading long retrieved policy passages. That per-token bill grows with every customer. At high, steady volume, renting GPUs and running the model yourself can cost less per answer — you've swapped a usage bill for a fixed infrastructure bill. The crossover depends on your traffic, but it's real.

3. Control

When you self-host, the model doesn't change under you. A hosted model can be updated, deprecated, or retired on the provider's schedule — and suddenly your carefully tested prompts behave differently. On your own GPUs the weights are frozen until you choose to move. You also get to fine-tune freely, pin an exact version for an audit, and guarantee latency isn't at the mercy of someone else's busy afternoon.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's team ships a hosted-API prototype in two weeks and everyone's thrilled. Then the risk committee asks one question: "Does a customer's account number ever travel to a third party?" The answer is yes — and in their jurisdiction that's a non-starter for production. The project doesn't die; it pivots. They keep the hosted API for the internal, no-customer-data developer tooling, and they stand up a self-hosted open-weight model behind the bank's firewall for anything that touches real customers. Same app, two engines, chosen by what data flows through them.

Going deeper — where the cost lines actually cross

People argue about the API-versus-self-host bill in the abstract; it's clearer with rough numbers. A hosted small/open-weight-class model often prices around $0.10–0.50 per million input tokens and $0.30–1.50 per million output tokens. A self-hosted GPU — say an NVIDIA H100 — rents on-demand for roughly $2–4 an hour, which is about $1,500–3,000 a month running flat out (cheaper on a 1-year reservation). Put those together. If BankAssist handles 10 million chats a month, each with ~1,500 input and ~300 output tokens, that's about 18 billion tokens; at a blended ~$0.20 per million that's roughly $3,600/month on a hosted API. Two self-hosted H100s cost ~$4,000–6,000/month plus engineers to run them. So at that volume the API is still competitive — the crossover favours self-hosting only when volume climbs higher, the model is small enough to pack many users per GPU, or a reservation cuts the hourly rate. The lesson: don't assume self-hosting is cheaper; model it with your traffic, your token lengths, and the fully-loaded cost of the humans who keep GPUs alive.

There's a third, quieter axis: latency control. A hosted frontier API can spike to several seconds under its own load on a busy afternoon, and you can't do anything about it. Self-hosting lets you provision for your peak and hit a latency SLA you own — valuable when a customer is watching a reply form in real time.

In production

Self-hosting is not free lunch — it's a different bill. You now own GPU capacity planning, uptime, scaling for peak hours, security patching of the serving stack, and an on-call rotation for when a node dies at 2 a.m. A hosted API hides all of that behind someone else's SLA. The mature pattern in banks is hybrid: hosted APIs where data sensitivity allows and volume is modest, self-hosted open-weight models where residency demands it or volume makes it cheaper. Decide per use-case, not once for the whole company.

⚙️ In production

Cost: self-hosting converts a variable per-token bill into a fixed GPU bill plus staff; reserve capacity for the floor and burst to on-demand or a hosted API for spikes. Latency: own your p95 by provisioning for peak, not average — a GPU at 100% utilisation queues requests and latency explodes. Scale: plan replicas for peak concurrency, not daily mean; banking traffic has sharp 9 a.m. and payday peaks. Failure modes: a dead GPU node, a driver/CUDA mismatch after a patch, or an OOM under a traffic spike — all need health checks, automatic restart, and a fallback (a second replica or a hosted API in break-glass mode). Monitoring: GPU utilisation, memory headroom, queue wait, tokens/sec, and error rate per replica. Security & compliance: for a bank, pin the exact model weights and serving-stack version so an audit can reproduce an answer months later; keep the serving container in the bank's VPC with no outbound internet; patch the stack for CVEs on a schedule; and log that no customer data crossed the boundary — that evidence is often what the regulator actually asks for.

💡 Key idea

The self-host decision is usually driven by data residency first, then cost at scale, then control. If none of those bite, call the API and spend your energy elsewhere.

⚠ Watch out

Don't self-host just to feel in control. Running a model well is a real operational discipline — GPUs, drivers, scaling, monitoring. Teams that self-host "because it's cooler" often ship slower and spend more than they would have on an API. Let a regulation or a spreadsheet make the call, not a vibe.

Use self-hosting when a regulation forbids data leaving your boundary, or steady volume makes fixed GPU cost beat a growing per-token bill, or you need a frozen, auditable model version. Do NOT self-host when volume is modest, data residency allows a hosted call, and you'd be standing up a GPU fleet just to run a weaker open model than the hosted one you could have called.

🧠 Remember it

API = takeaway. Self-host = your own kitchen. You open the kitchen when the food isn't allowed to leave the house — or when you're feeding a crowd every single day.

The serving engines: vLLM, SGLang, TGI, Ollama, LM Studio

A raw model file is just weights on disk. A serving engine is the program that loads it onto the GPU and turns requests into answers, fast — and the right engine depends on whether you're on a laptop or running a fleet.

Here's a point that trips people up: downloading a model doesn't let you talk to it, any more than owning an engine block lets you drive to work. You need a program that loads the weights, manages the GPU's memory, accepts requests, runs the model, and streams tokens back. That program is a serving engine (also called an inference server). Picking the right one is most of the self-hosting game. Let's meet the main ones and what each is actually for.

vLLM — the production workhorse

vLLM is the default choice for serving open-weight models to many users at once on GPUs. Its claim to fame is a clever memory trick called PagedAttention that lets it pack far more concurrent conversations onto one GPU than naive approaches. It speaks the OpenAI API format, so your existing code barely changes. If BankAssist is going to production on its own GPUs, vLLM is the first thing to try.

SGLang — the throughput challenger

SGLang is a newer high-performance engine in the same league as vLLM, and often faster for certain workloads. Its signature feature is RadixAttention, a form of prefix caching: when many requests share the same beginning — say, BankAssist's long system prompt and the same policy passages — SGLang reuses the computation for that shared prefix instead of redoing it every time. For RAG and agent workloads with big repeated prompts, that's a meaningful win.

TGI — the one to know about, not reach for

TGI (Text Generation Inference) is Hugging Face's serving engine and was a popular production choice for years. Worth knowing because you'll see it in older systems and docs. But as of December 2025, TGI entered maintenance mode, and Hugging Face now recommends vLLM or SGLang for new deployments. Translation: don't start a new banking project on TGI — recognise it, inherit it if you must, but build new on vLLM or SGLang.

Ollama — the easy local runner

Ollama is the friendliest way to run a model on your own machine. One command pulls a model and runs it, CPU or GPU, Mac or Windows or Linux. Under the hood it uses llama.cpp and the GGUF format (a compact, quantized file format for running models on everyday hardware), which makes it great on laptops and workstations. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible endpoint too. Ollama is built for development, prototyping, and single-user use — not for serving thousands of concurrent customers.

LM Studio — the no-code desktop app

LM Studio is a graphical desktop app: click to download a model, chat with it in a built-in window, and flip on a local OpenAI-compatible server. Zero command line. It's perfect for analysts, product folks, and engineers who just want to try models locally without touching a terminal. Like Ollama, it's a desktop tool — it has no horizontal scaling or load balancing, so it's not a production server.

The lovely part is that all five speak the same OpenAI-compatible API. That means the same client code points at any of them — you just change the base URL. Prototype against Ollama on your laptop, then flip the URL to a vLLM server in the data centre for production, and the application barely notices.

# The same client code talks to ANY of these engines — only the base_url changes.
from openai import OpenAI                       # the standard OpenAI client, reused for self-hosted engines

client = OpenAI(                                # build a client pointed at our OWN server, not OpenAI's
    base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1",        # a local vLLM server; swap to :11434 for Ollama, same shape
    api_key="not-needed-locally",               # self-hosted servers often ignore the key, but the field is required
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(          # the familiar chat call — identical to hosted OpenAI usage
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",   # the open-weight model this engine has loaded onto the GPU
    messages=[{"role": "user",                  # one user turn; the engine applies the model's chat template
               "content": "What is BankAssist's overdraft fee policy?"}],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)          # the generated answer, streamed from your own GPU
▶ Output
The standard overdraft item fee is $35, with one courtesy waiver available per 12-month period on request. (served locally — no data left the bank)

That one property — a shared API shape — is what makes self-hosting approachable. You don't rewrite your app to change engines; you change a URL.

Going deeper — how to actually choose between vLLM and SGLang

Both are top-tier GPU engines, and both moved fast through 2025, so treat any single benchmark as a snapshot. The practical differences that survive: vLLM is the broadest and best-supported — its rewritten V1 engine is now the default, it has the widest model coverage, the most quantization formats, built-in prefix caching, tensor parallelism behind a single flag, and modern speculative-decoding methods. It's the safe default. SGLang tends to win on workloads with heavy shared prefixes — its RadixAttention caches the computation for a repeated prompt beginning across many requests. BankAssist's traffic is exactly that shape: the same long system prompt and the same policy passages at the top of thousands of requests. On such traffic SGLang's prefix reuse can cut time-to-first-token sharply. The honest advice: start on vLLM, and benchmark SGLang on your own prompts if prefix reuse is high and you're chasing the last slice of throughput. Do not pick on a leaderboard number from someone else's model and hardware — the ranking flips between releases.

A subtle edge case: these engines expose an OpenAI-compatible API, not a byte-identical one. Features like structured outputs, logprobs, or certain sampling parameters can differ slightly from hosted OpenAI. Test the specific features your app relies on against the engine before you promise behaviour, rather than assuming perfect parity.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the engine is free; the GPU is the bill, so the metric that matters is tokens per second per GPU at your target latency — a faster engine is literally cheaper. Latency: watch p95 time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token separately; prefix caching (SGLang RadixAttention, vLLM prefix cache) mostly helps the first. Scale: one engine process serves one (or a few) GPUs; for more traffic you run multiple replicas behind a load balancer and shard big models across GPUs with tensor parallelism. Failure modes: a model that won't fit (OOM at load), a request longer than --max-model-len rejected, a replica wedged after a driver update; health-check each replica and drain-restart on failure. Monitoring: vLLM exposes Prometheus metrics (running vs waiting requests, GPU-cache usage, tokens/sec) — scrape them and alert on queue growth. Security & compliance: run the engine container inside the bank's network with authentication in front of it (the raw server often trusts any API key), pin the engine version for reproducibility, and never expose the inference port to the public internet.

⚙️ Under the hood — why not just run the model in a plain Python loop?

You can load a model with plain Hugging Face Transformers and call model.generate() in a loop. It works for one request at a time and it's great for learning. But it wastes the GPU terribly under real traffic: it can't efficiently interleave many users, its memory management is crude, and throughput collapses. Serving engines exist precisely to solve that — smart batching, paged memory, streaming — which is why you reach for vLLM rather than a hand-rolled loop the moment real users show up.

⚠ Watch out

Ollama and LM Studio feel so easy that teams are tempted to put them behind a production app. Don't. They're single-node desktop tools without real concurrency, autoscaling, or load balancing. Use them to prototype; serve production traffic with vLLM or SGLang.

Reach for vLLM as your production default; reach for SGLang when shared-prefix reuse is high and you've measured a win on your own traffic; reach for Ollama / LM Studio only on a laptop. Do NOT start a new banking project on TGI (maintenance mode) or put a desktop runner behind real customers.

🧠 Remember it

vLLM/SGLang for the fleet, Ollama/LM Studio for your laptop, TGI for the museum. All five speak OpenAI, so the code is the same — only the URL moves.

How inference actually works — and why the KV cache matters

A model writes one token at a time, re-reading everything before it on each step. The KV cache is the sticky-note system that saves it from re-reading the whole page over and over.

To serve a model well you need a feel for what it's doing when it "answers." It isn't typing a finished sentence from a drawer. It's predicting one token at a time — a token being a chunk of text, roughly a word-piece. To predict the next token, the model looks back at every token so far (the prompt plus everything it has written) and asks "given all this, what comes next?" Then it appends that token and does it again. Answer length is literally how many times this loop runs.

There are two phases, and they behave very differently:

  • Prefill — the model reads your whole prompt in one big parallel pass. Fast per token, because it's all processed at once. This is the wait before the first word appears.
  • Decode — the model generates the answer one token at a time, each step depending on the last. This is the steady stream of words you watch appear.

Now the crucial problem. In the decode phase, predicting token #100 means attending to tokens #1–99. Predicting token #101 means attending to tokens #1–100. Naively, every single step would re-process the entire history from scratch — enormous, wasteful repetition. The fix is the KV cache.

What the KV cache is

When the model processes a token, it computes two internal vectors for it, called the key and the value (the K and V). These capture "what this token offers to future tokens." Here's the insight: a token's key and value never change once computed. So instead of recomputing them for the whole history on every step, the engine computes each token's K and V once and stores them in GPU memory — the KV cache. Each new step only computes K and V for the one new token, then reads the cached K and V for everyone before it.

Think of it as sticky notes. Without the cache, answering each new word means re-reading the entire conversation from the top. With the cache, you've left a sticky note summarising each previous word — so you just glance at the notes and add one. That's the difference between a system that crawls and one that flies.

⚙️ Under the hood — the KV cache is a memory hog

The cache is what makes decode fast, but it's hungry. Its size grows with every token in the context and every concurrent user. A long RAG prompt (lots of retrieved policy text) times hundreds of simultaneous chats can eat more GPU memory than the model weights themselves. This is the central tension of serving: you have a fixed pool of GPU memory, the weights take a fixed slice, and whatever's left is split among all the KV caches. Run out, and you can't admit another user. That's why memory management is the heart of a serving engine.

And that memory problem is exactly what vLLM's PagedAttention solves. A naive engine reserves one big contiguous block of memory per request for its KV cache — sized for the longest answer it might produce — and most of that reservation sits empty, wasted. PagedAttention instead chops the KV cache into small fixed-size pages and hands them out on demand, exactly like an operating system pages memory. Little waste, so you fit far more users on the same GPU. That single trick is why vLLM squeezes dramatically more concurrency out of a card than a plain loop.

Going deeper — the levers that shrink the cache

Because the KV cache is the thing that runs you out of memory, model and engine designers attack it directly, and knowing the levers helps you reason about capacity. First, grouped-query attention (GQA) and its extreme, multi-query attention (MQA): modern models let several attention "heads" share one set of keys and values instead of each keeping its own, which can cut KV-cache size several-fold with almost no quality loss. Most current open models (Llama 3, Qwen, Mistral) already use GQA — it's a big reason they serve so many users per GPU. Second, prefix caching: when thousands of BankAssist requests start with the same system prompt and the same retrieved policy block, the engine can compute that shared prefix's K and V once and reuse it, saving both prefill compute and cache memory. Third, quantizing the KV cache itself (storing K and V in 8-bit, or FP8) roughly halves its footprint for a small accuracy cost — a knob (--kv-cache-dtype in vLLM) you turn when memory, not quality, is the binding constraint. Fourth, eviction and offloading: under pressure an engine can pause (preempt) a request and recompute or swap its cache, trading a little latency for the ability to admit more users. A concrete feel for scale: an 8B-class model costs on the order of 0.1–0.2 MB of KV cache per token, so a single 4,000-token conversation is ~0.5–0.8 GB — multiply by hundreds of users and you see why the crowd, not the weights, fills the card.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist launches and the dashboard looks fine at 50 concurrent chats. On payday morning concurrency jumps to 400, each chat carrying a long retrieved policy passage. Nothing crashed — but new customers suddenly wait seconds for a seat, because the KV-cache pool filled and the engine started queueing. The fix wasn't a bigger model; it was turning on prefix caching for the shared system prompt, trimming the retrieved context from eight passages to four, and adding a second replica for the peak. The crowd's cache, not the weights, had been the ceiling all along.

In production

Two numbers you'll be judged on come straight from this mechanism. TTFT (time to first token) is dominated by prefill — how long until the first word shows up — and it grows with prompt length, which is why bloated RAG prompts feel sluggish to start. TPOT (time per output token) is the decode speed — how fast words stream after that. Long retrieved contexts hurt TTFT; the KV cache and batching govern TPOT. When BankAssist "feels slow," measure which of the two it is before you touch anything — they have different cures.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the KV-cache pool, not the weights, usually caps how many conversations a GPU holds, so cache efficiency (GQA models, prefix caching, trimmed context) is directly money. Latency: report TTFT and TPOT separately; a long retrieved context quietly inflates TTFT across every concurrent user. Scale: the engine pre-reserves a cache pool at start-up; when it's full, new requests queue — so capacity planning is really "how many simultaneous conversations fit in the pool." Failure modes: OOM if the pool is mis-sized, and silent latency creep as average context length grows over time. Monitoring: track GPU KV-cache utilisation %, queue wait time, and average context length — a rising context length is an early warning of a coming capacity wall. Security & compliance: the KV cache holds the plaintext of customer prompts in GPU memory while a request runs; keep it on bank-controlled hardware, ensure it's cleared between requests (don't leak one customer's cache into another's prefix reuse), and never offload it to shared or external storage.

⚠ Watch out

Don't reason about GPU memory as "weights only." The KV cache is invisible until traffic arrives, then it dominates — and a prompt that grew from 2,000 to 6,000 tokens tripled your per-user cache without anyone touching the model. A subtle banking hazard: aggressive prefix sharing across users can, if mis-configured, reuse one customer's cached tokens for another — verify your engine only shares the truly-common system prefix, never user data.

Lean on the KV cache (it's always on) — but actively manage context length when concurrency is high and prompts are long. Do NOT enable cross-request KV sharing on segments that contain customer-specific data.

🧠 Remember it

Prefill reads the prompt; decode writes one token at a time. The KV cache is the sticky notes that stop the model re-reading the whole page every word — fast, but it eats GPU memory per token and per user.

Continuous batching: serving a crowd without making anyone wait

A GPU is happiest doing many things at once. Continuous batching keeps it busy by letting new requests hop onto the ride the instant a seat opens, instead of waiting for the next departure.

A GPU is a massively parallel chip — it can run one request or a hundred for almost the same clock time, because it's built to do huge batches of math at once. So serving one user at a time leaves the GPU mostly idle. The way to use it well is batching: run many requests together. The question is how you batch, and the answer makes or breaks your throughput.

Static batching (the old, clumsy way)

The simple idea: collect, say, 8 requests, run them as a group, wait for all 8 to finish, then start the next group. The problem? Answers have wildly different lengths. One request writes a 10-token "Yes, it's waivable." while another writes a 500-token explanation. With static batching, the seven short answers sit finished but stuck, hostages waiting for the one long answer before anyone gets released and the next batch can begin. The GPU runs half-empty and latency suffers. It's like a minibus that won't leave until every passenger has reached their stop.

Continuous (dynamic) batching — the modern default

Here's the clever upgrade that engines like vLLM and SGLang use. In the decode phase, the model generates one token per step for every conversation in flight. Continuous batching works at the token-step level: after each step, any request that just finished is released immediately, and any new request waiting in the queue joins the batch right away to fill the empty seat. Nobody waits for the slowest member of a fixed group. The batch is a living thing — people get on and off at every stop while the bus keeps rolling.

The payoff is large: continuous batching can multiply throughput several times over static batching on the same hardware, because the GPU almost never sits idle waiting for a straggler. This is a big part of why vLLM serves so many more users per GPU than a naive setup.

The throughput-versus-latency dial

Here's the tradeoff you'll actually tune. Bigger batches mean higher throughput (more total answers per second, so lower cost per answer) — but each individual user's tokens come a touch slower, because the GPU is splitting attention across more people, so latency per user rises. Smaller batches give each user snappier responses but serve fewer people per GPU, raising cost. There's no free win; there's a knob. Where you set it depends on the job.

Favour low latency

An interactive BankAssist chat where a customer watches words appear. Keep batches modest so each reply streams fast. You'll pay for more GPU per user, but the experience feels instant.

Favour high throughput

An overnight batch job summarising 50,000 transaction disputes. Nobody's watching a spinner, so pack batches large and squeeze maximum answers per GPU-hour. Cheapest per answer.

In production

You don't usually set a batch size directly; you set limits and the engine fills batches up to them. In vLLM the dials are things like --max-num-seqs (how many requests may run concurrently) and --max-num-batched-tokens (the token budget per step). Set them against a target: "p95 time-to-first-token under 1 second at 200 concurrent chats." Then watch the queue — if requests pile up waiting for a seat, you're GPU-bound and need a bigger batch budget, another replica, or a smaller model. The metric that tells the story is queue wait time: healthy serving keeps it near zero.

⚙️ In production

Cost: continuous batching is the single biggest lever on cost-per-answer — it can lift throughput several-fold over static batching on the same GPU, so a well-tuned batch budget directly shrinks the GPU bill. Latency: the knobs trade against each other — a larger --max-num-batched-tokens raises throughput but can delay a user's tokens; tune to a p95 TTFT/TPOT target, not to peak utilisation. Scale: one replica saturates, then you add replicas behind a load balancer; set --max-num-seqs so a single replica stays inside its KV-cache pool. Failure modes: the queue growing without bound (a thundering herd at peak) manifests as soaring TTFT while GPU use looks "fine" — shed load or autoscale before the queue explodes. Monitoring: running vs waiting requests, queue wait time, batch size, and tokens/sec; alert on queue wait crossing your SLA. Security & compliance: many customers' prompts share one GPU batch at once, so enforce tenant isolation at the app layer, rate-limit per caller to stop one client starving others, and make sure request logs don't mingle data across customers.

⚠ Watch out

Chasing maximum throughput can quietly wreck the customer experience. Crank batch sizes too high and the GPU is wonderfully "utilised" while every user watches their reply dribble out slowly. Tune to a latency target first (what the customer feels), then push throughput up to the edge of breaking it — not the other way round.

Favour big batches when nobody's watching a spinner — overnight bulk jobs, dispute summarisation, embedding backfills — to buy the cheapest cost-per-answer. Favour small batches when a customer is reading a live reply. Do NOT tune to GPU-utilisation alone; high utilisation with a slow per-user stream is a worse product, not a better one.

🧠 Remember it

Static batching is a minibus that won't leave till everyone's home; continuous batching lets riders hop on and off at every stop. Bigger batch = more throughput, slower per user. It's a dial, not a free lunch.

Weight quantization for serving: GGUF, AWQ, GPTQ, bitsandbytes

Quantization shrinks a model by storing its numbers with fewer digits — like saving photos as JPEGs. Done right, the model fits on a smaller GPU and runs faster, for a tiny, usually invisible, drop in quality.

A model's weights are billions of numbers. By default each is stored in 16 bits (two bytes) — that's "full precision" for serving, called FP16 or BF16. A 7-billion-parameter model therefore needs about 14 GB just for weights (7 billion × 2 bytes). Quantization stores each number with fewer bits — commonly 4 — so the same model shrinks to roughly a quarter of the size. Suddenly a model that needed a big expensive GPU fits on a modest one, loads faster, and often generates faster too (less memory to shuffle).

The catch: fewer bits means less precision, like a lower-quality JPEG. The art of quantization is squeezing the file while keeping the picture looking the same. Modern 4-bit methods are remarkably good — often within a point or two of full precision on quality tests — which is why quantized serving is routine, not exotic. Let's meet the four names you'll keep seeing. They split cleanly by where you're running.

GGUF — for CPUs, laptops, and Apple Silicon

GGUF is the format used by llama.cpp (and therefore by Ollama and LM Studio). It's really a container that holds a model at any of many quantization levels — you'll see tags like Q4_K_M (a solid 4-bit default) or Q8_0 (8-bit, higher quality, bigger). Its superpower is running well on CPUs, Macs, and mixed hardware — the only one of the four with good non-NVIDIA support. When BankAssist developers run a model on their laptops, it's GGUF underneath.

AWQ — for fast GPU serving

AWQ (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) is tuned for serving on GPUs. "Activation-aware" means it looks at which weights matter most in practice and protects those from the rounding, so quality holds up well at 4-bit. Paired with fast GPU kernels, AWQ is a leading choice for 4-bit serving in vLLM. If you're self-hosting a quantized model on GPUs for production, AWQ is often the first thing to try.

GPTQ — the broad GPU alternative

GPTQ is another GPU-oriented 4-bit method, around for longer, with a huge library of ready-made quantized models. Quality and speed are close to AWQ and model-dependent. The practical rule: if a model has an AWQ build, lean AWQ; if it only has a GPTQ build, GPTQ is perfectly good. It's about which checkpoint exists for the model you want.

bitsandbytes — easy, on-the-fly, mainly for training

bitsandbytes quantizes the model as it loads, with no separate pre-quantized file to prepare — flip a flag and the weights are compressed in memory (its 4-bit format is called NF4). That convenience makes it the default for QLoRA fine-tuning (training a small adapter on a quantized base). For pure serving its throughput is lower than AWQ or GPTQ, so you'll usually train with bitsandbytes and then convert to AWQ/GPTQ/GGUF to deploy.

FormatBest homeReach for it when…
GGUFCPU, Mac, laptops (llama.cpp / Ollama)Running locally for dev, or on non-NVIDIA hardware.
AWQGPU production serving (vLLM)You want fast, high-quality 4-bit serving on GPUs.
GPTQGPU production servingThe model you want only has a GPTQ build, or it's what your stack supports.
bitsandbytesFine-tuning (QLoRA), quick loadsTraining on a quantized base, or a one-off load without prep.
⚙️ Under the hood — this is NOT the embedding quantization you may have met in RAG

A frequent mix-up. In the RAG world you also hear "quantization" — but there it means shrinking the embedding vectors stored in your vector database (turning each 32-bit number in a vector into an 8-bit or even 1-bit value) to save storage and speed up similarity search. That's vector quantization: it compresses the search index, and the thing it trades is retrieval recall. Weight quantization, this chapter's topic, compresses the language model's parameters on the GPU, and the thing it trades is generation quality. Same word, two completely different objects: one shrinks what you search, the other shrinks what answers. Keep them apart or you'll confuse everyone in a design review.

Here's how little it takes to serve a quantized model with vLLM — the quantization lives in the model checkpoint, and the engine just loads it:

# Serve a 4-bit AWQ model on a GPU with vLLM — one command.
vllm serve TheBloke/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-AWQ \  # a pre-quantized AWQ checkpoint — ~4GB instead of ~16GB
    --quantization awq \                          # tell vLLM to use AWQ kernels for the 4-bit weights
    --max-model-len 8192 \                         # cap context length — keeps KV-cache memory in check
    --port 8000                                    # serve the OpenAI-compatible API on this port
▶ Output
INFO: Loaded model in AWQ (4-bit). KV cache: 31,200 tokens free. Uvicorn running on http://0.0.0.0:8000

Notice what the quantization bought you: the 8B model that wanted ~16 GB now loads in ~4 GB, which frees most of the GPU's memory for the KV cache — meaning more concurrent users. Quantization isn't only about fitting; it directly buys you capacity.

Going deeper — the kernel matters more than the format, and real quality numbers

Two things surprise people who quantize for the first time. First, on quality, 4-bit is closer to full precision than the fear suggests but it is not free. On a public coding benchmark (HumanEval), community tests put AWQ and GGUF's Q4_K_M around ~52% against a full-precision baseline near ~56%, with GPTQ a little lower around ~46% — a few points, and exactly the kind of gap that can move a number or a rare term in a banking answer. Second, and less obvious: which GPU kernel runs the 4-bit math matters more than which format you picked. The same AWQ checkpoint on a large model has been measured at roughly 740 tokens/sec with the optimised Marlin kernel versus ~70 tokens/sec on a default kernel — a 10× swing from a flag, not a re-quantization. GPTQ with Marlin lands close behind. So "AWQ vs GPTQ" is often really "did I enable the fast kernel for my GPU and vLLM version?" — and the ranking between them flips release to release. The takeaway: pick a format your engine supports well, make sure the fast kernel is active, and benchmark on your model and card rather than trusting a blog's leaderboard.

Two more current options worth knowing. FP8 (8-bit floating point) is increasingly the sweet spot on recent NVIDIA GPUs: near-lossless quality — in one test matching BF16 on a math benchmark while 4-bit lost six-plus points — at roughly half the memory of FP16, with hardware acceleration. If you have the GPU memory, FP8 buys speed and capacity with almost no quality risk, which is attractive for high-stakes banking answers. And a warning on mixing worlds: GGUF runs poorly inside GPU engines like vLLM (one test ~93 tok/s) — GGUF is for llama.cpp/Ollama on CPU/Mac, AWQ/GPTQ/FP8 are for GPU serving. Don't cross the streams.

⚙️ In production

Cost: quantization is capacity — a 4-bit 8B frees ~10 GB that becomes KV cache and therefore more concurrent users per GPU, or lets a model fit a cheaper card. Latency: fewer bytes to move usually speeds decode, but only with the right kernel active (Marlin for AWQ/GPTQ, native FP8 paths) — verify tokens/sec, don't assume. Scale: smaller weights mean fewer GPUs for the same model, or the same GPUs serving more replicas. Failure modes: a checkpoint quantized for one kernel that your engine can't accelerate (silent 10× slowdown), or a quality regression that passes "it sounds fine" but fails a numeric check. Monitoring: keep a frozen evaluation set and re-score it after every quantization or engine upgrade; track tokens/sec to catch a kernel regression. Security & compliance: treat a quantized model as a new model version for audit — record the exact checkpoint hash, method, and bit-width, and re-run your accuracy and safety evals so you can show the regulator the quantized model still meets the bar it was approved at.

⚠ Watch out

Don't quantize blindly for a banking workload. Quality loss, though usually small, isn't uniform — it can hit the exact things you care about, like precise numbers, long chains of reasoning, or rare terminology. Always re-run your own evaluation set after quantizing. "It still sounds fluent" is not the same as "it still quotes the fee correctly." For high-stakes answers, verify, don't assume.

Quantize when memory or cost is the binding constraint and your eval set confirms the quality holds — prefer FP8 when you can afford it, AWQ/GPTQ (with the fast kernel) for aggressive 4-bit GPU serving, GGUF for laptops. Do NOT quantize the highest-stakes numeric or compliance answers without a passing eval, and do NOT run GGUF on a production GPU engine.

🧠 Remember it

Quantization = saving the model as a JPEG: much smaller, usually looks the same. GGUF for laptops, AWQ/GPTQ for GPU serving, bitsandbytes for training. And weight-quant ≠ embedding-quant — one shrinks the answerer, the other shrinks the search.

Speculative decoding: a fast junior drafts, the expert checks

Instead of the big model writing every token itself, a tiny fast model guesses several tokens ahead, and the big model verifies them all in one quick pass — accepting the good guesses for free.

Here's the painful truth of how a model writes an answer: the big model produces one token at a time, and each step is a full, heavy pass through billions of parameters. That's the latency floor. Speculative decoding is a brilliant trick to beat it without changing the output.

Picture a senior analyst writing a report with a sharp junior beside them. The junior, who's fast but less authoritative, scribbles the next few words they expect the senior would write. The senior then reads those few words in a single glance and says "yes, yes, yes, no" — keeping the run of correct guesses and correcting at the first wrong one. When the junior guesses well, the senior produces several words for the effort of reading one. That's exactly the mechanism.

How it works

  1. A small, fast draft model proposes the next few tokens (say 4) quickly and cheaply.
  2. The big target model checks all 4 proposals in a single forward pass — and because that pass works on multiple tokens at once (like prefill), it's barely slower than generating one.
  3. The target accepts the proposed tokens that match what it would have produced, and rejects from the first mismatch onward, generating the correct token there itself.
  4. Repeat. On a good run you got several tokens for roughly the cost of one big-model step.

The guarantee that makes this safe for banking: the output is mathematically identical to what the target model would have produced alone. The draft model only proposes; the target model has the final say on every single token. You get speed, not a different (riskier) answer. In practice this can roughly double or triple single-stream generation speed when the draft guesses well.

There's also a draft-model-free cousin called n-gram / prompt-lookup decoding: instead of a small model, it guesses the next tokens by copying repeated phrases already in the context. It shines when answers echo the prompt a lot — summarisation, or RAG answers that quote retrieved policy text verbatim. No extra model to host, free speedup where it applies.

Going deeper — EAGLE, and the number that decides it all

The simplest form uses a separate small model from the same family as the draft. The method that's become the 2025 state of the art does something cleverer: EAGLE (and its successor EAGLE-3) trains a tiny, lightweight head that predicts drafts from the target model's own internal features, so the draft "thinks" almost exactly like the big model — which pushes acceptance high. In vLLM you turn it on by passing a speculative_config naming the method and the draft, so adding it is a config change, not a code rewrite. The one number that governs whether any of this pays off is the mean accepted length: how many drafted tokens the target keeps per verification step. A realistic figure on a well-matched EAGLE-3 setup is around 2.5 — meaning you produce ~2.5 tokens for roughly the cost of one big-model step. If your acceptance on your traffic comes out near 1, speculation is costing more than it saves; if it's 2–3, it's a clear win. Banking traffic that quotes policy text verbatim tends to accept well (the answer is predictable); open-ended advice accepts less. Always measure acceptance on your own prompts before committing — a vendor's benchmark on different traffic tells you almost nothing.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist runs an overnight job that drafts thousands of near-identical fee-dispute letters — same policy wording, just different names and amounts. Daytime customer chat already packs the GPUs, so speculation there would waste compute on rejected guesses. But the overnight job runs on an otherwise-idle GPU, and its output is highly repetitive, so the draft's guesses are accepted most of the time. The team enables EAGLE-style speculative decoding only for that off-peak, high-overlap job, roughly doubling its single-stream speed, and leaves it off during the busy, fully-batched day. Same model, same answers — speed turned on exactly where the GPU had room and the draft guessed well.

In production

Speculative decoding helps most when the GPU is underused — low traffic, few concurrent users, where latency per request is what you're fighting. When the GPU is already packed via continuous batching (high traffic), its spare capacity is gone, and speculation can even hurt by spending compute on guesses that get rejected. So it's workload-dependent, not a global "on." The dial that tells you whether it's paying off is the acceptance rate: how often the target keeps the draft's guesses. High acceptance (a draft that mirrors the target on your traffic) means big wins; low acceptance means wasted work — turn it off. Measure on your real traffic before committing.

⚙️ In production

Cost: speculation spends extra compute on drafts, so it only lowers cost-per-answer when acceptance is high and the GPU had spare capacity — on a saturated daytime fleet it can raise cost. Latency: its whole purpose is cutting per-request latency (TPOT) for single or low-concurrency streams; expect roughly 1.5–2.5× on well-matched workloads, near-zero when acceptance is low. Scale: treat it as a per-workload toggle — on for off-peak/low-concurrency and highly-repetitive jobs, off (or auto-off) when the batch is already full. Failure modes: a mismatched draft that tanks acceptance and quietly slows you down; hosting a second (draft) model also adds its own memory and ops. Monitoring: watch mean accepted length and the resulting TPOT — if accepted length drifts toward 1, disable it. Security & compliance: because the output is provably identical to the target model alone, speculation needs no new model approval — but the draft model still runs on bank hardware and must sit inside the same trust boundary and version-pinning regime as the target.

⚠ Watch out

A bad draft model is worse than none. If the junior guesses poorly, the senior rejects constantly and you've paid for the draft and the full verification with little to show. Pick a draft from the same family as the target (so they "think alike"), and always check the acceptance rate on your own prompts rather than trusting a blog's benchmark.

Turn it on when latency per request matters, the GPU has spare capacity (off-peak or low concurrency), and acceptance on your traffic is high — repetitive, quote-heavy outputs are ideal. Do NOT run it on an already-saturated high-concurrency fleet, or with a draft that mirrors the target poorly.

🧠 Remember it

A fast junior drafts, the expert checks in one glance. Same answer, more speed — when the junior guesses well (high acceptance) and the GPU has room to spare.

GPU sizing: will this model even fit?

Before you rent a GPU you need to answer one question on the back of an envelope: does the model, plus room for all my users' conversations, fit in its memory? Here's the simple math.

Running out of GPU memory isn't a slowdown — it's a hard stop. The process dies with an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) error, or refuses to admit the next user. So sizing is a survival skill. The good news: a rough estimate needs only grade-school arithmetic and three ingredients.

Total GPU memory you need ≈ weights + KV cache + overhead. Take them one at a time.

1. The weights

This is the biggest, most predictable chunk: parameters × bytes-per-parameter. The bytes depend on precision:

  • FP16 / BF16 (full serving precision): 2 bytes each.
  • 8-bit quantized: 1 byte each.
  • 4-bit quantized: about 0.5 bytes each.

So a 7B model in FP16 ≈ 7 × 2 = 14 GB. The same model at 4-bit ≈ 7 × 0.5 = 3.5 GB. A handy shortcut: in FP16, GB ≈ twice the billions of parameters; at 4-bit, roughly half.

2. The KV cache

This is the sneaky one that sinks sizing estimates. The KV cache grows with every token of context × every concurrent user. A rough per-token cost for an 8B-class model is on the order of 0.1–0.2 MB per token. Multiply by your context length and your concurrent requests:

KV cache ≈ per-token cost × context length × concurrent users

That product can dwarf the weights. 200 users each holding a 4,000-token RAG conversation, at ~0.13 MB/token, is roughly 0.13 × 4,000 × 200 ≈ 104 GB of KV cache — far more than the 14 GB of weights. This is why "the model is only 14 GB, so a 16 GB card is fine" is the classic rookie miscalculation: it ignores the crowd.

3. Overhead

Add a cushion — roughly 10–20% — for activations, the engine's own buffers, and fragmentation. Never plan to fill a GPU to 100%; leave headroom or you'll OOM under a traffic spike.

Let's turn the envelope into a tiny, runnable estimator — the kind of check you'd do before provisioning:

# Back-of-envelope GPU sizing for a self-hosted model.
params_billion   = 8          # model size — an 8B open-weight model (e.g. Llama 3.1 8B)
bytes_per_param  = 0.5        # 4-bit quantized weights ≈ 0.5 bytes each (use 2 for FP16)
kv_mb_per_token  = 0.13       # rough KV-cache cost per token for an 8B-class model, in MB
context_len      = 4000       # typical tokens per conversation (RAG prompt + answer)
concurrent_users = 100        # how many chats we must serve at the same time

weights_gb = params_billion * bytes_per_param          # 8 * 0.5 = 4 GB for the weights
kv_gb      = kv_mb_per_token * context_len * concurrent_users / 1024  # MB → GB for the whole crowd's caches
overhead   = 0.15 * (weights_gb + kv_gb)               # ~15% cushion for activations and engine buffers
total_gb   = weights_gb + kv_gb + overhead             # the number that must fit inside the GPU

print(f"weights={weights_gb:.0f}GB  kv={kv_gb:.0f}GB  total≈{total_gb:.0f}GB")  # the verdict
▶ Output
weights=4GB kv=51GB total≈63GB → fits on one 80GB GPU, with room to spare

Read what the numbers scream: the weights are 4 GB, but the KV cache for 100 users is 51 GB. The crowd, not the model, is your real memory cost. That reframes every lever: quantizing the weights frees a little; capping context length and controlling concurrency frees a lot. If it doesn't fit, your options are a smaller or more-quantized model, shorter context, fewer concurrent users per GPU, or spreading the model across multiple GPUs (tensor parallelism, which vLLM does with a single flag).

Going deeper — picking the card, and spreading across several

Once you can estimate the bill, two practical questions follow. Which GPU? Today's common serving cards, by memory: ~24 GB (NVIDIA A10/L4 — fine for a quantized 7–8B with modest concurrency), ~48 GB (L40S), ~80 GB (A100/H100 — the workhorse for mid-size models at real concurrency), and ~141 GB (H200). Memory decides what fits; the card's compute decides how fast it runs. For BankAssist's quantized 8B at a few hundred concurrent chats, a single 80 GB card is the natural home — the earlier estimate landed at ~63 GB.

What if the model is too big for one card? You split it. Tensor parallelism shards each layer's math across GPUs that work on every token together — it's how a 70B model (≈140 GB in FP16) runs across two 80 GB cards, and in vLLM it's one flag, --tensor-parallel-size 2. It needs a fast interconnect (NVLink) between the cards or the chatter between them becomes the bottleneck. Pipeline parallelism instead puts different layers on different GPUs (even different machines) and passes activations down the line — better when the cards aren't tightly linked. Rule of thumb: tensor-parallel within a box, pipeline-parallel across boxes. And a sharper way to read the KV math backwards: if you fix the GPU and the model, the free memory divided by per-user cache cost tells you your concurrency ceiling — e.g. ~60 GB of pool ÷ ~0.5 GB per 4k-token chat ≈ 120 simultaneous conversations before requests start queueing.

In production

Real serving engines don't make you guess per request — vLLM pre-reserves a KV-cache pool from the free memory after loading weights, and once that pool is full, new requests queue rather than crash. So sizing becomes capacity planning: your memory sets your KV pool, your KV pool sets how many concurrent conversations you can hold, and that sets how many replicas you need for peak traffic. A banking twist: long contexts are expensive in a hidden way — every extra 1,000 tokens of retrieved policy text you stuff into prompts multiplies across every concurrent user and eats the pool. Trimming RAG context isn't just about quality; it's directly GPU capacity you're buying back.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the number of replicas to cover peak concurrency is your GPU bill, and it's set by per-user KV cost — so quantization, GQA models, prefix caching, and context trimming all translate straight into fewer cards. Latency: leave headroom; a GPU driven to 100% memory and compute queues requests and p95 latency spikes well before you "run out." Scale: size for peak (payday mornings), not daily average, and plan an autoscaling or spillover path rather than one heroic over-provisioned box. Failure modes: hard OOM at load if you under-provision, and graceful-but-painful queueing when the KV pool fills under a spike — both are capacity-planning misses, not bugs. Monitoring: GPU memory headroom, KV-pool utilisation %, queue wait, and average context length (a slow creep here erodes capacity invisibly). Security & compliance: capacity plans for a bank must survive the regulated peak, so document the sizing assumptions (model, bit-width, context cap, concurrency) as part of the change record, and keep a tested fallback so a capacity miss never becomes a customer-facing outage.

⚠ Watch out

Never size for the weights alone. "The 70B model is 140 GB in FP16, so two 80 GB GPUs are plenty" ignores the KV cache entirely — under real concurrency you'll OOM on day one. Always add the crowd's cache to the bill, and always leave overhead.

Use this envelope math when choosing a card or deciding how many replicas a peak needs — it's fast and good enough to provision from. Do NOT trust it as the final word for go-live: measure the real KV-pool size the engine reports and load-test at peak concurrency before you promise an SLA.

🧠 Remember it

Need ≈ weights + KV cache + 15%. Weights ≈ 2× the billions (FP16) or ½× (4-bit). And the KV cache — users × context — is usually the slice that bites. Size for the crowd, not just the model.

Local models for development — and choosing across providers

The fastest way to learn serving is to run a model on your own laptop in two commands. And once you can run anything anywhere, the real skill is choosing which engine or provider each job deserves.

You don't need a data centre to get hands-on. Ollama runs a real open-weight model on your laptop — with your data never leaving the machine, which makes it perfect for experimenting with sensitive banking prompts safely. Two commands and you're talking to a model:

# Pull a model once (downloads the GGUF weights), then chat with it.
ollama pull llama3.1:8b          # download the 8B model — a ~4.7GB quantized GGUF file, cached locally
ollama run llama3.1:8b           # start an interactive chat right in the terminal
▶ Output
>>> What is an overdraft fee?
An overdraft fee is a charge a bank applies when you spend more than your account balance... (running entirely on your laptop)

The same Ollama instance also exposes an OpenAI-compatible server at http://localhost:11434/v1, so your application code can talk to your laptop model with the exact client you'd use for a hosted API — only the base URL differs. That's the beauty of the shared API shape: write once, point anywhere.

# Point the standard OpenAI client at Ollama running on your own machine.
from openai import OpenAI                     # same library you'd use for hosted OpenAI

dev = OpenAI(                                 # a client aimed at the local Ollama server
    base_url="http://localhost:11434/v1",     # Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint — note the port
    api_key="ollama",                         # any non-empty string; Ollama ignores it locally
)
reply = dev.chat.completions.create(          # identical call shape to the production code
    model="llama3.1:8b",                      # the model we pulled — runs on the laptop's CPU/GPU
    messages=[{"role": "user",                # a test banking prompt, safe because nothing leaves the laptop
               "content": "Draft a polite overdraft-fee explanation."}],
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)       # the answer, generated locally — zero data egress
▶ Output
Thank you for reaching out. An overdraft fee of $35 applies when a transaction exceeds your available balance. You're eligible for one courtesy waiver every 12 months — just let us know.

This is the everyday development loop in a bank: prototype against a local model where you can throw real-looking prompts around freely, then flip the base URL to your production vLLM server when it's time to ship. The code doesn't change.

Choosing across the whole landscape

Put it all together and you have a decision you'll make again and again: for this job, do I use a hosted API or self-host, and with which engine? Here's the practical map.

Your situationGood choiceWhy
Prototyping on a laptop, sensitive promptsOllama / LM StudioZero setup, data stays local, OpenAI-compatible so code ports later.
Production, data must stay in the bankSelf-host vLLM or SGLangResidency satisfied; high concurrency on your own GPUs.
Production, data residency is fine, modest volumeHosted API (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google)No infrastructure to run; cheapest until volume is large.
Huge steady volume, cost-sensitiveSelf-host (quantized) on vLLMFixed GPU cost beats a growing per-token bill at scale.
Need the very strongest reasoning, no residency blockHosted frontier modelTop closed models often still lead; don't self-host a weaker one just to self-host.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist ends up running three engines at once, and that's healthy, not messy. Developers prototype on Ollama laptops with realistic (synthetic) customer data — nothing leaves their machines.
