Because the failure is silent, the only defence is to measure extraction quality directly, before any retrieval question is asked. Three cheap signals catch most disasters. First, a coverage check: what fraction of pages produced almost no text? A scanned batch that returns empty strings shows up instantly. Second, a structure check: did the tables you expected actually come out as tables, or as flat lines of numbers? Third, a round-trip spot check: keep a small "gold set" of pages where a human wrote down the right answer, re-parse them on every pipeline change, and diff. The point is to turn an invisible ceiling into a number on a dashboard.

def parse_health(pages):                            # pages: list of extracted-text strings, one per page
    total = len(pages)                              # denominator for the coverage ratio
    empty = sum(1 for t in pages if len(t.strip()) < 30)  # near-empty page = scan or failed extraction
    digit_soup = sum(                               # pages that are mostly loose numbers = flattened tables
        1 for t in pages
        if sum(c.isdigit() for c in t) > 0.4 * max(len(t), 1)
    )
    empty_rate = empty / total                      # the coverage signal we alarm on
    if empty_rate > 0.1:                             # >10% blank pages = the ceiling just dropped
        raise ValueError(f"{empty_rate:.0%} of pages empty — parser failing silently")
    return {"empty_rate": empty_rate, "table_risk_pages": digit_soup}  # emit as metrics

print(parse_health(extracted_pages))               # run this on every ingest, not just at launch
▶ Output

{'empty_rate': 0.02, 'table_risk_pages': 3}

Nothing here is clever — it's a smoke alarm. An empty_rate that jumps from 2% to 30% overnight means a source started shipping scans, and you now know before a customer gets a blank answer.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. The quality gate itself is almost free, but it governs the biggest cost lever you have: whether a page escalates to an expensive vision parser. A good gate keeps 95%+ of pages on the cheap tier while still catching the failures — that ratio is the difference between a $500 and a $50,000 backfill.

Scale & failure modes. At millions of pages, the silent failures compound: empty extractions, tables flattened to soup, and reading order scrambled on multi-column pages. None throw. Catch them with the coverage/structure metrics above, sampled continuously, and route failing pages to a dead-letter queue for re-parsing rather than indexing nothing.

Monitoring. Dashboard the empty-page rate, table-risk rate, and gold-set accuracy per source and per parser version. Alarm on deltas, not absolutes — a source changing format is the event you must catch.

Security & compliance (a bank). A silently mis-parsed figure is a compliance incident waiting to happen (a wrong rate, a transposed account number). Keep the gold-set accuracy and parser version in your audit trail so you can prove, after the fact, that the extraction met a documented bar on the day the answer was given.

⚠ Watch out

The seductive mistake is to "fix" a wrong answer by swapping the embedding model or adding a reranker. If the text was destroyed at parse time, you will spend weeks tuning retrieval and move the number not at all. Always confirm the correct text is actually in the index, verbatim, before touching anything downstream.

✅ When to use / when not

Treat parsing as the first suspect whenever an answer is wrong, missing, or oddly generic. Do invest in better extraction when your coverage or structure metrics are poor — that raises the ceiling for everything downstream. Don't keep pouring effort into embeddings or rerankers while the parse-health metrics are red; you'd be polishing a ceiling you can't push through.

🧠 Remember it

Garbage in, garbage ranked. A great retriever on badly-parsed text just finds your mistakes faster.

PDFs and tables — where most banking knowledge hides, and most parsers fail

A PDF is a layout, not a document; tables are the hardest part of it, and banking runs on tables.

Here's the thing almost nobody tells you: a PDF file doesn't actually store sentences. It stores instructions like "place the glyph '6' at x=220, y=118." The human eye assembles those positioned marks into words and tables. A parser has to reconstruct that — guess the reading order, group marks into words, and recognise when a cluster of numbers is really a table. It's less like reading and more like archaeology.

And banking is unusually table-heavy: rate cards, amortization schedules, fee grids, financial statements, KYC checklists. So for a bank, table extraction is the main event, not a side quest.

The golden rules for tables

  • Extract tables separately and store them as Markdown or HTML, which preserve rows, columns and merged cells — not as flattened text.
  • Put the header on every row. A chunk that reads "30-year: 6.9%" is self-contained; a chunk that reads "6.9%" is a landmine. Repeating the column name into each row makes every row answerable on its own.
  • Never split a table mid-row. Cutting between a value and its label orphans both.
  • For long tables that span many pages, keep the header attached to each page's slice, and consider adding a one-line natural-language summary of the table for the embedding ("Rate card: fixed mortgage rates by term, Nov 2026") so topic-level questions find it.
  • Validate cells. In finance, a misread digit is a disaster. Check numbers against expectations (do the rows of a statement sum to the total? are account numbers the right length?).

A simple, real extraction with pdfplumber (great for digitally-born PDFs) that turns a table into header-per-row text:

import pdfplumber                                  # pure-python PDF reader, strong at tables on born-digital PDFs

with pdfplumber.open("rate_card_2026.pdf") as pdf: # context manager closes the file for us
    page = pdf.pages[0]                            # first page holds the rate table
    table = page.extract_tables()[0]               # returns rows as lists of cells; [0] = first table

header = table[0]                                  # first row is the column headers ("Term", "Rate")
rows = []                                          # collect one self-contained line per data row
for r in table[1:]:                               # skip the header row; iterate the data rows
    pairs = [f"{h}: {c}" for h, c in zip(header, r)]  # pair each cell WITH its column name
    rows.append(" | ".join(pairs))                # join into one readable, chunk-safe line

print("\n".join(rows))                             # each line now stands on its own
▶ Output

Term: 15-year | Rate: 6.2%
Term: 20-year | Rate: 6.5%
Term: 30-year | Rate: 6.9%

The trick is the zip(header, r) — it marries every value to its column name so "6.9%" never floats away from "30-year." For heavily ruled financial tables, Camelot (camelot.read_pdf(path, flavor="lattice")) is a strong alternative that reads the cell borders directly.

⚙️ Under the hood

Why Markdown/HTML for storage instead of just text? Because they encode structure a model already understands. Merged cells, spanning headers, and nested columns survive as HTML rowspan/colspan or Markdown pipes. When the LLM later reads a retrieved table, that structure helps it answer "what's the fee in the third tier?" correctly. For a very wide or very long table, also emit a short NL summary and embed that for discovery, while keeping the full table as the citation payload.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. pdfplumber and Camelot run locally for fractions of a cent per page but are slow on dense pages (hundreds of milliseconds). Vision-based table extractors read the hardest tables far better at roughly $0.01–0.05 per page — real money across a million-page archive, so reserve them for pages a cheap extractor demonstrably failed.

Scale & failure modes. The two failure shapes are missed tables (the extractor returns prose where a table was) and misaligned cells (a value lands in the wrong column) — both silent. Validate structurally: do the detected columns match the header count on every row? Do numeric columns parse as numbers? Do subtotal rows sum? Quarantine pages that fail validation instead of indexing them.

Monitoring. Track tables detected per document, cell-count consistency, and numeric-parse failure rate. A drop in "tables detected" after a source redesign is your signal that a rate card is now invisible to the assistant.

Security & compliance (a bank). A transposed digit in a rate or fee table is a mis-selling and compliance risk, not a cosmetic bug. Keep the original table image or cell coordinates as the citation payload so a human can verify any figure the assistant quotes, and log the parser/version that produced each table.

⚠ Watch out

Chunkers that split by character count will cheerfully cut a 40-row amortization table in half, stranding rows 21–40 with no header. Always make your chunker table-aware: a table is one unit, or is split only at row boundaries with the header re-attached.

✅ When to use / when not

Use pdfplumber for born-digital tables with whitespace alignment, and Camelot's lattice mode for tables with visible cell borders (ruled financial statements). Escalate to a vision parser only when both fail your validation on that page. Don't treat a table as prose text, and don't route "add up these rows" questions through similarity search — that arithmetic belongs in a query engine over the extracted table.

🧠 Remember it

A number without its header is a rumour. Keep every cell married to its column.

Hard pages — multi-column layouts, figures & charts, and OCR for scans

Columns scramble reading order, pictures carry meaning no text layer holds, and scanned paper has no text at all — each needs its own fix.

Not every page is a tidy wall of text. Three kinds of pages trip up naive parsers, and a bank's archives are full of all three.

Multi-column layouts

Product brochures and research notes often use two or three columns. A parser that reads strictly left-to-right across the whole page will weave the columns together like shuffling two decks of cards — a sentence from column one, then a fragment from column two, then back again. The result reads like nonsense. The fix is a parser that detects column boundaries and reads each column top-to-bottom before moving right. Layout-aware parsers do this; plain text extractors often do not.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist ingests a two-column "Switch to us" mortgage flyer. Column one lists benefits; column two lists eligibility. A naive read produces "Lower rates You must earn no setup fee at least $30,000 free valuation and hold…" — benefits and rules braided into gibberish. A customer then gets told the wrong eligibility rule. The flyer looked fine to the parser; the reading order quietly betrayed it.

Figures and charts

A chart of "default rates by region" holds real knowledge, but there's no sentence to extract — it's pixels. The modern move is vision captioning: send the figure image to a vision-capable model and ask it to describe the chart in words ("Bar chart: default rate highest in Region C at 4.1%, lowest in Region A at 1.2%"). You then embed that caption so the figure becomes searchable, and keep the image itself as the citation.

import base64                                       # to inline the image bytes as a data URL
from openai import OpenAI                           # official OpenAI SDK

client = OpenAI()                                   # reads the API key from the environment, never hard-coded
img_b64 = base64.b64encode(open("default_rates.png","rb").read()).decode()  # chart cropped out of the PDF page

resp = client.responses.create(                     # Responses API: current way to send text + image together
    model="gpt-4.1",                                # a vision-capable model
    input=[{                                         # one user message carrying a prompt AND the figure
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "input_text",                  # the instruction: describe for SEARCH, state the numbers
             "text": "Describe this chart for retrieval. State every value and the trend in one line."},
            {"type": "input_image",                 # the image part the model actually looks at
             "image_url": f"data:image/png;base64,{img_b64}"},
        ],
    }],
)
caption = resp.output_text                           # the searchable sentence we embed; image stays as citation
print(caption)                                       # verify it captured the numbers, not vague fluff
▶ Output

Bar chart of default rate by region: Region C highest at 4.1%, Region A lowest at 1.2%; overall rising left to right.

The prompt is doing the real work: "state every value" forces the model to pull the numbers off the axes instead of writing a vague "a chart showing default rates." You embed that caption for discovery and keep the original image as the thing a human can click to verify.

OCR for scanned documents

OCR (Optical Character Recognition) turns a picture of text back into actual characters. Under the hood it finds the text regions on the page, slices them into lines and then into individual letter shapes, and matches each shape to the character it most closely resembles. You need it whenever a PDF is a scan — a photographed loan agreement, an old signed KYC form — because those have no text layer at all. The usual tools:

  • Tesseract — the classic open-source OCR engine (via pytesseract); free, runs locally, good on clean scans.
  • AWS Textract — a cloud OCR service that also understands forms and tables.
  • Azure AI Document Intelligence — Microsoft's cloud service, strong on layout, forms and tables together.
import pytesseract                                 # python wrapper around the Tesseract OCR engine
from pdf2image import convert_from_path            # turns each PDF page into an image Tesseract can read

pages = convert_from_path("scanned_kyc.pdf", dpi=300)  # 300 DPI: enough detail for OCR to read small digits
text = ""                                          # accumulate recognised text across all pages
for img in pages:                                 # OCR works on one page image at a time
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(img)       # the actual recognition: pixels → characters

if len(text.strip()) < 20:                         # sanity check: near-empty means OCR failed silently
    raise ValueError("OCR produced almost nothing — bad scan?")  # fail LOUD, don't index an empty doc
print(text[:60])                                   # peek at the first line to confirm it's sensible
▶ Output

KNOW YOUR CUSTOMER FORM Full name: Priya Sharma Acc

The raise line matters more than it looks. OCR's most dangerous failure is returning an empty or near-empty string without complaining — so we check the length and fail loudly rather than silently index nothing.

⚠ Watch out

OCR confuses look-alikes: 0/O, 1/l/I, 5/S, 8/B. In a chatty document that's harmless. In an account number, a sort code, or a loan amount it's catastrophic. Always validate OCR'd numbers — check lengths, checksums, and totals — before trusting a single digit of finance.

💡 Key idea

Text, pictures, and scans are three different problems. Plain text extraction handles the first, vision captioning the second, OCR the third. Using only one tool for all three is how knowledge silently goes missing.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. These three cures are the expensive end of parsing. OCR at 300 DPI is CPU-heavy (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per page); cloud OCR (Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence) bills per page; vision captioning is an LLM call per figure. So you run them only on pages that need them — scans, figure-bearing pages, multi-column layouts — gated by a cheap detector, not on the whole corpus.

Scale & failure modes. OCR fails silently to an empty or near-empty string (so fail loud on length, as above). Vision captioning can hallucinate values that aren't on the chart — a dangerous failure for a bank — so prompt it to say "not legible" rather than guess, and keep the image for human verification. Multi-column detection misfires on unusual layouts; sample and eyeball.

Monitoring. Track OCR empty-output rate, average OCR confidence (Tesseract and the cloud services return per-word confidence), caption length/plausibility, and the share of pages escalated to each cure. A rising OCR-empty rate means scan quality dropped at the source.

Security & compliance (a bank). Scans of KYC forms and signed agreements are dense PII; if you use a cloud OCR or vision service, confirm it meets the bank's data-residency and no-training contractual terms, or keep OCR on-prem (Tesseract) inside the trust boundary. Always validate OCR'd account numbers, sort codes and amounts against checksums and lengths before trusting a digit.

✅ When to use / when not

Use layout-aware reading for multi-column pages, vision captioning for charts and diagrams, and OCR for any scan with no text layer. Don't OCR a born-digital PDF (its text layer is perfect and free), don't caption a chart whose data already exists as a table elsewhere, and don't trust a vision caption's numbers for a figure without keeping the source image to check against.

🧠 Remember it

Columns scramble, charts go mute, scans go blank. Three symptoms, three cures: layout reading, captioning, OCR.

Choosing a parser — and the tiered pipeline that beats any single one

There is no one best parser; the winning design is cheap-first, expensive-only-when-needed, and tested on your hardest pages.

Parsers come in three families, and each trades speed and cost against layout fidelity. Knowing the families lets you pick deliberately instead of by vibes.

FamilyExamples (2026)Great atWeak at
Basic textPyMuPDF (pymupdf), pdfiumFast, exact text from digitally-born PDFs; nearly freeScans (returns empty); complex tables
Heuristic / layoutUnstructured, Docling, pdfplumber, CamelotReading order, headings, tables via rules & layout modelsMessy scans; very unusual layouts
Vision-firstLlamaParse, Reducto, Azure AI Document IntelligenceHardest pages: scans, dense tables, odd layoutsSlower and 10–100× costlier per page

The mistake is to pick one family for everything. A basic text extractor on a scanned loan deed returns nothing. A vision model on a million clean memos burns your budget for no gain. The grown-up answer is a tiered (hybrid) pipeline with fallback: try the cheap parser first, measure whether it actually worked, and only escalate the pages that failed.

import pymupdf                                      # PyMuPDF: the fast, cheap tier-1 extractor

def parse_pdf(path):
    doc = pymupdf.open(path)                        # open once; iterate its pages
    out = []                                        # collect (page_number, text) results
    for i, page in enumerate(doc):                  # enumerate gives us the page number for citations
        text = page.get_text()                      # tier 1: pull the text layer (free if it exists)
        if len(text.strip()) < 30:                  # QUALITY GATE: too little text = scan or odd layout
            text = vision_parse(path, i)            # escalate ONLY this page to the pricey vision parser
        out.append((i + 1, text))                   # store 1-based page number with its text
    return out                                      # tier-1 handled most pages; vision touched only the hard ones

The whole design lives in one line: if len(text.strip()) < 30. That character-count heuristic decides, per page, whether the cheap parser was good enough or whether this page deserves the expensive one. Most pages pass; your bill stays small; the hard pages still get read.

✅ Tip

Test on your hardest pages, not your average ones. Build a small "torture set" — your ugliest scanned deed, your most merged-cell rate sheet, your worst two-column flyer — and judge every parser on those. Average pages make every parser look fine; the hard pages are where the choice actually matters.

Going deeper — the cost math that justifies tiers

The tiered design isn't just tidy engineering; it's the only way the budget survives. Suppose a bank has 1,000,000 pages and 8% of them are genuinely hard (scans, dense tables, odd layouts). Run everything through a vision parser at $0.02/page and you pay ~$20,000 per full backfill — repeated every time you re-ingest. Run the cheap text extractor first (effectively free) and escalate only the hard 8%, and the vision bill falls to ~$1,600. Same accuracy on the pages that matter, a tenth of the cost. The quality gate's threshold is the dial that sets that ratio: too loose and hard pages slip through as empty; too tight and you escalate clean pages you didn't need to. Tune it against your torture set, not a guess.

A quick 2026 map of the families: PyMuPDF / pdfium for fast local text; Docling (IBM, open-source, runs on-prem — handy for compliance-sensitive banks) and Unstructured for layout and reading order; pdfplumber / Camelot for tables; and the hosted vision-first tier — LlamaParse, Reducto, Azure AI Document Intelligence — for the hardest pages. None wins everywhere; independent tests keep showing different leaders per document type, which is exactly why you benchmark on your documents.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Tier 1 is milliseconds and ~free; the vision tier is seconds and cents per page. Your p95 latency and your monthly bill are both dominated by the escalation rate, so that single number is the one to watch and tune.

Scale & failure modes. A hosted vision parser is an external dependency: it has rate limits, outages and timeouts. Wrap it with retries, a circuit breaker, and a queue so a slow vendor stalls only the hard pages, not the whole corpus. Keep a local fallback so ingestion never fully stops.

Monitoring. Track escalation rate, per-tier latency and error rate, per-tier cost, and gold-set accuracy by tier. An escalation rate creeping from 8% to 30% is both a cost alarm and a signal that a source changed format.

Security & compliance (a bank). Hosted parsers mean documents leave your walls — confirm data-residency, encryption and no-training terms before sending PII-laden pages, or keep sensitive classes on an on-prem parser (Docling, PyMuPDF, Tesseract). Record the parser name and version per document so every answer is reproducible and auditable.

⚠ Watch out

Record which parser (and which version) read each document in your manifest. When you upgrade a parser, its output can shift, which quietly changes your chunks and embeddings. Treat a parser change as a re-ingestion event, not a silent swap.

✅ When to use / when not

Use the cheap text tier as the default for the whole corpus; escalate only pages that fail the quality gate; reserve the hosted vision tier for your genuinely hard minority. Don't standardise on a single parser "to keep it simple" — one family is always wrong for some of your documents. And don't send sensitive documents to a hosted parser without clearing the data-handling terms first.

🧠 Remember it

Cheap first, escalate on failure, test on the torture set. That one sentence is a production parsing strategy.

Parsing JSON & JSONL — it's already structured, so don't crush it

JSON arrives with its meaning already labelled; flatten it to a blob and you throw that gift away.

JSON (and JSONL, which is just one JSON object per line) is the format of APIs and exports. Unlike a PDF, it comes pre-organised: keys name their values, and nesting shows what belongs to what. The rookie move is to stringify the whole thing and chunk it by character count. That shreds the structure — customer.accounts[0].balance becomes a puddle of braces.

The right way

  • Keep the key path as context. "Account[0] balance: $4,210" is far more useful than a bare "4210."
  • Chunk on object boundaries, not byte counts. One record = one chunk. Never split mid-object, or you get invalid, meaningless fragments.
  • For big arrays (a list of 10,000 transactions), chunk per record or in windows, so unrelated records don't blend into one vague vector.
  • Often, don't vector-index it at all. If a question is "what's this customer's balance?", that's an exact lookup by ID, not a fuzzy similarity search. Keep the raw JSON for exact lookup and citation; embed a readable rendering only for fuzzy questions.
import json                                        # stdlib JSON parser; no extra install needed

record = {                                         # one customer record as it might arrive from an API
    "customer": "Priya Sharma",
    "accounts": [{"type": "current", "balance": 4210.50, "currency": "USD"}],
}

def render(obj, prefix=""):                         # walk the JSON and emit "path: value" lines
    lines = []                                      # collect human- and search-friendly lines
    if isinstance(obj, dict):                       # dict → recurse into each key, extending the path
        for k, v in obj.items():
            lines += render(v, f"{prefix}{k}.")     # keep the key path so context survives
    elif isinstance(obj, list):                     # list → index each item so records stay separate
        for i, v in enumerate(obj):
            lines += render(v, f"{prefix}{i}.")
    else:                                           # a leaf value → emit the full path and the value
        lines.append(f"{prefix.rstrip('.')}: {obj}")
    return lines

print("\n".join(render(record)))                   # a flat-but-labelled view, ready to embed
▶ Output

customer: Priya Sharma
accounts.0.type: current
accounts.0.balance: 4210.5
accounts.0.currency: USD

Every value still carries its path, so an embedding of "accounts.0.balance: 4210.5" means something, while a raw "4210.5" would not.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist ingests a nightly JSONL export of the product catalogue — one product object per line, 1,400 lines. A naive loader concatenates the file and chunks it every 1,000 characters, slicing straight through the middle of a product object so "overdraft" and its fee land in different chunks. A customer asks about overdraft fees and gets a fragment that mentions overdrafts but not the number. The fix is boring and total: one line = one object = one chunk, each rendered as labelled "path: value" text. Now every product answers on its own.

Going deeper — flatten, summarise, or keep raw?

The "path: value" rendering is the workhorse, but deeply nested or array-heavy JSON needs judgement. Three patterns cover almost everything. Flatten shallow records into labelled lines (shown above) — great for a product or a customer profile. Summarise when a record is large and mostly numeric: emit one natural-language sentence ("Current account, USD, balance snapshot, opened 2019") for the embedding and keep the raw JSON as the citation payload, so discovery is semantic but the exact data is still exact. Keep raw and don't embed when the questions are lookups by key, not fuzzy searches — more on that below. A subtle trap in all three: JSON values are typed (numbers, booleans, null), and stringifying them loses that; keep the raw typed object alongside the text so a downstream query can still do real comparisons (balance > 1000) that a string can't.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. JSON parsing is trivially fast; the cost comes from over-embedding. A 10,000-transaction export turned into 10,000 vectors is 10,000 embedding calls and 10,000 index rows that mostly answer nothing. Decide per field whether it's worth embedding at all — most volatile numeric fields are not.

Scale & failure modes. Stream large files with a line-by-line (JSONL) or incremental parser — loading a multi-gigabyte export fully into memory will OOM a worker. Guard against malformed lines (skip and log, don't crash the batch), schema drift (a key renamed upstream silently breaks your path logic), and mixed types in the same field.

Monitoring. Track records parsed vs. records skipped (malformed), unexpected new keys per source (schema-drift alarm), and the ratio of records you embed vs. keep raw. A spike in skipped records means an upstream export changed shape.

Security & compliance (a bank). API exports are PII-dense (names, account numbers, balances). Redact or tokenise sensitive fields before they reach the vector index, carry the record's access scope into metadata, and never embed a volatile balance — a stale number quoted as current is a reportable error.

⚠ Watch out

Account balances change by the minute. Embedding today's balance bakes a stale number into your index that will be confidently wrong next week. For anything volatile, prefer a live lookup — query the system of record at the moment of the question — over an embedded snapshot.

✅ When to use / when not

Use the "keep the labels, split on records" rendering for slow-changing, descriptive JSON (product catalogues, config, data dictionaries) worth a semantic search. Don't vector-index JSON when the real question is an exact lookup by id or an aggregation — keep it raw for direct query — and never embed volatile fields like balances or live rates.

🧠 Remember it

JSON is pre-labelled — keep the labels, split on records, never mid-object.

Parsing CSV, TSV, Excel & spreadsheets — relational data in disguise

A spreadsheet is a little database wearing a document costume; treat it like data, not prose.

CSV and TSV are plain tables (comma- or tab-separated). Excel adds multiple sheets, merged cells, formulas and charts. They all share one truth: each row is a record, and the header row names the fields. So the parsing recipe mirrors the PDF-table rule — row as chunk, with the column headers repeated into every row so each record stands alone.

Excel's extra traps

  • Multiple sheets — carry the sheet name as metadata ("Q3 Fees" vs "Q4 Fees"); the same row means different things on different sheets.
  • Merged cells — a value merged across rows must be copied down to each row, or the alignment breaks silently.
  • Formulas — store the computed value (=SUM(B2:B10) → 13400), not the formula string. Read the file in "data only" mode.
  • Number & date formats — locale bites: "1.000,50" (European) vs "1,000.50" mean the same amount; Excel also stores dates as integers. Normalise early, or you corrupt every figure.
from openpyxl import load_workbook                 # openpyxl reads modern .xlsx files

wb = load_workbook("fee_income.xlsx", data_only=True)  # data_only=True → get formula RESULTS, not "=SUM(...)"
ws = wb["Q3 Fees"]                                 # pick the sheet; its name is meaningful metadata

rows = list(ws.iter_rows(values_only=True))        # each row as a tuple of cell values
header = rows[0]                                    # first row holds the column names
for r in rows[1:]:                                 # iterate the data rows
    record = " | ".join(f"{h}: {v}" for h, v in zip(header, r))  # marry each value to its header
    print(f"[sheet=Q3 Fees] {record}")             # prepend sheet name so the record is fully self-contained
▶ Output

[sheet=Q3 Fees] Product: Overdraft | Fees $: 13400 | Txns: 512
[sheet=Q3 Fees] Product: Wire transfer | Fees $: 8900 | Txns: 140

When to NOT use vector search at all

Here's the advanced bit that saves teams months. Vector search cannot do arithmetic. If a manager asks "What was total fee income in Q3?", no amount of similarity search will add up the rows — it'll just fetch a few that look relevant. For aggregate and numeric questions, route the query to a query engine instead: generate SQL (Text-to-SQL) or a pandas operation over the structured table and compute the real answer. Reserve RAG for "what does this column mean?" questions over the data dictionary.

Route to RAG

"What does the 'NSF fee' column mean?" — a definition question. Fuzzy match over the data dictionary wins.

Route to a query engine

"Total Q3 fee income? Which product earned most?" — aggregation. Text-to-SQL / pandas computes it exactly; vector search cannot.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Reading spreadsheets is cheap, but a large .xlsx with formulas forces a choice: data_only=True returns cached results instantly but is blank if the file was never opened in Excel to compute them; recomputing formulas yourself is slower and needs a calc engine. Decide per source and document it.

Scale & failure modes. The silent killers are locale (European "1.000,50" vs. "1,000.50"), Excel's date-as-integer storage, merged cells that leave blanks on every row but the first, and multi-row headers that shift every value one column over. None throw — they just corrupt numbers. Normalise locale and dates on ingest, forward-fill merged cells, and flatten multi-row headers before mapping.

Monitoring. Validate on read: row-count per sheet, numeric-parse failures, and reconciliation checks (do the row subtotals equal the stated total?). Alarm when a sheet's column count or header text changes between runs — that's a layout change that will misalign everything.

Security & compliance (a bank). Finance spreadsheets carry customer and account data; apply the same redaction and ACL metadata as any source. Because a misread figure here can flow into a regulatory number, keep the original cell reference (sheet!A1) as the citation so any quoted value is traceable back to the exact cell.

⚠ Watch out

Multi-row headers ("Fees" spanning two sub-columns) and merged cells are the top cause of silently misaligned spreadsheet data. If a parser reads one cell into the wrong column, every downstream number is wrong and nothing errors. Spot-check a few parsed rows against the original before trusting the lot.

✅ When to use / when not

Use the row-as-record, header-on-every-row rendering for descriptive, slow-changing tables (fee schedules, product grids, branch lists) and for "what does this column mean?" questions. Don't use vector search for aggregation or arithmetic ("total Q3 fee income") — route those to Text-to-SQL or pandas over the structured table — and don't embed spreadsheets of volatile, fast-changing numbers.

🧠 Remember it

Spreadsheets: row = record, header on every row, values not formulas — and send the "add it up" questions to SQL, not search.

Parsing Word & PowerPoint — the structure is the gift

Office documents hand you headings, lists and speaker notes for free; keep that structure as chunk boundaries and metadata.

Policy manuals live in Word (.docx); training and product decks live in PowerPoint (.pptx). Unlike a PDF, these formats still know their own structure — this paragraph is "Heading 2," that block is a bulleted list, this slide has speaker notes. That's a gift. Use the heading hierarchy as natural chunk boundaries, and store the heading path as metadata so retrieval can filter and cite precisely.

Word (.docx)

  • Walk paragraphs in order; when you hit a Heading style, start a new section and remember the path ("Credit Policy > 4 Collateral > 4.2 Valuation").
  • Extract embedded tables through the table rules (header-per-row), not as loose text.
  • Decide deliberately about tracked changes and comments: are redlines signal (the live policy) or noise (old suggestions)? Accept or drop them on purpose.

PowerPoint (.pptx)

  • One slide is a sensible chunk. Pull the slide's text boxes and the speaker notes — the notes often hold the real explanation the bullets only hint at.
  • Grab embedded tables and images; a diagram-of-text with no caption is otherwise lost.
from docx import Document                           # python-docx reads .docx files

doc = Document("credit_policy.docx")               # load the policy manual
section_path, chunks = [], []                       # track current heading path + collected chunks

for p in doc.paragraphs:                            # paragraphs come in reading order
    style = p.style.name                            # style tells us if this is a heading
    if style.startswith("Heading"):                 # a heading starts a new, labelled section
        level = int(style.split()[-1])              # "Heading 2" → level 2
        section_path = section_path[: level - 1]     # trim deeper levels when we step back up
        section_path.append(p.text)                  # push this heading onto the path
    elif p.text.strip():                            # a non-empty body paragraph
        chunks.append({                             # store text WITH its heading breadcrumb
            "text": p.text,
            "section_path": " > ".join(section_path), # e.g. "Credit Policy > 4 Collateral > 4.2 Valuation"
        })

print(chunks[0]["section_path"])                    # confirm the breadcrumb was captured
▶ Output

Credit Policy > 4 Collateral > 4.2 Valuation

🏦 Picture this

A loan officer asks BankAssist, "How do we value collateral?" Because the parser kept the heading path, the assistant doesn't just return a floating paragraph — it answers and adds "from Credit Policy, section 4.2 Valuation." The officer trusts it because it can be checked. That breadcrumb came straight from the .docx heading styles the parser bothered to keep.

PowerPoint hides its best content in the speaker notes — the bullets say "Early repayment," the notes say what it actually costs. Here's how to pull slide text and notes together with python-pptx:

from pptx import Presentation                        # python-pptx reads .pptx decks

deck = Presentation("mortgage_training.pptx")       # load the training deck
for i, slide in enumerate(deck.slides, start=1):    # one slide is a sensible chunk; keep its number
    body = [sh.text for sh in slide.shapes if sh.has_text_frame]  # every text box on the slide
    notes = ""                                      # default: no notes
    if slide.has_notes_slide:                        # guard — not every slide has notes
        notes = slide.notes_slide.notes_text_frame.text  # the hidden explanation presenters read aloud
    chunk = {                                        # one self-contained chunk per slide
        "slide": i,                                 # citation: "slide 7"
        "text": "\n".join(body),                    # the visible bullets
        "notes": notes,                             # KEEP notes — often the real content
    }
    print(f"slide {i}: {len(chunk['notes'])} chars of notes")  # confirm notes were captured
▶ Output

slide 1: 0 chars of notes
slide 7: 240 chars of notes

Slide 7's 240 characters of notes are exactly the kind of explanation that never makes it onto a bullet — drop them and the deck looks ingested but its substance is gone.

Going deeper — tracked changes, comments and the "which version is true?" problem

Office files carry history that a plain text dump quietly flattens. In Word, tracked changes mean the file holds both the old and the proposed wording; python-docx by default reads the current text, but a document mid-review can mix accepted and pending edits, so you must decide on purpose whether redlines are the live policy or stale suggestions. Comments ("legal to confirm this clause") are reviewer chatter, not policy — usually drop them, but keep them if the use case is reviewing the review. And every Office file has core properties (author, last-modified, title) worth capturing as metadata for freshness and provenance. The guiding rule: these formats know their own structure, so your job is to preserve it as boundaries and metadata, not to melt it into one blob.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Office parsing is local and cheap. The cost risk is index bloat: a 300-slide deck with the same footer and logo on every slide becomes 300 near-identical chunks unless you de-dupe the template boilerplate first.

Scale & failure modes. Floating text boxes parse out of reading order; images-of-text (a screenshot of a table) vanish unless you OCR them; embedded objects (an Excel sheet inside a slide) need routing to the right parser. Very large decks and manuals should be streamed, and corrupt or password-protected files handled gracefully, not fatally.

Monitoring. Track chunks per document (a deck producing 1 chunk means parsing failed; 300 identical ones means boilerplate leaked), notes-captured rate for decks, and the share of slides that are image-only (candidates for OCR/captioning).

Security & compliance (a bank). Word and PowerPoint files hide data in comments, tracked changes, hidden slides and document metadata — a reviewer's note may name a customer. Scrub or deliberately handle those before indexing, carry the ACL and version into metadata, and keep the heading/slide path as the citation so every answer is checkable.

⚠ Watch out

Floating text boxes in Word and PowerPoint can parse out of reading order, and images-of-text with no alt text vanish entirely. Also beware template boilerplate — the same footer on every one of 300 slides will flood your index with identical, meaningless chunks.

✅ When to use / when not

Use the heading path (Word) and per-slide-plus-notes (PowerPoint) as natural chunk boundaries whenever you ingest native Office files — the structure is handed to you free. Don't convert a .docx to PDF first and parse that (you throw the structure away and inherit PDF's layout problems), and don't blindly index comments and tracked changes as if they were the live policy.

🧠 Remember it

Headings are free chunk boundaries; speaker notes are the hidden explanation. Keep both.

Parsing HTML & web pages — strip the chrome, keep the content

A web page is mostly menus, banners and ads; your job is to rescue the article hiding inside.

Bank help-centres, FAQs and product pages are HTML. The trouble is that a typical page is maybe 20% real content and 80% chrome — navigation bars, cookie banners, "related articles," footers, ads. If you embed the whole page, every chunk is dominated by the same menu text, and your search quality collapses because everything looks alike.

The recipe

  • Main-content extraction. Use a "readability"-style tool that finds the article body and discards the chrome. Internally it scores each block of the page by how much real sentence text it holds versus links and menu markup, then keeps the text-dense block and drops the rest. Libraries like trafilatura do this well.
  • Map the structure. Headings (<h1>…<h6>), lists (<li>) and tables carry meaning — preserve them, don't flatten to one blob.
  • Keep link targets and the canonical URL as metadata, plus the last-modified date for freshness and citation.
  • Watch for JavaScript-rendered pages. If the content only appears after scripts run, the raw HTML is empty; you need a headless browser (like Playwright) to render it first.
import trafilatura                                  # library specialised at pulling article text from web pages

html = trafilatura.fetch_url("https://bank.example/help/overdraft-fees")  # download the raw page
content = trafilatura.extract(                      # extract ONLY the main content, dropping nav/ads
    html,
    include_tables=True,                            # keep fee tables — they're the whole point of the page
    include_links=False,                            # drop link clutter from the body text
    with_metadata=True,                             # also return title, date, URL for citation + freshness
)
print(content[:70])                                 # confirm we got the article, not the menu bar
▶ Output

Overdraft fees | An arranged overdraft costs $0; unarranged is $5/day

One call did the heavy lifting: trafilatura.extract found the article and left the navigation behind, while with_metadata=True kept the URL and date so answers stay citable and fresh.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist crawls the public help-centre. Every one of 600 pages shares the same left-hand menu — "Accounts · Cards · Loans · Contact us" — and the same cookie banner. Ingest the raw HTML and every chunk is 80% that menu, so when a customer asks about overdraft fees, retrieval returns five pages that all look equally relevant because they all contain the same navigation soup. After switching to main-content extraction, each chunk is just its article, the overdraft page stands out, and the right answer rises to the top. The menu was never knowledge — it was camouflage.

Going deeper — rendered pages, sitemaps and freshness

Three realities separate a toy scraper from a production one. First, JavaScript rendering: many modern bank pages ship almost-empty HTML and build the content in the browser, so a plain fetch returns a shell. For those you need a headless browser (Playwright, Puppeteer) to run the scripts first, then extract — slower and heavier, so detect the empty-shell case and only render when needed. Second, discovery: don't guess URLs — read the site's sitemap.xml and robots.txt to find pages and respect what you're allowed to crawl. Third, freshness and identity: keep the canonical URL, the last-modified header, and an ETag so incremental sync re-fetches only changed pages, and so citations point at a stable address rather than a tracking-parametered one.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. A static fetch plus readability extraction is milliseconds and ~free. Headless-browser rendering is seconds per page and memory-hungry, so it's the cost driver — gate it behind an empty-content check so 90% of pages stay on the fast path.

Scale & failure modes. Crawlers break on redirects, soft-404s (a "not found" page served with status 200), infinite calendar/pagination loops, locale duplicates, and rate limits. Respect robots.txt, throttle politely, cap crawl depth, and de-dupe on content hash or canonical URL so twenty copies of one page don't flood the index.

Monitoring. Track pages fetched vs. rendered, extraction-empty rate (a site redesign can break your readability selectors overnight), duplicate rate, and HTTP error mix. A jump in empty extractions means the page structure changed under you.

Security & compliance (a bank). Only crawl the public site, or authenticated internal pages with explicit permission and credentials in a secrets manager — never scrape a customer-authenticated portal. Strip tracking parameters and any session tokens from stored URLs, and keep the canonical URL + fetch date in the citation so answers are provably sourced.

⚠ Watch out

Bank help-centres often publish the same page in many locales and near-duplicate variants. Without de-duplication, your index fills with twenty copies of the overdraft page, and retrieval wastes slots returning the same thing. De-dupe on content hash or canonical URL.

✅ When to use / when not

Use readability-style main-content extraction (trafilatura) for help-centres, FAQs and product pages, keeping headings, tables and the canonical URL. Add a headless browser only for pages that render content via JavaScript. Don't embed whole raw pages (the chrome drowns the signal), and don't crawl pages you don't have permission to, or behind a customer login.

🧠 Remember it

HTML is a sandwich: eat the filling, bin the wrapper. Keep the article and its URL; drop the menus.

Parsing XML — exploit the schema, and never trust it blindly (XXE)

Banking XML is schema-driven gold — and a classic security trap if you parse it with the wrong tool.

XML is everywhere in banking plumbing, and unlike a free-form PDF it's schema-driven: standards like ISO 20022 (payment messages — pain, pacs, camt), FpML (derivatives) and FIXML (trading) define exactly which elements mean what. That's a gift — parse by the schema, map each element to a named field, and keep the namespace and schema version as metadata.

Because it's structured, treat XML much like JSON: map elements to fields, validate against the schema (XSD) on ingest, and embed a readable rendering for semantic search while keeping the typed data for exact use.

The security trap: XXE

Here's the part that catches people. XML has a feature called external entities — a document can say "go fetch this file or URL and paste it here." A malicious XML file can abuse that to read /etc/passwd, reach internal servers, or hang your pipeline. This attack is called XXE (XML External Entity). You defeat it simply: use a hardened parser that disables entity resolution. The defusedxml library is the standard, drop-in safe choice.

from defusedxml.ElementTree import fromstring       # defusedxml: same API as stdlib but XXE-safe by default

xml = """<Document xmlns="urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:camt.053.001.08">
  <Stmt><Acct><Id><IBAN>GB29NWBK60161331926819</IBAN></Id></Acct></Stmt>
</Document>"""                                      # a snippet of an ISO 20022 bank statement message

root = fromstring(xml)                              # parse safely — external entities are refused, not fetched
ns = {"c": "urn:iso:std:iso:20022:tech:xsd:camt.053.001.08"}  # namespaces must be declared to query elements
iban = root.find(".//c:IBAN", ns).text             # pull the IBAN by its schema path, not by guessing
print(f"camt.053 statement for IBAN {iban}")        # render a readable line; schema version kept as metadata
▶ Output

camt.053 statement for IBAN GB29NWBK60161331926819

Two lessons sit in this snippet. First, the namespace dictionary ns — without it, find can't locate elements, because ISO 20022 tags are namespaced. Second, and more important, importing from defusedxml instead of the standard library is the entire XXE defence: same code, safe by construction.

🏦 Picture this

A partner bank sends BankAssist a daily camt.053 statement feed as XML. Because the pipeline parses by the ISO 20022 schema, each <Ntry> becomes a labelled transaction — amount, currency, booking date, counterparty — and the namespace version rides along as metadata, so a later camt.053.001.09 upgrade doesn't silently misread the old files. One day a crafted file arrives with an external-entity trick pointing at an internal config server. Because the parser is defusedxml, the entity is refused, not fetched — the attack is a non-event. Had the pipeline used the stdlib parser, that one file could have exfiltrated internal data. Same XML, two very different outcomes.

Going deeper — validate, don't just read; and watch the billion-laughs bomb

Structure is only a promise until you check it. On ingest, validate against the XSD so a malformed or mislabelled message is rejected loudly instead of indexed as half-truth — in payments a missing mandatory field is a processing failure, not a cosmetic one. Beyond XXE, hardened parsers also block the "billion laughs" attack, where nested entity expansions blow up a tiny file into gigabytes of memory and crash your worker; defusedxml caps that too. For very large XML (a multi-gigabyte end-of-day feed), use streaming / iterative parsing (iterparse) and clear each element after processing, rather than building the whole tree in memory. And keep the typed values: an amount is a decimal with a currency, not a string — preserve that so downstream reconciliation can actually compare numbers.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. XML parsing is CPU-cheap, but validation and tree-building scale with document size. For big feeds, stream with iterparse to keep memory flat; a full-DOM parse of a multi-gigabyte file will OOM the worker.

Scale & failure modes. Namespace drift (a new schema version), optional elements that are sometimes absent, and malformed partner files are the routine failures. Validate against the XSD, default missing optionals safely, and dead-letter files that fail validation rather than indexing garbage. The security failures — XXE and entity-expansion bombs — are defeated by using defusedxml everywhere, not just where you remembered.

Monitoring. Track schema-validation pass rate, unknown-namespace occurrences, rejected-file count, and parse memory/time per file. A rise in validation failures means a partner changed their format.

Security & compliance (a bank). ISO 20022 / FpML / FIXML messages are the bank's most sensitive data — payments and trades. Parse untrusted XML only with a hardened parser inside the trust boundary, log provenance (sender, message id, schema version) for audit and non-repudiation, and carry access scope into metadata so a payments message isn't retrievable by the wrong team.

⚠ Watch out

Never feed untrusted XML to Python's default xml.etree.ElementTree or lxml without hardening — both will resolve external entities. For any XML that arrived from outside your trust boundary (a partner bank, a customer upload), defusedxml is not optional.

✅ When to use / when not

Use schema-driven mapping (parse by XSD, keep namespace + version as metadata) for standards-based banking XML, and embed a readable rendering while keeping the typed data for exact use. Always parse with defusedxml. Don't stringify-and-chunk XML by character count (you shred the schema), and don't vector-index payment/trade messages when the real need is exact field lookup or reconciliation.

🧠 Remember it

Use the schema, fear the entity. Map by XSD; parse with defusedxml so a document can't read your filesystem.

Parsing email — .eml, .msg, and the nightmare of quoted threads

An email thread is a Russian doll of quoted replies, signatures and attachments; naive parsing indexes the same text a dozen times.

Complaints and disputes arrive as email — .eml (standard format) or .msg (Outlook's format). Email is deceptively messy because a single "message" is really a thread of nested, quoted replies, each carrying the full text of the ones before it, plus signatures, legal disclaimers, and attachments. If you index each reply whole, the original complaint text gets embedded ten times over — massive redundancy that drowns your index and skews retrieval.

The recipe

  • Split the thread into individual messages; strip the quoted history so each message appears once.
  • Strip signatures and disclaimers — the "This email is confidential…" block is not knowledge.
  • Parse the headers (from, to, date, subject) into metadata; keep the message-ID lineage for audit.
  • Recurse into attachments — a PDF statement attached to a dispute goes through the PDF parser; a spreadsheet through the spreadsheet parser.
  • Redact PII early — dispute emails are dense with names, card numbers and addresses.
from email import policy                            # modern email API with sensible Unicode handling
from email.parser import BytesParser                # parses raw .eml bytes into a message object

with open("dispute_thread.eml", "rb") as f:        # emails are bytes; open in binary mode
    msg = BytesParser(policy=policy.default).parse(f)  # policy.default decodes headers & charsets for us

meta = {                                            # headers become clean metadata
    "from": msg["from"], "to": msg["to"],
    "subject": msg["subject"], "date": msg["date"],  # date supports freshness & sorting the thread
}
body = msg.get_body(preferencelist=("plain",))     # prefer plain text over the HTML alternative part
text = body.get_content() if body else ""          # guard against a message with no readable body

for att in msg.iter_attachments():                 # walk attachments to send through their own parsers
    print("attachment:", att.get_filename())       # e.g. the disputed statement PDF

print(meta["subject"])                             # confirm headers parsed
▶ Output

attachment: statement_oct.pdf
Re: Unrecognised $35 charge

For Outlook's .msg files the standard library won't help; use the extract-msg library, which exposes the same pieces (sender, subject, body, attachments). After parsing, the crucial clean-up step is stripping the quoted "On Tuesday, X wrote:" history so each message is stored once, not re-embedded in every reply.

🏦 Picture this

A customer disputes a $35 charge over a five-email back-and-forth with support. The final reply quotes the entire thread beneath it, so the original "I don't recognise this charge" sentence physically appears in all five messages. Index each message whole and that one complaint gets embedded five times — it now dominates retrieval, crowding out the agent's actual resolution. After splitting the thread and stripping quoted history, each message is stored once: the complaint appears once, the resolution appears once, and a later query "how was the $35 dispute resolved?" surfaces the right message instead of five echoes of the question.

Going deeper — reconstructing the thread and the attachment tree

Email is a tree, not a list. The headers Message-ID, In-Reply-To and References let you rebuild the real reply structure even when subjects drift ("Re: Re: Fwd:"), which matters for audit: you want to prove the exact order of who said what. Stripping quoted history is the hard craft — clients mark quotes differently ("On Tue, X wrote:", leading ">", or an Outlook divider), so a robust de-quoter uses several heuristics and is tested on your real mail, not one sample. Attachments are their own tree: a dispute email may carry a PDF statement (route to the PDF parser), a spreadsheet of transactions (spreadsheet parser), even a nested .eml forwarded inside — recurse, and tag each extracted piece with the parent message id so the chunk knows which complaint it belongs to.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Parsing a message is cheap; the cost comes from attachments (each runs its own, sometimes expensive, parser) and from not de-duplicating quoted text, which multiplies embedding calls and index rows. Strip quotes before you embed and the bill and the noise both fall.

Scale & failure modes. Expect encoding chaos (quoted-printable, base64, exotic charsets — policy.default handles most), huge or malicious attachments (cap sizes, scan for malware, sandbox extraction), .msg vs .eml differences (extract-msg for Outlook), and broken threading. Dead-letter the files you can't parse; never let one malformed mailbox halt the batch.

Monitoring. Track messages per thread after de-quoting (should be far fewer chunks than raw replies), attachment-extraction success rate, de-dupe ratio, and PII-redaction coverage. A low de-dupe ratio means quoted history is leaking into the index.

Security & compliance (a bank). Dispute and complaint mail is saturated with PII — names, card numbers (PAN), addresses. Redact or tokenise before indexing (PCI-DSS forbids storing full card numbers), keep sender/recipient and message-id lineage for audit and legal hold, and carry access scope so complaint threads aren't retrievable by unrelated teams.

⚠ Watch out

Emails ship a plain-text and an HTML version of the same body. Index both and you double-count every message. Pick one (plain text is cleaner) and ignore the other.

✅ When to use / when not

Use thread-splitting, quote-stripping and attachment recursion whenever email is a knowledge source (complaints, disputes, support history). Don't index raw whole messages (you bury the signal under quoted echoes), and don't embed email bodies before redacting PII — a card number in a vector index is a reportable breach.

🧠 Remember it

One thread, many echoes. Split into messages, strip the quotes and signatures, chase the attachments, index each line once.

Databases & APIs — rows into text, or questions into SQL

Live systems-of-record are a retrieval source too, but they change by the second — snapshotting them into a vector index is a recipe for confidently stale answers.

The richest knowledge in a bank isn't in documents at all — it's in the core-banking database and internal APIs: balances, transactions, card statuses, today's rates. There are two honest ways to bring this into an AI assistant, and choosing between them is one of the most consequential design calls you'll make.

Path A — rows into text (ingest the stable parts)

For data that changes slowly — product catalogues, branch lists, fee schedules — you can render each row into a self-contained sentence, embed it, and index it like any document. Same rule as spreadsheets: carry the column names and a stable row ID.

from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text         # SQLAlchemy: a safe, standard way to query SQL databases

engine = create_engine("postgresql://ro_user@corebank/products")  # read-only user — least privilege for ingestion
with engine.connect() as conn:                     # context manager returns the connection to the pool
    rows = conn.execute(text(                       # text() parameterises SQL safely, no string-concat
        "SELECT product_id, name, monthly_fee FROM products"
    )).mappings()                                   # .mappings() gives dict-like rows keyed by column
    for r in rows:                                 # render each row into a labelled sentence
        line = f"Product {r['name']} (id {r['product_id']}): monthly fee ${r['monthly_fee']}"
        print(line)                                 # this sentence is what gets embedded + indexed
▶ Output

Product Everyday Current (id C1): monthly fee $0
Product Premier Current (id C7): monthly fee $12

Path B — questions into SQL (query the volatile parts live)

For data that changes fast — a balance, a pending transaction, a live rate — never embed it. A balance embedded last Tuesday will be quoted as fact next month, and a wrong balance is a serious incident. Instead, let the assistant call the live system at the moment of the question: translate the user's words into a parameterised query or API call (Text-to-SQL or a tool call), run it against the system-of-record, and use the fresh result.

Embed it (Path A)

Slow-changing knowledge: product terms, fee schedules, policy, branch hours. Safe to snapshot into the index.

Query it live (Path B)

Fast-changing facts: balances, transactions, today's rate, card status. Always a live lookup — never a stale embedding.

🏦 Picture this

A customer asks, "What's my balance, and what's the monthly fee on my account?" BankAssist splits the job: the fee comes from the indexed product row (slow-changing, Path A); the balance comes from a live call to core banking at that instant (fast-changing, Path B). The customer gets one smooth answer — but behind the scenes, each fact came from the source that keeps it honest.

Going deeper — Text-to-SQL safely, and keeping Path A fresh

Path B's "turn words into a query" is powerful and dangerous. A model that writes raw SQL against your core banking tables can, if tricked, write DELETE or read another customer's rows. The safe pattern is to never let the model touch arbitrary SQL: expose a small set of parameterised, read-only queries (or one tool per allowed question — "get_balance(account_id)"), run them as a least-privilege read-only user, and enforce row-level security tied to the authenticated customer at the database, below the model. The model chooses which safe query and supplies parameters; it never composes free-form SQL. Meanwhile Path A has its own quiet duty: "slow-changing" is not "never-changing," so re-ingest product and fee tables on a schedule and delete the old chunks, or your "stable" fee schedule becomes last year's fee schedule.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Path A is a one-time embed then cheap retrieval. Path B adds a live round-trip at question time — database or API latency lands directly in the user's wait, so cache briefly where safe, set tight timeouts, and have a graceful fallback message when the system-of-record is slow.

Scale & failure modes. Live queries can overload the core banking DB under traffic — always hit a read replica, never production OLTP, and rate-limit. The headline failure mode is still stale embeddings of volatile data (a balance quoted months late). Guard Path A with scheduled re-ingestion and delete-then-reindex; guard Path B with timeouts, circuit breakers and a read replica.

Monitoring. Track live-query p95 latency and error/timeout rate, replica lag, cache hit rate, and — for Path A — the age of the newest ingested row per table (an alarm when a "slow" source hasn't refreshed in too long).

Security & compliance (a bank). This is the highest-risk source: enforce row-level security at the database tied to the authenticated customer, use a read-only least-privilege account, never let the model emit free-form SQL, log every live query for audit, and keep all of it inside the trust boundary. Filtering results in the prompt is not access control.

⚠ Watch out

Two production killers here. First, stale embeddings of volatile data — the single most common way a RAG system gives a confidently wrong number. Second, access control: enforce row-level security at the database or API, tied to the actual customer's identity, so one customer can never retrieve another's rows. Filtering in the prompt is not security.

✅ When to use / when not

Use Path A (embed it) for slow-changing, descriptive data worth a semantic search — product terms, fee schedules, branch hours. Use Path B (query live) for anything fast-changing or customer-specific — balances, transactions, today's rate, card status. Don't embed volatile facts (ever), and don't route "add it up" or exact-lookup questions through vector search when a parameterised query answers them precisely.

🧠 Remember it

Slow facts you store; fast facts you fetch. Embed the fee schedule, call live for the balance.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Knowledge Layer (RAG) — Chunking

Before a bank's documents can answer questions, they have to be cut into pieces of the right size. This chapter is the whole story of that cut — why we make it, how to size it, and the clever ways to make it smarter.

Why we cut documents into pieces at all

You can't hand a machine a 300-page policy manual and ask "what's my overdraft fee?" — it needs small, findable pieces.

Let's meet our bank for the whole chapter. BankAssist is a helpful assistant that answers customer questions using the bank's own documents: the account agreement, the fees schedule, the loan policy manual, the card dispute guide. These documents are long. The overdraft rules alone might be buried on page 47 of a 300-page PDF.

Now, how does an assistant "find" an answer inside all that text? It doesn't read the whole thing every time. Instead, before any customer ever asks a question, BankAssist does a one-time preparation step: it breaks every document into small pieces, turns each piece into a special number-list called an embedding (a row of numbers that captures the meaning of the text, so pieces about similar topics end up with similar numbers), and stores them. Later, when a customer asks something, BankAssist turns the question into numbers too, and grabs the handful of pieces whose numbers are closest. Those pieces are then shown to the language model to write the answer.

That act of breaking a document into pieces is called chunking, and each piece is a chunk. It sounds boring. It is secretly one of the most important decisions in the whole system.

Why not just keep whole documents?

Three hard walls force us to chunk. Each one is worth understanding, because they explain every tuning choice in this chapter.

  • Embedding limits. The model that turns text into those meaning-numbers can only read so much at once (its input limit). Feed it a whole 300-page manual and it either refuses or silently truncates. And even when it accepts a lot of text, squeezing a huge document into one fixed row of numbers blurs everything together — the overdraft rule, the wire-transfer rule, and the ATM rule all average into one muddy vector that matches nothing well.
  • Retrieval precision. We want to hand the language model just the overdraft paragraph, not the entire manual. Small, focused chunks let the search point at exactly the right spot. A whole-document match tells you "the answer is somewhere in these 300 pages" — useless.
  • Context budget. The language model that writes the final answer also has a limited input (its context window) and you pay per word you put in it. You can only afford to show it a few chunks. So each chunk must be small enough that several fit, yet complete enough to actually contain an answer.
🏦 Picture this

A customer asks BankAssist, "What's the fee if I overdraw my account?" If the fees schedule was stored as one giant chunk, the search returns the whole schedule — ATM fees, wire fees, statement fees, everything — and the model has to hunt through noise. If instead the schedule was chunked into one small piece per fee type, the search returns exactly the overdraft paragraph. Same document, wildly different answer quality. The only thing that changed was how we cut it.

💡 Key idea

Chunking is the act of cutting documents into small, searchable pieces. We do it because the meaning-model has an input limit, because small pieces are easier to pinpoint, and because the answer-model can only afford to read a few pieces. Get the cut wrong and no fancy trick downstream can save you.

Going deeper — the real numbers behind the three walls

Those three walls aren't vague. They have exact sizes, and knowing them turns "chunk small-ish" into real engineering. Take the embedding model BankAssist actually uses — OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small. It accepts at most 8,191 tokens of input per call (about 32,000 characters, or roughly 12 pages). Feed it more and the API rejects the request outright; you don't get a half-answer, you get an error. So a 300-page manual (around 150,000 tokens) can't be embedded whole no matter what — the wall is a hard number.

But hitting the limit isn't even the real problem; the real problem is the blur. Every chunk, whether it's 50 tokens or 8,000, is squeezed into the same fixed-length vector — for this model, 1,536 numbers. Think of that vector as a tiny summary with a fixed budget. A 100-token chunk about overdrafts gets all 1,536 numbers to describe one idea, so the summary is sharp. An 8,000-token chunk covering overdrafts, wires, and ATM fees has to describe all three with the same 1,536 numbers, so each idea gets a blurry third of the budget. That's why a question about overdrafts matches the small chunk strongly and the giant chunk weakly — even though both technically "contain" the answer.

The context-budget wall has numbers too. The answer model might have a 128,000-token window, but you would never spend it all on retrieved text — it's slow and you pay per token in and out. A sane BankAssist retrieval budget is maybe 4,000–6,000 tokens of chunks per question. At 500-token chunks that's 8–12 pieces; at 4,000-token chunks it's one, maybe two. Small chunks give the model several independent shots at the answer; huge chunks give it one bulky guess.

⚙️ In production

At BankAssist scale the chunk count is the bill. Say the bank has 50,000 documents averaging 20 pages (~10,000 tokens each) — half a billion tokens. At 500-token chunks that's about 1 million chunks to embed. One-time embedding cost on text-embedding-3-small (around $0.02 per million tokens) is only a few dollars for the raw text — cheap — but the vectors you must now store and search are the real cost: 1 million vectors × 1,536 dimensions × 4 bytes ≈ 6 GB of index that has to live in fast memory for low-latency search. Halve the chunk size and you double the vector count and roughly double that memory bill. Failure modes: documents re-ingested on every edit (re-embedding the same unchanged pages — fix with a content hash so only changed chunks re-embed); a scanned PDF that OCR'd to garbage, producing thousands of junk chunks nobody notices. Monitoring: track chunks-per-document and alert on outliers — a document that suddenly produced 10× its usual chunks is usually a parsing bug. Compliance: each chunk must carry its source document id and a retention tag, because when a customer exercises their deletion rights the bank must be able to find and purge every chunk derived from their data — an index with no back-pointer to the source is a regulatory liability.

⚠ Watch out

The seductive mistake is "the model has a huge context window now, so let me just use enormous chunks and skip the hard part." It backfires twice: the embedding blurs (retrieval gets worse, not better), and you blow your per-question token budget on one bulky piece instead of several sharp ones. A bigger window is not a licence to stop chunking carefully.

When to chunk vs. when not to: chunk any document longer than a few hundred tokens that will be searched — which is nearly all of a bank's policy, product, and help content. You can skip chunking only for genuinely tiny, self-contained records that already fit comfortably in one sharp vector (a single FAQ answer, a one-line product-rate row); splitting those just creates fragments with no benefit.

🧠 Remember it

A chunk is a bite. Too big and you choke; too small and you starve. The whole chapter is about the right bite size.

chunk_size and chunk_overlap — the two dials that matter most

Almost every splitter has the same two knobs: how big each piece is, and how much neighbouring pieces share.

chunk_size is how large each chunk is allowed to get — measured in characters or in tokens (a token is roughly a word-piece; "overdraft" might be one or two tokens). chunk_overlap is how much text the end of one chunk repeats at the start of the next. If chunk 1 ends with "…a fee of $35 is" and overlap is on, chunk 2 begins with "…a fee of $35 is charged per item." The overlap is a deliberate, repeated seam.

Why overlap exists: the split-sentence rescue

Here is the problem overlap solves. Imagine BankAssist's overdraft rule is this sentence:

"If your balance goes below zero, an overdraft fee of $35 is charged per transaction, up to a maximum of five fees per day."

Now suppose we chunk with no overlap and the cut lands right in the middle:

ChunkText it holds (no overlap)
Chunk A"If your balance goes below zero, an overdraft fee of $35 is charged per transaction,"
Chunk B"up to a maximum of five fees per day."

A customer asks: "How many overdraft fees can I be charged in one day?" The answer — "five per day" — lives in Chunk B. But Chunk B alone doesn't even mention "overdraft fee"; it just says "up to a maximum of five fees per day." Its embedding is weak and vague, so the search may never pick it. The sentence was cut at the knees.

Now turn on chunk_overlap. The start of Chunk B repeats the tail of Chunk A:

ChunkText it holds (with overlap)
Chunk A"If your balance goes below zero, an overdraft fee of $35 is charged per transaction,"
Chunk B"…an overdraft fee of $35 is charged per transaction, up to a maximum of five fees per day."

Now Chunk B is self-contained. It says "overdraft fee" and "five fees per day." Its embedding is strong, the search finds it, and the model answers correctly. That repeated seam is the whole point of overlap: it stops ideas from dying at the boundary.

How to choose the two numbers

Think about what kind of questions you get and what your embedding model likes.

  • Small chunks (say 200–300 tokens) are sharp and precise — great for short, factual questions ("what's the overdraft fee?"). But they may lack surrounding context, so an answer that needs a whole paragraph can slip through the cracks.
  • Large chunks (say 800–1000 tokens) carry more context and are better for "explain the whole process" questions — but they dilute the embedding (many topics averaged together) and eat your context budget fast.
  • Overlap is usually set to 10–20% of chunk_size. Too little and you get the split-sentence problem above. Too much and you bloat your index with repeated text — more storage, more cost, and the same sentence keeps showing up in multiple search hits.
⚙️ Under the hood

Overlap is not free. If your document is 10,000 tokens and you use 500-token chunks with 100-token overlap (20%), you don't get 20 chunks — you get about 25, because every chunk re-stores 100 tokens of its neighbour. That's roughly 25% more vectors to embed, store, and search. At three documents that's nothing. At three million documents, that 25% is a real line on the cloud bill. So overlap buys recall, and you pay for it in index size. Choose the smallest overlap that still rescues your split sentences.

Going deeper — the dials interact, and overlap fights duplication

The two dials aren't independent. Overlap is usually expressed as a fraction of chunk_size, so the same "20%" means very different things at different sizes: 20% of a 200-token chunk is 40 tokens (barely a sentence — often too little to rescue a split rule), while 20% of a 1,000-token chunk is 200 tokens (a whole paragraph repeated, which bloats the index). As you shrink chunks for precision, you often need to raise the overlap fraction to keep seams safe — small chunks have proportionally more seams to protect.

There's a second, subtler cost to overlap that the storage number hides: near-duplicate hits. Because neighbouring chunks share text, a single important sentence can live in two or three chunks at once. When BankAssist searches "overdraft fee cap," it may get back three chunks that are 70% the same text, crowding out other genuinely different chunks from the top-k (the handful of best-matching chunks the search hands back for a question). You spent your context budget on one idea repeated. The fix downstream is de-duplication (drop a retrieved chunk that overlaps heavily with one already chosen), but the cheaper fix is simply not over-setting overlap in the first place.

A concrete tuning table for BankAssist's text: for short factual policy Q&A, ~400 tokens with ~50-token overlap (12%); for narrative "walk me through…" procedures, ~800 tokens with ~120-token overlap (15%); for dense fee tables already cut by row, often zero overlap because each row is self-contained and overlap would just smear one rate into the next row's chunk.

⚙️ In production

Cost & scale: overlap is a multiplier on everything downstream — more chunks means more embedding calls at ingest, more vectors in memory, and more candidates the search must score at query time, so a careless 30% overlap quietly adds ~40% to your vector-store memory bill. Latency: overlap doesn't change per-query latency much (the index just has more entries), but a larger chunk_size does — bigger chunks mean more tokens shipped to the answer model per question, which is the dominant latency and cost term at the response stage. Failure modes: the classic bug is changing chunk_size or overlap and re-indexing only new documents, leaving the corpus with two incompatible chunking schemes — half the answers come from 300-token chunks and half from 800, and retrieval quality becomes a coin flip. Always re-index the whole corpus when you change either dial, and stamp each chunk with the chunking-config version so you can detect a mixed index. Monitoring: alert on the near-duplicate rate in top-k results — a sudden rise usually means overlap was bumped too high. Compliance: overlap means a sentence appears in multiple chunks, so a redaction or deletion must sweep every chunk the text landed in, not just one.

⚠ Watch out

Setting overlap as a fixed token count and then changing chunk_size is a silent trap. A 100-token overlap is a sane 20% on a 500-token chunk but a wasteful 50% on a 200-token chunk — you can end up storing each sentence three or four times without realizing it. Always reason about overlap as a percentage of the current chunk_size.

When to use overlap and when not: use overlap (10–20%) for flowing prose where an idea can straddle a cut — policies, guides, agreements.
