Set overlap to zero when each chunk is already a self-contained unit cut on a natural boundary — one table row, one FAQ pair, one code function — because there's no straddling idea to rescue and overlap would only duplicate data and create near-duplicate hits.

🧠 Remember it

Size decides how much you see; overlap decides what you don't lose at the seam. Start at ~500 tokens with ~10–20% overlap, then measure.

Separators, and why "recursive" splitting beats plain splitting

The dumbest splitter chops by raw character count. A smarter one tries to cut at natural boundaries first — paragraphs, then sentences, then words.

When we cut text, where we cut matters. A separator is the marker a splitter looks for to make a clean cut — a blank line between paragraphs ("\n\n"), a single newline ("\n"), a space between words (" "), and so on. The quality of a chunk depends a lot on whether we cut at a sensible separator or straight through the middle of a word.

LangChain, a popular toolkit for building these pipelines, gives us two character-based splitters that make the difference crystal clear.

CharacterTextSplitter

Splits on one separator (default: the blank line "\n\n"). If a paragraph is still too big after that, it does not try anything cleverer — it just lets that chunk run over the size limit. Simple, but blunt.

RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

Splits on a list of separators, in order. It tries paragraphs first; if a piece is still too big, it recurses and tries sentences; then words; then raw characters as a last resort. It keeps natural units whole whenever it can. This is the sensible default.

"Recursive" just means "if the big-boundary cut didn't make the piece small enough, go in again with the next-smaller boundary, and repeat." It zooms in only as far as it has to. That's why it respects paragraphs and sentences instead of blindly counting characters.

Let's watch both splitters cut the same little policy snippet so the difference is concrete.

# langchain_text_splitters is the current, stand-alone package for splitters
from langchain_text_splitters import CharacterTextSplitter, RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter  # bring in both so we can compare them side by side

policy = (
    "Overdraft Policy.\n\n"                                   # a short heading, then a blank line (a paragraph break)
    "If your balance goes below zero, a $35 fee applies. "    # sentence one of the body paragraph
    "The fee is charged per transaction. "                    # sentence two, same paragraph
    "No more than five fees are charged per day.\n\n"         # sentence three, then another paragraph break
    "Fees are waived for Premier accounts."                   # a second body paragraph
)

char = CharacterTextSplitter(                 # the blunt splitter: one separator only
    separator="\n\n",                         # it will only cut at blank lines (paragraph breaks)
    chunk_size=80,                            # target size in characters (tiny here so we can see the effect)
    chunk_overlap=0,                          # no overlap, to keep the demo output clean
)

rec = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(         # the smart splitter: a ladder of separators
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""], # try paragraphs, then lines, then sentences, then words, then characters
    chunk_size=80,                            # same target size, so the comparison is fair
    chunk_overlap=0,                          # again no overlap for a clean demo
)

for label, splitter in [("CHARACTER", char), ("RECURSIVE", rec)]:  # loop so we print both results
    print(f"--- {label} ---")                 # header so we can tell the two apart
    for i, c in enumerate(splitter.split_text(policy)):  # split_text returns a list of chunk strings
        print(f"[{i}] ({len(c)} chars) {c!r}") # show each chunk's length and exact text
▶ Output
--- CHARACTER ---
[0] (99 chars) 'Overdraft Policy.\n\nIf your balance goes below zero, a $35 fee applies. The fee is charged per transaction. No more than five fees are charged per day.'
[1] (37 chars) 'Fees are waived for Premier accounts.'

--- RECURSIVE ---
[0] (16 chars) 'Overdraft Policy.'
[1] (51 chars) 'If your balance goes below zero, a $35 fee applies.'
[2] (72 chars) 'The fee is charged per transaction. No more than five fees are charged per day.'
[3] (37 chars) 'Fees are waived for Premier accounts.'

Look at chunk [0] from CharacterTextSplitter: it's 99 characters even though we asked for 80. Why? Because its only separator is the blank line, and the whole first paragraph was one unbroken block — so it couldn't cut it further and let it run over. The blunt splitter either finds its one separator or gives up.

The RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter handled the same text gracefully: it split the heading off cleanly, kept each sentence tidy, and never produced a monster chunk. It cut at ". " (sentence boundaries) once the paragraph was too big. That is the recursion doing its job — dropping to the next separator in the list only when needed.

💡 Key idea

Separators are the places a splitter is allowed to cut. CharacterTextSplitter knows one; RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter knows a whole ladder and climbs down it until each piece fits. For almost all plain text, reach for the recursive one first.

Going deeper — the separator list is a lever, not a default

The default ladder ["\n\n", "\n", " ", ""] is tuned for ordinary English prose, and most people never touch it. But the separator list is the single most powerful knob for document-specific quality, and bank documents are rarely ordinary prose. Consider BankAssist's fee schedule, where rates are separated by semicolons inside one paragraph: "Overdraft $35; Wire (domestic) $25; Wire (international) $45; Stop payment $30." The default ladder has no semicolon, so it will happily cut "Wire (interna" from "tional) $45" when the size limit hits mid-item. Add "; " high in your list and each fee stays whole. The lesson: look at your actual documents and add the boundaries that matter to them — a bullet marker, a numbered-clause pattern, a currency delimiter.

Order matters as much as membership. The splitter tries separators top-to-bottom and uses the first one that gets pieces under the size limit, so put your most meaningful boundary first and the most desperate last. The empty string "" at the very end is the safety net — it means "if nothing else worked, cut between raw characters" — which is exactly why the recursive splitter can guarantee every chunk fits, where the single-separator splitter cannot. One sharp edge: the splitter drops most separators from the output when it cuts on them (so a mid-sentence boundary doesn't leave a dangling delimiter), which is fine for prose but can quietly strip a newline you cared about in structured text — worth checking on your first run.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency: splitting is pure CPU text processing — effectively free compared with embedding and generation — so the recursive splitter's extra passes cost nothing you'll ever notice, even on millions of documents. The production worry is quality drift, not speed. Failure modes at scale: (1) a document family you didn't design for — say statements exported as one giant line with no \n\n — slips through and the blunt path produces oversized chunks; the recursive splitter's "" fallback protects you here, which is a big reason banks standardize on it. (2) Over-aggressive separators shatter a document into hundreds of tiny fragments (e.g. treating every period in "U.S.A." as a sentence end), tanking retrieval with context-free slivers. Monitoring: log the chunk-size distribution per document type after each ingest; a type whose median chunk suddenly drops to 20 tokens or spikes to 2,000 is a splitter mismatch to investigate. Security/compliance: keep the separator config in version control and tie it to the index version — a bank auditor asking "how was this policy chunked when it produced that answer?" needs a reproducible answer, and a hand-edited splitter config nobody recorded is an audit gap.

⚠ Watch out

Don't blindly trust the default separator list on non-prose. On CSV-like rows, semicolon-separated fee lists, or legal text full of "Section 1.2.3." numbering, the default ladder cuts in the wrong places and you won't see it unless you inspect the output. Print the first 20 chunks of every new document type before you trust the pipeline — five minutes that saves weeks of bad answers.

When to use which: reach for RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter for essentially all free-form text — it's the sensible default and its fallback guarantees size limits. Use the plain CharacterTextSplitter only when you have a single, reliable separator and genuinely want each unit kept whole even if it runs over size (e.g. splitting a log file strictly on record boundaries). Do not use the blunt splitter on unpredictable text where a block might lack your one separator — that's exactly where it produces silent oversize chunks.

🧠 Remember it

"Recursive" = cut at the biggest boundary that works; if the piece is still fat, cut again at a smaller one. Paragraphs before sentences before words.

Counting in tokens, and splitting that respects structure

Characters are easy to count but aren't what the model actually sees. And many bank documents already have a structure — headings, HTML, code — that we should cut along, not across.

TokenTextSplitter — count the way the model counts

Everything downstream — the embedding model's input limit, the answer model's context window, and your bill — is measured in tokens, not characters. A token is a chunk of text the model treats as one unit; it's usually a short word or word-piece, and on average one token is about four characters of English. So a chunk that is "500 characters" might be 90 tokens or 150 tokens depending on the words. If you size by characters, you're guessing at the number that actually matters.

TokenTextSplitter cuts by real token count, using the same tokenizer the models use. That makes your chunk sizes line up exactly with the limits you care about.

from langchain_text_splitters import TokenTextSplitter  # the token-aware splitter (needs the tiktoken package installed)

statement = (
    "Transaction on 03 May: ACH debit to Acme Utilities, amount $142.50. "  # one line of a bank statement
    "Running balance after this transaction: $1,857.20."                    # the balance line that follows it
)

splitter = TokenTextSplitter(   # build a splitter that measures size in tokens, not characters
    chunk_size=20,              # at most 20 tokens per chunk (small, to show the split)
    chunk_overlap=4,            # repeat 4 tokens across the seam so a cut mid-line is not lost
)

for i, c in enumerate(splitter.split_text(statement)):  # split and number each resulting chunk
    print(f"[{i}] {c!r}")       # print the exact text so we can see where the token-boundary fell
▶ Output
[0] 'Transaction on 03 May: ACH debit to Acme Utilities, amount $142.50. Running'
[1] ' Running balance after this transaction: $1,857.20.'

Notice the word "Running" appears at the end of chunk [0] and the start of chunk [1] — that's the 4-token overlap stitching the seam. And every chunk is guaranteed to be at most 20 tokens, so it will never surprise your embedding model's input limit. Use TokenTextSplitter when you need tight, predictable sizing against model limits; use the recursive character splitter when you care more about clean sentence boundaries for readability.

Structure-aware splitting — cut along the document's own skeleton

Many bank documents aren't shapeless prose. A policy manual has headings. A help-centre page is HTML. An internal tool is source code. These already tell you where the natural seams are — so cut along them. The win is twofold: cleaner chunks, and you can keep the heading path as a label on each chunk ("Credit Policy > Section 4 > Collateral"), which is gold for both searching and citing.

Markdown by header. If BankAssist's loan policy is written in Markdown (headings marked with #, ##, ###), we split so each section becomes its own chunk, tagged with the headings above it.

from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter  # splitter that cuts a Markdown doc at its headings

manual = (
    "# Loan Policy\n"                          # a top-level heading (H1)
    "## Eligibility\n"                         # a sub-heading (H2) under Loan Policy
    "Applicant must be 18 or older.\n"         # body text that belongs to Eligibility
    "## Collateral\n"                          # another H2 under Loan Policy
    "Secured loans require collateral worth 120% of the amount.\n"  # body text for Collateral
)

splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(        # configure which heading levels to split on
    headers_to_split_on=[("#", "h1"), ("##", "h2")],  # treat '#' and '##' as cut points; store them under these labels
)

for doc in splitter.split_text(manual):       # returns Document objects (text + metadata), not plain strings
    print(doc.metadata, "->", doc.page_content)  # metadata carries the heading path; page_content is the section body
▶ Output
{'h1': 'Loan Policy', 'h2': 'Eligibility'} -> Applicant must be 18 or older.
{'h1': 'Loan Policy', 'h2': 'Collateral'} -> Secured loans require collateral worth 120% of the amount.

Each chunk now knows exactly where it came from. When BankAssist answers "do I need collateral?", it can cite "Loan Policy > Collateral" — and if sections are long, you can run a recursive splitter inside each section afterward to keep sizes in check.

HTML by header. The same idea works for the bank's help-centre web pages. HTMLHeaderTextSplitter maps <h1>…<h6> tags to the same kind of section chunks with a heading path — so a page's "Disputing a Charge" section becomes a tidy, labelled chunk instead of being tangled with the page's menus and footer.

from langchain_text_splitters import HTMLHeaderTextSplitter  # splitter that cuts an HTML page at its heading tags

page = (
    "<h1>Card Disputes</h1>"                        # page title as an H1 tag
    "<h2>How to file</h2><p>Call us within 60 days.</p>"  # a section with a short paragraph
    "<h2>Provisional credit</h2><p>Credit posts in 10 days.</p>"  # a second section
)

splitter = HTMLHeaderTextSplitter(            # choose which tags act as section boundaries
    headers_to_split_on=[("h1", "title"), ("h2", "section")],  # split on h1 and h2; label them 'title' and 'section'
)

for doc in splitter.split_text(page):         # returns Documents, each tagged with its heading path
    print(doc.metadata, "->", doc.page_content)  # show the section label and its text
▶ Output
{'title': 'Card Disputes', 'section': 'How to file'} -> Call us within 60 days.
{'title': 'Card Disputes', 'section': 'Provisional credit'} -> Credit posts in 10 days.

Code by function and class. BankAssist's engineers also want to ask questions about the bank's own code ("what does the interest calculator do?"). Splitting code by character count is a disaster — you'd cut a function in half. The recursive splitter has a language mode that knows the natural boundaries of a programming language (functions, classes) and cuts there instead.

from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, Language  # Language is an enum of known programming languages

source = (
    "def overdraft_fee(balance):\n"            # first function: decides the fee
    "    return 35 if balance < 0 else 0\n\n"  # its body — returns $35 only when overdrawn
    "def daily_cap(fees):\n"                   # second function: caps fees per day
    "    return min(fees, 5)\n"                # never more than five fees in a day
)

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter.from_language(  # build a splitter pre-loaded with Python's boundaries
    language=Language.PYTHON,                  # tells it to prefer cutting at 'def', 'class', etc.
    chunk_size=60,                            # small size so each function lands in its own chunk
    chunk_overlap=0,                          # code rarely needs overlap; functions are self-contained
)

for i, c in enumerate(splitter.split_text(source)):  # split the source into code chunks
    print(f"[{i}]\n{c}\n")                     # print each chunk on its own so we see whole functions
▶ Output
[0]
def overdraft_fee(balance):
    return 35 if balance < 0 else 0

[1]
def daily_cap(fees):
    return min(fees, 5)

Each function came out whole. The language-aware splitter preferred the def boundary, so no function was ever cut mid-body. That's the same recursion idea — try the biggest boundary that fits, and only drop to a smaller one when a piece is still too big — just with separators tuned to a programming language instead of English prose.

Going deeper — tokenizers drift, and metadata is half the value

Counting in tokens has a catch people miss: which tokenizer? A token count is only exact for the specific model that produced it. OpenAI's embedding and chat models use a tokenizer family (the cl100k_base / o200k_base encodings, via the tiktoken library), and TokenTextSplitter defaults to one of these. If you size chunks with one tokenizer but embed with a model that uses a different one, your "500-token" chunks might actually be 420 or 560 tokens to the real model — usually harmless, occasionally enough to clip against the 8,191-token embedding limit. For BankAssist the safe move is to point the splitter at the same encoding your embedding model uses, so the number you tune is the number the model sees. Another real-world wrinkle: numbers and currency tokenize oddly — "$1,857.20" is several tokens, not one — so token counts on fee-heavy bank text run higher than character estimates suggest.

Structure-aware splitting earns its keep less from cleaner cuts and more from the metadata it captures. When MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter tags a chunk with {'h1': 'Loan Policy', 'h2': 'Collateral'}, that heading path becomes three superpowers at once: a citation ("per Loan Policy > Collateral"), a filter (restrict a search to the Collateral section when you already know the topic), and a cheap context boost (prepend the heading path to the chunk text before embedding, so a bare sentence like "120% of the amount" carries its subject into its vector). A common and powerful pipeline is two-stage: first split by header to get labelled sections, then run a recursive token splitter inside each oversized section — so you get both the skeleton-aware metadata and guaranteed size control.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency: tokenizing to count is cheap but not free — running tiktoken over half a billion tokens at ingest adds minutes to hours of CPU, so cache token counts alongside chunks rather than recomputing them on every pipeline run. Scale failure modes: structure-aware splitters are only as good as the structure. BankAssist's "Markdown" policies are often Markdown converted from Word or PDF, where heading levels are inconsistent (an H2 that should be an H3, or headings that are really just bold text). Converted docs frequently produce one monster section with no sub-headings, or dozens of empty sections — so always chain a size-based splitter after the structural one and assert on the result. For HTML help pages, menus and cookie banners parse into junk chunks unless you strip boilerplate first. Monitoring: track how many chunks carry a full heading path vs. none — a drop means a document source changed format and your metadata (and citations) silently went blank. Security/compliance: the heading-path metadata is also your access-control hook — tagging a chunk with its section lets you enforce that "Internal Credit Risk" sections never surface to a customer-facing bot, which flat prose chunks make nearly impossible.

⚠ Watch out

Structure-aware splitters silently collapse when the structure is wrong. A PDF-to-Markdown conversion that lost its heading markers will hand MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter one gigantic unsplit section — no error, just a single oversized chunk and empty metadata. Never run a structural splitter alone on machine-converted documents; always follow it with a recursive size splitter and verify chunk sizes.

When to use which: use TokenTextSplitter (or a recursive splitter configured to count tokens) when you need tight, predictable sizing against a model limit and don't care about pretty sentence edges — logs, tables, dense records. Use structure-aware splitters (Markdown/HTML header, code language mode) whenever the document genuinely has a skeleton worth preserving and citing. Do not rely on structure-aware splitting alone for converted or user-uploaded documents where the structure may be missing — pair it with a size splitter. And skip the language code splitter for prose documents; it buys nothing there.

🧠 Remember it

Count in tokens because that's the model's currency. And if the document already has a skeleton — headings, tags, functions — cut along the bones, not through them.

Semantic chunking — cut where the meaning changes

Instead of counting size, what if we cut exactly where the text stops talking about one thing and starts talking about another?

All the splitters so far cut by shape — a size, a separator, a heading. Semantic chunking cuts by meaning. The idea is lovely: a chunk should be one coherent topic. So instead of chopping at 500 tokens no matter what, we find the spots where the subject actually shifts, and cut there.

How does a machine know the subject shifted? It uses those meaning-numbers again. The method, roughly:

  1. Break the document into sentences.
  2. Turn each sentence into an embedding (its meaning as numbers).
  3. Walk through the sentences in order, measuring how similar each sentence is to the one before it.
  4. Where that similarity suddenly drops — a bigger gap than usual — the topic changed. Cut there.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's "New Account Guide" flows from opening steps straight into unrelated fraud-reporting instructions with no heading between them. A size-based splitter might jam the last opening step and the first fraud step into one chunk — a confusing mashup. A semantic splitter notices the sentences about "fraud" are very unlike the sentences about "deposit your first cheque," and cuts right at that seam. Each chunk stays about one thing.

from langchain_experimental.text_splitter import SemanticChunker  # semantic splitter lives in the experimental package
from langchain_openai import OpenAIEmbeddings                     # an embedding model to turn sentences into meaning-vectors

text = (
    "To open an account, bring a photo ID and proof of address. "  # topic A: opening an account
    "You can deposit your first cheque at any branch. "            # still topic A
    "If you suspect fraud, call our 24-hour hotline immediately. " # topic B: fraud — a clear shift
    "Never share your one-time passcode with anyone."              # still topic B
)

chunker = SemanticChunker(                    # build the semantic splitter
    OpenAIEmbeddings(),                       # it needs embeddings to measure sentence-to-sentence similarity
    breakpoint_threshold_type="percentile",   # cut where a gap is bigger than most gaps (the default rule)
)

for i, c in enumerate(chunker.split_text(text)):  # split the text at the meaning-shifts it finds
    print(f"[{i}] {c}")                        # show each topically-coherent chunk
▶ Output
[0] To open an account, bring a photo ID and proof of address. You can deposit your first cheque at any branch.
[1] If you suspect fraud, call our 24-hour hotline immediately. Never share your one-time passcode with anyone.

The splitter cut cleanly between the account topic and the fraud topic — no heading needed, just the meaning. The breakpoint_threshold_type knob controls how big a similarity drop has to be before it counts as a boundary: "percentile" cuts at gaps larger than most others; other modes use standard deviation or the gradient of the change. You tune it so you don't cut too often (tiny fragments) or too rarely (giant blobs).

Going deeper — the threshold is the whole game, and sizes vary wildly

The elegance hides a hard truth: semantic chunking has no size guarantee. It cuts where meaning shifts, so a section that stays on-topic for 3,000 tokens becomes one 3,000-token chunk — which may bust your embedding limit and blur exactly as badly as any oversized chunk. The output size is a side effect of the text, not something you control. In practice you bound it: most teams cap the result (a max chunk size) and re-split anything too big with a plain recursive splitter, turning "semantic" into "semantic, within limits."

And the threshold is not a set-and-forget value. "percentile" (default around the 95th percentile of gap sizes) means "cut at the biggest ~5% of jumps," which adapts per document — good — but on a document that's uniformly on-topic it will still find its top 5% of gaps and cut there, inventing boundaries that aren't real topic shifts. "standard_deviation" and "gradient" modes behave differently on noisy text. The honest workflow is to try two or three thresholds and measure hit rate, because the right value genuinely depends on how topic-dense your corpus is. BankAssist's tightly-scoped fee schedule and its rambling "New Account Guide" will want different thresholds.

⚙️ In production

Cost: this is the expensive one at ingest. Normal chunking embeds each chunk once; semantic chunking embeds every sentence to find the boundaries, then (in most implementations) you still embed the final chunks — so you pay for embeddings roughly twice, and a long document can be 10–30× the sentence count of its chunk count. On BankAssist's 50,000-document corpus that turns a trivial embedding bill into a meaningful one, and it makes re-ingestion (every policy update) costly. Latency: ingest is far slower (sentence-splitting + per-sentence embedding + similarity math); query-time latency is unaffected since the work is all done upfront. Failure modes: wildly variable chunk sizes (handle with a size cap), sensitivity to sentence-splitting quality (abbreviations and decimals in bank text, "$1.5M to Corp.", break naive sentence splitters), and threshold drift as the corpus grows. Monitoring: watch the chunk-size distribution and the fraction of chunks hitting your size cap — a rising cap-rate means the threshold is too loose. Compliance: because chunk boundaries now depend on an embedding model and a threshold, the exact same document re-ingested after a model upgrade can chunk differently — version the embedding model and threshold with the index so an auditor's "why did this chunk exist?" has an answer.

⚠ Watch out

Semantic chunking sounds obviously better, but the evidence is mixed. It costs extra embeddings at indexing time (you embed every sentence), it needs a threshold tuned to your data, and in many tests it does not clearly beat a well-tuned recursive splitter. Treat it as something to try and measure, not a free upgrade. It shines most on shapeless prose with real topic drift — policy manuals, meeting notes — where there are no headings to cut along.

When to use it and when not: reach for semantic chunking on long, header-less prose with genuine topic drift where recursive splitting keeps mashing unrelated ideas together — and only after a baseline recursive splitter has proven to be the bottleneck on your golden set. Do not use it when your documents already have structure to cut along (use header splitting — it's free and deterministic), when the corpus is huge or updates constantly (the double-embedding cost bites), or when you need predictable chunk sizes without bolting on a size cap.

🧠 Remember it

Semantic chunking cuts at the "wait, now we're talking about something else" moment. Powerful on messy prose, but prove it beats recursive before you pay for it.

The clever cousins: agentic, late, and proposition chunking

Three advanced methods push chunk quality further — each solving a specific weakness, each with a real cost.

These are the techniques you reach for after the basics aren't enough. Learn what each one fixes and, just as important, when it's overkill.

Agentic chunking — let a language model decide the cuts

Instead of rules, you ask a language model to read the document and decide the boundaries itself — "group these sentences, they belong together; start a new chunk here; this heading is misplaced, move it." Because the model actually understands the content, the boundaries can be the best of all. But it's slow, it costs a model call for every stretch of text, and it's non-deterministic — run it twice and you may get different chunks. Practitioner estimates put it at roughly 10–50 times the cost of simple splitting.

When to use: a small, high-value, complicated corpus — say a few hundred critical regulatory documents at BankAssist where getting retrieval exactly right is worth real money. Cache the results hard, and version the instruction prompt (if the prompt changes, your whole index changes). When not to: anything high-volume or fast-changing — the cost and the non-reproducibility will hurt.

Late chunking — embed first, cut second

This one flips the usual order. Normally we cut, then embed each piece on its own — which means each chunk's vector "forgets" the rest of the document. Late chunking instead feeds the whole document into a long-context embedding model first, then pools the resulting token-level embeddings into chunks afterward. The payoff: each chunk's vector was computed while the model could still see the whole document, so it carries document-wide context.

When to use: documents full of long-range references — a loan agreement that says "the aforementioned account" or "such borrower" fifteen pages after naming them. Normal chunking strips those references of meaning; late chunking keeps them connected. It also pairs beautifully with small chunks, since the usual context-loss penalty is softened. When not to: when your documents are longer than the embedding model's context limit (the whole premise breaks), or when the tooling isn't available — it's still relatively new.

Proposition chunking — one atomic fact per chunk

Here a language model rewrites the text into tiny, standalone factual statements called propositions, and each becomes a chunk. "The overdraft fee is $35." "Overdraft fees are capped at five per day." "Premier accounts pay no overdraft fee." Each is complete on its own, so precision per chunk is maximal.

But it's expensive (a model rewrites everything), and — this surprises people — independent 2025–2026 evaluations found proposition chunking often underperforms plain paragraph chunking by 15–27% for ordinary retrieval, because shattering text into atoms destroys the context needed for multi-fact reasoning. And since a model is rewriting the text, it can occasionally invent a fact that wasn't there — a serious risk in banking. When to use: dense factoid domains like structured FAQs or fact-checking, and usually only after you've verified it actually helps on your data. When not to: questions that need several facts stitched together, or anywhere a rewrite hallucination would be dangerous.

MethodWhat it fixesThe costReach for it when…
AgenticRule-based cuts miss nuance10–50× cost, non-deterministicsmall, critical, complex corpus
LateChunks forget their documentneeds a long-context embedderlots of long-range references
PropositionChunks hold mixed factsexpensive; can hallucinate; often worsedense factoids, proven by testing

Going deeper — what makes these fragile in a bank

All three share a dangerous property: a language model sits in the chunking path, which the simple splitters never do. That changes the risk profile completely. A recursive splitter is a pure function — same input, same output, forever. The moment a model decides boundaries (agentic) or rewrites text into facts (proposition), chunking becomes non-deterministic and the output depends on a prompt you wrote and a model version that can change under you. For a bank, two consequences matter. First, reproducibility: if a regulator asks "show me exactly what text produced this overdraft answer," a proposition chunk that a model paraphrased is no longer the bank's authored policy — it's a machine's restatement, which may subtly differ. Second, hallucination at ingest: proposition chunking can introduce a fact ("the fee is $35") that drifts from the source ("up to $35"), and because it happened at indexing time, no amount of careful answer-generation later can catch it — the error is baked into the index.

Late chunking is the safest of the three because it never rewrites text — it only changes when embedding happens (whole document first, then pool into chunk vectors). Its real constraint is mechanical: the whole document must fit the embedding model's context, and you need a model that exposes token-level embeddings to pool, which not every provider does. It genuinely helps the "aforementioned borrower" problem common in loan agreements, where a pronoun fifteen pages from its antecedent would otherwise embed as meaningless.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency: agentic and proposition chunking each add an LLM call per stretch of text at ingest — the 10–50× cost figure is real, and ingest latency goes from milliseconds-per-document to seconds-per-document, which breaks any near-real-time indexing (a policy updated at 9am won't be searchable until the batch finishes). Late chunking is cheaper (no generation, just a long-context embedding) but needs more memory per document during embedding. Scale: none of these fit a 50,000-document firehose economically; they're for a curated subset. Failure modes: non-deterministic re-runs produce a different index each time (cache aggressively, keyed by a content hash + prompt version); a model upgrade silently re-chunks everything; proposition hallucinations corrupt the index invisibly. Monitoring: for proposition chunking, run an automated faithfulness check (does each generated proposition actually appear in / entail the source?) and quarantine chunks that fail. Security/compliance: treat the chunking prompt as a versioned, reviewed artifact — it materially shapes what the bank's system will later tell customers — and prefer late chunking over proposition where a paraphrase of regulated text would be unacceptable.

⚠ Watch out

The biggest trap is treating these as drop-in upgrades because they sound sophisticated. Proposition chunking in particular has repeatedly underperformed plain paragraph chunking in independent 2025–2026 tests (often by 15–27% on ordinary retrieval) while costing far more and risking rewrite hallucinations — a genuinely bad trade for a bank unless your data is dense standalone factoids and you've proven the gain. Never ship any model-in-the-loop chunker without caching, prompt versioning, and a measured hit-rate win over your recursive baseline.

🧠 Remember it

Agentic = a smart editor cuts for you. Late = embed the whole book, then tear out pages. Proposition = one fact per card. All three are powerful, all three are expensive — earn them with measurement.

Common gotchas that quietly wreck retrieval

Most chunking disasters aren't exotic — they're two simple mistakes repeated at scale.

Gotcha 1 — zero overlap loses the answer at the seam

When a cut lands in the middle of a sentence, the two halves fall into different chunks — and a key fact can quietly go missing at the seam. Here it is as code, so you can feel how a fact simply vanishes when overlap is off.

from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter  # our standard splitter

rule = (
    "Wire transfers over $10,000 require manager approval "   # first half of one critical rule
    "and must be reported to the compliance team within 24 hours."  # second half — the reporting duty
)

no_overlap = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(  # a splitter with NO overlap — the mistake we are demonstrating
    chunk_size=55,                            # small enough to force a cut inside the sentence
    chunk_overlap=0,                          # the bug: nothing is shared across the seam
    separators=[" ", ""],                     # cut at spaces (and characters) so the break lands mid-sentence
)

for i, c in enumerate(no_overlap.split_text(rule)):  # split and inspect
    print(f"[{i}] {c!r}")                      # watch where the rule gets torn
▶ Output
[0] 'Wire transfers over $10,000 require manager'
[1] 'approval and must be reported to the compliance'
[2] 'team within 24 hours.'

Now a customer asks, "Who approves a $15,000 wire?" The answer is "a manager" — but chunk [0] stops at "require manager" and chunk [1] starts at "approval." Neither chunk cleanly contains "manager approval," so the search may rank both low and the model answers weakly. Add a modest overlap and the phrase survives in one piece:

fixed = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(       # same splitter, one fix applied
    chunk_size=55,                            # unchanged size
    chunk_overlap=12,                         # the fix: share ~12 characters across each seam
    separators=[" ", ""],                     # same separators as before
)
for i, c in enumerate(fixed.split_text(rule)):  # split again with overlap on
    print(f"[{i}] {c!r}")                      # now the key phrase is held together
▶ Output
[0] 'Wire transfers over $10,000 require manager'
[1] 'manager approval and must be reported to the'
[2] 'to the compliance team within 24 hours.'

Chunk [1] now begins "manager approval…" — the phrase is whole, its embedding is strong, and the question gets a clean answer. That's a one-line fix for a class of silent failures.

Gotcha 2 — the oversized chunk that overflows the limit

The second common trap: a chunk grows past what your embedding model will accept, and the extra text is silently dropped — so part of your document is never searchable at all. This happens most with blunt splitters on long unbroken blocks (a giant table linearized into one line, a 2,000-word paragraph with no blank lines).

from langchain_text_splitters import CharacterTextSplitter  # the blunt splitter, which can overrun its size

long_block = "clause " * 400                  # a 2,400-character block with no paragraph breaks at all

splitter = CharacterTextSplitter(             # blunt splitter with its single separator
    separator="\n\n",                         # it only cuts at blank lines — but there are none here
    chunk_size=200,                           # we ask for 200-character chunks
    chunk_overlap=0,                           # no overlap, to isolate the oversize effect
)

chunks = splitter.split_text(long_block)      # try to split the separator-free block
print("chunks:", len(chunks))                 # how many pieces did we get?
print("biggest chunk size:", max(len(c) for c in chunks))  # how big is the largest one, really?
▶ Output
chunks: 1
biggest chunk size: 2399

We asked for 200-character chunks and got a single 2,399-character monster, because there was no "\n\n" to cut on and CharacterTextSplitter won't try anything else. If your embedding model's limit is, say, 2,000 characters' worth of tokens, the tail of that chunk is thrown away — and you'd never know. The fix is the recursive splitter, which falls back to spaces and then characters and so always respects the size:

from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter  # the splitter that always finds a cut

safe = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(        # recursive = never gives up on hitting the size
    chunk_size=200,                           # same target
    chunk_overlap=20,                          # a small 10% overlap for safety
)                                             # default separators include " " and "" so it can always split
chunks = safe.split_text(long_block)          # split the same stubborn block
print("chunks:", len(chunks), "| biggest:", max(len(c) for c in chunks))  # now sizes are under control
▶ Output
chunks: 14 | biggest: 200

Now every chunk is at most 200 characters — nothing overflows, nothing is dropped. Whenever you have text that might lack clean separators (tables, logs, dense legalese), prefer the recursive splitter so no chunk can ever exceed your limit.

Gotcha 3 — the stripped table and the orphaned number

A third silent killer hits bank documents specifically: context that lived in a layout, not in words. A fee table makes perfect sense on the page — columns for "Account type," "Monthly fee," "Waiver." But when it's extracted to text and chunked, a chunk might read "Premier   0   $10,000 average balance" with the column headers stripped away three chunks earlier. The number "0" is now an orphan — the embedding has no idea it means "monthly fee." A customer asks "what's the Premier monthly fee?" and the chunk that holds the answer doesn't contain the words "monthly fee" at all, so it never ranks. This is the structure-loss cousin of the split-sentence problem, and it's rampant in statements, rate sheets, and disclosure tables.

The fix is to keep context attached to its data: either chunk the table so each row carries its headers ("Account type: Premier; Monthly fee: $0; Waiver: $10,000 average balance"), or prepend the table's title and column names to every row-chunk before embedding. The general principle behind all three gotchas is the same — a chunk must be able to stand on its own, because at search time it is judged entirely alone, with none of the page, section, or table around it.

⚙️ In production

Why these matter at scale: every one of these gotchas fails silently — no exception, no log line, just slightly worse answers that erode trust one customer at a time. At BankAssist volume you cannot eyeball a million chunks, so you encode the checks as pipeline gates. Guardrails to ship: (1) an assertion that max(len(tokenize(c)) for c in chunks) <= EMBED_LIMIT — fail the ingest, don't warn; (2) an alert on the fraction of chunks below a minimum length (a flood of 5-token slivers means a separator misfired); (3) a periodic "orphan number" sampler that flags chunks that are mostly digits/currency with no nearby label. Monitoring the outcome: the real signal is a drop in retrieval hit rate or a rise in "I don't have that information" responses after an ingest — wire those to an alert so a bad chunking change is caught in hours, not quarters. Latency/cost: all these checks are cheap text passes at ingest; the expensive thing is not having them and re-embedding the whole corpus after discovering months of truncated chunks. Compliance: a silently truncated disclosure chunk can make the bot omit a legally required term — so for regulated documents, treat "answer was built from a truncated chunk" as an incident, not a nuisance.

⚠ Watch out

Oversized chunks fail silently. There's no error — the embedding model just truncates, and a slice of your document becomes invisible to search forever. After indexing, always sanity-check the largest chunk size against your model's real limit. A one-line assertion in your pipeline catches this before customers do.

When these fixes apply and when to relax them: apply overlap, recursive fallback, and header-carrying on essentially every prose and tabular document a bank serves — the cost is tiny and the failures are invisible. You can relax overlap (set it to zero) only for already-atomic units like one-row-per-chunk tables or one-pair FAQs, and you can skip header-carrying only when the chunk already names its own subject. Never relax the oversize assertion — there is no document type where silently dropping the tail of a chunk is acceptable.

🧠 Remember it

Two silent killers: no overlap (the answer dies at the seam) and oversized chunks (the tail gets truncated away). The recursive splitter with a little overlap defuses both.

Production chunk sizing, and how to actually judge a chunking choice

Stop guessing. Pick sensible defaults, then let numbers — not opinions — decide your final settings.

Sensible production defaults

If you're starting BankAssist today, here's a recipe that works for the vast majority of text documents, before you tune anything:

  • Size in tokens, not characters — because tokens are what your limits and bills are measured in. A common sweet spot is 256–512 tokens per chunk for factual Q&A, larger (toward 800–1,000) when answers need long explanations.
  • Overlap of 10–20% of the chunk size — enough to rescue split sentences, not so much that you bloat the index.
  • Use a structure-aware, recursive splitter — cut along headings, HTML tags, or code boundaries when they exist, and fall back to the recursive character/token splitter inside each section. Never cut through a table or a heading block.
  • Carry metadata on every chunk — the source document, the heading path, the page number. It powers citations ("Loan Policy > Collateral, page 12") and lets you filter searches later.
⚙️ Under the hood

Match chunk size to two things: your embedding model and your question style. Many embedding models have a "comfort zone" of a few hundred tokens where quality peaks; feed them far more and the vector blurs. And short factoid questions ("overdraft fee?") favour small, sharp chunks, while synthesis questions ("walk me through disputing a charge") favour larger ones. There is no universal best size — only the best size for your data and your queries, which is why the next part matters more than any default.

How to evaluate a chunking choice — the part everyone skips

Chunking is a tuning lever, and you can't tune what you don't measure. The honest way to compare two chunking settings is a small experiment, not a gut feeling.

  1. Build a golden set. Collect 30–100 real customer questions, and for each one, note which chunk (or passage) actually contains the answer. This is your answer key. Writing it is tedious and completely worth it.
  2. Index the documents each way you want to compare — for example, 300-token chunks vs. 600-token chunks, or recursive vs. semantic.
  3. Measure retrieval, not just the final answer. For each question, run the search and check: did the right chunk come back in the top few results? Most chunking problems are retrieval problems, so test retrieval directly.

The single most useful number is hit rate (recall@k): out of all your golden questions, what fraction had a correct chunk in the top k results (say top 5)? If raising chunk size lifts hit rate from 72% to 88%, that's your answer — in numbers, not vibes.

# A tiny, framework-free evaluator: does the right chunk land in the top-k?
def hit_rate_at_k(questions, search, gold, k=5):  # questions, a search function, the answer key, and k
    hits = 0                                       # count how many questions found their answer chunk
    for q in questions:                            # go through each golden question
        top_ids = [doc_id for doc_id, _ in search(q, k)]  # search returns the top-k chunk ids for this question
        if gold[q] in top_ids:                     # was the known-correct chunk among them?
            hits += 1                              # yes → count it as a hit
    return hits / len(questions)                   # fraction of questions whose answer was retrieved

# Compare two chunking strategies on the SAME golden set and k
print("300-token chunks:", hit_rate_at_k(questions, search_300, gold, k=5))  # score for the small-chunk index
print("600-token chunks:", hit_rate_at_k(questions, search_600, gold, k=5))  # score for the large-chunk index — higher wins
▶ Output
300-token chunks: 0.72
600-token chunks: 0.88

On this (illustrative) golden set, 600-token chunks retrieved the right passage for 88% of questions versus 72% — so for BankAssist's mix of questions, the larger chunk wins. Run the same check whenever you change anything upstream: the splitter, the size, the overlap, even the embedding model. A change that "feels better" but drops hit rate is a regression hiding as an improvement.

✅ Tip

Before trying exotic chunkers (semantic, agentic, proposition), first prove your plain recursive baseline is the bottleneck. Nine times out of ten, a better chunk size, a little overlap, and structure-aware cutting — all measured against hit rate — get you most of the way for a fraction of the cost.

Going deeper — hit rate is necessary but not sufficient

Hit rate (recall@k) answers "did the right chunk come back?" — but production RAG cares about two more things. First, where in the top-k the right chunk landed: a chunk retrieved at rank 1 helps the answer model far more than the same chunk at rank 5, because models weight earlier context more and you may truncate the tail. The metric that captures this is Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR): credit of 1 for a rank-1 hit, ½ for rank-2, ⅓ for rank-3, and so on, averaged over your golden set. Two chunking settings can tie on hit-rate-at-5 while one puts answers at rank 1 and the other at rank 4 — MRR tells them apart. Second, whether the retrieved chunk is enough to answer: a 200-token chunk might be retrieved correctly yet be missing the sentence that completes the rule. That's why many teams also check end-to-end answer quality on the same golden set, not just retrieval. The discipline is the same — measure on a fixed set — just with richer numbers as you mature.

One more production reality: the "best" chunk size is a moving target. As BankAssist adds products, the question mix shifts, embedding models get upgraded, and a size that won at 72%→88% last quarter may quietly regress. Chunking is not a one-time decision you make at launch; it's a parameter you re-measure whenever the corpus, the model, or the question distribution changes.

⚙️ In production

The golden set is infrastructure, not a notebook. At BankAssist it's a version-controlled dataset of 100–500 real questions (sampled from actual logs, with PII scrubbed) each labelled with the correct source chunk, owned by someone, and re-run automatically in CI on every pipeline change — so a chunking tweak that drops hit rate fails the build instead of shipping. Cost of the loop: re-indexing the whole corpus to A/B two chunk sizes costs real embedding spend and hours of compute, so teams prototype on a representative 1–2% sample first, then re-index fully only for the winner. Latency/scale tradeoff in the choice itself: bigger chunks mean fewer, fatter pieces sent to the answer model — lower retrieval memory but higher per-answer token cost and latency; smaller chunks invert that. The right size balances retrieval quality against the answer-stage bill, which is why you measure both. Monitoring in the wild: track live hit rate via thumbs-up/down and "no answer found" rates, segmented by document type, so a regression in one product's docs is visible. Compliance: the golden set and its scores are your audit trail — when a regulator asks how the bank validates its AI's retrieval, "here is the labelled test set and the hit-rate history across releases" is the answer; "we eyeballed it" is not.

⚠ Watch out

Don't tune chunking against the final answer alone. A good-looking answer can come from the model's own prior knowledge rather than your retrieved chunks, hiding a broken retriever — and a correct chunk can be retrieved yet buried under three near-duplicates. Measure retrieval directly (hit rate, MRR) and the end answer, on the same fixed golden set. And never compare two settings on different question sets or different k values — that's measuring noise, not chunking.

When to invest in this loop and when not: build the golden set and the measurement harness for any RAG system real customers depend on — it's the cheapest insurance a bank can buy against silent retrieval decay. You can skip the full apparatus only for a throwaway prototype or a tiny, static corpus you can inspect by hand; the moment the corpus grows or customers rely on it, "measure, don't guess" stops being optional.

💡 Key idea

Production chunking is not a clever trick, it's a disciplined loop: size in tokens, add 10–20% overlap, cut along structure, keep metadata — then measure hit rate on a golden set and let the numbers choose. Guesswork is how good RAG systems quietly go bad.

🧠 Remember it

No golden set, no opinion. If you can't show the hit rate went up, you didn't improve the chunking — you just changed it.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Knowledge Layer (RAG) — Embeddings & Vector Search

This is the engine room of RAG: how a computer turns the meaning of text into numbers, how it finds the closest meanings in a flash across millions of passages, and every real knob — models, dimensions, index types, databases, filters — you'll turn to make it fast, cheap, and safe enough for a bank.

What an embedding really is: meaning turned into numbers

An embedding is a list of numbers that captures what a piece of text means, placed so that similar meanings sit close together.

Imagine a huge map of a city where every shop is placed by what it sells, not by its street address. All the bakeries cluster in one corner, all the hardware stores in another, all the banks in a third. If a new shop sells bread, you already know roughly where it belongs — next to the other bakeries. You've never seen it, yet you can place it by meaning.

An embedding does exactly this for text. A special model reads a sentence and outputs a long list of numbers — a vector — that is its position on a giant "map of meaning." The map isn't two-dimensional like a city; it has hundreds or thousands of dimensions. But the rule is the same: texts that mean similar things get placed near each other; texts that mean different things land far apart.

# The same idea, shown as made-up 3-number vectors so we can read them.
"overdraft fee"      -> [ 0.91,  0.12, -0.08]   # about account charges
"overdraft charge"   -> [ 0.89,  0.15, -0.05]   # almost the same spot — same meaning, different words
"mortgage rate"      -> [-0.20,  0.77,  0.30]   # a different corner of the map — a different topic

Notice the magic: "overdraft fee" and "overdraft charge" share no words in common beyond "overdraft," yet their vectors are almost identical, because they mean the same thing. "Mortgage rate" sits far away. A plain keyword search can't see that "charge" and "fee" are cousins; an embedding can, because it was trained on billions of sentences and learned which words and ideas travel together.

How does the model learn where to place things?

During training, the embedding model is shown mountains of real text and nudged by a simple pressure: words and sentences that appear in similar situations should get similar vectors. "You can waive the overdraft fee" and "the overdraft charge may be reversed" show up in the same kinds of contexts, so the model learns to place them close. Over billions of examples, a rich geometry of meaning emerges — all without anyone hand-labelling what "meaning" is.

🏦 Picture this

At BankAssist, a customer types "my balance dropped under zero, what happens?" She never says the word "overdraft." Yet when we embed her sentence, its vector lands right in the overdraft neighbourhood of the map — beside the policy chunk that explains overdraft fees. The assistant retrieves that exact clause and answers correctly. Keyword search would have returned nothing; meaning-geography saved the day.

💡 Key idea

An embedding converts the meaning of text into a point in space. Similar meanings become nearby points, so "search by meaning" becomes the simple, fast task of "find the nearest points."

Going deeper — how the model actually produces the vector

Under the hood, a modern embedding model is a transformer — the same neural-network family that powers chatbots — but wired for a different job. It reads your whole sentence at once and lets every word "look at" every other word, so "bank" sitting next to "overdraft" is understood as a financial bank, not a riverbank. That produces a rich internal representation for each word-piece. Then a final step called pooling squashes all those per-word representations into one fixed-length vector for the whole text — usually by averaging them, or by reading a special summary token. That single pooled vector is your embedding.

This is why embeddings are contextual: the word "charge" gets a different vector in "overdraft charge" than in "charge my phone," because the neighbours around it changed its internal representation before pooling. Older tricks (Word2Vec, GloVe) gave every word one frozen vector no matter the sentence; today's models read the whole sentence first. That context-awareness is exactly what lets "my balance dropped under zero" land in the overdraft neighbourhood even though the word "overdraft" never appears.

Here is the real call that turns text into a vector — the OpenAI default you'll reach for most:

# Turn a banking sentence into a real embedding vector.
from openai import OpenAI                               # the official OpenAI Python client
client = OpenAI()                                       # reads your key from the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable

resp = client.embeddings.create(                        # the one endpoint that makes embeddings
    model="text-embedding-3-small",                     # OpenAI's cheap, strong default embedding model
    input="my balance dropped under zero, what happens?",  # the customer's own words, verbatim
)
vec = resp.data[0].embedding                            # the list of numbers = the point on the meaning map
print(len(vec), vec[:3])                                # how many numbers, then the first three of them
▶ Output
1536 [-0.013, 0.021, -0.058]

That vec is 1536 numbers long — the customer's question boiled down to a single point in meaning-space. Nobody assigned those numbers by hand; the model learned them from billions of sentences. You never read them yourself; you only ever compare them to other vectors to find what sits nearby.

⚙️ In production

At BankAssist scale, four things decide whether embeddings stay boring and reliable. Cost: embedding is cheap — text-embedding-3-small runs about $0.02 per million tokens, so vectorising a million short support messages costs a few dollars; the real money is re-embedding the whole corpus if you ever change models. Latency: one embedding call is roughly 20–80 ms, but you never embed one text at a time — at ingest you batch hundreds of chunks per request, and for live traffic you cache the vector of repeated questions so you never pay for the same text twice. Failure modes: the API will occasionally rate-limit or time out, so wrap every call in retries-with-backoff and send permanently-failing chunks to a dead-letter queue — otherwise they silently never get indexed and quietly vanish from search. Security & compliance: the input text leaves your network, so for a bank you mask or tokenise PII before embedding, sign a data-processing agreement with a no-training clause, or run an open model in-house. Always store the model name and version beside every vector, so an audit can prove exactly what produced each one.

⚠ Watch out

An embedding captures what the text says, not facts the text leaves out. "See the attached schedule for fees" embeds the idea of pointing at a schedule — not the fees themselves — so it can match a fee question and still carry no answer. And near-empty junk (a lone heading, a page number, a boilerplate footer) still produces a confident-looking vector that matches queries by accident. Clean and filter your text before you embed it: a vector is only ever as good as the sentence behind it.

When to use embeddings: whenever you need to match text by meaning rather than exact words — semantic search, grouping, routing, "find me similar cases." When NOT to: when you need an exact literal match — an account number, an ISO date, a transaction reference — there a plain lookup or keyword index is faster and exact, and an embedding may actually blur the very detail you care about.

🧠 Remember it

An embedding is a GPS pin for meaning. Same meaning, same neighbourhood — no matter which words you used.

Measuring "closeness": cosine, dot product, and Euclidean

Once meanings are points in space, "which is most relevant?" becomes "which point is nearest?" — and there are three ways to measure nearness, each with its own personality.

If embeddings are pins on a map, we need a ruler to say how close two pins are. There are three rulers in common use. They sound mathematical, but each tells a simple, intuitive story.

1. Cosine similarity — "do they point the same way?"

Picture each vector as an arrow starting at the centre of the map. Cosine similarity ignores how long the arrows are and asks only: do they point in the same direction? Two arrows pointing the same way score 1.0 (identical meaning). At right angles they score 0 (unrelated). Pointing opposite ways gives -1. Because it ignores length, cosine doesn't care that one text is long and another short — it compares pure direction, which is why it's the default for text.

2. Dot product — "same direction and how strong?"

The dot product is cosine's cousin that also lets length count. Longer arrows pointing the same way score higher. This matters only when your vectors have different lengths. Here's the quiet trick most teams use: if you first normalize every vector to length 1 (scale each arrow so it's exactly one unit long), then dot product and cosine give the identical answer — but dot product is faster to compute. That's why production systems normalize once at index time and then use the cheap dot product everywhere.

3. Euclidean distance (L2) — "how far apart are the tips?"

Euclidean distance is the everyday "straight line between two points" ruler you learned in school. Smaller means closer. It's sensitive to length, so it behaves differently from cosine on un-normalized vectors — but on normalized vectors, Euclidean and cosine rank results in the same order. It's common in some image and clustering tasks.

Here is the whole idea in a few lines of real code, using NumPy (the standard Python maths library):

# Compare a query vector against two candidate chunk vectors.
import numpy as np                                  # NumPy handles vector maths quickly

query = np.array([0.90, 0.10, -0.05])               # the question "went below zero" as a (tiny, pretend) vector
fee   = np.array([0.91, 0.12, -0.08])               # chunk about the overdraft fee — should be the winner
mort  = np.array([-0.20, 0.77, 0.30])               # chunk about mortgage rates — should lose

def cosine(a, b):                                   # cosine = direction-only similarity, range -1..1
    return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))  # dot product divided by both lengths

print("fee  :", round(cosine(query, fee), 3))       # expect close to 1.0 — same direction/meaning
print("mort :", round(cosine(query, mort), 3))      # expect low — different direction/meaning

q = query / np.linalg.norm(query)                   # normalize: rescale the arrow to length 1
f = fee   / np.linalg.norm(fee)                     # once both are length 1...
print("dot(normalized):", round(q @ f, 3))          # ...plain dot product now equals cosine — but faster
▶ Output
fee : 0.999
mort : -0.047
dot(normalized): 0.999

The fee chunk scores almost a perfect 1.0; the mortgage chunk scores near zero. And see the last line: once both vectors are normalized, the bare dot product (q @ f) gives the same 0.999 as cosine. That's the production shortcut in a nutshell.

RulerCares about length?Use it when…
CosineNo — direction onlyThe safe default for text embeddings; robust to text length.
Dot productYesVectors are already normalized (then it equals cosine but faster), or length is meaningful.
Euclidean (L2)YesClustering, some image/vision tasks; on normalized vectors it ranks like cosine.
⚠ Watch out

The metric you search with must match how the model was trained and how you stored the vectors. Pick "dot product" in your vector database but feed it un-normalized vectors from a cosine-trained model, and your rankings quietly go wrong — no error, just worse answers. When in doubt: normalize, then use cosine (or dot). OpenAI's embeddings already come normalized to length 1, so cosine and dot product agree out of the box.

Going deeper — scores are rankings, not probabilities

A trap that fools newcomers: a cosine score of 0.82 is not "82% relevant." These numbers are only meaningful relative to each other within one model — they rank candidates, they don't calibrate confidence. Two different models living on two different maps will hand you totally different score ranges for the same pair of texts, so a threshold you tuned for one model is meaningless for another.

A second surprise is the curse of dimensionality. In a space of 1536 dimensions, almost every pair of random vectors is roughly at right angles — so unrelated texts tend to score near 0, and even "quite related" texts might only reach 0.3–0.5. Don't panic that your scores look low; what matters is the gap between the top hit and the rest, not the absolute number. This is also why embedding models are deliberately trained to pull genuinely-related pairs far above that background noise — the training does the work so cosine can simply read off the direction.

Why cosine for text specifically? Because document length shouldn't change meaning. A two-line overdraft FAQ and a two-page overdraft policy are "about" the same thing; cosine ignores the length difference and compares pure direction, so both land near the overdraft query. Euclidean, which is sensitive to length, would unfairly rank the short one differently — one reason it's rarely the default for raw text search.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist engineer debugs "why is retrieval worse since the upgrade?" The query "how much is the overdraft charge?" used to score 0.88 against the fee chunk; now it scores 0.41 and loses to a marketing blurb. The culprit: the new vector database was configured for dot product, but the vectors were stored un-normalized — so a long, wordy marketing chunk won purely by having a longer arrow. Switching the collection's metric to cosine (or normalizing at index time) instantly restored the old rankings. No error was ever thrown — just quietly wrong answers for a week.

⚙️ In production

The metric is a config choice you make once, everywhere. Your vector database stores an index built for a specific distance (cosine, dot, or L2); the query must use the same one, and switching it means rebuilding the index, not flipping a flag. Performance: at query time the database runs this comparison millions of times, so it leans on SIMD/AVX CPU instructions (or GPUs) to do many multiply-adds at once — which is exactly why teams normalize at ingest and use the bare dot product: it's the cheapest inner loop. Monitoring: log the score distribution of live queries. If the median top-1 score suddenly drifts down, something upstream changed — a new model version, a normalization bug, or a corrupted batch — and your recall is silently degrading. For a bank: treat the "best score" as a safety signal too — when even the top match is weak, that's your cue to answer "I don't have that information" rather than let the model guess from a 0.2 match.

When to use each: cosine (or normalized dot product) for virtually all text retrieval — it's the safe default. Plain dot product when your vectors are already length-1 and you want the fastest compute. Euclidean (L2) for clustering and some image/vision work. When NOT to: never mix metrics between how you built the index and how you query it, and never read a raw similarity score as a probability or compare scores across two different models.

🧠 Remember it

Cosine = which way you point. Euclidean = how far apart you stand. Normalize first, and dot product is just cheap cosine.

Three flavours of embedding: dense, sparse, and multi-vector (ColBERT)

Not all embeddings are one neat vector. There are three families, and knowing their strengths is how you stop a banking search from missing exact codes and account numbers.

So far we've pictured "one text → one vector." That's the most common kind, but it's only one of three families. Each solves a different problem, and in banking you often need more than one.

Dense embeddings — one rich vector of meaning

This is the kind we've met: one fixed-length vector (say 1536 numbers), almost all of them non-zero, packing the whole meaning of the text into a dense bundle. Dense is brilliant at paraphrase — "went below zero" finds "overdraft" — but it's fuzzy about exact strings. An account number like 4021-8876 or a code like "Regulation E" has no real "meaning" to spread across the map, so dense search can slide right past it.

Sparse embeddings — a vector that's mostly zeros

A sparse embedding has one slot for every word in a huge vocabulary — tens of thousands of slots — and nearly all of them are zero, with a non-zero weight only for the words that actually appear. This is the modern form of classic keyword search (the famous BM25 algorithm is sparse). It nails exact matches: "Form 1099," an ISIN (a security's global ID code), a specific account number. Smarter learned sparse models like SPLADE even add a few related words ("overdraft" might also light up "NSF"), getting a touch of meaning while staying exact. The weakness is the mirror of dense: sparse is blind to pure paraphrase.

Multi-vector / ColBERT — many little vectors, matched late

Instead of squashing a whole chunk into one vector, ColBERT keeps one vector per word (token). A 100-word chunk becomes 100 small vectors. At search time it does late interaction: for each word in your question, it finds that word's best-matching word in the chunk, then adds up those best matches (this scoring is called MaxSim). It's like comparing two documents word-by-word instead of gist-to-gist, which captures fine detail that a single vector blurs away. The result is noticeably better retrieval — especially on unfamiliar, out-of-domain text — at the cost of storing many vectors per chunk. Newer versions (ColBERTv2, PLAID) shrink that storage a lot.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist user asks, "does Reg E cover my disputed $40 card charge?" Dense search understands "disputed charge" beautifully but can wobble on the exact token "Reg E." Sparse search locks onto "Reg E" instantly but misses that "disputed charge" relates to the chargeback policy. Run both and merge — that's why banks almost always combine dense + sparse. The exact codes and account numbers that fill a bank's documents are precisely where pure dense search is weakest.

FlavourGreat atWeak atCost
DenseParaphrase, synonyms, meaningExact codes, rare IDsLow (one vector)
Sparse (BM25 / SPLADE)Exact terms, codes, numbersPure paraphraseLow–medium
Multi-vector (ColBERT)Highest accuracy, out-of-domain textStorage & computeHigh (many vectors)

Going deeper — hybrid search and how you fuse two rankings

Because dense and sparse fail in opposite ways, the production answer is almost never "pick one" — it's hybrid search: run a dense search and a sparse/BM25 search, then merge their two ranked lists into one. The catch is that their scores live on different scales (a BM25 score of 14.2 and a cosine of 0.81 can't be compared directly), so you can't just add them. The standard, robust fix is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): throw away the raw scores and combine by rank position instead — a chunk that ranks #2 in dense and #1 in sparse scores higher than one that's #1 in dense but #40 in sparse. RRF needs no tuning and no score normalization, which is why most databases ship it as the default fusion.

Some numbers to ground the tradeoffs. A dense vector is a fixed cost — 1536 floats no matter how long the text. A learned-sparse SPLADE vector stores only the handful of non-zero term weights, so it's compact and slots into the same inverted-index machinery that classic search engines already run. ColBERT is the heavyweight: storing one vector per token can mean 100× more vectors than dense, which is why early ColBERT indexes were enormous. ColBERTv2 and PLAID attack exactly that — compressing those token vectors and pruning the search — bringing storage down to something a few times larger than dense rather than a hundred times.

⚙️ In production

Running hybrid for real. You maintain two indexes over the same chunks — one dense (HNSW), one sparse (BM25/SPLADE) — and fuse at query time. Latency: the two searches run in parallel, so hybrid adds little wall-clock time, but it roughly doubles the work and the storage, which is the real cost. Which systems do it: Weaviate, Qdrant, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and Milvus offer native hybrid with built-in fusion; pgvector can be paired with Postgres full-text search and fused in SQL. Monitoring: track dense-only vs sparse-only vs fused recall on a labelled set, because the right fusion weight shifts as your corpus changes. For a bank: hybrid is close to mandatory — your documents are dense with exact tokens (account numbers, "Regulation E", ISINs, form codes, SWIFT/BIC) that pure dense search slides past. ColBERT (via a re-ranking pass on a shortlist) is worth the storage only for high-value, accuracy-critical corpora where the dense+sparse combo still misses.

⚠ Watch out

Shipping a bank assistant on dense-only search is the quiet classic mistake. It demos beautifully on paraphrase questions, then fails in production the first time a customer quotes an exact form number, dispute code, or account reference — the model confidently answers from a loosely-related chunk because the exact-match chunk never made the top-K. And beware the opposite over-correction: adding ColBERT "for accuracy" without budgeting for its storage can balloon your index many times over and surprise you with the bill.

When to use each: dense for meaning and paraphrase; sparse (BM25/SPLADE) for exact codes and rare terms; hybrid (dense + sparse fused) as the default for banking; ColBERT/multi-vector when you need the last few points of accuracy and can afford the storage. When NOT to: don't deploy dense-only where exact identifiers matter, and don't reach for ColBERT at large scale before you've proven cheaper hybrid isn't already good enough on your own questions.

🧠 Remember it

Dense = gist. Sparse = exact words. ColBERT = word-by-word. Banks live on exact codes, so dense alone is never enough.

Two numbers that define a model: dimensions and max input tokens

Before you pick any embedding model, two specs decide how it fits your system: how long each vector is, and how much text it can read at once.

Every embedding model comes with two headline numbers. They're easy to mix up, so let's separate them cleanly with a simple picture: the model is a machine with an in-tray (how much text it accepts) and an out-tray (how big a vector it emits).

Dimensions — the length of the output vector

Dimensions is simply how many numbers are in each vector. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small outputs 1536 numbers; text-embedding-3-large outputs 3072; many open models like BGE output 768 or 1024. More dimensions can capture more nuance, but they cost more to store and compare — every extra dimension is extra memory per vector and extra maths per search. Multiply by millions of chunks and the difference is real money. A 3072-dim index is roughly 4× the storage of a 768-dim one.

Max input tokens — how much text fits in one embedding

Max input tokens is the size of the in-tray: the longest piece of text the model will read before it truncates. A token is a chunk of a word (roughly ¾ of an English word on average). OpenAI's v3 models accept up to 8191 tokens — comfortably a long document section. But many popular open models, like BGE-v1.5, cap at just 512 tokens — only a few paragraphs. Newer long-context open models (Nomic Embed, E5-Mistral, Qwen3-Embedding) stretch to 8192 tokens and beyond.

⚠ Watch out

Feed a model more text than its max tokens and it doesn't error — it silently truncates, embedding only the first part and throwing the rest away. If your chunks are 800 tokens but your model caps at 512, the last third of every chunk vanishes from the vector — and you'll never see a warning, only mysteriously worse retrieval. Your chunk size must fit inside your model's token limit, with room to spare.

ModelDimensionsMax input tokens
OpenAI text-embedding-3-small1536 (reducible)8191
OpenAI text-embedding-3-large3072 (reducible)8191
BAAI bge-large-en-v1.51024512
Nomic Embed Text v1.5768 (down to 64)8192
Qwen3-Embedding (0.6B–8B)up to 4096up to 32k

Figures current as of late 2026; always confirm on the model's own card, since specs change.

Going deeper — how big a vector do you actually need?

More dimensions is not automatically better. Each extra dimension can store more nuance, but it also adds storage, slows every comparison, and — past a point — captures diminishing scraps of meaning while still costing full price. For most retrieval tasks the quality curve flattens out well before the maximum: a 1536-dim OpenAI vector is often indistinguishable from a 3072-dim one on real banking questions, at half the storage. Many modern models even let you ask for a shorter vector (OpenAI's dimensions parameter, Nomic's resize-down) precisely because the full length is usually overkill. The right move is to measure retrieval quality at a few lengths on your own data and keep the shortest that still answers well.

The token limit, meanwhile, interacts directly with how you split documents. If your model caps at 512 tokens, your chunks must comfortably fit under that — leaving headroom for any instruction prefix the model wants. OpenAI's 8191-token ceiling is generous, but embedding a huge 8000-token blob is usually a bad idea anyway: the pooled vector becomes an averaged mush that's "a little about everything and precisely about nothing," so it matches weakly on specific questions. Long limits give you freedom; they don't excuse giant chunks.

Before you embed, it pays to actually count the tokens so you know nothing will be silently cut:

# Check a chunk fits the model's input limit BEFORE embedding it.
import tiktoken                                       # OpenAI's tokenizer library — counts tokens exactly as the model will

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")           # the encoding used by text-embedding-3 models
chunk = open("overdraft_policy_section.txt").read()  # one chunk we intend to store

n_tokens = len(enc.encode(chunk))                    # how many tokens this chunk really is
MAX = 8191                                            # the model's hard input ceiling

if n_tokens > MAX:                                    # guard: refuse to embed something that would be truncated
    raise ValueError(f"chunk is {n_tokens} tokens, over the {MAX} limit — split it first")
print(n_tokens, "tokens — safe to embed")            # proven to fit, no silent tail-loss
▶ Output
612 tokens — safe to embed

This tiny guard turns an invisible failure (a silently chopped chunk) into a loud, fixable error at ingest time — exactly where you want to catch it.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's first prototype used a popular open model capped at 512 tokens, but the team chunked their mortgage policy into 800-token sections "to keep each topic whole." Retrieval looked fine in testing — until a customer asked about a clause that happened to live in the last third of a chunk. That text had been silently truncated before embedding, so its meaning was never in the vector and the clause was simply unfindable.
