The fix wasn't a better model; it was matching the chunk size to the in-tray: 400-token chunks with overlap, comfortably inside the 512 limit.

⚙️ In production

Storage math you can do on a napkin. A float32 vector costs dimensions × 4 bytes. So 10 million chunks at 1536 dims ≈ 10M × 1536 × 4 ≈ 61 GB of raw vectors — and an HNSW index adds roughly another 30–50% on top for its graph links, all of it wanting to live in RAM for speed. Jump to 3072 dims and you've doubled that bill for often-negligible quality gain. Latency scales with dimensions too: every comparison is a dot product over that many numbers, millions of times per query. Monitoring: log a counter whenever an input hits the token ceiling and gets truncated — a rising count means your chunker drifted and search quality is eroding. For a bank: fix your dimension and token-limit choices before you index millions of documents, because changing either later means re-embedding the whole corpus — a budgeted migration, not a quick edit.

When to use more dimensions / a longer token limit: when measured accuracy on your data genuinely improves, or your natural passages are long and self-contained. When NOT to: don't default to the biggest model "to be safe" — oversized vectors waste RAM and money for little gain, and oversized chunks produce mushy, weakly-matching vectors. Pick the smallest dimensions and chunk size that still answer your real questions.

🧠 Remember it

Tokens in, dimensions out. Your chunk must fit the in-tray, or the tail silently disappears.

Choosing an embedding model: hosted, open-source, and the instruction trap

The model you embed with sets the ceiling on retrieval quality — so choosing well matters, and one quiet "prefix" rule trips up almost every team that tries open-source.

There's no single "best" embedding model; there's the best one for your constraints — accuracy, cost, languages, and whether your data is allowed to leave your walls. Let's walk the real options a banking team weighs in 2026.

Hosted / API models — easiest to start

You call an API, you get vectors back. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small is the cheap, strong workhorse (1536 dims); text-embedding-3-large (3072 dims) is more accurate and a bit pricier (around $0.13 per million tokens). Others in this lane include Cohere and Voyage (Voyage models are notably strong on finance/legal text and quantization). The upside: zero infrastructure, great quality, instant start. The catch for banks: your text leaves your network. For regulated data you'll need the right data-processing agreement, or a private deployment — or you go open-source.

Open-source models — run them yourself, keep data in-house

You download the model and run it on your own machines, so customer text never leaves the bank. The strong families to know:

  • BGE (BAAI, from China) — long the open-source favourite; bge-large-en-v1.5 is a reliable English model; bge-m3 adds multilingual and can produce dense + sparse + multi-vector at once.
  • E5 (Microsoft) — the e5 and multilingual-e5 families; the bigger e5-mistral and -instruct variants are strong and long-context.
  • GTE (Alibaba) — "General Text Embeddings"; gte-large and the gte-Qwen2 models are well-rounded performers.
  • Nomic — nomic-embed-text-v1.5 is fully open (Apache-2.0), long-context (8192 tokens), and resizable from 768 down to 64 dims.
  • Qwen3-Embedding (Alibaba) — a 2025 family (0.6B / 4B / 8B) that topped the multilingual leaderboard; excellent if you need many languages and can host a larger model.

The instruction trap: "query:" and "passage:" prefixes

Here's the mistake that silently wrecks open-source retrieval for newcomers. Many of these models are instruction-tuned: they were trained expecting you to prepend a little label telling the model whether a text is a search query or a document to be found. Skip the label and quality quietly drops — no error, just worse results. The labels differ by model family:

  • E5: prepend "query: " to questions and "passage: " to documents. (The -instruct variant uses a different "Instruct: …\nQuery: …" format and no prefix on documents — mixing these up is a classic bug.)
  • Nomic: prepend "search_query: " to questions and "search_document: " to documents.
  • BGE v1.5: add a short instruction to queries only (optional — it gives a small boost); documents need nothing.
  • OpenAI: no prefixes — just send the raw text. Simpler, which is part of its appeal.
# Using an open-source E5 model locally with sentence-transformers.
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer   # popular library for running open embedding models

model = SentenceTransformer("intfloat/multilingual-e5-large")  # downloads & runs the model on your own hardware

# The prefixes are MANDATORY for E5 — this is the step beginners forget.
docs = ["passage: Overdraft item fee is $35; one waiver per 12 months."]  # "passage: " marks text to be stored/found
query = "query: how much is the overdraft charge?"       # "query: " marks the user's question

doc_vecs = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)  # normalize so we can use cosine/dot directly
q_vec    = model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)  # embed the query the SAME way as the docs

score = q_vec @ doc_vecs[0]                               # dot product on normalized vectors = cosine similarity
print(round(float(score), 3))                            # high score = the chunk answers the question
▶ Output
0.874

The normalize_embeddings=True flag does the length-1 rescaling for us, so the plain dot product on the last line is cosine similarity. And notice both the document and the query go through the same model — just with their correct prefixes.

✅ Tip

Don't agonise over the leaderboard's #1. Shortlist two or three models that fit your constraints (languages, token limit, can-it-stay-in-house), then test them on your own questions and documents. A model that tops a public benchmark on Wikipedia can lose to a humbler one on dense banking policy text. Your corpus is the only benchmark that counts.

Going deeper — the 2026 hosted field, beyond OpenAI

OpenAI is the easy default, but the hosted field has widened. Google's Gemini Embedding (gemini-embedding-001) is a strong general model with resizable output — you can ask it for a shorter vector to save storage (up to 3072 dims) — and it has topped parts of the public leaderboard. Voyage AI refreshed its line in early 2026 (the voyage-4 family), and remains a favourite for finance and legal text and for aggressive quantization. Cohere's Embed v4 leans into multimodal (text + images in one space) with a very long input window — useful when your "documents" include scanned statements or screenshots. On the open side, Qwen3-Embedding (0.6B / 4B / 8B) leads much of the multilingual board, and research models like NV-Embed push the English scores — but a bigger open model means a bigger GPU bill to serve it. The lesson isn't "chase the leader"; it's that there are now several credible choices, and the winner is decided on your corpus, not a leaderboard.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist shortlisted three models: OpenAI text-embedding-3-large (hosted, easiest), a multilingual open model (data stays in-house), and a finance-tuned hosted model. On a public benchmark the finance model looked best. But the team's real test — 300 actual customer questions against their own policy library — flipped the result: the "worse" open model actually won on their dense, jargon-heavy mortgage text, and kept every byte inside the bank's network, which the compliance team required. The leaderboard would have sent them the wrong way; their own 300 questions sent them the right way.

⚙️ In production

Hosted vs self-hosted is an operations decision, not just an accuracy one. A hosted API means no GPUs to run, elastic scale, and a per-token bill (roughly $0.02–$0.15 per million tokens), but your text leaves the building — so you need a data-processing agreement, a no-training guarantee, and often a specific region. Self-hosting an open model keeps data in-house and makes marginal embedding "free," but you now own GPU capacity, autoscaling, batching, and uptime; at bank query volumes that's a real platform to run. Either way: pin the exact model version, because a silent vendor update can shift the map under your stored vectors; budget for re-embedding when you upgrade; and load-test the throughput you'll actually need (embeddings sit on the hot path of every search and every ingest). For many banks the pragmatic answer is a hosted model behind a private endpoint, or an open model served in your own VPC.

⚠ Watch out

The instruction-prefix trap bites in a sneaky way: you must embed documents and queries with the same model but often with different prefixes ("passage: " vs "query: " for E5). Apply the wrong prefix — or the document prefix to a query — and recall quietly drops with no error. Worse, if you re-index documents later and forget the prefix that time, half your corpus now sits in the wrong place on the map. Bake the prefixes into one shared embedding function used by both the ingest path and the query path, so they can never drift apart.

When to use hosted: you want to ship fast, have no ML-ops team, and your data policy permits an external call (with the right agreement). When to use open-source / self-hosted: data must stay in-house, you need many languages or heavy volume where per-token fees add up, or you want full version control. When NOT to: don't pick a model off a leaderboard without testing it on your own questions, and don't self-host a large open model unless you're ready to run GPUs reliably.

🧠 Remember it

Hosted = fast start, data leaves. Open-source = data stays, you host. And for open models: forget the prefix, forget your recall.

Spending less without losing much: Matryoshka and quantization

Storing millions of big vectors gets expensive fast. Two clever tricks — shrinking the vector's length, and shrinking each number's precision — can cut storage by 4×, 32×, even more, with surprisingly little accuracy lost.

At scale, the dominant cost of a vector search system is memory — millions of vectors, each a long list of high-precision numbers, held in RAM for speed. Two independent levers shrink that bill. They stack.

Matryoshka embeddings — one model, many sizes

Named after Russian nesting dolls, Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) trains a model so that the first chunk of each vector is itself a complete, usable embedding. A 1536-dim vector from text-embedding-3-large can be cut to its first 512 — or 256 — numbers and still work well, because the most important meaning was packed into the front. You don't re-embed anything; you just keep fewer numbers. That's how OpenAI's dimensions parameter works, and why Nomic can hand you anything from 768 down to 64.

# Ask OpenAI for a SHORTER vector to save storage — Matryoshka in action.
from openai import OpenAI                     # official OpenAI client
client = OpenAI()                             # reads your API key from the environment

resp = client.embeddings.create(              # the embedding call
    model="text-embedding-3-large",           # a 3072-dim model by default
    input="Overdraft item fee is $35.",       # the chunk to embed
    dimensions=512,                           # ask for only the first 512 numbers — 6x smaller, no re-training
)
print(len(resp.data[0].embedding))            # confirms we got a 512-length vector back
▶ Output
512

You just turned a 3072-dim index into a 512-dim one — roughly 6× less storage — with a single parameter and no re-embedding. Measure the small accuracy drop on your data and keep the shortest length that still answers well.

Quantization — fewer bits per number

Each dimension is normally a float32 — a high-precision number using 4 bytes. Quantization stores it more coarsely:

  • int8 — squeeze each number into a single byte. ~4× smaller, and with a rescoring pass accuracy stays close to the full-precision original.
  • binary — keep just one bit per number: is it positive or negative? Up to 32× smaller. Astonishingly, on high-dimensional vectors this still retrieves surprisingly well — because with thousands of dimensions, even "just the signs" carries a lot of the meaning.

The rescoring pattern — cheap first, precise second

Binary vectors sound too lossy to trust alone, and used alone they are. The production move is a two-pass rescoring (also called oversampling): do a fast, rough search with the tiny binary vectors to pull a generous candidate list (say the top 200), then re-rank just those few using the full-precision vectors. You get binary's ~32× storage saving and near-full accuracy, because the expensive precise comparison only runs on a handful of survivors. Every serious vector database — Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Elasticsearch — supports this.

⚠ Watch out

Shrink too far and recall falls off a cliff. Binary without rescoring, or Matryoshka truncated below its "quality knee," can quietly drop the right chunk. Never trust vendor compression claims blindly — measure recall against your full-precision index on your queries, then back off to the smallest setting that still passes. Compression is a dial you tune with evidence, not a switch you flip on faith.

Going deeper — the two levers stack, and each has a "knee"

Matryoshka and quantization are independent, so they multiply. Take a 3072-dim float32 vector, truncate it to 1024 dims (Matryoshka, ~3× smaller), then store those as int8 (quantization, ~4× smaller) and you're at roughly 12× smaller with modest accuracy loss; go binary instead of int8 and the savings climb further. But each lever has a quality knee — a point where recall was holding steady and then falls off a cliff. For Matryoshka, cutting from 1536→512 might cost you almost nothing while 512→128 suddenly craters; for quantization, int8 is usually near-lossless with rescoring while raw binary without rescoring can drop 10–20 points of recall. The knee's location depends on your model and your data, which is exactly why you measure rather than guess.

Why does binary work at all? With thousands of dimensions, the pattern of signs (which dimensions are positive vs negative) already encodes most of the direction of the vector — and direction is what cosine cares about. Comparing two binary vectors becomes a bitwise XOR plus a popcount (count the differing bits), an operation modern CPUs do blisteringly fast — which is the other half of binary's appeal: not just 32× smaller, but dramatically cheaper to compare in the first sweep.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's archive of statements, emails, and dispute threads grew to 40 million chunks, and the full-precision HNSW index needed hundreds of gigabytes of RAM — a painful server bill. The team switched the cold archive to binary vectors with int8 rescoring: the first pass sweeps all 40 million tiny binary vectors to grab the top 200 candidates, then re-ranks just those 200 with fuller-precision vectors. Memory dropped by well over an order of magnitude, p99 latency actually improved (the sweep is faster), and measured recall stayed within a point of the original. One dial, measured carefully, turned an eye-watering RAM bill into a rounding error.

⚙️ In production

Every serious vector database ships these as settings. Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate and Elasticsearch all support int8/binary quantization with an oversample-and-rescore pass; OpenAI and Nomic expose Matryoshka via a dimensions parameter. The rescore knob matters: you oversample the first pass (grab top 200 to return 5) — too little oversampling and binary's roughness drops the real winner before the precise pass can rescue it; too much and you lose the speed benefit. Tune it against recall. Memory tiering: a common bank pattern is hot data (recent, frequently queried) on full-precision HNSW and cold archives on binary+rescore — right precision for the right tier. Monitoring: keep a small full-precision ground-truth index and re-measure recall after any compression change, every model upgrade, and periodically in production, because a corpus that drifts can move the knee. Caution for audits: record which precision produced which result tier, so a compliance review can reason about why an answer was or wasn't retrieved.

When to use compression: at scale (millions of vectors) where RAM is your dominant cost, especially for large, rarely-updated archives. When NOT to: on small collections (a few hundred thousand vectors) compression saves pennies and just adds complexity — keep full precision. And never ship binary (or deeply-truncated Matryoshka) without a rescoring pass and a measured recall number; unrescored binary alone is a quiet recall disaster.

🧠 Remember it

Matryoshka trims the vector's length; quantization trims each number's bits. Sweep cheap, judge precise — that's rescoring.

Living with embeddings: the same-model rule, re-indexing, and other uses

A few operational truths separate a demo from a system you can run for years — starting with the one rule you can never break.

The same-model rule (the one you must never break)

Different embedding models build different maps of meaning. A vector from OpenAI and a vector from BGE are coordinates on two totally different maps — comparing them is like using Paris street numbers to navigate Tokyo. So the ironclad rule: you must embed your documents and your queries with the exact same model (and version). If you ever switch models, every stored vector becomes meaningless and you must re-embed your entire corpus from scratch — a full migration, not a config tweak. Always store the model name and version alongside your vectors so you know what built them.

⚠ Watch out

The silent killer: mixing vectors from two models (or two versions of one model) in a single index. There's no error — searches just return subtly wrong, garbage-adjacent results, and teams burn days blaming the retriever. Changing your embedding model invalidates the whole index. Plan re-embedding as a scheduled, budgeted migration with a blue/green swap, never an afterthought.

Two habits that save money and sanity

  • Normalize once. Scale every vector to length 1 at index time, so cosine and the cheaper dot product agree and your database can use its fastest path.
  • Batch your embedding calls. Sending 1000 chunks one at a time is slow and, on APIs, expensive in overhead. Send them in batches (e.g. 100–2048 texts per call) — far fewer round-trips, much faster indexing.

The MTEB leaderboard — a starting point, not a verdict

The MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) is a public leaderboard on Hugging Face that scores embedding models across dozens of tasks and many languages. It's the standard first stop for a shortlist — but treat it the way you'd treat a car's advertised fuel economy: useful for comparison, not a promise about your commute. Scores drift monthly, some models quietly over-fit the benchmark, and a leader on general web text can underperform on dense financial jargon. Use MTEB to pick two or three candidates, then let your own data decide the winner.

Embeddings aren't just for RAG

Once you can turn text into meaning-vectors, a whole toolbox opens up — handy to know, because these are some of the highest-value, lowest-effort wins in a bank:

  • Deduplication — near-identical complaints or help-centre pages have near-identical vectors; cluster them to find and merge duplicates.
  • Classification — embed an incoming complaint and see which labelled cluster it's nearest to ("card fraud" vs "fee dispute") — a cheap, fast classifier with no training loop.
  • Recommendation — "customers who read this product page" → find the nearest product vectors to suggest related offerings.
  • Anomaly detection — a transaction description or support message whose vector sits far from every normal cluster is an outlier worth a second look — a useful signal in fraud and AML screening.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's team embedded six months of support tickets — not for RAG, but to cluster them. Overnight, thousands of free-text complaints sorted themselves into tidy neighbourhoods: "disputed card charge," "app login fails," "overdraft surprise." Suddenly the bank could see which problems were growing, route new tickets automatically, and spot three near-duplicate help articles to merge. Same embeddings, zero extra models — just a different use of the map.

Going deeper — store the metadata that makes the rule enforceable

The same-model rule is only safe if you can prove which model built each vector. The habit that saves you is tagging every stored vector with its provenance, so a mismatch becomes visible instead of silent:

# Store provenance beside every vector so the same-model rule is auditable.
record = {                                        # one row we upsert into the vector database
    "id": "doc_8842_chunk_3",                     # stable id so we can re-embed or delete this exact chunk later
    "vector": vec,                                # the embedding itself
    "payload": {                                  # metadata travels with the vector
        "embed_model": "text-embedding-3-small",  # WHICH model drew this point on the map
        "embed_version": "2024-01",               # and which version — vendors update models silently
        "embed_dims": 1536,                       # the dimension count, so a mismatch is caught on read
        "source": "overdraft_policy.pdf",         # where the text came from, for citations and re-ingest
    },
}

Now a query path can assert embed_model matches the model it's about to query with, and your re-index job knows exactly what to rebuild. Without this, a model mix-up is invisible until users complain.

⚙️ In production

Re-embedding is a migration, so run it like one. When BankAssist upgrades its embedding model, it does not edit the live index — it builds a new index from scratch with the new model while the old one keeps answering, validates recall against a labelled question set, then swaps traffic (blue/green) and retires the old index. Cost & time: re-embedding tens of millions of chunks is hours of compute and a real (if modest) API bill — plan it, don't improvise it. Dual-write window: during the rebuild, new documents must be embedded into both indexes, or the new one launches already stale. Batch economics: ingest paths send hundreds-to-thousands of texts per call, and OpenAI's Batch API runs embeddings at roughly half price for non-urgent backfills. Monitoring: watch top-1 score distribution and a recall sample after the swap — if they sag, roll back to the still-warm old index. For a bank: keep the old index around until the new one has proven itself in production, and log the model/version per vector so audits can always answer "what produced this answer?"

When to switch embedding models: when a new model measurably beats your current one on your own questions, or compliance/data-residency forces a move — and you've budgeted a full re-index. When NOT to: never swap models casually or mix two models' vectors in one index; and don't re-embed chasing a leaderboard bump that doesn't show up on your evaluation — the migration cost rarely pays back.

🧠 Remember it

One map, one model. Change the model, re-draw the whole map. And remember embeddings cluster, classify, and flag outliers — not just retrieve.

What a vector database does, and why "approximate" beats "exact"

A vector database has one superpower: given a query vector, find its nearest neighbours among millions — in milliseconds. The secret is being willing to be almost perfect.

You have ten million chunk-vectors on your meaning-map. A question arrives, you embed it, and now you need the handful of stored vectors closest to it. How?

The exact way — and why it doesn't scale

The honest approach is brute force: compare the query to every single stored vector, sort by closeness, return the top few. This is called Flat or exact search, and it gives 100% correct results — the true nearest neighbours, guaranteed. The problem is speed: ten million comparisons per query, every query. Fine for ten thousand vectors; hopeless for ten million at a customer-facing speed.

The approximate way — the big idea behind vector DBs

Here's the insight that makes vector search practical: you almost never need the perfect nearest neighbours — you need very-nearly-the-nearest, extremely fast. Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search builds a clever index ahead of time so that at query time it only examines a small, promising slice of the data instead of all of it. It might miss the true #7 result and return #9 instead — a tiny quality cost — in exchange for being hundreds of times faster. That trade is almost always worth it, and it's what every production vector database is built around.

We measure the quality cost with recall: of the true top-K nearest neighbours, what fraction did the approximate search actually find? Recall of 0.95 means it found 19 of the true top 20 — usually plenty. The whole game of tuning a vector index is the recall-vs-speed-vs-memory triangle: push one corner and the others move.

✅ Tip

Always keep a small Flat (exact) index on a sample of your data as a "ground truth." Run your ANN index against it and measure recall. Reporting query speed without recall is meaningless — a lightning-fast index that returns the wrong chunks is worse than useless. Speed and recall are a pair; never quote one alone.

Going deeper — a database does more than nearest-neighbour math

"Find the nearest vectors" is the headline, but a real vector database earns its keep on the un-glamorous parts around it. It has to filter (return only this customer's chunks) while searching, not after. It has to handle updates and deletes — documents change, customers exercise their right to be forgotten — without rebuilding the whole index each time. It has to persist to disk so a restart doesn't lose everything, replicate for high availability, and back up for recovery. And it has to do nearest-neighbour search and all of that concurrently, under load, at a stable latency. The ANN index is the engine; the database is the whole car.

The quality/speed trade isn't one fixed setting either — it's a curve. Every index exposes knobs that let you buy more recall with more time per query (or more memory). Teams plot recall vs queries-per-second (QPS) and pick the point that meets their latency budget at their target recall, rather than treating "fast" or "accurate" as absolutes.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist starts with 50,000 policy chunks. At that size, honestly, a brute-force scan returns the exact nearest neighbours in a few milliseconds — no fancy index needed. But as the bank ingests statements, emails, and dispute threads, the collection crosses 10 million vectors, and brute force now takes hundreds of milliseconds per query — unacceptable when thousands of customers are chatting at once. Switching to an approximate index drops per-query time back to single-digit milliseconds at 98% recall. The customers never notice the missing 2% (it was the 20th-best chunk, not the 1st); they absolutely would have noticed a two-second wait.

⚙️ In production

Four numbers define a vector-search service: recall (did it find the right chunks?), p99 latency (how slow is the worst 1% of queries?), QPS (how many concurrent searches can it sustain?), and memory footprint. You tune the index to hit a target like "recall ≥ 0.95 and p99 < 50 ms at 500 QPS." Scale: past one machine you shard (split vectors across nodes) and replicate (copies for throughput and failover). Failure modes: a cold cache after restart makes the first queries slow until the index is warm; an index that doesn't fit in RAM spills to disk and latency explodes; and recall silently drifts down as data grows if you never re-check it. For a bank: this service holds customer data, so it needs encryption at rest and in transit, access controls, audit logging of queries, backups, and a disaster-recovery plan — the same bar as any system of record, because effectively it is one.

⚠ Watch out

Vendor benchmarks are measured on clean, unfiltered, in-memory data — your production reality is messier. Recall measured with no metadata filter can be far higher than recall when you also demand "only this customer's docs," because filtering interacts with the ANN graph in ways that can starve the search. Always benchmark recall and latency with your real filters, at your real scale, on your real queries. A number from a vendor slide is a sales artifact, not a production guarantee.

When to use a vector database: once you're past roughly 100,000 vectors, or need concurrent queries, metadata filtering, live updates, persistence, and HA — i.e. anything customer-facing. When NOT to: for a few thousand vectors in a prototype, an in-memory brute-force search (or a library like FAISS) is simpler, exact, and plenty fast — don't stand up distributed infrastructure for a problem a laptop solves.

🧠 Remember it

A vector DB trades a crumb of recall for a feast of speed. "Nearly the nearest, right now" beats "exactly the nearest, eventually."

Inside the index: Flat, HNSW, IVF, and PQ

Four index designs power almost every vector database. Each makes a different bet on the recall-speed-memory triangle — and knowing them lets you pick (and tune) the right one for your scale.

"Approximate search" isn't one algorithm; it's a family of index structures. Here are the four you'll actually meet, told as four strategies a librarian might use to find a book fast.

Flat — read every spine

Flat is the brute-force baseline: compare the query to every vector. Perfect recall, no tuning, but linear slowdown as data grows. Use it up to roughly 10,000–100,000 vectors, or as the ground-truth yardstick for measuring everything else.

HNSW — a network of "who's near whom"

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small-World graph) is the default in most vector databases, and the best all-rounder. Picture a social network of vectors: each vector is linked to its nearest neighbours, with a few long-range "express" links layered on top. To search, you drop in anywhere and keep hopping to whichever linked neighbour is closer to the query — like asking "who do you know that's nearer?" and following the chain. You reach the neighbourhood in a handful of hops instead of scanning everything. It's fast with high recall; the price is memory — the whole graph plus vectors must sit in RAM. Three knobs tune it:

  • M — how many neighbour links each vector keeps. Higher = better recall, more memory.
  • efConstruction — how hard it works while building the graph. Higher = better graph, slower build.
  • efSearch — how many candidates it explores per query. Higher = better recall, slower search. This is your live recall/latency dial.

IVF — sort books into labelled shelves first

IVF (Inverted File) first clusters all vectors into, say, 1000 groups (nlist), each with a centre. At query time it finds the few nearest cluster-centres and only searches inside those cells (nprobe of them) — ignoring the rest. Far less memory than HNSW; the dial is nprobe (search more cells = higher recall, slower). It needs a quick "training" step to learn the clusters, and suits very large, fairly static collections.

PQ — shorthand the books to save shelf space

PQ (Product Quantization) is a compression trick, usually bolted onto IVF (giving IVF-PQ). It chops each vector into small sub-pieces and replaces each with a short code from a learned codebook — shrinking memory dramatically, at some accuracy cost. It's how you fit billions of vectors in memory. Because the codes are approximate, IVF-PQ is almost always paired with a full-precision rescoring pass (sweep cheap with the codes, judge precise on the survivors).

IndexRecallSpeedMemoryBest for
FlatPerfect (100%)Slow at scaleFull<100K vectors; ground-truth baseline
HNSWVery highVery fastHigh (all in RAM)The default for most apps
IVFTunable (nprobe)FastLowerLarge, mostly-static corpora
IVF-PQLower (rescore to recover)FastLowestBillions of vectors on a budget
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist starts with 50,000 policy chunks on plain HNSW — fast, simple, perfect for the scale. A year later, after ingesting every statement, email, and dispute thread, the index hits 40 million vectors and the RAM bill screams. The team moves the cold, rarely-touched history to IVF-PQ with rescoring (tiny memory, recall recovered on the second pass) and keeps the hot, recent policy docs on HNSW. Right tool, right tier — the defaults that worked at 50K would have bankrupted them at 40M.

⚠ Watch out

Defaults that sing at 100K vectors can collapse at 10M. The classic traps: efSearch left too low so recall silently craters as data grows; rebuilding an HNSW graph from scratch on every tiny update instead of upserting; and assuming HNSW's RAM scales linearly (it doesn't — plan memory before you hit the wall).

Going deeper — build time, deletes, and the disk option

Each index has a hidden cost beyond search speed. HNSW builds slowly: inserting millions of vectors while wiring up neighbour links takes real time and lots of RAM, and deletes are awkward — most implementations tombstone the node (mark it dead) rather than truly remove it, so a corpus with heavy churn slowly bloats and eventually wants a rebuild. IVF needs training: it must first learn its cluster centres from a sample, and if your data distribution drifts over months, those centres go stale and recall sags until you retrain. PQ trades accuracy for size, which is why it's almost always rescored.

There's also a fourth family worth knowing: disk-based indexes like DiskANN (and the Vamana graph behind it). Instead of demanding everything in RAM like HNSW, they keep most of the graph on fast SSD and only a compressed summary in memory — so you can serve billions of vectors from one machine at a fraction of HNSW's memory cost, trading a little latency for a huge drop in RAM spend. Several databases now offer it as the "big but budget" option between HNSW and IVF-PQ.

⚙️ In production

Pick the index by scale and update pattern, then tune with evidence. HNSW is the right default up to a few million vectors on a healthy RAM budget; set efSearch from a recall measurement, not a guess, and raise it if recall drifts as data grows. IVF (or IVF-PQ) suits large, mostly-static corpora where memory is the constraint — and remember to retrain the clusters after big data changes. IVF-PQ or DiskANN is how you reach hundreds of millions to billions affordably, always with a rescore pass. Operational gotchas: budget build time and RAM before you hit the wall (HNSW memory is super-linear, not linear); upsert incrementally rather than rebuilding on every change; and keep a Flat ground-truth index on a sample so you can measure recall continuously. For a bank: churny data (customers deleted for GDPR, documents superseded) favours indexes that handle deletes gracefully — or a scheduled rebuild window — so tombstones don't quietly rot your index.

When to use each: Flat for <100K vectors or as the recall yardstick; HNSW as the all-round default for low-latency apps that fit in RAM; IVF for large static collections where memory matters; IVF-PQ or DiskANN for billions on a budget. When NOT to: don't run HNSW once the index no longer fits in RAM (latency falls off a cliff), don't use IVF for tiny or highly-dynamic data (the training overhead isn't worth it), and never ship PQ without a full-precision rescore.

🧠 Remember it

Flat = read all. HNSW = hop the graph. IVF = shelf then search. PQ = shorthand to save space. HNSW for speed, IVF-PQ for billions.

The vector database landscape: picking the right home for your vectors

A dozen vector stores compete for your workload. You don't need to memorise them — you need a map of which one fits which situation.

Once you understand indexes, choosing a database is mostly about operations: do you already run Postgres? Do you need it managed? How big will you get? Here's the honest lay of the land in 2026, grouped by the decision you're actually making.

Libraries vs. databases

First, a distinction that trips people up. FAISS (from Meta) is a library, not a database — a brilliant, battle-tested toolkit of ANN index implementations that you embed in your own code. It has no server, no metadata filtering, no persistence out of the box; you build those around it. Many actual databases use FAISS-like techniques under the hood. Reach for FAISS for research, notebooks, or when you want total control and will handle the plumbing yourself.

The practical choices, by situation

  • pgvector — a PostgreSQL extension. If you already run Postgres, start here. Your vectors live right beside your relational data, you get real transactions and SQL filtering for free, and there's no new system to operate. Perfect until you genuinely outgrow it.
  • Chroma — the easy on-ramp for prototyping and local development, loved in the LangChain world; runs in-process with one line. Chroma Cloud (2025) added a production-grade distributed backend for when the prototype graduates.
  • Qdrant — a fast, Rust-built dedicated database with first-class metadata filtering and native quantization. A strong pick for latency-sensitive apps and multi-tenant systems with heavy filtering — which describes a lot of banking.
  • Weaviate — a dedicated database known for built-in hybrid search (vector + BM25 together) and a module ecosystem. Good when you want dense + sparse out of the box.
  • Milvus — built for massive scale; its rule-of-thumb home is tens of millions to billions of vectors with distributed, GPU-accelerated indexing. Reach for it when the others start straining.
  • Pinecone — fully managed and closed-source: you never touch a server, it just scales. Ideal when you have no ops team and want production RAG without running infrastructure (you trade control and cost for that convenience).
  • LanceDB — an embedded, columnar store (think "SQLite for vectors") great for local-first, multimodal, and analytics-flavoured workloads, with data on cheap object storage.
  • Elasticsearch / OpenSearch — if you already run them for keyword search, they now do vector (HNSW) + BM25 hybrid in one place. Convenient when your org already lives in the Elastic stack.
✅ Tip

For a first banking project, the boring answer is usually right: if you're already on PostgreSQL, start with pgvector. You avoid running a whole new system, keep vectors transactionally beside customer data (which simplifies compliance and backups), and you can always migrate to a dedicated store once you've measured a real limit. Don't adopt a billion-scale database for a 200,000-chunk problem.

Going deeper — the 2026 shape of the market

Two trends have reshaped the choices. First, pgvector grew up: paired with the pgvectorscale extension it adds a disk-friendly index and better filtered search, pushing the "just use Postgres" answer much further up the scale curve than it used to go. Second, serverless decoupled storage from compute: Pinecone's serverless tier (and similar object-storage-backed designs) keep vectors on cheap storage and spin up compute per query, so you pay for what you use instead of renting always-on RAM. Milvus continues to own the distributed, GPU-accelerated, billions-of-vectors end. The upshot: the "right" database depends less on raw capability (most do HNSW + filtering + hybrid now) and more on your operating model — who runs it, where the data may live, and how spiky your traffic is.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist already ran PostgreSQL for customer records, so the team started RAG on pgvector — vectors sat in the same database as the relational data, inside the same security perimeter, covered by the same backups and the same SQL access controls. Compliance loved it: no new system to certify. It comfortably served the first 800,000 policy chunks. Only when the archive project pushed them toward tens of millions of vectors with heavy per-customer filtering did they migrate the hot path to Qdrant for its fast filtered search — a deliberate move backed by a load test, not a reflex to "get a real vector database" on day one.

⚙️ In production

For a bank, the database choice is half compliance, half operations. Data residency: a managed cloud store is wonderfully easy, but you must confirm the data stays in an approved region and sits under the right agreement — or choose a self-hosted/on-prem option (pgvector, Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate all self-host). Multi-tenancy: one customer's vectors must never leak into another's results, so you need strong, index-level filtering or per-tenant collections, not a hopeful WHERE clause. HA & DR: replication, snapshots, and a tested restore — this holds customer data. Cost model: self-hosted means you pay for RAM/SSD and ops staff; managed/serverless means a usage bill but no 3am pages. Audit: log who queried what. Monitoring: the same recall/latency/QPS dashboard regardless of vendor — the database brand doesn't exempt you from measuring.

⚠ Watch out

Two traps. First, premature scale: standing up a distributed, billion-scale cluster for a 200,000-chunk problem buys you operational pain and no benefit — match the tool to the measured size. Second, benchmark theatre: every vendor publishes numbers where they win, on their chosen dataset and filters. Ignore the marketing and run a bake-off on your corpus, your filters, and your latency budget. And for a managed service, never skip the question "where does my data physically live and who can touch it?" — for a bank that answer can veto an otherwise-perfect database.

When to use pgvector: you already run Postgres and are below the tens-of-millions range — it's the lowest-risk start. When to move to a dedicated store: you've measured a real limit — latency under heavy filtering, scale past what Postgres serves comfortably, or a need for built-in hybrid. When NOT to: don't adopt a new database on hype, and don't pick a managed service whose data location or terms your compliance team can't approve.

🧠 Remember it

FAISS is a library; the rest are databases. Start where your data already lives (pgvector), scale to a dedicated store only when you've measured the need.

The retrieval dials: metadata filtering, top-K, MMR, and score thresholds

Finding the nearest vectors is only half the job. These four controls decide which of them you actually keep — and in a bank, one of them is a hard security requirement, not a nicety.

Raw nearest-neighbour search gives you a ranked list. But a good retrieval step shapes that list: it restricts what's allowed, chooses how many to keep, removes redundancy, and drops weak matches. Four dials, each fixing a specific failure.

Metadata filtering — and why it's non-negotiable in banking

Every chunk you store can carry metadata: tags like customer_id, department, product, region, sensitivity, date. A metadata filter narrows the search to chunks that match conditions — "only mortgage docs," "only from 2025," "only this customer's records." It makes retrieval more precise and faster.

But in banking it's far more than a precision tweak — it's the access-control boundary (ACL). A retail customer must never retrieve another customer's statement, and a junior agent must never surface documents above their clearance. You enforce this by filtering on identity/permission metadata inside the retrieval query, so forbidden chunks are never even candidates.

⚠ Watch out

The number-one enterprise RAG breach: filtering for permissions in the prompt instead of in the retriever. If you fetch everyone's chunks and then ask the model "please only use the ones this user is allowed to see," the model has already read the forbidden text — and a clever question (or a prompt injection) can make it leak. Authorization must happen in the query filter, before vectors are ever compared. Deny by default; never trust the model to police access.

# Retrieval WITH a mandatory access-control filter (Qdrant-style client).
hits = client.query_points(                       # run the vector search
    collection_name="bank_docs",                  # the collection of stored chunk vectors
    query=q_vec,                                   # the embedded user question
    query_filter={                                 # ACL + scope filter applied DURING search, not after
        "must": [                                  # every condition here must hold for a chunk to qualify
            {"key": "customer_id", "match": {"value": user.customer_id}},  # only THIS customer's data — the security boundary
            {"key": "sensitivity", "match": {"value": "standard"}},        # exclude docs above the user's clearance
        ]
    },
    limit=5,                                       # top-K: keep the 5 best qualifying chunks
    score_threshold=0.30,                          # drop anything below this similarity — weak matches are noise
).points                                           # the final, authorized, trimmed result list

Notice the filter runs as part of the search: chunks belonging to other customers are never scored, never retrieved, never seen by the model. That's the difference between a filter and a security control.

Top-K — how many to keep

Top-K is simply how many chunks you return. Too few (K=1) risks missing the chunk that holds the answer; too many (K=50) floods the prompt with noise, raises cost, and can bury the good chunk in the middle where models read least carefully. A common sweet spot is K=3 to 10 — then tune against real questions. If you add a re-ranking step, you often retrieve a larger K first and let the re-ranker narrow it.

MMR — kill the duplicates

Plain top-K has a blind spot: the 5 closest chunks might all be near-copies of each other — the same overdraft sentence repeated across five documents — so you waste all five slots on one fact and miss the related fact about waivers. MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance) fixes this by balancing two goals: pick chunks that are relevant to the query but also different from what's already picked. The result is a diverse, non-redundant set that covers more of the answer. A tuning knob (often called lambda) slides between "pure relevance" and "maximum diversity."

Score threshold — refuse to answer on thin evidence

A score threshold discards any chunk whose similarity falls below a floor. Its real value is the empty result: if nothing clears the bar, your best move is often to say "I don't have information on that" rather than let the model improvise from weak, barely-related text. In a bank, an honest "I can't find that" beats a confident, unfounded answer every time.

🏦 Picture this

A customer asks BankAssist, "what fees hit my account last month?" The ACL filter instantly restricts the search to her records — no one else's can even be scored. The score threshold throws out barely-relevant marketing chunks. MMR notices that three retrieved chunks all repeat the monthly-maintenance fee and keeps just one, freeing a slot for the overdraft fee and the ATM fee. Top-K=5 delivers a tidy, varied, authorized set. Remove any one dial and the answer gets worse, noisier — or, without the ACL filter, catastrophic.

Going deeper — how filtering actually runs, and tuning the rest

"Filter during search" hides a real engineering subtlety: pre-filter vs post-filter. A naive engine does the vector search first and then throws away results that don't match the filter (post-filtering) — which is dangerous, because if a customer only owns 3 of the top-100 vectors, you asked for 5 and got 3, or worse, zero. A good engine applies the filter as it traverses the index (pre-filtering) so it keeps searching until it has 5 qualifying hits. On graph indexes like HNSW this is tricky — an over-tight filter can strand the search in a region with no allowed neighbours — so mature databases (Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus) implement filtered-HNSW carefully. For a bank this isn't academic: post-filtering plus a strict ACL can silently return nothing, and a nothing answer is at least safe, but it's still a bug.

The other three dials reward tuning. Top-K is often dynamic: retrieve a wide net (say 50) feeding a re-ranking step, then keep the final few — wide for recall, narrow for the prompt. MMR's lambda slides between pure relevance (λ=1) and maximum diversity (λ=0); around 0.5–0.7 usually gives variety without drifting off-topic. Score thresholds must be calibrated per model and per corpus — because, as scores aren't probabilities, a 0.3 floor that's sensible for one model may reject everything for another. Set it by looking at the score distribution of known-good vs known-bad matches on your own data.

⚙️ In production

Filtering is where security meets performance. Derive the ACL filter from the authenticated session (the customer's verified identity and role) — never from anything the user typed, or a prompt-injected "I am an admin" could widen the net. Performance: a high-selectivity filter (one customer out of millions) can slow ANN search, so index the filter fields and prefer databases with true pre-filtering; for very small per-tenant sets, a direct filtered lookup can even beat ANN. Audit: log the filter applied and the chunk ids returned for every query — in a bank you must be able to prove, months later, that user X could only ever have seen their own data. Monitoring: track the rate of empty results (a spike means your threshold is too high or your corpus has a gap) and the rate of filter-starved queries. Failure mode to rehearse: what does the assistant say when the filter legitimately returns nothing? "I don't have that information" — not a guess.

When to use each dial: ACL filter always (it's mandatory, not optional); score threshold whenever a wrong-but-confident answer is costly (most banking cases); MMR when your corpus has lots of near-duplicate chunks; a larger top-K when a re-ranker will narrow it afterward. When NOT to: don't set the score threshold so high it starves good answers, don't crank top-K so large the real answer gets lost in the middle of a bloated prompt, and never rely on the model to self-enforce permissions in place of a real query filter.

🧠 Remember it

Filter for who's allowed, threshold for what's strong, MMR for what's fresh, top-K for how many. In a bank, the ACL filter isn't a dial — it's the wall.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking 🔐 security

Scaling the vector store: sharding, replication & tiering

One machine answers vector searches beautifully — until the index no longer fits in its memory or the queries no longer fit in its day. This is how a vector database grows past a single box.

Earlier topics in this chapter explained what a vector database does and which one to pick; this one is about what happens when your data outgrows any one of them. Picture a single very fast librarian who has memorised where every book sits. She's unbeatable — until the library holds more books than she can remember, or more visitors arrive than she can greet in a minute. At that point you don't find a smarter librarian; you hire several, split the shelves between them, and keep spare librarians on standby. That is sharding, replication, and tiering, in one breath.

Why one node isn't enough

Vector search is fast because the index lives in RAM. So the first wall is simple arithmetic: a float32 vector costs dimensions × 4 bytes. BankAssist's full knowledge base is about 90 million chunks at 1536 dimensions, so the raw vectors alone are 90M × 1536 × 4 ≈ 550 GB — and an HNSW graph index adds roughly another 30–50% for its links, pushing you past 700 GB. No ordinary server has that much memory, and even if one did, you'd have a single point of failure holding the entire bank's knowledge. The second wall is traffic: one node has a ceiling on queries per second (QPS), and as it saturates, tail latency (p99) climbs — the 99th-percentile query that used to take 30 ms starts taking 300. You scale out to beat both walls at once.

Sharding — split the vectors across nodes

Sharding (horizontal partitioning) cuts the collection into pieces called shards and puts each on a different node, so no single machine holds — or searches — everything. There are two ways to decide which vector goes where. Random / hash sharding spreads vectors evenly by hashing their id (Qdrant uses consistent hashing by default), which balances load perfectly but scatters every topic across every shard. Semantic / metadata sharding routes by a key you choose — per-tenant, per-region, or per-product — so all of one customer's (or one country's) vectors live together. That makes a filtered query touch only the relevant shard, which is faster and cleaner for data-residency rules (EU data stays on EU nodes), at the cost of possible hot spots if one tenant is huge.

A normal query has to reach data that's now spread out, so the database does a scatter-gather: the router node fans the query out to all shards, each shard returns its own local top-k, and the router merges and re-ranks those partial lists into the global top-k. Your code still makes one call; the fan-out is hidden. The cost is that overall latency is governed by the slowest shard, so one lagging node drags the whole query. Two more realities: adding a shard triggers rebalancing — vectors move between nodes to even out the load, which consumes bandwidth and must be done carefully live (Qdrant fixes shard count at creation, so growth often means more replicas or a planned re-index rather than a flag flip). And filtered search interacts with shards: a metadata filter either narrows the fan-out to the shards that can match (great when you sharded on that key) or still hits every shard and filters locally (fine, just not cheaper).

Replication — copies for throughput and survival

Replication keeps more than one copy of each shard on different nodes. It buys you two things. First, read throughput: queries for a shard can be answered by any of its replicas, so two replicas roughly double the QPS that shard can serve. Second, high availability: if a node dies, a replica takes over and searches keep working — no 3 a.m. outage. The usual arrangement is leader/follower: one replica (the leader) accepts writes and streams them to the followers. That introduces the classic trade-off — eventual consistency. For a brief moment after a write, a follower may still serve the old data, so a freshly-ingested document might not appear in the very next search. Qdrant exposes this directly with a write_consistency_factor (how many replicas must acknowledge a write before it counts), letting you dial between "fast writes" and "every replica agrees before we move on."

Hot / cold tiering — not everything deserves RAM

Keeping 700 GB in RAM across every node is expensive, and the honest truth is that most queries hit a small, recent slice of the data. Tiering keeps hot (recent, frequently-hit) vectors in RAM and pushes cold vectors to SSD. The key technology here is DiskANN — a disk-friendly index (used by pgvectorscale's StreamingDiskANN and offered by Milvus and others) that holds the hot part of the graph in memory and streams the rest from disk, trading a few milliseconds of latency for a fraction of the RAM bill. The complementary trick is quantization: store compressed vectors so more fit per node. Int8 scalar quantization cuts 4 bytes per dimension down to 1 (that 550 GB becomes ~138 GB); binary quantization cuts it to a single bit (~17 GB), with a cheap re-scoring pass on the full vectors to recover accuracy.

Multi-tenancy at scale

A bank serves many tenants — business units, white-label partners, or millions of individual customers — and there are two ways to isolate them. A collection or shard per tenant gives the strongest isolation (one tenant's index is physically separate, easy to delete or move for residency) but costs more and scales badly past a few thousand tenants. One shared index with a tenant filter on every query is far cheaper and simpler, but leans entirely on that filter being correct, and risks the noisy neighbour problem — one giant tenant's traffic or data slowing everyone else. The common middle path: shard by the tenant key so each tenant's data clusters together (isolation-ish) while still sharing infrastructure (cheap), and always derive the tenant filter from the authenticated session, never from user input.

Managed vs self-host — what each gives you

The scaling machinery differs sharply by product. Qdrant does explicit sharding (consistent hashing or a custom shard key) and replication with a tunable write-consistency factor. Milvus is built distributed-first, with storage/compute separation and data split into ~512 MB segments spread across worker nodes — the heavy option for ten-billion-vector scale. Pinecone hides all of it: its serverless tier decouples storage (vectors kept as immutable files on object storage like S3) from compute that's paged in on demand, so you never size a shard — you just pay per query and storage (its older pod model is now legacy; "always use serverless"). pgvector alone doesn't shard; you reach for Postgres read replicas (streaming replication) for read scaling, add pgvectorscale for the DiskANN tiering, and use Citus to shard across nodes when one Postgres box isn't enough.

# A sharded + replicated collection, then one scatter-gather query. (Qdrant)
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models        # official Qdrant Python client
client = QdrantClient(url="http://qdrant:6333")        # connect to any node in the cluster

client.create_collection(                              # create the collection ONCE, cluster-wide
    collection_name="bank_docs",                       # BankAssist's ~90M chunk vectors live here
    vectors_config=models.VectorParams(                # describe each stored vector
        size=1536,                                     # text-embedding-3-small dimensions
        distance=models.Distance.COSINE,               # the metric the index is built for
    ),
    shard_number=12,                                   # split 90M vectors across 12 shards (~7.5M each)
    replication_factor=2,                              # keep 2 copies of every shard — HA + read throughput
    write_consistency_factor=2,                        # a write must reach BOTH replicas before it's "done"
)

hits = client.query_points(                            # ONE call — the router fans it out to all 12 shards
    collection_name="bank_docs",                       # each shard returns its own local top-k...
    query=q_vec,                                        # the embedded customer question
    limit=5,                                            # ...then the router merges + re-ranks to the global top-5
).points
print(len(hits), "results merged from 12 shards")      # scatter-gather, hidden behind one call
▶ Output
5 results merged from 12 shards

Three lines of config turn a single-node collection into a 12-shard, 2-replica cluster — 24 physical shard copies in all — and the query code doesn't change at all. The fan-out, the per-shard top-k, and the merge all happen below your call.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's knowledge base grows to ~90 million chunks — well over 700 GB once indexed, far past any single server. The team splits it into 12 shards of ~7.5 million vectors each and runs 2 replicas per shard, so losing a node during a rollout never takes search down. Peak traffic comes from the mobile app each morning; the extra replicas soak up those reads. Cold archival policy from five years ago lives on a DiskANN tier on SSD, while this quarter's hot documents stay in RAM, and int8 quantization keeps per-node memory sane. EU customer vectors are pinned to EU-region shards for residency. The whole thing answers one query_points call in under 50 ms at p99.

⚙️ In production

Capacity planning is the job. Start from RAM: raw vectors are N × dims × bytes, then add ~30–50% for the HNSW graph, then size each shard so its slice fits comfortably in one node's memory (aim to use ~60–70%, never 100%). For BankAssist's 90M×1536 ≈ 550 GB raw (~770 GB indexed), roughly 12 shards of 64 GB-class nodes fit with headroom. Replicas for QPS and recall: add replicas until a shard comfortably serves your peak QPS at the p99 you need while staying at your target recall — one replica is zero fault tolerance, so two is the floor for a bank. Monitor per shard, not just globally: a single slow or memory-pressured shard drags every scatter-gather query, so watch per-shard latency, QPS, memory, and replica lag. Rebalancing moves data and competes with live traffic — do it in a window and throttle it; because Qdrant fixes shard count at creation, plan capacity ahead or budget a re-index. Backup/DR: snapshot per shard, store copies cross-region, and actually rehearse a restore — replicas protect against a dead node, not a bad deploy or a fat-fingered delete. Cost: RAM dominates the bill, so tiering and quantization are the biggest levers you have.

⚠ Watch out

The commonest scaling mistake is scaling too early. A 50,000-vector prototype is about 300 MB — it fits in RAM on a laptop and answers in single-digit milliseconds. Sharding it adds scatter-gather latency, rebalancing headaches, and operational cost to buy capacity you will not use for years; you have turned a one-line deployment into a distributed system for nothing. The other trap is the mirror image: a too-tight metadata filter on a graph index can strand a scatter-gather query in a shard with no qualifying neighbours and quietly return too few results. When NOT to shard: any corpus that fits in one node's RAM with room to grow — don't shard until a single box genuinely can't hold the index or can't serve the QPS. Reach for vertical scaling (a bigger box) and replicas first; reach for shards only when one machine truly can't hold the data.

🧠 Remember it

Shard to fit the data, replicate to survive and serve, tier to save the RAM. Scatter-gather is one question asked of every shelf, answered as one.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking 📈 scale

Knowledge Layer (RAG) — Smarter Retrieval

Plain search finds similar text; smart retrieval finds the right text. This chapter is the toolbox that turns a shaky RAG demo into an assistant a bank would trust — told as a story, one fix at a time.

Reshaping the question: rewriting, multi-query, and RAG-Fusion

The fastest way to retrieve better is not a better database — it's asking a better question before you search.

Imagine a customer types into BankAssist: "got charged again even tho i was told it'd be free??" That is a real human sentence — messy, emotional, full of "it" and "again" that only make sense in a conversation. Now picture handing that exact sentence to a librarian and asking her to find the matching page in a 400-page fee policy. She'd struggle, because the policy doesn't talk like an angry customer. It says "Monthly maintenance fee waiver conditions." The words don't line up, so the search misses.

Query transformation is the simple idea of cleaning up or reshaping the question before it hits the search, so it looks more like the documents you're searching. There are three everyday moves, from simplest to strongest.

Move 1 — Query rewriting

Ask a cheap, fast language model to turn the messy question into a clean, standalone search query. "got charged again even tho i was told it'd be free" becomes "conditions under which the monthly maintenance fee is waived." This also fixes the biggest retrieval bug in chat: follow-up questions. If the previous turn was about overdrafts and the customer now asks "and what about the fee for that?", the word "that" means nothing to a search engine. Rewriting folds the history in: "what is the overdraft fee?"

Move 2 — Multi-query

One question often has many right phrasings, and you can't know which one matches the document's wording. So generate several — three or four paraphrases — search with all of them, and pool the results. One paraphrase says "fee waiver," another says "avoid monthly charge," another says "free checking requirements." Between them, they cast a wider net and are far more likely to catch the one chunk that holds the answer. This lifts recall (the chance the right chunk is somewhere in what you fetched).

Move 3 — RAG-Fusion

RAG-Fusion is multi-query with one clever extra step. After searching with each paraphrase you don't just dump all results in a pile — you fuse the ranked lists intelligently so that chunks which show up near the top of many lists bubble to the very top. The fusing is done with a little formula called Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and it's worth understanding because it shows up everywhere.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) — the formula you'll actually use

Here's the problem RRF solves. When you search two different ways, each gives back a ranked list — but their scores aren't comparable. A keyword search might score things 0–30; a meaning search scores things 0–1. You can't just add those numbers. RRF's trick: throw away the scores and keep only the rank (1st, 2nd, 3rd…). A chunk's final score is the sum, across every list, of one divided by (a constant k plus its rank in that list):

Why the + k (usually 60)? It softens the gap between rank 1 and rank 2. Without it, being #1 would be worth double being #2, and a single list could dominate. With k=60, ranks 1 and 2 are almost equal, so a chunk only wins by showing up high in many lists — exactly the consensus you want. You rarely need to tune k; 60 is the field default and works well.

Here's RRF in a few lines of plain Python — no library needed, which is the beauty of it.

# Fuse several ranked lists of chunk-IDs into one list, RRF-style.
def reciprocal_rank_fusion(ranked_lists, k=60):   # each list is best-first chunk IDs; k smooths rank gaps
    scores = {}                                   # chunk_id -> running fused score
    for one_list in ranked_lists:                 # loop over every retriever's result list
        for rank, chunk_id in enumerate(one_list, start=1):  # rank 1 = top; enumerate gives position
            scores[chunk_id] = scores.get(chunk_id, 0) + 1 / (k + rank)  # add this list's contribution
    return sorted(scores, key=scores.get, reverse=True)  # highest total score first = final order

dense  = ["c3", "c7", "c9"]      # meaning-search ranked these for one paraphrase
sparse = ["c3", "c1", "c7"]      # keyword-search ranked these for another
print(reciprocal_rank_fusion([dense, sparse]))   # c3 is #1 in BOTH lists, so it clearly wins
▶ Output
['c3', 'c7', 'c1', 'c9']

Notice c3 comes first, and by a clear margin: it was ranked #1 in both lists, so its two top contributions (1/61 + 1/61 ≈ 0.0328) beat everything else. That's consensus winning — a chunk that two different searches both put first. c7 takes second because it placed respectably in both lists, while c1 and c9 each appeared in only one. The exact same function fuses multi-query results, and it also fuses keyword and meaning search together — the hybrid-search pattern.

🏦 Picture this

A customer asks BankAssist, "why'd my free account suddenly start costing me?" Rewriting turns it into "monthly maintenance fee waiver conditions." Multi-query also spins off "how to keep checking free" and "minimum balance to avoid fees." Each phrasing finds a slightly different slice of the policy; RRF fuses them so the one chunk listing the three waiver conditions — minimum balance, direct deposit, or student status — lands on top. The customer gets the complete answer, not just the fragment their original wording happened to match.

Going deeper — how many phrasings, and from which model

The knobs that matter are few. How many paraphrases? Three to five is the sweet spot; beyond that you mostly add cost and near-duplicates. How much variety? Generate them with a little temperature (around 0.6–0.8) so the phrasings genuinely differ — at temperature 0 you often get four near-identical rewrites that all miss the same way. Which model? A small, fast one. Rewriting is not deep reasoning, so gpt-4.1-mini is plenty and keeps the added latency to a few hundred milliseconds. Here is the generation step itself, which the earlier RRF function then fuses.

# Multi-query: ask a cheap model for several search-ready phrasings of one question.
from openai import OpenAI                 # official OpenAI SDK
client = OpenAI()                         # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

def make_paraphrases(question, n=4):      # returns n alternative phrasings to search with
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1-mini",             # small/fast — rephrasing needs no heavy reasoning
        temperature=0.7,                  # some randomness so the phrasings actually differ
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"Give {n} short, different search queries for this bank question, "
            f"one per line, no numbering:\n{question}"}],
    )
    lines = resp.choices[0].message.content.splitlines()  # one phrasing per line
    return [q.strip("-• ").strip() for q in lines if q.strip()]  # tidy bullets/spaces, drop blanks

print(make_paraphrases("why'd my free account start costing me?"))  # search with ALL of these, then RRF
▶ Output
['monthly maintenance fee waiver conditions', 'how to keep a checking account free', 'minimum balance to avoid the monthly fee', 'why was an account fee charged']

Always keep the original question in the pool you fuse, so a creative rewrite can never erase a chunk the plain wording would have found. And measure the payoff the honest way: compute recall@k (the share of questions whose gold chunk is in the top-k) with and without the transformation on a fixed test set. If recall barely moves, you are paying for latency you don't need.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency: every question now costs one small rewrite call plus up to N searches. Four paraphrases means roughly 4× the retrieval load — at a million questions a month that is millions of extra embed-and-search operations. Fire the N searches concurrently (async or a thread pool) so wall-clock time stays near one search plus the ~200–400 ms rewrite, not N searches end to end. Cache rewrites for templated or repeated questions. Failure modes: the model returns fewer lines than asked, emits an empty string, or drifts off-topic — always fall back to the raw question when parsing fails. Monitoring: track recall@k before/after and a query-drift score (embedding similarity between the original and each rewrite); alert when drift spikes, because that is intent being silently rewritten. Security/compliance: the rewrite prompt carries raw customer text that may contain account numbers or names — redact PII before it leaves your perimeter or use a zero-retention endpoint, and never log the unmasked text (GLBA/PCI). When to use / when NOT: use when recall is genuinely your bottleneck and for multi-turn chat where follow-ups need the history folded in; skip for single-shot, high-volume lookups where latency and cost dominate and recall is already healthy.

⚠ Watch out

Every transformation costs an extra language-model call and more searches, which means more latency and more money per question. Multi-query with four paraphrases does roughly four times the retrieval work. Use these when recall is genuinely your problem — not by reflex. And watch for query drift: an over-creative rewrite can quietly change what the customer actually asked.

🧠 Remember it

Rewrite = tidy the question. Multi-query = ask it several ways. RAG-Fusion = ask several ways, then let consensus (RRF) pick the winners.

Bridging the gap: HyDE and step-back prompting

Sometimes the question and the answer are written in such different styles that no rewrite helps — so you generate a bridge between them.

There's a sneaky mismatch at the heart of RAG. A BankAssist customer asks a short question. Your documents are long, formal answers. In meaning-space, a question and its own answer can sit surprisingly far apart, because one is a query ("can I stop a direct debit?") and the other is dense policy prose ("A standing authorisation may be revoked by the account holder up to one business day prior to the scheduled settlement…"). Two techniques build a bridge across that gap.

HyDE — write a fake answer, then search with it

HyDE stands for Hypothetical Document Embeddings, and the idea is wonderfully cheeky. Instead of searching with the question, you first ask the language model to write what a good answer might look like — even though it's guessing and might be wrong — and then you search with that. Why would a made-up answer help? Because a fake answer is written in the style of real answers: it uses document-like words and sentence shapes, so its embedding lands much closer to the genuine policy text than the bare question ever could. You're not using the fake answer's facts — you throw those away. You're only using its shape to go fishing in the right part of meaning-space.

# HyDE: let the model draft a plausible answer, then retrieve with the draft.
from anthropic import Anthropic            # official Anthropic SDK for Claude
client = Anthropic()                       # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

question = "Can I cancel a direct debit before it's taken?"  # short, casual customer wording

draft = client.messages.create(            # one cheap, fast call to invent a document-shaped answer
    model="claude-haiku-5-5",              # small fast model — this is a throwaway draft, not the final reply
    max_tokens=200,                        # keep it short; we only need the "shape", not an essay
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": f"Write a short bank-policy paragraph answering: {question}"}],
).content[0].text                          # the hypothetical paragraph — we embed THIS, not the question

# embed(draft) now lands near the real "revoking a standing authorisation" clause
hits = vector_store.search(embed(draft), k=5)  # retrieve using the draft's vector, not the question's
▶ Output
Top hit: "Deposit Agreement §6.3 — Revoking a standing payment authorisation"

The draft probably got a detail wrong (maybe it guessed the wrong cut-off time). Doesn't matter — it still steered us to §6.3, where the real cut-off lives. The real model answer at the end is grounded in that retrieved clause, not in the guess.

Step-back prompting — zoom out first

Step-back prompting is the opposite move: instead of guessing a specific answer, you ask a more general question first. A customer asks, "will I be charged if my balance hits exactly zero on a Sunday?" That's very specific, and searching for it directly may find nothing. So you "step back" to the principle: "what are the bank's overdraft and negative-balance rules?" You retrieve the general policy, and then answer the specific edge case using those grounded principles. It's how a good human expert works — understand the rule, then apply it to the odd case.

⚙️ Under the hood

Both tricks were most valuable in the early days of RAG, when retrievers were weak. As hybrid search and rerankers got good, the gains from HyDE shrank — a strong retriever already bridges much of the style gap. Today HyDE earns its keep mainly in sparse, specialised domains where you have little data and odd jargon. Step-back still shines for reasoning-heavy policy questions. Treat both as targeted fixes, not default layers.

Going deeper — tuning the bridge, and why it fades

Three practical levers make both tricks safer. First, keep the draft short: for HyDE you only want the shape of an answer, so a 100–150 token draft from a small model (gpt-4.1-mini) is both cheaper and less likely to wander than a full essay. Second, generate more than one draft and average their vectors: the original HyDE paper embeds several hypothetical answers plus the query itself and averages them, which smooths out any single hallucinated draft. Third, always fuse with the plain-question hits (the same RRF idea) so a bad guess can be out-voted rather than trusted alone.

Now the honest part: both techniques were born when retrievers were weak, and their edge has shrunk as hybrid search and rerankers matured. On modern benchmarks a strong hybrid-plus-reranker stack already closes most of the question-document style gap, so HyDE's lift is often small — and sometimes negative, because the extra generation adds latency and a chance to drift. Its gains survive best in sparse, specialised, low-data domains with odd jargon, which is exactly where a cold-start banking knowledge base starts before you have tuned anything. Step-back prompting ages better, because "learn the governing rule, then apply it" genuinely helps reasoning-heavy policy questions that no amount of retrieval tuning fixes on its own.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency: both tricks add a generation step before retrieval — typically 300–800 ms and a small per-query token bill on top of the search itself, which matters on a live chat path. Cache drafts for common questions and keep max_tokens tight. Scale: because the draft is generated per query (not per document), there is no index blow-up — the cost is purely at query time. Failure modes: a HyDE draft that hallucinates the wrong product drags retrieval with it; a step-back question that zooms out too far retrieves generic fluff. Guard both by always retaining the original-question hits in the fused set. Monitoring: log the embedding distance between the draft and the top retrieved chunk, and A/B the technique against a no-HyDE arm on recall@k — turn it off the moment it stops earning its latency. Security/compliance: the draft-generation prompt sees the raw customer question, so the same PII-redaction and zero-retention rules apply as for any LLM call in a bank. When to use / when NOT: use HyDE for sparse/specialised cold-start corpora and step-back for reasoning-heavy policy edge cases; do NOT bolt them on as default layers once a hybrid+reranker stack already gives you good recall — you would only be buying latency.

⚠ Watch out

HyDE's fake answer can hallucinate itself off-topic — if the draft wanders to the wrong product, it drags retrieval with it. And step-back can over-generalise: zoom out too far and you lose the specific detail the customer actually needed. Always keep the original question in play too (fuse HyDE/step-back hits with plain-question hits), so a bad guess can't sink the whole search.

🧠 Remember it

HyDE = "pretend you know the answer, then go find it." Step-back = "learn the rule before judging the exception."

Understanding the question: decomposition, routing, and self-query

Before you search at all, three smart questions help: Is this really one question? Where should it even go? And is there a hard filter hiding inside it?

Not every question should be fired straight at your vector store as-is. Three lightweight "understanding" steps decide how and where to retrieve — and skipping them is behind a surprising number of wrong answers.

Query decomposition — break a fat question into small ones

BankAssist customers love to ask two or three things in one breath: "Compare the fees and the early-closure penalty on your 1-year and 3-year fixed deposits." A single search for that whole sentence retrieves a muddle — a bit about fees, a bit about penalties, nothing complete.
