MATCH (a)-[:OWNED_BY|CO_SIGNS*1..3]-(p:Person)   // walk 1 to 3 relationship hops to linked people
MATCH (p)-[:OWNS]->(c:Company)-[:HOLDS]->(l:Loan {type: 'business'})  // reach their business loans
RETURN DISTINCT p.name AS person, c.name AS company, l.id AS loan_id   // return the connected results
"""
# The *1..3 is the multi-hop part: it follows chains up to three links deep,
# which a single vector search over text chunks simply cannot do.

records = neo4j_session.run(QUERY)         # run the walk against the graph database
subgraph = [dict(r) for r in records]      # the connected facts we retrieved

# Now hand the subgraph to the LLM as grounded context, exactly like text chunks:
context = "\n".join(f"{r['person']} owns {r['company']} holding loan {r['loan_id']}"
                    for r in subgraph)     # render the graph facts into readable lines
print(context)                             # this context grounds the final answer
▶ Output
Priya owns Acme Ltd holding loan BL-4471 Omar owns Vega Traders holding loan BL-5093

The *1..3 is the magic: it follows chains up to three links deep in one query. That's the multi-hop connection a pile of text chunks can never surface, because the link between "this account" and "that business loan" was never written in a single sentence anywhere.

⚙️ Under the hood

Building the graph is the expensive part. You run an LLM over your documents to extract entities and relationships ("this contract links Priya to Acme Ltd as director"), which costs real money and depends heavily on the extraction prompt quality. The usual production pattern is hybrid: use normal vector RAG for ordinary factoid questions, and reach into GraphRAG only for the multi-hop, "connect the dots" questions where it earns its keep. Keep the graph fresh with change-data-capture (a feed that automatically picks up new and changed records the moment they happen), because a stale fraud graph misses the newest ring.

Going deeper

The two retrieval styles have very different performance shapes. Local search is a bounded graph traversal — fast and cheap, because you start at one node and the number of hops is capped (the *1..3 in the query). The danger isn't cost; it's the super-node: one entity with tens of thousands of edges (a payment processor everyone transacts with, a shared corporate address) that, when you walk through it, explodes a three-hop query into millions of paths. Production graphs defend against this by capping fan-out, skipping hub nodes above a degree threshold, and weighting edges so the walk prefers meaningful links. Global search has the opposite shape: it reads precomputed community summaries, so query-time is cheap, but it only works because expensive LLM summarization happened at index time — you pay once, up front, to make whole-corpus questions affordable forever after.

The quality ceiling of the whole system is set at extraction and entity resolution, not retrieval. If the extractor misses that a contract names Priya as a director, no clever Cypher will ever recover that edge. If resolution fails to merge "P SHARMA" and "Priya Sharma," the multi-hop path simply isn't there to walk. This is why GraphRAG is worth it only where relationships are the answer — fraud rings, AML layering, KYC entity resolution, counterparty exposure — and wasteful where a plain vector lookup suffices. A newer research direction worth tracking, Microsoft's LazyGraphRAG, defers the expensive extraction and summarization to query time and reports a small fraction of full GraphRAG's indexing cost, which attacks the single biggest objection to graphs: the upfront build bill.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Construction is the dominant cost (an LLM call per chunk to extract, plus a call per community to summarize) — indexing a large corpus can be thousands of LLM calls and hours of wall-clock time; query-time local search, by contrast, is a sub-second database walk. Scale. Store the graph in a graph database built for it (commonly Neo4j); watch node degree, because super-nodes turn innocent traversals into runaway queries — cap hops and fan-out. Failure modes. Missed or wrong extractions (phantom or absent edges), under-merging (one customer looks like five strangers, hiding a ring) and over-merging (two people fused into one, inventing links), and graph staleness (a fresh fraud ring the nightly build hasn't captured yet). Monitoring. Track extraction failure rate, the share of entities routed to human review at resolution, graph freshness lag, and per-query hop count and latency. Security & compliance for a bank. The graph concentrates linked personal and financial data, so it inherits the full weight: per-entity (row-level) access control so an investigator only sees permitted subgraphs, immutable audit logs on every write and every query, PII governance, and data-residency control over where the graph DB physically lives. A wrongly merged identity can freeze an innocent customer's account, so borderline merges carry a confidence score and go to a human, not an auto-merge.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's AML team gets an alert on one account. With plain RAG they'd read that account's file and stop. With GraphRAG, a local-search walk fans out three hops and surfaces two other customers who co-sign with the account holder and quietly control companies holding business loans — a classic layering pattern. The graph didn't just answer a question; it revealed a ring no single document described.

⚠ Watch out

GraphRAG is overkill for simple factoid QA — "what's the overdraft fee?" needs no graph, and building one for it is wasted money and maintenance. Use graphs where the relationships are the answer (fraud rings, KYC entity resolution, exposure analysis), and remember the graph is only as good as the extraction that built it. Garbage entities in, garbage connections out.

🧠 Remember it

Vector RAG finds the right passage. GraphRAG finds the right path. Reach for the graph when the answer is a connection, not a sentence.

Multimodal RAG: retrieving over images, tables, and charts

A lot of a bank's knowledge isn't clean text — it's scanned statements, charts in reports, and complex tables. Multimodal RAG retrieves over those directly.

Not every answer lives in a paragraph. A customer's question might depend on a chart in a research report, a table on a scanned rate sheet, or the layout of a scanned loan agreement where columns and stamps carry meaning. Flatten those to plain text and you lose the very structure that held the answer. Multimodal RAG retrieves over visual content — images, tables, charts, whole scanned pages — not just extracted text.

There are two broad approaches, and the second is the frontier shift worth knowing:

Approach 1 — Describe, then embed

Run OCR and image captioning to turn every picture, chart, and table into text, then embed that text like anything else. Simple and works with your existing text pipeline — but it's only as good as the OCR, and a misread table or a vague caption silently loses the answer.

Approach 2 — Embed the page image itself

Newer models (ColPali, ColQwen, and single-vector options like voyage-multimodal) embed the page image directly — no brittle OCR step. At answer time, a vision model reads the retrieved page image. Far more robust on messy layouts, scanned docs, and dense tables.

The page-image approach is a genuine leap for banking's scanned, table-heavy documents. Models like ColPali (accepted at ICLR 2025) treat each page as an image, break it into patches, and use late interaction (matching each query word to the best-matching patch of the page) to score relevance — skipping OCR entirely.

At generation time the retrieved page image is passed straight to a vision-capable model, which can read the table or chart and answer. Here's that final step with the Anthropic Messages API, which accepts images directly.

# Multimodal generation: let a vision model read the retrieved page image.
import anthropic, base64
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

with open("retrieved_statement_page.png", "rb") as f:   # the page our image-retriever returned
    img_b64 = base64.standard_b64encode(f.read()).decode()  # models take images as base64 text

resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",          # a current vision-capable Claude model
    max_tokens=512,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "image", "source": {   # attach the page image as grounding, like a text chunk
            "type": "base64", "media_type": "image/png", "data": img_b64}},
        {"type": "text", "text": "From this statement page, what was the total of all fees charged?"},  # the question, asked against the image
    ]}],
)
print(resp.content[0].text)             # the model reads the table in the image and answers
▶ Output
The statement shows three fees — a $35 overdraft fee, a $12 wire fee, and a $5 paper-statement fee — totaling $52.

The model read a table inside an image and summed it. No OCR step mangled the "$35" into "$36," because the pixels went straight to a model that can see.

⚙️ Under the hood

Page-image models like ColPali store many vectors per page (one per image patch), so the index is far larger than single-vector text — hundreds of vectors per page instead of one. That's the cost of avoiding OCR. Teams weigh it against the single-vector multimodal models (Cohere Embed 4, voyage-multimodal), whose quality gap has been narrowing on benchmarks like ViDoRe V2 (and its successors, which added long and cross-document queries to keep the test hard). Always keep page-and-document provenance on every image so answers can still cite "page 3 of your March statement."

Going deeper

The two approaches aren't rivals so much as a precision-vs-robustness dial. "Describe then embed" keeps your familiar text pipeline and is cheap to search, but it inherits every OCR mistake and every vague caption — a misread "$35" becomes "$36" forever, silently. "Embed the page image" (ColPali-style late interaction, where each query word matches the best-matching patch of the page) is far more robust on messy scans and dense tables, but the late-interaction index stores hundreds of vectors per page, so it's much larger and heavier to serve. Many banks run a hybrid: cheap text retrieval over the clean, born-digital documents, and page-image retrieval reserved for the scanned, table-heavy, or stamped documents where layout carries meaning. A practical middle path is layout-aware parsing up front — a parser that understands a page's structure (titles, tables, figures, reading order) and extracts clean, structure-preserving chunks before anything is embedded, so even the text pipeline stops mangling tables.

This is exactly the niche that RAGFlow (open-source, Apache 2.0, by InfiniFlow) fills. RAGFlow is a layout-aware RAG engine built around deep document understanding: its DeepDoc module runs layout analysis and table-structure recognition on PDFs, scans, slides, and spreadsheets, so complex formats are chunked along their real structure instead of being flattened into a text blob. It pairs that with multi-path recall and fused re-ranking, can call a multi-modal model to interpret images embedded inside a PDF or DOCX, and — importantly for a bank — produces grounded citations with visual highlights that point back to the exact region of the source page, giving the traceability auditors ask for. It's a strong default when your corpus is messy, layout-heavy institutional documents (statements, rate sheets, scanned agreements) and you want a batteries-included engine rather than assembling parsing, indexing, retrieval, and citation yourself. The edge case even layout-aware tools struggle with is the truly degraded scan — faint faxes, handwriting, skewed photos — where you still want a human-in-the-loop fallback for anything high-stakes.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Vision inference is expensive per page and slower than text — budget both the larger page-image index (hundreds of vectors/page) and the per-answer cost of a vision model reading the retrieved page; cache parsed/embedded pages so a document is only processed once. Scale. Late-interaction indexes grow fast; use vector pooling (e.g. a pooling factor of 2 can cut storage by over half for a couple of points of quality) or fall back to single-vector multimodal embeddings for high-volume corpora. Failure modes. OCR/caption errors in the describe-then-embed path, degraded or rotated scans that defeat even layout-aware parsers, and tables whose structure the parser splits wrongly. Monitoring. Track parse success rate per document type, retrieval hit rate on a visual golden set, and vision-model cost per answered question; sample low-confidence parses for human review. Security & compliance for a bank. Scanned documents are dense with PII (IDs, signatures, account numbers), so every image must be governed exactly like text: redaction before it reaches a model, access control on the image store, data-residency control over where images and the vision model run, and a vetted, compliance-approved model path — never send a customer's scanned passport to an un-reviewed endpoint. Keep page-and-document provenance on every image so each answer can cite its exact source page.

⚠ Watch out

Vision inference is expensive per page, and reading sensitive documents (IDs, signed agreements, statements) means PII flows through the model — redact and govern it exactly as you would text, and mind data-residency rules. Don't send a customer's scanned passport to a model path you haven't vetted for compliance.

🧠 Remember it

When the answer is in a picture, chart, or scanned table, don't flatten it to text and pray — retrieve the image and let a model with eyes read it.

RAFT: fine-tuning a model to use context and ignore distractors

RAFT trains the model to be a great open-book test-taker for your domain — using the relevant pages and deliberately ignoring the irrelevant ones mixed in.

Give a student an open-book exam and slip five wrong chapters into the pile along with the one right chapter. A weak student gets distracted and quotes the wrong page. A well-trained student calmly ignores the decoys, finds the relevant chapter, and cites it. RAFT — Retrieval-Augmented Fine-Tuning — is how you train a model to be that well-prepared student for your bank's specific documents.

Everything so far has been prompt-time tricks that leave the model's weights untouched. RAFT is different: it fine-tunes the model (updates its weights) so it's natively good at your domain's open-book RAG. The clever part is the training data. Each example is built as:

  • a question,
  • the golden document(s) that actually answer it,
  • distractor documents — plausible but irrelevant passages, deliberately mixed in,
  • a chain-of-thought answer that cites the golden text and reasons step by step.

By training on golden-plus-distractor piles, the model learns the skill that production retrieval always demands: your retriever will hand me some junk along with the gold — use the gold, ignore the junk. The RAFT paper (arXiv 2403.10131, 2024) reported solid gains on domain datasets over both plain fine-tuning and standard RAG.

You don't write the training loop by hand — you call a fine-tuning API with examples in this golden-plus-distractor shape. Here's how one training example looks and how you'd kick off the job.

# RAFT: one training example mixes the golden doc with distractors.
example = {
  "messages": [
    {"role": "system",
     "content": "Answer using ONLY the provided context. Ignore irrelevant passages."},  # the behaviour we're training in
    {"role": "user", "content":
       "Context:\n"
       "[1] Overdraft item fee: $35; one courtesy waiver per 12 months.\n"   # the GOLDEN passage
       "[2] Branch lobby hours are 9am-4pm weekdays.\n"                       # a DISTRACTOR (plausible, irrelevant)
       "[3] Wire transfers post same business day.\n\n"                       # another DISTRACTOR
       "Question: Can the overdraft fee be waived?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content":
       "Reasoning: Passage [1] covers overdraft fees; [2] and [3] are unrelated. "  # chain-of-thought that names the gold and dismisses decoys
       "[1] states one courtesy waiver per 12 months.\n"
       "Answer: Yes - once every 12 months as a courtesy, on request. [cite: 1]"},  # grounded, cited answer
  ]
}

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()
job = client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(   # launch a fine-tuning job on your RAFT dataset
    training_file="file-raft-banking",  # an uploaded file of thousands of examples like the one above
    model="gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14",    # a current base model you're allowed to fine-tune
)
print(job.status)                       # track the job; the result is a domain-specialized model id
▶ Output
validating_files

After training, you deploy the returned fine-tuned model behind your normal RAG pipeline. It still gets retrieved passages at answer time — but now it's been drilled to lean on the relevant ones and shrug off the noise, which makes it far more robust when retrieval is imperfect (and retrieval is always a little imperfect).

⚙️ Under the hood

RAFT bridges two worlds people usually treat as rivals: fine-tuning (behaviour baked into weights) and RAG (facts supplied at answer time). It doesn't memorize the facts — it learns the skill of using supplied facts well. That's why it suits a stable, high-value domain: a bank's product and policy corpus that changes slowly but must be answered precisely. You still update facts by re-indexing documents; you re-train only when the domain shape shifts.

Going deeper

The single most important RAFT hyperparameter is the fraction of training examples that contain no golden document at all — only distractors. The RAFT paper (arXiv 2403.10131, 2024) found that mixing in a share of "golden-free" examples, where the correct answer must come from the model's own trained knowledge because the retrieved context is all noise, makes the model more robust, not less: it learns both to lean on good context when it exists and to not be derailed when retrieval whiffs entirely. Too few golden-free examples and the model over-trusts whatever it's handed; too many and it starts ignoring context it should use. That ratio is the dial you tune on a validation set. The second lever is the chain-of-thought answer: training the model to first name which passage is relevant and why, then answer with a citation, is what teaches the "ignore the decoys" skill — strip the reasoning and you mostly get a plain fine-tune.

Where RAFT bites is maintenance and the fact/skill split. RAFT does not learn your facts — it learns the skill of using facts — so when a fee changes you re-index documents, you do not retrain. You retrain only when the shape of the domain shifts: new product lines, new document formats, new question types the model fumbles. That makes RAFT suitable for a slow-moving, high-value corpus and a poor fit for anything volatile. The failure mode to fear is over-fitting to the training corpus: a model drilled only on last year's product docs can become brittle and over-confident on genuinely new questions, so you always hold out a fresh evaluation set the training never touched and watch for regression on out-of-distribution queries.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. The upfront cost is the heaviest of any technique here — building a labeled dataset with hand-constructed distractors, running the fine-tuning job, and evaluating it — but inference is cheap and fast: a RAFT model is just a model, with no extra grader or loop calls at answer time, which is part of its appeal. Scale. Serving a fine-tuned model is as scalable as serving any model; the scaling pain is the data pipeline that produces training examples and the cadence of retraining. Failure modes. Over-fitting (brittle on new questions), a stale fine-tune lagging a drifted domain, and training-data leakage of live customer PII into the weights. Monitoring. Track accuracy on a held-out golden set over time, regression on out-of-distribution questions, and the groundedness/citation rate of the fine-tuned model versus the base model — if the gap closes, it's time to retrain or reconsider. Security & compliance for a bank. Never train on raw customer data — synthesize or de-identify training examples, because anything baked into weights can resurface and cannot be "deleted" like an index row (a right-to-erasure headache); version and document every model and its exact training set for model-risk governance and audit; and validate the fine-tuned model through the same approval gate as any model that talks to customers before it ships.

⚠ Watch out

RAFT is the heaviest option here: you need a labeled dataset with hand-built distractors, training infrastructure, and a re-training plan as the domain drifts. Over-fit to your training corpus and the model gets brittle on anything new. Only climb to RAFT when measurement shows prompt-time methods (good retrieval, reranking, CRAG gating) have hit a ceiling — not as a first move.

🧠 Remember it

RAFT = open-book exam prep. Train on gold mixed with decoys so the model learns to use the right page and ignore the rest.

Conversational RAG: turning a follow-up into a standalone question

In a real chat, people say "and can it be waived?" — retrieval needs to rewrite that into a full, self-contained question before it searches.

Real conversations are full of shortcuts. A customer asks, "What's the overdraft fee?" BankAssist answers "$35." Then they type, "and can it be waived?" To a human, "it" obviously means the overdraft fee. But a retriever that searches the raw text "and can it be waived?" has no idea what "it" is — it searches a meaningless fragment and fetches junk. Conversational RAG fixes this with one step: rewrite the follow-up into a standalone question using the chat history, then search.

So "and can it be waived?" becomes "Can the overdraft fee be waived?" — a complete question that retrieves the right clause. This rewrite step is sometimes called a history-aware retriever or query condensation.

The rewrite is a single, cheap LLM call that takes the recent history and the new turn and returns one self-contained question. Here it is in plain code.

# Conversational RAG: rewrite a follow-up into a standalone question before searching.
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

history = [                              # the recent conversation so far
    {"role": "user", "content": "What's the overdraft fee?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "The overdraft item fee is $35."},
]
follow_up = "and can it be waived?"      # a vague turn — "it" only makes sense with history

def condense(history, follow_up):        # produce a self-contained search query
    convo = "\n".join(f"{m['role']}: {m['content']}" for m in history)  # flatten history to text
    prompt = (
        "Given the chat history and the follow-up, rewrite the follow-up as a "
        "STANDALONE question that needs no history. Return only the question.\n"  # we want just the rewritten query
        f"History:\n{convo}\n\nFollow-up: {follow_up}"
    )
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1-mini",            # small + fast; this runs on every conversational turn
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.content.strip()

standalone = condense(history, follow_up)
print(standalone)                        # THIS is what we embed and send to the retriever
# ...now run your normal retrieval + generation on `standalone`, not on the raw follow-up.
▶ Output
Can the overdraft fee be waived?

That one rewrite is the difference between retrieving the exact waiver clause and retrieving nothing useful. The popular frameworks wrap this for you — LangChain offers a create_history_aware_retriever helper that does exactly this condense-then-retrieve dance — but as you can see, it's a short, understandable step you could write yourself.

⚙️ Under the hood

Two subtleties matter in production. First, don't rewrite when there's no history — on the first turn, pass the question straight through; rewriting a standalone question can distort it. Second, keep the history window bounded: feed the rewriter the last few turns, not the entire transcript, or the condense call gets slow and the model over-stuffs the query. And remember the answer generation still gets the full conversation for tone and continuity — only the retrieval query is the condensed, standalone version.

Going deeper

The rewrite step quietly does more than resolve pronouns. It handles topic carry-over ("what about for a Gold account?" after a fee question), ellipsis ("and the wire one?" meaning the wire fee), and correction turns ("no, I meant the savings account"). Each is a case where the raw turn is nonsense to a retriever but obvious to a human reading the history. The hardest and most dangerous case is the topic switch: the customer finishes with overdrafts and asks "and can it be waived?" where "it" now means a new thing they haven't named yet. A rewriter anchored on stale history will confidently resolve "it" to the old topic and fetch the wrong clause. The defenses are to feed only the last few turns (so old topics age out), and to let the rewriter return the question unchanged when it can't confidently resolve a reference, rather than forcing a guess.

A second refinement is to decouple the retrieval query from the generation context cleanly. The condensed standalone question is the only thing you embed and search; the answer model still receives the full recent conversation so it keeps tone, remembers the customer's name, and doesn't repeat itself. Mixing these up — searching on the full transcript, or answering from only the condensed line — is a common bug that either floods retrieval with irrelevant history or makes the bot sound amnesiac. For multilingual banks there's a further wrinkle: a customer who code-switches mid-chat can produce a follow-up in one language referring to an answer in another, and the rewriter must normalize to the language your index is built in before it searches.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. One small-model condense call per conversational turn — the cheapest technique in this chapter, and almost always worth it; keep it on a fast model so it adds tens of milliseconds, not seconds. Scale. It runs on every multi-turn request, so cache nothing stateful but do bound the history window (last 3–5 turns) to keep the call fast and the cost flat as conversations grow long. Failure modes. Mis-resolved references on topic switches (the subtle, high-impact bug), over-rewriting a question that was already standalone, and the first-turn case where there's no history to use. Monitoring. Log the original turn and the rewritten query side by side — when a conversational answer looks wrong, the rewrite is the first suspect; track how often rewrites change the query and sample them for correctness. Security & compliance for a bank. The condense prompt carries recent conversation, which can contain account numbers and balances — treat that history as sensitive (redact or tokenize PII before it enters the rewrite prompt and before it lands in logs), and scope the history strictly to the authenticated session so one customer's context can never leak into another's rewrite.

⚠ Watch out

A sloppy rewrite silently poisons retrieval. If the model mis-resolves "it" — say the customer switched topics and "it" now means the wire fee, not the overdraft fee — you'll confidently fetch and answer about the wrong thing. Log the rewritten query alongside the original; when a conversational answer looks wrong, the rewrite is the first place to look.

🧠 Remember it

Before you search a chat turn, fill in the blanks from history: turn "can it be waived?" into "can the overdraft fee be waived?" Rewrite, then retrieve.

How these fit together — and when each is worth the extra cost

All of these are upgrades to the same humble idea (fetch, then answer). The engineering skill is knowing which upgrade fixes which failure — and resisting the ones you don't need.

It's easy to feel you must bolt on everything. You shouldn't. Each technique in this chapter buys a specific improvement in exchange for latency, cost, or complexity. A great engineer adds one only after measurement shows the plain pipeline failing in exactly the way that technique fixes. Here's the whole toolbox on one page.

TechniqueWhat it addsExtra costReach for it when…
Agentic RAGModel decides, repeats & routes retrieval in a loopHigh (many LLM calls, non-deterministic)Questions vary widely; some need multiple hops or sources
Self-RAGReflects on whether to retrieve and whether the answer is groundedMedium (extra reflection calls)Hallucinations slip through; you need a groundedness gate
CRAGGrades retrieved docs; falls back when they're weakMedium (a grader call per doc + fallback)Retrieval sometimes returns junk and the model builds on it
Adaptive RAGRoutes by question complexity to the cheapest pathLow (one tiny classifier call) — usually saves moneyA wide mix of easy and hard questions
GraphRAGRetrieves connected subgraphs for multi-hop linksHigh (graph construction + maintenance)The answer is a connection: fraud rings, AML, exposure
Multimodal RAGRetrieves over images, tables, charts, scanned pagesHigh (vision inference, large index)Knowledge lives in pictures, charts, or scanned docs
RAFTFine-tunes the model to use context & ignore distractorsVery high (training data + infra + retraining)A stable, high-value domain where retrieval noise hurts
Conversational RAGRewrites follow-ups into standalone queriesLow (one condense call per turn)Any multi-turn chat — this one is nearly always worth it

A sensible way to climb: start with plain retrieval. Add conversational rewriting the moment it's a chat (cheap, almost always helps). Add adaptive routing to control cost. Add CRAG grading and Self-RAG grounding checks where wrong answers are costly. Reach for agentic loops only when questions genuinely need multiple steps. Bring in GraphRAG for relationship questions and multimodal for visual documents — both for whole classes of questions the others simply can't answer. Save RAFT for last, when prompt-time tricks have hit a wall on a stable, high-value domain.

✅ Tip

These techniques stack. A mature BankAssist might rewrite the follow-up (conversational), route by complexity (adaptive), grade the docs (CRAG), check the answer is grounded (Self-RAG), and for AML questions walk a graph (GraphRAG) — all in one request. But it earned each layer by measuring a real failure first, not by collecting features.

Going deeper

When you stack these, the order matters as much as the choice. A sensible composed pipeline runs cheap-and-early, expensive-and-late: condense the follow-up first (so everything downstream sees a clean query), then route by complexity (so easy questions exit before you spend a cent on graders), then retrieve, then grade the documents (CRAG) and drop junk, then generate, then check the draft is grounded (Self-RAG) before it ships. Put the groundedness check last, because it's the final safety net; put routing early, because its whole job is to stop you paying for the later stages. The one thing you must resist is letting the layers multiply latency blindly: four sequential small-model calls in front of the answer can quietly turn a 1-second bot into a 4-second one, and users feel every extra second more than they value the marginal accuracy.

The deeper discipline is that every added layer is also an added failure surface and an added thing to monitor. A grader that silently starts rubber-stamping, a router that drifts after a prompt tweak, a rewrite that mis-resolves a pronoun — each can degrade quality without throwing a single error. So a mature system treats the whole chain as one observable unit: a trace per request with a span per stage, and a small golden evaluation set that runs on every change so you can see which layer moved the numbers. That is what separates "we added some clever RAG" from "we run a measured, debuggable knowledge system."

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Stacking multiplies both — each gate is another model call in the critical path, so maintain an explicit per-request latency and token budget and let the adaptive router short-circuit the expensive layers for easy questions; measure p95 latency per intent, not just the average. Scale. The cheap gates (condense, route, grade) are your highest-QPS calls — run them on small models in their own rate-limit pools so a traffic spike on grading never starves the main answer model. Failure modes. Silent degradation of any single gate, latency creep from layer pile-up, and composite non-determinism that makes bugs hard to reproduce. Monitoring. One distributed trace per request with a span per stage; dashboards for cost-per-answered-question, per-stage latency, groundedness-pass rate, refusal rate, and escalation-to-human rate; and a golden-set regression run on every deploy. Security & compliance for a bank. The composed pipeline touches customer PII at several stages (history in the rewrite, documents in retrieval, drafts in the grader), so apply redaction and access control at each stage, keep an end-to-end audit trail that ties the final answer to the exact sources and gate verdicts behind it, and give it all a single human-escalation exit for anything the system can't confidently and safely answer.

⚠ Watch out

The frontier-RAG trap is adding cleverness the plain pipeline never needed — a loop, a grader, a graph — and shipping something slow, expensive, and fragile that solves a problem you didn't have. Every technique here is a fix for a specific, observed failure. If you can't name the failure it fixes, you don't need it yet.

🧠 Remember it

Diagnose, then upgrade. Junk docs → CRAG. Hallucination → Self-RAG. Mixed difficulty → Adaptive. Multi-hop → Agentic/Graph. Pictures → Multimodal. Chat → Conversational. Stable, noisy domain → RAFT.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Building the knowledge graph behind GraphRAG

Walking a graph is the easy half. The real work — and the real cost — is turning a mountain of messy documents into clean, connected nodes and edges in the first place.

Retrieving over a knowledge graph assumes the graph already exists. But nobody hands you one. You start with the same raw stuff as any RAG system: account statements, KYC forms, loan contracts, wire-transfer logs, support transcripts. A graph is not sitting inside those documents waiting to be read — you have to construct it. Think of it like a detective's cork-board: the case files are just paper until someone pins the photos up and runs red string between the people who know each other. Building the graph is running that string, at scale, with an LLM holding the spool.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist wants to answer "which customers linked to this flagged account also hold business loans?" — but first someone has to notice that the contract calls her "Priya R. Sharma," the wire log calls her "P SHARMA," and the KYC form calls her "Sharma, Priya" — and that all three are the same person, who happens to be a director of Acme Ltd. Until that string is pinned, the graph has three strangers where there is really one customer, and every multi-hop answer built on top is quietly wrong.

In plain terms

Graph construction is a pipeline with four big steps, and the whole GraphRAG payoff rests on getting them right:

  1. Extract — read each document with an LLM and pull out entities (nodes) and relationships (edges).
  2. Resolve — merge the duplicates, so "P SHARMA" and "Priya Sharma" become one node.
  3. Cluster & summarize — group the graph into communities and write a plain-English summary of each.
  4. Maintain — keep all of the above fresh as new data streams in, without rebuilding from scratch every night.

Step 1 — Schema-guided extraction into triples

The core move is simple: feed the LLM a chunk of text and ask it to return triples — little (subject, relation, object) facts like (Priya Sharma, DIRECTOR_OF, Acme Ltd). Each triple becomes two nodes and one edge. Do this across every document and the triples stitch themselves into a graph.

But a free-form "extract whatever you see" prompt is a trap: one chunk invents a works_for edge, the next says employed_by, a third says EMPLOYEE_OF, and now the same real relationship is scattered across three edge types the query can never join. The fix is a lightweight ontology — a short, fixed menu of allowed entity types and relation types — handed to the model so it classifies into your vocabulary instead of improvising. For a bank, that menu is small and concrete:

Entity types (nodes)Relation types (edges)
Customer, Account, Transaction, Counterparty, Company, Loan, AddressOWNS, CO_SIGNS, SENT_MONEY_TO, DIRECTOR_OF, HOLDS, SHARES_ADDRESS_WITH

That tiny schema is the single highest-leverage thing you can do for graph quality. It keeps the vocabulary closed, makes edges joinable, and turns a vague extraction task into a classification task the model is good at. Here is the extraction itself, using OpenAI structured outputs so the model is forced to return valid triples in your schema — no fragile JSON parsing, no invented edge names.

# Schema-guided entity/relationship extraction: raw text -> clean triples.
from openai import OpenAI                       # official OpenAI SDK
from pydantic import BaseModel                  # declares the exact shape we demand back
from typing import Literal                      # pins fields to a fixed menu of values

client = OpenAI()                               # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

NODE = Literal["Customer","Account","Company","Loan","Counterparty"]   # our ontology: allowed node types
EDGE = Literal["OWNS","CO_SIGNS","DIRECTOR_OF","HOLDS","SENT_MONEY_TO"] # our ontology: allowed edge types

class Triple(BaseModel):                        # one fact = two nodes + one edge
    subject: str                                # e.g. "Priya Sharma" (verbatim from the text)
    subject_type: NODE                          # must be one of the allowed node types
    relation: EDGE                              # must be one of the allowed edge types
    object: str                                 # e.g. "Acme Ltd"
    object_type: NODE                           # must be one of the allowed node types

class Graph(BaseModel):                          # the wrapper the model returns
    triples: list[Triple]                       # zero or more facts found in this chunk

chunk = ("Priya Sharma, a director of Acme Ltd, co-signs account "   # one document chunk
         "AC-88 with Omar Reed. Acme Ltd holds business loan BL-4471.")

resp = client.responses.parse(                  # structured-output call: guarantees the schema
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                       # cheap, fast model — extraction runs on EVERY chunk
    input=[                                      # the prompt
        {"role": "system", "content":           # tell it to use ONLY our ontology
            "Extract banking entities and relationships. "
            "Use only the given types. Skip anything that doesn't fit."},
        {"role": "user", "content": chunk},     # the text to mine
    ],
    text_format=Graph,                          # the model MUST fill this exact structure
)

for t in resp.output_parsed.triples:            # resp.output_parsed is a validated Graph object
    print(f"({t.subject}) -[{t.relation}]-> ({t.object})")  # emit each edge for the graph DB
▶ Output
(Priya Sharma) -[DIRECTOR_OF]-> (Acme Ltd) (Priya Sharma) -[CO_SIGNS]-> (AC-88) (Omar Reed) -[CO_SIGNS]-> (AC-88) (Acme Ltd) -[HOLDS]-> (BL-4471)

Those four lines are the graph for one chunk. Run the same call over a million chunks and you have a graph for the whole bank. Notice what the Literal menus bought you: every edge is one of five known types, so a Cypher query can actually join them. That is schema-guided extraction in one picture — the model does the reading; the ontology does the disciplining.

🧠 Remember it

Give the model a menu, not a blank page. Free-form extraction invents a new edge name every chunk; a tiny ontology keeps every edge joinable.

Step 2 — Entity resolution (the same thing, spelled five ways)

Extraction happily creates a new node every time it sees a name. So "Priya Sharma," "P SHARMA," and "Sharma, Priya" land as three separate customers — and three disconnected customers break every multi-hop walk, because the string that should link them was never pinned. Entity resolution (also called deduplication or record linkage) is the step that decides "these refer to the same real-world thing" and merges them into one node.

In practice you blend three signals, cheapest first:

  • Deterministic keys — if two nodes share a verified identifier (customer ID, tax number, IBAN), merge immediately. This catches most of the volume for almost no cost.
  • Fuzzy matching — normalize and compare names, addresses, and dates of birth (string similarity, phonetic keys). Good for typos and reordered names.
  • Embedding similarity — embed the name-plus-context and merge nodes whose vectors are very close. Catches the hard cases that spelling alone misses.

Get this wrong in either direction and you pay: under-merging leaves one customer looking like five strangers and hides the fraud ring; over-merging fuses two different Priya Sharmas into one node and invents links that don't exist. In a bank, a wrongly merged identity can mean a frozen innocent account, so resolution usually keeps a confidence score and routes the borderline merges to a human.

⚙️ Under the hood

Resolution isn't a one-pass job — it's an ongoing reconciliation. A common pattern is blocking then scoring: first bucket candidate nodes cheaply (e.g. same surname soundex + same postcode) so you never compare every node against every other, then run the expensive fuzzy/embedding score only within each bucket. Microsoft's GraphRAG indexer leans on the LLM itself here too, asking it to decide whether two similarly named entities are the same before it finalizes the graph.

Step 3 — Communities and their summaries

Local search ("everything connected to this account") only needs clean nodes and edges. But global questions — "what themes run across all our fraud cases this quarter?" — can't be answered by walking from one starting point, because there is no single starting point. This is the problem Microsoft's GraphRAG solved with an indexing trick: community detection plus community summaries.

After the graph is built, a clustering algorithm (GraphRAG uses Leiden) partitions it into communities — tightly connected clusters of entities — and does so hierarchically: fine-grained clusters at the bottom, which roll up into broader clusters above them. Then an LLM writes a plain-English summary (a "community report") for each community: its key entities, its main relationships, its overall theme. A global question is answered by reading these precomputed summaries and combining their partial answers — never by reprocessing the raw documents. That is why GraphRAG can reason over an entire corpus: the expensive thinking was done once, at index time, and frozen into summaries.

💡 Key idea

Local search walks the graph to answer "how is X linked to Y?" Global search reads community summaries to answer "what's going on across everything?" The summaries are the thing that makes whole-corpus questions affordable — you build them at index time so you don't pay for them at query time.

Step 4 — Incremental maintenance

A bank's data never holds still — new accounts, new wires, new counterparties every minute. If building the graph costs real money (it does), you cannot rebuild it from scratch every night. The production pattern is incremental: hook into the source systems with change-data-capture, run extraction only on the new or changed documents, resolve those fresh entities against the existing graph, and then recompute communities and summaries only for the clusters that actually moved. A stale fraud graph is worse than useless — it misses exactly the newest ring you most need to catch — so freshness is a first-class requirement, not a nice-to-have.

Storage and tooling

The graph has to live somewhere queryable. The default home is a graph database — most commonly Neo4j — which stores nodes and edges natively and speaks Cypher for the multi-hop walks. (Some teams keep nodes and edges in a relational or vector store with graph extensions; the choice is about scale and the queries you run.) You rarely hand-build the whole pipeline. Three tool families dominate, and they trade control for convenience:

ToolWhat it gives youBest when
Microsoft GraphRAGEnd-to-end indexer: extraction → Leiden communities → community reports, plus local & global searchYou want the full "global summaries" capability out of the box
LlamaIndex PropertyGraphIndexPluggable extractors (including schema-guided ones) over a property-graph store; the newer successor to its older KnowledgeGraphIndexYou want control over extraction and a Neo4j backend
LangChain LLMGraphTransformerOne class that turns documents into graph documents (nodes + relationships), usually written straight into Neo4jYou want the lowest-effort "text in, graph out" path

A reasonable default: prototype with LangChain's LLMGraphTransformer to see a graph fast, move to LlamaIndex's PropertyGraphIndex when you need schema control, and adopt Microsoft GraphRAG when global, corpus-wide questions matter. All three can store into Neo4j, so the backend survives the tool choice.

⚙️ In production

Construction is LLM-heavy, and that is the dominant cost. Extraction runs at least one LLM call per chunk, and community summarization adds another LLM call per community across every level of the hierarchy — so indexing a large corpus can mean hundreds to many thousands of LLM calls and hours of wall-clock time before you can ask a single question. Banks control this with the usual levers: a small cheap model for extraction (like the gpt-4.1-mini above), batching and parallelism across chunks, caching so unchanged documents are never re-extracted, and strictly incremental updates. Watch the bill the way you'd watch any batch job — cost per 1,000 documents, extraction failure rate, and the share of nodes that needed human review at resolution. Because the graph holds linked personal and financial data, it inherits the full compliance weight: per-entity access control, audit logs on every write, PII handling, and data-residency rules on where the graph DB lives. A newer research direction, Microsoft's LazyGraphRAG, defers the expensive extraction to query time and reports a small fraction of full GraphRAG's indexing cost — worth watching if upfront indexing cost is the blocker.

⚠ Watch out

Don't build a graph you don't need. Construction and maintenance are expensive and never truly "done," so a graph only pays off where the relationships are the answer: multi-hop link analysis, AML and fraud rings, KYC entity resolution, exposure and counterparty risk. For ordinary factoid questions ("what's the overdraft fee?") a vector store is cheaper, simpler, and just as correct. And remember the whole structure rests on step one — garbage extraction and sloppy resolution produce confident, well-connected nonsense. The graph is only ever as trustworthy as the triples and the merges underneath it.

✅ Tip

Treat the ontology as a product decision made with the fraud and AML teams, not a coding detail. The entity and relation types you choose decide which questions the graph can ever answer. Start with a handful of types that map to real investigations, ship it, and widen the schema only when a question you actually get keeps falling through the gaps.

🧠 Remember it

Extract, resolve, summarize, refresh. The LLM reads the documents; the ontology disciplines the edges; resolution merges the duplicates; communities make the global view cheap — and you pay for all of it once, up front, so queries stay fast.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Knowledge Layer (RAG) — Evaluation

A RAG system that "looks good in the demo" is a rumour, not a fact. This chapter shows you how to turn that rumour into numbers you can trust — so when BankAssist answers a customer, you already know how often it's right, and you'd catch it the moment it slips.

Why you must grade retrieval and generation separately

A RAG answer is really two machines bolted together. If you only grade the final answer, you'll never know which machine broke.

Imagine a librarian and a writer working as a team. A customer asks a question. The librarian runs to the shelves and brings back a stack of pages. The writer reads only those pages and composes the reply. If the final letter is wrong, there are two very different reasons it could be wrong — and the fix for each is the opposite of the other:

  • The librarian brought the wrong pages. No matter how brilliant the writer is, she can only work with what's on the desk. This is a retrieval failure.
  • The librarian brought the right pages, but the writer ignored them, misread them, or made something up. This is a generation failure.

If you only look at the final letter and say "that's wrong," you've learned almost nothing. Do you go fix the search system, or do you go fix the prompt and the model? You're guessing. And in a bank, guessing-driven engineering means weeks spent tuning the writer when the librarian was the problem all along.

So you measure each machine on its own. You check: did retrieval fetch the passages that actually contain the answer? Separately, you check: given those passages, did the model write an answer that stays true to them? Two scores, two owners, two fixes.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist tells a customer the wire-transfer fee is "$15." It's actually $25. The team argues for a week: "the model is hallucinating, let's swap to a bigger model." Then someone finally checks the retrieval score and discovers the fee schedule chunk was never fetched at all — the search returned an old marketing page that mentioned a "$15 promotional transfer." The model was perfectly faithful to the wrong page. The bug was the librarian, not the writer. A bigger model would have confidently repeated the same wrong number.

💡 Key idea

Retrieval sets the ceiling; generation decides how close to the ceiling you get. If the right text was never retrieved, no prompt, no model, and no reranker can produce a correct, grounded answer. So you always read the retrieval score first.

Going deeper — the four quadrants of a RAG failure

Once you hold two scores instead of one, every answer falls into one of four boxes, and each box has a different owner and a different fix. Think of it as a two-by-two grid: retrieval good or bad, on one axis; generation good or bad, on the other.

  • Retrieval good, generation good — the happy path. The right pages were fetched and the answer stayed true to them. Ship it, then keep watching, because live traffic will still surprise you.
  • Retrieval good, generation bad — the pages were on the desk but the writer fumbled: it hallucinated an extra fact, ignored a page, or answered a different question. Owner: the prompt/model team. Fix: tighten the prompt, raise the model, add a "answer only from context" instruction.
  • Retrieval bad, generation good — the most dangerous box, because it looks fine. The writer faithfully, fluently, confidently wrote an answer grounded in the wrong pages. A faithfulness score alone would wave this through. Only the retrieval score exposes it. Owner: the search team.
  • Retrieval bad, generation bad — everything is broken; start with retrieval, because fixing the writer is pointless while the desk holds the wrong pages.

The quadrant you're in is not visible from the final answer. Two customers can get the same wrong "$15 fee" reply — one because retrieval fetched a stale page (box three), one because the model ignored a correct page (box two). Same symptom, opposite cure. That is the entire argument for two scores in one sentence: the symptom is shared, the cure is not.

How the split works in practice. You attach the two scores to every logged answer. Retrieval is graded against a ground-truth list of which chunks should have been fetched (an offline measurement, because it needs labels). Generation is graded by asking a second model — a judge — whether each claim in the answer is supported by the chunks that were fetched (this needs no labels, so it can run on live traffic too). The pair travels together through your dashboards, so a human or an alert can read the quadrant at a glance instead of re-deriving it from a transcript.

⚙️ In production

Two scores means two dashboards, two alerts, two on-call owners. At a bank, wire these as separate signals so a 3 a.m. page says which machine broke, not just "quality down."

  • Cost & latency. The retrieval score is almost free — it's arithmetic over IDs, microseconds per query, so compute it on 100% of traffic. The generation (faithfulness) score costs a judge LLM call or several per answer, so never run it inline in the customer's request path (it would add seconds and dollars to every chat). Instead sample — score, say, 1–5% of live answers asynchronously off the logs. For BankAssist at 200k chats/day, scoring 2% with a mini judge model is a few thousand cheap calls a day, not 200k expensive ones.
  • Scale & failure modes. The two machines rot in different ways. Retrieval degrades slowly and silently when the knowledge base changes — a re-indexing job drops a document, an embedding model is swapped, a parser update mangles tables. Generation degrades suddenly when a prompt or model version changes. Separate charts catch separate rots.
  • Monitoring. Alert on each score independently with its own threshold (e.g. page on-call if sampled faithfulness drops below 0.9 for an hour, or if retrieval recall on the nightly golden run drops 3 points). A blended "quality" line hides both.
  • Security & compliance. When a regulator or an internal audit asks "why did the assistant tell a customer the wrong fee?", the two-score record is your evidence: you can show it was a retrieval miss (stale document in the index) versus a model hallucination, which are different remediation obligations. Keep both scores in the immutable audit log alongside the answer.
⚠ Watch out

A single end-to-end "accuracy" number is the most popular and most useless RAG metric. It can stay flat while your retrieval quietly rots, or drop for reasons you can't diagnose. Treat it as a headline, never as a diagnosis. The two component scores are where the truth lives.

When to split (almost always) vs when not to: in any system where a wrong answer has a real cost — a bank, healthcare, legal — always grade the two machines apart; the diagnostic power is worth the extra plumbing. The only time a single end-to-end number is defensible is a throwaway prototype you'll never debug, where you just want one rough "is it in the ballpark" signal before investing further.

🧠 Remember it

Librarian or writer? Grade them apart, read retrieval first. You can't fix a two-part machine with a one-part score.

Retrieval metrics, with one tiny worked example

Five small numbers answer one big question: did we fetch the right passages, and did we rank them well? Let's compute all five by hand on a single banking query.

Retrieval metrics all start from the same two ingredients. First, a query. Second, a ground-truth list of which chunks in your knowledge base are actually relevant to that query — the ones a careful human marked as "yes, this helps answer it." Then your retriever returns a ranked list of chunks, and we compare its list against the truth.

Here is our running example. A customer asks BankAssist:

"What is the overdraft fee, and can it be waived?"

Two chunks in the knowledge base are genuinely relevant (our ground truth): C-fee ("Overdraft item fee: $35") and C-waiver ("one courtesy waiver per 12 months on request"). The retriever fetches its top 5, ranked:

RankChunk the retriever returnedRelevant?
1Overdraft marketing blurb✗ no
2C-fee — "$35 item fee"✓ yes
3ATM withdrawal limits✗ no
4C-waiver — "one waiver / 12 months"✓ yes
5Savings interest rates✗ no

Now the five metrics, each a different question about this list.

Hit rate (did we get any relevant chunk?)

Hit rate@k asks the simplest yes/no: is there at least one relevant chunk in the top k? Here, at k=5, yes (ranks 2 and 4 are relevant), so hit rate@5 = 1. But at k=1 — looking only at the very top result — the answer is no, because rank 1 is the marketing blurb, so hit rate@1 = 0. Measured across your whole test set, hit rate is "the fraction of questions where we fetched something useful at all." It is your crude floor.

Recall@k (did we get all the relevant chunks?)

Recall@k = (relevant chunks found in top k) ÷ (total relevant chunks that exist). We found both relevant chunks (C-fee, C-waiver) within the top 5, and there are 2 in total, so recall@5 = 2 / 2 = 1.0. This is the metric that most directly measures the ceiling we keep warning about: if recall is low, the answer is doomed before the model even starts, because the needed text isn't on the desk.

Precision@k (how much of what we fetched was junk?)

Precision@k = (relevant chunks in top k) ÷ k. We fetched 5 chunks and 2 were relevant, so precision@5 = 2 / 5 = 0.4. Precision is about noise: the 3 irrelevant chunks still get pasted into the prompt, costing tokens and tempting the model to wander. High recall with low precision means "we found it, but we buried it in clutter."

MRR (how high was the first relevant chunk?)

Mean Reciprocal Rank rewards putting a relevant chunk near the top. For one query it's simply 1 ÷ (rank of the first relevant result). Our first relevant chunk sits at rank 2, so the reciprocal rank is 1 / 2 = 0.5. MRR is the average of that across all your queries. If the right chunk had been at rank 1, you'd score 1.0; at rank 10, just 0.1. It captures "how far does the reader have to dig?"

NDCG (the full ranking grade)

NDCG (Normalised Discounted Cumulative Gain) is the richest metric: it rewards relevant chunks and penalises them for sitting low in the list, using a gentle logarithmic discount. It comes in two steps.

First, DCG (the gain we actually got). Each relevant chunk contributes 1 / log2(rank + 1). Our relevant chunks are at ranks 2 and 4:

  • rank 2 → 1 / log2(3) = 1 / 1.585 = 0.631
  • rank 4 → 1 / log2(5) = 1 / 2.322 = 0.431
  • DCG = 0.631 + 0.431 = 1.062

Second, IDCG (the ideal gain — what a perfect ranking would score, with both relevant chunks at the very top, ranks 1 and 2):

  • rank 1 → 1 / log2(2) = 1 / 1 = 1.000
  • rank 2 → 1 / log2(3) = 0.631
  • IDCG = 1.000 + 0.631 = 1.631

Then NDCG = DCG ÷ IDCG = 1.062 / 1.631 = 0.651. A perfect ranking scores 1.0; our messy one scores 0.65 because the relevant chunks were pushed down to ranks 2 and 4 instead of 1 and 2. NDCG is the metric you tune a reranker against, because it's the one that notices ordering.

⚙️ Under the hood — why the log2 discount?

People read from the top. A chunk at rank 1 is almost always seen; a chunk at rank 20 might as well not exist. The log2(rank+1) denominator shrinks each chunk's contribution as it sinks, modelling that fading attention — and it fades gently (logarithmically), not off a cliff, which matches how a model skims a prompt. Dividing by the ideal (IDCG) just rescales every query to the same 0–1 range, so a query with 5 relevant chunks and a query with 1 are comparable.

Here's the whole worked example as a few lines of code, so you can see the metrics are just arithmetic, not magic.

# Our retriever's top-5 result for one query, newest-style: 1 = relevant, 0 = not.
import math                                   # we only need log2 for NDCG

relevant_flags = [0, 1, 0, 1, 0]             # ranks 1..5; C-fee at 2, C-waiver at 4
total_relevant = 2                            # how many relevant chunks exist in the whole KB

hit_rate = 1 if any(relevant_flags) else 0    # did we fetch at least one relevant chunk?
recall = sum(relevant_flags) / total_relevant # fraction of all relevant chunks we found
precision = sum(relevant_flags) / len(relevant_flags)  # fraction of fetched chunks that were relevant

first_hit = next(i for i, r in enumerate(relevant_flags, start=1) if r)  # rank of first relevant (=2)
mrr = 1 / first_hit                           # reciprocal of that rank

# DCG: each relevant chunk adds 1/log2(rank+1); irrelevant chunks add nothing.
dcg = sum(r / math.log2(rank + 1) for rank, r in enumerate(relevant_flags, start=1))
# IDCG: the ideal is all relevant chunks packed at the top (ranks 1,2,...).
idcg = sum(1 / math.log2(rank + 1) for rank in range(1, total_relevant + 1))
ndcg = dcg / idcg                             # rescale so a perfect ranking = 1.0

print(f"hit={hit_rate} recall={recall} prec={precision} mrr={mrr} ndcg={ndcg:.3f}")
▶ Output
hit=1 recall=1.0 prec=0.4 mrr=0.5 ndcg=0.651

The numbers tell a story at a glance: we found everything (recall 1.0, the ceiling is fine) but we ranked it poorly (precision 0.4, MRR 0.5, NDCG 0.65). The fix here is a reranker to push the relevant chunks up, not a change to the embeddings.

⚙️ Under the hood — picking your k, and graded relevance

Two production refinements. First, choose k to match reality: if you feed the model the top 5 chunks, measure recall@5 and precision@5, not recall@100 — a chunk retrieved at rank 40 that never reaches the prompt is useless, and measuring it flatters you. Second, NDCG also supports graded relevance (a chunk can be "perfect = 3", "helpful = 2", "slightly on-topic = 1" instead of just 0/1). Graded labels make NDCG far more sensitive, but they cost more to produce — binary is the pragmatic default to start.

Going deeper — which metric to optimise, and the real numbers

These five metrics do not move together, and choosing which to chase is a real engineering decision. A useful rule of thumb from production RAG teams:

  • If recall@k is low, nothing else matters yet. Recall is the ceiling. Fix it first by changing what goes into the index: smaller or overlapping chunks, a better embedding model, hybrid search (dense vectors plus keyword/BM25 — BM25 being the classic keyword-matching score that ranks a chunk by how many of the query's exact words it contains) so exact terms like account numbers and reg codes aren't lost, or simply a larger k. Chasing NDCG while recall is 0.6 is polishing a car with no engine.
  • Once recall is high, chase NDCG and MRR. These are about order, and order is what a reranker fixes. A cross-encoder reranker typically lifts NDCG@10 by a meaningful margin (often several points) at the cost of a few tens of milliseconds per query — it re-scores the top candidates with a model that reads query and chunk together.
  • Watch precision when you feed many chunks. Low precision means the prompt is full of distractors, which both costs tokens and, in long contexts, causes the model to "lose" the right chunk among the noise (the well-known "lost in the middle" effect). If precision@k is 0.3, consider retrieving fewer, better chunks.

A concrete target set for a banking knowledge base: recall@10 above 0.90 (you almost never want to miss the policy page), MRR above 0.7 (the right page is usually first or second), and NDCG@10 above 0.8 after reranking. Numbers below these are not "fine" — they are a backlog.

⚙️ In production

Retrieval metrics are the cheap, always-on half of eval — lean on them hard.

  • Cost & latency. Unlike generation metrics, these are pure arithmetic over chunk IDs — no LLM calls, no dollars, sub-millisecond. You can recompute them on every single query in production if you log which chunks were retrieved and have labels. The real cost is labelling: a human deciding which chunks are truly relevant. That human-label budget, not compute, is what caps the size of your measured set, which is why synthetic label generation matters at scale.
  • Scale. For a bank with tens of thousands of documents, the labelled "relevant chunks" ground truth drifts every time the knowledge base is re-indexed — chunk boundaries shift, IDs change. Pin labels to stable document anchors (a section ID, a policy number), not to volatile chunk indices, or your recall will "drop" purely because the chunker renumbered everything.
  • Monitoring & failure modes. Track recall@k and NDCG@k as time series on your golden set, run nightly. The classic silent failure: an embedding-model or index upgrade that improves average recall but tanks it on one critical category (say, fee-dispute queries). Segment the metrics by topic so a win in one area can't mask a regression in another a regulator cares about.
  • Security & compliance. Log the retrieved chunk IDs (not necessarily the full text) with every answer. When an answer is challenged, you can reconstruct exactly which documents the system saw — essential for a bank proving it acted on the current, approved policy and not a withdrawn one.
⚠ Watch out

Never report latency without recall, or recall without k. "Our retriever is fast" is meaningless if it's fast because it gave up early and recall collapsed. And a tiny or unrepresentative labelled set will lie to you confidently — 20 easy questions can show 100% recall while the hard long-tail queries your customers actually ask are failing silently.

When to use which: use recall@k whenever the question is "could we possibly answer this?" (the default health check). Use NDCG/MRR when you're tuning ordering or a reranker. Do not optimise NDCG while recall is still low, and do not rely on precision as a quality signal when you deliberately over-fetch and let a reranker trim — precision will look bad by design.

🧠 Remember it

Recall = did we find it. Precision = how much junk came with it. MRR = how high was the first good one. NDCG = the whole ranking, graded. Hit rate is just recall's yes/no cousin.

Generation metrics: faithfulness, answer relevancy, answer correctness

Now we grade the writer. Given the pages on the desk, did the model write something true, on-topic, and actually correct?

Once retrieval has done its job, three questions decide whether the generated answer is any good. They sound similar but catch completely different failures.

Faithfulness / groundedness — "is every claim backed by the pages?"

This is the hallucination detector, and the single most important generation metric in banking. Faithfulness asks: of all the factual claims in the answer, what fraction are actually supported by the retrieved context? The recipe is mechanical:

  1. Break the answer into separate atomic claims.
  2. For each claim, check: can it be found in or inferred from the retrieved chunks?
  3. Faithfulness = (supported claims) ÷ (total claims).

Say BankAssist answers: "The overdraft fee is $35, and it is automatically waived for all senior citizens." That's two claims. Claim one ("$35") is right there in C-fee — supported. Claim two ("automatically waived for all seniors") appears nowhere in the retrieved context — the model invented it. So faithfulness = 1 / 2 = 0.5. A score below 1.0 means the model said something the pages don't back — in a bank, that invented second claim is a compliance incident waiting to happen.

Answer relevancy — "did it actually answer what was asked?"

Answer relevancy ignores truth entirely and asks only: does the response address the user's question, or does it wander, pad, or dodge? A faithful answer can still be irrelevant. If the customer asks "can the overdraft fee be waived?" and BankAssist replies with a perfectly accurate paragraph about how overdrafts are calculated but never mentions waiving, that's faithful (every word is true) yet low on relevancy (it didn't answer the question). A common way to measure it automatically: ask a model to generate a few questions that the answer would be a good reply to, then check how close those are to the real question.

Answer correctness — "is it right, compared to the gold answer?"

Answer correctness compares the answer to a human-written reference answer (your "gold" answer). It blends two things: factual overlap (does it state the same facts as the reference?) and semantic similarity (does it mean the same thing?). This is the closest metric to "is it simply correct," but it needs a gold answer for every test question — which is expensive to create and the reason you build a golden dataset — a curated set of questions paired with known-correct answers. Faithfulness and relevancy need no reference and can run on live traffic; correctness needs a reference and lives in your offline test set.

Faithful but wrong

Retrieval fetched an outdated fee page saying "$15." The model faithfully repeats "$15." Faithfulness = 1.0 (true to the page), but answer correctness = low (the real fee is $25). This is why faithfulness alone isn't enough — it only proves the writer obeyed the pages, not that the pages were right.

Correct but unfaithful

The model happens to know the real fee from training and says "$25" — which is correct — even though the retrieved page said "$15." Correctness = high, faithfulness = low. Dangerous: it got lucky this time, but a model that ignores its context will eventually "guess" wrong with total confidence.

Here's how you'd score faithfulness and the two relevancy/recall metrics with RAGAS, a popular open-source RAG-eval library. (APIs here change between versions — pin the version you install.)

# pip install ragas langchain-openai   — versions drift, so pin them in your project.
from ragas import SingleTurnSample                 # one (question, answer, context) test row
from ragas.metrics import Faithfulness, ResponseRelevancy, LLMContextRecall  # three metric classes
from ragas.llms import LangchainLLMWrapper          # lets RAGAS drive any LangChain chat model as the judge
from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI             # the model that will act as the LLM judge

judge = LangchainLLMWrapper(ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4.1-mini"))  # a cheap, capable judge model

sample = SingleTurnSample(                           # one evaluation record...
    user_input="What is the overdraft fee, and can it be waived?",  # the question asked
    response="The overdraft fee is $35; one courtesy waiver is allowed per year.",  # what BankAssist replied
    retrieved_contexts=[                             # the chunks retrieval put in front of the model
        "Overdraft item fee: $35.",
        "One courtesy overdraft waiver per 12 months on request.",
    ],
    reference="Overdraft fee is $35, waivable once every 12 months on request.",  # gold answer, for recall/correctness
)

faithfulness = Faithfulness(llm=judge)              # fraction of answer claims supported by the context
relevancy    = ResponseRelevancy(llm=judge)         # does the answer address the question (no reference needed)
recall       = LLMContextRecall(llm=judge)          # did the context contain everything the gold answer needs

score = await faithfulness.single_turn_ascore(sample)  # returns a float 0..1; await because the judge call is async
print(round(score, 2))                              # 1.0 here: both claims are backed by the retrieved chunks
▶ Output
1.0

Notice the division of labour: Faithfulness and ResponseRelevancy are reference-free (they only compare the answer to the question and the retrieved context), so you can run them on live production traffic. LLMContextRecall compares against the gold reference, so it belongs in your offline test set where references exist. (A note on versions: in recent RAGAS releases these capitalised metric classes are the current API, but importing names from ragas.metrics can raise a deprecation warning as the library reorganises — one more reason to pin the exact version in your project.)

Going deeper — why faithfulness is the metric a bank watches hardest

Of the three, faithfulness is the compliance metric. A relevant-but-unfaithful answer — fluent, on-topic, and quietly wrong about a fee or a legal right — is exactly the output that gets a bank fined or sued. So faithfulness gets the strictest treatment: it is often run on a large sample of live traffic, gated in CI, and alerted on. The mechanics matter here. Because faithfulness decomposes the answer into atomic claims and checks each one against the context, a single fabricated clause drags the score down even if ninety percent of the answer is perfect — which is the behaviour you want, because that one clause is the one that hurts a customer.

There is a subtlety worth internalising: a high faithfulness score is necessary but not sufficient. It only proves the answer is true to the retrieved pages. If retrieval handed the model a stale or wrong page, a faithful answer is faithfully wrong — which is precisely why faithfulness lives next to the retrieval scores and the gold-answer-based correctness metric, never alone. The "faithful but wrong" and "correct but unfaithful" cases above are not edge cases; in a large deployment they happen every day, and only the combination of all three generation metrics plus retrieval recall tells the whole story.

One more real-world wrinkle: faithfulness is expensive. Decomposing claims and verifying each against the context is typically several LLM calls per answer, not one. Answer relevancy's reverse-question trick is also multi-call. This is the single biggest driver of your eval bill, and it shapes every production decision below.

⚙️ In production

Generation metrics are LLM-judged, so they cost money, wobble, and must be sampled — plan for all three.

  • Cost. Each faithfulness score can fire 3–10 judge calls (claim extraction + per-claim verification). At BankAssist's volume you cannot score every answer; pick a cheap but capable judge (a gpt-4.1-mini-class model), sample a few percent of live traffic, and reserve the expensive full judge for the offline golden set and for answers a cheaper filter already flagged as risky.
  • Latency. Never block the customer on a faithfulness check — it would add seconds. Score asynchronously from the logs. The exception is a lightweight guardrail check (a single fast call) that can run inline to suppress a clearly-ungrounded answer before it reaches a customer; that is a different, cheaper check than full faithfulness scoring.
  • Scale & failure modes. Judge scores drift when the judge model is silently upgraded by the provider. Pin the judge model version. Re-baseline your dashboards whenever you intentionally change it, or a tooling change masquerades as a quality change.
  • Monitoring. Track sampled faithfulness and relevancy as live time series, segmented by product area. A drop in faithfulness on "overdraft" queries after a prompt tweak is an actionable, scoped alert; a single blended number is not.
  • Security & compliance. Store the judge's reasoning (the claim-by-claim breakdown), not just the number. When an answer is disputed, the breakdown showing which claim was unsupported is your audit trail — and it is far more convincing to a regulator than "our metric said 0.6."
⚠ Watch out

These scores are produced by another LLM reading and judging — they are estimates, not ground truth, and they wobble run to run. Pin the metric library version and the judge model: a metric definition or judge upgrade can shift every number overnight, and you'll mistake a tooling change for a quality regression. The judge also carries biases of its own, so calibrate it against human ratings before trusting its scores.

When to use which: run faithfulness and relevancy everywhere, including live traffic, because they need no reference. Reach for answer correctness only where you have a gold answer (the offline golden set) — do not try to force correctness onto live traffic, because without a reference it degenerates into a second, noisier relevancy check and tells you nothing new.

🧠 Remember it

Faithful = true to the pages. Relevant = answers the question. Correct = matches the gold answer. You can be any two without the third — so measure all three.

The RAG Triad: three checks that box in hallucination

Three relevance checks, arranged in a triangle, cover every link in a RAG answer. If all three hold, a made-up answer has almost nowhere to hide.

The RAG Triad (popularised by the TruLens evaluation project) is a beautifully simple mental model. A RAG answer involves exactly three things: the question, the retrieved context, and the answer. Draw them as a triangle, and each edge is one quality check:

  • Context Relevance (question ↔ context): is the retrieved context actually relevant to the question? This grades the librarian.
  • Groundedness (context ↔ answer): is the answer supported by the retrieved context — same idea as faithfulness? This grades the writer's honesty.
  • Answer Relevance (question ↔ answer): does the answer actually address the question? This grades the writer's aim.

Why does covering all three edges matter so much? Because each edge catches a failure the others miss, and a hallucination has to slip past all three to survive:

  • If context relevance is high but groundedness is low → the right pages were fetched, but the model made something up anyway. A generation/prompt problem.
  • If context relevance is low → retrieval failed; the model is working from the wrong pages, so even a grounded answer is grounded in the wrong thing. A retrieval problem.
  • If groundedness is high but answer relevance is low → the model dutifully summarised the context but never actually answered the customer. A prompt/instruction problem.

That's the real gift of the triad: it's not just three scores, it's a diagnostic decision tree. The pattern of which edge is weak tells you exactly which part of the pipeline to go fix — the same separate-the-machines principle, now with a name for each failure.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist starts getting complaints. The team runs the triad over a sample of live chats. Context relevance: 0.92 (good — retrieval is finding the right policy pages). Answer relevance: 0.90 (good — answers are on-topic). Groundedness: 0.61 (bad). Instantly they know where to look: retrieval is fine, but the model is padding answers with plausible-sounding extras the policies never stated. The fix is a tighter prompt ("answer only from the provided context; if it's not there, say so"), not a new embedding model. The triad turned a vague "customers are unhappy" into a one-line fix.

⚙️ Under the hood — reference-free by design

All three triad checks are computed by an LLM judge comparing two of the three items — and crucially, none of them needs a human-written gold answer. That's deliberate: it means you can run the triad continuously on live production traffic, sampling real customer chats and scoring them in near-real-time. Context recall and answer correctness (which need references) stay in the offline lab; the triad is your always-on smoke alarm.

Going deeper — the triad's judges are themselves imperfect

It's tempting to treat the three triad numbers as truth. They aren't — they're the output of three LLM judges, each with its own accuracy. Public benchmarks of these exact judges are sobering and worth knowing.
