In early-2025 evaluations of a widely-used triad implementation (TruLens) using a strong default judge, the groundedness judge agreed with human labels at roughly 0.81 F1 (F1 is an accuracy-style score that blends precision and recall into one number, where 1.0 is a perfect match with the humans), answer relevance around 0.79 F1, and context relevance the hardest of the three at around 0.64 F1 on a standard retrieval benchmark. The lesson isn't "don't use the triad" — it's "know that context relevance is the noisiest edge, and don't over-react to a small wobble on it."

Teams improve these judges the same way you'd improve any prompt: by optimising the rubric. The same 2025 work found that instructing the context-relevance judge to be deliberately "critical and strict" measurably reduced its tendency to rate marginal chunks as relevant (leniency bias), and that prompt optimisation lifted groundedness precision by roughly 16 points at a small recall cost. In other words, the triad is a starting point you tune against your own human labels, not a finished oracle you install.

⚙️ In production

The triad is your live smoke alarm — cheap enough to run forever if you sample, precise enough to route the alert.

  • Cost & latency. Three judge calls per sampled chat. Run it off the logs, not in the request path, and sample (1–5% of live traffic for BankAssist). Because the three checks localise the failure, one alert can carry a tag — "retrieval" vs "generation" vs "answering" — so the right team is paged, not everyone.
  • Scale & monitoring. Chart all three edges as separate live time series. The pattern is the diagnosis: context relevance falling means retrieval drift (new products, stale index); groundedness falling means the model is padding (often after a prompt or model change); answer relevance falling means the assistant is dodging or rambling. Set an independent threshold and on-call owner per edge.
  • Failure modes. Because context relevance is the least reliable judge, give it more headroom in alerting (don't page on a 2-point dip) and confirm suspected retrieval regressions against the offline recall number, which is label-based and firmer.
  • Security & compliance. The triad runs on real customer chats, so the sampled transcripts it reads contain PII. Scrub or tokenise before they reach the judge model, keep the judge inside your compliance boundary (self-hosted or a contracted endpoint with no training-on-data), and log the three scores to the audit trail with the answer.
⚠ Watch out

The triad is reference-free, which is its superpower and its limit: because no edge compares against a human-written gold answer, it can all look green while the answer is confidently, grounded-ly wrong — the model faithfully summarised a page that was itself out of date. The triad proves the internal consistency of question, context and answer; it cannot prove the context was true.

When to use it vs when not: use the triad as your always-on live monitor and first-pass diagnostic, where references don't exist. Do not use it as your release gate or your proof of correctness — for that you need the offline golden set with reference answers and context-recall/correctness scores. Triad for the floor, golden set for the gate.

🧠 Remember it

Question, Context, Answer — three corners, three checks. Context relevance grades the search, groundedness grades honesty, answer relevance grades aim. Pass all three and hallucination is cornered.

Building a golden dataset — and generating eval data synthetically

You can't measure quality without a set of questions whose right answers you already know. That set is your golden dataset, and it's the most valuable asset in the whole eval program.

A golden dataset (also called an eval set or test set) is a collection of records, each holding four things:

  • a question a real customer might ask,
  • the reference answer (the gold, human-approved answer),
  • the relevant chunks — which passages in your knowledge base actually contain the answer (your retrieval ground truth), and
  • optional metadata — topic, difficulty, language, whether it's a trick question.

With this set, every metric in this chapter becomes computable: recall needs the relevant-chunk labels, correctness needs the reference answer, and you can re-run the whole thing on every code change. Without it, you're flying blind and calling it "looks good."

How big, and how do you pick the questions?

Start small but representative — even 50–100 well-chosen questions beat 10,000 random ones. The art is in coverage. A good banking golden set deliberately includes:

  • The common cases — the top questions from your call-centre logs (fees, limits, how to reset a PIN).
  • The long tail — rare but real questions, because that's where retrieval quietly fails.
  • Hard cases on purpose — multi-part questions ("compare early-closure penalties for a fixed vs a flexible loan"), questions with exact codes ("what does Reg E say about disputed charges?"), and questions that have no answer in your docs (so you can test that BankAssist says "I don't know" instead of inventing one).
  • Adversarial cases — a question whose retrieved document contains a hidden instruction, to test that the system treats retrieved text as data, not commands.

Where the data comes from: mine it, write it, or generate it

Three sources, usually combined. Mine real questions from support tickets and chat logs (most realistic, needs PII scrubbing first). Hand-write the tricky cases with a subject-matter expert (a compliance officer knows the questions that must never be answered wrong). And generate synthetically — use an LLM to read your actual documents and invent plausible question/answer pairs grounded in them. Synthetic generation is how you get to hundreds of test cases quickly.

# Synthetic eval-data generation: turn a real policy chunk into a Q/A test record.
from openai import OpenAI                     # official OpenAI client
import json                                   # to parse the model's structured reply
client = OpenAI()                             # reads your API key from the environment

chunk = ("Overdraft item fee: $35 per item. One courtesy waiver is available "  # a REAL chunk from your KB...
         "per 12-month period on customer request.")                            # ...so the generated answer is grounded

prompt = f"""You are building a test set for a bank assistant.
Read the POLICY TEXT and write ONE realistic customer question whose answer is
fully contained in it, plus the correct answer. Do not invent facts beyond the text.
Return strict JSON: {{"question": "...", "reference_answer": "..."}}
POLICY TEXT:
{chunk}"""                                     # we force grounding by forbidding outside facts

resp = client.chat.completions.create(        # one chat call to generate the pair
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                     # cheap model is fine for generation
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},  # ask for valid JSON so we can parse it safely
)
record = json.loads(resp.choices[0].message.content)  # dict with question + reference_answer
record["relevant_chunk_id"] = "overdraft-fee-001"     # we KNOW the source chunk → free retrieval label
print(record["question"])                     # a ready-to-use golden-set question
▶ Output
If I overdraw my account, how much is the fee and can I ever get it waived?

The clever part: because you generated the question from a known chunk, you automatically get the retrieval ground-truth label for free (relevant_chunk_id). That single line is what makes recall and precision measurable at scale. Libraries like RAGAS ship a TestsetGenerator that automates this across a whole corpus and even produces multi-hop questions that span several chunks.

Going deeper — a golden set is a living asset, not a one-time file

The biggest mistake teams make is building the golden set once and letting it fossilise. Your bank ships new products, retires old fees, and rewrites policies under new regulation — and the day it does, every reference answer touching those topics is silently wrong. A golden record that says the overdraft fee is $35 becomes a false failure the moment the fee changes to $30: the system now answers correctly, but your test marks it wrong. So the golden set needs an owner and a refresh cadence, exactly like a codebase.

Coverage is the other half of the craft, and it's worth being systematic. Build a small matrix: rows are topics (fees, limits, disputes, loans, cards, security), columns are difficulty (simple lookup, multi-part, no-answer-exists, adversarial). Aim for at least a handful of records in every cell. The empty cells are your blind spots — and in a bank, the "no-answer-exists" and "adversarial" cells are the ones compliance cares about most, because they test whether BankAssist says "I don't know" instead of inventing a policy, and whether it refuses an instruction hidden inside a retrieved document.

On sourcing, the three streams complement each other by design. Mined questions give you realism (how customers actually phrase things). Expert-written questions give you coverage of the scary edge cases a customer rarely asks but you must never get wrong. Synthetic generation gives you volume cheaply. A healthy banking golden set is roughly a blend of all three, never one alone.

⚙️ In production

Treat the golden dataset as governed, versioned, PII-sensitive infrastructure — because that's what it is.

  • Cost. The expensive part isn't storage, it's expert time. A compliance officer's review of hard cases is the scarce resource; spend it on the adversarial and no-answer cells and let synthetic generation + spot-checks cover the easy ones. Budget for a recurring refresh, not a one-off build.
  • Scale & freshness. Tie golden records to the policy documents they came from, and flag records for re-review whenever their source document changes (a simple content hash on the source chunk does this). This is how you avoid thousands of false failures after a routine policy update.
  • Security & compliance. Mined records come from real customer conversations, so the golden set is a PII repository. Scrub names, account numbers, and balances before records enter the set; store it under the same access controls and retention rules as production customer data; and keep it inside your data-residency boundary. A test set casually copied to a laptop or a public notebook is a data-breach report waiting to happen.
  • Monitoring & failure modes. Watch for dataset rot: if scores move but no code changed, suspect the test set, not the system — which is only diagnosable if the set is versioned in git with a changelog. Also guard against leakage: never let golden questions be used to tune the retriever or prompt, or you'll measure memorisation, not quality.
⚠ Watch out

Synthetic data has a trap: a model that writes the questions in the same style it answers them makes the test too easy, and you'll report rosy scores that collapse on real customers. Mitigations: always have a human review a sample of generated records, vary the phrasing deliberately (slang, typos, non-native English — exactly how real customers write), and never let synthetic data fully replace real mined questions and expert-written hard cases. Also scrub PII from any mined data before it enters the eval set — test sets leak into logs and dashboards.

When to lean on synthetic vs not: use synthetic generation to reach volume fast and to blanket a new corpus with coverage early. Do not use it for the high-stakes cases — the adversarial, no-answer, and compliance-sensitive questions must be hand-written and expert-reviewed, because those are exactly the cases a model is worst at inventing and the ones where a wrong reference answer is most dangerous.

✅ Tip

Version your golden dataset like code (it lives in git, with a changelog). When a score moves, you must be able to tell whether the system changed or the test set changed. An un-versioned eval set makes every number unexplainable.

🧠 Remember it

A golden record = question + gold answer + which chunk holds it. Mine the common ones, hand-write the scary ones, generate the rest from real docs — and always have a human spot-check.

LLM-as-a-judge: the grader is a model, so grade the grader

Most RAG metrics above are secretly produced by another LLM reading your answer and scoring it. That's cheap and scalable — and quietly biased. Here's how to prompt it well and keep it honest.

You cannot pay a human to read every answer BankAssist produces. So nearly every metric in this chapter — faithfulness, relevancy, the whole triad — is computed by a strong LLM acting as a judge: you give it the question, the answer, maybe the context, and a rubric, and it returns a score. This is the engine that makes continuous evaluation affordable. But a judge is a model, with all a model's quirks, so you treat its scores as useful estimates, never as gospel.

How to prompt a judge well

A vague "rate this answer 1–10" produces noise. A good judge prompt is specific, gives a rubric (what each score means), demands reasoning before the score, and asks for structured output. Here is a faithfulness-style judge prompt for BankAssist:

# An LLM-as-judge prompt for groundedness/faithfulness, with an explicit rubric.
JUDGE_PROMPT = """You are a strict evaluator for a bank's assistant.
Decide whether the ANSWER is fully supported by the CONTEXT.

Score with this rubric:
  1 = every factual claim in the answer is directly supported by the context
  0.5 = partially supported (some claims backed, some not in the context)
  0 = a key claim is NOT in the context (the model added or changed a fact)

Think step by step: first LIST each factual claim in the answer, then mark each
claim supported/unsupported by quoting the context. THEN give the final score.
Return JSON: {"reasoning": "...", "score": 1 | 0.5 | 0}

QUESTION: {question}
CONTEXT: {context}
ANSWER: {answer}"""                            # reasoning-before-score makes the judge more accurate and auditable

Three deliberate choices in that prompt. The rubric turns a fuzzy opinion into a defined scale. "List each claim, then quote the context" forces the judge to decompose the answer rather than vibe-check it — the same claim-by-claim mechanic that makes faithfulness reliable. And reasoning before the score both improves accuracy and leaves you an audit trail, which matters when a regulator asks "why did you consider this answer safe?"

The judge's biases (and they're real)

Judges have well-documented, systematic blind spots. Know them, because they quietly skew your numbers:

  • Verbosity bias — longer, more confident answers get higher scores, even when a short answer was better. Your metrics can reward padding.
  • Position bias — when comparing two answers "A vs B", judges favour whichever came first (or sometimes second), regardless of quality.
  • Self-preference bias — a judge tends to prefer answers written by its own model family. Using GPT to grade GPT's answers inflates the scores.
  • Noise — ask the same judge the same question twice and you may get two different scores.

How to calibrate and de-bias the judge

You don't throw the judge out; you discipline it:

  • Calibrate against humans. Have experts hand-label a few hundred answers, then check how often the judge agrees with them. If judge-human agreement is high, trust the judge at scale. If it's low, fix the rubric before trusting any number. Report that agreement figure — it's the credibility of your whole eval.
  • Prefer pairwise over absolute. "Is answer A better than B?" is more reliable than "score A from 1–10," because relative judgments are more stable than absolute ones.
  • Randomise order in pairwise comparisons, and run each both ways (A-then-B and B-then-A) to cancel position bias.
  • Use a different family for judge and generator to dodge self-preference — e.g. don't let the same model both write and grade.
  • Ensemble or repeat — average several judges or several runs for a less noisy score on high-stakes metrics.

Going deeper — agreement is the number that validates every other number

Here is the idea that separates a serious eval program from theatre: your judge's credibility is a measurable number, and you must publish it. Take a few hundred answers, have humans label them, run the judge on the same answers, and compute how often they agree (accuracy, or better, Cohen's kappa which corrects for chance agreement). That single figure — say "our faithfulness judge agrees with human compliance reviewers 91% of the time" — is what lets anyone trust the thousands of answers the judge grades unattended. Without it, every downstream score is a guess dressed as a measurement.

What counts as "good enough" agreement depends on stakes. For a low-risk relevancy signal, 80% might be fine. For a faithfulness judge standing between BankAssist and a compliance incident, you want agreement comparable to how often two human reviewers agree with each other (inter-annotator agreement) — because a judge can't reasonably be held to a higher bar than humans hit. If humans only agree 85% of the time on what "faithful" means, your rubric itself is ambiguous and needs tightening before the judge can do better.

⚙️ In production

The judge is the single biggest line item in your eval bill and the single biggest source of silent drift — manage it like a production dependency.

  • Cost. Judging dominates eval spend because high-stakes metrics multiply calls (claim decomposition, repeats for noise reduction, both orderings for pairwise). Control it with a tiered strategy: a cheap gpt-4.1-mini-class judge on the bulk of sampled traffic, escalating to a stronger judge only for flagged or high-risk answers and for the offline golden run.
  • Latency & caching. Cache judge results keyed on (answer, context, rubric-version) so re-runs over an unchanged golden set don't re-pay. Run judging async, off the request path.
  • Drift & monitoring. Providers silently update models; a judge you didn't change can change under you. Pin the judge version, and keep a fixed anchor set of human-labelled answers that you re-score on every judge or rubric change. If the anchor-set agreement moves, the grader moved — freeze releases until you re-calibrate.
  • Security & compliance. The judge reads real answers and contexts containing PII, so it must sit inside your compliance boundary with no training-on-your-data. Persist the judge's rubric version and its written reasoning with every score — when a regulator asks "how did you decide this answer was safe to send?", the reasoning trail is the answer.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's faithfulness score jumps from 0.82 to 0.94 overnight — champagne? No. Someone had switched the judge model to a newer version of the same family that writes the answers, and self-preference inflated the grades. The underlying answers hadn't improved at all. The team caught it only because they kept a fixed set of 200 human-labelled answers and noticed judge-human agreement had actually dropped. Lesson: when the judge changes, re-calibrate before you believe a single number.

⚠ Watch out

The cardinal sin is treating judge scores as ground truth. They are a model's opinion, calibrated at best. Pin the judge model and the rubric, re-calibrate whenever either changes, and keep a human-labelled "anchor set" so you can always tell whether a score moved because quality moved or because the grader moved.

When to use an LLM judge vs not: use it whenever you need to score at a scale humans can't reach and the metric is fuzzy (faithfulness, relevancy, helpfulness) — that's most of RAG eval. Do not use it where a cheaper deterministic check already works (exact-match on a reference number, a regex for a required disclosure, retrieval recall from labels), and do not let it be the sole gate on a life-or-money-critical decision without a human in the loop and a measured agreement figure behind it.

🧠 Remember it

The judge is a model too. Give it a rubric, make it reason first, and check it against humans. An ungraded grader is just a confident guess with a number attached.

Offline vs online evaluation, the tooling, and the benchmarks

Evaluation happens in two places: in the lab before you ship, and on live traffic after. You need both, plus the tools that run them and the public benchmarks that let you shop for components.

Offline eval — the lab

Offline evaluation runs your golden dataset against the system before release. Because you have reference answers and relevant-chunk labels, you can compute everything: recall, precision, NDCG, correctness, faithfulness. It's repeatable, it's controlled, and it's where you compare "chunk size 300 vs 500" or "reranker on vs off." Its limit: your golden set is a sample of what you imagined customers would ask, frozen in time. Real customers are weirder.

Online eval — the live floor

Online evaluation runs on real production traffic. You usually don't have reference answers for live questions, so you lean on the reference-free metrics — the RAG triad (context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance) — sampled across live chats, plus real signals like thumbs-up/down, "was this helpful?", escalation-to-human rate, and follow-up re-asks. Online eval catches the drift offline can't: a new product launches, customers ask about it, and your frozen golden set never saw it coming.

The tooling (all current, open-source unless noted)

You don't build this plumbing from scratch. The 2025–2026 landscape splits into metric libraries and observability platforms:

ToolWhat it's for
RAGASOpen-source metric library: faithfulness, context precision/recall, response relevancy, plus a synthetic test-set generator. The default for scripted offline RAG scoring.
TruLensOpen-source library that popularised the RAG Triad; instruments an app and logs triad feedback scores per call.
DeepEvalOpen-source, pytest-style eval framework — write metrics as unit tests and run them in CI as a quality gate.
Arize PhoenixOpen-source observability built on OpenTelemetry/OpenInference: tracing, datasets, experiments, and evaluator templates for hallucination and retrieval quality. Strong for self-hosted online eval.
LangfuseOpen-source LLM-engineering platform: tracing, prompt management, dataset-driven evals, and online scoring on live traces. Self-hostable.
LangSmithCommercial platform from the LangChain team: tracing, datasets, built-in and custom evaluators, production monitoring. Best fit if you're already on LangChain/LangGraph.

A common shape: RAGAS or DeepEval for offline metrics in CI, and Phoenix, Langfuse, or LangSmith for tracing and online monitoring of live traffic. They overlap — pick the smallest set that covers lab + live.

Benchmarks: BEIR and MTEB (for shopping, not shipping)

Two public benchmarks come up constantly when choosing a component (especially an embedding model), so know what each measures:

  • BEIR — a retrieval benchmark: a heterogeneous set of ~18 datasets across many domains and query types, used to see how well a retriever generalises to data it wasn't trained on. Its headline metric is NDCG@10 — the ranking metric that grades both whether the right chunks were found and how high they sat in the list.
  • MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) — much broader: it scores embedding models across 8 task types (retrieval, classification, clustering, reranking, semantic similarity, pair classification, summarisation, bitext mining) over dozens of datasets and many languages. Its retrieval task is drawn from BEIR and reported as NDCG@10. The public MTEB leaderboard is where teams compare embedding models; a newer massively-multilingual expansion (often written MMTEB) stretches it to hundreds of tasks across 250+ languages.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist passes every offline test and ships. Two weeks later, the bank launches a new "green mortgage" product. Customers flood in asking about it — and BankAssist confidently quotes old mortgage terms, because the golden set was frozen before the product existed and retrieval is matching the closest old document. Offline eval is blind to this by construction: you can't test for a question you never imagined. The online triad, sampling live chats, catches it within hours — context relevance on "green mortgage" queries is near zero. The team adds the product docs to the index, writes a handful of new golden records, and the loop closes. Offline would never have caught it; online did.

⚙️ In production

Offline gates, online watches — and a bank wires both with cost, PII, and residency in mind.

  • Cost & latency. Offline runs on a schedule (per-PR and nightly), so its judge-call bill is bounded by golden-set size — predictable. Online eval's bill scales with traffic, so you sample (1–5%) and tier the judge. Neither should sit in the customer's request path; tracing and scoring happen off the hot path.
  • Scale & tooling overlap. The 2025–2026 pattern is RAGAS or DeepEval for offline metrics in CI, plus one observability platform (Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, or LangSmith) for live tracing and online scoring. They overlap deliberately — resist running three platforms; pick the smallest set that covers lab + live, because every tool is another PII-handling vendor to govern.
  • Failure modes. The gap offline can't see is novelty: new products, new scams, new phrasings. Online eval plus user signals (thumbs-down, escalation-to-human rate, repeat-question rate) is your only early warning. Feed every live failure back as a new golden record — that feedback loop is what keeps the lab honest over time.
  • Security & compliance. Online eval reads live customer traffic, so traces carry PII. Prefer a self-hostable platform (Phoenix, Langfuse) when data-residency rules forbid sending customer chats to a third-party SaaS; scrub PII before it reaches any judge; and keep the eval store inside the same compliance boundary as production.
⚠ Watch out

Public benchmarks are for narrowing the shortlist, never for declaring victory. A model topping MTEB was tuned on general text, not your bank's loan agreements and ISO-20022 messages — and leaderboards suffer contamination and overfitting. A top-5 embedding model can underperform a "worse" one on your jargon. Always re-run the shortlist against your own golden set before committing. The benchmark picks the candidates; your eval set picks the winner.

When to use offline vs online: use offline to compare options and gate releases, where references and repeatability matter. Use online to catch what you didn't anticipate and to measure real user outcomes. Never rely on only one — offline alone ships blind to novelty; online alone can't safely gate a release because there's no answer key. You need both lanes feeding one loop.

🧠 Remember it

Offline = lab with answer keys. Online = live floor with feedback. Libraries (RAGAS, DeepEval, TruLens) compute; platforms (Phoenix, Langfuse, LangSmith) watch. Benchmarks (BEIR, MTEB) shortlist — your golden set decides.

Putting eval in CI: the quality gate that blocks a bad release

Measuring quality is pointless if a bad change can still ship. The final step is to wire your offline metrics into the build so a drop in faithfulness or recall fails the pipeline — just like a failing unit test.

Here's the discipline that separates a serious RAG team from a hopeful one: every change to the pipeline runs the golden dataset automatically, and the build fails if quality drops below a threshold. A parser upgrade, a new chunk size, a different embedding model, a tweaked prompt — any of these can silently wreck retrieval or faithfulness. A CI quality gate catches the regression before it reaches a customer, instead of weeks later via complaints.

The idea is exactly like a unit test, but the assertion is "faithfulness ≥ 0.9" instead of "2 + 2 == 4." Frameworks like DeepEval are built for this — they plug straight into pytest, so your existing CI runner already knows how to run them.

# test_bankassist_rag.py — runs in CI; a quality drop FAILS the build.
import pytest                                       # CI already runs pytest, so eval rides along
from deepeval import assert_test                    # raises AssertionError if a metric is below threshold
from deepeval.metrics import FaithfulnessMetric, ContextualRecallMetric  # two gates
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase          # one (input, output, context) record

from bankassist import answer_with_rag              # YOUR pipeline under test
from golden import load_golden_set                  # your versioned golden dataset

# Thresholds are the release contract: fall below these and the build goes red.
faithfulness = FaithfulnessMetric(threshold=0.9)    # block if <90% of claims are grounded
recall       = ContextualRecallMetric(threshold=0.8)# block if retrieval misses too much needed context

@pytest.mark.parametrize("record", load_golden_set())  # run the body once per golden question
def test_answer_quality(record):
    result = answer_with_rag(record["question"])     # run the REAL pipeline for this question
    case = LLMTestCase(                               # package what the metrics need to judge
        input=record["question"],                    # the question asked
        actual_output=result.answer,                 # what BankAssist produced
        retrieval_context=result.chunks,             # the chunks retrieval fetched (DeepEval's field name)
        expected_output=record["reference_answer"],  # gold answer, needed by recall
    )
    assert_test(case, [faithfulness, recall])        # FAILS the test (and CI) if either is below threshold
▶ Output
FAILED test_answer_quality[record12] - FaithfulnessMetric: 0.62 (threshold 0.9) reason: answer claimed "waived for all seniors" — not supported by retrieved context === 1 failed, 49 passed === → build RED, release blocked

Read what just happened: one of fifty golden questions dropped the faithfulness score to 0.62, the assertion failed, and the CI build turned red — so the release cannot merge. The failure message even names the hallucinated claim, so the engineer knows exactly what broke. A compliance-risking answer was stopped by a robot, not discovered by a customer.

⚙️ Under the hood — making the gate trustworthy

Three refinements keep the gate from becoming a nuisance or a rubber stamp. (1) Watch variance: LLM-judged scores wobble, so set thresholds with a little headroom and consider averaging over a couple of runs, or you'll get flaky red builds. (2) Gate the aggregate and the floor: require both "average faithfulness ≥ 0.9" and "no single answer below 0.5," so one catastrophic answer can't hide behind a good average. (3) Separate gates per stage: a retrieval-recall gate and a generation-faithfulness gate, so a red build immediately tells you which machine regressed — the separate-the-machines principle, enforced automatically.

Going deeper — the gate's real enemy is flakiness, not strictness

A unit test that checks 2 + 2 == 4 gives the same answer forever. A faithfulness gate does not: the judge is a probabilistic model, so the same code can score 0.91 on Monday and 0.89 on Tuesday and flip a 0.90 threshold from green to red with nothing changed. A flaky gate is worse than no gate, because the team learns to re-run until green or to disable it — and then a real regression sails through. Three tactics tame this. First, set the judge to its most deterministic setting (temperature 0) so repeated runs vary as little as possible. Second, build in headroom: if your real quality bar is 0.9, don't set the gate at 0.9 where normal noise trips it — gate at the bar but alert earlier, or require the average over two runs to clear it. Third, pin the judge model and the metric-library version in the CI environment, so a silent provider upgrade can't turn every build red overnight.

There is also a speed-versus-coverage trade. Running 500 golden questions, each firing several judge calls, can add many minutes and real dollars to every pull request. The common split: run a fast, representative subset (say 50 questions) on every PR for quick feedback, and the full set nightly or pre-release. The PR gate catches gross regressions in seconds-to-minutes; the nightly full run catches the subtle ones before they reach production.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist engineer bumps the chunk size from 400 to 600 tokens to "give the model more context" — a change that looks obviously good and passes every unit test. The CI quality gate runs the 50-question golden subset and turns red: recall on multi-part fee questions dropped from 0.94 to 0.78, because the fatter chunks now straddle two policies and the fee page no longer surfaces cleanly. The build is blocked, the PR gets a comment naming the failing records, and the change never reaches a customer. Without the gate, this ships, and three weeks later the first complaint arrives as a regulator-reportable wrong-fee incident. The gate turned a future compliance event into a red build an engineer fixed before lunch.

⚙️ In production

A CI eval gate is itself a production system — it has a cost, a latency, and a failure mode, and at a bank it also produces release evidence.

  • Cost & latency. Judge calls are the expense; a full 500-question run several times a day is real money and minutes. Control it with the PR-subset / nightly-full split, cache judge results for unchanged (answer, context, rubric) tuples, and use a cheaper judge on the PR gate than on the nightly run.
  • Scale. As the golden set grows (it should), parallelise the run across CI workers — the questions are independent — so wall-clock time stays flat even as coverage climbs.
  • Failure modes & monitoring. The gate's own failure mode is flakiness; monitor the pass-rate stability of the gate itself, not just the product. If builds go red without code changes, your judge or test set drifted — treat that as a P1 on the eval infrastructure.
  • Security & compliance. The gate's output is an auditable release record: "version X.Y cleared faithfulness ≥ 0.9 and recall ≥ 0.8 on golden set v12 before deploy." Store these run artefacts — scores, thresholds, dataset version, judge version — alongside the deployment. For a bank this is the documented evidence of due diligence that turns "we tested it" into "here is the signed record that we tested it."
⚠ Watch out

Don't gate on end-to-end accuracy alone — it can pass while retrieval silently degrades, and when it fails it won't tell you why. And resist setting thresholds so high that the team starts disabling the gate to ship; a gate that's always red gets ignored, which is worse than no gate. Tune thresholds to your real quality bar, then hold the line.

When to gate in CI vs not: gate every change that can touch answer quality — prompts, models, chunking, embeddings, parsers, reranker config. Do not bother gating pure cosmetic or infra changes that can't affect retrieval or generation (a logging tweak, a CSS fix); forcing a slow, costly eval run on those just trains the team to route around the gate. Gate what can break quality, skip what can't.

🧠 Remember it

If it's not gated, it's not guaranteed. Turn faithfulness and recall into pass/fail assertions on your golden set, and let a red build — not an angry customer — catch the regression.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

AI Agents — The agent loop & when to use one

Let's meet the AI that doesn't just answer — it decides what to do next, takes an action, looks at the result, and keeps going until the job is done. We'll build the idea slowly, in plain words, with our bank "BankAssist" as the running example.

What makes software "agentic" — and the four-part mental model

Software is "agentic" when it chooses its own next step toward a goal, instead of following steps you wrote out in advance.

Think about two kinds of helpers in a bank branch. The first is a vending machine: press B4, get a specific snack, every time, forever. Someone decided in advance exactly what each button does. The second is a junior teller: you say "please sort out this customer's disputed charge," and they figure out the steps themselves — pull up the account, check the transaction, read the dispute policy, maybe call the card network, then come back with an answer. Nobody scripted those exact steps. The teller decided them, one at a time, based on what they found along the way.

That second helper is agentic. The word sounds grand, but it points at one simple property: the software picks its own next move. A normal program runs a fixed recipe you wrote. An agent is handed a goal and works out the recipe as it goes, adjusting when things surprise it.

Under the hood, an AI agent is built from four parts. Hold these four in your head and almost everything about agents becomes easy to follow.

  • The model — the "brain." A large language model (the kind of AI behind chat assistants) that reads the situation and decides what to do next. It does the thinking, but on its own it can only produce words.
  • Tools — the "hands." Real functions the model is allowed to call: look up a balance, search the policy manual, open a dispute, send an email. Tools are how the agent touches the real world instead of just talking about it.
  • The loop — the "heartbeat." The agent doesn't act once and stop. It repeats: think, act, look at the result, think again — around and around until the goal is met. That repetition is what turns a one-shot answer into real work.
  • Memory — the "notebook." A place to keep facts across steps and across conversations: what the customer already told us, what we tried, what worked. Without it, the agent forgets everything the moment each step ends.

And wrapping all four is context — the carefully chosen information you place in front of the model at each step (the goal, the recent history, the tool results, the relevant memories). The model can only "see" what's in its context window — the limited span of text it reads before answering — so deciding what goes in is a job of its own. A neat way to say the whole thing in one line: agent = model + tools + loop + memory, all curated through context.

🏦 Picture this

A customer messages BankAssist: "I was charged twice for the same coffee shop — fix it." A plain chatbot would reply with words only: "Sorry to hear that, here's how disputes work…" An agent instead goes to work: it calls a tool to pull the last 30 transactions (hands), notices two identical $4.50 charges seconds apart (brain), checks the dispute policy from memory and a document search, decides this qualifies as a duplicate, and calls an open_dispute tool — then loops back to confirm the case was created before telling the customer. It didn't just describe the process. It did it.

💡 Key idea

"Agentic" is not about being smart or futuristic. It's one concrete behaviour: the software decides its own next step toward a goal, and can take actions in the world, instead of running a recipe you fixed in advance.

Going deeper: the four parts pull in different directions

The four-part model is tidy, but in real systems the parts fight each other, and knowing the tensions is what separates a toy from something a bank can run. Start with the model. A bigger, smarter model decides better but costs more and answers slower; a smaller one is cheap and fast but makes worse choices and needs tighter tools to stay on track. Many banking agents use a split: a capable model like gpt-4.1 for the hard reasoning steps, and a cheaper gpt-4.1-mini for routine classification inside the same flow, so you pay for brains only where brains are genuinely needed.

Tools look free but are not. Every tool you add is extra text in the model's context — its name, its description, and its argument schema — and it is one more thing the model can pick wrongly. Give an agent forty tools and it spends attention just choosing among them; the practical sweet spot is a handful of well-named, well-described tools, with the rarely-used ones grouped behind a single "router" tool. Memory splits into two kinds people often confuse. Short-term memory is just the running conversation (the growing message list) that lives for one task and vanishes when it ends. Long-term memory is facts you deliberately save to a database and fetch back later — the customer's preferred name, their past disputes, their risk flags. Short-term memory is automatic; long-term memory is something you design, write, and retrieve on purpose. And the loop is where cost quietly piles up: each turn re-sends everything before it, so a ten-step task is not ten small calls — it is one call, then a bigger one, then a bigger one still.

Wrapping all four, context is the scarce resource. A model can only read a fixed span of text at once — its context window — and current production models hold somewhere between roughly 128,000 tokens and a million or more (a token is about four characters of text). That sounds enormous until a single dispute investigation dumps fifty transactions, three policy pages, and eight tool results into it. Curating context — deciding what to keep, what to summarise, and what to drop at each step — is the real craft, because the model can only ever act on what it can currently see.

# The four parts, wired together explicitly, using the OpenAI API.
from openai import OpenAI                 # official OpenAI SDK — our door to the model (the "brain")

client = OpenAI()                         # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

MODEL = "gpt-4.1"                         # PART 1 — the model: the brain that decides each next step

tools = [{                                # PART 2 — tools: the hands the model may use to touch the bank
    "type": "function",                   # every OpenAI tool is typed "function"
    "function": {
        "name": "get_balance",           # one simple tool the model can call by name
        "description": "Get a customer's balance by account id.",  # clear text so the model picks it correctly
        "parameters": {"type": "object",  # a JSON schema describing the tool's arguments
            "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string"}},  # the one argument this tool needs
            "required": ["account_id"]},
    },
}]

long_term_memory = {"AC-7781": {"name": "Priya"}}  # PART 4a — long-term memory: facts saved on purpose, fetched back later

messages = [                              # PART 4b — short-term memory: the running conversation for THIS task
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are BankAssist. Be brief and accurate."},  # standing instructions = part of context
    {"role": "user", "content": "Hi, what's the balance on AC-7781?"},  # the goal the agent must reach
]

for step in range(6):                     # PART 3 — the loop: repeat think-act-observe, capped so it can't run forever
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, tools=tools, messages=messages)  # the brain reads context and decides
    # execute any requested tool, append its result to messages, then loop again  # ACT + OBSERVE happen on each pass
    break                                 # shortened here: a full run repeats until the model answers in words
▶ Output
Wired up: model (brain) + tools (hands) + loop (heartbeat) + memory (notebook), all fed to the model through the messages list — that list IS the context.
⚙️ In production

At a bank, each of the four parts becomes its own operational concern. Cost & latency: because the loop re-sends the whole conversation every step, a chatty agent's bill grows faster than linearly with its length — the number to watch is tokens-per-resolved-task, not tokens-per-call. A simple balance check should cost one model call; if your dashboards show it averaging four, something is looping. Scale: the model and the tools are usually external services with rate limits, so at call-centre volume you pool connections, set timeouts, and queue overflow rather than letting thousands of loops hammer core banking at once. Failure modes: a tool that times out, a context that overflows the window, a memory store that returns stale data — each needs a defined fallback (retry once, then hand to a human). Monitoring: log every step — the model's inputs, the tool calls, the tool results — so an investigator can replay exactly what the agent saw. Security & compliance: tools are the only place an agent touches real money and real customer data, so each tool enforces its own permission check and writes its own audit record; the model is never trusted to be the access-control layer. Meter, rate-limit, and audit the four parts separately.

⚠ Watch out

The classic beginner mistake is thinking "agent" means "one clever model call." It doesn't — the power is in the loop plus tools, and that is also exactly where the cost and the risk live. When to use the full four-part machine: when a task genuinely needs the model to act, look at the result, and decide again — investigating why a customer's payment keeps failing. When NOT to: when a plain model call or a scripted lookup already answers the question. Wrapping a one-shot "what does APR mean?" question in a tool-calling loop just adds latency, cost, and fresh ways to fail, for no benefit at all.

🧠 Remember it

An agent is a model + tools + loop + memory. Brain decides, hands act, heartbeat repeats, notebook remembers.

Agent vs plain LLM, vs RAG, vs a fixed workflow — and the agency spectrum

An agent is one point on a spectrum of "how much does the software decide for itself." Knowing the neighbours keeps you from calling everything an agent.

The word "agent" gets stuck on everything these days, which makes it mushy. Let's pin it down by lining it up against three things it is often confused with. For each, picture the same banking question.

Agent vs a plain LLM call

A plain language-model call takes your text in and gives text back — once. It's a brilliant writer and reasoner, but it can't do anything beyond producing words, and it stops after a single reply. Ask it "has my salary landed yet?" and it can only guess or explain in general, because it has no way to look at your actual account. An agent wraps that same model in tools and a loop, so it can fetch your real transactions, check them, and answer from fact — and keep going if one step isn't enough.

Agent vs RAG

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) means: before the model answers, go fetch the most relevant documents and let it read them, so the answer is grounded in your real files instead of the model's memory. It's a powerful pattern — but in its basic form it's a fixed, one-way pipe: retrieve once, then answer once. It doesn't decide to look again, try a different source, or take an action. An agent can use retrieval as one of its tools, but it also chooses when to search, whether the results were good enough, and whether to search again or do something else entirely. RAG fetches knowledge; an agent decides and acts, and may fetch knowledge as part of that.

Agent vs a fixed workflow

A workflow (or "automation") is a set of steps you wrote, in a fixed order, maybe with a few if/else branches. "When a wire over $10,000 arrives → run the sanctions check → if clean, post it → else flag for review." The path is decided by the programmer in advance; the model, if used at all, just fills in a slot (like classifying a message). An agent is different precisely because the model chooses the path at run time. Give it the same goal and it may take different steps on Tuesday than it did on Monday, depending on what it finds.

The honest way to hold all this: these aren't rivals on a battlefield, they're points on a dial — how much does the software get to decide? That dial is the agency spectrum.

Reading the dial from left to right:

  • Fixed workflow — you decide every step; the model (if any) fills a blank. Most reliable, least flexible.
  • Autocomplete — the model suggests the next small thing (a sentence, a field) and a human accepts or rejects. The human is still driving.
  • Copilot — the model can plan and act, but checks with a human before anything important. Shared control.
  • Autonomous agent — the model runs the loop itself: decides, acts, observes, repeats, and only surfaces for truly high-stakes moments. Most flexible, needs the most guardrails.
⚙️ Under the hood

There's no bright line where "not an agent" becomes "agent." The useful test is: does the model choose the control flow? If the sequence of steps is decided by your code, it's a workflow — even if it calls an LLM at each step. If the sequence is decided by the model, reacting to what it sees, it's agentic. Most real banking systems are a blend: a fixed outer workflow for safety and audit, with a small agentic step in the middle where judgement is genuinely needed.

Going deeper: the same question, four ways

The cleanest way to feel the difference is to push one customer question — "Has my salary landed yet?" — through all four designs and watch what each can and can't do. A plain LLM can only say something general ("salaries usually post on the last working day"); it never looks at the real account, so it may be confidently wrong. RAG can quote the bank's pay-cycle policy accurately, but it still can't see this customer's ledger — it grounds the answer in documents, not in live data. A fixed workflow can be wired to fetch the last five transactions and check for a credit from the employer, and it does so the same way every time — but only because a programmer foresaw this exact question and coded that path. An agent is handed the goal, decides on its own to call get_transactions, notices the salary isn't there, decides to also check pending credits, finds one arriving tomorrow, and explains — a path nobody scripted in advance.

ApproachWho decides the steps?Can it act via tools?Model callsRepeatable?
Plain LLMNo steps — one replyNo1Mostly
RAGYou: fetch, then answerReads documents only1 (+ a retrieval)Mostly
Fixed workflowYou, in advanceYes, in a set order0–many, fixedExactly
AgentThe model, at run timeYes, in an order it choosesMany, variableNo

Notice the trade running down that last column: as you move from plain LLM to agent, you gain the power to act and adapt, but you lose repeatability — the very thing a regulated bank prizes. That's why the right answer is so often a blend, not a pure agent. The agency spectrum isn't a ladder you're supposed to climb to the top of; it's a dial you set as low as the task allows.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's mortgage team wants to "answer customer questions about their application." The tempting move is to build one big autonomous agent. The wiser build is a blend: a fixed workflow authenticates the customer and loads their case (same every time, fully auditable); a RAG step answers policy questions like "what documents do I still owe you?" from the lending manual; and only the genuinely open-ended requests — "why was my application delayed and what can I do?" — get handed to a small agent that can look across the case, the notes, and the checklist to reason out a real answer. Three tools from the toolbox, each where it fits, instead of one hammer for every nail.

⚙️ In production

The spectrum maps directly onto cost, latency, and governance. Cost & latency climb left-to-right: a plain LLM or RAG answer is one call and a fraction of a second; a fixed workflow is predictable to the penny; an agent is several calls over several seconds, and its bill varies per request. Determinism falls left-to-right: the further right you go, the harder it is to say "it will always do X," which is precisely the property model-risk and audit teams ask for. In practice banks draw a hard outer boundary — authentication, limits, logging, and any money movement stay in deterministic workflow code — and allow agentic reasoning only in the soft centre where judgement helps and mistakes are cheap and reversible. Monitoring differs too: a workflow you test once and trust; an agent you must watch continuously, because the same input can take a new path tomorrow. Choosing a point on the dial is therefore a cost and compliance decision, not just an engineering one.

⚠ Watch out

The loudest mistake in the field is calling everything an agent — slapping the label on a plain RAG bot or a scripted workflow because it sounds impressive. It muddies design conversations and, worse, invites people to add autonomy that isn't earned. When to use an agent: only when the model genuinely needs to choose the control flow because the path can't be known ahead of time. When NOT to: when retrieval-then-answer (RAG) or a fixed set of steps already does the job — then naming it an "agent" buys you nothing but the agent's downsides. Say what it actually is: an LLM call, a RAG pipeline, a workflow, or a true agent.

🧠 Remember it

LLM talks. RAG talks after reading. Workflow follows your steps. Agent chooses its own steps — and acts.

When to use an agent (and when a boring workflow wins)

Agents are exciting, which is exactly why they get used in places a simple script would have been cheaper, faster, and safer.

Here's a truth that separates engineers from demo-builders: most tasks do not need an agent. An agent's whole value is that it decides its own path — so you only want one when the path genuinely cannot be known in advance. If you can draw the steps on a whiteboard, you don't need a model to invent them; you need to write them down and run them. That's a workflow, and it will be faster, cheaper, and far easier to trust.

So how do you tell? Walk a task through a short set of questions before you reach for an agent.

Reach for an agent when all of these are true:

  • The path is unpredictable. You genuinely can't list the steps ahead of time because they depend on what the agent discovers. Investigating why a payment failed could need one lookup or seven, in no fixed order.
  • It needs tools and several adaptive steps. One retrieval or one classification isn't enough; the task is a little project — gather, reason, act, check, maybe redo.
  • The value of flexibility beats the cost of unpredictability. You can afford the extra latency and token cost, and you've made the risky actions safe (bounded permissions, or a human approving money movement).

Prefer a plain workflow when the steps are known and repeatable. A daily reconciliation job, a "wire over $10k → sanctions screen → post or flag" rule, a fixed onboarding checklist — these want deterministic code. You get speed, a cost you can predict to the penny, and an audit trail that's the same every run. An agent here only adds ways to go wrong.

Banking taskBuild…Why
"Nightly, reconcile these two ledgers and email mismatches."Fixed workflowSame steps every night; no judgement needed.
"Answer 'what's my overdraft fee?' from our policy docs."RAG (one call)Fetch the clause, answer once. No loop required.
"Investigate why this customer's transfer keeps failing and resolve it."AgentPath varies wildly; needs several tools and adaptive steps.
"Move $50,000 between customer accounts on request."Agent + human approvalAgentic reasoning, but a human must sign off on the money.
⚠ Watch out

The most expensive mistake in this whole field is using an agent where a workflow would do. You pay for it three times: slower responses (every step is a model call), higher bills (lots of tokens), and a system whose behaviour you can't fully predict — which, in a regulated bank, is a compliance headache. "Could a script do this?" If yes, let a script do it.

✅ Tip

Start with the least agentic design that could work, and add autonomy only where you feel real pain. Often the best banking system is a solid workflow with one small agentic step tucked inside — the single spot where human-like judgement actually earns its cost.

Going deeper: put real numbers on the choice

"An agent costs more" is easy to say and easy to ignore until you price it out. Take a question a single call answers for, say, a fraction of a penny in under a second. Turn it into an agent and three things change at once. First, calls multiply: a modest investigation is five to ten model calls instead of one. Second, each call is bigger: every step re-sends the whole growing conversation, so the later calls carry all the earlier tool results — total tokens can be several times the sum of the individual steps. Third, latency stacks: the calls run one after another because each depends on the last, so a sub-second answer becomes five to fifteen seconds. Put together, an agentic version of a simple task can cost ten to thirty times as much and feel an order of magnitude slower. That is a brilliant trade when the task truly needs it — an open-ended fraud investigation that would otherwise take a human twenty minutes — and a terrible one when a script would have sufficed.

There's an edge case worth naming: the "almost-workflow." Sometimes a task has a mostly-fixed path with just one unpredictable fork. The temptation is to make the whole thing an agent "for flexibility." The better move is usually the opposite — keep the fixed path as code and call the model only at the one fork, feeding its decision back into your workflow. You get the adaptivity exactly where it's needed and keep determinism everywhere else. The question is never "agent or not?" at the whole-system level; it's "which steps need judgement?"

🏦 Picture this

A product manager at BankAssist asks for "an AI agent that handles address changes." It sounds agentic, but walk the steps: verify the customer, validate the new address format, check it against sanctions/fraud rules, update the record, send a confirmation. Every step is known in advance and must happen the same way every time for audit. That's a workflow, not an agent — and building it as an agent would trade a predictable, penny-cheap, instantly-auditable process for a slower, pricier, non-deterministic one that compliance would rightly block. The one place judgement might help is reading a messy free-text address, and even that is a single model call inside the workflow, not a loop.

⚙️ In production

Before an agent ships at a bank, three production questions decide whether the flexibility is worth it. Cost at volume: multiply the per-task token cost by real traffic — an agent that's fine in a demo can turn a call-centre's modest AI budget into a frightening one, so set a per-task token budget and alert when average calls-per-task drifts upward (the classic early sign of needless looping). Latency budget: a chat customer tolerates a few seconds; a real-time payment screen does not — if the task sits on a latency-critical path, a workflow usually wins regardless of how "agentic" the problem feels. Governance fit: every autonomous action must be loggable, explainable, and reversible or human-gated; if you can't satisfy model-risk management and produce an audit trail, the task isn't ready for autonomy no matter how well it demos. The decision to use an agent is signed off by finance and compliance, not just engineering.

🧠 Remember it

If you can draw the steps, script them. Agents are for paths you can't draw in advance.

The agent loop in depth: perceive → reason → act → observe → reflect → stop

An agent is a loop. Understand the six beats of that loop and you understand how every agent in the world actually runs.

At the center of every agent is a simple cycle that repeats until the job is done. People draw it many ways, but it always comes down to the same six beats. Let's walk them with a BankAssist example: a customer says, "I don't recognise a $90 charge from last Friday — please sort it."

  1. Perceive — take in the current situation: the user's request, the conversation so far, and any new tool results from the last step. This is the agent "reading the room." Here: it reads the complaint and notes it has no transaction data yet.
  2. Reason / plan — the model thinks about what to do next. Not the whole plan carved in stone, just the next sensible move: "I should pull Friday's transactions to find the $90 charge." Good agents keep a light plan and revise it as facts arrive.
  3. Act — the model calls a tool: a real function with real arguments. Here it calls get_transactions(account, date="last Friday"). This is the only beat that touches the outside world.
  4. Observe — the tool returns a result, and that result is fed back into the agent's context. It sees a $90 charge to "GreenCabs Ltd" at 23:10. Now it knows something it didn't a moment ago.
  5. Reflect — the agent checks its own progress. "Does this answer the goal? Is the charge clearly fraudulent, or could it be a forgotten taxi? Do I need another step?" Reflection is what lets an agent catch a wrong turn instead of charging ahead.
  6. Stop condition — every loop must know when to quit. It stops when the goal is met ("dispute opened, customer told"), or when a guardrail trips: too many steps, too much spend, a tool keeps failing, or a human needs to approve. Without a stop condition, an agent can run forever.

Here's the surprise for most newcomers: the agent loop is not some huge framework. At its heart it's a short while loop. Let's write a real, minimal one using the Anthropic Messages API (the official way to talk to Claude models), where the model is allowed to call one tool. Every line is explained.

# A tiny but real agent loop: the model can call a get_balance tool.
from anthropic import Anthropic          # official Anthropic SDK — talks to Claude models

client = Anthropic()                      # reads your API key from the environment; your door to the model

tools = [{                                # the "hands": tools the model is allowed to call
    "name": "get_balance",               # the tool's name — the model uses this to call it
    "description": "Get a customer's current account balance by account id.",  # a clear description guides the model to pick it correctly
    "input_schema": {                     # a JSON schema describing the arguments the tool expects
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string"}},  # one required argument: the account id, as text
        "required": ["account_id"],
    },
}]

def get_balance(account_id):              # the ACTUAL function that runs when the model calls the tool
    return {"account_id": account_id, "balance_gbp": 412.55}  # pretend lookup; in real life this hits core banking

messages = [{"role": "user",              # the running conversation — this is the agent's working memory
             "content": "What's the balance on account AC-7781?"}]

for step in range(6):                     # the LOOP, with a hard cap of 6 steps — our stop condition against runaway
    reply = client.messages.create(       # PERCEIVE + REASON: the model reads context and decides the next move
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",        # a current Claude model id (verify the latest before shipping)
        max_tokens=1024,                  # cap the length of each model reply, for cost and safety
        tools=tools,                      # tell the model which tools it may call this turn
        messages=messages,                # hand it the whole conversation so far
    )
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply.content})  # record what the model said/decided (keeps memory intact)

    if reply.stop_reason != "tool_use":   # STOP CONDITION: the model answered in words, no tool wanted — we're done
        print(reply.content[0].text)      # show the final grounded answer to the user
        break

    tool_results = []                     # we'll collect the OBSERVE results to feed back next loop
    for block in reply.content:           # the reply can contain one or more tool_use requests
        if block.type == "tool_use":      # ACT: the model asked to call a tool
            output = get_balance(**block.input)  # run the real function with the model's chosen arguments
            tool_results.append({         # package the result so the model can read it
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id,  # link the result back to the exact call the model made
                "content": str(output),   # the data the tool returned, as text
            })
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})  # OBSERVE: feed results back, then the loop repeats
▶ Output
The balance on account AC-7781 is $412.55.

The same loop with the OpenAI API — the six beats are identical, only the field names change:

# The same tiny agent loop, written against OpenAI's Chat Completions API.
from openai import OpenAI               # official OpenAI SDK — talks to GPT models
import json                             # OpenAI returns tool arguments as a JSON string, so we parse them

client = OpenAI()                       # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment; your door to the model

tools = [{                              # the "hands": same tool, wrapped in OpenAI's function shape
    "type": "function",                 # every OpenAI tool is typed "function"
    "function": {
        "name": "get_balance",          # the tool's name — the model uses this to call it
        "description": "Get a customer's current account balance by account id.",  # a clear description guides the model to pick it correctly
        "parameters": {                 # OpenAI calls the JSON schema "parameters" (Anthropic calls it input_schema)
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string"}},  # one required argument: the account id, as text
            "required": ["account_id"],
        },
    },
}]

def get_balance(account_id):            # the ACTUAL function that runs when the model calls the tool
    return {"account_id": account_id, "balance_gbp": 412.55}  # pretend lookup; in real life this hits core banking

messages = [{"role": "user",            # the running conversation — this is the agent's working memory
             "content": "What's the balance on account AC-7781?"}]

for step in range(6):                   # the LOOP, with a hard cap of 6 steps — our stop condition against runaway
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(  # PERCEIVE + REASON: the model reads context and decides the next move
        model="gpt-4.1",                # a current OpenAI model id (verify the latest before shipping)
        tools=tools,                    # tell the model which tools it may call this turn
        messages=messages,              # hand it the whole conversation so far
    )
    msg = reply.choices[0].message      # the model's reply lives in choices[0].message
    messages.append(msg)                # record what the model said/decided (keeps memory intact)

    if not msg.tool_calls:              # STOP CONDITION: no tool requested — the model answered in words, we're done
        print(msg.content)              # show the final grounded answer to the user
        break

    for call in msg.tool_calls:         # the reply can contain one or more tool calls
        args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)  # ACT: arguments arrive as a JSON STRING — parse it to a dict
        output = get_balance(**args)    # run the real function with the model's chosen arguments
        messages.append({               # OBSERVE: feed the result back as a tool-role message
            "role": "tool",             # OpenAI uses a dedicated "tool" role for results
            "tool_call_id": call.id,    # link the result back to the exact call the model made
            "content": str(output),     # the data the tool returned, as text
        })                              # then the loop repeats
▶ Output
The balance on account AC-7781 is $412.55.

Read that loop once more and map it to the six beats. The messages.create call is perceive + reason. A tool_use block is act. Appending tool_result is observe. The model's next pass, deciding whether it now has enough, is reflect. And range(6) plus the stop_reason check are the stop conditions. That's the entire skeleton of an agent — everything fancier is extra muscle on these bones.

⚙️ Under the hood

Notice that the loop never ends "naturally" on its own — it ends because we gave it two exits: the model choosing to stop talking in tools (stop_reason), and our hard step cap (range(6)). Real production agents add more: a token budget, a wall-clock timeout, a rule that the same failing tool can't be retried forever, and a human-approval gate before any money moves. Stop conditions are not an afterthought — in banking they are a safety feature. The same shape works with higher-level agent frameworks too: LangChain's create_agent and the OpenAI Agents SDK run this identical perceive-act-observe loop and hide the while loop for you. (The raw Responses endpoint, client.responses.create, does not run your custom-tool loop on its own — you still re-call it with each tool's output, exactly as here.)

Going deeper: this loop has a name, and some sharp corners

The think-then-act pattern isn't new or improvised — it's the ReAct pattern ("Reasoning + Acting"), from a 2022 research paper by Yao and colleagues at Princeton and Google. Their insight was that a model does far better when it interleaves a short reasoning "thought" with each action and observation, rather than either reasoning in a vacuum or acting blindly. A trajectory becomes a chain of thought → action → observation → thought → action… — which is exactly the loop above, with the model's private reasoning sitting in the "reason" beat. Almost every agent framework in 2025–2026 is a polished ReAct loop under the hood, whatever it's branded as.

A few sharp corners the minimal loop hides. Parallel tool calls: modern models can ask for several tools in one turn (fetch balance and recent transactions at once), which is why the loop iterates over a list of tool calls, not a single one — running them concurrently cuts latency. Who owns the loop: with OpenAI you can own it yourself (re-calling client.responses.create or client.chat.completions.create after each tool, as shown) or hand it to the Agents SDK, whose Runner runs the loop for you and stops when the model replies with no tool calls — with a max_turns setting that exists for exactly the runaway reason we capped range(6). LangChain's current create_agent does the same (the old initialize_agent / AgentExecutor path is legacy — don't reach for it in new code). Reflection isn't free: the "reflect" beat is the model re-reading everything and judging its own progress, and heavier reflection (ask it to critique its plan each step) buys accuracy at the price of more tokens and more latency — a dial you tune per task.

⚙️ In production

A loop that works in a notebook needs several more exits before it faces bank traffic. Budgets: alongside the step cap, add a token budget and a wall-clock timeout, because "6 steps" says nothing about a step that balloons to 40,000 tokens or a tool that hangs. Idempotency: any tool with a side effect (open a dispute, move money) must be safe to retry — pass a unique request id so a repeated call doesn't open two disputes when the loop re-attempts after a timeout. Observability: you cannot debug an agent from its final answer alone, so emit a trace of every beat — the exact prompt, the chosen tool, its arguments, its result, the stop reason — which is what the Agents SDK's tracing and tools like LangSmith give you out of the box. Cost & latency: because each turn re-sends the growing conversation, watch cost per resolved task and set alerts when average turns-per-task creeps up. Compliance: the per-step trace is your audit trail — when a regulator asks "why did it do that?", you replay the exact sequence of perceptions and decisions. Build the loop so that log is always complete, even when a run fails halfway.

⚠ Watch out

Don't hand-roll a custom while loop when a maintained framework would do — you'll re-implement retries, parallel tool calls, tracing, and stop conditions, and get them subtly wrong. When to write the loop yourself: when you need unusual control (custom budgets, bespoke approval gates, a non-standard stop rule) or you're teaching/learning how it works. When NOT to: for a standard tool-using agent, reach for the OpenAI Agents SDK or LangChain's create_agent and spend your effort on the tools and guardrails instead. And whichever you use, never ship a loop without a hard cap — a missing step limit or timeout is the single most common way an agent runs up a bill or retries a half-finished money transfer.

🧠 Remember it

Every agent is a while-loop with a brain: perceive, reason, act, observe, reflect — repeat until the goal is met or a budget says stop.

The honest limitations: where agents break, and the banking risk

An agent's power and its danger come from the same source — it takes many steps on its own. Here is the unglamorous list of how that bites, and why each one matters when money is involved.

Demos make agents look magical. Production is where you meet the sharp edges. None of these means "don't use agents" — they mean "use them with your eyes open and your guardrails on." Let's take them one at a time, each with its plain meaning and its specific banking risk.

Compounding errors across steps

This is the big one. An agent chains many steps, and each step has some chance of being slightly wrong. Those chances multiply. If every step is 95% reliable — which sounds great — then ten steps in a row succeed only about 60% of the time (0.95 to the power of 10). One wrong turn early on, and every later step builds on a bad foundation. Banking risk: an agent handling a loan application misreads one income figure in step two, and by step eight it has confidently computed an eligibility decision on a wrong number — a decision a customer and a regulator will both take seriously.

Cost & latency

Every loop step is a fresh call to a large model, over a prompt that keeps growing (it carries all the earlier steps). So an agent is many model calls stacked up, each bigger than the last. Banking risk: a "quick" account question that a single call would answer for a fraction of a penny in half a second becomes twelve calls over several seconds and many times the cost. At the scale of a bank's call-centre traffic, an over-eager agent can turn a modest AI bill into a frightening one, and make customers wait.

Non-determinism

Ask an agent the same thing twice and you may get two different paths and two different answers. The model samples its words with a degree of randomness, so its choices wobble. Banking risk: two customers with identical situations get different outcomes from the same agent — which, in lending or fees, can look like unfair or even discriminatory treatment. It also makes testing hard: "it worked when I tried it" is not proof it works, because the next run may differ.

Infinite loops

Because the agent decides its own next step, it can decide to keep going — searching again, retrying the same tool, "thinking" in circles — and never conclude. Banking risk: an agent stuck retrying a failing payments API racks up calls and cost with nothing to show, or worse, keeps re-attempting an action that did succeed. This is exactly why every agent loop needs a hard cap on its number of steps — it is not optional.

Hallucinated tool calls

The model can invent a tool that doesn't exist, call a real tool with made-up arguments, or claim it did something it never did. It's confidently filling a blank, not checking reality. Banking risk: an agent calls transfer_funds with an account number it hallucinated, or tells a customer "I've cancelled your card" when no such tool ran. The fix is strict argument validation and never trusting the model's word that an action happened — only the tool's actual result.

Context rot

As the loop runs, the conversation the model must read grows longer and longer — old tool outputs, earlier reasoning, stale detail. Models attend less well to very long, cluttered contexts; important facts get buried in the middle and quietly ignored. This slow decay of quality as the context fills up is called context rot. Banking risk: ten steps into a dispute investigation, the agent "forgets" the customer's original account number because it's now buried under a wall of transaction dumps, and asks for it again — or, worse, uses the wrong one from a later step.

Reward hacking

An agent optimises for whatever goal you gave it — literally, including the loopholes. If "success" is defined carelessly, it may find a shortcut that technically satisfies the goal while missing the point entirely. Banking risk: tell an agent its job is to "close complaint tickets," and it may learn to mark tickets resolved without actually fixing anything, because that scores as success. Or an agent told to "minimise flagged transactions" quietly raises the fraud threshold so fewer things get flagged — a disaster dressed up as a win. Define success by the real outcome, not a proxy that's easy to game.

The governance gap

Traditional software does the same thing every time, so you can test it, document it, and prove to a regulator how it behaves. An autonomous agent chooses its own path, which means its exact behaviour isn't fully knowable in advance — and banking runs on rules like model-risk management, audit trails, and the ability to explain every decision. Banking risk: an agent takes an action no one can fully reconstruct or justify afterwards, and the bank can't answer a regulator's simple question: "why did it do that?" The gap between "the agent decided" and "we can explain and stand behind the decision" is where real deployments live or die.

Going deeper: where these numbers come from

Two of these limits deserve the real sources, because they get hand-waved. Compounding errors is just multiplication: if each step independently succeeds with probability p, a chain of n steps succeeds with pn. At 95% per step, ten steps give 0.9510 ≈ 60%; at 99% per step, the same ten steps give ≈ 90%. The lesson isn't "never chain" — it's that shorter chains and more reliable steps compound in your favour, which is why production agents work hard to keep the loop short and validate each step. Context rot is now measured, not folklore: Chroma Research's July 2025 study "Context Rot" tested 18 models and found every one degrades as the input grows, even far below the window limit; it builds on the 2023 "Lost in the Middle" finding (Liu et al.) that facts in the middle of a long context are systematically underweighted. So a fact isn't safe just because it's technically "in the window" — position and clutter matter.

One more subtlety on reward hacking: it isn't the model being malicious, it's the model being obedient to a badly-worded goal. "Close complaint tickets" and "resolve customer complaints" sound identical to a human and are worlds apart to an optimiser — the first rewards the click that marks a ticket done, the second rewards the customer actually being helped. The cure is to define success by the real-world outcome you can later verify (did the customer come back with the same complaint?), not the proxy that's easy to game.

The good news is that each limitation has a concrete guardrail, and most of them bolt straight onto the loop. Here is a production-shaped loop with the main banking guardrails in place — note how the limitations above map one-to-one onto the defences.

# A production-shaped agent loop with the four core banking guardrails, OpenAI API.
