from openai import OpenAI               # official OpenAI SDK — talks to GPT models
import json, time                       # json parses tool arguments; time powers the wall-clock budget

client = OpenAI()                       # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

ALLOWED = {"get_balance", "get_transactions"}  # whitelist: the only tools the model is permitted to run
MAX_STEPS, MAX_SECONDS = 8, 20          # stop conditions: cap steps AND wall-clock time (vs infinite loops & runaway cost)

def valid_args(name, args):             # guard vs HALLUCINATED arguments: check shape before acting
    return name == "get_balance" and isinstance(args.get("account_id"), str)  # only accept a string account_id

def run_tool(name, args):               # the single gate every tool call passes through
    if name not in ALLOWED:             # guard vs HALLUCINATED tools: refuse names we never registered
        return {"error": f"unknown tool {name}"}  # tell the model, don't crash — it can recover
    if name == "transfer_funds":        # guard vs IRREVERSIBLE actions: never auto-run money movement
        return {"error": "transfer needs human approval"}  # force a human gate instead of acting
    return {"account_id": args["account_id"], "balance_gbp": 412.55}  # validated → the real lookup would go here

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What's the balance on AC-7781?"}]  # the goal (short-term memory)
start = time.time()                     # mark the start so we can enforce the time budget

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):           # guard vs INFINITE LOOPS: a hard step cap, not a hope
    if time.time() - start > MAX_SECONDS:  # guard vs runaway LATENCY/COST: bail if we've spent our time budget
        break
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", tools=tools, messages=messages)  # perceive + reason
    msg = reply.choices[0].message      # the model's decision for this turn
    messages.append(msg)                # keep memory intact for the next pass
    if not msg.tool_calls:              # normal stop: the model answered in words, no tool wanted
        print(msg.content); break
    for call in msg.tool_calls:         # models may request several tools at once
        args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)  # OpenAI sends arguments as a JSON string — parse it
        if not valid_args(call.function.name, args):  # guard vs BAD ARGS: validate before touching anything
            result = {"error": "invalid arguments"}   # reject cleanly; let the model try again
        else:
            result = run_tool(call.function.name, args)  # act, through the permission gate above
        log_for_audit(call, result)     # COMPLIANCE: record every action and its outcome for the audit trail
        messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": str(result)})  # observe
▶ Output
The balance on account AC-7781 is $412.55. (Step cap, time budget, tool whitelist, argument validation, a human gate on transfers, and an audit log all enforced on every turn.)

Read it against the limitations list: the step cap and time budget answer infinite loops and runaway cost/latency; the whitelist and the transfer gate answer hallucinated tool calls and irreversible actions; valid_args answers hallucinated arguments; and log_for_audit answers the governance gap. The one thing code alone can't fix is non-determinism — for that you lean on evaluation (run the agent over a fixed test set repeatedly and measure the spread) rather than a single guardrail.

When to accept these limits and use an agent anyway: when the task's value genuinely needs adaptive, multi-step autonomy and the risky actions are bounded or human-gated — a fraud investigation, a complex dispute. When NOT to: when the task is high-stakes and irreversible with no room for a wrong path (straight-through money movement, final credit decisions), or when a workflow would do the job — there, the limitations above are not worth paying for.

⚙️ In production

At a bank these limitations become a standing monitoring and governance programme, not a one-time checklist. Monitoring: track success rate per task type, average steps and tokens per task (a creeping average signals loops or context rot), tool error rates, and how often a run hits a cap — caps firing often means the task is mis-scoped. Failure modes to alarm on: repeated identical tool calls (a loop), rising "unknown tool / invalid argument" rejections (the model drifting), and tasks that hit the human-approval gate unexpectedly. Security & compliance: every tool enforces its own authorization and writes an immutable audit record; irreversible actions sit behind a human; and because behaviour isn't fixed, the agent goes through model-risk management like any other decisioning model — documented, evaluated on a held-out set before release, and re-evaluated when the underlying model version changes. Cost control: per-task token budgets with hard stops, plus a cheaper model (gpt-4.1-mini) for routine sub-steps, keep the bill from scaling with the bank's full traffic. The guardrails in the code above are the floor; the monitoring around them is what lets a bank actually sleep at night.

⚠ Watch out

Almost every item above shares one root: the agent acts over many steps with some autonomy. So the cures rhyme, too — cap the steps and the spend, validate every tool argument, keep the context lean, define success by real outcomes, log every action for audit, and put a human in front of anything irreversible (moving money, closing accounts, sending letters). Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. In a bank, turn it up slowly and keep your hand on it.

💡 Key idea

An agent's strength (it takes many steps on its own toward a goal) is its weakness. Every limitation here is the shadow of that one trait. Engineering a safe agent is mostly the craft of keeping that autonomy useful without letting it run away.

🧠 Remember it

More steps = more power and more ways to fail. Cap it, validate it, trim it, log it, and gate the scary actions behind a human.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

AI Agents — Tools & Function Calling

A chatbot can only talk. An agent can act — check a balance, look up a policy, freeze a lost card — and the bridge from talking to acting is a single idea called a tool. This chapter tells the whole story of tools, from "what even is one" to the hard-won production habits that keep a money-moving agent safe.

What a tool really is: the model asks, your code acts

A tool lets the model request an action in plain structured form — but your own code is what actually runs it.

Imagine a brilliant new hire on their first day at the bank. They know banking inside out, they're fast, they're polite. But they have no login, no keyboard access to the core system, and no phone. If a customer asks "what's my balance?", the new hire can't look it up themselves. What they can do is write a sticky note: "Please fetch the balance for account 4471." They hand you the note. You — a trusted staff member with the right login — read it, run the actual lookup, and hand back the number. The new hire then reads the number aloud to the customer.

That sticky note is a tool call. The language model (the "brain" behind the agent) is the new hire. It never touches your database, your payment rails, or the internet by itself. It can only produce a neat, machine-readable request that says "I would like to call the tool named get_balance with account = 4471." Your code catches that request, decides whether to honour it, runs the real function, and feeds the result back. The model then keeps talking as if it had done the work itself.

This split is the single most important thing to understand about tools, so let's say it bluntly: the model proposes, your code disposes. The model cannot execute anything. It only emits text that describes a call. Everything that has real-world effect — reading a record, moving money — happens inside code you wrote and control.

🏦 Picture this

A customer tells BankAssist: "Did my salary land yet?" The model can't see the account. So it emits a request to call get_recent_transactions for that customer. BankAssist's backend checks the customer is logged in, runs the real query against the core-banking API, and returns the last five transactions. The model reads them and replies, "Yes — a credit of $2,400 from 'ACME PAYROLL' posted this morning." The model never saw the database. It just asked, and your code answered.

Why engineers designed it this way

Letting the model only request actions is not a limitation — it's the whole safety model. Because every real action passes through your code first, you get a natural checkpoint. Before running transfer_money, your code can check the amount, confirm the customer's identity, log the attempt, and even pause for a human to approve. If the model were allowed to reach out and move money directly, you'd have no such gate. The "model proposes, code disposes" design means the risky part always stays on your side of the fence.

💡 Key idea

A tool is a function you expose to the model. The model can only output a structured request to call it; your code runs the function and returns the result. The model's power to act is always borrowed through your code.

Going deeper

Three subtleties hide inside this simple picture. First, a tool call is still just tokens. When the model "requests" get_balance, it is predicting text the same way it predicts a sentence — the API merely formats that prediction into a tidy structured block for you. That means the model can hallucinate a call to a tool that doesn't exist, or invent arguments; your code must treat every request as a claim to be checked, never a command to obey. Second, the round trip costs real time and money. Each tool call means the model stops, you run code, and then you call the model again with the result — so a single customer question that needs two tools is three model invocations, not one. Third, the model never truly "knows" whether the action happened. It only knows what you told it in the tool result. If your code silently fails and returns nothing, the model will often just make something up. The gap between "the model asked" and "the thing actually happened" is exactly where banking bugs live.

⚙️ In production

Treat the request/execute boundary as your control plane, because at a bank it is where cost, safety, and compliance all land.

  • Cost & latency: every tool call adds one more model round trip. A two-tool answer can mean 3–5× the tokens and 2–4 seconds of extra wall-clock time versus a plain reply. Budget tool calls per request and stream the final answer so the customer isn't left staring at a spinner.
  • Failure modes: the model may request a non-existent tool, send malformed arguments, or "act" in prose without ever emitting a call. Your dispatcher must reject unknown tool names, and your prompt/logging must catch the "pretended to act" case.
  • Monitoring: log every proposed call (name, arguments, decision to run or refuse) and every result. Track tool-call volume, rejection rate, and latency per tool — a spike in rejections usually means a prompt or schema regression.
  • Security & compliance: because the model holds no credentials and touches nothing directly, the only place money can move is inside your code. That makes the boundary the natural spot for authentication, authorization, rate limits, and the immutable audit trail a regulator will later ask to see.
⚠ Watch out

The classic beginner mistake is treating a tool request as if the action already happened — logging "transfer complete" the moment the model emits the call, before your code has actually run (or refused) it. The model proposing transfer_money means nothing until your function returns success. Confuse "asked" with "done" and you will tell customers their money moved when it never did.

Use tools when the agent needs live data it cannot know (a balance, today's rate) or must change something in the real world. Don't add a tool when a static system-prompt fact or a plain retrieved document already answers the question — every extra tool is more latency, more tokens, and one more thing the model can misfire.

🧠 Remember it

The model writes the sticky note; you do the actual work. No note ever moves money on its own.

The tool definition: name, description, and a JSON-Schema of parameters

You describe each tool to the model with three things — a name, a sentence of purpose, and a strict shape for its inputs.

For the model to request a tool, it first has to know the tool exists and what it needs. You tell it that with a small spec called a tool definition. Every provider uses the same three pieces:

  • Name — a short machine-friendly handle, like get_balance. This is what the model types on the sticky note.
  • Description — one or two plain sentences telling the model what the tool does and when to use it. This is the single biggest lever on whether the model picks the right tool.
  • Parameters — the inputs the tool accepts, written as a JSON Schema: a tiny contract that lists each field, its type, whether it's required, and any allowed values.

JSON Schema is just a standard way to describe the shape of a JSON object. If that phrase is new: it's a small block that says "this object has a field called account_id which is a string and is required, and a field called currency which must be one of GBP, USD, or EUR." The model reads this schema and fills in values that fit.

Here is a complete tool definition for BankAssist, in the shape Anthropic's API expects (OpenAI and Gemini use the same JSON-Schema core, just wrapped differently — OpenAI nests it under function.parameters, Gemini under function_declarations):

{
  "name": "get_balance",                                  # the exact handle the model will call
  "description": "Return the current available balance for ONE of the signed-in customer's own accounts. Use when the customer asks how much money they have, or whether a payment will clear. Do NOT use for transaction history.",  # says what it does AND when to use / not use it
  "input_schema": {                                       # JSON Schema describing the arguments
    "type": "object",                                     # arguments always arrive as a JSON object
    "properties": {                                       # the list of allowed fields
      "account_id": {                                     # one field the model must supply
        "type": "string",                                 # constrain the type so the model can't send a number or list
        "description": "The account number, e.g. '4471'." # per-field help makes the model fill it correctly
      },
      "as_of": {                                           # an optional field
        "type": "string",
        "format": "date",                                 # nudge the model toward YYYY-MM-DD
        "description": "Optional date for a historical balance; omit for today."
      }
    },
    "required": ["account_id"]                             # account_id must be present; as_of may be skipped
  }
}

Read that schema like a form the model has to fill in. It can leave as_of blank, but it must write something in account_id, and that something must be a string. When the model emits its sticky note, it will produce an object like {"account_id": "4471"} that satisfies this contract.

Why a tight schema matters so much

A loose schema is like a form with one giant blank box labelled "details." People write anything, and half of it is wrong. A tight schema is a form with labelled fields, dropdowns, and required stars — it's nearly impossible to fill in badly. The same is true for the model. The more you constrain the shape, the less room there is for the model to invent a malformed or dangerous call.

Tighten a schema with these tools:

  • Types — "type": "string" / "integer" / "boolean" stops the model sending the wrong kind of value.
  • Enums — "enum": ["GBP","USD","EUR"] means only those three currencies are even expressible. The model literally cannot ask for a currency you don't support.
  • Numeric bounds — "minimum": 0 on an amount blocks negative transfers at the schema level.
  • Formats & patterns — "format": "date" or a regex "pattern" for an account number nudges values into the right shape.
  • required — forces the model to supply the fields your function cannot run without.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's first transfer_money tool took a plain amount number and a free-text currency string. A test user asked to "send fifty quid" and the model emitted {"amount": -50, "currency": "quid"} — a negative amount in a currency that doesn't exist. Nothing crashed; the call simply flowed into code that wasn't ready for it. The team tightened the schema: amount became a number with "minimum": 0.01, and currency became an enum of ["GBP","USD","EUR"]. After that, the negative and nonsense-currency calls became literally unexpressible — the model could no longer even write them. One schema edit removed a whole class of bugs.

⚙️ Under the hood

The schema isn't just documentation — many providers can enforce it. OpenAI's "strict" mode and similar features use constrained decoding, meaning the model is physically prevented from emitting tokens that would break the schema: an enum field can only output one of its listed values. Even where enforcement isn't available, the schema is injected into the model's context as part of the prompt, so a precise schema measurably improves how often the model calls the tool correctly. Either way, treat the schema as a prompt, not an afterthought.

⚙️ In production

At a bank the tool definition is a shared contract, so treat it like one.

  • Cost & context: every tool's full definition — name, description, and schema — is injected into the prompt on every turn. Fifty verbose tools can burn thousands of input tokens per request before the customer has even spoken. Keep descriptions tight and the active toolset small.
  • Versioning: schemas drift. Version your tool definitions (e.g. get_balance.v2) and roll them out behind a flag; a field renamed in the schema but not in your function is a silent production break. Keep a test that validates each live schema against the real function signature.
  • Enforcement limits: strict/constrained decoding guarantees the shape, not the semantics. It can force account_id to be a string; it cannot force it to be this customer's account. Server-side validation is still mandatory.
  • Monitoring & compliance: track per-tool schema-validation failures and argument-rejection rates. For audit, log the exact schema version a given call was made against, so a disputed transaction can be replayed with the precise contract that was in force.
⚠ Watch out

Never trust the model's arguments blindly, even with a strict schema. A schema guarantees the shape (it's a string, it's one of three currencies) — not the truth (that this customer is allowed to see that account). Always re-validate in your code: check ownership, check limits, check sanity. The schema stops malformed calls; your code stops unsafe ones.

Use a tight schema with enums, bounds, and patterns when the field has a known, finite, or rule-bound set of valid values (currencies, account types, amounts). Don't force a rigid schema when the input is genuinely open-ended free text (a dispute description, a search query) — over-constraining there just makes the model fight the form and emit malformed calls.

🧠 Remember it

Name = the handle. Description = the "when". Schema = the "shape". A tight schema is a form with dropdowns, not a blank box.

Writing names and descriptions the model actually understands

The description is a mini-prompt: it should pull the model in for the right questions and push it away from the wrong ones.

Here's a truth that surprises new agent builders: the hardest part of tools isn't the code behind them — it's the words you use to describe them. The model chooses tools by reading their descriptions and matching them to the user's request. Vague words lead to wrong choices. So think of each description as doing two jobs at once: a trigger (making the model reach for this tool at the right time) and an anti-trigger (making it not reach for this tool at the wrong time).

Names: short, verb-first, unambiguous

Good tool names read like commands: get_balance, list_transactions, freeze_card, open_dispute. Start with a verb, keep it lowercase with underscores, and make sure no two names could be confused. Avoid cutesy or overloaded names like handle_account — the model can't tell what "handle" means and will misfire.

Descriptions: say what, say when, say when-NOT

Compare these two descriptions for the very same function:

❌ Weak

"Gets transactions."

No hint about whose transactions, over what period, or when to pick it over a balance lookup. The model will guess — and overlap with get_balance will cause it to call the wrong one.

✅ Strong

"List the signed-in customer's recent transactions for one account, newest first. Use when the customer asks about payments, deposits, 'did X arrive', or spending history. Do NOT use to get a single current balance — use get_balance for that."

It names the subject, the ordering, the trigger phrases, and the anti-trigger that keeps it out of get_balance's lane.

Notice the three moves in the strong version. First, it states exactly what comes back ("recent transactions ... newest first"). Second, it lists real trigger phrases a customer might use ("did X arrive", "spending history") so the model recognises the match. Third, it draws a boundary ("Do NOT use to get a single current balance") so overlapping tools don't collide. That boundary line is the anti-trigger, and it's the part most people forget.

The same two tools, defined for the model

Here are the two neighbours written out as OpenAI tool definitions. Read the description strings as prompts — each one has a come-here and a stay-away pointing at its sibling:

tools = [                                                    # the toolbox we hand the model
  {
    "type": "function",                                     # every OpenAI tool is typed "function"
    "function": {
      "name": "get_balance",                                # verb-first, lowercase, unambiguous
      "description": (                                       # what + when + when-NOT, all in one string
        "Return the single current available balance for ONE account. "   # WHAT it returns
        "Use when the customer asks how much they have, if a payment will clear, or 'am I overdrawn'. "  # come-here triggers
        "Do NOT use for lists of payments or history — use list_transactions for that."  # stay-away anti-trigger -> sibling
      ),
      "parameters": {                                       # JSON Schema for the arguments
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string", "description": "e.g. '4471'"}},
        "required": ["account_id"]
      }
    }
  },
  {
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
      "name": "list_transactions",                          # the neighbour that kept getting confused
      "description": (
        "List the signed-in customer's recent transactions for ONE account, newest first. "  # WHAT + ordering
        "Use for 'did X arrive', deposits, spending history, or 'what did I spend on groceries'. "  # come-here triggers
        "Do NOT use to get a single current balance — use get_balance for that."  # stay-away anti-trigger -> sibling
      ),
      "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
          "account_id": {"type": "string", "description": "e.g. '4471'"},
          "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 50, "description": "How many to return."}
        },
        "required": ["account_id"]
      }
    }
  }
]

The code behind these two functions never changed. The only thing that fixed the routing was the English in the two description strings — each naming the other as its boundary. That is the whole lesson in one snippet: tool selection is a writing problem first and a code problem second.

🏦 Picture this

Before the anti-trigger line existed, a customer asked BankAssist, "What's my balance?" and the agent called list_transactions, dumped twenty rows, and made the customer do the maths. After adding "Do NOT use to get a single current balance — use get_balance for that" to the description, the agent routed straight to get_balance. One sentence of English fixed a routing bug that no amount of code could.

✅ Tip

When two tools keep getting confused, don't reach for the code first. Add a one-line boundary to each description pointing at the other ("for X, use the other tool"). Descriptions are the cheapest, fastest knob you have for tool selection.

⚙️ In production

Descriptions are code that ships — so manage them like code.

  • Token cost: every description is in the prompt on every turn. A 60-word description across 20 tools is ~1,600 tokens of fixed overhead per request. Wordsmith for precision, then trim; measure the token count of your whole tool block.
  • Regression testing: a description change can silently re-route traffic. Keep a labelled set of real customer utterances mapped to their correct tool, and re-run tool-selection accuracy on every description edit — the same way you'd run unit tests on code.
  • Monitoring: watch for "near-miss" pairs — tools that get called interchangeably. A confusion matrix over logged calls shows exactly which two descriptions need a sharper boundary line.
  • Security & compliance: descriptions are model-visible and can surface in reasoning the customer sees, so they must never contain secrets, internal system names, or PII. For a bank, treat the tool-description file as reviewable content, not throwaway strings.
⚠ Watch out

Don't stuff secrets, internal IDs, or instructions-to-the-user into tool descriptions. The model reads them every turn, they cost tokens, and they can leak into reasoning the user sees. Keep descriptions about the tool's purpose and boundaries, nothing else.

Invest in rich trigger/anti-trigger descriptions when tools overlap or the catalogue is large and routing errors are costly. Don't over-engineer the wording when you have two or three clearly distinct tools — there, a plain one-line purpose is enough, and extra prose just burns tokens.

🧠 Remember it

Every description needs a come-here (trigger phrases) and a stay-away (what it's not for). The stay-away is the line beginners skip and seniors never do.

Native function calling: one real round trip, line by line

Modern model APIs have tool use built in — here is a full propose → execute → observe → answer loop you can run today.

"Native function calling" just means the model API understands tools directly: you pass tool definitions in the request, and when the model wants a tool it returns a special structured block instead of plain text. You don't parse the model's prose hoping to find a JSON blob — the API hands you a clean object. Let's walk one complete round trip with the current Anthropic Messages API (model claude-sonnet-5-5). The same four beats appear in every provider; only the field names differ.

Step 1 — Send the question and the tools

import anthropic                                           # the official Anthropic SDK
client = anthropic.Anthropic()                             # reads your API key from the environment

tools = [{                                                 # the list of tools we expose this turn
    "name": "get_balance",                                # the handle the model will call
    "description": "Current available balance for one of the signed-in customer's accounts.",  # what + when
    "input_schema": {                                     # JSON Schema for the arguments
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {
            "account_id": {"type": "string", "description": "e.g. '4471'"}  # one required field
        },
        "required": ["account_id"]
    }
}]

messages = [                                               # the running conversation we pass each turn
    {"role": "user", "content": "What's the balance on my 4471 account?"}  # the customer's question
]

resp = client.messages.create(                            # first call: ask the model, offering the tools
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",                            # a current tool-capable model
    max_tokens=1024,                                      # cap the reply length
    tools=tools,                                          # hand the model its toolbox
    messages=messages                                     # the conversation so far
)

Step 2 — The model proposes a tool call

Because the question needs live data, the model doesn't answer — it asks for the tool. The response's stop_reason is "tool_use", your signal that a tool was requested rather than a final answer.

print(resp.stop_reason)                                   # -> "tool_use": the model wants a tool, not done yet

tool_req = next(b for b in resp.content                   # scan the content blocks...
               if b.type == "tool_use")                   # ...for the tool_use block (there can be several)

print(tool_req.name)                                      # -> "get_balance": which tool it chose
print(tool_req.input)                                     # -> {"account_id": "4471"}: the arguments it filled in
print(tool_req.id)                                        # -> "toolu_01A...": the unique id that ties request to result
▶ Output
tool_use
get_balance
{'account_id': '4471'}
toolu_01A09q90...

Step 3 — Your code runs the real function

This is the part the model can't do. Here you also enforce safety: confirm the customer owns account 4471 before touching the database.

def get_balance(account_id, user):                        # your real function
    assert account_id in user.owned_accounts              # SECURITY: ownership check, never trust the model's arg
    return {"account_id": account_id, "available": 812.40, "currency": "GBP"}  # real query result

result = get_balance(**tool_req.input, user=current_user) # run it with the model's args + the trusted user

Step 4 — Hand the result back; the model answers

Now you append two things to the conversation: the model's own tool request (so it remembers what it asked), and a tool_result carrying the answer, matched by that id. Then you call the API again.

messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})  # keep the model's tool_use block in history
messages.append({                                         # add the result as a user-role tool_result
    "role": "user",
    "content": [{
        "type": "tool_result",                            # this block type carries a tool's output
        "tool_use_id": tool_req.id,                        # MUST match the id from step 2, or the model is confused
        "content": str(result)                             # the data, as a string the model can read
    }]
})

final = client.messages.create(                           # second call: model now has the data
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    tools=tools,                                          # still pass tools in case it wants another
    messages=messages
)
print(final.content[0].text)                              # the grounded, human-readable answer
▶ Output
Your account 4471 has an available balance of $812.40.

The same round trip with the OpenAI API — the four beats are identical; only the field names change:

from openai import OpenAI                                   # the official OpenAI SDK
import json                                                 # OpenAI hands tool arguments back as a JSON string
client = OpenAI()                                           # reads your API key from the environment

tools = [{                                                  # the same tool, in OpenAI's function wrapper
    "type": "function",                                     # every OpenAI tool is typed "function"
    "function": {
        "name": "get_balance",                              # the handle the model will call
        "description": "Current available balance for one of the signed-in customer's accounts.",  # what + when
        "parameters": {                                     # OpenAI's name for the JSON Schema (Anthropic says input_schema)
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string", "description": "e.g. '4471'"}},
            "required": ["account_id"]
        }
    }
}]

messages = [                                                # the running conversation we pass each turn
    {"role": "user", "content": "What's the balance on my 4471 account?"}  # the customer's question
]

resp = client.chat.completions.create(                      # STEP 1 — ask the model, offering the tools
    model="gpt-4.1", tools=tools, messages=messages         # a current tool-capable model
)
msg = resp.choices[0].message                               # STEP 2 — the model proposes a tool call
call = msg.tool_calls[0]                                    # tool_calls[] replaces Anthropic's tool_use blocks
print(call.function.name)                                   # -> "get_balance": which tool it chose
print(call.function.arguments)                              # -> '{"account_id":"4471"}': a JSON STRING, not a dict

def get_balance(account_id, user):                          # STEP 3 — your code runs the real function
    assert account_id in user.owned_accounts                # SECURITY: ownership check, never trust the model's arg
    return {"account_id": account_id, "available": 812.40, "currency": "GBP"}  # real query result

args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)                  # parse the JSON string into a dict first
result = get_balance(**args, user=current_user)             # run it with the model's args + the trusted user

messages.append(msg)                                        # STEP 4 — keep the model's tool-call message in history
messages.append({                                           # add the result as a tool-role message
    "role": "tool",                                         # OpenAI's dedicated role for tool output
    "tool_call_id": call.id,                                # MUST match the id from step 2
    "content": str(result)                                  # the data, as a string the model can read
})
final = client.chat.completions.create(                     # call again — the model now has the data
    model="gpt-4.1", tools=tools, messages=messages
)
print(final.choices[0].message.content)                     # the grounded, human-readable answer
▶ Output
get_balance
{"account_id":"4471"}
Your account 4471 has an available balance of $812.40.

That's the entire pattern: propose (model emits tool_use), execute (your code runs the function), observe (you send back a tool_result with the matching id), answer (model writes the reply). If the model needs several tools, it simply loops: your code keeps feeding results until stop_reason is no longer "tool_use" and a final text answer arrives.

The same loop across providers

Every major provider offers native function calling with the same four beats; only the vocabulary changes. You don't need to memorise this — just recognise the shape when you move between SDKs.

StepAnthropic (Messages)OpenAI (Chat Completions)Google (Gemini)
Define toolstools=[{name, description, input_schema}]tools=[{type:"function", function:{name, description, parameters}}]tools=[{function_declarations:[...]}]
Model askstool_use block; stop_reason="tool_use"message.tool_calls[]; each has id, function.arguments (JSON string)a part with functionCall{name, args}
You replytool_result block with tool_use_idmessage with role:"tool", tool_call_ida part with functionResponse{name, response}
Args come asparsed object (.input)JSON string — you must json.loads itparsed object

Going deeper — the OpenAI Responses API

OpenAI now recommends its Responses API (client.responses.create) as the default for new projects. It is the same four beats; the tool shape is just flatter — name, description, and parameters sit at the top level of each tool rather than nested under a function key, and the model's output arrives as typed items you iterate.

from openai import OpenAI                                   # same SDK, newer endpoint
client = OpenAI()

tools = [{                                                   # Responses API: flat tool shape (no "function" wrapper)
    "type": "function",
    "name": "get_balance",                                  # name is top-level here
    "description": "Current available balance for one of the signed-in customer's accounts.",
    "parameters": {                                         # still plain JSON Schema
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string"}},
        "required": ["account_id"]
    }
}]

resp = client.responses.create(                             # STEP 1 — ask, offering the tools
    model="gpt-4.1", tools=tools,
    input=[{"role": "user", "content": "Balance on my 4471 account?"}]  # "input", not "messages"
)
for item in resp.output:                                    # STEP 2 — scan output items for a call
    if item.type == "function_call":                        # a tool request item
        args = json.loads(item.arguments)                   # arguments are still a JSON string
        result = get_balance(**args, user=current_user)     # STEP 3 — your code runs it
        resp = client.responses.create(                     # STEP 4 — return the result, ask again
            model="gpt-4.1", tools=tools,
            previous_response_id=resp.id,                   # chains onto the prior turn — no manual history
            input=[{                                        # the output of the call, matched by call_id
                "type": "function_call_output",
                "call_id": item.call_id,                    # MUST match the call's id
                "output": str(result)
            }]
        )
print(resp.output_text)                                     # the grounded answer

The vocabulary shifts (input/output, function_call/function_call_output, call_id, previous_response_id) but the rhythm is identical: propose, execute, observe, answer. Chat Completions remains fully supported, so existing code keeps working — reach for Responses when you start something new or want built-in state chaining.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's first integration forgot to echo the assistant's own tool-call message back into history before sending the tool_result. The second API call then saw a result with no matching request — the model replied, "I'm not sure what that number refers to," and asked the customer to repeat themselves. The fix was a single line: append the model's tool-call message, then the result, with the ids lined up. The loop is unforgiving about that pairing — drop either half and the model loses the thread.

⚙️ In production

The humble tool loop is where most agent latency, cost, and flakiness actually live.

  • Latency: every tool means an extra model round trip. A three-tool task is four model calls end to end; at ~1–2 s each that is a 4–8 s reply. Stream the final answer, run independent tools concurrently, and keep tool count per turn low.
  • Cost: the full conversation — including every prior tool result — is re-sent on each call, so tokens grow super-linearly across a long tool chain. Trim or summarise stale tool outputs once they've been used.
  • Failure modes: malformed-JSON arguments (wrap json.loads in try/except), mismatched ids, and the model "finishing" without calling a tool it clearly needed. Enforce a max-steps ceiling so a loop can't run away.
  • Monitoring & compliance: assign a trace id per request and log every model call, tool call, arguments, result, and the final answer. For a bank, that full trace is both your debugger and your audit record.
⚠ Watch out

Two gotchas trip everyone. (1) With OpenAI, function.arguments is a JSON string, not a dict — parse it with json.loads before use, and wrap that in a try/except because the model can occasionally emit invalid JSON. (2) The id that links request to result (tool_use_id / tool_call_id) must match exactly; mismatch it and the model loses track of which result answers which call, especially when several tools run at once.

⚠ Watch out

Old tutorials use dead APIs. OpenAI's single function_call / role:"function" format is superseded by the tools / tool_calls / role:"tool" format shown here, and OpenAI's newer Responses API is now its recommended default for new projects (same concepts, input/output items). If you see initialize_agent, function_call=, or a role:"function" message, you're reading a 2023-era example — don't copy it.

Use native function calling when your provider supports it (all major ones do) — it is the safe, structured default for giving a model tools. Don't hand-roll prompt-parsed "JSON in the text" tool use when native calling is available; parsing prose for a JSON blob is brittle and was only ever a workaround for models that lacked the feature.

🧠 Remember it

Four beats, always: propose → execute → observe → answer. The little matching id is the thread that stitches a result back to its request.

Routing: picking the right tool as the toolbox grows

A handful of tools is easy; fifty tools quietly wrecks the model's aim — so you narrow the choices before the model ever sees them.

When BankAssist has three tools, the model picks well almost every time. But a real bank has dozens: balances, transactions, standing orders, card controls, disputes, statements, branch locators, loan quotes, FX rates, and on and on. Here's the uncomfortable fact: tool-selection accuracy drops as the number of tools grows. More choices mean more near-duplicates, more descriptions competing for attention, and more ways to pick wrong. Beyond roughly ten to twenty active tools, quality starts to sag.

The fix is the same one a big shop uses: don't make the customer wander every aisle. Put up signs, and send them to the right department first. There are two main techniques.

Two-stage routing (a small decision first)

Instead of handing the model all fifty tools, you first run a cheap, fast step that decides which category the request falls into — "this is a card question" — and then expose only that category's handful of tools to the main model. The first stage can be a small classifier model, or even a quick LLM call with a short menu of departments.

Retrieval over tools (search your toolbox)

When you have hundreds of tools, even departments aren't enough. Treat the tools themselves like documents: write a short description of each, embed those descriptions into a vector store, and at query time search for the handful of tools whose descriptions best match the user's request. You then pass only those top few to the model. This is often called "RAG over tools," and it's exactly how large tool catalogues — including those exposed through the Model Context Protocol (a standard way to plug external tool servers into agents) — stay manageable. The model never sees the full catalogue; it only ever sees the five or ten tools retrieval surfaced.

⚙️ Under the hood

Routing isn't free: a router adds a step, and retrieval can miss the right tool if its description is poorly written (the same "write good descriptions" lesson, now with higher stakes — a tool that isn't retrieved can't be called). Measure it. Build a test set of real requests with their correct tools, and track tool-selection accuracy as you add tools. If accuracy sags past a dozen tools, that's your signal to add a routing layer, not more tools to the flat list.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist grew from 8 tools to 34 as new features shipped, all handed to the model in one flat list. Nobody changed the prompt, yet complaints crept up: customers asking to "freeze my card" sometimes got routed to report_fraud or open_dispute instead, because three card-and-fraud tools had overlapping descriptions. The flat list had quietly pushed tool-selection accuracy from 97% down to 84%. The team added a lightweight router that first picked a department (Accounts, Cards, Disputes, Payments) and exposed only that department's 4–6 tools. Accuracy jumped back to 96% — with no change to any individual tool.

⚙️ In production

Routing is itself a system with its own cost, latency, and failure modes.

  • Latency & cost: a two-stage router adds a step. Keep stage one cheap — a small/fast model (e.g. gpt-4.1-mini) or an embedding lookup — so you spend a few hundred milliseconds there to save a wrong, expensive main-model call. RAG-over-tools adds a vector search (single-digit ms) plus the embedding of the query.
  • The miss problem: a tool that routing doesn't surface simply cannot be called. Set retrieval to return a generous top-k (say 8–10), and always keep a small set of "always-on" safety tools (like escalate_to_human) outside the router.
  • Monitoring: track two numbers separately — router accuracy (did it pick the right department/tools?) and end-to-end tool accuracy. A healthy end number with a poor router number means your main model is quietly compensating, which is fragile.
  • Security & compliance: routing is also a blast-radius control. A customer-service session never needs the admin or back-office tools in view at all; scoping the toolset by role and channel means an injected instruction can't reach a tool that was never on the menu.
⚠ Watch out

The most common routing mistake is exposing 40+ tools "just in case." Selection quietly collapses and nobody notices until customers get wrong answers. Keep the active toolset small per turn; group the rest behind routing or retrieval.

Add a routing layer when your catalogue passes roughly a dozen active tools or selection accuracy starts to sag on your test set. Don't add routing when you have a handful of distinct tools — the extra step just adds latency and one more thing to get wrong, with no accuracy to gain.

🧠 Remember it

Don't hand the model the whole toolbox. Point to the drawer first. Few tools in view = sharp aim.

Parallel tool calls and the independence rule

When several lookups don't depend on each other, run them at once — but only when they truly don't depend on each other.

A customer opens the app and asks, "Give me a full picture of my current account." To answer well, BankAssist needs the balance, the last few transactions, and the card status. None of those three depends on the others — the balance query doesn't need the transaction result, and vice versa. So why run them one after another, paying three round trips of latency? Modern model APIs can emit several tool calls in a single turn, and your code can run them concurrently, then feed all the results back together.

import asyncio                                             # run functions concurrently

# The model returned THREE tool_use blocks in one response:
#   get_balance(4471), list_transactions(4471), get_card_status(4471)

async def run_all(tool_reqs, user):                        # dispatch every requested tool at once
    tasks = [run_tool(t, user) for t in tool_reqs]         # one coroutine per tool call
    return await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)  # wait for all; keep going if one fails

results = asyncio.run(run_all(tool_reqs, current_user))    # ~1x latency instead of 3x

# Send back one tool_result per call, each matched by its own id:
tool_results = [                                           # pair each result with the request it answers
    {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": t.id, "content": str(r)}  # id links result -> request
    for t, r in zip(tool_reqs, results)
]

The three queries finish in about the time of the slowest single one, instead of all three added up. For a dashboard-style question that's the difference between a snappy reply and an awkward pause.

The independence rule

Here is the line you must never cross: only parallelise calls that don't need each other's results. Independent reads — balance, transactions, card status — are perfect. But a chain is not. Consider "transfer $200 from savings to current, then tell me the new current balance." You cannot fetch the "new balance" at the same time as the transfer, because the new balance only exists after the transfer completes. Those steps are dependent and must run in order. Parallelising them would read a stale balance, or worse, race.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist once parallelised "move $200 to savings, then confirm savings balance." The balance read fired at the same instant as the transfer and returned the old figure. The customer was told their money hadn't arrived — a support call and a very confused afternoon. The fix was one rule: reads that stand alone run together; anything that depends on a previous step runs after it.

⚙️ Under the hood

Parallelism has three sharp edges. Partial failure: one of five calls errors — use return_exceptions=True (or equivalent) so the others still return, and send each error back as data so the model can react. Rate limits & stampedes: firing many calls at once can hammer a downstream core-banking API; cap concurrency and respect rate limits. Cost: more calls means more tokens and more API load — parallelise to cut latency, not to do needless work.

⚙️ In production

Parallelism trades a little complexity for a lot of latency — control it deliberately.

  • You can turn it off: OpenAI exposes parallel_tool_calls=False on the request when you want the model to emit one call at a time (useful for strict ordering or when a downstream system can't take concurrent load). Left at its default, the model may propose several calls in one turn.
  • Cap concurrency: don't fire an unbounded fan-out at a core-banking API. Wrap the dispatch in a semaphore (e.g. max 5 in flight) so a dashboard question can't stampede a downstream service and trip its rate limiter.
  • Latency math: three independent reads at ~400 ms each run as one ~400 ms wait instead of 1.2 s — real savings on a "full picture" screen. But measure the slowest call, because the batch is only as fast as its laggard; add a per-call timeout so one slow tool can't stall the whole set.
  • Failure & monitoring: use return_exceptions=True so a partial failure still returns the rest, and send each error back as its own tool result. Log per-tool latency and the concurrency level; a rising p95 on one tool is your early warning.
⚠ Watch out

Writes are rarely safe to parallelise. Two transfers fired together can double-spend, trip race conditions, or violate ordering a ledger depends on. Default to sequential for any tool that changes state, parallel only for independent reads.

Parallelise when the calls are independent reads whose results don't feed each other (balance + transactions + card status). Don't parallelise when one step needs another's output, or any step changes state — those run in strict order, alone.

🧠 Remember it

Parallel is for readers that don't wait on each other. If step B needs step A's answer, B waits. If a step changes money, it goes alone.

Errors and retries: return failures to the model as data

Tools fail all the time — the trick is to hand the model a clean, honest error it can reason about, and to know which failures are worth retrying.

In a demo, tools always work. In production, they time out, return 500s, hit rate limits, and get fed bad inputs. An agent that can't cope with a failing tool will either freeze, loop forever on the same broken call, or — worst of all — pretend the call succeeded and make up an answer. Robust tool use is mostly about handling the unhappy path well.

The foundational habit is simple: when a tool fails, send the failure back to the model as a normal tool result — just marked as an error. Don't crash the whole agent, and don't hide the failure. Give the model a short, structured error string, and let it decide what to do next (apologise, try a different tool, ask the customer for clarification).

def run_tool(req, user):                                  # one safe wrapper around every tool
    try:
        data = DISPATCH[req.name](**req.input, user=user) # look up and run the real function
        return {"type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": req.id,
                "content": str(data)}                     # success: return the data
    except PermissionError as e:                          # a TERMINAL error — retrying won't help
        return {"type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": req.id,
                "content": f"ERROR (do not retry): {e}",  # tell the model plainly, so it can explain to the user
                "is_error": True}                         # flag it as an error result
    except (TimeoutError, ConnectionError) as e:          # a RETRIABLE error — a transient hiccup
        return {"type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": req.id,
                "content": f"ERROR (transient, safe to retry): {e}",
                "is_error": True}

Notice what the error strings say. They're written for the model to read, not for a log file. "ERROR (do not retry)" tells the model not to bang on a locked door; "safe to retry" invites another attempt. The model is surprisingly good at acting on plain-English hints like these.

Retriable vs terminal — know the difference

🔁 Retriable (transient)

Timeouts, connection drops, HTTP 429 (rate limit), 503 (service busy). The call might work if you try again. Retry with exponential backoff: wait 1s, then 2s, then 4s, so you don't hammer a struggling service.

🛑 Terminal (permanent)

HTTP 400 (bad input), 401/403 (not allowed), 404 (no such account), a validation failure. Retrying the identical call will fail identically. Don't retry — surface it so the model can change course or tell the customer.

The loop guard

Even with good errors, an agent can get stuck repeating the same action — model calls a tool, it fails, model tries the exact same call, fails again, forever. Always cap the loop. Two cheap guards: a hard limit on total tool calls per request (say, 10), and a check that refuses to run the identical call twice in a row.

MAX_STEPS = 10                                            # never let the agent loop forever
seen = set()                                              # remember calls we've already made

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):                             # hard ceiling on tool-use rounds
    key = (req.name, str(req.input))                     # a fingerprint of this exact call
    if key in seen:                                      # same tool + same args as before?
        return "Stopping: repeated identical tool call."  # break the loop, hand back to a human
    seen.add(key)                                        # record it so a repeat is caught
    # ... run the tool, feed the result back, continue ...
🏦 Picture this

A customer asked BankAssist to move $300 to their savings pot during a brief core-banking slowdown. The transfer tool timed out after 8 seconds, so the agent — trying to be helpful — retried it. Both attempts had actually reached the ledger: $600 left the current account. The customer noticed, a dispute was opened, and an engineer spent an afternoon reconciling. The fix was tiny: the agent now generates one idempotency key per transfer intent and passes it on every attempt, so the ledger recognises the second call as a duplicate and returns the first result instead of moving money again. A timeout is now safe to retry.

⚙️ In production

Error handling is the difference between a demo and a system real customers trust.

  • Backoff with jitter: plain exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s) is good; add random jitter so a fleet of agents retrying after an outage doesn't synchronise into a thundering herd that re-crashes the service.
  • Budgets & circuit breakers: cap total retries per request and trip a circuit breaker per downstream tool — if transfer_money is failing 50% of calls, stop calling it and tell customers plainly rather than hammering a sick service.
  • Idempotency everywhere that writes: every state-changing tool takes a client-generated key; the backend dedupes on it. Without this, no write is ever safe to retry.
  • Monitoring & compliance: alert on retry rate, terminal-error rate, and loop-guard trips (an agent stuck repeating a call is a prompt or data bug). Log every error returned to the model — for a bank, "what did the agent know and when" must be reconstructable from the trace.
⚠ Watch out — the idempotency trap

Retrying a read is harmless. Retrying a write can be a disaster: a timed-out transfer_money might have actually succeeded before the timeout, so a blind retry sends the money twice. The fix is an idempotency key: generate a unique id for the transfer and pass it with every attempt, so the backend recognises a repeat and refuses to double-execute. Never retry a money-moving tool without one.

⚠ Watch out

Never swallow an error silently and return a cheerful empty result — the model will confidently invent an answer ("your balance is $0.00"). An honest error beats a fake success every time, especially in banking.

Retry when the failure is transient (timeout, 429, 503) and the call is a read or carries an idempotency key. Don't retry when the error is terminal (400/401/403/404, validation) or the tool changes state without an idempotency key — surface it instead and let the model change course.

🧠 Remember it

Errors are data for the model, not crashes for you. Retriable? Back off and try again (with an idempotency key for writes). Terminal? Tell the truth and move on. Always cap the loop.

A real banking tool catalog, sorted by risk tier

Group every tool by how much damage it can do — read, knowledge, or action — and let that tier decide the guardrails around it.

Not all tools deserve the same trust. A tool that reads a balance is a world apart from one that moves money, even though both are just functions. The cleanest way to keep an agent safe is to sort your tools into risk tiers and apply heavier controls as the risk climbs. Here's a realistic BankAssist catalogue.

TierWhat it doesExample toolsControls
🟢 Read
(customer's own data)		 Fetches live, personal data. No side effects, but exposes real customer information. get_balance, list_transactions, get_card_status, get_statement Enforce ownership (user can only read their own accounts); log access; safe to retry; safe to parallelise.
🔵 Knowledge
(general facts)		 Looks up non-personal information — policies, rates, product terms, branch hours. search_policy, get_fx_rate, find_branch, get_product_terms Lowest risk; no personal data; safe to retry and parallelise. Keep sources trusted and current.
🔴 Action
(changes state)		 Does something irreversible or money-moving. The dangerous tier. transfer_money, freeze_card, open_dispute, update_address, close_account Idempotency keys; step-up identity checks; amount/risk thresholds; human approval for high-risk; run sequentially; full audit trail.

Why bother sorting? Because the tier tells you, at a glance, how much protection each tool needs — and it stops you accidentally treating a transfer like a balance check. A few rules fall straight out of the tiers:

  • Read & Knowledge tools are safe to retry and to run in parallel. Most of an agent's calls live here.
  • Action tools get the heavy machinery: an idempotency key so retries can't double-execute, a re-check that this user is authorised for this action, and — above a risk threshold — a human in the loop before anything happens.
  • Keep read and write tools separate. Don't build one manage_card that both checks status and cancels the card; split them, so the risky half carries its own guardrails.

Lightweight tools worth knowing — and where they fit the tiers

Most agent tools are your own banking functions, but a few small, battle-tested third-party services show up again and again. Each one slots neatly into the risk tiers above, which tells you at a glance how to guard it.

ServiceWhat it doesTierWhy it fits an agent
SerperGoogle Search results as structured JSON (organic, news, places) via a single POST.🔵 KnowledgeGives the agent fresh, public web facts — "what's today's Bank of England base rate?" — that no internal DB holds.
SendGridTransactional email API (/v3/mail/send).🔴 ActionLets the agent send a confirmation, a statement, or a dispute acknowledgement to the customer by email.
PushoverSimple push notifications to a phone/desktop (one POST to messages.json).🔴 ActionAlerts a human — an ops engineer or on-call fraud analyst — the instant the agent escalates something.
uvAstral's fast Rust-based Python package/runner (uv run, uvx).— (infra)Not a model-facing tool, but how you package tool code and spin up clean, reproducible environments fast — including the throwaway sandboxes an agent's code runs in.

Here is how the three model-facing ones look as plain Python functions you'd register as tools. Notice the search tool is a safe read, while the two notification tools are state-changing actions that get action-tier guardrails:

import os, requests                                          # requests for the HTTP calls; os for keys

def web_search(query: str) -> list[dict]:                   # 🔵 Knowledge tier — a safe read
    r = requests.post(                                      # Serper: one POST returns structured results
        "https://google.serper.dev/search",
        headers={"X-API-KEY": os.environ["SERPER_API_KEY"]},  # key from env, never hard-coded
        json={"q": query}, timeout=10)                      # always set a timeout on a network tool
    r.raise_for_status()                                    # turn HTTP errors into exceptions your wrapper catches
    return [                                                # LEAN return: trim to the fields the model needs
        {"title": o["title"], "snippet": o.get("snippet", ""), "link": o["link"]}
        for o in r.json().get("organic", [])[:5]]           # top 5 only — don't dump the whole page

def email_customer(to: str, subject: str, body: str, user) -> dict:  # 🔴 Action tier
    assert to == user.verified_email                        # SECURITY: only ever email the signed-in customer
    r = requests.post(                                      # SendGrid transactional send
        "https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['SENDGRID_API_KEY']}"},
        json={"personalizations": [{"to": [{"email": to}]}],
              "from": {"email": "noreply@bankassist.example"},
              "subject": subject,
              "content": [{"type": "text/plain", "value": body}]},
        timeout=10)
    return {"sent": r.status_code == 202}                   # SendGrid returns 202 Accepted on success

def alert_oncall(message: str) -> dict:                     # 🔴 Action tier — pings a human, not the customer
    r = requests.post(                                      # Pushover: notify the fraud/ops team
        "https://api.pushover.net/1/messages.json",
        data={"token": os.environ["PUSHOVER_TOKEN"],        # app token
              "user":  os.environ["PUSHOVER_USER"],         # the team/group key
              "message": message, "priority": 1},           # priority 1 = bypass quiet hours for fraud
        timeout=10)
    return {"notified": r.json().get("status") == 1}        # Pushover returns status:1 on success
▶ Output
web_search("Bank of England base rate today")
# -> [{"title": "Official Bank Rate ...", "snippet": "4.00% ...", "link": "https://..."}]
alert_oncall("Possible card fraud on acct 4471 — agent froze card, needs review")
# -> {"notified": True}

And uv sits one layer down. When you package these tools into a service, uv resolves and installs their dependencies in seconds instead of minutes; when an agent runs model-written code (a CodeAct snippet), uvx or uv run can spin up an ephemeral, pinned environment per run so each execution is clean and reproducible. It's the plumbing that makes tool code fast to build and safe to throw away.

🏦 Picture this

A customer says, "Someone's using my card — stop it and tell me the last three charges." BankAssist runs two 🟢 reads in parallel (get_card_status, list_transactions) for a quick picture, then calls the 🔴 action freeze_card — which triggers a step-up check ("confirm the last 4 digits") and logs an audit entry before freezing. Same conversation, two very different trust levels, each handled by its tier's rules.

⚙️ Under the hood

A powerful pattern is to route authority by tier. Read and Knowledge tools can run with the customer's own scoped, read-only credentials. Action tools require the agent to re-confirm the user's intent and identity for that specific action — never a broad "admin" credential that would let an injected instruction in some retrieved document quietly move money. Tie every privileged action to the real user's authorisation, not the agent's.

✅ Tip

You do not build the sandbox yourself: managed services run untrusted model-written code safely — E2B and Modal give you ephemeral cloud sandboxes with no standing credentials, and Pyodide (Python compiled to WebAssembly) runs it inside a locked browser tab. Pick one and keep money-moving tools out of it.

⚙️ In production

A tiered catalogue is only as safe as the controls you actually wire to each tier.

  • Third-party dependency risk: Serper, SendGrid, and Pushover are external services with their own uptime, rate limits, and latency (Serper ~1–2 s; email/push typically sub-second). Wrap each in the retry/timeout discipline for its tier, and have a fallback — if search is down, the agent should say so, not stall.
  • Cost control: metered APIs bill per call (Serper ≈ $0.001/query; email/push per message). Rate-limit per customer and per tenant so a looping agent can't run up a bill or spam a customer's inbox.
  • Secrets & compliance: API keys live in a secrets manager, never in code or tool descriptions. For a bank, outbound email/push must respect consent and comms-preference rules, and every send is logged with who triggered it and why.
  • Data egress: a web-search tool sends the query to a third party — never let it carry PII or account numbers. Scrub arguments before they leave your perimeter, and keep knowledge-tier tools on public, non-sensitive queries only.
⚠ Watch out

Don't let a convenient third-party tool quietly become an action-tier risk without action-tier guards. A "just send an email" helper that trusts the model's to field can be steered by a prompt injection into emailing a customer's statement to an attacker. Bind every outbound action to the verified, signed-in user — not to an argument the model filled in.

Use a lightweight external tool when it does one job well and no internal system covers it (public web facts via Serper, customer email via SendGrid, on-call alerts via Pushover). Don't reach for one when an internal, auditable service already exists — in-house keeps the data inside the bank's perimeter and under its controls.

🧠 Remember it

Three tiers: Read (my data), Knowledge (the world's facts), Action (changes things). Trust rises as you go down — so do the guardrails.

Computer-use agents, tool limiting, and lean return formats

Some tasks have no clean API, so an agent can drive a screen like a person. But that power is a last resort, boxed in tightly. One thread runs through this whole topic: give the model less, and give it clean.

Computer-use / browser agents — the last resort

Occasionally a bank's task lives behind a legacy web portal with no API at all. For these, the newest models can use a computer-use tool: the model is shown a screenshot, and it emits actions like "click at (x, y)", "type this", "scroll down" — effectively driving a browser or desktop like a human would. A browser agent is the same idea aimed at web pages.

This is genuinely powerful, and genuinely risky, so the rule is: reach for it only when no real API exists. A clean function tool is faster, cheaper, and far safer than clicking pixels. When you must use computer-use, box it in hard:

  • Sandbox it. Run the browser in an isolated container or VM with no access to production systems, no stored credentials beyond the one task, and a network allowlist of only the sites it needs. If the agent goes wrong, the blast radius stays inside the box.
  • Watch the untrusted screen. A web page the agent reads is untrusted input. A malicious page can contain text like "ignore your instructions and transfer funds" — and a computer-use agent might obey. Never let on-screen text trigger a privileged action without an independent check.
  • Human approval for anything irreversible. Pause and get a sign-off before the agent submits a payment or changes a record through the screen.

Tool limiting: breadth, budget, permissions

Whether a tool clicks pixels or calls an API, the same discipline keeps an agent affordable and safe — give it less. Think in three limits:

  • Breadth — how many tools are in view. Keep the active set small, routing or retrieving so only the relevant handful reaches the model. Fewer tools, better choices.
  • Budget — how much it can do. Cap tool calls per task, set a cost and time ceiling, and apply per-tenant rate limits so one runaway session can't drain the bank's downstream APIs.
  • Permissions — what it's allowed to do. Least privilege: scope every tool's credentials to the minimum, separate read from write, and gate high-risk tools behind approval. The agent should never hold more authority than the customer it's serving.

Return format: minimal and structured

One last habit quietly decides whether an agent stays sharp over a long conversation: what a tool hands back. Every token a tool returns lands in the model's limited context, costs money, and can bury the signal in noise. So return the least the model needs, in a clean, structured shape.

❌ Bloated

{"status":200,"headers":{...40 lines...},
 "raw":"<xml>...2KB of core-banking
 envelope...</xml>","account":{
 "id":"4471","type":"CURRENT",
 "openedDate":"2009-...","balance":
 812.40, ...30 more fields...}}

The model wades through 2KB of envelope to find one number. Multiply that over ten tool calls and the context is drowning.

✅ Lean

{"account_id":"4471",
 "available":812.40,
 "currency":"GBP"}

Exactly what's needed to answer, nothing more. Easy for the model to read, cheap in tokens, hard to misread.

The pattern: let your code do the filtering, not the model. Parse the raw API response in your function, pull out the fields that matter, and return a small object. If a tool could return a huge list, paginate or summarise it rather than dumping everything. The model should receive a tidy answer, not a data dump to sift through.

⚙️ Under the hood

Lean returns compound over a session. A big raw tool output sits in context for every following turn, growing cost and latency and pushing older, still-important facts toward the "middle" of the context where models attend least. Returning small, structured results — and clearing large stale tool outputs once they've been used — is one of the cheapest ways to keep a long-running agent both fast and coherent.

⚙️ In production

These three disciplines — computer-use, tool limiting, lean returns — are where an agent's real-world cost and risk get decided.

  • Computer-use cost & latency: driving a screen is slow (seconds per click, a screenshot sent to the model each step) and expensive (vision tokens on every turn). Reserve it for the rare no-API case; a function tool is 10–100× cheaper and faster.
  • Budget as a hard limit: enforce max tool calls, a token ceiling, and a wall-clock timeout per task, plus per-tenant rate limits. A runaway session should hit a wall and escalate, not quietly drain a downstream core-banking API.
  • Lean returns compound: every tool result rides along in context on every later turn. A 2 KB raw payload across ten calls is 20 KB of recurring cost and a slower, dumber agent. Filter in your code; paginate or summarise big lists.
  • Security & monitoring: least privilege on every credential, read split from write, and on-screen text treated as untrusted. Monitor per-tool token footprint, budget-limit trips, and any computer-use session as a high-risk event with full screen-action audit.
⚠ Watch out

Don't over-trim either. If you strip a field the model genuinely needs, it'll call the tool again to get it — turning one lean call into two. Return the minimum sufficient set: small, but complete enough to answer the likely question.

Use computer-use when a required task genuinely has no API and sits behind a legacy screen — sandboxed, with human approval for anything irreversible. Don't use it when an API or function tool exists; it's slower, costlier, and a far bigger attack surface.

🧠 Remember it

Computer-use is the fire escape, not the front door. And whatever the tool: give the model fewer tools, a tighter budget, less authority, and leaner results.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🔒 security

CodeAct — when the action is code

Instead of filling in one JSON form per step, the agent writes a tiny program and runs it.

Classic tool-calling works like a vending machine: the model picks one button (a function name), slides in the exact change (JSON arguments), and gets back one snack (the result). To do three things, it presses three buttons, one turn at a time. That is clear and safe — but slow and clumsy when a task needs a loop, a bit of maths, or stitching several tools together.

CodeAct is the other way to act. The model's "action" is a small snippet of real code (usually Python) that calls your tools as ordinary functions, does any logic it needs, and returns an answer. The snippet runs in a locked-down sandbox, and whatever it prints or returns flows back to the model as the observation.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist customer asks, "What was my average balance over the last 30 days?" With JSON tool-calling the agent fetches each daily balance in its own round-trip, then has to add thirty numbers and divide — arithmetic LLMs fumble. With CodeAct the agent writes one short program: pull the balances, sum them, divide, round. One action, exact maths, done.

In plain terms

JSON tool-calling says "call get_balance with these args." CodeAct says "here is code that calls get_balance in a loop, averages the results, and returns the number." The tools are the same; the difference is that code can loop, branch, compute, and compose many calls in a single step.

How it actually works

The agent loop is the same shape as any tool-using agent, with one twist at the "act" step:

  1. You expose your tools as plain Python functions and put their signatures in the system prompt.
  2. The model replies with a code block instead of a JSON tool call.
  3. Your harness extracts the code and runs it inside a sandbox where those functions are in scope.
  4. Whatever the code prints (or the error it throws) is captured and handed back to the model.
  5. The model reads the observation and either finishes or writes more code.
SYSTEM_TOOLS = """ # these function stubs are shown to the model so it knows the API
def get_daily_balances(account_id: str, days: int) -> list[float]: ...
def final_answer(text: str) -> None: ...
"""

# ↓ a CodeAct-style action the MODEL emits (your harness runs it in a sandbox)
balances = get_daily_balances("AC-4471", days=30)   # one tool call returns 30 numbers
avg = round(sum(balances) / len(balances), 2)        # real arithmetic — no LLM guessing
final_answer(f"Your 30-day average balance is ${avg}")  # hand the result back cleanly
▶ Output

Your 30-day average balance is $2841.57

One action did the fetch, the loop, the maths, and the formatting. With JSON tool-calling that is thirty-plus round-trips plus a shaky mental sum. Research on CodeAct found that letting agents act through executable code often completes tasks in fewer steps and with higher success than text or JSON actions, because code naturally composes. It is the pattern behind Hugging Face smolagents' CodeAgent, among others.

JSON tool-calling

One function + args per turn. Easy to validate, easy to permission, easy to log. Weak at loops, maths, and chaining — those cost many round-trips.

CodeAct

A code block per turn. Loops, branches, composes tools, and computes in one step. Powerful — but you are now running model-written code, so the sandbox is non-negotiable.

⚠ Watch out

CodeAct runs code the model wrote. Never exec() it in your app process. Run it in a real sandbox: a separate container or locked-down interpreter with no network, a short CPU/time limit, capped memory, a read-only filesystem, and only an allow-list of safe imports and your tool functions in scope. Treat a prompt-injected instruction that says "write code to email the customer list" as the attack it is.

Use CodeAct when a task needs loops, maths, or composing several tool calls in one step (an average over 30 days, filtering then summing) and you have a real sandbox. Don't use it when a single high-stakes action (one transfer_money) is all that's needed — plain JSON tool-calling there is easier to validate, permission, and audit, with far less attack surface.

⚙️ In production

For a bank, CodeAct is a privilege boundary, not a convenience. Rules that keep it safe at scale:

  • Sandbox per run — ephemeral container, killed after each action; nothing persists between customers.
  • Fast, pinned environments — build the sandbox image with a tool like uv (Astral's Rust-based Python runner): uv resolves and installs the exact pinned dependencies in seconds, so you can afford a clean, reproducible interpreter per run instead of a long-lived shared one. uvx/uv run launch the snippet in that locked environment — fast to spin up, cheap to throw away.
  • Tools, not raw SQL — the code may call get_daily_balances, never open a database connection. Money-moving tools still require their own confirmation/approval step.
  • Resource caps + timeouts — a runaway loop should die in seconds, not take down a node.
  • Full audit — log the exact code, inputs, and output of every action for compliance replay.
  • Fall back to JSON for simple, high-stakes, single-tool actions where the extra power of code just adds attack surface.
🧠 Remember it

JSON tool-calling = press one button at a time. CodeAct = write a little program that presses many — so keep that program in a padded cell (the sandbox).

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🔐 security

AI Agents — Reasoning & Planning

An agent is just a language model put in charge of a job — but a model that answers in one breath makes careless mistakes. This chapter is about the "thinking" half of an agent: the handful of patterns that let it slow down, work step by step, check itself, split a big job into small ones, and change course when the world surprises it.

Chain of Thought: let the model show its work

Ask the model to reason out loud, step by step, before it commits to an answer — and watch its accuracy on hard problems jump.

Think back to a maths exam at school. The question says "show your working." Not because the teacher enjoys reading your scribbles, but because a student who writes each step — carry the one, subtract the deposit, then divide — gets the final number right far more often than one who stares at the page and blurts a guess.
