The scribbling is the thinking. Take the paper away and even a clever student fumbles.

Language models are exactly the same. Chain of Thought (CoT) just means: before the model gives its final answer, you let it write out the intermediate reasoning. In the simplest form you literally add the words "Let's think step by step" to your instruction, and the model starts laying out its reasoning instead of leaping to a conclusion.

Why spreading the work over more tokens actually helps

Here's the part that surprises people, and it's worth getting right. A language model does a fixed amount of computation to produce each token (a token is roughly a word-piece). It cannot "think harder" on a single token — one token is one fixed dose of compute. So if you force the answer into the very first token, the model gets exactly one dose of compute to solve the whole problem. That's like demanding the final exam answer with no paper allowed.

When the model instead writes a sentence of reasoning first, every one of those reasoning tokens is another dose of compute, and — crucially — each new token can look back at all the reasoning so far. The problem gets chewed on across dozens of steps instead of one. You are literally buying the model more computation by letting it write more, and giving it a scratchpad to store half-finished thoughts. That is the whole trick: more tokens of reasoning = more compute spent = better answers on anything multi-step.

🏦 Picture this

A customer asks BankAssist: "I borrowed $12,000 at 6% simple interest for 3 years. I've already paid $1,500. What's left to pay?" Answering in one shot, a model often jumps straight to a round-ish number and gets it wrong. Told to think step by step, it writes: "Interest = 12000 × 0.06 × 3 = $2,160. Total owed = 12,000 + 2,160 = $14,160. Minus $1,500 paid = $12,660." Same model, same question — the working is what made it right.

The four flavours of Chain of Thought

CoT isn't a single switch; it comes in four strengths you'll reach for in different situations.

  • Zero-shot CoT. The lazy, brilliant one-liner. You just append "Let's think step by step" (or "reason it out before answering") and the model produces its own reasoning. No examples needed. This alone rescues a lot of arithmetic and logic.
  • Few-shot CoT. You show the model two or three worked examples — question, full reasoning, answer — before the real question. The model copies the style of reasoning. Use this when you want the reasoning to follow your bank's particular method (e.g. "always check eligibility before quoting a rate").
  • Self-consistency. Instead of trusting one chain, you ask the model the same question several times, let each run reason its own way, and then take the majority answer. Reasoning can wander down a wrong path once; it rarely wanders down the same wrong path five times. Voting cancels out the flukes.
  • Reasoning models. The newest models have CoT baked in. Instead of you prompting for steps, the model is trained to produce a long internal reasoning pass on its own before answering — often called "extended" or "adaptive" thinking. You don't write "think step by step"; the model already does, and decides how long to think based on how hard the question looks.

Here's self-consistency in real code. We ask a reasoning-capable model the same tricky question a few times and vote. (In practice, for exact money maths you'd hand the sum to a calculator tool — more on that in the warning below — but this shows the voting mechanic clearly.)

# Self-consistency: sample several independent reasoning runs, then vote.
from anthropic import Anthropic      # official Anthropic SDK — the client for Claude models
from collections import Counter      # a tiny helper to tally which answer won the vote
import re                            # used to pull the final number out of each reply

client = Anthropic()                 # reads your API key from the environment; your door to the model

question = (                          # one awkward, multi-step banking question
    "A customer has 3 accounts: $1,240.50, $880, and an overdraft of -$300. "
    "What is their total net balance? Reason step by step, then end with "
    "'ANSWER: <number>'."        # we force a fixed last line so we can parse the result
)

def ask_once():                      # one independent reasoning run
    resp = client.messages.create(   # the core call that sends a prompt and gets a reply
        model="claude-opus-5-5",     # a current reasoning-capable model (thinks before answering)
        max_tokens=1024,             # enough room for the reasoning plus the final line
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],  # the conversation so far: just our question
    )
    text = resp.content[0].text      # the model's written reply (first text block)
    match = re.search(r"ANSWER:\s*(-?[\d.]+)", text)  # grab the number after 'ANSWER:'
    return match.group(1) if match else None          # return that number, or None if it didn't comply

votes = [ask_once() for _ in range(5)]            # run the SAME question 5 times — each reasons its own way
winner = Counter(v for v in votes if v).most_common(1)[0]  # pick the answer that appeared most often
print("votes:", votes)               # see the spread — usually 4-of-5 agree
print("final:", winner[0], f"({winner[1]}/5 agreed)")  # report the majority answer and its confidence
▶ Output
votes: ['1820.50', '1820.50', '1820.50', '1220.50', '1820.50']
final: 1820.50 (4/5 agreed)

The same self-consistency vote with the OpenAI API:

# Self-consistency with OpenAI: sample several independent reasoning runs, then vote.
from openai import OpenAI            # official OpenAI SDK — the client for GPT models
from collections import Counter      # a tiny helper to tally which answer won the vote
import re                            # used to pull the final number out of each reply

client = OpenAI()                    # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment; your door to the model

question = (                          # one awkward, multi-step banking question
    "A customer has 3 accounts: $1,240.50, $880, and an overdraft of -$300. "
    "What is their total net balance? Reason step by step, then end with "
    "'ANSWER: <number>'."        # we force a fixed last line so we can parse the result
)

def ask_once():                      # one independent reasoning run
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(  # the core call that sends a prompt and gets a reply
        model="gpt-4.1",             # a current OpenAI model
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],  # the conversation so far: just our question
    )
    text = resp.choices[0].message.content   # the model's written reply
    match = re.search(r"ANSWER:\s*(-?[\d.]+)", text)  # grab the number after 'ANSWER:'
    return match.group(1) if match else None          # return that number, or None if it didn't comply

votes = [ask_once() for _ in range(5)]            # run the SAME question 5 times — each reasons its own way
winner = Counter(v for v in votes if v).most_common(1)[0]  # pick the answer that appeared most often
print("votes:", votes)               # see the spread — usually 4-of-5 agree
print("final:", winner[0], f"({winner[1]}/5 agreed)")  # report the majority answer and its confidence
▶ Output
votes: ['1820.50', '1820.50', '1820.50', '1220.50', '1820.50']
final: 1820.50 (4/5 agreed)

Notice run four slipped (it forgot the overdraft is negative), but it was outvoted. That is self-consistency earning its keep: five cheap-ish reasoning passes beat one, because the mistakes don't line up. The cost, of course, is that you paid for five answers instead of one — so you save it for questions where being wrong is expensive.

⚙️ Under the hood

Why do reasoning models feel so much stronger than "think step by step" bolted onto an older model? Because they were trained on millions of good reasoning traces and rewarded for reaching correct answers, so their internal chains are tidier and self-correcting — they'll often catch their own slip mid-thought ("wait, that account is an overdraft, so it's negative"). The practical upshot: on a reasoning model you usually should not stuff the prompt with your own "step by step, first do X then Y" scaffolding. It already reasons; over-instructing it can actually lower quality. Set how hard it should think (a low/high "effort" dial) and let it cook.

Going deeper

Self-consistency is not free accuracy — it's accuracy you buy by the sample. The gains are real but they plateau: on hard reasoning benchmarks, voting over about five samples captures most of the lift, and beyond roughly 10–15 samples the curve flattens while your bill keeps climbing in a straight line. There is also a wall voting can never cross — if every chain makes the same early mistake (a misread of the question, a wrong policy assumption), the majority is confidently wrong. Voting cancels random slips, not shared blind spots.

Reasoning models shift the tuning from wording to a budget dial. Instead of crafting "think step by step" phrasing, you set a reasoning-effort level (low / medium / high) or a thinking-token budget, and the model spends more internal compute on harder questions. Two edge cases bite banks here: (1) on an easy question a high-effort model can overthink — burning tokens and latency to second-guess a correct first instinct; and (2) stacking your own verbose "first do X, then Y" scaffolding on top of a trained reasoner often lowers quality, because you are fighting the reasoning it already does well. Match the dial to the difficulty and otherwise get out of its way.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Reasoning is not free output — a reasoning pass can produce several times the tokens of a blunt answer, and self-consistency multiplies that again by your sample count (five votes is roughly five times the spend). Reasoning also adds seconds of latency, so a customer-facing BankAssist turn should stream a "working on it…" state or cap the thinking budget rather than leave the chat frozen. Scale. Do not put every message through deep reasoning: route it. A cheap classifier sends "what's my branch's phone number?" straight to a one-shot answer and reserves CoT or a reasoning model for genuine multi-step work (eligibility, disputes, comparisons) — typically a small minority of traffic. Failure modes & monitoring. Track tokens per turn, the vote-agreement rate (a 3/5 split is a low-confidence flag worth escalating), and the parse-success rate of the forced ANSWER: line — a sudden drop usually means a prompt or model change broke your extraction. Security & compliance. Never surface the raw chain of thought to a customer: it can leak PII, internal policy wording, and footholds an attacker could use to steer the model. Store the reasoning trace separately in an audit log — for any reasoning that feeds a regulated decision (a lending or fraud outcome) that trace is your explainability record, so retain it under the same rules as the decision itself.

⚠ Watch out

Three traps. (1) Plausible-but-wrong reasoning. A chain of thought that reads convincing can still reach a false answer — fluent is not the same as correct. (2) Never trust CoT for exact arithmetic. Models reason in words, not in a calculator; for interest, amortisation, or any figure that touches money, make the agent call a real calculation tool and reason about the result, not instead of it. (3) Don't show raw reasoning to customers. The chain can contain half-formed guesses, internal policy notes, or clues an attacker could use to steer the model. Keep it in your logs, show the customer only the final, checked answer.

When to use it, when not. Reach for CoT on anything multi-step: eligibility logic, "compare these two products," troubleshooting a failed payment. Skip it for trivial lookups ("what's the branch's phone number?") — there the reasoning just adds latency and cost for no gain. And remember CoT alone is not an agent: it thinks, but it cannot yet do anything in the world. Giving the model tools and a think-act-observe loop (the ReAct pattern) is what closes that gap.

🧠 Remember it

More words of thinking = more compute. One token gets one shot; a chain of tokens gets many. Show the working, vote when it matters, and never let the model do money-maths in its head.

ReAct: a loop of think, act, observe

Give the model tools and let it alternate between reasoning and using them — thinking a bit, acting, looking at what came back, thinking again.

Chain of Thought lets a model think. But a banker who only thinks, and never looks anything up, is just guessing eloquently. Real work needs a loop: have a thought, check something, see the result, think again. Picture a detective. She doesn't solve the case in one monologue; she forms a hunch, knocks on a door to test it, hears the answer, updates her hunch, and knocks on the next door. Thought, action, observation — around and around until the case is closed.

ReAct (short for Reason + Act) is exactly that loop for an AI agent. At each turn the model does one of two things: it writes a Thought (private reasoning about what to do next), or it issues an Action — a call to a tool you've given it, like "look up this account's balance." Your code runs that tool and feeds the result back as an Observation. The model reads the observation, thinks again, and either acts once more or decides it's ready to answer. It is the single most common pattern in production agents, because it keeps the reasoning grounded in real data instead of floating free.

🏦 Picture this — a real ReAct trace

A customer asks BankAssist: "Did my salary land yet, and am I overdrawn?" Watch the agent work the problem one honest step at a time:

Thought: I need two facts — the current balance, and whether a salary credit arrived. Start with the balance.
Action: get_balance(account="chk-001")
Observation: {"balance": -42.17, "currency": "USD"}
Thought: Balance is negative, so yes, currently overdrawn by $42.17. Now check for a recent salary credit.
Action: get_transactions(account="chk-001", days=3, type="credit")
Observation: []  (no credits in the last 3 days)
Thought: No salary has landed. That explains the negative balance. I have both answers.
Final answer: "Your salary hasn't arrived yet, and your account is currently $42.17 overdrawn. Once the credit lands it should clear the overdraft."

See how the reasoning and the facts take turns? The model never guessed the balance — it fetched it. That grounding is the whole point: ReAct ties each thought to a real observation, so the agent can course-correct when reality doesn't match its hunch.

Here is the loop in code. The key idea: you call the model, and if it asks to use a tool you run the tool, hand the result back, and call the model again — repeating until it stops asking for tools.

# A minimal ReAct loop with real tool-calling.
from anthropic import Anthropic      # official SDK for Claude models
client = Anthropic()                 # picks up your API key from the environment

tools = [                            # the "doors" the agent is allowed to knock on
  {"name": "get_balance",            # tool 1: look up an account balance
   "description": "Current balance for one account.",  # the model reads this to decide when to use it
   "input_schema": {"type": "object",
     "properties": {"account": {"type": "string"}},     # it must supply an account id
     "required": ["account"]}},
  {"name": "get_transactions",       # tool 2: list recent transactions
   "description": "Recent transactions, newest first.",
   "input_schema": {"type": "object",
     "properties": {"account": {"type": "string"},
                    "days": {"type": "integer"}},        # how far back to look
     "required": ["account"]}},
]

def run_tool(name, args):            # YOUR code that actually talks to the core-banking system
    if name == "get_balance":
        return {"balance": -42.17, "currency": "USD"}    # (stubbed here; real call would hit an API)
    if name == "get_transactions":
        return []                    # no recent credits — salary hasn't landed

messages = [{"role": "user",         # the conversation starts with the customer's question
    "content": "Did my salary land yet, and am I overdrawn? Account chk-001."}]

for step in range(6):                # CAP the loop — never let an agent spin forever
    resp = client.messages.create(   # ask the model what to do next
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
        tools=tools, messages=messages,                  # give it the tools and the history so far
    )
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})  # record what the model said/asked (keeps the thread intact)

    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":                   # the model stopped asking for tools → it's ready to answer
        print(resp.content[-1].text)                     # print the final answer and leave the loop
        break

    results = []                     # gather the result of every tool the model asked for this turn
    for block in resp.content:       # one assistant turn can request several tools at once
        if block.type == "tool_use": # this block is an Action (a tool request)
            out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)      # run it → this is the Observation
            results.append({"type": "tool_result",       # package the observation to send back
                            "tool_use_id": block.id,      # link the result to the exact request it answers
                            "content": str(out)})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})  # feed all observations back, then loop and think again
▶ Output
Your salary hasn't arrived yet, and your account is currently $42.17 overdrawn. Once the credit lands it should clear the overdraft.

The same ReAct loop with the OpenAI API:

# A minimal ReAct loop with OpenAI tool-calling.
from openai import OpenAI            # official SDK for GPT models
import json                          # tool arguments come back as a JSON string
client = OpenAI()                    # picks up OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

tools = [                            # the "doors" the agent is allowed to knock on
  {"type": "function", "function": {
     "name": "get_balance",          # tool 1: look up an account balance
     "description": "Current balance for one account.",  # the model reads this to decide when to use it
     "parameters": {"type": "object",
       "properties": {"account": {"type": "string"}},     # it must supply an account id
       "required": ["account"]}}},
  {"type": "function", "function": {
     "name": "get_transactions",     # tool 2: list recent transactions
     "description": "Recent transactions, newest first.",
     "parameters": {"type": "object",
       "properties": {"account": {"type": "string"},
                      "days": {"type": "integer"}},        # how far back to look
       "required": ["account"]}}},
]

def run_tool(name, args):            # YOUR code that actually talks to the core-banking system
    if name == "get_balance":
        return {"balance": -42.17, "currency": "USD"}    # (stubbed here; real call would hit an API)
    if name == "get_transactions":
        return []                    # no recent credits — salary hasn't landed

messages = [{"role": "user",         # the conversation starts with the customer's question
    "content": "Did my salary land yet, and am I overdrawn? Account chk-001."}]

for step in range(6):                # CAP the loop — never let an agent spin forever
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(  # ask the model what to do next
        model="gpt-4.1", tools=tools, messages=messages,  # give it the tools and the history so far
    )
    msg = resp.choices[0].message    # the model's reply lives in choices[0].message
    messages.append(msg)             # record what the model said/asked (keeps the thread intact)

    if not msg.tool_calls:           # the model stopped asking for tools → it's ready to answer
        print(msg.content)           # print the final answer and leave the loop
        break

    for call in msg.tool_calls:      # one assistant turn can request several tools at once
        out = run_tool(call.function.name, json.loads(call.function.arguments))  # run it → this is the Observation
        messages.append({"role": "tool",          # package the observation to send back
                         "tool_call_id": call.id,  # link the result to the exact request it answers
                         "content": str(out)})     # feed it back, then loop and think again
▶ Output
Your salary hasn't arrived yet, and your account is currently $42.17 overdrawn. Once the credit lands it should clear the overdraft.
⚙️ Under the hood

The original ReAct papers had the model print the words "Thought:" and "Action:" as plain text, and you parsed that text with fragile regular expressions. Modern APIs do it far more robustly with native tool-calling: the model returns a structured tool_use block with the tool name and arguments already as clean JSON — no parsing guesswork. The "Thought" still happens (as the model's reasoning, visible or internal), but the "Action" is now a typed, validated object. If you build agents on top of a framework, this loop is what libraries like LangChain's create_agent give you out of the box — a ReAct-style loop with the tool plumbing handled.

Going deeper

ReAct is the default loop almost every framework ships — LangChain and LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, the Claude Agent SDK, CrewAI and others all wrap this think-act-observe cycle for you. That ubiquity is earned, but it has a price tag: an agent that narrates a thought before every action typically emits two to four times the tokens of a plain tool-caller for the same result, and each loop step is a full model round-trip. A chatty six-step loop is six sequential calls plus six tool round-trips — the latency and cost add up fast when multiplied across a contact centre's traffic.

The subtle edge cases are about grounding quality. If an observation is huge (a 500-row transaction dump), it bloats the context on every subsequent turn, so you summarise or paginate tool outputs before feeding them back. If a tool is slow, the whole loop stalls — so independent lookups should fire in parallel rather than one thought at a time. And the model can "observe" an error and then cheerfully pretend it succeeded on the next turn, so error observations must be explicit and unmistakable, not a silent empty result.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Budget per conversation, not per call: cap the loop (the range(6) above is a real safety rail) and set a token and time budget for the whole turn. Each step is a serial round-trip, so your p95 latency (the slow end of the range — what 95% of turns finish under) is roughly steps × (model time + slowest tool) — trim both by keeping thoughts short and tool outputs lean. Scale & failure modes. The classic production incidents are infinite loops (same tool, same arguments, forever), tool timeouts that aren't surfaced, and context bloat that silently doubles cost by turn five. Detect repeated identical actions and break; wrap every tool call in a timeout that returns a clear error observation; trim or summarise large results. Monitoring. Log every Thought / Action / Observation as a structured trace (this is what LangSmith-style observability gives you) with per-step tokens, tool latency, and tool error rates; alert on loops that hit the step cap, which is your early warning of a broken tool or a confusing prompt. Security & compliance for a bank. Tools are where an agent touches real money, so enforce least privilege (a support agent gets read-only balance and transaction tools, never a transfer tool), validate and authorise every tool argument server-side against the authenticated customer (so a prompt-injected "now fetch account chk-999" is rejected), and keep an immutable audit trail of which tool ran with which inputs for every customer action.

⚠ Watch out

ReAct's failure modes all come from the loop. Infinite loops: an agent can call the same tool with the same arguments over and over — always cap the number of steps (the range(6) above) and detect repeats. Tool errors: if a banking API returns an error, feed that error back as an observation (with a clear message) so the model can react to it — don't let an exception kill the agent silently, or it will hallucinate that the call succeeded. Context bloat: long, chatty thoughts and huge tool outputs pile up in the conversation, raising cost and latency every turn — keep observations trimmed to what matters.

When to use it, when not. ReAct is your default whenever the agent needs to touch the world — fetch data, call services, check live facts. It's overkill for a pure one-shot question that needs no tools (just use Chain of Thought), and it can be inefficient for a long, predictable workflow where you already know the steps in advance — which is exactly what planning the whole route up front (the Plan-and-Execute pattern) fixes.

🧠 Remember it

ReAct = the detective loop: hunch → knock on a door → hear the answer → better hunch. Think, act, observe, repeat — and always cap the loop.

Plan-and-Execute: decide the whole route first

Instead of thinking one step at a time, have a smart model write the full plan up front, then let a cheaper, faster worker carry out each step.

Imagine two ways to do the weekly shop. The first: wander the supermarket deciding what you need aisle by aisle, doubling back when you remember the milk. The second: write the full list at home, then walk the aisles ticking items off. For a big shop, the list wins — you think once, carefully, then execute quickly without re-deciding at every shelf.

That's Plan-and-Execute. A ReAct agent re-thinks before every single action, which means a full, expensive reasoning call on each tiny step. For a long task that's slow and pricey. Plan-and-Execute splits the job in two: a planner (a strong model) looks at the whole goal once and writes an ordered list of steps; then an executor (often a cheaper, faster model, or even plain code) runs each step in turn. You pay for deep thinking once, not twenty times.

🏦 Picture this

A customer applies for a small personal loan through BankAssist. The job has a known shape every time: check who they are, pull their credit, test it against lending policy, then decide. A ReAct agent would wake up the big model four times to "figure out what to do next" — but there's nothing to figure out; the steps are the same for every applicant. So BankAssist plans the four steps once with a strong model, then lets a small, cheap model execute each one. Faster for the customer, and a fraction of the cost per application.

# Plan with a strong model, execute each step with a cheaper one.
from anthropic import Anthropic
import json
client = Anthropic()

goal = "Process a $5,000 personal loan application for customer C-7781."

# --- 1) PLAN: ask the strong model for an ordered list of steps ---
plan_resp = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",         # the capable (pricier) model — used ONCE
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
        f"Goal: {goal}\n"
        "Return ONLY a JSON list of short step strings, in order."}],  # ask for a clean, parseable plan
)
steps = json.loads(plan_resp.content[0].text)   # turn the model's JSON text into a Python list
print("PLAN:", steps)

# --- 2) EXECUTE: run each step with the cheap, fast model ---
for i, step in enumerate(steps, 1):  # walk the plan in order, one step at a time
    out = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-5-5",    # the cheap, fast model — does the routine legwork
        max_tokens=512,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"You are executing step {i} of a loan workflow: '{step}'. "
            "Do just this step and report the result in one line."}],  # keep each executor call tightly scoped
    )
    print(f"step {i}: {out.content[0].text}")    # show what the executor did for this step
▶ Output
PLAN: ['Verify customer identity', 'Pull credit score', 'Check against lending policy', 'Make decision and explain']
step 1: Identity verified for C-7781 (ID + address match on file).
step 2: Credit score retrieved: 742 (good).
step 3: Policy check: income multiple within limit; no adverse flags.
step 4: Approved $5,000 at 9.9% APR — score and affordability both pass.

The same plan-then-execute split with the OpenAI API:

# Plan with a strong OpenAI model, execute each step with a cheaper one.
from openai import OpenAI
import json
client = OpenAI()

goal = "Process a $5,000 personal loan application for customer C-7781."

# --- 1) PLAN: ask the strong model for an ordered list of steps ---
plan_resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1",                 # the capable (pricier) model — used ONCE
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
        f"Goal: {goal}\n"
        "Return ONLY a JSON list of short step strings, in order."}],  # ask for a clean, parseable plan
)
steps = json.loads(plan_resp.choices[0].message.content)  # turn the model's JSON text into a Python list
print("PLAN:", steps)

# --- 2) EXECUTE: run each step with the cheap, fast model ---
for i, step in enumerate(steps, 1):  # walk the plan in order, one step at a time
    out = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1-mini",        # the cheap, fast model — does the routine legwork
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"You are executing step {i} of a loan workflow: '{step}'. "
            "Do just this step and report the result in one line."}],  # keep each executor call tightly scoped
    )
    print(f"step {i}: {out.choices[0].message.content}")  # show what the executor did for this step
▶ Output
PLAN: ['Verify customer identity', 'Pull credit score', 'Check against lending policy', 'Make decision and explain']
step 1: Identity verified for C-7781 (ID + address match on file).
step 2: Credit score retrieved: 742 (good).
step 3: Policy check: income multiple within limit; no adverse flags.
step 4: Approved $5,000 at 9.9% APR — score and affordability both pass.

Reach for Plan-and-Execute when…

The task is long and fairly predictable — a multi-stage workflow where the steps are knowable up front (onboarding, loan processing, a reconciliation run). You want lower cost and latency, and a plan you can log, review, or even get a human to approve before anything runs.

Reach for ReAct when…

The task is short or unpredictable — you genuinely don't know step two until you see the result of step one (open-ended troubleshooting, exploratory questions). Here, committing to a full plan up front is premature; think-act-observe fits better.

Going deeper

The economics are the whole point. ReAct wakes the expensive model before every step; Plan-and-Execute pays for deep thinking once and then runs the steps on a cheaper, faster model — for a stable four- or five-step workflow that can cut both cost and latency substantially, because a small model answering a tightly-scoped "do just this step" prompt is a fraction of the price of a reasoning model re-deciding the whole task each time. The catch is adaptability: when a result invalidates the plan, recovery is costlier than ReAct's local retry, because you often have to go back to the planner and regenerate the remaining route.

Two refinements make it robust in practice. First, a plan-validation step: before executing, a second model (or a rules check) reviews the proposed plan against known constraints — do all the named tools exist, is the order legal, does it respect policy? Catching a bad plan on paper is far cheaper than discovering it halfway through execution. Second, checkpointing: record which steps have completed so a mid-run failure resumes from the last good step instead of restarting the whole job — without it, Plan-and-Execute is surprisingly fragile on long workflows.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. The win is one strong-model call amortised over many cheap executor calls — ideal for predictable, high-volume flows like loan intake or nightly reconciliation where the shape never changes. Measure the blended cost per completed job, not per call, and watch that replans don't quietly erase the saving. Scale & failure modes. The headline risk is a bad plan propagating: a planner that invents a non-existent tool or an illegal step sends the executor marching off a cliff. Constrain the planner to the real, named tool list; add the validation gate above; and treat a plan as revisable, never sacred. Monitoring. Because the plan is produced up front, it is a first-class artefact — log it, diff plans over time, track plan-validation pass rate and per-step success rate, and alert when executors start failing a step that used to pass (a sign the world or a downstream API changed). Security & compliance for a bank. The explicit written plan is a compliance gift: for a lending or account action you can route the plan to a human for approval before any step runs, and you keep the exact approved sequence in the audit log. Pin the planner and executor model versions so an approved workflow's behaviour doesn't drift silently under you.

⚠ Watch out

The danger of planning first is a bad plan propagating. If the planner misjudges the task — or worse, invents a step that uses a tool you don't actually have — the executor dutifully marches off a cliff. Two defences: (1) constrain the planner to the real, named list of available tools so it can't dream up fictional ones, and (2) never treat a plan as sacred — when a step fails, the agent must be able to stop and make a new plan rather than ploughing ahead. That revise-the-plan skill — making a fresh plan when a step fails instead of ploughing ahead — is important enough to treat as its own pattern, replanning.

🧠 Remember it

Write the shopping list before you walk the aisles. Plan once with the smart model, execute with the cheap one — great for long, known jobs, wasteful for short, surprising ones.

Tree of Thoughts: explore branches, keep the best

For truly hard problems, don't follow a single line of reasoning — grow several, score them, cut the weak ones, and sometimes back up and try a different branch.

A chess player doesn't play the first move that pops into her head. She pictures a few candidate moves, imagines how each might play out, judges which position looks strongest, and discards the rest. If a promising line turns sour three moves deep, she backtracks and explores a different branch. That is search, not a straight line — and it's the idea behind Tree of Thoughts (ToT).

Chain of Thought walks one path from question to answer. If that path takes a wrong turn early, the whole chain is doomed. Tree of Thoughts instead treats reasoning as a tree: at each step the model proposes several different next thoughts (the branches), a scorer rates how promising each one looks, the agent keeps the best few and prunes the rest, and it can backtrack if a branch turns out to be a dead end. It's deliberate trial-and-error, done in parallel.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's fraud team flags a payment that might be fraud but might just be unusual — a large transfer to a new payee in another country. A single chain of thought would pick one explanation and run with it. Tree of Thoughts instead generates three candidate explanations ("stolen credentials," "customer paying an overseas invoice," "family transfer"), scores each against the evidence on file (device fingerprint, past payees, the customer's travel notes), prunes the two that fit the facts poorly, and expands the strongest into a concrete recommendation. When a problem has several plausible stories and getting it wrong is costly, exploring beats guessing.

# Tree of Thoughts, one level deep: propose, score, keep the best.
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()

problem = ("A $4,200 transfer to a new overseas payee was flagged. "
           "Propose ONE short hypothesis for what's going on.")

# --- 1) BRANCH: generate several independent candidate thoughts ---
branches = []                        # will hold the candidate hypotheses
for _ in range(3):                   # grow 3 branches — each is a different line of reasoning
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=200,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": problem}])
    branches.append(r.content[0].text.strip())       # collect this branch's hypothesis

# --- 2) SCORE: ask the model to rate each branch against the evidence ---
evidence = "Known device, customer added a travel note for France last week."
def score(hypo):                     # a judge call: how well does this hypothesis fit the facts?
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=10,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"Evidence: {evidence}\nHypothesis: {hypo}\n"
            "Rate fit 0-10. Reply with the number only."}])  # force a bare number so we can sort
    return int("".join(c for c in r.content[0].text if c.isdigit()) or 0)

# --- 3) PRUNE: keep only the top-scoring branch ---
best = max(branches, key=score)      # pick the hypothesis with the highest fit score
print("Kept:", best)                 # the survivor would be expanded further in a deeper tree
▶ Output
Kept: Likely a legitimate holiday payment — the device is recognised and the customer flagged travel to France, matching an overseas payee.

The same branch-score-prune with the OpenAI API:

        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": problem}])

# --- 2) SCORE: ask the model to rate each branch against the evidence ---
evidence = "Known device, customer added a travel note for France last week."
def score(hypo):                     # a judge call: how well does this hypothesis fit the facts?
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", max_tokens=10,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"Evidence: {evidence}\nHypothesis: {hypo}\n"
            "Rate fit 0-10. Reply with the number only."}])  # force a bare number so we can sort
    return int("".join(c for c in r.choices[0].message.content if c.isdigit()) or 0)

# --- 3) PRUNE: keep only the top-scoring branch ---
best = max(branches, key=score)      # pick the hypothesis with the highest fit score

▶ Output
Kept: Likely a legitimate holiday payment — the device is recognised and the customer flagged travel to France, matching an overseas payee.
⚙️ Under the hood

Two dials decide a tree's cost: breadth (how many branches per step) and depth (how many steps deep you go). Cost grows roughly like breadthdepth — a modest tree of 4 branches, 4 deep is already 256 paths, each needing model calls to generate and to score. That exponential blow-up is why ToT is rare in everyday, latency-sensitive banking chat. The quality of the whole search also rests entirely on the scorer: a weak judge happily prunes the right answer and keeps a bad one. If you can't score branches reliably, a tree just burns money exploring nonsense.

Going deeper

Put real numbers on the blow-up. A modest tree with breadth 4 and depth 3 is already on the order of 20-plus generation calls plus 20-plus evaluator calls for a single answer, versus one forward pass for a plain chain — and practitioners quote rough cost multipliers of 50–150× for a real ToT search (and 100–300× for heavier hybrids that bolt reflection and Monte-Carlo search onto the tree). A controlled 2025 study comparing one-shot, chain-of-thought, tree-of-thought and reflection under a fixed compute budget found the uncomfortable truth: on most tasks the simpler methods matched or beat the tree while costing far less. ToT only pulls ahead where the problem genuinely contains search.

Two edge cases decide whether a tree is worth it. First, the evaluator is the whole ballgame — a tree is only as smart as the scorer steering it, and a weak LLM judge will happily prune the right branch and expand a wrong one, burning money to search worse than a straight line. Where you can, score with an external verifier (a rules engine, a schema validator, a balance or policy check) rather than another model call. Second, modern reasoning models already do a lot of internal search, so explicit ToT now earns its keep mainly where you need transparency and control — an auditable record of which options were considered and why one was chosen — or where a cheap proposer paired with an expensive verifier beats one big model.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. ToT is the most expensive pattern in this chapter by a wide margin, and the branch generations plus scoring make it slow — which is why it almost never sits on the hot path of live banking chat. Reserve it for low-volume, high-stakes work (complex fraud triage, a contested dispute with several resolutions) run slightly off-line, not for the millions of routine lookups. Scale. Never run full search: bound breadth and depth hard, and use a bounded beam (keep only the top-k branches at each level) so cost stays roughly linear instead of exponential. Failure modes & monitoring. The dangers are an unbounded tree whose cost and latency explode on one query, and a mis-calibrated scorer that quietly steers every search wrong. Cap total model calls per query as a circuit breaker; log branches explored, prune decisions, and score distributions; and track cost-per-resolved-case so a runaway tree shows up immediately. Validate the evaluator offline against known-good outcomes before trusting it live. Security & compliance for a bank. The upside is explainability — the retained tree of considered options and their scores is a ready-made record of why a fraud or dispute decision was reached, which is exactly what an auditor or regulator asks for. Keep that trace, and keep the discarded branches out of anything the customer sees.

⚠ Watch out

ToT is the sledgehammer of reasoning patterns — powerful and expensive. The classic mistakes: using it on problems a single well-prompted chain would solve (you pay 50× for no gain); trusting a weak evaluator to steer the search; and letting breadth and depth grow unbounded until a single customer query costs pounds and takes a minute. Always bound both dials, and only reach for a tree when you have measured that single-chain reasoning genuinely fails on your hardest cases.

When to use it, when not. Worth the cost for high-stakes, low-volume problems with real search in them — complex fraud triage, a tricky dispute with several possible resolutions, planning an optimal sequence of eligibility checks. Not worth it for the 95% of banking questions that are straightforward lookups or simple multi-step reasoning; there, Chain of Thought or ReAct is faster, cheaper, and plenty.

🧠 Remember it

Tree of Thoughts = think like a chess player: branch, score, prune, backtrack. Brilliant for hard searches, far too costly for easy questions — and only as good as its scorer.

Reflection & Reflexion: let the agent check its own work

Before an agent calls a job done, have it critique its own draft against hard evidence — and when it's wrong, let it keep a written note of the lesson so it does better next try.

A careful writer never sends the first draft. She reads it back, spots the clumsy sentence, fixes it, and only then hits send. A good chef tastes the sauce before it leaves the kitchen. That second look — reviewing your own output and improving it — is Reflection. When the agent also remembers what went wrong, so the same mistake doesn't recur, that stored lesson is what the research calls Reflexion: reflection plus a little verbal memory.

The loop is simple. An actor produces a draft answer or plan. A critic examines it and says "good — ship it" or "no, here's what's wrong." If the critic rejects it, the actor tries again, this time with the critique in hand. Reflexion adds one thing: the critique is saved as a lesson ("I forgot to check the overdraft was negative"), so across many attempts the agent accumulates a growing list of its own gotchas.

The single most important word in that diagram is grounded. A critic that just asks the model "are you happy with your answer?" is nearly useless — models are agreeable and will cheerfully rubber-stamp their own nonsense. A grounded critic checks each claim against something real: the actual tool output, the retrieved policy text, a validator, a calculator. It's the difference between "does this feel right?" and "does every number here match the evidence?"

🏦 Picture this — a grounded critic catching a mistake

A customer asks whether a $35 overdraft fee can be waived. BankAssist's actor drafts: "Yes, we waive the $35 fee automatically every month." Before sending, the grounded critic compares that claim to the retrieved policy clause, which actually reads "one courtesy waiver per 12 months, on request." The critic flags it: "Claim 'automatically every month' contradicts the policy ('once per 12 months, on request')." The actor rewrites: "The $35 fee can be waived once in a 12-month period if you request it." No false promise ever reaches the customer — because the check was against the real text, not the model's mood.

# Reflection with a GROUNDED critic: check the draft against real evidence.
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()

question = "Can my $35 overdraft fee be waived?"
evidence = "Policy 4.2: one courtesy overdraft-fee waiver per 12 months, on request."  # the retrieved truth
lessons = []                         # Reflexion memory: notes we carry into each retry

def actor(extra=""):                 # produce a draft answer, optionally warned by past lessons
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=300,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"{question}\nEvidence: {evidence}\n{extra}"}])      # 'extra' injects the critique on a retry
    return r.content[0].text.strip()

def critic(draft):                   # the grounded check: is every claim backed by the evidence?
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=200,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"Evidence: {evidence}\nDraft: {draft}\n"
            "Does the draft ONLY state things supported by the evidence? "
            "Reply 'PASS' or 'FAIL: <reason>'."}])            # force a verdict we can branch on
    return r.content[0].text.strip()

draft = actor()                      # first attempt
for attempt in range(3):             # bound the retries — never reflect forever
    verdict = critic(draft)          # judge the current draft against the policy
    if verdict.startswith("PASS"):   # critic is satisfied the claims are grounded
        print("SHIP:", draft); break
    lessons.append(verdict)          # remember why it failed (Reflexion's growing note)
    draft = actor("Previous attempt was wrong. " + verdict)  # retry, this time told exactly what to fix
▶ Output
SHIP: Your $35 overdraft fee can be waived once within a 12-month period if you request it. Would you like me to log that request now?

The same grounded reflection loop with the OpenAI API:

# Reflection with a GROUNDED critic, OpenAI version: check the draft against real evidence.
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()

question = "Can my $35 overdraft fee be waived?"
evidence = "Policy 4.2: one courtesy overdraft-fee waiver per 12 months, on request."  # the retrieved truth
lessons = []                         # Reflexion memory: notes we carry into each retry

def actor(extra=""):                 # produce a draft answer, optionally warned by past lessons
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", max_tokens=300,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"{question}\nEvidence: {evidence}\n{extra}"}])      # 'extra' injects the critique on a retry
    return r.choices[0].message.content.strip()

def critic(draft):                   # the grounded check: is every claim backed by the evidence?
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4.1", max_tokens=200,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
            f"Evidence: {evidence}\nDraft: {draft}\n"
            "Does the draft ONLY state things supported by the evidence? "
            "Reply 'PASS' or 'FAIL: <reason>'."}])            # force a verdict we can branch on
    return r.choices[0].message.content.strip()

draft = actor()                      # first attempt
for attempt in range(3):             # bound the retries — never reflect forever
    verdict = critic(draft)          # judge the current draft against the policy
    if verdict.startswith("PASS"):   # critic is satisfied the claims are grounded
        print("SHIP:", draft); break
    lessons.append(verdict)          # remember why it failed (Reflexion's growing note)
    draft = actor("Previous attempt was wrong. " + verdict)  # retry, this time told exactly what to fix
▶ Output
SHIP: Your $35 overdraft fee can be waived once within a 12-month period if you request it. Would you like me to log that request now?
⚙️ Under the hood

Reflection shines brightest when there's a cheap, objective signal to check against — did the code run, does the number match, is the claim in the source text, did the generated SQL return rows? Those give the critic solid ground. When the only judge is the model's own opinion, reflection gets shaky: it may "fix" a correct answer into a wrong one, or declare a wrong answer perfect. The production move is to lean on external verifiers wherever you can — a schema validator, a unit test, a second model from a different family, a lookup against ground truth — and to treat pure self-opinion as the weakest form of critique.

Going deeper

Reflection multiplies calls, so count them before you commit. A single actor-critic round is already two to three model calls instead of one; a Reflexion loop that allows, say, three attempts of a multi-step task with a critique between each can easily reach a dozen or more calls for one answer. That is fine when correctness is worth it — and wasteful when the critic adds nothing. The deciding factor is whether you have a cheap, objective signal to check against: did the code run, does the number reconcile, is the claim actually in the retrieved policy text, did the generated SQL return rows? Where such a signal exists, reflection is some of the best money you'll spend; where the only judge is the model's own taste, it gets shaky.

The edge cases are failure directions. An ungrounded critic tends to rubber-stamp — models are agreeable and will bless their own nonsense — adding cost and zero safety. The opposite failure is a confident critic that "fixes" a correct answer into a wrong one, or two drafts that oscillate forever, each attempt undoing the last. Both are why grounding and a hard retry cap matter more than the loop itself: a second model from a different family, or better still a non-model verifier, breaks the shared-blind-spot trap that self-critique falls into.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Each reflection pass is another round-trip, so reserve it for answers where being wrong is expensive — customer-facing policy answers, generated code, structured outputs that must validate — and skip it on trivial replies. Budget for the worst case (max attempts × calls per attempt), not the happy path. Scale & failure modes. The two incidents that bite are rubber-stamping (an ungrounded critic that always passes, giving false assurance) and unbounded reflect-retry loops that churn cost with no convergence. Fix the first by feeding the critic real evidence or an external verifier; fix the second with the range(3)-style cap and an escalation path when it still can't pass. Monitoring. Track how often the critic rejects (a reject rate near 0% usually means a lazy critic, not a perfect actor), average attempts to pass, and the escalation rate; alert when attempts-to-pass creeps up. Security & compliance for a bank. Ground the critic against the authoritative source — the retrieved policy clause, the real calculator result — so a customer never gets a confidently-wrong promise like "we waive the fee every month." Keep both the rejected drafts and the final shipped answer in the audit log: showing that a grounded check caught and corrected an error is powerful evidence of a controlled, compliant process.

⚠ Watch out

Two failure modes to guard against. Rubber-stamping: an ungrounded critic that always says "looks good" adds cost and zero safety — give it real evidence to check against, or don't bother. Reflect-retry loops: without a cap, an agent can critique-and-redo endlessly, or even oscillate between two wrong answers forever. Always bound the attempts (the range(3) above) and, if it still can't pass, escalate to a human rather than shipping an unchecked guess.

When to use it, when not. Add reflection to any task where quality matters and you can check it — customer-facing answers that must match policy, generated code, structured outputs that must validate. Skip it for trivial replies where a second pass just doubles cost for no real risk.

🧠 Remember it

Reflection = taste the sauce before you serve it — but taste it against the recipe (real evidence), not your mood. Reflexion just means writing the lesson on a sticky note for next time.

Task decomposition: break a goal into a map of subtasks

Split a big job into small, named subtasks and draw the arrows showing which depend on which — some must wait their turn, others can run side by side.

Ask anyone to cook a Sunday roast and they instinctively decompose it: peel the potatoes, season the meat, preheat the oven, make the gravy. Some steps have an order — you can't carve before you roast. But others are independent — you can peel potatoes while the oven heats. A good cook sees both the sequence and the parallelism. That mental map of "what must come before what" is exactly what task decomposition gives an agent.

Formally, you turn one big goal into a set of smaller subtasks and record the dependencies between them — subtask D needs the results of B and C; A and B don't need each other at all. That structure is a DAG (a Directed Acyclic Graph): "directed" because the arrows point from a task to the ones that depend on it, and "acyclic" because there are no loops (nothing can depend on itself, directly or in a circle). The DAG tells the agent two priceless things: the order it must respect, and which steps it can safely run at the same time to save time.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist handles a loan application. Verifying the customer's identity and pulling their credit score are completely independent — no reason to do them one after the other. So the agent fires both off at the same time, and the customer waits for the slower of the two, not the sum. Only once both come back can it assess affordability; only after that can it run the policy check; only then can it decide. The DAG squeezes out the waiting that a naive one-step-at-a-time agent would suffer — the same four-second job finishes in two.

# Decompose a goal into a DAG, then run independent tasks in parallel.
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor   # lets independent tasks run at the same time

tasks = {                            # each task lists the tasks it DEPENDS ON
    "A_verify_id":   [],             # no dependencies — can start immediately
    "B_credit":      [],             # no dependencies — can start immediately
    "C_afford":      ["A_verify_id", "B_credit"],  # needs identity AND credit first
    "D_policy":      ["C_afford"],   # needs affordability first
    "E_decide":      ["D_policy"],   # the final step, needs the policy check
}

def run(task):                       # stand-in for "do this subtask" (call a tool / model)
    return f"{task} done"

done = {}                            # remembers which tasks have finished
while len(done) < len(tasks):        # keep going until every task is complete
    ready = [t for t, deps in tasks.items()           # find tasks whose dependencies are all done...
             if t not in done and all(d in done for d in deps)]  # ...and that haven't run yet
    with ThreadPoolExecutor() as pool:                # run this whole ready batch together
        for t, result in zip(ready, pool.map(run, ready)):  # parallel execution of independent tasks
            done[t] = result         # record each result as it completes
    print("ran in parallel:", ready) # show which tasks went off together this round
▶ Output
ran in parallel: ['A_verify_id', 'B_credit']
ran in parallel: ['C_afford']
ran in parallel: ['D_policy']
ran in parallel: ['E_decide']

The scheduler is tiny but does the clever thing: each round it finds every task whose prerequisites are already satisfied and runs that whole batch together. Round one fires A and B side by side; the later rounds fall into sequence because each truly needs the one before it.

⚙️ Under the hood

Who draws the DAG? Two options. For a fixed workflow like loan processing, you (the engineer) hard-code the graph — it's the same every time, so there's no reason to pay a model to re-derive it. For an open-ended goal ("research this company's exposure to three counterparties"), you ask a planner model to produce the decomposition — list the subtasks and their dependencies as JSON — and then your code schedules it. The parallel branches are also a natural fit for sub-agents: give each independent subtask its own focused agent with a clean context, and have them report short summaries back to a coordinator, so no single agent's context gets cluttered with everyone's raw work.

Going deeper

The payoff from a DAG is wall-clock time on the critical path, not fewer steps. If verifying identity takes 1.5s and pulling credit takes 2s, running them in sequence costs 3.5s but running them in parallel costs 2s — the customer waits for the slower of the two, not the sum. Across a five- or six-task flow with two or three independent branches, that routinely halves perceived latency. Recent research pushes this further: manager-driven agents that keep a live DAG, launch parallel sub-agents on every "ready" node, and re-plan as results arrive report success-rate gains of up to around 25% on complex tasks over a single static plan — the structure helps accuracy, not just speed.

The edge cases are both directions of dependency error. Inventing a dependency that isn't real forces independent steps into a needless queue and throws away the parallelism. Missing a real dependency is worse and quieter: run the policy check before the credit score lands and you decide on missing data — a correctness bug no exception will flag. And over-decomposition has its own cost: shatter a job into forty micro-tasks and the coordination overhead and extra model calls can outweigh the work itself. Split along the genuine seams, and remember a DAG is acyclic by definition — if your "plan" contains a cycle (A waits on B which waits on A), that is a modelling bug, not a schedule.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Parallelism trades a burst of concurrent load for lower latency — great for the customer, but it means several tool and model calls fire at once, so size downstream rate limits and connection pools for the peak, not the average. For a fixed flow like loan intake, hard-code the DAG; only pay a planner model to derive the graph for open-ended goals. Scale. The independent branches map naturally onto sub-agents — give each its own clean context and have it report a short summary to a coordinator, so no single context fills up with everyone's raw work. Failure modes & monitoring. A failed node must not silently let dependents run on missing data; mark the branch failed and block its descendants. Watch for a partial failure where three of four parallel branches succeed — decide up front whether that is a retry, a degraded answer, or an escalation. Log per-node latency and failure rate and the critical-path time so you can see which branch is the bottleneck. Security & compliance for a bank. Parallel sub-agents each touching customer data multiply the surface area, so scope every sub-agent's tools and data access to exactly its subtask (the identity-verification agent can't see transaction history it doesn't need), and keep a per-node audit trail. For regulated decisions, record the whole graph — which subtasks ran, in what order, and what each returned — as the decision's provenance.

⚠ Watch out

The two opposite errors. Inventing dependencies that aren't there forces steps into a needless sequence and throws away the speed-up — if A and B truly don't need each other, don't chain them. Missing a real dependency is worse: run the policy check before the credit score is in and you'll decide on missing data, a silent correctness bug. And resist over-decomposition — shattering a job into forty micro-tasks adds coordination overhead and model calls that can cost more than they save. Split along the real seams of the work, not finer.

When to use it, when not. Decompose whenever a goal has genuinely separable parts, especially independent ones you can run in parallel, or when it's complex enough that a map keeps the agent honest. For a simple, single-step request, skip it — there's nothing to break apart, and the graph is just ceremony.

🧠 Remember it

Decomposition = the Sunday-roast plan: list the steps, draw the arrows for what must wait, and run the rest side by side. Honour real dependencies; never invent fake ones.

Replanning: change course without spinning in circles

When reality doesn't match the plan, make a new plan — but put firm limits in place so the agent adapts a few times rather than thrashing forever.

Your car's sat-nav plots a route. You miss a turn. A good sat-nav doesn't sulk or blindly tell you to drive into a wall — it quietly reroutes. But imagine one that recalculated the entire journey every two seconds, or kept flipping between two routes at a junction, never committing: you'd never arrive. That tension — adapt when things change, but don't dither — is the heart of replanning.

A plan is a guess about the future, and the future loves to surprise you. A tool times out. A credit API returns "customer not found." A policy rule the planner assumed turns out not to apply. When an agent's plan collides with reality like this, the mature response is to stop, look at what actually happened, and make a fresh plan from the new situation — not to keep executing steps that no longer make sense. That's replanning: the agent revises its plan mid-flight when observations diverge from expectations.

But replanning has a dark twin: thrashing. An agent that replans too eagerly can get stuck — retry the same failing step, loop between two plans, or churn out plan after plan while making no real progress, burning time and money the whole way. So replanning is only safe when it comes wrapped in guardrails.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist is processing a loan with a four-step plan (verify identity, pull credit, check policy, decide). At step two, the credit API returns an error: "no file found for this customer." A rigid agent would ignore it and barrel on to the affordability check with no score — garbage in, garbage out. A thrashing agent would hammer the same broken call fifty times. A well-guarded agent does neither: it notices the divergence, makes a new plan ("try the alternative bureau; if that also fails, request manual documents"), and — crucially — if it has already replanned twice without progress, it stops and hands the case to a human underwriter with a clear note of what it tried. Adapt, but know when to tap out.

# Replanning with guardrails that stop the agent from thrashing.
MAX_STEPS   = 10                     # hard ceiling on total actions — the ultimate backstop
MAX_REPLANS = 2                      # how many times we'll redraw the plan before giving up

replans = 0                          # count the re-plans we've done so far
recent  = []                         # remember recent actions to catch repeats (no-progress check)
plan    = make_plan(goal)            # the starting plan (from a planner model or a fixed template)

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):        # GUARDRAIL 1: never loop more than MAX_STEPS times
    action = plan.pop(0)             # take the next action off the front of the plan
    result = execute(action)         # run it and watch what happens (the observation)

    if result.ok:                    # reality matched the plan — carry on
        if not plan: break           # plan finished, nothing left to do — success
        continue

    # --- the step diverged; decide whether to re-plan or bail ---
    if recent.count(action) >= 2:    # GUARDRAIL 2: same action failing again = no progress
        escalate(goal, reason="stuck repeating an action"); break  # hand to a human instead of thrashing
    recent.append(action)            # log this failed action for the repeat check

    if replans >= MAX_REPLANS:       # GUARDRAIL 3: too many re-plans already
        escalate(goal, reason="replan budget exhausted"); break    # stop churning, get a human

    plan = make_plan(goal, note=result.error)  # make a FRESH plan informed by what went wrong
    replans += 1                     # spend one of our limited re-plans

Every path out of trouble is bounded. The loop can't run past MAX_STEPS; the agent can't repeat a failing action more than twice; it can't replan more than MAX_REPLANS times. Hit any limit and it escalates to a human rather than spinning. That's the whole art: free to adapt, but never free to thrash.

⚙️ Under the hood

How does an agent know it's "making progress" versus thrashing? A few practical signals, beyond the simple repeat-detection above. State change: did this step actually move the world forward (a new fact gathered, a sub-goal completed), or did it leave things exactly as before? Budget burn: track tokens, tool calls, wall-clock time, and even money spent — a hard budget is the bluntest but most reliable guardrail. Loop detection: watch for the agent cycling through the same small set of states. In durable, long-running banking workflows you also checkpoint progress so that a replan builds on completed work instead of redoing it — you revise the route ahead, you don't re-drive the miles already covered.

Going deeper

Replanning is what separates a brittle demo from an agent that survives real-world flakiness — and the hard part is telling honest adaptation from thrashing. The practical progress signals are concrete: did this step actually change state (a new fact gathered, a sub-goal closed) or leave the world exactly as before; is the agent cycling through the same small set of actions; and how much of the budget — tokens, tool calls, wall-clock, money — has it burned for how much progress? A hard budget is the bluntest guardrail but also the most reliable: when it is spent, you stop, full stop. Research on long-horizon agents keeps finding the same thing — allowing only an initial static plan gives poor success rates, while bounded re-planning on a live task graph markedly improves them. Adaptation helps; unbounded adaptation destroys.

The subtle edge case is side effects. A fresh plan that quietly discards completed work is merely wasteful when the steps were read-only — but dangerous when a step already did something irreversible, like initiating a payment. Re-running it double-charges. The fixes are checkpointing (a replan builds on completed steps, it doesn't re-drive them) and idempotency keys on every side-effecting action (a retry with the same key is a no-op, not a second charge). And every replanning agent needs a human exit: some cases simply aren't the agent's to solve, and escalating with a clear note of what was tried is a feature, not a failure.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Replanning means regenerating the remaining route with the strong model, so each replan is a real cost spike — bound the number of replans (MAX_REPLANS above) and the total steps (MAX_STEPS) so a single stuck case can't run up an open-ended bill or leave a customer waiting indefinitely. Scale & failure modes. The named enemies are what the three guardrails invert: a runaway step count, the same action failing on repeat, and endless replan churn. Detect repeated identical actions, cap replans, and always escalate to a human when any limit trips rather than looping. In durable, long-running workflows, checkpoint progress so a replan — or a crash and restart — resumes from the last good step. Monitoring. Track replans per task, escalation rate, budget burn per outcome, and the distribution of why plans diverged (which tool or API most often triggers a replan is your reliability hot-spot). Alert on any task that hits its step or replan ceiling. Security & compliance for a bank. Make every side-effecting step idempotent so a replan or retry can never double-initiate a payment or a fee, and keep an immutable log of each plan revision with the observation that triggered it — for a regulated action you must be able to show exactly why the agent changed course and that it handed off to a human underwriter when it reached its limits.

⚠ Watch out

The nastiest replanning bug is a plan that throws away good progress. If "make a fresh plan" silently discards the three steps that already succeeded, the agent redoes work — and if those steps had real side-effects (say, it already initiated a payment), redoing them can double the action. Protect side-effecting steps with idempotency so a retry can't double-charge, and make the new plan build on what's done rather than starting from zero. And never ship an agent that can replan without a human exit — some problems simply aren't the agent's to solve, and knowing when to escalate is a feature, not a failure.

When to use it, when not. Replanning earns its place in longer, autonomous workflows that run against flaky real-world systems — exactly where things will go sideways. For a short, single-shot interaction, you don't need the machinery: if it fails, just surface the error and stop. The guardrails, though, are non-negotiable the moment any agent is allowed to loop at all.

🧠 Remember it

Replanning = a good sat-nav: reroute when you miss a turn, but don't recalculate every two seconds. Bound the steps, the repeats, and the re-plans — and when the limits hit, hand the wheel to a human.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

AI Agents — Memory & Context Engineering

An agent is only as good as what it can remember and what it chooses to look at right now — so let's learn, in plain words, how to give BankAssist a memory it can trust and a workspace it keeps tidy.

Short-term memory: the context window is the agent's RAM

Everything the model can "see" in one turn — the instructions, the chat so far, the tool results — lives in a single bounded space called the context window. Think of it as working memory, like RAM in a computer.

Imagine a brilliant new teller at BankAssist's branch. She has a small desk. Whatever papers are on the desk right now are the only things she can read while she helps you — the forms you handed her, the sticky note with your account number, the policy page she pulled out. The desk is fast and right in front of her, but it's small. Pile on too many papers and some slide off the edge and are gone.

That desk is the context window. It is the chunk of text a language model (the "brain" behind the agent) reads in one shot before it replies. It holds the system prompt (the standing instructions, like "You are BankAssist, never reveal another customer's data"), the conversation so far, any documents you retrieved, the tool results that came back, and the answer being written. All of it competes for the same limited space, measured in tokens — a token is roughly three-quarters of a word.

Why "short-term"

Two things make this memory short-term. First, it is bounded: a model has a maximum window (today, often 128K to 1M tokens depending on the model — big, but never infinite). Second, it is gone at the end: when the session closes, the window is cleared, exactly like RAM losing its contents when you power off. Tomorrow the agent remembers nothing of today unless you deliberately saved it somewhere lasting.

🏦 Picture this

A customer tells BankAssist at the start of a chat: "I'm travelling to Spain next week, don't flag my card." Fifteen messages later she asks, "will my card work abroad?" If that first sentence is still on the desk, the agent answers perfectly. But if the chat ran long and early turns slid off the edge, the agent has genuinely forgotten the trip — not because it's dim, but because the paper left the desk. That single failure is why long-term memory and context engineering exist.

Going deeper — bigger desks don't end the problem

It's tempting to think "just use a model with a million-token window and never worry." Three realities stop that. You pay per token on every turn, so stuffing a huge window is expensive and repeated each message. Bigger windows are slower — more to read means more latency while the customer watches a spinner. And models read a crowded desk worse: attention spreads thin, and the one line that mattered can get skimmed. A big desk helps, but a tidy desk wins.

💡 Key idea

Short-term memory = the context window = the agent's RAM. It is fast, finite, shared by everything, and wiped at session end. Managing it well is half of building a good agent.

In production — the window is a line item on every invoice

⚙️ In production

Cost. You pay for every token on the desk on every turn. A BankAssist chat that drags 40K tokens of history through 20 turns bills 800K input tokens for one conversation — before a single reply is counted. At a few dollars per million input tokens that is real money across the millions of chats a bank handles a month, which is why trimming the desk is a cost lever, not a nicety.

Latency. Bigger inputs mean a longer time-to-first-token; a desk that grows unchecked turns a snappy one-second reply into a four-second wait while the customer watches a spinner. Prompt caching (the provider reusing an unchanged front-of-desk at a steep discount) helps a lot — but only if the stable prefix, the system prompt and tool definitions, stays byte-identical turn to turn. Reorder or edit that prefix and the cache misses, so both cost and latency jump.

Failure mode & monitoring. The signature production failure is a hard context-limit error mid-conversation: the agent simply refuses once the desk overflows. Track tokens-per-turn and percent-of-window-used as first-class metrics, alert before you reach the ceiling, and keep a compaction step ready to fire. Compliance: everything on the desk is transmitted to the model provider — never let unmasked card numbers, full account numbers, or passwords sit in the window; mask at the edge so they are never sent at all.

⚠ Watch out

Don't treat the window like infinite scratch paper. The most common rookie bug is appending every tool result and every turn forever "to be safe" — the desk silently grows until one customer's long session trips the hard limit and the agent dies mid-sentence. A window is a budget you actively manage, not a bucket you keep filling.

When to lean on short-term memory, and when not: use the window for the here-and-now of a single conversation — the current task, the last few turns, the documents needed for this answer. Do not use it as storage for anything that must survive the session or be recalled tomorrow; the moment a fact needs to outlive the chat, write it to long-term memory instead of hoping it stays on the desk.

🧠 Remember it

The context window is a desk, not a filing cabinet. Fast and in reach — but small, and cleared at closing time.

Long-term memory and its three flavours: episodic, semantic, procedural

To remember across sessions, the agent needs a filing cabinet outside the desk. Borrowing from how human memory works, we split that store into three kinds — events, facts, and know-how.

Short-term memory is the desk; long-term memory is the filing cabinet behind it. It lives outside the context window, usually in a database, and the agent pulls the right folder onto the desk only when it's needed. Psychologists have long split human long-term memory into types, and the same split turns out to be a wonderfully practical way to organise an agent's store.

1. Episodic memory — specific events that happened

This is the diary. Each entry is a thing that occurred, tied to a time: "On 3 March, the customer disputed a $40 overdraft fee and we waived it." Episodic memory answers "what happened before?" It is how BankAssist can say, "I see we waived a fee for you back in March," instead of treating a returning customer like a stranger.

2. Semantic memory — durable facts and knowledge

This is the fact sheet. It strips the timeline away and keeps the standing truths: "This customer prefers email over phone. Holds one mortgage and two credit cards. Primary language: Spanish." Semantic memory answers "what is true about this person or the world?" It changes slowly and is what powers real personalisation.

3. Procedural memory — how to do things

This is the staff handbook. It holds skills and routines: how to run a card-dispute, the exact steps to verify identity, the tone BankAssist always uses. In practice this often lives in the system prompt, in tool definitions, and in learned rules ("for Spanish-speaking customers, greet in Spanish"). Procedural memory answers "how do we do this?"

⚙️ Under the hood — what actually gets stored

You rarely dump raw chat into long-term memory. Instead you distill: after a session, a cheap model reads the transcript and extracts a few durable items — "customer travelling to Spain (episodic, expires after trip)," "prefers Spanish (semantic)." Each item is saved as a short text with metadata: the user_id it belongs to, a timestamp, and a type tag. Storing distilled facts instead of raw turns keeps the cabinet small, searchable, and auditable — and in banking, auditable matters.

⚠ Watch out

Long-term memory tied to a customer is personal data. Every item must be scoped to one user_id and locked so one customer's memories can never surface in another's chat. A memory leak across customers isn't a bug in banking — it's a reportable data breach.

⚙️ In production

Where each flavour lives & what it costs. At scale the three drawers map to different stores. Semantic facts are few and high-value — a few dozen per customer — so they are cheap to keep and are often pinned straight onto the desk. Episodic events grow without bound (every interaction adds one), so they live in a vector store and are fetched by relevance, never all loaded. Procedural memory is shared across all customers — one copy of "how to run a dispute" — so it lives in the system prompt and tool definitions, versioned with the code.

Latency & scale. Reading a semantic fact is a single key-value lookup (single-digit milliseconds); episodic recall is a vector search (tens of milliseconds) you run only when the turn actually needs history. Partition every store by user_id so one customer's growing episodic pile never slows another customer's lookup.

Failure modes & monitoring. The dangerous one is a stale semantic fact — "has a mortgage" after the mortgage was repaid — because semantic memory is read as ground truth. Attach a source and a last_confirmed timestamp to each fact, and monitor how often a recalled fact is later contradicted.
