Compliance for a bank: semantic and episodic memory are personal data under GDPR/CCPA — they need per-customer encryption, access logs, retention limits, and a working delete path; procedural memory is not personal data and is governed like code.

When to use each, and when not: reach for episodic when "what happened last time" changes the answer (a repeat complaint, a prior waiver); semantic for durable personalisation (language, products held, preferences); procedural for behaviour that must be identical for every customer. Do not store a volatile, time-boxed fact ("travelling next week") as a semantic truth — it belongs in episodic memory with an expiry, or it will outstay its welcome and mislead the agent.

🧠 Remember it

Three drawers: Episodic = diary (what happened), Semantic = fact sheet (what's true), Procedural = handbook (how we do it).

Recall is retrieval: RAG over the agent's own past

Here's the quiet secret of agent memory — "remembering" is just searching. The agent runs the very same retrieve-the-relevant-bits trick, except the library it searches is its own history.

You might have met RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) as a way to answer questions from a bank's documents: embed the docs into meaning-vectors, store them, and at question time fetch the closest passages to put in front of the model. Memory recall is the same machine pointed inward. Instead of searching policy PDFs, the agent searches its saved memories about this customer, and pastes the most relevant ones onto the desk before replying.

So "the agent remembered my trip" really means: it embedded the new question, searched the memory store, and the trip note came back as a close match. Memory isn't a mystical property — it's a write path (save distilled facts) plus a read path (retrieve the relevant ones). Two things make memory recall different from ordinary document RAG, and both are non-negotiable in a bank.

1. User-scoping — search only this customer's drawer

Document RAG searches one shared library. Memory RAG must search only the current customer's memories. That means every query carries a hard filter: user_id = this_customer. This isn't a nice-to-have for relevance; it's the wall that stops Mrs. Khan's history leaking into Mr. Rao's chat.

2. Recency — newer memories usually matter more

A policy document from 2019 is as true as one from today. But a memory from last week often beats one from two years ago: people move house, close accounts, change preferences. So memory recall blends two signals — similarity (how well the memory matches the question) and recency (how fresh it is) — into one score.

# Recall = retrieval over the agent's own memories, scoped and recency-aware.
import math, time                              # math for the decay curve; time for "how old is this memory"

def recall(query, user_id, store, k=5, half_life_days=30):
    hits = store.search(                        # vector search over saved memories, same as document RAG
        query=query,                            # the customer's new message, embedded to a meaning-vector
        filters={"user_id": user_id},           # HARD wall: only THIS customer's memories — never anyone else's
        limit=20,                               # over-fetch 20, then we re-score and keep the best few
    )
    now = time.time()                           # current time, to measure each memory's age
    for h in hits:                              # blend similarity with freshness for every candidate
        age_days = (now - h.created_at) / 86400 # seconds → days since the memory was written
        decay = 0.5 ** (age_days / half_life_days) # half-life curve: weight halves every 30 days
        h.score = h.similarity * decay          # a close-but-stale memory loses to a fresh relevant one
    hits.sort(key=lambda h: h.score, reverse=True) # best combined score first
    return hits[:k]                             # paste only the top k onto the desk — keep it tight
▶ Output
recall("will my card work abroad?", "cust_88213") → ["2d ago: customer travelling to Spain next week (do not flag card)", "40d ago: prefers travel alerts by SMS"]

Walk through what just happened. The customer's question became a vector and searched only her own memories. The two-day-old travel note scored highest because it was both relevant and fresh; an older preference still made the cut but ranked below it. Those two lines get pasted onto the desk, and now the agent answers as if it "remembered." The half_life_days dial controls how fast old memories fade — shorter for volatile facts, longer for stable ones.

✅ Tip

Over-fetch, then re-score. Pull 20 candidates by similarity alone, then apply recency and keep the top 5. If you filter by recency too early you can throw away the one old memory that was the perfect answer ("in 2021 the customer opted out of marketing — permanently").

Going deeper — the knobs that decide recall quality

Three dials shape every recall. The over-fetch width (how many candidates you pull before re-scoring — 20 here) trades recall against cost; too narrow and the perfect old memory never enters the race. The half-life sets how fast memories fade: a few days for volatile context like "annoyed about a fee today," many months for stable traits. And the final k (how many you paste) trades completeness against desk space — more memories mean more tokens and more chance of burying the one that matters. Tune these on real transcripts, not by guesswork: measure whether the memory that should have answered actually landed in the top k.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Every recall is an embedding call plus a vector query on the customer's turn — budget tens of milliseconds and a fraction of a cent, paid on the turns where you decide to recall. Don't recall on every turn blindly; a cheap gate ("does this message reference the past or need personalisation?") skips the lookup for small talk and saves both.

Scale & failure modes. With millions of customers the store must be partitioned by user_id so each search touches only one customer's shard. The quiet failure is the silent miss: the right memory exists but ranks below k and never reaches the desk, so the agent looks forgetful. Monitor recall-hit-rate on a labelled set, and log which memories were injected so you can audit why the agent said what it said.

Security. The user_id filter is a hard security boundary, not a relevance tweak. Enforce it server-side from the authenticated session — never from anything the model or the user can set — so a prompt-injected "search customer 99999's memories" is impossible. In a bank, a cross-customer recall is a reportable breach.

⚠ Watch out

Recency weighting cuts both ways. Crank the decay too hard and a permanent, load-bearing memory — "customer opted out of marketing for good," "legally barred from wire transfers" — gets out-ranked by last week's small talk and falls out of the top k. Mark such facts as non-decaying (or store them as semantic truths), so freshness can never bury a standing legal or consent flag.

When to recall, and when not: recall when the answer depends on this customer's history or preferences. Do not fire a recall for generic knowledge questions ("what's the SWIFT cut-off time?") — that's shared policy search, not personal memory, and querying the memory store for it just adds latency and risks pasting irrelevant personal notes onto the desk.

🧠 Remember it

Memory recall = RAG pointed at yourself, with two guardrails bolted on: scope to the user, and let the old stuff fade.

Forgetting on purpose: summarizing, aging, and the right to be forgotten

A memory that only ever grows becomes slow, expensive, and dangerous. The skill isn't remembering everything — it's deciding what to compress, what to let fade, and what to delete outright.

Left alone, an agent's memory bloats. Every chat adds notes; conflicting facts pile up ("lives in Madrid" and later "lives in Lisbon"); old tool dumps clog the desk. Three techniques keep memory healthy, and in a bank a fourth — deletion on demand — is the law.

Summarization & compression — trade detail for space

When a conversation runs long, you don't keep every word. You summarize older turns into a compact running note: "Customer verified identity; disputed a $40 fee; fee waived; now asking about travel." You drop the chatty back-and-forth and keep the decisions and facts. This frees desk space while preserving the thread. It is lossy on purpose — you accept losing wording to keep meaning.

Decay — let weak memories fade

Recall scores memories partly on recency — how fresh each one is. Decay is the same idea applied to the whole store: a memory's strength drops over time, and memories that are never recalled and have decayed past a floor get pruned. Like a human forgetting a one-off detail from years ago, the agent quietly lets trivia go.

TTL & supersession — expiry dates and overwrites

Some memories have a natural TTL (time-to-live): "travelling to Spain next week" should self-delete after the trip. Others are superseded: when "lives in Lisbon" arrives, the old "lives in Madrid" shouldn't sit alongside it causing contradictions — the new fact replaces the old. Good memory systems resolve these conflicts at write time, keeping only the current truth plus, where audit demands, a dated history of the change.

⚠ Watch out — the right to be forgotten

Under rules like GDPR, a customer can demand you erase their data. For agent memory this is harder than it sounds. The fact wasn't just written as text — it was embedded into a vector, maybe copied into a cache, maybe baked into a summary of a long chat. Deleting the original note is not enough; the meaning can still live in the vector and the summary. A compliant delete must chase down every copy: the raw memory, its embedding, any cache entry, and any summary that absorbed it. Design deletion in from day one — retrofitting it is agony.

⚙️ Under the hood — don't summarize away the load-bearing facts

Compression has a sharp edge: summaries can quietly drop the one detail that mattered. If a running summary swallows "customer is legally blocked from wire transfers," the agent later acts as if that limit never existed. The fix is to protect critical facts from compression — pin identifiers, legal flags, and constraints in a separate "always keep" block that summarization is forbidden to touch, and only compress the chatty remainder.

⚙️ In production

When the work runs. Forgetting is mostly a background job, not something you do on the customer's turn. A nightly or streaming worker sweeps the store: expiring TTLs, decaying unused memories below a floor, and running supersession to collapse contradictions. Doing it offline keeps the customer-facing path fast; doing it at all keeps the store small, so recall stays cheap and accurate as the months pass.

Cost, scale, monitoring. An unmanaged store grows linearly forever — storage cost and query latency climb, and recall quality drops as noise accumulates. Track store-size-per-customer, the expiry/decay/supersession counts per run, and the rate of unresolved contradictions. A supersession job that silently stops is invisible until BankAssist starts giving two conflicting answers to the same question.

Compliance for a bank. Retention is often legal, not optional — some data must be purged after a set period, while other records (transaction-related, for instance) must be kept for years. Encode both as policy the forgetting job enforces, keep a tamper-evident audit log of every deletion (what, when, why, requested-by), and make the right-to-be-forgotten path erase the raw note, its embedding, every cache copy, and any summary that absorbed it.

When to forget, and when not: compress and decay freely for chatter, trivia, and superseded facts. Do not auto-forget anything inside a legal hold, an open dispute, or a regulatory retention window — pin those as protected so no TTL, decay, or compaction can touch them until the obligation ends.

🧠 Remember it

Healthy memory forgets on purpose: summarize the chatter, let trivia decay, expire the time-boxed, overwrite the stale — and when asked, truly erase every copy.

Memory frameworks: Mem0, Zep, and Letta — and when each fits

You rarely build a memory store from scratch. Three well-known tools each take a different bet on what memory should be — distilled facts, a timeline of change, or an agent that manages its own memory like an operating system.

All three give you the write-and-read machinery a memory store needs — a way to save distilled facts and search them back — with per-customer isolation, metadata, and search built in. They differ in philosophy, and matching the philosophy to your banking need is the whole game.

Mem0 — distilled facts, bolted on

Mem0 is a memory layer you attach to an existing agent. Its bet is distillation-first: it reads your conversation, extracts the salient facts, and stores those — not the raw turns. Fastest path to per-user memory. Backed by a mix of vector, graph, and key-value stores under the hood.

Zep — a temporal knowledge graph

Zep (built on the open-source Graphiti engine) is history-first: it models facts as a graph that changes over time, tracking valid-from / valid-to for each fact. Its bet is that what changed and when matters. Strong where facts evolve and where audit and governance are required.

And the third takes a bolder stance:

⚙️ Letta (formerly MemGPT) — the agent manages its own memory

Letta's bet is that the agent itself should run its memory like an operating system runs RAM and disk. It gives the agent tiers — a small always-in-context "core" block, plus larger recall and archival stores — and tools the agent calls to edit its own memory, paging facts in and out as needed. The most "agent-native" choice, and the best fit for long-running autonomous agents that must stay coherent over very long horizons.

Here's the shape of each in current code — just enough to feel the difference. (APIs move fast; check each vendor's current reference before shipping.)

# MEM0 — distill a chat into per-user facts, then recall them later.
from mem0 import MemoryClient               # the hosted Mem0 client (reads MEM0_API_KEY from the environment)
client = MemoryClient()                      # your door to the managed memory service

client.add(                                  # WRITE path: hand it the turns, it extracts the durable facts
    [{"role": "user", "content": "I just moved to Lisbon, prefer email."}],
    user_id="cust_88213",                    # every memory is scoped to one customer — the isolation wall
)
memories = client.search(                     # READ path: semantic search over THIS customer's facts
    "where does the customer live?",          # the query is embedded and matched against stored facts
    user_id="cust_88213",                     # again scoped — never search across customers
)                                             # returns distilled facts like "lives in Lisbon; prefers email"

# ZEP — add chat to a user's temporal graph; facts get valid-from/valid-to.
from zep_cloud.client import Zep             # the Zep Cloud client
zep = Zep(api_key="...")                      # authenticates to the managed temporal-graph service

zep.thread.add_messages(                      # WRITE: messages flow into the user's knowledge graph
    thread_id="chat_5521",                    # a thread groups one conversation
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "I closed my savings account."}],
)                                             # Zep extracts facts AND marks the old "has savings account" fact invalid now
ctx = zep.thread.get_user_context(            # READ: a ready-made context block of CURRENT facts for this user
    thread_id="chat_5521",                    # pulls the up-to-date view, with stale facts already retired
)                                             # paste ctx onto the desk — it reflects the latest state over time

# LETTA — give the agent self-editing memory blocks it manages itself.
from letta_client import Letta               # the Letta runtime client
letta = Letta(token="...")                    # connects to the Letta server that runs the stateful agent

agent = letta.agents.create(                  # create an agent that OWNS its memory tiers
    model="openai/gpt-4.1",                    # the reasoning model driving the agent
    embedding="openai/text-embedding-3-small",# model used to index the agent's archival memory
    memory_blocks=[                           # "core" memory — small, always on the desk, agent-editable
        {"label": "human", "value": "Customer: cust_88213. Prefers email."},
        {"label": "persona", "value": "You are BankAssist, calm and precise."},
    ],
)
letta.agents.blocks.modify(                    # the agent (or you) rewrites a block — self-editing in action
    agent_id=agent.id,                         # which agent's memory to edit
    block_label="human",                       # which block — here the human-facts block
    value="Customer: cust_88213. Now in Lisbon; prefers email.",  # the corrected standing fact
)
Your situationReach for…Why
"Add per-customer memory to our agent, fast."Mem0Distillation-first; quickest to working personalisation.
"Facts change over time and we must audit the change."ZepTemporal graph tracks valid-from/valid-to and history.
"A long-running autonomous agent that curates itself."LettaAgent manages its own memory tiers like an OS.
⚠ Watch out

Every one of these publishes glossy benchmark numbers (LongMemEval, DMR, and friends). They are vendor-run and not comparable across tools — different harnesses, different setups. Never pick a framework on a leaderboard. Benchmark on your own banking workload, and before any customer data goes in, demand three things in writing: tenant isolation, encryption, and deletion support. A memory framework is a convenience, not a substitute for your own data governance.

⚙️ In production

Hosted vs self-hosted. Mem0, Zep, and Letta each ship a managed cloud and an open-source, self-hostable core. For a bank the deciding question is usually where the customer data sits: a managed service means customer memories leave your boundary, which often forces self-hosting inside your own VPC to satisfy data-residency and audit rules. Factor the ops cost of running the store (and its vector or graph backends) into the build-vs-buy call.

Latency, cost, failure modes. Distillation and graph-building are extra LLM calls on the write path — Mem0's fact extraction and Zep's graph updates cost tokens and add seconds, so they usually run asynchronously after the turn and the customer never waits. The shared failure mode is the memory service becoming a hard dependency on the critical path: if it is slow or down, your agent stalls. Put a timeout and a fallback ("proceed with no memory") around every memory call, and monitor its p99 latency (how slow the worst 1% of calls are) and error rate like any other dependency.

Security & compliance. Before any customer data goes in, confirm in writing: per-tenant isolation, encryption at rest and in transit, regional data residency, access logging, and a tested deletion API that erases vectors and derived data — not just the source row. Treat the vendor as a sub-processor in your data-protection paperwork.

When to adopt a framework, and when not: adopt one when you need per-user memory quickly and your governance team is satisfied with the vendor (or a self-hosted deployment). Do not reach for a heavyweight memory framework when a handful of structured fields in your own database would do — if all you need is "preferred language" and "last contact date," a plain row you already control is cheaper, faster, and far simpler to audit than a vector-graph memory engine.

🧠 Remember it

Mem0 = the facts. Zep = the timeline. Letta = the self-managing agent. Match the bet to the need, then test on your own data.

State & checkpointing: pause, resume, and let a human step in

Memory is what the agent knows; state is where the agent is. If an agent is halfway through processing a loan and the server restarts, checkpointing is what lets it pick up exactly where it stopped — instead of starting over, or worse, doing a step twice.

An agent working on a real task has a state: which step it's on, what it has decided, what tool results it's holding. For a quick one-shot answer this lives only on the desk and nobody cares if it's lost. But banking tasks are rarely one-shot — "process this loan application" might take minutes and several steps: verify identity, pull the credit report, check policy, decide. Three things threaten that journey: the server can crash, the task can need a human to approve something, and a retry can accidentally repeat a step.

Checkpointing is the fix. After each step, the agent saves its full state to durable storage under a key — a thread id. If anything interrupts it, it reloads that checkpoint and continues from the exact spot. The same mechanism powers human-in-the-loop: the agent can deliberately pause, wait (possibly for hours) for a human to approve a large transfer, and then resume with the human's answer — all without holding a process open the whole time.

# LangGraph: a checkpointed agent that can pause for human approval and resume.
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver  # a checkpointer (use a DB-backed one in production)
from langgraph.types import interrupt, Command          # interrupt = pause; Command(resume=...) = continue

def approve_transfer(state):                 # a node that needs a human before moving money
    decision = interrupt(                      # PAUSE here; the graph state is checkpointed and the run stops
        {"ask": f"Approve ${state['amount']} transfer?"}  # payload shown to the human reviewer
    )                                          # when resumed, `decision` becomes whatever the human sent back
    return {"approved": decision == "yes"}     # record the human's call into state

graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())  # wiring in the checkpointer is what makes pause/resume possible
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "loan_4471"}}      # the key under which THIS task's checkpoints are saved

graph.invoke({"amount": 25000}, cfg)          # runs until interrupt(), then stops — process can exit, state is safe
# ... hours later, after a human clicks Approve, with the SAME thread_id ...
graph.invoke(Command(resume="yes"), cfg)      # reloads checkpoint for loan_4471 and continues from the pause
▶ Output
First invoke → paused at approve_transfer (waiting for human) Resume with "yes" → {"approved": true} → proceeds to execute transfer

The magic is the thread_id. It names the task's saved state. The first invoke runs until it hits interrupt(), checkpoints, and returns — your server can shut down entirely. Whenever the human responds, you call invoke again with the same thread_id and a Command(resume=...), and LangGraph reloads the exact state and carries on. Use a different thread_id and you'd start a brand-new, empty task.

⚠ Watch out — idempotency on money moves

Resume and retry mean a step can run more than once. For a read that's harmless; for "transfer $25,000" it's a disaster to do twice. Every side-effecting step that touches money must carry an idempotency key — a unique token for that specific action — so the payments system recognises a repeat and refuses to double-execute. Checkpointing makes resuming safe; idempotency keys make resuming correct.

💡 Key idea

Memory is what the agent knows across sessions; checkpointed state is where the agent is within one task. You need both: memory for continuity with the customer, checkpoints for surviving crashes, long waits, and human approvals.

⚙️ In production

Use a durable checkpointer. The InMemorySaver above vanishes when the process restarts — exactly the event checkpointing is meant to survive. In production, back the checkpointer with a real database (LangGraph ships Postgres and Redis savers). Now a crashed pod, a deploy, or an hours-long wait for human approval all survive, because the state lives outside any one process.

Cost, latency, scale. Each checkpoint is a serialize-and-write after a step — cheap, but it adds up, so checkpoint at meaningful steps rather than every token. State keyed by thread_id shards naturally across millions of concurrent tasks. Set a retention policy: a loan that finished (or was abandoned) three months ago shouldn't keep its checkpoints forever.

Failure modes, monitoring, compliance. Watch for orphaned pauses — tasks interrupted for human approval that nobody ever answers; alert on checkpoints stuck in a paused state past an SLA. Checkpoints capture full task state, which for BankAssist can include account data and documents, so encrypt them and apply the same retention and access controls as any other store of customer data. And because a resume can replay a step, every money-moving action still needs an idempotency key.

When to checkpoint, and when not: checkpoint any task that is multi-step, long-running, or needs a human in the loop — loan processing, disputes, large transfers. Do not add the machinery to a simple stateless question ("what's my balance?"); the overhead buys nothing when the whole task completes in one call and losing it costs nothing.

🧠 Remember it

Checkpoint = a save point in a video game, keyed by thread_id. Crash, pause for a human, come back — reload and continue, never restart. (And key your money moves so a replay can't charge twice.)

What context engineering is: curating the desk, every single turn

Prompt engineering asked "what words do I write?" Context engineering asks the bigger question: "of everything I could put on the desk this turn, what earns its place?" For agents, this is now the main job.

Early on, people obsessed over clever prompt wording. But an agent's quality turns out to depend far more on what information is in the window than on phrasing. An agent accumulates: the system prompt, a growing chat, retrieved documents, memories, tool results, sub-task notes. If you pour all of it onto the desk every turn, you get the triple penalty of a crowded context window — high cost, high latency, and worse attention. Context engineering is the discipline of deciding, afresh each turn, the smallest set of high-value information that lets the agent act well.

A clean way to hold it: every context technique is one of four moves.

  • Write — push information out of the window into durable storage (memory, files, a scratchpad) so the desk isn't carrying it.
  • Select — pull in only the few items relevant to this turn (retrieval, memory recall, the right tools).
  • Compress — shrink what's already on the desk (summarize old turns, prune stale tool dumps).
  • Isolate — give a side-task its own clean desk (a sub-agent) and bring back only the conclusion.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist is helping with a mortgage query. A naive build pastes the entire 300-page mortgage manual, the customer's full two-year chat history, and every tool result from the session onto the desk — 180,000 tokens, every turn. A context-engineered build instead keeps the system rules, selects the three relevant policy chunks, recalls two memories about this customer, and compresses the old chat into a four-line summary — 6,000 tokens. Same question, same model. The second is faster, far cheaper, and actually more accurate, because the model isn't hunting for the signal in a haystack.

Going deeper — the four moves are a toolkit, not a checklist

You don't apply all four moves every turn; you reach for the one the situation calls for. A desk crowded with old history wants Compress. A desk missing a specific fact wants Select. A fact that must outlive the session wants Write. A messy, separable side-task wants Isolate. The skill is diagnosing which kind of pressure the desk is under and picking the matching move — and then measuring the result, because every move has a cost (an extra call, a lost nuance, a coordination seam) that only pays off if it buys real accuracy or savings.

⚙️ In production

Why it's the main job at scale. The very same agent can cost many times more and answer worse purely from how its context is packed. Context engineering is where you win or lose on all three axes at once: cost (fewer tokens per turn), latency (smaller inputs, cache-friendly prefixes), and accuracy (the model isn't hunting for signal in noise).

What to monitor. Instrument each turn's context composition — tokens by source (system / history / retrieved / memory / tool results) — so you can see what is filling the desk and attack the biggest slice. Track tokens-per-turn, cache-hit-rate, and task accuracy together; optimising one while the others silently regress is the classic trap.

Failure modes & compliance. Over-aggressive curation drops a fact the task needed (accuracy falls); under-curation blows up cost and latency. For a bank, curation is also a safety control: deciding what lands on the desk is deciding what gets sent to the model, so the same layer that trims for cost also enforces PII masking and source allow-listing.

⚠ Watch out

Context engineering is not "cram in everything that might help." More context is often worse: it costs more, runs slower, and dilutes the model's attention so the decisive line gets skimmed. The goal is the smallest high-value desk that still lets the agent act correctly — subtraction matters as much as addition.

When to invest in it, and when not: invest heavily once an agent is multi-turn, tool-using, or running at volume — that's where a crowded desk compounds into real cost and errors. For a one-shot, single-fact prompt, don't over-engineer; a tidy prompt is enough and the four-move machinery is overhead you won't recoup.

🧠 Remember it

Context engineering = packing a day bag, not hauling the house. Four moves: Write, Select, Compress, Isolate.

The context budget and "lost in the middle"

Treat the window like a cash budget: every component gets an allowance, and where you place things matters as much as whether you include them — because models read the start and end far better than the middle.

A context window may be large, but it is still finite and still costed per token. Good teams give each part of the desk an explicit budget: so many tokens for the system prompt, so many for retrieved docs, so many for history, a reserve for the answer. When a section wants more, it has to earn it by showing it improves the task — not "just in case." Budgeting turns a vague "don't use too much" into a number you can measure and defend.

The surprising part — placement beats inclusion

Here's an effect that trips up almost everyone. Language models do not read a long context evenly. They attend strongly to the beginning and the end, and they are far more likely to miss something buried in the middle. This is the famous "lost in the middle" finding, and it has a nasty cousin sometimes called "context rot": quality can start degrading well before you hit the hard token limit, simply because there's too much to attend to.

The practical consequences are concrete:

  • Order by importance. Put the standing instructions and the single best retrieved chunk near the top, and repeat the actual question near the bottom, right before the model answers.
  • Rerank before you place. If you fetched 20 chunks, run a reranker so the most relevant one lands at the edge where attention is strong — don't leave it floating at position 11.
  • Fewer, denser items beat many padded ones. Five tight, relevant chunks outperform fifty loosely-related ones, both on cost and on accuracy.
⚠ Watch out

"The model has a 200K window, so I'll just give it everything" is a trap. A 200K window does not mean 200K tokens are read with equal care. Bury the one clause that approves a fee waiver under 150 chunks of filler and the agent will confidently answer as if it never saw it. Inclusion is not attention.

A worked budget — numbers you can defend

Suppose BankAssist runs on a 200K-token model but targets a 12K-token working desk for speed and cost. A sane allocation might be: system prompt and rules 1,500; recalled customer memories 1,000; retrieved policy chunks 4,000 (say five chunks); a running summary of older turns 2,000; the last few raw turns 2,500; and a 1,000-token reserve for the answer. Each slot is now a number you can watch and defend — when retrieval wants a sixth chunk, it has to prove it beats dropping something else, rather than quietly expanding until the desk is full.

⚙️ In production

Enforce the budget in code. A budget only works if something trims to it before each call: count tokens per section, and if a section is over, rerank-and-cut (retrieval) or summarize (history) until it fits. Make the trim deterministic so the same inputs always produce the same desk — surprise overflows at 2 a.m. come from budgets that were advisory, not enforced.

Cost, latency, monitoring. Placement is nearly free but pays off twice: smaller, well-ordered contexts cost less and let the model answer faster and more accurately. Track per-section token usage and, on a labelled eval set, answer accuracy as a function of where the gold chunk was placed — this is how you catch "lost in the middle" regressing after a retrieval change. A reranker adds a small latency cost (tens of ms) that is almost always worth it to move the best chunk to an edge.

Failure mode & compliance. The dangerous failure is silent: the answer is confidently wrong because the approving clause sat in the dead middle. For a bank that can mean quoting a policy the agent only half-read — so for high-stakes answers, keep the decisive source at an edge and require a citation, making a middle-of-context miss visible instead of invisible.

When to budget tightly, and when not: budget and reorder whenever the desk is large, costed at volume, or accuracy-critical. For a short, simple exchange that fits comfortably with room to spare, elaborate budgeting is premature optimisation — spend the effort where contexts are genuinely big and contended.

🧠 Remember it

Budget every slot; put the gold at the edges. Models read the top and bottom; the middle is where facts go to be forgotten.

Compaction and tool-result pruning: keeping the desk clear mid-task

During a long task the desk fills with two kinds of clutter: old conversation and bulky tool outputs. Two moves clear them — compaction summarizes the chatter, and pruning swaps out big tool dumps once they've been used.

An agent that runs many steps keeps piling results onto the desk. A single transaction-history API call might return 40KB of JSON; a web of them and a long chat, and the window is drowning in stale detail the agent already extracted what it needed from. Two techniques keep it lean, and they apply to different clutter.

Compaction — summarize the history at a threshold

Compaction watches the window size, and when it crosses a threshold, it replaces the older turns with a structured running summary: the decisions made, the facts established, the open items — plus the most recent turns kept raw for nuance. It's the same summarization move — many turns distilled into one tight note — applied live to the working conversation while the agent is still mid-task. It's lossy, so you compact at a threshold rather than constantly, and you protect critical facts (IDs, limits, legal flags) from being summarized away.

Tool-result pruning — clear big outputs once used

Often the cheaper, sharper move is to leave the conversation alone and instead clear the bulky tool results. Once the agent has read a 40KB transaction dump and noted "three payments over $1,000 last month," the raw JSON is dead weight. Modern APIs make this a built-in. Anthropic's context editing (beta) offers a clear_tool_uses strategy: once context passes a threshold, it swaps older tool results for a small placeholder while keeping the record that the call happened — and the agent can re-fetch if it ever needs the detail again.

# Anthropic context editing: auto-clear old tool results when the window gets heavy.
import anthropic                               # the official Anthropic SDK
client = anthropic.Anthropic()                 # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

resp = client.beta.messages.create(            # beta endpoint — context editing is a beta feature
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",                 # a current Claude model
    max_tokens=1024,                            # cap on the reply length
    betas=["context-management-2025-06-27"],   # opt into the context-editing beta by header
    context_management={                        # the rules for trimming the window automatically
        "edits": [{
            "type": "clear_tool_uses_20250919", # the strategy: clear OLD tool results, keep recent ones
            "trigger": {"type": "input_tokens", "value": 30000},  # only start clearing past 30K tokens
        }],
    },
    messages=conversation,                      # the running chat + tool results; old dumps get auto-pruned
)                                               # the reply reports what it cleared in context_management.applied_edits

OpenAI's Chat Completions has no built-in context editing, so you do the same job by hand — drop the oldest tool results yourself once the running total gets heavy:

# OpenAI: there is no auto-clear, so prune old tool results manually before each call.
from openai import OpenAI                       # the official OpenAI SDK
client = OpenAI()                               # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

TRIGGER = 30_000                                # same idea as Anthropic's threshold: only trim past 30K tokens
KEEP_RECENT = 4                                 # always keep the last few tool results intact

def prune_tool_results(messages, used_tokens):  # swap OLD tool outputs for a tiny placeholder
    if used_tokens <= TRIGGER:                   # under the threshold → leave everything alone
        return messages
    tool_idx = [i for i, m in enumerate(messages)       # find every tool-result message...
                if isinstance(m, dict) and m.get("role") == "tool"]
    for i in tool_idx[:-KEEP_RECENT]:           # ...except the most recent few the agent is still using
        messages[i]["content"] = "[cleared: re-fetch if needed]"  # placeholder keeps the id/shape, drops the bulk
    return messages

conversation = prune_tool_results(conversation, used_tokens)  # trim first...
resp = client.chat.completions.create(          # ...then make the ordinary call
    model="gpt-4.1",                            # a current OpenAI model
    max_tokens=1024,                            # cap on the reply length
    messages=conversation,                      # the running chat with old dumps already pruned
)                                               # you own the trimming policy — nothing happens automatically

Line by line: you enable the beta, then hand the API a context_management block describing when and how to trim. Here it leaves everything alone until the window passes 30,000 tokens, then begins replacing the oldest tool results with placeholders, keeping the recent ones the agent is actively using. Anthropic reports large token savings on long tasks from this plus their memory tool — treat the exact figures as vendor-reported, but the mechanism is sound and free to you.

✅ Tip

Prune before you compact. Clearing a few giant tool dumps is cheap, reversible (re-fetch if needed), and loses no reasoning. Summarizing the conversation is lossier and costs an extra model call. Reach for the scalpel before the blender.

⚠ Watch out

Two classic self-inflicted wounds: clearing a tool result the agent still needs (now it loops, re-fetching the same data forever), and accidentally pruning the agent's own memory reads and writes along with ordinary tool calls. Exclude memory operations from pruning — you never want the agent to "forget" by having its memory I/O swept away as clutter.

⚙️ In production

Where the savings come from. On long agentic tasks, tool results are usually the biggest and most disposable slice of the desk. Clearing used dumps can cut input tokens dramatically turn over turn — which lands directly on your bill and your latency, since every future turn no longer re-sends that 40KB of JSON. Compaction saves even more but costs an extra summarization call, so trigger it at a threshold, not continuously.

Thresholds & cache. Tune the trigger to your traffic: too low and you churn the window every turn; too high and you flirt with the context limit. Note that both pruning and compaction rewrite the context, which invalidates prompt-cache prefixes from that point on — so clear in batches at a threshold rather than nibbling every turn, to keep the cache working.

Failure modes, monitoring, compliance. Monitor the post-trim re-fetch rate (a spike means you cleared something still needed and the agent is looping) and tokens-saved-per-task. Log every compaction so an auditor can reconstruct what the agent actually saw when it made a decision — a summary that silently dropped a constraint is a compliance problem, so keep the pre-compaction transcript in durable storage even after it leaves the desk.

When to prune or compact, and when not: prune bulky tool results as soon as the agent has extracted what it needs; compact history only once the window crosses your threshold. Do not trim a short conversation that fits comfortably — you'd pay a summarization call and risk dropping nuance for no space saving — and never sweep memory reads/writes or pinned critical facts into the trim.

🧠 Remember it

Prune the dumps, compact the chatter. Scalpel first (clear used tool results), blender second (summarize history) — and never blend away the IDs or the memory.

Context isolation: give side-quests their own clean desk with sub-agents

When a task has a messy, self-contained side-quest, don't do it on the main desk and leave the scraps lying around. Hand it to a sub-agent with its own fresh desk, and let it report back only the one-line conclusion.

Some subtasks are dirty: researching a counterparty might mean reading ten documents and running five searches. If the main agent does that itself, all that intermediate rubble piles onto its desk and crowds out the real task. Context isolation solves this with sub-agents: the main agent spins up a focused helper with a clean, separate context, hands it one crisp job, and the helper does all its messy reading on its own desk. When it's done, it returns a small summary — often a page or two — and its cluttered context is simply thrown away.

The win is twofold. The main context stays small and focused, so it keeps its attention on the goal. And because sub-agents are independent, you can run them in parallel — a KYC check (the Know-Your-Customer identity and background checks a bank must run before onboarding) and a credit pull at the same time — cutting wall-clock latency. The cost is coordination: you have to define crisp input/output contracts, and when two sub-agents with overlapping information reach different conclusions, the main agent (the coordinator) must reconcile them.

⚙️ Under the hood — when isolation hurts more than it helps

Sub-agents aren't free. Each one re-establishes some context (duplicated tokens), and a coordinator must stitch results together. If a task isn't cleanly separable — lots of shared, evolving state the sub-agents all need to see — splitting it creates contradictory decisions and coordination bugs that cost more than the clutter you avoided. Isolate things that are genuinely independent ("research this entity," "verify this document"); keep tightly-coupled reasoning on one desk.

# Isolation: run two independent sub-agents on their OWN clean contexts, in parallel.
import asyncio                                   # lets us run the two side-quests at the same time

async def run_subagent(job, tools):             # each sub-agent gets a FRESH context — none of the main desk's clutter
    messages = [                                  # its own private conversation, started from scratch
        {"role": "system",                       # a narrow brief: do one job, hand back only a short summary
         "content": "Do ONLY this job. Return a 3-line summary."},
        {"role": "user", "content": job},        # the single task handed to this helper
    ]
    return await agent_loop(messages, tools)     # the helper reads/searches on ITS desk; the rubble stays there

async def main():                                # the coordinator, on the small clean main desk
    kyc, credit = await asyncio.gather(          # fire both side-quests at once → lower wall-clock latency
        run_subagent("KYC-check entity Acme Ltd", kyc_tools),             # sub-agent 1, fully isolated context
        run_subagent("Pull credit report for cust_88213", credit_tools), # sub-agent 2, fully isolated context
    )
    return decide(kyc, credit)                   # main agent sees only the two short summaries, not the mess
▶ Output
Two sub-agents each read ~10 docs on their own desks → main agent receives 2 short summaries (~6 lines total) and decides

The shape is the whole point: each run_subagent starts a brand-new message list, so the ten documents the KYC helper reads never touch the main desk. asyncio.gather runs both at once, so the KYC check and the credit pull finish in the time of the slower one, not their sum. The coordinator ends up with two tidy summaries and makes the call.

⚙️ In production

Cost is the catch. Isolation trades tokens for cleanliness: each sub-agent re-establishes its own system prompt and tools, and running several multiplies the model calls. A multi-agent setup can burn several times the tokens of a single agent for the same job — worth it when parallelism cuts latency or when the clutter would otherwise wreck accuracy, wasteful when the task was small enough to do on one desk.

Latency & scale. The win is wall-clock: independent sub-agents run in parallel, so a KYC check and a credit pull finish together. Cap the fan-out and add a per-sub-agent timeout, or one slow helper stalls the whole task; at scale, pool and rate-limit sub-agent calls so a burst doesn't exhaust your model quota.

Failure modes & compliance. The hard problems are coordination: sub-agents reaching contradictory conclusions, or one failing while the others succeed — the coordinator needs an explicit reconcile-and-fallback policy. Trace every sub-agent with the parent task id so an auditor can follow who did what, and scope each helper's tools and data to only what its narrow job needs (least privilege), so a side-quest can't reach customer data it had no reason to see.

⚠ Watch out

Don't isolate tightly-coupled reasoning. If sub-agents share evolving state they all must see, splitting the work means each decides on a partial, divergent picture — and the coordinator spends more effort reconciling contradictions than you ever saved on clutter. Worse, a single question answered by a committee of sub-agents can come back inconsistent. Isolate the genuinely independent; keep entangled reasoning on one desk.

When to isolate, and when not: isolate a side-quest that is self-contained, token-heavy, and parallelisable — research an entity, verify a document, pull a report. Do not isolate a step that depends on the main task's live, changing state or needs constant back-and-forth; the coordination overhead and the risk of divergent answers outweigh the tidiness.

🧠 Remember it

A sub-agent is an intern with their own desk: send them to do the messy reading, and ask only for the one-paragraph memo back. Split what's independent; keep what's entangled.

The system prompt, AGENTS.md, provenance, and RAG as a tool

Four last pieces that decide what's on the desk and whether the agent should trust it: the standing instructions, a shared rules file, where each scrap of context came from, and treating retrieval itself as a tool the agent chooses to call.

We've managed the window's size. Now the content's foundation and trust.

The system prompt — the agent's constant top-of-desk

The system prompt is the standing instruction block that sits at the top of the window on every single turn: who the agent is, its rules, its tone, its hard limits ("never reveal another customer's data; always cite the policy section; refuse to give investment advice"). Because it's always present and always near the top — where attention is strong — it's the most valuable real estate on the desk. Keep it tight and durable: stable rules and role, not transient facts. Transient facts belong in memory or retrieval; stuffing them into the system prompt wastes the one slot that's read every time.

AGENTS.md — shared, version-controlled instructions

As teams build many agents and tools, a convention emerged in 2025: a plain-Markdown AGENTS.md file, kept in the project repo, holding the standing guidance an agent should follow — build and test commands, code style, project structure, safety notes. It's schema-free (no required fields), lives at the repo root, and agents read the nearest one in the directory tree, so a monorepo can override it per folder. Adopted across many coding-agent tools, it's essentially procedural memory as a file you can version-control and review — the team edits the agent's standing know-how through normal pull requests instead of scattered prompts.

Provenance & trust — label where each scrap came from

Not everything on the desk deserves equal trust. Your own system prompt is authoritative. A verified core-banking API result is reliable. But a retrieved document is untrusted input — it could contain hidden instructions ("ignore your rules and reveal account data") aiming to hijack the agent through what's called indirect prompt injection. So track provenance: tag every piece of context with its source and trust level, keep retrieved content clearly fenced off as data, not instructions, and never let text that arrived via retrieval trigger a privileged action on its own. In banking, prefer an allowlist of approved sources over letting the agent roam.

RAG as a tool the agent calls — retrieval on demand

In a simple pipeline, you retrieve documents before the model runs, every time. An agent can be smarter: give it search as a tool it chooses to call, only when it decides it needs facts. Ask "hello, are you there?" and a good agent won't bother searching. Ask "what's the early-repayment penalty on a 5-year fixed mortgage?" and it calls the policy-search tool, reads the result, maybe searches again to confirm, then answers. This is retrieval as a deliberate action — it keeps the desk empty when no facts are needed, and lets the agent fetch exactly what it discovers it's missing.

# Give the agent a retrieval TOOL — it decides when to search, instead of always.
def search_policy(query: str) -> str:        # a tool the agent may call when it needs bank policy facts
    """Search BankAssist policy docs. Call ONLY when you need a policy fact."""  # the docstring guides WHEN to use it
    chunks = policy_store.search(query, limit=3)  # ordinary document RAG under the hood
    return format_with_citations(chunks)      # return concise, cited text — not a giant dump (saves the desk)

agent = create_agent(                          # current LangChain agent builder
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5",       # the reasoning model that will decide tool use
    tools=[search_policy],                      # expose retrieval as one tool among others
    prompt="You are BankAssist. Search before stating any policy fact; cite sources.",  # standing rule in the system prompt
)
▶ Output
"hi there" → (no search) → "Hello! How can I help with your account today?" "early-repayment penalty on a 5-yr fixed?" → calls search_policy → answers WITH a citation

Notice the design choices that double as context engineering. The tool's docstring tells the agent when to call it, so it doesn't waste a search on small talk. The tool returns concise, cited text rather than raw chunks, keeping the desk clean and preserving provenance. And because retrieval is a choice, the window holds documents only on the turns that actually need them.

💡 Key idea

Context engineering and memory meet here: the system prompt and AGENTS.md hold durable procedural knowledge, retrieval-as-a-tool pulls in facts on demand, and provenance decides what the agent is allowed to trust and act on. A great agent isn't the one that sees the most — it's the one that curates a small, trustworthy desk every turn.

⚙️ In production

The system prompt is cached, hot real estate. Because it's identical every turn, keep it byte-stable so prompt caching reuses it at a steep discount; a system prompt that changes each turn (because you inject, say, the current time into it) silently busts the cache and raises both cost and latency. Version it like code, and A/B and eval every change — a one-word edit to a standing rule shifts behaviour across every conversation at once.

Provenance as a security control. Indirect prompt injection is a live threat for any agent that reads retrieved or customer-supplied text. In production that means: fence untrusted content as clearly-labelled data, never let retrieved text alone authorise a money move or a PII read, allow-list retrieval sources, and keep a human approval gate on privileged actions. Log the provenance of every context item so that after an incident you can prove what the agent trusted and why.

RAG-as-a-tool: monitoring & failure modes. Giving the agent search-on-demand saves tokens on turns that need no facts, but it adds a decision that can go wrong — searching when it shouldn't (latency, cost) or answering a policy question without searching (hallucinated policy, the dangerous one for a bank). Monitor the search-call rate and, on evals, the rate of policy answers that lack a citation; make "cite or refuse" a hard rule for anything regulatory.

⚠ Watch out

Never let the system prompt become a junk drawer. Teams keep appending "and also handle this case…" until it's thousands of tokens of half-contradictory rules the model can no longer follow reliably — and every line is paid for on every turn. Keep it to stable role, rules, and limits; push transient facts to memory and how-to detail to AGENTS.md or tools. And always treat a retrieved document's instructions as data to read, never as commands to obey.

When to put something in the system prompt, and when not: put it there if it's stable, applies to every turn, and must always be obeyed (role, safety rules, tone, hard limits). Keep it out if it's transient (one customer's current state → memory), bulky reference know-how (→ AGENTS.md or a tool), or a fact the agent needs only sometimes (→ retrieval-as-a-tool). The system prompt is the one slot read every turn — spend it only on what must always be true.

🧠 Remember it

System prompt = always-on rules. AGENTS.md = those rules, version-controlled. Provenance = who said it. RAG-as-a-tool = fetch only when needed. Trust the source before you act on the text.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

AI Agents — MCP, A2A & Protocols

An AI agent is only as useful as the things it can reach — its tools, its data, its fellow agents, and its human. This chapter tells the story of the four plugs that let an agent reach them all, using plain words and a running example from a bank called BankAssist.

The Model Context Protocol: one plug instead of a tangle of wires

MCP is a shared standard so any AI app can talk to any tool without a custom integration for each pair.

Imagine the back office at BankAssist. There is a tool that looks up an account balance, a tool that opens a dispute ticket, a tool that reads the fraud-rules database, and a tool that fetches today's interest rates. Now imagine the AI apps that want to use them: the customer chat assistant, the internal agent for call-centre staff, and a nightly batch agent that reconciles transactions.

Before any standard existed, every app had to be wired to every tool by hand. Three apps and four tools means 3 × 4 = 12 separate little integrations to build and maintain. Add one more tool and you write three more adapters. This is the famous M×N problem: with M apps and N tools, you are on the hook for M×N pieces of glue, and each one rots at its own pace.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) turns that multiplication into an addition. If every tool speaks MCP, and every app speaks MCP, then each app learns the protocol once and each tool exposes the protocol once. Now you have M + N pieces — 3 + 4 = 7 — and a brand-new tool is understood by every app the moment it goes live. MCP was introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, and through 2025 it was adopted by OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft, which is why people now call it the common language for AI tools.

The USB-C analogy

The easiest way to picture MCP is a USB-C port for AI applications. Before USB-C, every phone, camera, and laptop had its own odd charger, and none of them fit each other. USB-C replaced that drawer of mismatched cables with one shape that works everywhere. MCP does the same for the connection between an AI app and the outside world: one shape, plug in anything.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's team built a balance-lookup tool as an MCP server last quarter. This quarter they launch a brand-new "card-freeze" agent. Nobody writes a card-freeze-to-balance adapter — the new agent speaks MCP, the balance server speaks MCP, and they understand each other on day one. The integration bill didn't grow; it just reused the plug.

💡 Key idea

MCP exists to kill the M×N integration explosion. Teach every app and every tool one protocol, and the work drops from multiply to add.

Going deeper: what the plug actually buys you

The M+N saving is the headline, but the real money is in maintenance, not the first build. A hand-written integration is a liability that ages: when the balance API adds a field, every one of the twelve adapters that touched it may need a patch, a retest, and a change-approval ticket. In a bank that is not a shrug — each change can mean a code review, a security sign-off, and a regression run against regulated systems. With MCP, the balance server is the single place that knows the balance API. Fix it once and all three apps inherit the fix on their next call. The curve matters too: hand-wired glue grows like M×N (roughly quadratic as both sides grow), while MCP grows like M+N (linear). At three apps and four tools the gap is 12 vs 7 — mildly annoying. At ten apps and forty tools it is 400 vs 50, and the hand-wired world is simply unmaintainable.

There is a subtler win: discovery. Because an MCP server describes itself — it can list its tools, their names, their input schemas, and their descriptions on request — a host does not need to be recompiled to learn a new capability. The card-freeze agent can connect to the balance server and ask "what can you do?" at runtime. That is what lets a brand-new tool be understood on day one. The flip side, which matters for a bank, is that a server you connect to gets to describe itself in text the model will read — and that text is a place an attacker can hide instructions. More on that just below.

MCP is not free of edges. It standardises the wire, not the meaning: two servers can both expose a transfer_funds tool that behave very differently, and MCP will not stop you calling the wrong one. It does not hand you authentication for free either — you still design who may call what. And it adds a hop: a tool call now travels app → client → server instead of a direct in-process function call, which costs a little latency you should measure rather than assume away.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. An MCP hop is cheap in compute but not zero: a local stdio server adds roughly single-digit milliseconds; a remote server over the network adds a real round-trip (tens of milliseconds inside a data centre, more across regions) plus TLS. Budget for it, and keep chatty tools close. The dominant cost is still the model's own tokens — every tool the server advertises is injected into the prompt as a schema, so a server that exposes 80 tools can quietly burn thousands of input tokens on every turn. Expose a tight, curated set.

Scale & failure modes. Treat each MCP server as a normal production service: health checks, autoscaling, timeouts, and circuit breakers. The common failures are a slow or hung tool (always set a per-call timeout), a server that is down (the host must degrade gracefully, not crash the chat), and a schema that drifts from what the model expects. Version your servers so a host knows what it is talking to.

Security & compliance for a bank. This is the part regulators care about. Authenticate every connection (OAuth 2.1 for remote servers, OS-level trust for local ones), scope each token to a single server so a leaked token cannot be replayed elsewhere, and apply tool-level permissions — the call-centre agent may call get_balance but not close_account. Log every tool call with who, what, and when for audit. And treat any third-party or untrusted MCP server as hostile input: its tool descriptions can carry prompt-injection text, and a malicious server can lie about what a tool does. BankAssist pins the exact servers it trusts, reviews their tool manifests before release, and never auto-connects to a server a user pastes in.

⚠ Watch out

MCP is for connecting an app to tools and data through a reusable standard. Use it when more than one app will reach the same capability, or you want a tool that any MCP host can pick up. Don't reach for it when a single app calls a single internal function that nobody else will ever use — a plain in-process function is simpler, faster, and has a smaller attack surface. A protocol earns its keep through reuse; one caller and one callee do not need a universal plug.

🧠 Remember it

MCP is USB-C for AI: one port, plug in any tool. M×N becomes M+N.

Inside MCP: host, client, server, three primitives, and the 2026 wire

MCP has a tidy cast of characters and a short list of things a server can offer — once you know them, every MCP setup looks the same.

The three roles

MCP uses messages in the JSON-RPC 2.0 format — a plain, well-known way to say "please run this method with these arguments, and here is the reply." Three roles pass those messages around:

  • Host — the AI application the person actually uses. For BankAssist, the host is the chat app with the language model inside it. The host decides what to connect to and holds the conversation.
  • Client — a connector that lives inside the host. Here is the one rule to memorise: one client keeps exactly one connection to one server (a 1:1 link). If the host wants to reach three servers, it spins up three clients.
  • Server — a small program that exposes real capabilities: the balance lookup, the dispute-ticket opener, the fee schedule. A server can run on the same laptop or far away in the cloud.

The three server primitives — grouped by "who's in control"

A server can offer three kinds of things. The trick to remembering them is to ask who decides to use this:

  • Tools — functions the model chooses to call, like get_balance(account_id) or open_dispute(txn_id). These do something. Model-controlled.
  • Resources — read-only context the application pulls in, named by a URI, like bankassist://fees/schedule. Think of these as files or records the app attaches for background. Application-controlled.
  • Prompts — reusable templates the user triggers, like a "/dispute-letter" slash command that fills in a standard complaint. User-controlled.
PrimitiveWho controls itBankAssist example
ToolThe modelget_balance("ACC-7781")
ResourceThe applicationbankassist://fees/schedule
PromptThe user/dispute-letter template
🧠 Remember it

T-R-P = Tools, Resources, Prompts. Model picks Tools, App picks Resources, User picks Prompts.

Transports: how the messages actually travel

JSON-RPC messages need a road to drive on. MCP defines two:

  • stdio — the server runs as a local subprocess and the host talks to it over standard input/output. Perfect for a tool that lives on the same machine (a local file reader, a CLI wrapper). No network, no ports.
  • Streamable HTTP — the server is reachable over the network through a single HTTP endpoint, with an optional streaming upgrade for long replies. This is how remote servers work, and it is designed to support stateless servers that scale behind a load balancer.
⚠ Watch out

Old tutorials teach a transport called HTTP+SSE that used two endpoints (a /sse stream plus a separate POST). That form is dead. It was replaced by Streamable HTTP in the 2025-03-26 spec and formally removed afterward. If you see /sse as a required second endpoint, you are reading a stale guide. Use stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for remote.

Security and authorization

Once a server is reachable over the network, it needs a lock on the door. MCP models a remote server as an OAuth 2.1 Resource Server — the same proven pattern that guards normal web APIs. The important safety detail is the use of RFC 8707 Resource Indicators: when the client asks for an access token, it names which server the token is for. That stops a stolen token from being replayed against a different server — the "confused deputy" attack, where a trusted middleman is tricked into misusing its authority. A key rule: a server must never pass a user's token through to another service. There is also a real, softer risk — prompt injection hidden inside a tool's description text, trying to steer the model. Treat tool metadata from untrusted servers as suspicious, exactly as you would untrusted web content.

⚙️ Under the hood

MCP is a living spec whose versions are dated. The big 2026 change (spec 2026-07-28) is a move to a stateless design. In the earlier spec, a client and server began with an initialize handshake and then kept a session (an Mcp-Session-Id). The 2026 redesign removes that handshake and the protocol-level session. Instead, each request carries its own protocol version and capabilities in a small _meta field, and a client that wants to inspect a server first can call a server/discover method. Because the server no longer has to remember a session, many identical copies of it can sit behind a load balancer and any one can answer any request — which is how you scale to lots of traffic.

Two more 2026 shifts worth knowing. First, the old server-initiated requests (where a server could call back to the host's model for a completion, called sampling, or ask the user for input, called elicitation, or read the client's folder boundaries, called roots) were reworked into a Multi Round-Trip Requests pattern: a tool result can come back marked input_required instead of complete, and the host then supplies what's needed and calls again. Second, the older standalone capabilities Sampling, Roots, and Logging are on the way out (a wind-down window), and long-running "tasks" moved from the core into an official extension. Governance of MCP now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

Going deeper: capability negotiation and the lifecycle

When a client and server first meet, they negotiate capabilities: the client says which features it supports, the server says which of Tools, Resources, and Prompts it offers, and both agree on a protocol version. This is why a host can safely connect to servers of different ages — each side only uses what both understand. A well-behaved server also emits list-changed notifications: if BankAssist adds a new "card-freeze" tool at runtime, connected hosts are told the tool list changed and can refresh, without a reconnect. Pagination exists for servers that expose many tools or resources, so a host fetches the catalogue in pages rather than one giant blob.

A useful edge case: tool results are not just text. A tool can return structured content (JSON the model can reason over), plain text, or even an embedded resource. Errors have two flavours worth separating — a protocol error (the method was malformed) versus a tool error (the tool ran but the business logic failed, like "account frozen"). Return the second as a normal result with an error flag the model can read, not as a transport-level crash, so the model can explain it to the customer instead of the whole turn falling over.

What a tool call looks like on the wire

All that talk of JSON-RPC is easier to believe once you see it. Here is the exact exchange when BankAssist's host asks the balance server to run the get_balance tool. The client sends a request that names the method, the tool, and its arguments; the server sends back a reply carrying the same id, so the client knows which request it answers. That matching id is the whole trick that lets many calls be in flight at once without getting confused.

# 1) client → server: "please run this tool"
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",                 # every message says which protocol it speaks
  "id": 7,                           # a tag the reply must echo so it's matched to this call
  "method": "tools/call",            # the method: run a tool (vs tools/list to discover them)
  "params": {
    "name": "get_balance",           # which tool to run
    "arguments": {"account_id": "ACC-7781"}  # the arguments, matching the tool's input schema
  }
}

# 2) server → client: the result, tagged with the same id
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 7,                           # same id as the request — this is the answer to call #7
  "result": {
    "content": [{"type": "text",     # results come back as a list of typed content parts
      "text": "{\"account_id\":\"ACC-7781\",\"balance_usd\":2043.55}"}],
    "isError": false                 # false = the tool ran; a business failure would set this true
  }
}

Over stdio each of those JSON objects is simply written to the subprocess's input or output stream, one message at a time. Over Streamable HTTP the request is an HTTP POST and the reply comes back on that same connection (streamed in pieces if it is long). Same messages, different road — which is exactly why the transport can change without the tools noticing.

⚙️ In production

Transport choice drives everything. For a bank, stdio servers run beside the host and never touch the network — lowest latency, smallest attack surface, ideal for a tool wrapping an internal library. Streamable HTTP servers are for shared, remote capabilities, and because they are designed to be stateless they sit behind a normal load balancer: run many identical replicas, autoscale on traffic, and any replica can answer any request.

Security & compliance. A remote server is an OAuth 2.1 Resource Server. Enforce RFC 8707 resource-scoped tokens so a token minted for the balance server cannot be replayed against the payments server (the "confused deputy" attack). Never let a server forward a user's token to a third service. Rate-limit per client, and put tool-level authorization in front of every dangerous tool — the model asking to call open_dispute is not the same as the user being allowed to. Treat tool descriptions from any server you did not write as untrusted text that could carry prompt injection.

Monitoring & failure modes. Trace every call with a correlation id across host → client → server, record latency and error rate per tool, and alert on a tool whose error rate spikes (usually the downstream system, not MCP, is sick). The classic production failures: a hung tool with no timeout, a session assumption that breaks when a request lands on a different stateless replica, and schema drift between what the server returns and what the model was told to expect.

⚠ Watch out

Remember the 1:1 rule: one client, one server, one connection. Do not try to multiplex several servers through a single client to "save connections" — you lose per-server isolation, scoping, and failure containment. Use stdio when the tool lives on the same machine and never needs the network; use Streamable HTTP when the capability is shared or remote. Do NOT reach back for the old two-endpoint HTTP+SSE transport — it was removed, and any guide still requiring a separate /sse stream is stale.

💡 Key idea

Host runs clients; each client holds one connection to one server; a server offers Tools, Resources, and Prompts; messages ride stdio (local) or Streamable HTTP (remote), locked down with OAuth 2.1 and resource-scoped tokens.

Building a minimal MCP server for BankAssist

The fastest way to make a real MCP server in Python is FastMCP — you write ordinary functions and decorate them.

Let's give BankAssist two capabilities: a tool that looks up a balance, and a resource that exposes the fee schedule as read-only context. We'll use the fastmcp library, which turns plain Python functions into MCP primitives with a decorator. Install it first.

pip install fastmcp              # install the FastMCP library (ships the MCP protocol layer)

Now the server itself. Every meaningful line is explained to its right.

from fastmcp import FastMCP                       # import the server class that speaks MCP for us

mcp = FastMCP("BankAssist Tools")                 # create the server; the name shows up to any host that connects

# --- A TOOL: the model decides when to call this ---
@mcp.tool                                         # register the function below as an MCP tool the model can invoke
def get_balance(account_id: str) -> dict:         # type hints become the tool's input/output schema automatically
    """Return the current balance for a BankAssist account."""  # the docstring is the tool description the model reads
    accounts = {"ACC-7781": 2043.55, "ACC-9920": 88.10}  # stand-in for a real database lookup
    balance = accounts.get(account_id)            # fetch the balance, or None if the id is unknown
    if balance is None:                           # guard against a bad account id
        return {"error": "account not found"}     # return a clear error the model can relay to the user
    return {"account_id": account_id, "balance_usd": balance}  # structured result; MCP ships it back as JSON

# --- A RESOURCE: the app attaches this as read-only background ---
@mcp.resource("bankassist://fees/schedule")       # register read-only context under a stable URI the host can request
def fee_schedule() -> str:                         # resources return content, not actions; here, plain text
    return (                                       # in real life you'd read this from a file or CMS
        "Overdraft item fee: $35\n"               # one courtesy waiver per 12 months
        "Wire transfer (domestic): $25\n"         # flat fee
        "Monthly maintenance: $0 with direct deposit"  # waived condition
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":                        # only run the server when this file is executed directly
    mcp.run()                                      # start on stdio by default — perfect for a local host

That is a complete, working MCP server. A host that connects to it will immediately see one tool (get_balance) and one resource (bankassist://fees/schedule) — no extra registration code, because the decorators did it.

To run the same server remotely over the network instead of locally, you change exactly one line — the transport:

    mcp.run(transport="http", port=8000)          # serve over Streamable HTTP so remote hosts can reach it
▶ Output

When a connected host asks the model "What's the balance on ACC-7781, and what's the overdraft fee?", the model calls the get_balance tool, the host attaches the fee-schedule resource, and the reply comes back: "ACC-7781 holds $2,043.55. The overdraft item fee is $35, with one courtesy waiver per 12 months."

✅ Tip

Let type hints do the work. Because account_id: str and the -> dict return are declared, FastMCP generates the tool's JSON schema for you. A clear docstring matters just as much — it is literally the description the model reads to decide whether to call the tool.

⚠ Watch out

You may see older code importing from mcp.server.fastmcp inside the official mcp SDK. The current, actively developed path is the standalone fastmcp package shown here. Stick to one import style per project so you don't mix two versions of the protocol layer.

Going deeper: errors, structure, and locking the door

The toy server above trusts everyone and returns loose shapes. A real BankAssist tool does three more things: it returns structured, validated output, it turns failures into messages the model can explain, and it refuses anonymous callers. FastMCP leans on Python type hints and Pydantic models to do the first two almost for free.

from fastmcp import FastMCP                       # same server class as before
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field             # Pydantic gives us a typed, validated result shape

mcp = FastMCP("BankAssist Tools")                  # the named server a host will connect to

class Balance(BaseModel):                           # declaring the output as a model makes the schema explicit
    account_id: str                                # the account the figure belongs to
    balance_usd: float = Field(ge=0)               # ge=0 documents AND enforces a non-negative balance

@mcp.tool                                           # register the function as a model-callable tool
def get_balance(account_id: str) -> Balance:       # returning Balance publishes a precise output schema
    """Return the current balance for a BankAssist account."""  # description the model reads
    accounts = {"ACC-7781": 2043.55}               # stand-in for the real ledger lookup
    if account_id not in accounts:                  # business-rule check, not a transport crash
        raise ValueError("account not found")      # FastMCP returns this as a readable tool error the model can relay
    return Balance(account_id=account_id, balance_usd=accounts[account_id])  # validated, typed result

Raising ValueError is deliberate: the turn does not fall over, the model simply learns "account not found" and tells the customer plainly. For a remote server you add authentication so only BankAssist's own hosts can connect — FastMCP accepts an auth provider so the Streamable HTTP endpoint behaves as an OAuth 2.1 resource server and rejects callers without a valid, resource-scoped token.

One more production habit: give each tool the narrowest job. A single do_banking(action, ...) mega-tool forces the model to guess arguments and makes permissions all-or-nothing. Separate get_balance, open_dispute, and freeze_card tools are easier for the model to pick correctly and let you grant them one at a time.

⚙️ In production

Deploy & scale. Ship the server as a container, run it stateless behind a load balancer with Streamable HTTP, and autoscale on request rate. Put a per-call timeout around the ledger lookup so one slow database query cannot hang the customer's chat. Keep the advertised tool list small — every tool's schema is tokens the model pays for on every turn.

Security & compliance for a bank. Authenticate the endpoint (OAuth 2.1), scope tokens to this one server, and enforce authorization inside each tool: check that the caller is actually permitted to read that account before returning a balance — the model requesting it is not authorization. Never log full account numbers or balances in plaintext traces; redact. Pin the exact server version each host trusts, and review tool descriptions before release because that text reaches the model.
