Monitoring & failure modes. Emit a structured log per tool call (tool name, caller, latency, outcome, correlation id) and alert on error-rate spikes, which almost always mean the downstream system is unwell rather than MCP itself. Watch for schema drift after a deploy — a changed return shape the model was not told about is a silent source of wrong answers.

⚠ Watch out

Besides the import gotcha above, don't let a tool's docstring lie — the model trusts it as the tool's contract, and a vague or stale description is the number-one cause of the model calling the wrong tool. Build an MCP server when a capability will be reused by more than one host or you want it to be discoverable. Skip it when one app needs one private function — call the function directly and save yourself a network service to secure, scale, and monitor.

🧠 Remember it

@mcp.tool = a verb the model can do. @mcp.resource = a noun the app can read. Write the function, add the sticker.

A2A: letting agents work together as peers

Where MCP connects an agent to its tools, A2A connects an agent to another agent.

BankAssist is growing up. The customer-facing assistant is good at conversation, but a tricky fraud case needs a specialist: a separate Fraud Investigation agent, built by a different team, maybe on a different framework, maybe running on different servers. How does one agent hand work to another when neither can see inside the other's code?

That is the job of A2A (Agent-to-Agent), a protocol announced by Google in April 2025 and now governed by the Linux Foundation, with its stable v1.0 spec in place. The core idea: agents are opaque peers. The customer agent does not get to reach into the fraud agent's tools or memory. It simply sends a request and gets results back, the way two companies exchange a work order without sharing their internal systems.

Discovery: the Agent Card

Before you can delegate to an agent, you have to find it and learn what it can do. Every A2A agent publishes an Agent Card — a small JSON "business card" — at a well-known address: /.well-known/agent-card.json. The card lists the agent's identity, its endpoint URL, the skills it offers, the transports it supports, and how to authenticate. The card can be cryptographically signed so you can trust it is genuine.

{
  "name": "Fraud Investigation Agent",            # human-readable identity of the peer agent
  "description": "Analyses suspicious transactions and recommends holds.",  # what it's for
  "url": "https://fraud.bankassist.internal/a2a",  # endpoint where tasks are sent
  "version": "1.0.0",                              # version of this particular agent
  "skills": [                                       # the discrete things it can be asked to do
    {
      "id": "investigate-transaction",             # stable id a caller references
      "name": "Investigate a transaction",         # friendly label
      "description": "Score a transaction for fraud risk and advise."  # helps the caller choose
    }
  ],
  "securitySchemes": { "oauth2": { "type": "oauth2" } }  # how a caller must authenticate
}
⚠ Watch out

Older material points to /.well-known/agent.json and uses method names like tasks/send. Those are pre-1.0. The current discovery path is /.well-known/agent-card.json. If a tutorial also claims A2A is JSON-RPC only, it predates v1.0's multiple transport bindings (see below).

The nouns: Task, Message, Part, Artifact

A2A has a small, clear vocabulary. Picture the customer agent asking the fraud agent to look into a charge:

  • Task — the unit of work, with a unique id and a lifecycle. A task can be quick or run for a long time (fraud review might take minutes). It has a status you can poll.
  • Message — one turn in the back-and-forth, tagged with a role of user or agent. The caller sends a message; the specialist replies with messages.
  • Part — the actual content inside a message or artifact: a chunk of text, a file, a link, or structured data, each with a media type. One message can carry several parts.
  • Artifact — a tangible output of the task, such as the finished fraud report. Artifacts have an id and can be streamed back piece by piece as they're produced.

A reply is one of two shapes: a quick Message for an immediate answer, or a Task when the work will take a while and needs tracking.

⚙️ Under the hood

A2A v1.0 offers three equivalent transport bindings that all carry the same operations: JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTPS, gRPC, and HTTP+JSON/REST. An Agent Card can advertise several endpoints in priority order, so a caller picks the one it speaks. Security is standard enterprise fare: API keys, HTTP Bearer tokens, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, or mutual TLS. Because agents stay opaque, you can mix vendors and frameworks freely — the fraud agent could be built in a totally different stack and the customer agent would never know or care.

Going deeper: the task lifecycle and getting results back

A Task is not fire-and-forget; it moves through a lifecycle the caller can follow: submitted → working → then one of completed, failed, canceled, or input-required when the specialist needs more from the caller to continue. Because fraud review can take minutes, A2A gives the caller three ways to receive results. It can stream them over Server-Sent Events, watching status and artifacts arrive live. It can poll with a simple "get task by id" call, which suits a batch job that checks back later. Or it can register a push notification webhook so the fraud agent calls back when the task finishes — the right choice for work that outlives the original connection, such as a review that runs overnight.

Two edge cases matter in a bank. First, long-running tasks must survive disconnects — the task id is the handle, so the customer agent can drop the connection and reattach to the same task later. Second, input-required is how an opaque peer asks a question without breaking opacity: the fraud agent might pause and ask "confirm the cardholder's travel status?" and the task simply waits in that state until the caller supplies a message. Design your callers to handle that state, not just success and failure.

⚙️ In production

Latency & cost. A2A hops are coarse-grained — you are delegating a whole task, not a single function call — so the cost that dominates is the callee agent's own model and tool usage, which can be large and variable. Set deadlines on tasks, prefer streaming or push callbacks over tight polling (polling every second across thousands of tasks is its own load problem), and cache an agent's card rather than refetching it on every call.

Scale & failure modes. The classic failures are a peer that is slow or down (set task timeouts and a fallback path — a human queue, say), a card that advertises a skill the agent no longer supports (validate against the live card), and a webhook that never fires (always keep a poll-based reconciliation sweep as a backstop). Treat another team's agent as an external dependency with an SLA, because that is exactly what it is.

Security & compliance for a bank. Verify the Agent Card's signature before trusting it, authenticate every task with enterprise schemes (OAuth 2.0, OIDC, or mutual TLS), and authorize per skill — the customer agent may invoke investigate-transaction but not some admin skill the fraud agent also exposes. Because agents are opaque, you cannot see how the peer reaches its decision, so log the full task trail — card used, skill called, messages, returned artifact, and its signature — for audit and dispute handling. Keep the PII inside a task to the minimum the peer actually needs.

⚠ Watch out

A2A and MCP are not interchangeable. Use A2A when you are delegating a whole piece of work to a separate, autonomous agent — often built by another team or vendor, with its own reasoning you don't control. Do NOT use A2A to reach your own tools or data; that is MCP's job, and wrapping a database call as a fake "agent" adds a network peer, a card, and a task lifecycle for nothing. A rule of thumb: if the other side thinks, it's A2A; if it just executes, it's MCP.

🏦 Picture this

A customer disputes a $900 charge at 2 a.m. BankAssist's chat agent reads the Fraud agent's card, sees the investigate-transaction skill, and sends a Message that opens a Task. The Fraud agent works for ninety seconds, streaming "checking device history… checking merchant… scoring," then returns an Artifact: a signed report recommending a temporary hold. The chat agent relays the decision. Two agents, two teams, one clean handoff.

🧠 Remember it

A2A agents are opaque peers passing work orders. Find them by their card; the job is a Task, the chatter is Messages, the deliverable is an Artifact.

The wider protocol family: ACP, AG-UI, and AP2

Around MCP and A2A sits a small family of protocols — one that merged away, and two newer ones for talking to users and moving money.

ACP — merged into A2A

You will still read about ACP (Agent Communication Protocol), a REST-first agent protocol from IBM Research built for its BeeAI project. Here is the current reality so you don't go down a dead end: ACP has merged into A2A under the Linux Foundation. IBM announced the merge in 2025, the ACP repository was archived read-only with a migration guide, and BeeAI now runs on A2A. A2A v1.0's HTTP+JSON/REST binding covers the REST-first style ACP cared about. For anything new, use A2A.

⚠ Watch out

"ACP" is an overloaded name. The IBM one is retired into A2A. There is an unrelated "Agent Client Protocol" (editor-to-agent, from the Zed editor) and the old academic "Agent Communication Protocols." If a source treats IBM's ACP as a live competitor to A2A, it is out of date.

AG-UI — the agent-to-user layer

MCP and A2A both happen in the back office. But a customer sees a screen. AG-UI (Agent-User Interaction Protocol), launched by CopilotKit in May 2025, is the plug between an agent backend and a frontend. It is event-based: the agent streams a series of standard JSON events to the UI — text arriving word by word, "I'm calling a tool now," a patch to shared state, lifecycle signals — usually over SSE/HTTP. That is what powers a BankAssist chat window where you watch the answer type itself out, see "checking your balance…" appear as the tool runs, and even approve an action mid-stream (human-in-the-loop). It ships with JS and Python SDKs and adapters for the common agent frameworks.

AP2 — the agent-to-payments layer

The newest plug handles money. AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol), introduced by Google in September 2025 with 60+ partners (Mastercard, PayPal, American Express, and more), is an open protocol layered on top of A2A and MCP. Its whole purpose is to answer one nervous question: "How do we prove a human actually authorized this purchase the agent is about to make?"

The answer is Mandates — cryptographically signed credentials that form a tamper-evident audit trail. There are three:

  • Intent Mandate — what the user authorized in general, e.g. "renew my travel insurance before it lapses, under $200." For agent-acts-while-you-sleep cases it pre-encodes the rules (price caps, timing).
  • Cart Mandate — the user approves the exact assembled cart, locking the items and the price. If a human is present, they sign it; if delegated, the agent may generate it once the Intent conditions are met.
  • Payment Mandate — sent to the payment network to signal that an agent is involved and to carry the proof, linking the Intent and the Cart.
🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist customer tells the agent: "Pay my electricity bill each month, but never more than $150 without asking me." That rule becomes an Intent Mandate, signed. When the $118 bill arrives, the agent builds a Cart Mandate for that exact amount, and because it's under the cap, the matching Payment Mandate goes to the network with proof the human pre-authorized it. If next month's bill is $240, the agent must stop and ask — the mandate didn't cover it. Non-repudiable, and auditable after the fact.

Going deeper: how the newer plugs are actually built

AG-UI keeps its surface tiny on purpose: every message is a small JSON event that extends one base shape (a type, an optional timestamp, an optional raw payload). There are roughly sixteen event types in a handful of families — lifecycle (run started, finished, error), streaming text deltas, tool-call signals, and state snapshots/deltas that keep the frontend and agent looking at the same shared state. The frontend finds an agent through the runtime, runs it with a POST, and the runtime streams those events back, usually as SSE. That event stream is what lets a BankAssist user watch an answer type itself, see "checking your balance…", and approve an action mid-flight.

AP2's mandates are not just "signed blobs." They are built as W3C Verifiable Credentials — a standard, portable format for a digitally signed claim that anyone can check. In practice they are encoded as SD-JWT (a signed token that lets the holder reveal only the fields it chooses to), with key binding (a cryptographic link between the token and the holder's private key, so only the real holder can present it), and signed with ECDSA P-256 (a common, well-trusted signature algorithm). That choice is what makes them tamper-evident and non-repudiable: change one character and the signature breaks, so the signed mandate proves exactly who authorized what, and the key binding stops anyone else from reusing it. The three mandates chain together — the Payment Mandate references the Cart, which traces back to the Intent — so an auditor can replay the whole authorization story from one signed thread. AP2 rides on top of A2A (and works with MCP), so the payment authorization can travel across agent hops without any agent having to hold raw card details.

⚙️ In production

Where the cost and risk sit. AG-UI's load is a long-lived streaming connection per active user — size your frontend gateway for many concurrent SSE streams, send heartbeats, and handle reconnects so a dropped Wi-Fi signal doesn't lose the conversation. AP2's cost is governance, not compute: you are now holding cryptographic evidence that money was authorized, so key management, signature verification, and secure storage of mandates become first-class concerns.

Security & compliance for a bank. For AP2, verify every mandate signature before acting, never let an agent exceed the signed Intent (the $150 cap is enforced, not advisory), and retain the signed mandate chain as your audit trail for chargebacks and regulators — it is designed precisely to answer "did a human authorize this?" after the fact. For AG-UI, remember the event stream reaches the customer's browser: never stream secrets or internal reasoning you wouldn't show the user, and make human-in-the-loop approvals real server-side checks, not just UI prompts. The ecosystem moves fast — ACP already folded into A2A — so pin versions and avoid betting a core flow on a protocol still in early draft.

⚠ Watch out

Pick the plug by direction. Use AG-UI when you need to show live agent progress to a human and take input mid-stream; use AP2 when an agent moves money and you must prove human authorization. Do NOT hand-roll your own streaming or payment-authorization scheme because it feels quicker — you will reinvent reconnection, event ordering, and non-repudiation badly. And do NOT start a new build on IBM's ACP: it has merged into A2A, so use A2A instead.

💡 Key idea

The family divides by direction: MCP reaches tools, A2A reaches agents, AG-UI reaches the user's screen, and AP2 reaches the payment network with signed mandates as the receipt. ACP is no longer separate — it lives inside A2A.

🧠 Remember it

ACP folded into A2A. AG-UI = talk to the user. AP2 = pay, with signed mandates as the receipt.

The stack view: four directions, one agent

Each protocol owns one direction an agent reaches — put them together and you can see the whole machine.

It's easy to lose the forest for the trees, so here is the one picture that ties everything together. An AI agent reaches outward along four axes, and a different piece owns each one:

  • MCP is vertical — tools and data. It connects a single agent down to its capabilities: the balance lookup, the fee schedule, the fraud database. This is the agent reaching for its instruments.
  • A2A is horizontal — other agents. It connects an agent sideways to its peers: the customer agent delegating to the fraud agent. This is teamwork between equals.
  • Memory is temporal — across time. It connects the agent to its own past: what this customer asked last week, what was decided, what to remember. This is continuity.
  • Context engineering is the glue. It is the craft of deciding what to put in front of the model at each step — which tool results, which retrieved facts, which memories, how much — so the limited space is spent on what matters. Without it, the other three just flood the model with noise.

In plain terms: MCP and A2A and memory are sources; context engineering is the editor that decides what actually reaches the model's attention for the next decision.

MCP (vertical)

Connects one agent to tools, data, and read-only context. Write a tool once; any MCP host can use it. Think "reach down for an instrument."

A2A (horizontal)

Connects agents to each other as opaque peers that pass Tasks and return Artifacts. Mix vendors and frameworks. Think "hand work to a colleague."

These two combine neatly: an A2A agent very often uses MCP internally to reach its own tools. The fraud agent is an A2A peer to the customer agent, and at the same time it's an MCP host wiring itself to the fraud-rules database. Horizontal and vertical, working at once.

⚠ Watch out

Don't force one protocol to do another's job. Reaching your own tools? That's MCP, not A2A. Delegating to a separate specialist agent? That's A2A, not a giant MCP tool. Showing live progress to a human? That's AG-UI. Taking a payment? AP2. Using the wrong plug is where brittle, confusing systems come from.

Going deeper: how the four combine in one request

Follow a single BankAssist request and watch all four reaches fire. A customer opens the chat and types "something's wrong with a $900 charge." The agent streams its thinking to the screen over AG-UI ("looking into this…"). It pulls the customer's recent history from memory so it doesn't ask what it already knows. It reaches down through MCP to read the transaction and the fraud-rules resource. It decides the case needs a specialist and reaches sideways through A2A to the fraud agent, opening a task. Meanwhile context engineering is the quiet editor deciding, at each step, which of all that — which memories, which tool results, which A2A artifact — actually goes into the next prompt, because the model's attention is finite and stuffing everything in makes it worse, not better. The agent never holds all four sources in the prompt at once; it curates.

The important design insight is layering: these protocols compose rather than compete. An A2A peer almost always runs MCP internally to reach its own tools; an AP2 payment flow rides on top of A2A; AG-UI wraps the whole thing so a human can watch and approve. You rarely choose "MCP or A2A" — a mature system speaks all of them at once, each on its own axis.

⚙️ In production

Cost, latency & scale. The expensive axes are the model tokens that context engineering governs and the coarse A2A hops that invoke whole peer agents; MCP and AG-UI are comparatively cheap per call but add up under load. Budget per axis separately: cap the context size, set deadlines on A2A tasks, keep MCP tool catalogues lean, and size the AG-UI gateway for concurrent streams. A failure on one axis should degrade, not collapse — if the fraud agent (A2A) is down, the chat (AG-UI) should still answer from MCP and memory and queue the review.

Security, compliance & monitoring for a bank. Each axis needs its own controls: OAuth 2.1 and resource-scoped tokens plus tool permissions for MCP, signed cards and per-skill authorization for A2A, verified mandates for AP2, and "never stream secrets" for AG-UI. Tie them together with a single correlation id so one customer request is traceable end to end — screen event, memory read, tool call, peer task, and any payment mandate — which is exactly the audit trail a regulator will ask for. Monitor each axis's latency and error rate independently; a spike usually localises the fault to one plug.

💡 Key idea

MCP (tools, vertical) + A2A (agents, horizontal) + memory (temporal) are the three sources an agent draws on; context engineering is the discipline that decides what actually reaches the model — and it's what separates a demo from a dependable system.

🧠 Remember it

Down = MCP (tools). Across = A2A (agents). Back = memory (time). The editor = context engineering.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🔌 protocols

AI Agents — Architectures & Multi-Agent Patterns

An agent is just a language model put in a loop with some tools and a goal. This chapter is the quiet art of shape — how to arrange one agent, or many, so the thing actually works, stays affordable, and never moves a customer's money by accident.

The single-agent loop, and how to put guards on it

An agent is a model that thinks, picks a tool, sees the result, and repeats — until it decides it's done. Everything else in this chapter is a variation on that one loop.

Let's start with the simplest possible picture. A plain chatbot does one thing: you send a message, it writes a reply, done. An agent is different. It runs in a loop. On each turn it looks at the conversation so far, decides what to do next, and often that "what to do next" is call a tool — look up a balance, search a policy, open a dispute. The tool runs, the result comes back, and the agent loops again with that new information in hand. It keeps going until it has enough to answer, then it stops.

That loop has a name you'll hear everywhere: ReAct, short for "Reason + Act." The agent reasons ("I need the customer's recent transactions"), acts (calls the get_transactions tool), reads the observation (the rows that come back), and reasons again. Thought, action, observation, repeat.

Here is the whole thing from scratch, with no framework hiding the moving parts. It uses the Anthropic Messages API, which is the current way to let a model call your tools. Read it slowly — every line earns its place.

# A single banking agent built by hand, so you can see the loop with no magic.
from anthropic import Anthropic          # official Anthropic Python SDK
import time                              # so we can enforce a wall-clock timeout

client = Anthropic()                     # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment

tools = [{                               # the tools the agent is ALLOWED to use — nothing else
    "name": "get_balance",               # the name the model will call
    "description": "Return the current balance for an account id.",  # the model picks tools by this text, so be precise
    "input_schema": {                    # JSON Schema: what arguments are valid
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string"}},  # one typed argument
        "required": ["account_id"],
    },
}]

def run_tool(name, args):                 # your real code that actually does the work
    if name == "get_balance":             # match on the tool the model asked for
        return f"Balance for {args['account_id']}: $1,204.50"  # in reality: call your core-banking API here
    return "Unknown tool"                 # never trust the model to only ask for real tools

messages = [{"role": "user",             # the conversation starts with the customer's goal
             "content": "What's the balance on account AC-77?"}]

MAX_STEPS = 6                            # GUARD 1: hard cap on loop turns — stops runaway thrashing
DEADLINE  = time.time() + 20             # GUARD 2: wall-clock timeout — a customer won't wait forever
tokens_used = 0                          # GUARD 3: we'll tally tokens and stop if the budget blows
TOKEN_BUDGET = 20_000                    # a ceiling so one request can't cost a fortune

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):            # the loop — bounded, never "while True"
    if time.time() > DEADLINE:           # check the clock before each model call
        raise TimeoutError("agent ran out of time")  # fail loud, not silently forever

    resp = client.messages.create(       # one turn of thinking by the model
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5",       # a current, capable, cost-sensible model
        max_tokens=1024,                 # cap the reply length per turn
        tools=tools,                     # tell the model which tools exist
        messages=messages,               # the full running history
    )
    tokens_used += resp.usage.input_tokens + resp.usage.output_tokens  # tally real token cost
    if tokens_used > TOKEN_BUDGET:       # GUARD 3 fires
        raise RuntimeError("token budget exceeded")

    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})  # record what the model said/asked

    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":   # the model is done thinking and wants to answer
        print(resp.content[0].text)      # this is the final answer — leave the loop
        break

    tool_results = []                    # the model asked for one or more tools; run them
    for block in resp.content:           # its reply can mix text and tool-use blocks
        if block.type == "tool_use":     # only act on tool-use blocks
            out = run_tool(block.name, block.input)  # execute the requested tool safely
            tool_results.append({        # package the result the way the API expects
                "type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": block.id, # link the result back to the exact call
                "content": out,
            })
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_results})  # feed results back; loop continues
else:                                    # this runs only if the for-loop never 'break'ed
    print("Stopped: hit max steps without finishing.")  # GUARD 1 fired — we didn't converge
▶ Output
The balance on account AC-77 is $1,204.50.

The same hand-built loop with the OpenAI API — same three guards, only OpenAI's field names differ:

# The same single banking agent, built by hand on OpenAI's Chat Completions API.
from openai import OpenAI               # official OpenAI Python SDK
import time, json                       # time for the timeout; json to parse tool arguments

client = OpenAI()                       # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

tools = [{                              # the tools the agent is ALLOWED to use — nothing else
    "type": "function",
    "function": {
        "name": "get_balance",          # the name the model will call
        "description": "Return the current balance for an account id.",  # the model picks tools by this text, so be precise
        "parameters": {                 # JSON Schema: what arguments are valid
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"account_id": {"type": "string"}},  # one typed argument
            "required": ["account_id"],
        },
    },
}]

def run_tool(name, args):                # your real code that actually does the work
    if name == "get_balance":            # match on the tool the model asked for
        return f"Balance for {args['account_id']}: $1,204.50"  # in reality: call your core-banking API here
    return "Unknown tool"                # never trust the model to only ask for real tools

messages = [{"role": "user",            # the conversation starts with the customer's goal
             "content": "What's the balance on account AC-77?"}]

MAX_STEPS = 6                           # GUARD 1: hard cap on loop turns — stops runaway thrashing
DEADLINE  = time.time() + 20            # GUARD 2: wall-clock timeout — a customer won't wait forever
tokens_used = 0                         # GUARD 3: we'll tally tokens and stop if the budget blows
TOKEN_BUDGET = 20_000                   # a ceiling so one request can't cost a fortune

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):           # the loop — bounded, never "while True"
    if time.time() > DEADLINE:          # check the clock before each model call
        raise TimeoutError("agent ran out of time")  # fail loud, not silently forever

    resp = client.chat.completions.create(  # one turn of thinking by the model
        model="gpt-4.1",                # a current, capable, cost-sensible model
        tools=tools,                    # tell the model which tools exist
        messages=messages,              # the full running history
    )
    tokens_used += resp.usage.total_tokens  # tally real token cost (OpenAI reports it here)
    if tokens_used > TOKEN_BUDGET:      # GUARD 3 fires
        raise RuntimeError("token budget exceeded")

    msg = resp.choices[0].message       # the model's reply
    messages.append(msg)                # record what the model said/asked

    if not msg.tool_calls:              # no tool wanted → the model is done and wants to answer
        print(msg.content)              # this is the final answer — leave the loop
        break

    for call in msg.tool_calls:         # the model asked for one or more tools; run them
        out = run_tool(call.function.name, json.loads(call.function.arguments))  # execute the requested tool safely
        messages.append({               # package the result the way the API expects
            "role": "tool",
            "tool_call_id": call.id,     # link the result back to the exact call
            "content": out,
        })
else:                                   # this runs only if the for-loop never 'break'ed
    print("Stopped: hit max steps without finishing.")  # GUARD 1 fired — we didn't converge
▶ Output
The balance on account AC-77 is $1,204.50.

That's an agent. Not a framework, not magic — a for loop that lets a model call your functions and hands the results back until it's ready to answer. Frameworks like LangChain's create_agent wrap exactly this for you, but it's worth seeing the bones once, because every production failure lives in this loop.

⚙️ Under the hood — why the three guards are not optional

A model in a loop can misbehave in three expensive ways. It can thrash — call the same tool over and over, never converging (the MAX_STEPS guard catches this). It can hang — a slow downstream API stalls the whole turn while a customer stares at a spinner (the DEADLINE guard catches this). And it can binge — stuff more and more into context each turn until one question quietly costs dollars (the TOKEN_BUDGET guard catches this). An agent without these three is a demo. An agent with them is something you can point at real traffic.

Going deeper — where the tokens actually go

The subtle cost in this loop is that the whole history is re-sent on every turn. Turn one sends the question; turn two re-sends the question plus the model's tool request plus the tool result; turn three re-sends all of that again, and so on. A five-step answer doesn't cost five messages' worth of tokens — it costs roughly the sum of a growing pyramid. That's why the token guard matters more than it first looks, and why trimming or summarising old tool results between turns is the first optimisation you reach for on a chatty agent. One more edge case worth internalising: a single turn can contain several tool-use blocks at once (the model asks for the balance and the recent transactions together), so always loop over every block and return a result for each — a missing tool_result for even one call makes the next turn error out. And notice the structural choice in the code: it is a bounded for, never a while True. The else clause on the for is the quiet hero — it fires only when the loop finishes without a break, i.e. the agent used up all its steps without converging, which is precisely the runaway case you want to catch and report rather than hide.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Every loop turn is a full model round-trip (~0.5–2 s) plus the tool's own latency, and in a single agent they run in series — a 4-step answer easily takes 4–8 s, so stream progress to the customer rather than show a frozen spinner. Track p50/p95 steps-per-request and tokens-per-request; a creeping step count is your earliest warning that a prompt or a tool description is confusing the model.

Failure modes. The number-one production bug is an uncaught tool exception: a downstream timeout throws, the loop dies, and the customer sees a 500. Wrap run_tool so errors come back as a tool_result string ("balance service unavailable, please retry") — the model can then apologise or try another path instead of crashing. Add per-tool retries with backoff for flaky dependencies, and keep the three guards (steps, seconds, tokens) because each catches a different runaway.

Monitoring. Log every step — the model's reasoning, the tool name, its arguments, and the result — under one trace id. Emit metrics for timeout rate, budget-exceeded rate, and tool-error rate per tool, so you can see which dependency is dragging the whole agent down.

Security & compliance (bank). The model asking for a tool is not authorisation. Check the caller's entitlements inside run_tool so BankAssist can't read an account the customer doesn't own. Keep a strict tool allow-list, never let the model build a raw SQL query or a transfer instruction that isn't validated server-side, and redact PII (account numbers, balances) from logs before they reach your observability stack.

⚠ Watch out

Never write while True around a model call in production. A single bad prompt, a looping tool error, or a confused model will burn your budget and your on-call engineer's night. Bound every agent loop by steps, time, and tokens — all three, because each catches a different failure.

🧠 Remember it

An agent is a model in a bounded loop: think → act → observe → repeat. Three guards keep the loop honest — steps, seconds, tokens.

When one agent is plenty: start simple

The best multi-agent system is usually one good single agent. Reach for "more agents" only when a single loop has clearly run out of road.

There's a strong pull, once you learn about agents, to build a whole team of them — a planner, three specialists, a reviewer, a manager. It feels sophisticated. It is almost always the wrong first move. More agents means more model calls, more tokens, more places to fail, more things to debug at 2 a.m. The guidance from the teams who build these for a living is blunt: start with the simplest thing that works, and add complexity only when it earns its keep.

A single agent with a well-chosen set of tools handles a surprising amount. Think about what most banking requests actually need:

  • "What's my balance and last three transactions?" — two tool calls, one answer. One agent.
  • "Is this $40 charge a duplicate? If so, start a dispute." — look up the transaction, compare, call one write tool behind an approval. One agent.
  • "Explain the overdraft fee and whether mine can be waived." — retrieve the policy, read the account, answer. One agent.

None of these needs a committee. They need one capable loop with the right tools and good guards.

🏦 Picture this

A team building BankAssist started with a grand five-agent design: a greeter, a router, a retrieval specialist, a math specialist, and a "supervisor." It was slow, it was pricey, and when an answer came out wrong, nobody could tell which agent to blame. They tore it down to one agent with five tools. Latency dropped by two-thirds, cost dropped with it, and debugging became "read one trace" instead of "untangle five conversations." They added a second agent back only months later, for one genuinely separate job — fraud investigation — where it paid off.

So when IS a single agent not enough?

Honest signals that you've outgrown one loop — and should read the rest of this chapter:

  • The tool list is huge. Past roughly 15–20 tools, a single agent starts picking the wrong one. Grouping tools behind specialist sub-agents restores accuracy.
  • The context is drowning. One agent doing research across dozens of sources fills its context window with clutter and loses the thread. Separate agents with their own clean contexts fix this.
  • The work is genuinely parallel. Three independent lookups that each take seconds can run at once instead of one after another.
  • You need an independent check. A second agent reviewing the first's work (a different "pair of eyes") catches mistakes the author can't see.
✅ Tip

Write the single-agent version first, even if you're sure you'll need more. Measure where it actually fails. Then add exactly the structure that fixes that failure — and nothing more. Architecture should be a response to a measured problem, not a guess made on day one.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. A single agent is the cheap, fast baseline — roughly ~4× a plain chat in tokens, versus ~15× for a full multi-agent design. For the high-volume "balance / last three transactions" traffic BankAssist serves millions of times a day, that gap is the difference between an affordable product and a runaway bill, so the deliberate default architecture for routine intents is one loop.

Scale & failure modes. One agent means one trace to read when something breaks, one place to patch, one context to reason about — operational simplicity that matters more at 3 a.m. than any architecture diagram. The watch-point is the tool count: past roughly 15–20 tools a single agent's selection accuracy drops, so track per-tool mis-selection rate as your objective signal to start grouping tools behind specialists.

Monitoring & compliance (bank). Instrument the single agent well before you ever add a second — containment rate (answered without human escalation), tool-error rate, and cost-per-resolved-request. A clean, well-audited single agent is also far easier to take through a bank's model-risk and change-approval process than a web of interacting agents whose joint behaviour nobody can fully characterise.

⚠ Watch out — the "team of agents" trap

The expensive mistake here is splitting on a guess — building the planner-plus-specialists team on day one because it looks impressive, before a single real request has shown you where one agent fails. You pay the multi-agent tax (more tokens, more latency, more debugging) and buy nothing. When to add agents: only after you can point at a measured failure — misrouted tool picks, a drowning context, work that is genuinely parallel, or a need for an independent check. When NOT to: for a handful of tools and clean single-domain requests, stay with one agent — adding structure there only subtracts reliability.

🧠 Remember it

One agent until it hurts. Add agents to fix a pain you can point at — too many tools, drowning context, true parallelism, or the need for a second opinion.

Sequential pipeline: prompt chaining

When a job always follows the same fixed steps, don't make an agent "figure it out." Wire the steps in order, and check the work between them.

Not everything needs an agent that decides its own path. Many banking tasks are a fixed recipe: step one, then step two, then step three, every single time. For those, the simplest and most reliable shape is a chain — the output of one model call becomes the input to the next, in a straight line. This is often called prompt chaining, and strictly speaking it's a workflow (the steps are fixed by you) rather than a free-roaming agent (which chooses its own steps). That fixedness is a feature: it's predictable, cheap, and easy to test.

The quietly important part is that gate in the middle. Because the steps are fixed, you can drop a plain check between them — "did the extract step return a valid account number? a real amount?" — and stop the chain early if it didn't. That's far more reliable than hoping a single big prompt gets everything right in one shot.

# A 3-step complaint pipeline: extract → validate → draft. Fixed order, checked between steps.
def handle_complaint(text):
    fields = extract_fields(text)        # step 1: pull account id, amount, date from free text
    if not fields.get("account_id"):     # the GATE — a cheap code check, not another model call
        return route_to_human("missing account number")  # stop early instead of guessing downstream

    category = classify(fields)          # step 2: dispute type (duplicate charge, fraud, fee…)
    reply = draft_reply(fields, category)# step 3: write the customer response with the right template
    return reply                         # each step saw clean, validated input from the last
⚙️ Under the hood — why split one prompt into a chain?

You could ask one giant prompt to "extract the fields, classify the dispute, and write a reply." It often works, until it doesn't — and when it fails you can't tell which part failed. A chain gives each step one small, clear job, which each model does better; it lets you validate between steps; and it makes failures legible ("classify returned nonsense") so you can fix exactly that step. The trade is latency: three calls in a row take longer than one. For back-office work where accuracy beats speed, that trade is almost always worth it.

In production

Chains are the workhorse of banking back-office automation — document intake, KYC checks, statement generation — precisely because they're boring and predictable. You can unit-test each step. You can replay a failed run. You can put a different model on each step (a cheap model to extract, a stronger one to draft). The main risk is error propagation: a bad step-1 output silently poisons every step after it, so the gates aren't decoration — they're the safety rail. Monitor each step's success rate separately, not just the end result.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. A chain's latency is the sum of its steps — three sequential model calls at ~1 s each is a ~3 s floor before any tool work — so chains suit back-office jobs (overnight KYC batches, statement generation, document intake) more than live chat. The upside is per-step model choice: run extraction on gpt-4.1-mini and only the customer-facing draft on gpt-4.1, which often halves cost versus using one big model for every stage.

Failure modes & monitoring. The signature failure is silent error propagation — a wrong account number from step 1 flows cleanly through classify and draft, producing a confident, wrong answer. The gates are the fix, and you must monitor each step's pass rate and gate-rejection rate separately; a single end-to-end success metric hides which station is drifting. Because the order is fixed, you can replay any failed run from the exact step that broke rather than re-running the whole pipeline.

Scale & compliance (bank). Chains are a regulator's friend: deterministic order, a validation checkpoint between stages, and a clean record of what each stage produced. Make each step idempotent and checkpoint between them so a crashed overnight batch resumes mid-chain instead of re-processing (and re-charging) everything. Persist each stage's input and output for the audit trail — for a disputed BankAssist complaint, you can show exactly what was extracted, how it was classified, and why the reply said what it did.

⚠ Watch out — when NOT to chain

Don't force a chain onto work whose steps aren't fixed. If the path changes per request — sometimes you need a web lookup, sometimes three, sometimes none — a rigid chain will fight you. That's when you want an agent that decides its own steps, or an orchestrator — a lead agent that splits the goal into sub-tasks at run time. Chains are for recipes, not for exploration.

🧠 Remember it

A chain is an assembly line: same stations, same order, a quality check between each. Fixed steps → chain. Changing steps → agent.

Routing & handoffs: send it to the right desk

A small, fast classifier reads the request and sends it to the specialist built for exactly that job — the way a bank's front desk directs you to the right window.

Walk into a bank branch and you don't explain your whole problem to the first person you see. A greeter points you: "mortgages — window 3; disputes — window 5; new accounts — over there." That's routing. In an agent system, a lightweight step (often a small, cheap model) classifies the incoming request and hands it to the specialist prompt, agent, or tool-set that handles that category.

Why bother? Because one giant do-everything prompt is a jack of all trades and master of none. A prompt tuned only for card disputes, with only dispute tools and only dispute policy, outperforms a sprawling general prompt on dispute questions — and it's cheaper, because it's smaller. Routing lets you keep each specialist narrow and sharp.

There are two flavours of "send it elsewhere," and the difference matters:

Routing (decide up front)

A classifier picks the handler before the real work starts, usually once. Clean, cheap, predictable. Best when the categories are clear and a request belongs to exactly one.

Handoff (transfer mid-conversation)

An agent already talking to the customer decides "this needs the loans specialist" and transfers control, passing the conversation along. More flexible; used in frameworks like the OpenAI Agents SDK, where handoffs are a core primitive.

# Routing: a tiny, cheap model picks the lane; the heavy specialist does the work.
def route(message):
    label = client.messages.create(      # a small fast model, used only to classify
        model="claude-haiku-5-5",        # cheapest tier — classification is easy, don't overpay
        max_tokens=16,                   # we only need one short label back
        messages=[{"role": "user",
          "content": f"Reply with one word — cards, loans, or fraud:\n{message}"}],
    ).content[0].text.strip().lower()    # e.g. "cards"

    return {                             # map the label to the specialist that handles it
        "cards": cards_agent,
        "loans": loans_agent,
        "fraud": fraud_agent,
    }.get(label, default_agent)          # a safe fallback if the label is unexpected

The same router with the OpenAI API:

# Routing: a tiny, cheap OpenAI model picks the lane; the heavy specialist does the work.
def route(message):
    label = client.chat.completions.create(  # a small fast model, used only to classify
        model="gpt-4.1-mini",            # cheapest tier — classification is easy, don't overpay
        max_tokens=16,                   # we only need one short label back
        messages=[{"role": "user",
          "content": f"Reply with one word — cards, loans, or fraud:\n{message}"}],
    ).choices[0].message.content.strip().lower()  # e.g. "cards"

    return {                             # map the label to the specialist that handles it
        "cards": cards_agent,
        "loans": loans_agent,
        "fraud": fraud_agent,
    }.get(label, default_agent)          # a safe fallback if the label is unexpected

Notice the two-step wiring, because that's the whole point. The router makes one cheap classification call and hands back the specialist to run — it never answers the customer itself. The caller then runs that specialist on the original message, roughly handler = route(msg); reply = handler(msg). So the message takes one short hop (classify) and then all the expensive, tool-heavy work happens exactly once, inside the single lane the classifier picked — the router is a signpost, not a worker.

⚙️ Under the hood — handoffs in a real framework

In the OpenAI Agents SDK, a handoff is modelled as a special kind of tool call: the triage agent "calls" a handoff to, say, the loans agent, and control (plus the conversation) moves there. The cost to know: a handoff means at least two model calls — the triage decision, then the specialist — and the receiving agent usually sees the whole prior conversation unless you add an input filter to trim it. Handy, but not free.

In production

Routing's single biggest failure is the misroute: a fraud report classified as a general question and sent to the wrong, un-urgent desk. So: measure routing accuracy like any other model output; build a confident default/fallback lane for "not sure"; and for high-stakes intents (fraud, account closure) lean toward over-escalating rather than under. Keep the router model cheap and fast — it runs on every single request, so a slow router taxes everything.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. The router runs on every request, so keep it on the cheapest fast tier (gpt-4.1-mini) and ask for one short label — a 16-token classification adds tens of milliseconds and fractions of a cent, which is the whole point. A handoff, by contrast, costs at least two full model calls (triage, then specialist), and the receiving agent inherits the entire prior conversation unless you add an input filter to trim it, so budget for that extra context.

Failure modes & monitoring. The dangerous failure is the misroute: a fraud report landing in the general-questions lane. Measure routing accuracy against a labelled sample like any other model output, alarm specifically on fraud/escalation recall, and keep a confident fallback lane for low-confidence classifications rather than forcing a guess. For high-stakes intents, deliberately bias toward over-escalation — a wrongly-escalated fee question costs a minute of an agent's time; a missed fraud report costs far more.

Security & compliance (bank). Re-check entitlements at the specialist, not just the router — routing decides where, never whether the customer is allowed. Log the chosen lane and the classifier's confidence with each request; when BankAssist sends a card dispute to the cards agent, the trace must show why, so a complaint can be reconstructed months later.

⚠ Watch out — when NOT to route

If you only have two or three tools and one capable agent handles them all well, a router is pure overhead — an extra model call and an extra failure point for no gain. Routing earns its place when specialists genuinely diverge (different tools, different tone, different policy), not when you're just splitting hairs.

🧠 Remember it

Router = greeter at the door (picks the window before you start). Handoff = being walked to another window (transferred mid-conversation).

Parallel agents: sectioning vs voting

Run several model calls at once — either to split a job into independent pieces, or to ask the same question many times and take the consensus.

So far every shape has been one call after another. But some work doesn't need to wait in line. If three lookups are independent of each other, running them at the same time cuts your latency to the slowest one instead of the sum of all three. This is parallelization, and it comes in two distinct styles that people often confuse.

Sectioning — split the work

Break a task into independent sub-tasks and run each in parallel, then combine. Example: to assess a loan application, check credit, verify income, and scan for fraud flags — all at once — then merge into one decision packet.

Voting — repeat the work

Run the same task several times (or with different prompts) and combine the answers — majority vote, or "flag if any run says fraud." Trades money for reliability on a judgment call.

# Sectioning: three independent checks on a loan, run concurrently with asyncio.
import asyncio

async def assess_loan(app):
    credit, income, fraud = await asyncio.gather(  # fire all three at once; wait for all to return
        check_credit(app),               # sub-task 1 — independent of the others
        verify_income(app),              # sub-task 2 — runs at the same time
        scan_fraud(app),                 # sub-task 3 — also concurrent
    )                                    # total wait = the SLOWEST of the three, not the sum
    return combine(credit, income, fraud)# merge the three results into one decision packet
⚙️ Under the hood — why voting helps on judgment calls

Models are a little random. Ask the same hard question twice and you can get two answers. For a subjective or borderline call — "does this transaction pattern look like fraud?" — running it several times and taking the majority smooths out that randomness, the way polling three doctors beats trusting one. The variant "flag if any run says fraud" deliberately biases toward caution — perfect when a miss is far worse than a false alarm. The cost is linear: three runs cost roughly three times as much.

In production

Parallelism's traps are about coordination, not the model. Only parallelize calls that are truly independent — parallelizing steps that depend on each other causes races and wrong ordering. Handle partial failure: if the fraud check times out but credit and income return, do you proceed, retry, or hold? Decide that on purpose. And watch the thundering herd — ten parallel agents hammering one core-banking API can trip its rate limits or knock it over. Add concurrency limits and respect downstream quotas.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Sectioning is the rare pattern that buys latency back: three checks that would take ~2 s each in series finish in ~2 s when fired together, so a loan pre-check feels instant instead of sluggish. Voting trades the opposite way — three runs cost ~3× the tokens for one answer, so reserve it for genuinely borderline judgment calls where a wrong answer is expensive.

Failure modes. Plan for partial failure explicitly: if the fraud scan times out but credit and income return, decide in advance whether to proceed, retry just that branch, or hold the whole decision — never let one slow branch silently drop. Use asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True) so one exception doesn't cancel its siblings, and set a per-branch timeout so the slowest check can't stall the merge.

Scale & compliance (bank). Watch the thundering herd: ten parallel loan assessments each firing three calls hit a legacy core-banking API with thirty simultaneous requests and can trip its rate limits or knock it over. Put a concurrency semaphore around calls to shared downstream systems, respect their quotas, and record which branches contributed to each lending decision — fair-lending audits will ask exactly which signals drove each BankAssist outcome.

⚠ Watch out — when NOT to parallelize

If step B needs step A's output, they're sequential — no amount of asyncio changes that. And voting on a factual question ("what's the balance?") is pointless: the answer is in the system of record, so look it up once. Save voting for genuine judgment, and sectioning for genuinely independent work.

🧠 Remember it

Sectioning = divide the work; Voting = double-check the work. Both run at once and finish at the speed of the slowest branch.

Orchestrator–worker: a lead agent that delegates

A central "lead" agent breaks a fuzzy goal into sub-tasks on the fly, hands each to a worker agent, and stitches the results back together.

Parallel sectioning works when you know the sub-tasks ahead of time (credit, income, fraud — always those three). But sometimes you don't. "Investigate whether this account is part of a fraud ring" might need two sub-investigations or ten, and you can't know which until you start digging. That's the home of the orchestrator–worker pattern: a lead agent that decides the sub-tasks at runtime, spins up worker agents to handle them, and synthesizes their findings into one answer.

The key difference from fixed parallelism: in sectioning the split is hard-coded; here the orchestrator chooses the split dynamically based on what the problem turns out to need. This is exactly the shape Anthropic described for its multi-agent research system — a lead agent coordinating specialized sub-agents that work in parallel.

Why this beats one big agent for complex research: each worker gets its own clean context window. Instead of one agent cramming statements, counterparties, and watchlists all into a single overloaded context (and losing the thread), each worker focuses on one slice, then hands back a tight summary. The orchestrator's context stays clear — it only ever sees the summaries, not the raw mess each worker waded through.

⚙️ Under the hood — the delegation contract

The make-or-break detail is the instruction the orchestrator gives each worker. Vague delegation ("look into the counterparties") produces vague work and duplicated effort — two workers researching the same entity. Good orchestrators hand each worker a crisp contract: a clear objective, the tools it may use, the output format expected, and boundaries ("only these three accounts"). Think of it as a manager writing a good ticket, not shouting a general direction across the room.

In production

This is the most powerful and most expensive pattern in this chapter. Anthropic reported its multi-agent research system used about 15× the tokens of a plain chat — because every worker is a full agent with its own loop and context. So reserve it for high-value tasks where quality genuinely justifies the spend (deep fraud investigation, complex research), not routine Q&A. Guard it hard: cap the number of workers the orchestrator may spawn, cap each worker's own loop, and set a total token budget across the whole fan-out, or one query can quietly spin up a crowd.

⚙️ In production

Cost & scale (real numbers). Anthropic's published research system is the reference point: a lead agent spins up 3–5 subagents in parallel, the whole thing burns about 15× the tokens of a plain chat, and in their internal eval a Claude-Opus lead with Sonnet subagents beat a single agent by roughly 90%. Their own sizing rule is sober — simple fact-finding needs one agent and 3–10 tool calls; only genuinely complex research justifies 10+ subagents. Spend this pattern only where the answer is worth it.

Failure modes & guardrails. Two things blow up: fan-out (an orchestrator that keeps spawning workers) and vague delegation (two workers unknowingly researching the same entity). Cap the worker count, cap each worker's own loop, and set one total token budget across the whole fan-out. Give each worker a crisp contract — objective, allowed tools, output format, boundaries — or you pay for duplicated, unfocused work.

Monitoring & compliance (bank). Trace the whole tree under one id so a BankAssist fraud investigation's every sub-finding is attributable and replayable. Workers read untrusted data (news, filings, counterparty records), so treat their returned text as data, not instructions, and have the orchestrator cite sources in its synthesis — an investigator must be able to see where each conclusion came from before acting on it.

⚠ Watch out — when NOT to orchestrate

If the sub-tasks are known and fixed, use plain parallel sectioning — it's simpler and cheaper, no lead agent needed. And if the task is mostly one continuous line of reasoning that can't be cleanly split (workers would just wait on each other), a single strong agent beats a committee. Orchestration shines on divisible, open-ended, high-value work — and nowhere else.

🧠 Remember it

Orchestrator = a manager who writes tickets on the fly. Fixed sub-tasks → sectioning. Unknown sub-tasks → orchestrator. Powerful, but ~15× the tokens.

Planner–Generator–Evaluator: the self-improving loop

One agent produces a draft, a second agent critiques it against clear criteria, and the first revises — looping until the work is good enough.

Here's a truth about writing anything: the first draft is rarely the best draft. The same holds for model output. The evaluator–optimizer pattern (also called generator–evaluator, or planner–generator–evaluator when a planning step comes first) builds that revision cycle in. One role generates a candidate answer; a separate role evaluates it against explicit criteria and gives specific feedback; the generator revises. Round and round, until the evaluator is satisfied or you hit a cap.

The power comes from separation. The same model is a far better critic of someone else's work than of its own in-progress draft — giving the evaluator a fresh, focused role ("you are a compliance reviewer; check only these five rules") catches things the generator, busy producing, glides right past.

# Evaluator–optimizer: draft a customer reply, critique it, revise — up to 3 rounds.
def generate_reply(question, context):
    draft = generator(question, context)         # first attempt at the answer
    for round in range(3):                        # GUARD: never loop more than 3 times
        verdict = evaluator(question, draft)      # a separate "reviewer" role scores the draft
        if verdict["pass"]:                       # evaluator is satisfied against the rubric
            return draft                          # good enough — ship it
        draft = generator(                        # otherwise revise using the SPECIFIC feedback
            question, context,
            feedback=verdict["notes"],            # e.g. "missing the fee citation; tone too casual"
        )
    return draft                                  # ran out of rounds — return best effort (and flag it)
⚙️ Under the hood — it only works when "good" is checkable

This pattern pays off when you can state clear evaluation criteria. "Does the reply cite the exact policy clause? Is the tone formal? Are all required disclaimers present? Is the math correct?" — those are checkable, so the evaluator gives useful, actionable feedback. But if "good" is vague and subjective, the evaluator just waffles and the loop spins without improving. The sharper your rubric, the better this works. Best of all is an external verifier where one exists — a calculator that confirms the interest math, a schema validator that confirms the JSON — because an objective check beats one model's opinion of another's.

In production

Two dangers. First, the loop that won't converge: generator and evaluator ping-pong forever, each round costing tokens and time — so the round cap isn't optional, and you should log how often you hit it (a high rate means your rubric is bad or the task is too hard). Second, the rubber-stamp evaluator: a weak evaluator approves bad work, giving false confidence. Calibrate it against human-reviewed examples before you trust it. In banking this pattern is gold for anything customer-facing or compliance-sensitive — a reviewer agent checking that every outgoing reply carries the right disclaimers and citations before it's sent.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. Each revision round is at least two model calls (generate, then evaluate), so a 3-round loop can be 6+ calls for one reply — fine for a compliance-sensitive letter, far too slow for "branch hours". Cap the rounds hard and log how often you hit the cap: a high cap-hit rate means your rubric is unclear or the task is beyond the generator, not that you need more rounds.

Failure modes. Two classics. The non-converging ping-pong, where generator and evaluator never agree — the round cap is the backstop, and you return best-effort-plus-a-flag, never an infinite loop. And the rubber-stamp evaluator, a weak reviewer that approves bad work and gives false confidence; calibrate it against human-reviewed examples before trusting it, and prefer an objective checker (a calculator for the interest math, a schema validator for the JSON) over one model judging another wherever one exists.

Compliance (bank). This is the pattern for the last mile of customer-facing text: a reviewer role that checks every outgoing BankAssist reply carries the right disclosures, cites the exact fee clause, and gets the math right before send. Log the evaluator's verdict and the final draft together — "reviewed and passed against rules X, Y, Z" is exactly the evidence an audit will ask for.

⚠ Watch out — when NOT to use it

Skip the loop for simple, low-stakes answers — "what are your branch hours?" doesn't need a review committee, and the extra calls just add latency and cost. Use evaluator–optimizer where quality genuinely matters and you can define what "good" means. On trivial requests it's over-engineering.

🧠 Remember it

Writer + editor, in a loop. Works brilliantly when you can write the rubric; pointless when "good" is a shrug. Always cap the rounds.

Hierarchies and DAGs: wiring agents into a shape

Zoom out and these patterns combine. A tree of managers-over-workers is a hierarchy; a map of "this step feeds those steps" is a DAG.

Real systems rarely use one pure pattern. Once you have orchestrators, workers, routers, and chains, you start wiring them into larger shapes. Two shapes are worth naming because they describe almost every big agent system you'll meet.

Hierarchical agents — layers of management

A hierarchy is an orchestrator pattern with more than two levels. A top agent delegates to mid-level managers, who delegate to workers — like a bank's org chart. The top agent thinks in big strategy ("assess this corporate client's total risk exposure"); each layer down translates that into narrower work, until leaf workers do concrete tool calls. It's how you keep a very large task comprehensible: no single agent holds the whole thing in its head, just its own slice and the slice below it.

DAG agents — a map of dependencies

DAG stands for Directed Acyclic Graph — a fancy name for a simple picture: boxes connected by arrows, where the arrows never loop back on themselves. Each box is a step; an arrow means "this must finish before that can start." It's more flexible than a straight chain because steps can fan out and merge: two steps run in parallel, both feed a third. "Acyclic" (no cycles) is the safety property — because nothing loops back, the graph is guaranteed to finish. Frameworks like LangGraph let you define exactly this: nodes (steps) and edges (what-feeds-what), including conditional edges that pick the next node based on a result.

⚙️ Under the hood — why "acyclic" is a safety feature

A cycle (an arrow that eventually loops back) is how agents run forever. A DAG forbids cycles by construction, so the graph must reach an end — which is exactly the property you want for a workflow that touches money. When you do need a loop (like the evaluator–optimizer revision cycle), good frameworks make you add it deliberately and attach a cap, rather than letting cycles sneak in. The discipline of drawing your system as a DAG often reveals accidental loops before they reach production.

In production

Hierarchies buy comprehensibility at the cost of latency — every layer adds a round of model calls, so a four-deep hierarchy is slow and pricey; keep them shallow (two or three levels is usually plenty). DAGs are the backbone of durable workflow engines: because the graph is explicit, the engine can checkpoint after each node, retry a failed node, and resume without redoing finished work — essential for long-running banking processes like loan underwriting that must survive a crash. Define the graph explicitly rather than letting agents improvise the structure; an explicit graph is one you can test, visualize, and audit.

⚙️ In production

Latency & cost. Hierarchies pay for comprehensibility in round-trips: every layer adds a full delegate-and-summarise cycle, so a four-deep tree is slow and expensive and loses fidelity as instructions travel down and summaries travel back up. Keep them shallow — two or three levels is almost always enough; past that, each layer buys less than it costs.

Durability (why banks like DAGs). Because a DAG is an explicit graph, a workflow engine can checkpoint after each node, retry just the failed node, and resume a crashed run without redoing finished work — essential for long-running processes like loan underwriting that must survive a deploy or an outage. An explicit graph is also one you can unit-test, visualise, and hand to an auditor; an improvised agent structure is none of those.

Monitoring & safety. The acyclic property is a guarantee the workflow finishes; enforce it by defining the graph explicitly rather than letting agents improvise edges, and when you genuinely need a loop (a revision cycle) add it deliberately with a cap. Monitor per-node success rate and duration so you can see which node in a BankAssist underwriting flow is the bottleneck or the flake, and alarm on a node whose retry rate climbs.

⚠ Watch out — when NOT to go hierarchical

Deep hierarchies are a classic over-engineering trap. Each layer is pure coordination overhead — more latency, more cost, more places for the message to get garbled on the way down and the summary to get lossy on the way up. If two levels do the job, don't build four. And don't reach for a DAG framework when a plain function chain would do; the graph machinery earns its keep only when you truly need branching, parallelism, or durable resume.

🧠 Remember it

Hierarchy = org chart (layers of bosses). DAG = flowchart with no loops (guaranteed to finish). Keep hierarchies shallow; draw DAGs explicitly.

Debate and group chat: many voices, one answer

Put several agents in a room, let them argue or collaborate toward a shared goal, and often the group lands somewhere better than any one of them would alone.

The patterns so far have clear bosses and workers. Debate and group chat are looser: multiple agents talk to each other — sometimes arguing opposite positions, sometimes just collaborating — in a shared conversation, until they converge on an answer. The bet is the same one juries and review panels make: structured disagreement surfaces flaws that a single confident voice would hide.

In a debate, you deliberately assign opposing roles. For a loan approval: one agent argues for approving, another argues against, and a judge agent weighs both and decides. The "against" agent is forced to hunt for reasons to decline — concentration risk, a thin credit file, an income mismatch — that a single approval agent, nudging toward yes, might wave away. The friction is the feature.

Mechanically it's a simple loop around a shared text transcript. Each round, the pro agent is called with the running transcript and appends its argument; then the con agent is called with that updated transcript and appends its rebuttal. After a fixed number of rounds, the judge is called once with the full transcript and returns the decision. No agent talks directly to another — they pass messages only by reading and writing the one transcript they all share, which is also why capping the rounds matters: nothing else stops the back-and-forth.

In a group chat, several specialists share one conversation and chip in as relevant — a credit expert, a policy expert, a fraud expert all "in the room," each speaking up on their piece, a coordinator keeping order and deciding when the group is done.

⚙️ Under the hood — why debate sometimes beats a single call

A lone agent asked "approve this loan?" tends to pick a side early and then rationalize it — it rarely argues vigorously against its own leaning. Splitting the roles forces both cases to be made at full strength, and makes the reasoning explicit in the transcript. The judge then decides with both arguments laid out, which also gives you a far richer audit trail than a single yes/no — you can see why. The cost: every round is several model calls, so a three-round debate with three agents is roughly nine-plus calls for one decision.

In production

Debate and group chat are the priciest and slowest patterns here — many agents, many rounds, lots of tokens — so they're reserved for high-stakes, judgment-heavy decisions where the quality and the audit trail justify it (credit committees, complex fraud calls, policy-exception reviews), never for routine traffic. Watch three failure modes: conversations that never converge (so cap the rounds and have the judge decide on whatever's on the table), agents that pile on and agree too quickly (defeating the point — enforce the opposing roles), and runaway token cost (budget the whole debate, not each agent). Always have a decisive judge or coordinator; a leaderless group chat tends to wander.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency. This is the priciest shape in the chapter: every round is several model calls, so a three-round debate among three agents is roughly nine-plus calls — and a judge on top — for one decision. Budget the whole debate, not each agent, and cap the rounds so a non-converging argument can't run up the bill; have the judge rule on whatever is on the table when the cap is hit.

Failure modes. Three to watch: conversations that never converge, agents that pile on and agree too quickly (which defeats the point — enforce the opposing roles in the prompts), and runaway token cost. Always keep a decisive judge or coordinator; a leaderless group chat wanders and rarely lands on a clean decision.

Compliance (bank). The reason a credit committee or a policy-exception review justifies the spend is the audit trail: the shared transcript lays out the case for and against plus the judge's reasoning, which is far richer evidence than a lone yes/no. Persist the full transcript and the verdict; for a declined BankAssist loan, "here is the argument the decline agent made" is exactly what fair-lending review needs. Reserve this for the handful of high-stakes judgment calls a week, never routine traffic.

⚠ Watch out — when NOT to debate

For anything with a factual or computable answer, debate is theatre — "what's the payoff amount?" needs a lookup and a calculation, not a panel. And for routine, low-stakes requests the cost and latency are indefensible. Debate earns its keep only on genuinely contested judgment calls where being right matters more than being fast or cheap.

🧠 Remember it

Debate = a courtroom (pro, con, judge); group chat = a case meeting. Great for hard judgment calls, far too costly for routine ones. Always keep a judge.

The multi-agent trade-off: quality vs cost vs latency

Every extra agent buys you something — and charges you for it. The honest view: multi-agent can cost roughly 15× the tokens of a single chat.

It's tempting to read this chapter as "more agents = better." It isn't. Every pattern that adds agents is spending a very real resource to buy quality. Before you reach for a multi-agent design, you should be able to say out loud what you're buying and what it costs — because the bill is bigger than most people expect.

Anthropic shared a striking number from its own multi-agent research system: it used about 15× the tokens of an ordinary chat interaction (single agents already run around 4× a plain chat). The reason is simple once you see it — each sub-agent is a full agent, with its own loop, its own context, its own back-and-forth. Three sub-agents don't add a bit of overhead; they roughly triple the core work, on top of the orchestrator's own thinking. Tokens are the dominant cost driver, and multi-agent designs spend them lavishly.

So the decision is a three-way balance, and you rarely get all three:

You gain…You pay in…Worth it when…
Higher quality on hard, divisible tasksMany more tokens (up to ~15×)The answer is high-value and hard for one agent
Parallelism / independent reviewHigher latency per layer or hopQuality & thoroughness beat speed & cost
Cleaner, focused contextsMore failure points & harder debuggingA single context genuinely can't hold the task
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist handles two very different jobs. For "what's my balance?" — millions of times a day — a multi-agent design would be madness: 15× the cost and several times the latency to answer something one tool call nails. So that's a single agent. But for a quarterly deep-dive fraud investigation — a handful a week, each one potentially saving millions — the orchestrator-with-workers design is a bargain even at 15× tokens, because being thorough and right dwarfs the token bill. Same bank, opposite answers. The task's value decides the architecture.

⚙️ Under the hood — latency doesn't add the way cost does

Cost scales with total tokens across all agents. Latency depends on the shape. Agents in a chain (or a deep hierarchy) run one after another, so their times add up — a four-step chain feels four times as slow. Agents running in parallel only cost you the slowest one, so sectioning can be nearly as fast as a single call while doing far more work. This is why the same token budget can feel snappy or sluggish depending entirely on whether the agents run side by side or in a line.

⚙️ In production

Make the trade-off a measured decision. Before shipping any multi-agent design, put a number on both sides. Measure the single-agent baseline's quality (task success on a labelled set), its cost, and its p95 latency; then measure the multi-agent version the same way. Ship the bigger design only when the quality gain is real and the task's value covers the ~15× token bill — not because it looks sophisticated.

Governing the spend at scale. Route by value: BankAssist sends high-volume "what's my balance?" traffic to a single agent, and reserves the orchestrator-with-workers design for the handful of deep fraud investigations a week where thoroughness saves millions. Enforce per-request and per-tenant token budgets, alarm on cost-per-resolved-request drifting up, and dashboard tokens and latency split by architecture so a creeping multi-agent bill is visible long before finance notices.

Compliance angle. More agents means more surface to govern — each sub-agent's prompts, tools, and data access must pass the same model-risk review as the whole. A simple architecture isn't only cheaper to run; it is cheaper to approve and to defend to a regulator.

⚠ Watch out

The commonest expensive mistake in this whole field is reaching for a multi-agent design to look sophisticated, on a task a single well-built agent would handle for a fraction of the cost and latency. More agents is a cost you justify with a measured quality gain — never a default, and never a flex.

🧠 Remember it

Every agent is a bill. Multi-agent ≈ 15× the tokens. Spend it only where the task is valuable, divisible, and too hard for one loop.

Human-in-the-loop: approval gates, pause & resume

For anything that moves money or can't be undone, the agent stops, asks a person, and only continues once they say yes — and it can survive a crash while it waits.

Autonomy is wonderful right up until an agent does something irreversible with someone's money. In banking there's a bright line: some actions — large transfers, account closures, data exports, limit increases — must have a human's sign-off. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is how you draw that line in the architecture itself. The agent is free to think, gather, and propose; but before it acts on anything high-risk, it pauses and hands the decision to a person.

Approval gates — ask before you act

The core move is a risk-tiered gate. Not every action needs approval — gating everything just trains humans to rubber-stamp, which is worse than no gate. Instead, you tier by risk: auto-approve the low-stakes stuff, require a human for the dangerous stuff.

# Risk-tiered approval: cheap actions auto-pass, risky ones wait for a human.
def execute_transfer(amount, to_account, user):
    if amount <= 100:                      # low risk → let the agent proceed on its own
        return do_transfer(amount, to_account)      # fast path for everyday small moves

    approval = request_human_approval({    # high risk → PAUSE and ask a person
        "action": "transfer",
        "amount": amount,                  # show the human exactly what will happen
        "to": to_account,                  # enough context to judge — not just "approve?"
        "requested_by": user,
    })
