No framework means no surprise upgrades, no hidden prompt text, no mystery token spend — all things a compliance team loves.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's first production feature — "check my balance and recent transactions" — shipped as a hand-written tool-use loop over the Messages API: a few tools, a while loop, full logging the audit team could read line by line. Only when the roadmap added multi-step dispute handling with human approval did the team adopt LangGraph for that one workflow — and kept the simple loop for the simple feature. Two tools, each matched to its job. That restraint is the senior move.

✅ Tip

Start with no framework or the lightest one that fits. Add orchestration only when a real need appears (durable state, human approval, many agents). It's far easier to adopt a framework later than to tear one out of a system that outgrew it.

💡 Key idea

Frameworks are accelerators, not requirements. The best engineers pick the smallest tool that solves today's problem and leave room to grow — and sometimes that tool is a plain while loop.

🧠 Remember it

Choose by the hard part, not the hype. And remember: "none" is on the menu.

🧩 One more to know — Agno

Agno is a lightweight, high-performance Python framework for building agents: very fast agent instantiation, model-agnostic (swap OpenAI, Anthropic, or local models), with memory, knowledge/RAG, tools, and multi-agent "teams" built in. Reach for it when you want a small, quick footprint without the heavier abstractions of LangChain or the ceremony of a graph engine. For a bank, treat it like any framework dependency: pin the version, and keep money-moving tools behind your own authorization and audit regardless of what the framework makes easy.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

LangChain middleware — the one way to shape an agent in v1

Middleware is LangChain 1.0's big idea: small, stackable pieces of code that sit around the agent loop and let you add safety, budgets, retries, and routing without rewriting the agent.

A bare create_agent is a clean loop: think, call a tool, read the result, repeat. But a real BankAssist agent needs more: scrub card numbers before they hit the model, cap how many times it can call the model (money!), fall back to a cheaper model if the main one hiccups, and stop early after hours. In 2026 the answer to all of these is the same mechanism — middleware. It replaced the old one-off pre_model_hook/post_model_hook arguments entirely.

🏦 Picture this

Compliance hands you a list: "never send a full card number to a third-party model, never let one chat burn more than six model calls, and if the primary model errors, don't just fail — try the backup." You don't want that logic smeared through your tool functions. You want it as four tidy layers you can switch on, test, and audit one by one. That's middleware.

In plain terms

Think of middleware as security checkpoints wrapped around the model. Every request to the model walks out through your layers and every response walks back in through them. Each layer can look, change, block, or re-route — and you stack as many as you like.

The six hook types

There are two families of hook. Node-style hooks run at a fixed moment and return a state update (or None for "no change"):

  • before_agent — once, before the whole run starts.
  • before_model — before each model call.
  • after_model — after each model response.
  • after_agent — once, after the run finishes.

Wrap-style hooks surround a call and decide whether (and how) the real call even happens:

  • wrap_model_call — wraps each model call (retry it, swap the model, edit the response).
  • wrap_tool_call — wraps each tool call (retry a flaky tool, redact its output).

Ordering, decorators, and jump_to

Order matters and follows one rule: before_* hooks run first-to-last, after_* hooks run last-to-first, and wrap_* hooks nest — so the first middleware in your list is the outermost layer. For quick custom hooks you don't write a class; you use a decorator (@before_model, @after_model, @wrap_tool_call, and @dynamic_prompt for a system prompt that changes per turn).

A hook can also re-route the agent by returning {"jump_to": ...}. The three targets are "model" (jump to the model step), "tools" (jump to the tool step), and "end" (finish now). You must declare in advance which jumps a hook may make, with can_jump_to=[...].

from langchain.agents.middleware import before_model, AgentState  # decorator + the typed state
from langgraph.runtime import Runtime                    # gives the hook access to run context

@before_model(can_jump_to=["end"])                       # declare the jumps this hook is allowed to make
def block_after_hours(state: AgentState, runtime: Runtime): # runs before every model call
    if is_after_hours():                                 # a bank rule: no wire transfers after 5pm
        return {"jump_to": "end",                        # skip the model entirely and finish the run
                "messages": [{"role": "assistant",       # leave a polite final message
                    "content": "Wires are processed 9-5. I've logged your request."}]}
    return None                                          # None = no change, carry on normally

The built-ins you'll actually reach for

You rarely write your own. LangChain ships a shelf of middleware that covers most of a bank's production and security needs out of the box:

MiddlewareWhat it does for a bank
PIIMiddlewareDetect and redact / mask / hash / block PII (card numbers, emails, SSNs) before it reaches the model
ModelCallLimitMiddleware / ToolCallLimitMiddlewareHard budgets — cap model/tool calls per run or per thread so a loop can't run up the bill
ModelRetryMiddleware / ToolRetryMiddlewareAutomatically retry a failed model or tool call with backoff
ModelFallbackMiddlewareIf the primary model errors, transparently switch to a backup model
ContextEditingMiddleware (ClearToolUsesEdit)Prune old tool results from the context window once it gets long
LLMToolSelectorMiddlewareWhen the toolbox is big, use a cheap LLM pass to pre-pick the few relevant tools
SummarizationMiddlewareSummarise long histories so the conversation fits the window
HumanInTheLoopMiddlewarePause for human approval on sensitive tool calls
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langchain.agents.middleware import (                 # the built-in shelf
    PIIMiddleware, ModelCallLimitMiddleware, ModelFallbackMiddleware)

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1",                                # OpenAI as the default primary
    tools=[get_balance, open_dispute],
    middleware=[                                          # order = outermost first
        PIIMiddleware("credit_card", strategy="redact"), # scrub card numbers out before the model sees them
        PIIMiddleware("email", strategy="mask"),         # mask emails (keep shape, hide value)
        ModelCallLimitMiddleware(run_limit=6),           # never more than 6 model calls per run
        ModelFallbackMiddleware("openai:gpt-4.1-mini"),    # if gpt-4.1 errors, retry on the mini
    ],
)
⚙️ Under the hood — node hooks vs wrap hooks

The split is about power. A node hook (before_model, after_model) sees the state at a moment and returns an update — perfect for "look and tweak." A wrap hook (wrap_model_call, wrap_tool_call) is handed the actual call and a handler function; it decides whether to call it, can call it several times (that's how retry and fallback work), and can rewrite the result. That's why ModelFallbackMiddleware is a wrap hook: it catches the error from handler() and calls again with a different model. Because create_agent compiles to a LangGraph graph, every middleware hook is really just extra nodes and edges woven into that graph.

In production

Middleware is where your cross-cutting concerns live, so treat it like infrastructure. Order is a decision: put PII redaction outermost so nothing downstream ever sees raw secrets; put budgets early so they trip before you spend. Test each layer alone — a middleware that silently swallows a jump_to can make an agent "mysteriously" stop. Cost: LLMToolSelectorMiddleware and SummarizationMiddleware add their own model calls, so they pay off only when the toolbox or history is genuinely large. And audit: for a regulator, "we redact card numbers in a named, tested middleware layer applied to every agent" is a far stronger story than redaction scattered through business logic.

⚠ Watch out

The old pre_model_hook / post_model_hook arguments are gone — everything is middleware now. A hook that returns a jump_to it didn't declare in can_jump_to is an error. And remember the asymmetry: list order is first-to-last for before_* but the reverse for after_* — the first middleware wraps all the others.

When to use it — and when not

Use middleware for anything cross-cutting: safety, PII, budgets, retries, fallbacks, routing, dynamic prompts, context pruning. Don't hide core business logic in it — a tool that opens a dispute is a tool, not a middleware. And if you only need one tiny tweak, a single @before_model decorator beats a full class.

🧠 Remember it

Middleware = checkpoints around the model. before goes in order, after goes in reverse, wrap nests — and jump_to is the emergency exit.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

ToolRuntime and Deep Agents — tools that see state, agents that go deep

Two v1 upgrades: ToolRuntime is the single, clean way for a tool to reach the agent's state and memory, and Deep Agents is a batteries-included harness for long, multi-step work.

A tool is usually a plain function — get_balance(account_id). But real banking tools need context the model shouldn't supply: who is asking (so you don't leak another customer's data), the saved preferences from past chats, the live conversation so far. In 2024 you reached for a grab-bag of annotations — InjectedState, InjectedStore, InjectedToolCallId, get_runtime(). In v1 there is one tidy replacement: ToolRuntime.

ToolRuntime: one injected parameter

Add a runtime: ToolRuntime parameter to your tool. LangChain fills it in at call time, and — crucially — it's hidden from the model's tool schema, so the model never tries to supply it. Through it you reach everything the tool needs.

from langchain.tools import tool, ToolRuntime             # the tool decorator + the injected runtime

@tool
def recent_transactions(limit: int, runtime: ToolRuntime) -> str: # model only sees "limit"; runtime is injected
    """Return the customer's recent transactions."""     # docstring is still the model-facing description
    customer = runtime.context.customer_id               # .context = per-run, immutable (who's calling)
    currency = runtime.store.get(("prefs", customer), "currency")  # .store = long-term cross-session memory
    recent = runtime.state["messages"][-3:]              # .state = the live conversation so far
    return fetch_txns(customer, limit, currency)         # now safe: the ID came from context, not the model

The pieces on runtime: .state (the live graph state), .context (per-run data you passed in, like a verified customer_id or a DB handle), .store (long-term memory that survives across sessions), plus .stream_writer (emit progress), .tool_call_id, and .execution_info. One parameter, everything in reach.

⚠ Watch out

A 2024 tools tutorial that annotates arguments with InjectedState, InjectedStore, InjectedToolCallId, or calls get_runtime() is the stale pattern — all of it is unified under ToolRuntime now. And pulling a verified identity from runtime.context instead of a model-supplied argument isn't just tidy — it's a security control: the model can't spoof an account ID it was never allowed to set.

Deep Agents: a harness for long-horizon work

Some BankAssist jobs are big: "investigate this fraud complaint" might mean reading ten documents, checking five accounts, writing notes, and composing a report. A plain agent loop drowns — its context window fills with tool output and it loses the plot. Deep Agents (create_deep_agent, in the deepagents package) is a prebuilt layer that adds the three things long tasks need.

from deepagents import create_deep_agent                  # pip install deepagents

investigator = create_deep_agent(
    tools=[search_policies, get_balance, get_transactions], # your real banking tools
    instructions="You are BankAssist's fraud-complaint investigator.", # appended to the built-in harness prompt
    subagents=[...],                                     # optional: named specialists for isolated sub-tasks
)
result = investigator.invoke(                             # same invoke shape as any create_agent
    {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Investigate complaint #4412 end to end."}]})
⚙️ Under the hood — three middleware, always on

create_deep_agent is really create_agent with three middleware baked in: TodoListMiddleware (a write_todos tool so the agent plans and tracks pending/in-progress/done steps), FilesystemMiddleware (virtual ls/read_file/write_file/edit_file/glob/grep tools — a scratchpad to offload context instead of stuffing the window), and SubAgentMiddleware (a task tool that hands a sub-job to a subagent with its own clean context, then returns just the answer). It's the open-source cousin of how coding agents like Claude Code stay coherent over long jobs. The filesystem is pluggable — back it with real storage in production.

In production

Deep Agents trade tokens for coherence: planning and subagent calls cost extra model calls, so reserve the harness for genuinely long, multi-document tasks — a simple balance lookup doesn't need it. Point the filesystem at durable, access-controlled storage (not a process-local scratch), because for a bank those intermediate notes may be discoverable records. And keep the same middleware discipline from before: PII redaction and call budgets apply here too — a deep agent that fans out to subagents can multiply your spend fast.

When to use it — and when not

Use ToolRuntime in every v1 tool that needs identity, memory, or live state. Use Deep Agents for long-horizon investigation, research, or report-writing where context would otherwise overflow. Don't wheel out a deep agent for a one-shot question — the planning and filesystem overhead is pure cost there.

🧠 Remember it

ToolRuntime = one backpack holding state, context, and store. Deep Agents = plan, park, delegate — a to-do list, a filesystem, and subagents.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Structured output strategies & content blocks — typed in, typed out

Two provider-neutral upgrades in LangChain v1: ask an agent for a validated typed object with response_format, and read a model's reply through the typed content_blocks view instead of a raw string.

Banks want structure on both ends. On the way out of an agent, a dispute should come back as a record with a category and an amount — not a paragraph you have to re-parse. On the way in, when a model reasons or cites a policy, you want to read that reasoning and those citations in a clean, portable shape for your audit log. LangChain v1 has a first-class answer to each.

Structured output: ToolStrategy vs ProviderStrategy

Pass response_format to create_agent and the final answer is validated against your schema and handed back under structured_response. The clever part is how it's produced, and v1 gives two strategies:

ProviderStrategy

Uses the model's native structured-output feature (OpenAI, Anthropic, and other capable providers). Most reliable — the provider guarantees the shape.

ToolStrategy

Gets structure by making the model call a tool whose arguments are your schema. Works with any tool-calling model, so it's the universal fallback.

If you just pass a schema, LangChain auto-picks: ProviderStrategy when the provider supports native output, ToolStrategy otherwise. Either way the result is generated inside the agent loop — no extra LLM round-trip, so it's cheaper than a separate "now format this" call.

from langchain.agents import create_agent
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Dispute(BaseModel):                                 # the exact shape we want back
    category: str                                        # e.g. "duplicate charge"
    amount: float                                        # validated as a number
    urgent: bool                                         # validated as true/false

agent = create_agent(
    model="openai:gpt-4.1",
    tools=[lookup_merchant],
    response_format=Dispute,                             # bare schema → auto-selects the best strategy
)
out = agent.invoke({"messages": [{"role": "user",
    "content": "I was charged $450 twice at a hotel, please fix this fast!"}]})
print(out["structured_response"])                        # a validated Dispute, not a string to re-parse
▶ Output
category='duplicate charge' amount=450.0 urgent=True

Want to force one? Wrap it: response_format=ProviderStrategy(Dispute) or ToolStrategy(Dispute). A raw JSON-Schema dict isn't auto-detected — you must wrap it in a strategy explicitly. ToolStrategy also accepts a Union of several schemas (let the model pick which record type fits) and has built-in retry handling when validation fails.

Content blocks: one typed view across every provider

Reading a model's raw .content is a mess — every provider shapes reasoning, citations, and tool results differently. LangChain v1 adds message.content_blocks: a typed, provider-neutral list of blocks you can read the same way whether you're on OpenAI or Anthropic.

Block typeWhat it carries
textNormal output; citations ride in its annotations list
reasoningThe model's thinking trace (gold for an audit trail)
refusalAn explicit refusal, flagged as such
image / audio / video / fileMultimodal content
tool_callA tool the model wants you to run
server_tool_call / server_tool_resultA tool the provider ran server-side (e.g. hosted web search) and its result
non_standardThe escape hatch for anything provider-specific
for block in msg.content_blocks:                          # the typed, provider-neutral view
    if block["type"] == "reasoning":                     # capture the model's thinking...
        audit_log.record("reasoning", block["reasoning"]) # ...straight into the compliance trail
    elif block["type"] == "text":                        # the customer-facing answer
        for cite in block.get("annotations", []):        # citations live here, not as a separate block
            audit_log.record("cited", cite)              # which policy doc backed the answer
    elif block["type"] == "server_tool_result":          # e.g. a provider-run search
        audit_log.record("server_tool", block)
⚙️ Under the hood — opt-in serialization

.content_blocks is a view: it lazily derives the standard blocks from whatever the provider returned, so it's always available to read without changing anything. What's not on by default is writing those blocks back into the serialized .content — you opt in with output_version="v1" (on init_chat_model) or the LC_OUTPUT_VERSION=v1 env var. Turn it on when you want systems outside LangChain to read the standardized shape from the stored message.

In production

For a regulated bank these two features close real gaps. Typed output means a dispute or a risk rating lands in your database already validated — no brittle regex, no "the model wrote the number as words" incident. The content-block view means reasoning traces, citations, and server-tool results are first-class, auditable fields instead of strings you scrape. Cost note: ToolStrategy spends the tokens of a tool call to get its structure, and a weak model can fail validation and retry — so prefer a capable model (ProviderStrategy) for high-volume structured extraction.

⚠ Watch out

Don't pass a raw JSON-Schema dict to response_format expecting auto-selection — wrap it in ToolStrategy/ProviderStrategy. And don't read .content expecting the new typed structure: the typed shape is on .content_blocks, and writing it into .content needs the output_version="v1" opt-in.

When to use it — and when not

Use response_format whenever a downstream system needs a record, not prose. Use content_blocks whenever you need portable reasoning/citation/tool data — especially for audit. Don't force a schema onto a free-form chat reply, and don't reach for content blocks if a plain string answer is all you'll ever store.

🧠 Remember it

Provider = native, Tool = universal. And read the reply as blocks, not a string — reasoning and citations are in there, typed.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

LangGraph streaming — showing your work as it happens

LangGraph can stream a running graph in several modes at once — the finished state, the per-step deltas, the model's tokens, or your own custom progress messages — so a long workflow never looks frozen.

A BankAssist dispute workflow might take ninety seconds: verify identity, pull transactions, score fraud risk, draft a resolution. If the customer stares at a dead spinner that whole time, it feels broken. Streaming is how you turn that wait into a live progress feed — and LangGraph gives you a few different "channels" to stream, each answering a different question.

The modes

  • values — the full state after each step (good for "show me everything so far").
  • updates — just the change each node made, keyed by node name (good for a step tracker).
  • messages — the model's tokens as they're generated, anywhere in the graph, as (token, metadata) pairs you can filter by node.
  • custom — whatever you emit from inside a node via the stream writer (your own progress text).
  • tasks and checkpoints — lower-level events for debugging and observability (debug bundles both).
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "dispute-4412"}}
for mode, chunk in graph.stream(                          # ask for TWO modes at once → get (mode, chunk) tuples
        inputs, cfg, stream_mode=["updates", "custom"]):
    if mode == "updates":                                # a node just finished...
        print("step done:", chunk)                       # ...here's which node + its state delta
    elif mode == "custom":                               # a node emitted a progress note
        print("progress:", chunk)                        # push this straight to the customer's screen

To emit those custom notes, grab the writer inside a node — this is how you stream progress from the middle of a slow tool, not just at step boundaries:

from langgraph.config import get_stream_writer            # the in-node progress channel

def run_fraud_checks(state):
    writer = get_stream_writer()                          # grab the custom-stream writer
    writer({"progress": "checking device fingerprint"})   # surfaces instantly as a custom chunk
    score = score_fraud(state["txns"])                    # the slow work
    writer({"progress": "scoring complete"})              # another live update mid-node
    return {"fraud_score": score}
⚙️ Under the hood — modes vs the event stream

stream_mode is the everyday API. Under it sits a finer-grained one, astream_events, which emits a typed event for every step — model start/stream/end, tool start/end, chain boundaries — each tagged with the node and any tags you set. It takes a version= argument (pass "v2"; the API is still evolving). Reach for it when you need deep per-event hooks, like a custom trace exporter; reach for stream_mode for normal UI streaming. You can also mark a node or model not to stream its tokens when you don't want internal chatter leaking to the user.

In production

Streaming is a latency illusion that's worth real money: time-to-first-token is what customers feel, so stream messages for the final answer and custom for the long middle. Because messages streams tokens from anywhere — including tools and subgraphs — filter by node so you don't accidentally stream an internal reasoning step to a customer. Over a network, wrap the stream so a dropped connection resumes from the checkpoint rather than restarting the ninety-second job.

⚠ Watch out

On async Python older than 3.11, get_stream_writer() can't find the context — add a writer parameter to your node and pass it explicitly instead. And when you combine modes you get (mode, chunk) tuples, not bare chunks — forgetting that is a classic "why is my loop unpacking wrong" bug.

When to use it — and when not

Use updates for a step tracker, messages for a typewriter-style answer, and custom for progress from inside slow tools. Don't bother streaming a sub-second single call — the plumbing isn't worth it — and don't stream internal reasoning to end users without filtering by node first.

🧠 Remember it

Four lenses on one run: values = everything, updates = the diff, messages = the tokens, custom = your own play-by-play.

🏭 production

LangGraph durability & fan-out — tuning safety vs speed, and parallel work

Two production dials: durability modes let you trade checkpoint safety against speed, and the Send API fans one node out across many items for map-reduce-style parallelism.

LangGraph saves a checkpoint so a crashed run can resume. What's less obvious is that "durable" isn't all-or-nothing — how often it saves is a knob you turn. And when BankAssist needs to screen fifty transactions at once, you don't want a slow for-loop; you want them checked in parallel. Both are everyday production LangGraph.

Durability modes: exit, async, sync

Set durability= on invoke/stream to choose when checkpoints get written. Stronger modes survive more failures but add overhead:

ModeWhen it savesTrade-off
"exit"Only when the run finishes (or errors/interrupts)Fastest; no mid-run recovery — a crash loses intermediate state
"async"In the background while the next step runsGood speed and durability; a tiny crash window
"sync"Before the next step startsStrongest guarantee; some performance cost
cfg = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "wire-99"}}
graph.invoke(inputs, cfg, durability="sync")             # a $2M wire: write the checkpoint BEFORE each next step
graph.invoke(inputs, cfg, durability="async")            # a chat reply: background writes, barely any overhead
graph.invoke(inputs, cfg, durability="exit")             # a short, retryable batch: only persist at the end

This replaced the old boolean checkpoint_during flag. The rule of thumb: money and compliance → sync; most interactive work → async; cheap, idempotent (safe to run more than once), easily-restarted jobs → exit.

The Send API: map-reduce fan-out

A conditional edge usually picks one next node. The Send API instead launches a node once per item, each with its own input — even when you only learn the count at runtime. The parallel results merge back through a reducer, and a node marked defer=True waits until every branch is done before it runs (the "reduce" step).

import operator
from typing import Annotated, TypedDict
from langgraph.types import Send                           # the fan-out primitive

class State(TypedDict):
    transactions: list
    results: Annotated[list, operator.add]                 # reducer: parallel results CONCATENATE, not clobber

def fan_out(state):                                        # count is known only at runtime
    return [Send("screen_txn", {"txn": t})                 # one screen_txn run per transaction...
            for t in state["transactions"]]                # ...each with its own tiny input

builder.add_conditional_edges("load", fan_out, ["screen_txn"]) # the map step
builder.add_node("summarize", summarize, defer=True)       # the reduce step: waits for ALL branches
builder.add_edge("screen_txn", "summarize")
⚙️ Under the hood — why you need a reducer

When many screen_txn branches finish at once, they all try to write results. Without a reducer that's an InvalidUpdateError (two writers, one key). The Annotated[list, operator.add] reducer says "merge by concatenation," so every branch's finding is kept. defer=True is the clean alternative to a hand-rolled "have we finished yet?" counter: the node simply doesn't run until no tasks are pending anywhere in the graph — ideal when branches finish at different times.

In production

Fan-out is where cost and rate limits bite: fifty parallel screen_txn nodes can mean fifty concurrent model calls, so cap concurrency and expect provider throttling. Pair the two dials thoughtfully — a fan-out of risky writes probably wants durability="sync" so a crash mid-batch is recoverable; a fan-out of cheap read-only checks is fine on exit. And keep each Send payload small: you're copying input per branch, so pass an ID, not a megabyte of data.

⚠ Watch out

exit durability means no recovery from a mid-run crash — never use it for money movement. Fan-out without a reducer on the shared key throws InvalidUpdateError. And checkpoint_during= is deprecated — use durability=.

When to use it — and when not

Use sync durability for high-stakes steps, async as the sensible default, exit only for cheap restartable work. Use Send when the number of parallel sub-tasks is dynamic (N transactions, M documents). Don't fan out a fixed, tiny set — ordinary parallel edges are simpler — and don't reach for a deferred node when a plain edge already guarantees ordering.

🧠 Remember it

Durability: exit = fast, sync = safe, async = both-ish. Send = map, defer=True = reduce.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Shipping a LangGraph app — Assistants, config, and where your data lives

Deploying a graph means three things: a langgraph.json that describes your app, Assistants that version its config apart from its code, and a hosting choice that decides which country your customers' data sits in.

A graph that runs on your laptop is one thing; a graph a regulated bank runs in production is another. You need to declare what to deploy, ship per-customer or per-environment variations without forking the code, call the deployed graph from elsewhere, and — the question a bank asks first — guarantee that customer data never leaves an approved region. LangGraph's deployment surface (the managed server was renamed LangSmith Deployment in late 2025) answers each.

langgraph.json — the deployment manifest

A small file tells the server what your app is: its dependencies, which graphs to expose (and where to find them), and the env file.

{
  "dependencies": ["."],                                 # install this project
  "graphs": {"bankassist": "./app/graph.py:graph"},      # expose the "graph" object as "bankassist"
  "env": ".env"                                           # where secrets/config come from
}

Assistants — versioned config, not versioned code

This is the clean idea most people miss. An Assistant is a saved configuration of a graph — its model, its system prompt, its settings — kept separate from the graph's logic. One graph can back many assistants: a conservative config for retail customers, a higher-limit one for private banking, a cheap one for the staging environment, an A/B variant. Editing an assistant creates a new version, and you can promote or roll back between versions — so a bad prompt change is a one-click revert, not a redeploy.

from langgraph_sdk import get_client                       # the deployment SDK
client = get_client(url="https://deploy.bank.internal")   # point at your deployment

assistant = await client.assistants.create(               # a new config of the SAME graph
    "bankassist",                                         # which graph (from langgraph.json)
    config={"configurable": {"model": "openai:gpt-4.1",     # this assistant's settings...
                             "daily_limit": 250000}})      # ...e.g. private-banking limits
# editing it later creates a new VERSION you can promote or roll back

Note: Assistants are a deployment feature, not part of the open-source LangGraph library — they exist once your graph is deployed.

RemoteGraph — call a deployed graph like a local one

Once deployed, a graph is reachable as a RemoteGraph that behaves exactly like a local graph — invoke, stream, the lot — and can even be dropped in as a node inside another graph. That's how one team's deployed fraud-scoring graph becomes a subgraph in another team's workflow.

from langgraph.pregel.remote import RemoteGraph            # client-side handle to a deployed graph

fraud = RemoteGraph("fraud_scorer", url="https://deploy.bank.internal") # looks local, runs remote
fraud.invoke({"txns": [...]})                              # same API as any graph — can also be a node elsewhere

Where the data lives — the topology choice

  • Cloud — LangChain runs everything; you pick US or EU data residency. Simplest, fastest to ship.
  • Hybrid — the control plane (orchestration, UI) stays in LangChain's cloud, but the data plane runs in your own VPC (virtual private cloud — your walled-off slice of a cloud provider), so customer data and execution stay on your infrastructure. The data plane polls the control plane over HTTPS. A common fit when you want a managed experience and residency control.
  • Self-hosted — you run the entire stack in your own infrastructure; nothing leaves. Maximum control and isolation.

Hybrid and self-hosted are Enterprise-tier. For a bank, this choice usually comes before any code: "customer PII must stay in-region and in our VPC" points straight at hybrid or self-hosted.

⚙️ Under the hood — control plane vs data plane

The split that makes hybrid work: the control plane is the brains that schedule and manage deployments; the data plane is where your graph actually executes and where state (threads, checkpoints) is stored. In hybrid, only the data plane touches customer data, and it pulls instructions from the control plane over outbound HTTPS — so you don't have to open inbound holes in your network, and the sensitive bytes never leave your VPC. Note that in hybrid, observability traces still flow to the managed side, so check what metadata that includes against your policy.

In production

Three habits. Treat assistants as config-as-data: version them, and make "promote/rollback" your fast path for prompt and model changes — far safer than redeploying code to tweak a prompt. Use stateless runs by default and reach for threads only when you need conversation memory, to keep the deployment lean. And decide residency with compliance first: the topology is hard to change later, and "which region, which VPC, which traces leave the building" are audit questions you'll answer for the life of the system.

⚠ Watch out

The names moved: it's LangSmith Deployment now, not "LangGraph Cloud/Platform." Assistants live in the deployment, not the open-source library. And don't point a RemoteGraph at its own deployment — a graph calling itself through RemoteGraph can deadlock; use a local subgraph for same-deployment composition.

When to use it — and when not

Use the managed deployment when you want persistence, REST endpoints, and Studio without building them; use assistants to ship environment/customer variants cleanly; use hybrid or self-hosted when residency rules demand it. Don't stand up the full platform for a prototype — a local langgraph dev server is plenty until you have real traffic and real compliance needs.

🧠 Remember it

langgraph.json says what, Assistants version the config, RemoteGraph makes remote feel local — and the topology (Cloud → Hybrid → Self-hosted) decides where your data sleeps.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Low-code & visual agent builders — LangFlow, Flowise & n8n

Instead of writing the agent in Python, you draw it: drag boxes onto a canvas, wire them together, and the tool runs the same model-call / tool-use / retrieval primitives for you — great for prototyping and for business-owned flows, risky for anything that needs real versioning, testing, or scale.

Everything so far in this chapter has been code: imports, functions, graphs you type out. But a huge amount of AI work in 2026 is built by people who don't want to open an editor — product managers, operations analysts, support leads. For them a new breed of tool exists: the visual, low-code builder. You open a blank canvas in your browser, drag in a box for "the model," a box for "search our documents," a box for "call this tool," and draw arrows between them. Hit run and you have a working agent — no pip install, no deployment script, no pull request.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist gets thousands of written complaints a month — "my card was declined," "I was double-charged," "your app logged me out." Someone has to read each one, decide which team it belongs to (cards, payments, fraud, app support), set a priority, and draft a first reply. The rules for that routing change constantly as policy shifts — and the people who know the rules are the complaints-ops team, not the engineers. Visual builders let that ops team own and edit the routing flow themselves, while engineers keep their hands firmly on anything that touches money.

In plain terms — what a visual builder actually is

Think of it as LEGO for AI apps. Each brick (the tools call them nodes or components) is a pre-built piece — a model call, a document retriever, an HTTP request, an if/else branch, a memory store. You snap bricks together on a canvas instead of importing classes and calling methods. The canvas is the program. Under the hood these builders are almost always wrapping a code framework you already met — most of them sit on LangChain (and some on LlamaIndex) — so the boxes you drag are really create_agent, a retriever, and a tool-call loop wearing a friendly face.

The three you'll actually meet

LangFlow

A Python, open-source (MIT) visual builder for LangChain, now stewarded by DataStax (part of IBM). Its party trick: every flow can be exported — as JSON to move between environments, or as LangChain Python code — and served as a REST endpoint (POST /api/v1/run/<flow-id>) or even as an MCP server. Closest to "visual, but you can escape to code."

Flowise

A Node/JavaScript, open-source drag-and-drop platform, also built on LangChain (with LlamaIndex components). It splits work into a Chatflow (single agent/chatbot/RAG) and an Agentflow (multi-agent, a superset). Ships 100+ LLM, embedding, and vector-DB nodes, with embeddable chat widgets and a code-fallback node for custom JS/Python.

n8n is the odd one out — and often the most useful. It's a general workflow-automation tool (think "connect 500+ apps: Gmail, Salesforce, Slack, your database") that added first-class AI Agent nodes built on LangChain's JavaScript library. So the same canvas that moves a row from a form into your CRM can also pass a complaint through an LLM, branch on its category, and open a ticket — AI as one step in a broader business process, not the whole app. It's fair-code (the Sustainable Use License): the Community Edition is free to self-host; SSO, audit logs, and the like sit behind the Enterprise license.

ToolRuns onSweet spotEscape hatch
LangFlowPython / LangChainPrototyping LangChain RAG & agent flowsExport to Python or JSON
FlowiseNode.js / LangChainChatbots, RAG, multi-agent chatflowsCustom JS/Python node
n8nNode.js (AI nodes on LangChain)AI stitched into real business automationCode node + 500+ app integrations

Calling what you built — the flow becomes an API

The whole point of the export/deploy step is that your drawn flow turns into something the rest of the bank's systems can call like any other service. In LangFlow, for example, a published flow is just an HTTP endpoint — here's the ops team's complaint-router being called from a small Python service that engineers own:

import os, requests                                      # requests for the HTTP call; os for the key

FLOW_URL = "https://flows.bank.internal/api/v1/run/complaint-router"  # the flow the OPS team drew & published
headers = {"x-api-key": os.environ["LANGFLOW_API_KEY"]} # auth handled in OUR code, not the canvas

payload = {                                              # the request body the flow expects
    "input_value": "I was charged twice for the same transfer!", # the raw complaint text
    "input_type": "chat",                               # tell the flow this is a chat input
    "output_type": "chat",                              # we want the chat-style result back
}

resp = requests.post(FLOW_URL, json=payload, headers=headers, timeout=30) # call the flow; cap the wait
resp.raise_for_status()                                  # turn a 4xx/5xx into an error WE log & alert on
routed = resp.json()                                     # the flow's decision: {category, priority, draft_reply}
print(routed["category"], routed["priority"])           # e.g. "payments" "high" — now hand to our ticket system
▶ Output
payments high

Read what just happened: the business logic (how to classify and prioritise a complaint) lives on a canvas the ops team maintains, but the plumbing around it — the API key, the timeout, the error handling, the alerting, the hand-off to the real ticketing system — lives in engineer-owned code. That boundary is the entire art of using these tools safely in a bank.

⚙️ Under the hood — they generate the same primitives

A visual builder isn't a different kind of AI — it's a graphical front-end over the exact primitives in the rest of this chapter. A LangFlow or Flowise "Agent" node compiles to a LangChain tool-calling agent; a "Retriever" node is a vector-store retriever; a "Prompt" node is a prompt template; an "if" node is a conditional edge. n8n's AI Agent node is literally LangChain under the covers, with dropdowns to pick the agent type, the model, and the memory. That's why export-to-code works at all: the canvas is already describing a graph of Runnables, so it can serialise to JSON (to move between environments) or emit the Python/JS that builds the same thing. The friendly boxes and the code you'd hand-write are two views of one underlying graph.

🧠 Remember it

Low-code is the same engine with a steering wheel instead of a wrench. Let the business drive the flow; keep engineers under the hood of anything that moves money.

When they're the right tool — and when to drop to code

✅ Reach for a visual builder

  • Non-engineers own the logic — ops, support, marketing can edit it without a release.
  • Fast prototyping — prove a RAG or routing idea in an afternoon, demo it, then decide.
  • Business-owned, frequently-tweaked flows — routing rules, FAQ bots, internal helpers.
  • Glue work — n8n shines when AI is one step among many app integrations.

🛠 Drop to code instead

  • Complex control flow — deep branching, loops, retries, long-running state (that's LangGraph).
  • Serious versioning & testing — code review, unit tests, CI/CD, reproducible builds.
  • High scale & tight latency/cost control — you need to tune the loop, not a dropdown.
  • Audit & regulation — money movement, where every change needs a signed, traceable trail.

In production — export, deploy & governance

Prototyping is the easy 20%; running a visual flow for real customers is where the questions get sharp. Deployment: all three self-host (Docker is the common path), so a bank can keep the canvas and the data inside its own network rather than a vendor cloud — important when complaints contain PII. Promotion: treat the exported JSON as the artifact — move it dev → staging → prod through your normal release process, instead of hand-editing boxes straight in production. Access & secrets: API keys, model credentials, and database connections should live in the platform's credential store (or injected env vars), never typed into a node that anyone with canvas access can read; lock down who can edit flows, and keep SSO/audit features (Enterprise tier on n8n) on for anything customer-facing. Observability: wire the flow's calls into the same tracing and alerting as your coded services — a flow that silently starts mis-routing fraud complaints is a very expensive kind of quiet failure. And guardrails: the LLM in a box still needs input/output checks (no leaking a full card number, no acting on a prompt-injected complaint), exactly as it would in code.

⚠ Watch out — the real limitations

The friendliness hides four sharp edges. Versioning & diffing: a flow is a big JSON blob — a two-box change produces a messy, unreviewable diff, so "what changed and why" is genuinely hard (n8n's newer draft/publish lifecycle helps, but it's not git). Testing: there's no natural unit test for a canvas; regressions hide until a customer finds them. Scaling & performance: you don't control the agent loop, concurrency, or token spend as finely as in code, and complex logic gets clumsy fast. Vendor lock-in: export-to-code is a convenience, not a guarantee — a non-trivial flow rarely round-trips into clean, maintainable code, so "we'll just export it later" can quietly become a rewrite. Treat a visual flow as a prototype or a business-owned leaf, not the foundation of a core banking system.

How they fit with everything else

Don't think of visual builders as rivals to LangChain or LangGraph — they sit on top of them. A healthy BankAssist uses both, split by ownership and risk: engineers build the money paths (transfers, disputes, anything audited) in versioned, tested LangGraph code; the complaints-ops team maintains the complaint-routing flow visually in LangFlow or n8n; and the two meet at a clean API boundary — the ops flow classifies and drafts, then hands the real action to an engineer-owned service. The visual flow can even expose itself as an MCP server so a coded agent calls it as just another tool. Same primitives, same protocols — different hands on different parts.

⚠ Watch out

"Low-code" is not "no governance." The biggest failure mode in a bank isn't a broken box — it's a well-meaning analyst quietly editing a production flow that touches a customer outcome, with no review, no test, and no audit trail. Draw a hard line: flows that decide are fine for the business to own; flows that act on money belong in code.

When to use it — and when not

Use a visual builder to prototype quickly, to let non-engineers own and iterate on a flow, and to stitch AI into existing business automations (n8n especially). Don't use one as the backbone of a high-scale, heavily-audited, complex-logic system — reach for code (LangGraph for orchestration, the provider SDKs for control) the moment versioning, testing, latency, cost, or compliance become the hard part. The best teams let the two coexist along the money line.

🧠 Remember it

Canvas for the business-owned and fast-moving; code for the complex, scaled, and audited. If it moves money, it lives in git — not on a whiteboard.

🎯 interview 🏭 production

Evaluation & Production — Evaluating Agents

A clever agent demo is easy; a trustworthy one is hard. This chapter is a calm, hands-on tour of how you actually measure whether a banking agent works — not once, but reliably, safely, and the same way tomorrow as today.

Why grading an agent is so much harder than grading an answer

A chatbot gives one reply you can check. An agent takes a whole journey of steps — and there are many right journeys, the same input can go differently each time, and small slips pile up.

Imagine you hire two tellers and give them the same task: "close this customer's duplicate account and move the balance to their main account." You could grade a one-line answer easily — right number or wrong number. But a teller doesn't just say something; they do a sequence of things: look up the customer, verify identity, check the duplicate really is a duplicate, move the money, close the account, confirm. Two good tellers might do these steps in a slightly different order and both be correct. A third might reach the right end but skip identity verification — a disaster hiding behind a happy ending.

That is exactly why evaluating an agent (an AI that reasons, picks tools, and acts in a loop toward a goal) is a different sport from evaluating a single model reply. Three things make it hard:

  • Many valid paths. There is rarely one "correct" sequence. An agent might fetch the balance first or verify identity first and both be fine. So you usually cannot grade by comparing to one fixed script — you have to judge the outcome and the soundness of the path, not an exact match.
  • Non-determinism. Language models sample their next words with some randomness, so the same question can produce different steps on different runs. Run the task once and it passes; run it again and it loops or picks the wrong tool. A single green checkmark tells you almost nothing.
  • Compounding errors. An agent takes many steps, and each step has some chance of going wrong. Those chances multiply. A step that is 95% reliable sounds great — until the task needs ten of them in a row, and 0.95¹⁰ ≈ 60%. Little cracks become big failures over a long trajectory.
🏦 Picture this

The team demos BankAssist Agent handling a card-dispute workflow. It nails it live, everyone claps, it ships. In week one, roughly one in six disputes goes sideways: sometimes it files the dispute before confirming the transaction belongs to the customer, sometimes it loops asking for the card number it already has. Nothing was "broken." The demo was simply one lucky run of a non-deterministic, multi-step process. The team measured capability; production needed reliability.

Going deeper — pass@k vs pass^k

This is the single most important idea in agent evaluation, and it hides in two symbols that look almost the same.

  • pass@k — the task succeeds in at least one of k attempts. This measures best-case capability: "can it ever do this?" Great for research bragging rights.
  • pass^k — the task succeeds in all k attempts. This measures reliability: "will it do this every single time?" This is the one banks care about.

If an agent succeeds on a task with probability p on any given try, then (assuming tries are independent) pass^k = p^k. That exponent is brutal. Watch how fast "pretty good" collapses into "not good enough" as you demand consistency across more runs:

This is not just theory. The public tau-bench benchmark (which tests tool-using agents in realistic retail and airline customer-service domains) popularised pass^k precisely because strong models that look capable at pass^1 fall off sharply by pass^8 — their behaviour wobbles across runs. For a bank, an agent that moves money correctly 9 times out of 10 is not "90% done"; it is a liability.

💡 Key idea

Evaluate an agent on reliability across repeated runs (pass^k), not on one impressive demo (pass@1). A single success proves the task is possible, never that it is safe to ship.

In production

Because runs vary, a production eval never runs a scenario once. It runs each scenario N times (say 5–20), records the success rate and its spread, and gates releases on reliability thresholds — for example, "every money-movement scenario must pass ≥ 19 of 20 runs." You track cost and latency per run too, because an agent that retries forever can be "reliable" and still bankrupt you on tokens. The mental shift: an agent's quality is a distribution, and your job is to measure the shape of it, not sample it once.

⚙️ In production

A reliability-first harness isn't free. Running a golden set of ~300 scenarios 20 times each is 6,000 full agent loops per release — at roughly 8–15 tool calls and 20k–60k tokens each, that is real money (often tens of dollars of model spend and 30–90 minutes of wall-clock on a parallelised runner). BankAssist budgets for it: cheap read-only scenarios run on every merge, the full pass^k gate runs nightly and pre-release. Monitor the spread as well as the mean — a scenario that passes 20/20 one week and 15/20 the next is drifting even while it is still above threshold. Record per-run cost and p95 latency (the slow tail — 95% of runs finish faster than this) beside the success rate, because an agent that reaches "reliable" only by retrying ten times has quietly tripled your cost-to-serve and your tail latency, and in a bank both land on a dashboard someone has to answer for.

⚠ Watch out

Chasing pass^k blindly can push you to over-constrain the agent until it refuses anything unusual — "reliable" because it does almost nothing. Measure reliability and coverage (the fraction of real requests it even attempts). When to lean on pass^k: any flow that moves money, changes account state, or discloses data — demand 19/20 or better. When NOT to over-index on it: low-stakes, read-only, easily-reversible interactions (a balance explanation with a human in the loop), where pass@1 plus live monitoring is enough and a 20× eval bill isn't justified.

🧠 Remember it

pass@k = "can it?" · pass^k = "can it every time?" Banks ship on the hat (^), not the at (@).

Task success: assert on the world, not on the words

The headline metric is simple to say and easy to get wrong: did the agent actually achieve the goal? The trap is checking what it said instead of what it did.

When you grade a plain chatbot, the text is the deliverable. When you grade an agent, the text is just narration — the real deliverable is a change in the world: a payment moved, a card frozen, a dispute case opened, an address updated. So the gold-standard success check reads the final state of the systems the agent touched and asserts it matches what the task wanted.

Here is the mistake that burns teams. An agent ends with: "Done! I've frozen your card and opened a dispute for the $240 charge." It sounds finished. But did it call the freeze tool, or did it just hallucinate a confident summary? If your test only checks the chat text, it passes — and in production a customer's card is still live and draining. This failure is common enough to have a name: the agent that "sounds finished but never performed the action."

❌ Asserting on the chat text

Check: does the reply contain "card frozen"? Fragile and gameable — a fluent lie passes. Wording changes break the test. Proves nothing about the real system.

✅ Asserting on the final state

Check: is card.status == "FROZEN" and does a dispute row exist for $240? This is ground truth — it fails loudly when the action didn't happen, whatever the agent claimed.

The pattern is: run the agent against a sandbox copy of your systems that starts in a known state, let it act, then query that sandbox and assert the end-state. In code it looks refreshingly ordinary — it's just a test:

# A state-based success check for a "freeze card + open dispute" task.
def test_freeze_and_dispute(sandbox):                 # sandbox = a fresh fake of core-banking systems for this run
    sandbox.seed(card_id="C-1001", status="ACTIVE")   # put the world in a KNOWN starting state before the agent runs

    agent.run(                                        # let the agent loop, reason, and call its real tools against the sandbox
        "Freeze card C-1001 and dispute the $240 charge from ACME.",
    )

    card = sandbox.get_card("C-1001")                 # read the ACTUAL end state — not the agent's chat summary
    disputes = sandbox.list_disputes(card_id="C-1001")# read the other side effect we required

    assert card.status == "FROZEN"                    # the card must really be frozen in the system of record
    assert any(d.amount == 240 and d.status == "OPEN" # a dispute for the right amount must really exist and be open
               for d in disputes)
▶ Output
PASSED — card C-1001 status=FROZEN, 1 open dispute for $240.00

Notice there is not one check on the agent's wording. We seeded a known world, let the agent act, then interrogated the world. If the agent had only said it froze the card, card.status would still be "ACTIVE" and the test would fail — exactly as we want.

Going deeper — writing checkable success criteria

State-based checks force a healthy discipline: before you can test a task, you must define what success means as something a program can verify. "Handle the dispute well" is not checkable. "A dispute row exists with status OPEN, amount 240, reason code 10.4, linked to card C-1001" is. Many tasks need a small bundle of assertions: the right side effects happened, the wrong ones did not (no funds moved, no other card touched), and any required artefact (a case ID, a confirmation number) exists. For tasks whose output is free text (a customer explanation), you still assert what you can structurally — it mentions the dispute ID, it does not promise a refund timeline — and leave the softer judgement to a rubric scored by an LLM-as-judge.

⚠ Watch out

Beware the partial-success trap. An agent that froze the card but never opened the dispute is a failure, not "half a pass." Money-touching tasks are all-or-nothing: assert every required end-state, and also assert the forbidden ones didn't happen. A test that only checks the card status would have cheerfully shipped a workflow that silently drops disputes. When to use state-based checks: every task with a verifiable side effect (money moved, status changed, case opened) — in a bank that is nearly all of them. When NOT to: purely conversational turns with no system change, where there is no "world" to read — grade those with a rubric judge instead.

⚙️ In production

State-based checks need a sandbox that faithfully mirrors core banking: same schemas, same validation, same error codes, seeded to a known state and reset between runs. BankAssist runs these against a disposable per-run database snapshot so 6,000 nightly runs don't collide; the dominant cost is sandbox spin-up/tear-down latency, not tokens, so it pools warm sandboxes. The failure mode to watch is sandbox drift — a field production validates but the fake does not — which hands you green tests and red customers, so the sandbox schema is reconciled against production in CI. For compliance, every assertion doubles as evidence: "card C-1001 ended FROZEN, one dispute row for $240, no funds moved" is exactly the artefact an auditor asks for, so BankAssist persists the asserted end-state alongside each run as an immutable record.

🧠 Remember it

Grade the world, not the words. If the test can pass on a confident lie, you're testing the narration, not the agent.

Trajectory evaluation: grade the journey, not just the destination

Reaching the right end-state is necessary but not enough. In banking, how the agent got there can be the difference between a clean workflow and a compliance incident.

Two agents can both end with "balance disclosed to the customer." One verified the caller's identity first, then disclosed. The other disclosed the balance before checking who was asking. Same destination; one is routine, the other is a data-protection breach. State-based success checks (which assert only on the final world state) would pass both. That gap is why you also evaluate the trajectory — the ordered sequence of thoughts, tool calls, and observations the agent produced on its way to the answer.

There are two honest ways to grade a trajectory, and you'll use both:

  • Match against a reference path. You record one or more "known-good" trajectories and compare. But remember that there are many valid paths, so a strict step-for-step match is usually too brittle. Looser modes work better — check the agent used the right set of tools (order-free), or check it used at least the required tools and no forbidden ones.
  • Check invariants. Instead of matching a whole path, assert rules that must hold on every path. These are the gold of banking agent eval. The classic one: auth-before-disclosure — a tool that reveals private data must never be called before the identity-verification tool succeeds. Others: "no money-movement tool before a confirmation step," "never call an external tool with a raw account number in the arguments."

Invariant checks are just code that walks the recorded list of tool calls. They're small, fast, deterministic, and they encode your policy directly:

# An invariant: no private-data tool may run before identity is verified.
PRIVATE = {"get_balance", "list_transactions", "get_statement"}  # tools that disclose customer data

def check_auth_before_disclosure(trajectory):          # trajectory = ordered list of tool-call records from one run
    verified = False                                   # track whether identity verification has succeeded yet
    for call in trajectory:                            # walk the agent's steps in the order they happened
        if call.name == "verify_identity" and call.ok: # a SUCCESSFUL identity check flips the gate open
            verified = True
        if call.name in PRIVATE and not verified:      # a disclosure tool fired while the gate is still closed
            return False, f"{call.name} before verify_identity"  # fail loudly and say exactly which rule broke
    return True, "ok"                                  # the whole path respected the invariant
▶ Output
(False, 'get_balance before verify_identity')

Going deeper — reference-match modes

When you do compare to a reference path, pick the strictness that fits. Open-source tooling (for example LangChain's agentevals) offers ready-made modes: strict (same tool calls, same order — rarely what you want), unordered (same set of tools, any order), subset (the agent called only tools that appear in the reference — good for "no spurious actions"), and superset (the agent called at least the reference tools — good for "did the essentials"). For most banking workflows, unordered-plus-invariants is the sweet spot: don't over-specify the order, but hard-fail on the rules that actually matter.

⚙️ Under the hood

To grade a trajectory you must first capture one. That means your agent runtime emits a structured, replayable log of every step — the thought, the tool name, the exact arguments, the observation, timestamps, and whether the call succeeded. This log is called a trace, and it is the raw material for every technique in this chapter. If your agent can't produce clean traces, you can't evaluate its trajectory — so build tracing in from day one, not after the first incident.

In production

Invariants graduate from test asserts to live guardrails and online monitors. The same auth-before-disclosure check that gates a release also runs on sampled production traces, alerting when a real session violates it. Trajectory grading is also where you catch the slow-leak failures that outcome checks miss: pointless extra tool calls, loops that eventually succeed but burn 40 steps, retrieving far more customer data than the task needed. You log every trajectory with the user's identity scrubbed, keep an immutable audit trail (regulators will ask "prove the agent verified identity before disclosing"), and review flagged paths with a human.

⚙️ In production

Invariants are cheap to run — microseconds of pure Python over a trace — so BankAssist runs them on 100% of production traffic, not a sample: a missed auth-before-disclosure is a reportable breach, not a metric dip. The expensive part is capturing clean traces at scale; at millions of sessions a day, trace storage and PII redaction become the real cost line, so identifiers are redacted at emit time and full traces live in tiered storage (hot for 30 days, cold for the 5–7 years retention demands). Any live invariant violation alerts in real time, a disclosure-before-auth hit pages on-call, and the trail stays immutable: when a regulator asks "prove the agent verified identity before every balance disclosure last quarter," the answer is a query, not a scramble.

⚠ Watch out

Over-fitting to one golden trajectory is the classic trap: you record the path your best run took, match it strictly, and now every valid alternative path fails the eval — which trains the team to make the agent rigid, not reliable. When to use trajectory eval: whenever ordering or forbidden-action rules carry compliance weight (auth-before-disclosure, confirm-before-transfer, no raw account number in an external call). When NOT to: for creative or read-only steps where many orders are equally fine — there, grade the outcome and skip the path-matching entirely.

🧠 Remember it

Outcome says what; trajectory says how. In banking, a right answer reached the wrong way is still a breach. Encode your "must never" rules as invariants.

Tool-call accuracy: right tool, right arguments, nothing spurious

An agent acts through tools. Most agent failures aren't bad reasoning in the abstract — they're picking the wrong tool, filling in the wrong arguments, or calling a tool that shouldn't have been called at all.

Think of tools as the agent's hands. You can grade those hands on three separate questions, and mixing them up hides real bugs:

  • Selection — did it choose the right tool for the step? (Called transfer_funds when the customer only asked to check a balance is a selection error.)
  • Arguments — given the right tool, did it fill the parameters correctly? Right tool, wrong amount or wrong account is arguably the most dangerous bug in finance. transfer_funds(to="C-1001", amount=2400) when the task said $240 is a decimal-point disaster.
  • Spurious calls — did it call tools it shouldn't have? Extra, unrequested actions (a stray send_email, a needless second transfer) are failures even if the main goal was met.

Grading selection and spurious calls is set logic over the trace: compare the set of tools the agent used against the set it should have used. A common score is the proportion of the agent's calls that were correct — which naturally punishes both missing tools and spurious ones.

# Score tool selection + penalise spurious calls, using DeepEval's ToolCorrectnessMetric.
from deepeval.test_case import LLMTestCase, ToolCall          # a test case holds what happened; ToolCall records one call
from deepeval.metrics import ToolCorrectnessMetric            # compares tools-used vs tools-expected

case = LLMTestCase(
    input="Check the balance on card C-1001.",                # the user's request
    actual_output="Your available balance is $512.30.",       # the agent's final reply (not graded by THIS metric)
    tools_called=[ToolCall(name="verify_identity"),           # what the agent ACTUALLY called, in order
                  ToolCall(name="get_balance"),
                  ToolCall(name="send_marketing_email")],     # ← a spurious, unrequested action
    expected_tools=[ToolCall(name="verify_identity"),         # what SHOULD have been called for this task
                    ToolCall(name="get_balance")],
)

metric = ToolCorrectnessMetric(threshold=1.0)                 # demand a perfect match — no missing, no spurious
metric.measure(case)                                          # compute the score for this single case
print(round(metric.score, 2), metric.reason)                 # show the score and the human-readable reason
▶ Output
0.67 Called a tool not in expected set: send_marketing_email (2 of 3 calls correct)

The spurious marketing email dragged the score to 0.67 and, with a threshold of 1.0, failed the case — even though the balance was fetched correctly. That is the behaviour you want in a bank: unrequested side effects are bugs.

Going deeper — grading arguments is the subtle part

Selection is a set comparison; arguments need more care. Some argument fields must match exactly (account ID, amount, currency), some can be semantically equivalent (a free-text note), and some you deliberately ignore (a request timestamp). Good tooling lets you say this per field — for instance, LangChain's trajectory matchers accept overrides so you can require amount and to_account to match exactly while ignoring idempotency_key. Never grade all arguments with one blunt "exact-equals," or you'll either miss real bugs (loose match) or drown in false failures over irrelevant fields (strict match).

⚠ Watch out

The headline metric people quote is tool-selection accuracy, because it's easy to compute — and it quietly ignores the far more dangerous argument errors. An agent that always picks transfer_funds correctly but sometimes sends the money to the wrong account has 100% selection accuracy and a fraud report. Always grade arguments on the money-moving tools, exactly. When to use argument-level grading: always, on any money- or data-moving tool. When NOT to: don't exact-match cosmetic fields (free-text memos, timestamps, idempotency keys) — grading those only manufactures false failures.

In production

Tool-selection accuracy degrades as you add tools — with 50 near-duplicate tools, the agent can't reliably tell them apart. So production systems keep the active toolset small, give tools crisp non-overlapping descriptions, and measure selection accuracy explicitly as part of CI. On the argument side, the last line of defence lives in the tool itself: validate every argument before executing (reject a transfer with a negative or implausibly large amount), and use idempotency keys so a retried call can never double-execute a payment. Evaluation finds the bad calls; validation stops them.

⚙️ In production

As the toolset grows, selection accuracy falls, so BankAssist keeps the live toolset under ~15 per agent, gives each a crisp non-overlapping description, and tracks selection accuracy as a first-class CI metric that must not regress. For arguments, evaluation is the second line of defence, not the first: every money tool validates its own inputs (a positive amount within the customer's limit, an account that belongs to the customer) and carries an idempotency key so a retried call can't double-pay. At scale the dangerous failure is the rare wrong-argument call — 0.1% of a million daily transfers is 1,000 misrouted payments — so money tools log every argument for post-hoc audit, and any mismatch between the amount requested and the amount executed pages on-call immediately. The eval itself is cheap; the cost of not grading arguments is a fraud report.

🧠 Remember it

Three grades, not one: picked it, filled it, didn't overdo it. Selection is easy to measure and arguments are where the money is — grade both.

Step-level vs end-to-end evaluation

You can grade the whole journey as one pass/fail, or grade each step on its own. You need both — one tells you whether it works, the other tells you where it broke.

Picture debugging a long assembly line. End-to-end evaluation stands at the end and asks: did a good product come out? Step-level evaluation stands at every station and asks: did this station do its job with the input it was given? The first measures real success; the second localises the fault.

End-to-end (outcome)

Run the full task, check the final state (and trajectory). It's what you actually ship on — it reflects real success including how errors compound across steps. But when it fails, it doesn't tell you which step caused it.

Step-level (per step)

Feed a single step its input and check its output in isolation: "given this context, did the agent pick the right next tool?" Pinpoints the weak step and isolates blame — but a perfect score on every step in isolation doesn't guarantee the whole chain succeeds.

Why you can't rely on just one: step-level can hide compounding errors. Every station might score 95% alone, yet the ten-step chain still fails 40% of the time, because the small errors feed forward and multiply. Conversely, end-to-end alone gives you a red light with no diagnosis — you know the dispute workflow fails one run in six, but not whether it's the identity step, the lookup step, or the filing step.

The healthy workflow uses them together: gate releases on end-to-end reliability (that's what the customer feels), and diagnose regressions with step-level scores (that's how you fix them fast). When the end-to-end number drops after a change, the step-level scores tell you in minutes whether it was the new retrieval prompt or the reworked dispute tool.

⚙️ Under the hood

Step-level evaluation is possible only because you captured the trace. To grade "did step 3 pick the right tool given the context it had," you replay the recorded input to that step and judge its output. This also lets you build focused step datasets — a few hundred tricky "which tool next?" situations harvested from real traces — and re-run them cheaply on every prompt change, without paying for the whole end-to-end loop each time.

⚠ Watch out

Don't let a wall of green step-level scores lull you. Teams proudly report "every component is 95%+" and ship an agent that fails a quarter of real tasks, because they never multiplied the chain. Step scores don't add; they compound. End-to-end reliability is the only number that reflects what customers actually get. When to use step-level: for fast diagnosis and cheap per-step regression datasets. When NOT to rely on it: never gate a release on step scores — gate on end-to-end, because only the compounded number is what the customer feels.

⚙️ In production

The two views have very different economics. End-to-end runs are expensive — the full agent loop, every tool, ×N for reliability — so BankAssist runs the end-to-end gate pre-release and nightly. Step-level datasets, a few hundred harvested "which tool next?" situations, are cheap single model calls, so they run on every commit and localise a regression in minutes. Both are tracked release-over-release: when the end-to-end dispute-flow reliability drops from 97% to 88% after a prompt change, the step dashboard says in one glance that it was the file_dispute step, not retrieval. The audit value is in the linkage — BankAssist keeps the trace IDs that connect a failed end-to-end run to the exact step that broke, so every regression carries a documented root cause rather than a shrug.

🧠 Remember it

End-to-end = the scoreboard. Step-level = the game film. Ship on the scoreboard; debug with the film.

Unit-testing tools, integration-testing whole flows

An agent is software, so borrow the oldest trick in software quality: test the small pieces in isolation, then test them wired together — and because agents are random, run the wired-together tests many times.

The tools your agent calls are just functions with inputs and outputs. They have nothing to do with the language model, so they deserve plain, fast, deterministic unit tests — no LLM in the loop at all. A transfer_funds tool should reject a negative amount, reject an unknown account, be idempotent on retry, and move exactly the right sum. You can prove all of that with ordinary test cases that run in milliseconds and never flake.

# Plain unit tests for a tool — no agent, no LLM, fully deterministic.
def test_transfer_rejects_negative():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):                 # a negative transfer must be refused, not silently run
        transfer_funds(to="C-1001", amount=-50)     # guard against sign/decimal bugs at the source

def test_transfer_is_idempotent():
    key = "idem-abc123"                             # same idempotency key = "this is the same request"
    transfer_funds(to="C-1001", amount=240, idem=key)  # first call actually moves the money
    transfer_funds(to="C-1001", amount=240, idem=key)  # retry with SAME key must NOT move it again
    assert ledger.total_debits("C-1001") == 240     # exactly one debit — never a double-charge on retry
▶ Output
2 passed in 0.03s

With the tools individually trustworthy, you move up to integration tests: the whole agent loop, driving real (or sandboxed) tools end-to-end, on realistic scenarios. This is where the model's reasoning meets the tools, and where non-determinism bites — so a single run is meaningless. You run each scenario many times and measure the success rate over repeats. That's pass^k reliability — success measured across repeated runs — made operational.

# Integration test: run the full agent on one scenario N times, require high reliability.
def test_dispute_flow_reliability(sandbox):
    successes = 0
    N = 20                                           # repeat because the agent is non-deterministic — one run proves nothing
    for _ in range(N):
        sandbox.reset(card_id="C-1001", status="ACTIVE")  # every run starts from the SAME known world state
        agent.run("Freeze C-1001 and dispute the $240 ACME charge.")  # full loop: reason + real tool calls
        card = sandbox.get_card("C-1001")            # check the ACTUAL end state, not the chat text
        if card.status == "FROZEN" and sandbox.has_open_dispute("C-1001", 240):
            successes += 1                           # count only runs that achieved the real goal
    rate = successes / N                              # the reliability of this scenario, not a single verdict
    assert rate >= 0.95, f"dispute flow only {rate:.0%} reliable"  # gate on reliability, with headroom for money tasks
▶ Output
FAILED — dispute flow only 85% reliable (17/20)

That failure is the whole point. A one-shot test would have passed on a lucky run and shipped an 85%-reliable money workflow. Running it twenty times exposed the wobble before a customer did.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist has a staging environment — a faithful copy of production wired to sandboxed core-banking systems with fake accounts and no real money. Before any release, the full integration suite runs every customer scenario 20 times against staging. The card-dispute flow comes back at 85%. The team doesn't ship; they trace the 3 failing runs, find the agent occasionally files the dispute with a missing reason code, fix the tool's argument validation, and re-run until it's 20/20. Staging caught what the demo hid.

In production

Unit tests run on every commit (seconds, free). The heavier integration suite runs in CI before release against staging, and you keep running a sampled version against production traffic as a canary (a small, low-risk trial run on real traffic that warns you of trouble before a full rollout). Staging must mirror production closely — same tool schemas, same latency profile, realistic data shapes — because an agent that's reliable against instant fake tools can fall apart when a real core-banking API is slow or flaky. You also test the failure modes deliberately: inject a tool timeout, a 500 error, malformed data, and assert the agent recovers (retries, replans, or asks for help) instead of hallucinating success or looping forever.

⚠ Watch out

The silent killer is a staging environment that's too nice: instant, always-successful fake tools. Your integration suite goes green, then production's real core-banking API is slow, rate-limited, or returns a 500 — and the agent that never learned to handle that hallucinates success or loops forever. When to use unit tests: every tool, every commit — they're free and deterministic. When to use ×N integration tests: before every release and as a production canary. When NOT to trust a single integration run: ever — one green run of a random process proves nothing.

⚙️ In production

Reliability only transfers if staging mirrors production's failure profile, not just its happy path. BankAssist injects faults into the staging suite on purpose — tool timeouts, 429 rate limits, 500s, malformed payloads, partial writes — and asserts the agent retries, replans, or escalates to a human rather than faking success. The full ×20 suite over ~300 scenarios is the heavy CI job (30–90 minutes, parallelised); unit tests gate every commit in seconds. In production a sampled canary runs the same assertions against live-shadow traffic so a regression surfaces in hours, not at the next incident review. Compliance angle: the fault-injection results are the evidence that the agent degrades safely under stress — exactly the question operational-resilience rules (DORA-style) now ask directly.

🧠 Remember it
