        return answer                                   # spans close and flush to the tracing backend
▶ Output
The tracing tool shows a timeline for req-7f3a: retrieve 0.9s, generate 0.6s — with inputs stored as "acct ***4821", not the real number.

In production

You can't afford to trace and store every request in full at high traffic — the storage and cost add up. The usual pattern is sample normal traffic (keep, say, 1-in-100 full traces) but always keep 100% of errors and slow requests, because those are the ones you'll actually need. Traces are also the raw material for your operational metrics: you derive latency, cost, and error rates from the spans you're already recording.

Going deeper

Three details separate a trace you can actually debug from a pile of pretty bars. First, context propagation: the correlation ID (often the OpenTelemetry trace ID) must travel across process boundaries — stamped on the model call, carried in the HTTP headers to the balance service, and written into that service's own logs — or the story breaks at the first hop. Second, cardinality discipline: put high-variety values (customer IDs, request IDs) on the span as searchable attributes, not as metric labels, or you blow up your metrics backend. Third, cost per trace: full traces with inputs and outputs are heavy, so sampling is a real decision — and it should be tail-based (decide whether to keep a trace after you know it errored or ran slow) rather than head-based (decide at the start and miss the interesting ones). For an agent specifically, record the agent-native fields the generic OpenTelemetry conventions don't yet standardise: which step number, which tool, tokens in and out, cost, and the budget remaining.

⚙️ In production

Cost & scale: you can't store every full trace at high traffic — sample normal traffic (e.g. 1-in-100) but keep 100% of errors and slow requests, because those are the ones you'll need. Latency: emit spans asynchronously (batch and export off the hot path) so tracing never adds latency to the customer's request. Failure modes: an over-eager tracer that blocks or fills disk can take down the very service it watches — cap buffers and drop rather than block. Monitoring: traces are the raw material your latency, cost, and error metrics are derived from, so a gap in tracing is a gap in every dashboard. Security/compliance: traces capture real prompts and results — account numbers, balances, names — so PII must be redacted or masked before storage, with retention and access controls, or your debugging tool becomes an unencrypted copy of customer data.

⚠ Watch out

Storing raw prompts and tool results in a trace turns your observability stack into a shadow copy of customer data — redact before you store, always. Use tracing on every agent request so you can replay failures step by step; don't log unmasked PII, and don't head-sample so aggressively that you throw away the errors you most need to see.

🧠 Remember it

A trace is the replay; spans are the frames. One correlation ID to find it, inputs on every span to understand it, PII redacted so storing it doesn't become the next incident.

Metrics and structured logging: the numbers that tell you it's healthy

Traces tell you about one request. Metrics tell you about a million at once — and they're how you learn there's a problem before the customers do.

A trace is a microscope; a metric is a dashboard. Metrics are numbers you roll up over all traffic so you can see trends, set alarms, and answer "is the agent healthy right now?" at a glance. For a banking agent, four families of metric matter, and skipping any one leaves a blind spot.

FamilyWhat it answersExamples
QualityAre the answers any good?task success rate, groundedness/faithfulness score, guardrail block rate, human-escalation rate, thumbs-down rate
LatencyHow fast does it feel?time to first token, end-to-end p50 / p95 / p99
CostWhat is it costing us?tokens per request, dollars per request, dollars per resolved task
ReliabilityIs it working at all?error rate, tool-failure rate, retry rate, fallback rate, timeout rate

Percentiles, not averages

This is the single most important idea in the lesson. Averages lie. If 99 customers get a 1-second reply and one customer waits 40 seconds, the average is a cheerful 1.4 seconds — and it completely hides the person having a terrible experience. Percentiles fix this. The p95 latency is the value that 95% of requests come in under; p99 is the value 99% come in under. So "p99 = 8s" means one in a hundred customers waits at least 8 seconds. In a bank, that tail is exactly who complains, so you watch the tail, not the middle.

Structured logging

A log line like "transfer failed for user" is nearly useless at scale — you can't search it, count it, or chart it. Structured logging means writing logs as machine-readable records (JSON), with consistent fields, so you can filter and aggregate them like data.

# A structured log line: machine-readable fields, not a sentence.
log.info("tool_call", {                        # an event name plus a bag of searchable fields
    "correlation_id": "req-7f3a",              # ties this line back to its full trace
    "tool": "transfer",                        # which tool — lets you count failures per tool
    "status": "error",                         # outcome as a field you can filter and alert on
    "error_code": 503,                         # the specific failure — distinguishes retriable from terminal
    "latency_ms": 3012,                        # how long it took — feeds the latency percentiles
    "customer_id": "cust_***4821",             # MASKED id — enough to group by, never the raw value
})
▶ Output
Now you can ask: "count tool_call errors where tool=transfer and error_code=503 in the last hour" — a query, not a grep through prose.

In production

Metrics are what alarms hang on: "page me if p99 latency > 10s for 5 minutes," or "if fallback rate > 20%," or "if task success rate drops 5 points." Pick a handful of service level objectives (SLOs) — the targets you promise, e.g. "p95 under 4 seconds, success rate over 90%" — and alert when you're about to miss them, not after. Track cost per resolved task, not just per request: an agent that answers cheaply but needs three tries or a human handoff isn't actually cheap. And the same PII discipline from tracing applies to logs — mask before you write.

Going deeper

Two measurement subtleties trip up teams. First, you cannot average percentiles. The p99 of two servers is not the average of their two p99s — percentiles must be computed from the underlying distribution (histograms), which is why metrics systems store latency as bucketed histograms rather than a running mean. If your dashboard "averages the p95 across pods," it is lying to you. Second, pick the right percentile for the stakes: p50 tells you the typical experience, p95 the unhappy minority, p99 (and even p99.9) the tail that writes complaints — in a bank, that tail is exactly who you hear from. On the logging side, the win from structured logs is that they're queryable: "count tool_call errors where tool=transfer and error_code=503 in the last hour" is one query, not a grep through prose. Give every log line the correlation ID so a metric anomaly drills straight into the exact traces behind it. One edge case: cost per request flatters an agent that answers cheaply but needs three tries or a human, so always track cost per resolved task too.

⚙️ In production

Scale: metrics are cheap and aggregate (counters, histograms) while logs and traces are heavy and per-event — so alarm on metrics, then drill with logs and traces. Latency & cost: emit metrics and logs off the hot path; a synchronous write to a slow log sink can itself add latency. Failure modes: alerting on the average hides the tail — BankAssist can show a cheerful 1.4s mean while one customer in a hundred waits 40s. Monitoring: hang a handful of SLOs off these metrics (e.g. "p95 under 4s, success rate over 90%") and page before you breach, not after; good alarms read like "p99 > 10s for 5 minutes" or "fallback rate > 20%". Security/compliance: the same PII discipline as tracing — mask customer IDs and never write a raw account number into a log a wide team can query.

⚠ Watch out

Judging speed by the average is the classic blunder — it sits with the happy majority and never sees the suffering tail. Use percentiles (p95/p99) for latency and structured JSON logs for anything you'll search or alarm on; don't alert on means, don't average percentiles together, and don't write prose log lines you can't query at scale.

🧠 Remember it

Watch four families — quality, latency, cost, reliability — and judge speed by the tail (p95/p99), never the average. Log as data, not as sentences.

The observability toolkit: LangSmith, Langfuse, Phoenix & OpenTelemetry

You don't have to build tracing and metrics from scratch — a mature set of tools captures agent traces, scores quality, and tracks cost out of the box. The trick is choosing with your eyes open.

Once you accept that you need traces, spans, metrics, and quality scores, the obvious question is "what records all this?" A handful of purpose-built LLM observability tools do, each capturing the think-act loop, the prompts, the token counts, and the costs, then letting you search, replay, and evaluate them.

ToolIn one lineNotes
LangSmithThe hosted tracing + eval platform from the LangChain team.Deep fit if you use LangChain / LangGraph; works with any stack via its SDK. Commercial, SaaS or self-hosted.
LangfuseOpen-source tracing, evals, and prompt management.Self-host or cloud; framework-agnostic; ingests OpenTelemetry. Popular when teams want to own their data (handy in a bank).
Phoenix (Arize)Open-source tracing & evaluation, built on open standards.Uses OpenInference/OpenTelemetry; strong for digging into traces and running evaluations locally.
OpenTelemetry (OTel)Not a product — the open standard for traces and metrics.Its GenAI semantic conventions define standard field names for model calls. Emit OTel and you can send data to many backends.

Why does the OpenTelemetry row matter so much? Because it's the plug shape, not the appliance. OpenTelemetry is the industry-standard way to describe traces and metrics, and it has a growing GenAI convention that names the fields everyone should use for a model call — so different tools read the same data the same way.

✅ Tip

Lean toward OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation rather than wiring your code tightly to one vendor's SDK. If you emit standard GenAI spans, you can start with an open-source tool like Langfuse or Phoenix, and move to a commercial platform later without rewriting your agent. The plug fits many sockets.

⚙️ Under the hood

The GenAI conventions are still maturing — the names for plain chat and embedding calls are fairly settled, while the agent and tool-orchestration parts are newer and still shifting version to version. Practically, expect good coverage of model calls (model name, input/output tokens, cost) and expect to add some custom spans of your own for the agent-specific parts (which tool, which step, the budget remaining). Pin the versions of your instrumentation libraries so a field doesn't silently rename under you.

In production

In a bank, the deciding factors are often not features but data residency and control: can you self-host so customer prompts never leave your environment? Does it support PII redaction before storage? Can you set retention and access controls on the trace data? An open-source, self-hostable tool often wins here even if a SaaS product has shinier dashboards, because "where does the data live" is a compliance question first and a convenience question second.

Going deeper

The real decision isn't "which dashboard looks nicest" but "where does the data live and who controls it." These tools split along two axes. Open vs. commercial: Langfuse and Phoenix are open-source and self-hostable; LangSmith is a commercial SaaS (with a self-hosted enterprise tier). Vendor SDK vs. open standard: you can instrument against one vendor's SDK, or emit OpenTelemetry GenAI spans and keep your options open. The standard is maturing unevenly — plain chat and embedding spans (gen_ai.* attributes, token counts, model name) are fairly settled, while the agent and tool-orchestration spans (invoke_agent, execute_tool) are still in "development" status and shift version to version. The practical consequence: expect clean, portable coverage of model calls, and expect to add a few custom spans of your own for the agent-specific parts (which step, which tool, budget remaining), and to pin your instrumentation-library versions so a field doesn't silently rename under you.

⚙️ In production

Compliance drives the choice: in a bank the deciding question is data residency — can you self-host so customer prompts never leave your environment, set retention, and enforce access controls? That often tips the decision to an open-source, self-hostable tool (Langfuse, Phoenix) even over a shinier SaaS. Cost & scale: ingestion and storage are the real bill at high traffic, so sampling and PII redaction before storage are first-class concerns, not add-ons. Failure modes: wiring your agent tightly to one vendor's SDK is a lock-in risk — a migration later means re-instrumenting every call. Latency: all of these ingest asynchronously, so keep exporters off the hot path. Monitoring: whichever tool you pick, confirm it actually captures the fields you alarm on (tokens, cost, tool, error) before you trust its dashboards.

⚠ Watch out

Picking a tool for its dashboards and ignoring data residency is how customer prompts end up in a third-party SaaS a bank can't audit. Use OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation so you can switch backends later without rewriting your agent; don't hard-wire to one vendor's proprietary SDK, and don't adopt any tool that can't redact PII before storage or be self-hosted where compliance requires it.

🧠 Remember it

OpenTelemetry is the plug; LangSmith, Langfuse, and Phoenix are sockets. Wire to the standard and you can change your mind later.

Spending less without hurting answers: budgets and model routing

The fastest way to blow a budget is to send every tiny question to your most powerful model. The fastest way to fix it is to match the model to the job.

Running an agent costs money per token, and the loop multiplies it — a single task might make five model calls, each reading a growing conversation. Two levers keep the bill sane. The first is budgets — a step and token ceiling per task that caps the worst case a single request can run up. The second is model routing, and it's where the real savings live.

Model routing

Model providers offer a ladder of models — small-fast-cheap at the bottom, large-smart-expensive at the top. Within one family the gap is large: a frontier model can cost many times more per token than the small one. Sending "what's my balance?" to the top model is like couriering a postcard by armored truck. Routing means sending each request to the cheapest model that can actually handle it, and reserving the expensive one for the hard cases.

# Route each request to the cheapest capable model — and force the flagship when money is involved.
CHEAP = "claude-haiku-5-5"      # small, fast, low cost — great for simple lookups and classification
MID   = "claude-sonnet-5-5"     # balanced — multi-step chat, summaries
FLAG  = "claude-opus-5-5"       # most capable — hard reasoning and high-stakes decisions

def pick_model(request):                         # decide the model BEFORE spending on it
    if request.moves_money or request.is_dispute: # anything touching funds or a formal dispute
        return FLAG                              # never cheap out on high-stakes, irreversible actions
    if request.needs_reasoning:                  # multi-step, some judgment required
        return MID                               # the middle rung is plenty here
    return CHEAP                                 # balance checks, FAQs, intent routing — the cheap model nails these
▶ Output
"What's my balance?" → cheap model. "Dispute this $2,000 charge." → flagship. The bulk of traffic takes the cheap path, so the average cost per request drops sharply.
⚠ Watch out

Use the flagship for anything that touches money. Routing saves money on easy questions; it must never save money on consequential ones. A wrong balance read annoys someone; a wrong transfer or a wrong dispute decision is a real loss and a compliance event. When the downside is irreversible, pay for the best model — the savings on a cheap model are never worth a wrong move on someone's account. Use routing to send easy, high-volume traffic (balances, FAQs, intent classification) to a cheap model; don't route anything irreversible or money-moving to a cheaper tier to save a fraction of a cent.

⚙️ Under the hood

Before building an elaborate multi-model cascade, check the obvious alternative: the capable model at a lower effort setting. Newer models expose an "effort" dial that trades thoroughness for tokens, and a strong model at low effort often matches an older model at high effort — while keeping you on one model, which matters because prompt caches (a cached, reused context prefix) are tied to a specific model. A cascade across three models forfeits cache reuse between them. Routing is powerful; it's just not always the first lever. And judge by cost per completed task: a cheap model that needs three tries or a human handoff isn't cheap.

In production

Routing decisions are usually cheap themselves — a fast classifier, a few rules on the request type, or a tiny model deciding "simple vs. complex." You watch two numbers together: cost per request (should fall) and quality per tier (must not fall). A healthy routed system has most traffic on the cheap tier, a clean escalation path when the cheap model is unsure, and a hard rule that high-stakes work always lands on the flagship. Pin exact model IDs in that routing code — a generic alias can quietly resolve to a different model over time and change both your cost and your behavior overnight.

Going deeper

Routing comes in a few flavours, cheapest-to-build first. Rule-based routing keys off the request type ("balance → small model, dispute → flagship") and is transparent and auditable — a real plus in a bank. Classifier-based routing uses a tiny model or a few features to score difficulty, catching cases rules miss. Cascade routing tries the cheap model first and escalates only when its confidence is low — powerful, but it pays twice on the hard cases and forfeits prompt-cache reuse between models. On the OpenAI ladder the same logic applies: send the bulk of easy traffic to a small model like gpt-4.1-mini and reserve gpt-4.1 (or a reasoning model at higher effort) for genuine reasoning and anything consequential. Two numbers to respect: a frontier model can cost roughly an order of magnitude more per token than the small one in its family, so moving traffic down a rung is the single biggest cost lever — but measure cost per completed task, because a cheap model that needs three tries or a human handoff isn't cheap. And check the simpler lever first: a strong reasoning model at a lower effort setting often matches an older model at high effort while keeping you on one model, and one cache.

⚙️ In production

Cost & scale: a healthy routed fleet has most traffic on the cheap tier and a thin slice on the flagship, so average cost per request falls sharply while quality holds. Latency: the router itself must be fast — a few rules or a tiny classifier, not another heavyweight call. Failure modes: the subtle one is quality quietly dropping on a tier after a traffic-mix shift, so watch cost-per-request and quality-per-tier together. Monitoring: alarm if cheap-tier success rate falls or if too much traffic escalates to the flagship (your router is miscalibrated or the cheap model regressed). Security/compliance: pin exact model IDs in routing code — a generic alias can silently resolve to a different model overnight and change both cost and behaviour — and keep a hard rule that any money-moving or dispute decision always lands on the flagship.

🧠 Remember it

Cheapest model that can do the job — flagship whenever money is on the line. Save on easy, never on consequential.

Caching at two levels: prompt caching and semantic result caching

The cheapest token is the one you never pay for twice. Two kinds of cache — one inside the model call, one around it — do exactly that.

Agents repeat themselves constantly. The same long system prompt and tool list ride along on every single call. The same common questions arrive from thousands of customers. Caching means remembering work you've already done so you don't redo it. There are two distinct caches, operating at two different levels, and they stack.

1. Prompt caching

Every model call re-reads the same front matter: a big system prompt, the bank's policies, the tool definitions — maybe thousands of tokens that never change. Normally you pay to process all of it every time. Prompt caching lets the provider remember that stable prefix after the first call, so later calls that start with the same prefix are processed far faster and cheaper — cached reads cost a small fraction of normal input tokens.

# Mark the big, unchanging prefix so the provider caches it after the first call.
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    system=[
        {"type": "text",
         "text": BANK_POLICIES_AND_TOOLS,          # thousands of tokens that are identical on every request
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},   # "remember everything up to here" — the cache breakpoint
    ],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}], # the ONLY part that changes per request goes AFTER the cached prefix
)
print(response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)       # > 0 means the prefix was reused — caching is working
▶ Output
First call: cache is written (a small premium). Every later call within the cache window: the policy prefix is a cache read at a fraction of the price, and the response comes back faster.
⚠ Watch out

Prompt caching is a prefix match — the cache is reused only up to the first byte that differs. One changing character near the top (a timestamp, an unsorted tool list, a per-request ID in the system prompt) invalidates everything after it, and your cache hit rate silently drops to zero. Keep stable content first and volatile content last, and verify with cache_read_input_tokens that reads are actually happening.

2. Semantic caching

Prompt caching reuses part of the input. Semantic caching reuses the entire output. When a question comes in, you embed it (turn its meaning into a vector) and check whether you've recently answered a question that means the same thing. "How do I reset my PIN?" and "I forgot my PIN, what now?" are different words with one meaning — a semantic cache spots that and returns the stored answer without any model call at all.

⚠ Watch out

Two risks make this dangerous if you're careless. First, a false hit: "can I overdraft $100?" and "can I overdraft $1,000?" are close in meaning but need different answers — too loose a threshold serves the wrong one. Second, and worse, personalized or private answers must never be cached across customers. Caching "your balance is $4,000" and serving it to the next person is a data breach. Only cache answers that are general (policy, how-to, product facts), set a conservative similarity threshold, scope every cache key by tenant and permissions, and give entries a TTL so a changed policy doesn't get served stale. Use prompt caching on every agent (the system prompt rides every loop step) and semantic caching only for general, non-personal answers; don't ever cache a personalized or private answer across customers, and don't set the similarity threshold so loose that near-but-different questions collide.

⚙️ Under the hood

The clean rule: cache things that are the same for everyone and slow to change (policy explanations, fee descriptions, "how do I…" answers). Never cache things that are per-customer or fast-changing (balances, transaction lists, anything personal). Set a TTL that matches how fast the underlying facts move, and invalidate on re-index — when a policy document is updated, the cached answers built from it must expire too, or you'll confidently serve last week's rule.

In production

The two caches address different costs: prompt caching cuts the per-call cost of your always-present context (big win for agents, where the same system prompt rides every loop step), while semantic caching removes whole calls for repeated general questions. Track hit rate for both — a prompt-cache hit rate near zero usually means a silent invalidator up top, and a semantic-cache hit rate near zero means either your threshold is too strict or your traffic genuinely isn't repetitive. Watch false-hit complaints like a hawk; in banking, one wrong cached answer costs more than all the savings.

Going deeper

The two providers handle prompt caching differently, and it matters for your code. OpenAI's prompt caching is automatic: send a prompt over roughly 1,024 tokens and repeated prefixes are cached for you, billed at a reduced rate (around half the normal input price), with hits reported as cached_tokens in the usage — you don't mark anything, you just keep the stable content first. Anthropic's is explicit: you place a cache_control breakpoint (shown above), pay a small write premium on the first call, then read the prefix back at roughly a tenth of the input price within the cache window. Both are prefix caches, so the discipline is identical: anything that changes near the top — a timestamp, a per-request ID, an unsorted tool list — invalidates everything after it and your hit rate silently collapses. For semantic caching the knobs are the similarity threshold (too loose = false hits, too strict = no hits), the TTL (match it to how fast the underlying facts move), and the scope of the cache key. The single most important edge case in a bank: scope every semantic-cache entry by tenant and permission so a cached personal answer can never leak to the next customer, and invalidate on re-index so a refreshed policy expires the answers built from it.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the two caches attack different bills — prompt caching cuts the per-call cost of the always-present context (huge for agents, where the same system prompt rides every loop step), while semantic caching removes whole model calls for repeated general questions. Latency: a prompt-cache read is faster as well as cheaper, and a semantic-cache hit is instant (no model call at all). Scale: keep the semantic cache in a shared store — Redis is the common backend (often with a vector-search module for the similarity lookup) — so a cache hit is shared across every worker, not trapped in one process. Failure modes: a silent invalidator up top drops prompt-cache hit rate to zero; a loose threshold serves a wrong cached answer. Monitoring: chart hit rate for both caches and watch false-hit complaints like a hawk — in banking one wrong cached answer costs more than all the savings. Security/compliance: never cache balances, transactions, or anything per-customer; only cache policy, fees, and how-to answers that are the same for everyone.

🧠 Remember it

Prompt cache = reuse the question's front matter. Semantic cache = reuse the answer itself. Cache what's shared and stable; never cache what's personal or moving.

Feeling faster: parallel tool calls and streaming

Some speed comes from doing less work. This speed comes from doing the work in a smarter order — and from letting the customer start reading before you've finished writing.

Two techniques make an agent feel dramatically faster without changing a single answer. One cuts real wait time; the other cuts perceived wait time. Both matter, because a customer's patience is measured in how long they stare at a blank screen.

Parallel tool calls

To answer "give me a summary of my account," BankAssist might need three things: the balance, the recent transactions, and the card status. If it fetches them one after another — balance (0.4s), then transactions (0.5s), then card (0.3s) — that's 1.2 seconds of waiting stacked end to end. But these three don't depend on each other. Fired off together, the total wait is just the slowest one: 0.5 seconds. Modern model APIs can emit several tool calls in a single turn exactly so you can run them concurrently.

# Run three INDEPENDENT tool calls at the same time instead of one after another.
import asyncio                                    # Python's library for running work concurrently

async def account_summary(cust_id):              # builds the summary with the least possible waiting
    balance, txns, card = await asyncio.gather(   # gather runs all three at once, waits for all to finish
        get_balance(cust_id),                     # these three do NOT depend on each other —
        get_transactions(cust_id),                #   so there's no reason to wait for one before starting the next
        get_card_status(cust_id),                 # total wait = the slowest of the three, not their sum
    )
    return summarize(balance, txns, card)         # combine the three results once they're all back
▶ Output
Three lookups that would take 1.2s in a row complete in ~0.5s together — same data, less than half the wait.
⚠ Watch out

Only parallelize calls that are truly independent. If step two needs step one's result ("find the disputed charge, then fetch its merchant"), running them together is a race that produces wrong or missing data. And watch the downstream: firing many parallel calls from thousands of agents at once can overwhelm a shared service — a synchronized flood that knocks it over, the same pile-on a retry storm causes. Respect rate limits, and handle a partial failure (two succeed, one errors) gracefully rather than letting one bad result sink the whole batch. Use parallel calls for independent lookups and streaming for any long or customer-facing answer; don't parallelize dependent steps (where one needs another's result), and don't stream an unvalidated financial figure straight to the screen.

Streaming

A model generates its answer token by token. Without streaming, the customer waits in silence until the entire answer is ready, then it appears all at once — which for a long answer can feel like ages. With streaming, you send each token to the screen as it's produced, so words start appearing almost immediately. The total time is the same, but the experience is transformed: the time to first token — how long until something shows up — is what people actually feel, and streaming makes it tiny.

Streaming has a second, practical benefit for agents: long tasks won't trip an HTTP timeout, because data keeps flowing instead of one giant response arriving at the end. That's why providers often recommend streaming for any request with a large output or a long-running agentic loop.

⚙️ Under the hood

There's a real tension to manage: if you stream raw tokens straight to the customer, your output validation — the sober check that an answer is grounded, safe, and well-formed before it ships — hasn't run yet on the full answer. A common pattern is to stream the visible reasoning or progress while buffering the final actionable content — amounts, confirmations, advice — until it has passed the checks. In a bank you never want a half-formed, unvalidated financial claim to appear on screen just because it looked fast. Speed serves the customer; it never overrules safety.

In production

Parallel calls and streaming together are what make a multi-step agent feel snappy instead of sluggish. Measure their effect on time to first token and on p95 end-to-end latency, not just the average. The combination is especially powerful for the "gather several things, then explain" shape that banking summaries, disputes, and reviews all share: fetch in parallel, stream the explanation as it forms.

Going deeper

Separate the two kinds of "fast," because they're measured differently. Parallel tool calls cut real wall-clock time: fan out independent lookups and your wait collapses from the sum of their durations to the slowest single one — but only for truly independent work, and only up to the point where you start overwhelming a shared downstream with a burst of simultaneous calls, or hit its rate limit. Streaming cuts perceived time: the total generation takes exactly as long, but time to first token — the gap before anything appears — shrinks to near-zero, and that first-token latency is what a human actually feels. Streaming has a second, concrete payoff for agents: a long response that streams keeps the connection alive with a steady flow of data, so it won't trip an HTTP idle-timeout the way one giant response arriving at the end can. The sharp edge is the interaction with guardrails: raw tokens on the screen haven't passed output validation yet. The common pattern is to stream visible progress or reasoning while buffering the actionable content — amounts, confirmations, advice — until it has cleared the checks. Edge cases: handle a partial failure in a parallel batch (two succeed, one errors) without sinking the whole answer, and handle a stream that drops mid-flight.

⚙️ In production

Latency: measure the pair by time to first token and p95 end-to-end, never the average — streaming can leave the average unchanged while transforming the experience. Cost: parallelism doesn't change token cost, but firing many calls at once raises instantaneous load and can trip rate limits, which cost retries. Scale: cap fan-out width and respect downstream limits so a burst of parallel agents doesn't DDoS a shared core-banking API. Failure modes: a dependent pair run in parallel is a race that returns wrong or missing data; an unbuffered stream can show a half-formed financial claim. Monitoring: watch first-token latency and the partial-failure rate on parallel batches. Security/compliance: at BankAssist, money-words wait for validation even when everything else streams — speed serves the customer, it never overrules safety.

🧠 Remember it

Parallel calls cut the real wait; streaming cuts the felt wait. Fire independent tools together, show words as they come — but hold the money-words until they've passed the checks.

Durable execution and checkpointing: surviving a crash mid-task

A long-running agent is a long-running risk: the longer a task runs, the more likely a crash, restart, or deploy interrupts it. Durable execution means the task picks up where it left off — without redoing what it already did.

Short tasks are forgiving. But a loan-application agent might run for minutes across many steps — verify identity, pull credit, check policy, request a document, decide. If the server restarts at step four (a deploy, a crash, a cloud instance recycled), an agent that kept its state only in memory loses everything and starts from scratch. In banking that's not just annoying; if step three already pulled a credit report or sent a notice, starting over might do it twice.

Durable execution is the property that a workflow survives interruptions and resumes correctly. Its engine is checkpointing: after each meaningful step, you save the agent's state — the conversation, what's been decided, which step is next — to durable storage (a database, not memory). On restart, you reload the latest checkpoint and continue from there.

⚙️ Under the hood

You rarely hand-build this. Agent frameworks like LangGraph ship checkpointers that persist graph state after each node — use a durable backend (Postgres) in production, not the in-memory one, which is for local testing only. For heavier needs, a dedicated durable-workflow engine like Temporal treats each step as a replayable, crash-proof unit. One sharp detail to understand: on resume, the engine replays up to the last checkpoint, then re-executes the steps after it — including any model calls or API writes in those steps. That re-execution is exactly why idempotency — making a repeated step a safe no-op by stamping it with a stable key — is non-negotiable here.

In production

Checkpointing after every step on a large state can get expensive in storage and latency — so you balance how often you checkpoint against how much rework a crash can cost. Keep the full step-by-step history as your audit trail (a regulator may ask "show me every step this agent took on this loan"), and set retention and access controls on it like any other customer record. The combination — resumable state plus a complete decision log — is what lets a bank trust an agent with a workflow that takes minutes and touches real accounts.

Going deeper

"Durable" is a spectrum, and knowing where your tool sits saves you a nasty surprise. A checkpointer (LangGraph's, for instance) persists the graph's state after each node to a durable backend — use Postgres in production, never the in-memory saver, which is for local testing only. That survives a crash between steps. A full durable-execution engine (Temporal and the like) goes further: it treats each step as a replayable unit, owns retries, timers, and timeouts, and can resume a workflow that's been asleep for days. The two are often combined — LangGraph defines the agent's state and control flow while Temporal supplies the durable scheduling and human-in-the-loop approval gates. The detail that bites people: on resume, the engine replays history up to the last checkpoint and then re-executes the steps after it — including any model calls or API writes in those steps. So a step that pulled a credit report or sent a notice can run again on recovery. That re-execution is exactly why every side-effecting step must be idempotent (carry a stable key so a repeat is a no-op). Edge cases: very long histories can approach an engine's event-history limits, and checkpointing a huge state after every step costs storage and latency — so balance checkpoint frequency against how much rework a crash would cost.

⚙️ In production

Cost & latency: each checkpoint is a durable write, so checkpointing a large state after every step adds storage and per-step latency — checkpoint at meaningful boundaries, not blindly. Scale: a durable backend lets you recycle, deploy, and autoscale worker instances without losing in-flight loan applications. Failure modes: the headline risk is re-executing a side effect on resume (a second credit pull, a duplicate notice) — idempotency keys are the fix. Monitoring: track resume rate and time-lost-per-crash; a climbing resume rate means instances are churning. Security/compliance: the full step-by-step history is also your audit trail — a regulator may ask "show me every step this agent took on this loan" — so keep it complete, with retention and access controls, like any other customer record.

⚠ Watch out

Resume re-runs the steps after your last checkpoint, so a non-idempotent side effect (pull credit, send a notice, post a fee) can happen twice after a crash. Use durable execution for any workflow that runs for minutes or spans human waits (loan applications, multi-step onboarding); don't use the in-memory checkpointer in production, and don't let any re-executable step write without a stable idempotency key.

🧠 Remember it

Save your place after every step, in a real database. A crash should cost a reload, not a redo — and remember the engine re-runs the steps after your last checkpoint.

Async, event-driven agents and idempotent handlers

Not every task should make a customer wait on a live connection. The big, slow, bursty work belongs on a queue — and anything that reads from a queue must be safe to run more than once.

Picture the usual case: a customer waiting live for a reply. But much agent work in a bank is different: process this batch of 10,000 overnight loan applications, investigate this flagged transaction, generate month-end statements. These don't need an open connection and a human watching a spinner. They fit an event-driven shape: something happens (an event — "new application received"), it lands on a queue, and a worker agent picks it up and processes it whenever it can.

This decoupling is a gift for reliability. Traffic spikes get absorbed by the queue instead of crushing the agent — work simply waits its turn. A failed job can be retried from the queue. You can scale workers up and down independently of the thing producing events. The agent stops being a fragile live phone call and becomes a resilient assembly line.

Idempotent handlers

Queues make a promise that sounds reassuring and hides a trap: they deliver each message at least once. "At least once" means sometimes more than once — if a worker processes a job but crashes before confirming it's done, the queue assumes it failed and hands the same job to another worker. So your handler will occasionally run twice on the same event. If the handler sends an email, that's two emails. If it approves a loan or posts a fee, that's a disaster.

The defense is the same idea that makes a timed-out transfer safe to re-send: make the handler idempotent — running it twice has the same effect as running it once. You do this by recording that you've handled each event ID, and skipping anything you've already done.

# An idempotent event handler: safe even if the SAME event is delivered twice.
def handle_event(event):                          # may be called more than once for one event (at-least-once delivery)
    if already_processed(event.id):               # have we seen this exact event id before?
        return                                     # yes → do nothing, exit quietly (this is the whole safety net)
    result = run_agent(event.payload)             # the real work — e.g. assess a loan application
    with db.transaction():                        # do the write and the "done" mark together, atomically
        save_result(result)                        # persist the outcome
        mark_processed(event.id)                   # record the id so a redelivery hits the guard above
▶ Output
First delivery of evt_42: assessed and saved. A duplicate delivery of evt_42: the guard returns immediately — no second assessment, no second email.
⚠ Watch out

The "mark as processed" and the actual work must be committed together (one transaction) or keyed through the same idempotency guarantee. If you do the work, then crash before marking it processed, the job comes back and you redo it. If you mark it processed, then crash before doing the work, it's lost. Tie them together so there's no gap between "done" and "recorded as done." Use queues for big, bursty, or non-interactive work (overnight batches, flagged-transaction investigations, statement runs); don't put a live, customer-waiting turn behind a queue, and don't build a handler that breaks when the same event arrives twice.

In production

Give every queue a dead-letter queue — a side queue for messages that keep failing after N attempts — so one poison message can't get retried forever and block the line; a human reviews the dead-letter pile. Set visibility timeouts so a slow job isn't wrongly handed to a second worker mid-run. And carry the correlation ID from the originating event through every log and trace, so an overnight batch job is as debuggable as a live request. Event-driven design is how banks run agent work at scale reliably — but every bit of it rests on idempotent handlers.

✅ Tip

A concrete serverless version of this on AWS: events land on Amazon SQS (the queue), and an AWS Lambda function is the handler SQS invokes per message. Lambda scales the worker pool up and down automatically with the backlog, and messages that keep failing move to an SQS dead-letter queue after N tries. SQS still delivers at least once, so the Lambda handler must be idempotent exactly as above. (Equivalents elsewhere: Google Pub/Sub + Cloud Functions, or Azure Service Bus + Functions.)

Going deeper

"At-least-once" delivery is the heart of the matter, and it's a feature, not a bug — the queue would rather deliver a message twice than lose it. The cost is that your handler will occasionally see the same event twice (a worker did the work, then crashed before acknowledging it, so the queue re-delivers). Three mechanics make this safe. Idempotent handlers: record each event ID as processed and skip anything already done, committing the work and the "done" mark in one transaction so there's no gap between them. Visibility timeout: when a worker picks up a message it becomes invisible to others for a window — set that window longer than the job's real runtime or a slow job gets handed to a second worker mid-run. Dead-letter queue: after N failed attempts a message moves to a side queue for a human, so one "poison" message can't be retried forever and block the line. Ordering is the common surprise — most queues don't guarantee it, so don't assume event B arrives after event A unless you've chosen an ordered queue or a partition key. And carry the correlation ID from the originating event through every log and trace, so an overnight batch is as debuggable as a live chat.

⚙️ In production

Scale: the queue absorbs spikes — 10,000 overnight loan applications wait their turn instead of crushing the agent — and you scale workers up and down independently of the producers. Cost: background and batch work can run on a cheaper model tier and off-peak capacity. Latency: throughput, not per-request latency, is the metric that matters here; watch queue depth and age-of-oldest-message. Failure modes: duplicate processing (fixed by idempotency), poison messages (fixed by a dead-letter queue), and a slow consumer letting the backlog grow unbounded. Monitoring: alarm on queue depth, dead-letter count, and redelivery rate. Security/compliance: messages can carry PII, so encrypt them at rest and in transit, scope access to the queue, and keep the dead-letter contents under the same controls as any customer record.

🧠 Remember it

Queues deliver at least once, so handlers must survive running twice. Check the event ID, do the work and mark it done together, and keep a dead-letter queue for the jobs that just won't.

Rate limiting, quotas, and being a good neighbor

Your agent isn't alone — it shares a model provider, a core-banking API, and a database with everyone else. Limits are what keep one busy moment, or one buggy loop, from taking the whole system down.

Every service your agent depends on has a ceiling: the model provider allows so many requests or tokens per minute; the core-banking API allows so many calls per second. Cross it and you get rate-limited — the dreaded HTTP 429, "too many requests." Rate limiting runs in two directions, and you have to think about both.

Limits coming at you. When a provider rate-limits your agent, you must handle the 429 gracefully — back off and retry (it's a retriable error — wait, then try again), or fall back to another model or a queue. An agent that ignores 429s and hammers away just gets limited harder and serves nobody.

Limits you impose. You also protect your own downstream systems and enforce fairness by rate-limiting yourself. Set quotas — a budget of requests per customer, per tenant, per time window — so one customer (or one runaway loop, or one abuser) can't consume all the capacity and starve everyone else. The classic tool is a token bucket: each caller has a bucket that refills at a steady rate; each request spends a token; an empty bucket means "wait." It allows short bursts while capping the sustained rate.

⚙️ Under the hood

In a multi-step agent, one task can be many provider calls, so a per-request limit isn't enough — track usage per task and per tenant, and keep the counters in a shared store (like Redis) so the limit holds across all your worker instances, not just one. Respect the provider's own signals too: a 429 often comes with a Retry-After header telling you exactly how long to wait — obey it rather than guessing. And distinguish tiers: a provider may give batch or background work a separate, cheaper lane from latency-sensitive live traffic, so route accordingly.

In production

Quotas are a safety and a cost control. A per-tenant token quota caps what any one client can spend, turning "a bug in one integration bankrupted us overnight" into "that tenant hit its quota and got a clean 429." They're also an abuse control: a runaway or malicious caller is contained to their own bucket. Monitor who's hitting limits — a customer constantly throttled may need a higher tier or may be misusing the system, and either way it's a conversation, not a silent drop. Being a good neighbor to your downstream services is what keeps the whole platform up, not just your corner of it.

Going deeper

Rate limiting is two jobs wearing one name. Limits coming at you are the provider's 429s; the professional response is to back off and retry, and — critically — to obey the Retry-After header when one is present rather than guessing a wait. Limits you impose protect your own downstreams and enforce fairness between tenants. The classic algorithm is the token bucket: a bucket refills at a steady rate, each request spends a token, an empty bucket means wait or reject. Its charm is that it allows a short burst (up to the bucket size) while capping the sustained rate — which matches real traffic better than a rigid "N per second." A close cousin, the leaky bucket, smooths output to a constant rate with no burst. The agent-specific twist: one task is many provider calls, so a per-request limit badly under-counts — track usage per task and per tenant. And the counters must live in a shared store (Redis is typical) so the limit holds across all your worker instances, not just one process; a per-instance limiter silently allows N times the intended rate when you run N workers. Distinguish tiers too: many providers offer a separate, cheaper lane for batch or background work, so route latency-insensitive jobs there and keep the fast lane for live traffic.

⚙️ In production

Cost control: a per-tenant token quota turns "a bug in one integration bankrupted us overnight" into "that tenant hit its quota and got a clean 429" — it's a financial circuit breaker as much as a load control. Scale: shared counters (Redis) keep the limit correct across the whole fleet. Latency: the limiter check must be fast; a slow shared lookup on every call adds latency to everything. Failure modes: a per-instance limiter that multiplies the true rate; ignoring 429s and getting throttled harder. Monitoring: track who's hitting limits — a constantly throttled customer needs a higher tier or is misusing the system, and either way it's a conversation, not a silent drop. Security/compliance: quotas are also an abuse control — a runaway or malicious caller is contained to their own bucket and can't starve other BankAssist customers.

⚠ Watch out

A per-process rate limiter is a trap — run ten workers and you silently allow ten times the rate you intended, so keep the counters in a shared store. Use backoff-and-retry for 429s coming at you and per-tenant token buckets for the load you impose; don't ignore a Retry-After header, and don't rely on a per-instance limiter in a multi-worker fleet.

🧠 Remember it

Honor the limits above you, impose limits below you. Back off on a 429, give every tenant a bucket, and never let one caller drink the whole well.

Versioning everything and the continuous eval loop

An agent is never "finished." Models change, prompts change, policies change — so the real production skill is changing things safely, knowing instantly if a change helped or hurt, and being able to undo it.

Here's a trap unique to AI systems. You tweak the prompt to fix one annoying answer. It fixes that case — and silently breaks five others you didn't test. Because the model's behavior is emergent, a small change can ripple in ways you can't predict by reading the diff. Two disciplines tame this: version everything, and evaluate continuously.

Version everything

Treat every input that shapes the agent's behavior as a versioned artifact — not a thing you edit in place and forget. That means: the prompts, the model name and settings (temperature, effort), the tool definitions, the retrieval config (chunking, embedding model, top-K), and the eval dataset itself. When you can name "version 7," you can compare it to version 6, roll back to it after a bad deploy, and — crucially — tie each logged answer to the exact version that produced it. Without versioning, "it got worse last Tuesday" is an unsolvable mystery; with it, it's a two-minute diff.

🏦 Picture this

A model provider releases a new version and auto-upgrades the alias BankAssist points at. Overnight, the agent's tone shifts and it starts refusing some legitimate requests. Because the team pinned an exact model ID and logged it on every response, they spot the change in minutes, roll back to the pinned version, and re-run their eval set against the new model before adopting it on their schedule — not the provider's. Versioning turned a potential incident into a controlled upgrade.

Continuous eval loop

Evaluation isn't a one-time gate before launch; it's a loop that never stops. It has three tiers working together, and a banking agent needs all three.

  • Offline eval (before you ship). Keep a golden set — representative banking tasks with known-good outcomes — and run every proposed change against it automatically, as a gate in your deployment pipeline. If a change drops success rate or faithfulness, it doesn't ship. This is your regression net.
  • Online monitoring (while it's live). On real traffic, continuously sample answers and score them — groundedness, guardrail hits, escalation rate — using the metrics and traces you already record. This catches what the golden set didn't anticipate.
  • Human feedback (closing the loop). Capture thumbs-up/down, agent-handoff outcomes, and reviewer corrections. The gold here: feed the failures you find in production back into the golden set, so every real mistake becomes a permanent test the agent can never silently repeat.
⚙️ Under the hood

For a banking agent, consistency matters more than peak cleverness. Run each eval scenario several times and look at how often it succeeds every time, not just once — an agent that gets a transfer right 9 times out of 10 is not "90% good," it's a system that mishandles money one time in ten. Gate releases on this reliability, not on a single lucky run. And when you use a model to grade answers ("LLM-as-judge"), remember judges are biased and drift — calibrate them against human labels and don't treat a judge score as ground truth.

In production

Roll changes out gradually — a canary or small percentage first, watching the live metrics, before 100%. Keep rollback one command away, because you will need it. And connect this loop to the rest of your operational stack: the traces give you the examples, the metrics give you the signal, the versioning gives you the control, and the eval set gives you the verdict. That closed loop — change, measure, learn, and be able to undo — is what separates an agent you demo from an agent you operate.

Going deeper

Two ideas make continuous eval trustworthy rather than theatre. First, measure reliability, not peak capability. Because a model is non-deterministic, running a scenario once tells you little — run each eval case several times and score how often it succeeds every time (sometimes called pass^k). An agent that gets a transfer right 9 times in 10 is not "90% good"; it's a system that mishandles money one time in ten, and for a bank that's a gating failure. Second, trust your judge carefully. Using a model to grade answers ("LLM-as-judge") scales evaluation cheaply, but judges are biased (they favour longer, more confident answers and their own style) and they drift when the judge model updates — so calibrate the judge against human labels on a sample, and never treat a judge score as ground truth for a money decision. The highest-leverage habit is the feedback loop itself: every real failure you find in production becomes a new case in the golden set, so the same mistake can never silently recur. Version every input that shapes behaviour — prompts, model ID and settings, tool definitions, retrieval config (chunking, embedding model, top-K), and the eval set itself — and stamp the exact version onto every logged answer, so "it got worse last Tuesday" becomes a two-minute diff instead of an unsolvable mystery.

⚙️ In production

Deployment: roll changes out gradually — a canary or small percentage first, watching live metrics — with rollback one command away, because you will need it. Cost: offline eval against a golden set runs on every change as a pipeline gate, so budget those eval calls; online scoring samples live traffic rather than grading everything. Scale & failure modes: the trap unique to AI systems is a prompt tweak that fixes one case and silently breaks five others — the golden set is your regression net against exactly that. Monitoring: gate releases on reliability (success every time), not a single lucky run, and alarm on live quality drift. Security/compliance: pin exact model IDs so a provider's silent auto-upgrade can't change behaviour overnight, and keep the version history and eval results as part of the auditable record of how the agent was allowed to make each decision.

⚠ Watch out

A prompt change that fixes the case in front of you can quietly break five you didn't test — behaviour is emergent, so you can't read the diff and know. Use a versioned golden set as a release gate and continuous online scoring for everything that shaped behaviour; don't ship on a single passing run, don't trust an LLM judge as ground truth without calibration, and don't let a provider auto-upgrade a model you haven't re-evaluated.

🧠 Remember it

Version everything, eval forever, and turn every production failure into a test. You can't improve what you don't measure — and you can't recover from what you didn't version.

Putting it together: the end-to-end reliability pipeline

Each pattern in this chapter is one brick. The system design is the order you stack them in — because the same bricks in the wrong order protect nothing.

Imagine every request to BankAssist as water flowing through a series of gates. Budgets, routing, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, validation, caching, tracing — on their own each is a single valve. The skill that turns a demo into a production system is wiring them into one pipeline where each valve sits in exactly the right place. Put a gate in the wrong spot and it does nothing; worse, it can make things less safe. So the real lesson of system design here is a single question asked at every layer: what wraps what, and why?

Request path

Here is the journey of one customer turn, from the moment it arrives to the moment an answer streams back. The order is the design — each number explains why it sits where it does.

  1. Quota / rate limit — first, so a rejected caller costs almost nothing. Check the tenant's token bucket before you spend a cent of compute. A caller who's over quota gets a clean 429 at the door, not after an expensive model call. (Counters live in a shared store so the limit holds across every worker, not per-process.)
  2. Model router — pick the cheapest model that can do the job. A balance check goes to a small model; anything moving money or deciding a dispute is forced to the flagship. Routing happens before the loop so every step runs on the right-priced model.
  3. Agent loop, inside a budget. The think-act loop runs with a hard ceiling — max steps, max tokens, max wall-clock seconds. The budget is the seatbelt that guarantees no single request can run away.
  4. Each tool call, through the resilience stack. Every call the loop makes is wrapped — innermost a per-call timeout, around it retry with backoff and jitter, around that a circuit breaker, and a fallback when the breaker is open. Writes carry an idempotency key so a retry can never pay twice.
  5. Validation, twice. Arguments are checked before any tool runs (a hallucinated amount never reaches the payments API); the final answer is checked before the customer sees it, and it fails closed — a questionable answer is blocked and escalated, never shipped.
  6. Response, streamed. Safe content streams out token by token so it feels instant — but money-words wait until they've passed their checks.

Two concerns wrap all of the above. Observability is the outermost layer: one trace with a correlation ID threads every span, metric, and downstream log, with PII redacted before storage. And governance surrounds the whole system over time: every prompt, model ID, tool, and retrieval setting is versioned, and a continuous eval loop gates each change.

Order matters

The wrapping order isn't cosmetic — get it wrong and gates cancel each other out. The resilience stack around a single tool call is the sharpest example. The circuit breaker goes outside the retry, not inside: when a dependency is down and the breaker is open, the request must fail instantly to the fallback — if retry wrapped the breaker instead, you'd waste three backoff waits before discovering the door is shut. The timeout goes innermost, so each individual attempt is bounded; the retry then gives each bounded attempt another go. Here is that stack in code, with the order made explicit.

# Every tool call the loop makes goes through the SAME resilient stack — the ORDER is the point.
@breaker(key=tool_name)                            # OUTERMOST: if the dependency is down, fail instantly — skip the retries entirely
@with_retry(RETRIABLE, max_attempts=3)             # middle: retry only transient errors, with exponential backoff + jitter
@with_timeout(seconds=p99_of(tool_name) + 0.5)     # INNERMOST: bound each single attempt, sized from measured p99 (not a round number)
def call_tool(tool_name, args, idem_key):          # idem_key makes a repeated WRITE a safe no-op after an ambiguous timeout
    validate_args(tool_name, args)                 # check arguments BEFORE the action — money rules live here, not in the model
    return downstream.invoke(tool_name, args, idem_key)  # only reached once every guard above has passed
▶ Output
Dependency healthy: timeout bounds the call, it succeeds, returns. Dependency flapping: a 503 is retried with backoff. Dependency down: the breaker is open, so the call fails in milliseconds straight to the fallback — no wasted retries.

The same "order is the design" logic governs the request handler. Observability must be the outermost layer so it captures everything inside it, including failures. Quota comes first so a rejected caller is cheap. Output validation comes last and fails closed, so nothing unsafe slips out just because the layers before it were fast.

# The request handler — same principle: what wraps what, and why.
from openai import OpenAI                           # the official OpenAI SDK
client = OpenAI()                                   # reads the API key from the environment

def handle_turn(request, correlation_id):          # one customer turn, stamped with a trace id
    with tracer.start_span("turn") as span:        # OUTERMOST: every layer below emits spans into this one trace
        span.set("correlation_id", correlation_id) # one id threads logs, metrics, and downstream calls together
        enforce_quota(request.tenant)              # 1. gate FIRST — a rejected caller must cost almost nothing
        model = pick_model(request)                # 2. route: small model for easy, flagship for money
        budget = Budget(max_steps=8, max_tokens=60_000, deadline_s=8)  # 3. the seatbelt around the loop
        answer = agent_loop(request, model, budget, client)  # run think-act under the ceilings; tools use the stack above
        if not output_ok(answer):                  # 5. validate the FINAL answer before the customer sees it
            return escalate_to_human(request)      # fail CLOSED — a questionable answer is never shipped
        return stream(answer)                       # 6. safe content streams out; money-words waited for the check
▶ Output
An over-quota tenant is turned away in one cheap step. A healthy "dispute this charge" runs on the flagship, under budget, with every tool call protected and every answer validated — and the whole turn is one searchable trace.
🏦 Picture this

A customer types "dispute this $2,000 charge." The pipeline hums: the request passes quota; the router sees "money + dispute" and pins the flagship model; the loop starts with a 12-step budget. It fires three lookups in parallel (the charge, the merchant, the customer's history), each wrapped in timeout-retry-breaker. The fraud-scoring call times out — but the breaker for a different, already-sick service is open, so that fallback kicks in instantly instead of hanging. Argument validation confirms the dispute amount and ownership; the draft answer is checked and passes; it streams back. Mid-investigation the server is redeployed — but the task was checkpointed after each step, so a fresh worker reloads the state and resumes at step 7, not step 1. Every step of it is one trace under correlation_id=req-9c2e, ready if an auditor ever asks.

The moving parts

The pipeline above is logic; it has to run on real infrastructure. In production BankAssist is a stateless fleet of agent workers sitting behind an API gateway, sharing a small set of backing stores. "Stateless" is the key word: a worker keeps nothing important in its own memory, so you can kill, deploy, or autoscale workers freely, and any worker can pick up any task because the state lives in the shared stores, not the process.

Each store earns its place by holding exactly the state one pattern needs to survive a crash or span the whole fleet.

StateLives inWhy there
Rate-limit counters, semantic cacheRedis (shared, fast)The limit must hold across every worker, and a cache hit must be shared by all of them — a per-process store would silently allow N times the rate.
Checkpoints, idempotency ledger, audit trailPostgres (durable)Must survive a crash or deploy; the ledger dedupes repeated writes; the trail is the regulator's record of every step.
Background & batch jobsQueue + dead-letter queueAbsorbs spikes, redelivers safely at-least-once, and quarantines poison messages for a human.
Model callsProvider APIs, routed by tierBilled per token; the router sends each request to the cheapest capable model.
Traces, metrics, logsObservability backend (self-hosted for PII)Debug one request, alarm on a million — kept in-house so customer prompts never leave the bank's environment.

Now the components the handler above named but didn't show — here's what each actually looks like inside. Start with enforce_quota: a token bucket kept in the shared store so the limit is correct across the whole fleet.

# enforce_quota implemented: a token bucket in a SHARED store, so the limit holds fleet-wide.
import time                                             # we refill the bucket based on elapsed real time

def enforce_quota(store, tenant, rate=10.0, burst=20):  # rate = tokens refilled per second; burst = bucket size
    key = f"quota:{tenant}"                             # one bucket PER tenant — one caller can't starve the rest
    now = time.time()
    tokens, last = store.get(key, default=(burst, now)) # current tokens + when we last refilled them
    tokens = min(burst, tokens + (now - last) * rate)   # REFILL: add tokens for the time that has passed, capped at burst
    if tokens < 1:                                      # bucket empty → caller is over their sustained rate
        raise RateLimited(retry_after=1)                # clean 429 at the door, BEFORE any model spend
    store.set_atomic(key, (tokens - 1, now))            # spend one token; MUST be atomic (Lua/transaction) or two workers race
▶ Output
Steady traffic under the rate passes freely; a burst up to 20 is absorbed; sustained over-use empties the bucket and returns 429 retry_after=1 — cheaply, at the gate.

Next, agent_loop — the heart. This is where the three budget ceilings are actually enforced around real OpenAI calls, and where each tool call is routed through the resilient stack shown earlier.

# agent_loop implemented: the think-act loop that ENFORCES the budget and calls OpenAI each lap.
import time

def agent_loop(request, model, budget, client):        # budget carries the three ceilings: steps, tokens, clock
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": request.text}]
    start, tokens_used = time.time(), 0                 # track elapsed time and cumulative tokens for the ceilings
    for step in range(budget.max_steps):               # STEP ceiling: the loop literally cannot exceed it
        if time.time() - start > budget.deadline_s:    # CLOCK ceiling: out of time → stop cleanly, don't run on
            return wind_down("taking too long")        # fail safe, never a half-formed guess
        resp = client.responses.create(                # one paid model call — current OpenAI Responses API
            model=model, input=messages, tools=TOOLS,  # model chosen by the router; the tools it may call
        )
        tokens_used += resp.usage.total_tokens         # TOKEN ceiling: track real spend from the usage the API reports
        if tokens_used > budget.max_tokens:            # near the token cap → wind down rather than get chopped off
            return wind_down("budget reached")
        if resp.output_text:                           # the model produced a final answer — the happy path
            return resp.output_text
        for call in resp.tool_calls:                   # otherwise run the tool(s) it asked for...
            result = call_tool(call.name, call.args, call.idem_key)  # ...through the timeout→retry→breaker stack
            messages.append(tool_result(call, result)) # feed the observation back so the next lap can use it
    return wind_down("out of steps")                   # STEP budget hit → hand off safely, never keep guessing
▶ Output
A simple question finishes in 2 laps well under budget. A task that loops hits the step or token ceiling and winds down to a human — it can never run away or run up an unbounded bill.

The @breaker decorator is a small state machine, one instance per dependency. Here it is unrolled so you can see the three states change.

# The @breaker, implemented: the three-state machine that protects a sick dependency.
import time

class Breaker:                                         # create ONE per downstream dependency — never one global breaker
    def __init__(self, fail_max=5, cool_off=15):       # trip after fail_max fails; stay OPEN for cool_off seconds
        self.state, self.fails, self.opened_at = "closed", 0, 0

    def call(self, fn, fallback):                      # wrap one downstream call plus its plan B
        if self.state == "open":                       # breaker tripped — the dependency is presumed down
            if time.time() - self.opened_at < self.cool_off:
                return fallback()                      # still cooling off → fail FAST, don't even try the dead service
            self.state = "half_open"                   # cool-off elapsed → allow exactly ONE trial request
        try:
            result = fn()                              # attempt the real call
        except Exception:
            self.fails += 1                            # count this failure toward the threshold
            if self.fails >= self.fail_max or self.state == "half_open":
                self.state, self.opened_at = "open", time.time()  # trip (or RE-trip when the trial fails)
            return fallback()                          # degrade to plan B rather than erroring the customer
        self.fails, self.state = 0, "closed"           # success resets the count and closes the breaker — self-healing
        return result
▶ Output
Five failures flip it to OPEN; for 15s every call fails instantly to the fallback; then one trial runs — success closes it, failure reopens it. No human, no 3 a.m. page.

Finally, the piece that makes a long task survivable: a durable step that checkpoints its progress and records its writes in one transaction, so a resume never repeats a side effect.

# Durable step on Postgres: checkpoint progress AND dedupe side effects — survive a crash safely.
def run_step(db, task_id, step_no, do_work, idem_key):  # one durable step of a long-running task
    if db.seen(idem_key):                              # idempotency ledger: has this exact write already happened?
        return db.result_of(idem_key)                  # yes → return the stored outcome, do NOT run it again
    result = do_work()                                 # the real side effect (pull credit, post a fee, send a notice)
    with db.transaction():                             # commit the write-mark AND the checkpoint TOGETHER — no gap between them
        db.record(idem_key, result)                    # mark this write done, so a resume skips it (the dedupe)
        db.checkpoint(task_id, step_no, result)        # save progress, so a restart resumes at step_no + 1, not step 1
    return result
▶ Output
Crash after step 3: a fresh worker reloads checkpoint 3 and resumes at step 4. A step that already pulled a credit report finds its idem_key in the ledger and returns the saved result — no second pull.

Long tasks & batch

Not every request is a live chat turn, and the pipeline flexes for two other shapes. A long-running task (a loan application that runs for minutes across many steps) runs the same loop but under durable checkpointing — state saved to a real database after each step — so a crash or deploy costs a reload, not a redo. Background and batch work (investigate 10,000 flagged transactions overnight) goes onto a queue: worker agents pull jobs, each handler is idempotent so an at-least-once redelivery is harmless, and a dead-letter queue catches poison messages. Same resilience bricks, arranged for throughput instead of live latency.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the cheap layers come first on purpose — quota and routing shed and down-shift load before the expensive model runs, so the bill is shaped at the front door. Latency: the open-breaker fast-fail and streaming are what keep p95 sane under partial outages; measure time-to-first-token and p95 end-to-end, never the average. Scale: shared counters (rate limits), a shared semantic cache, and a durable checkpoint/queue backend are what let the pipeline run correctly across a whole fleet of workers rather than one process. Failure modes: the classic system-design bug here is a layer in the wrong order — a breaker inside a retry, validation that fails open, observability that misses the errors because it sits too far in. Monitoring: one correlation ID per request ties the four metric families (quality, latency, cost, reliability) back to the exact trace behind any anomaly. Security/compliance: no layer may trade away a safety control — degrade capability, never safety — and the versioned config plus the full step-by-step trace are the auditable record of how every decision was allowed to happen.

⚠ Watch out

The same bricks in the wrong order protect nothing: a circuit breaker inside a retry still hammers a dead service, validation that fails open ships the bad answer anyway, and tracing that sits inside the loop misses the crashes that happen around it. Use this layered pipeline for any production agent that touches real accounts; don't bolt the pieces on in random order, and don't assume a pattern works just because it's present — it only works where it sits in the stack.

🧠 Remember it

The bricks are the patterns; the architecture is their order. Cheap gates first, safety checks last and fail-closed, resilience wrapped breaker-outside-retry-outside-timeout, and observability around the whole thing.
