Building low-latency, high-performance agents (web & API)

All the speed tricks are useless until you know your number. This is the end-to-end playbook: pick a latency target, then spend every trick in the right place to hit it.

Caching, parallel tool calls, streaming, budgets — each is a separate lever, and the earlier topics covered them one at a time. This lesson is the playbook that ties them into one request path and adds the pieces that only make sense together: where to deploy, how to route, and how to measure. The goal is a text or chat agent on the web that feels instant, stays cheap, and holds up when traffic spikes.

Start with the latency budget

You cannot optimize what you have not named. So name two numbers. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is how long the customer stares at a blank box before anything appears. Total latency is how long until the answer is complete. These are different experiences: a page that starts streaming in 0.8s and finishes in 3s feels fast; one that shows nothing for 2.5s then dumps the whole answer feels broken — even though the second one is quicker overall. That gap between the clock and the feeling is perceived vs actual latency, and TTFT is the lever that moves perception. Set a hard target up front. For BankAssist chat we use: first token < 1s, full answer < 3s, p95 (not the average — averages hide the slow tail that angry customers live in).

Spend the budget: the levers, in order

Stream to the browser. The single biggest perceived-latency win. Open a Server-Sent Events (SSE) connection (a one-way stream from server to browser — simpler than a WebSocket and ideal for chat) and paint each token as it arrives. Pair it with an optimistic UI: show the user's message and a skeleton (a shimmering placeholder) the instant they hit send, so the box is never blank. Token-by-token rendering turns a 3-second wait into a conversation.

Choose and route the model. Default to a small, fast model — gpt-4.1-mini answers in roughly half the TTFT of a big model — and escalate to gpt-4.1 only when the task is genuinely hard (long reasoning, ambiguous policy). This "small-first" router is the highest-leverage cost and latency decision you make. Related ideas: distillation (train a tiny model to imitate a big one on your traffic) for self-hosted paths, speculative decoding (a cheap draft model guesses several tokens ahead and the big model verifies them in one pass — 2–3× faster generation, though it barely touches TTFT), and turning up reasoning effort only for the queries that need it.

Cache aggressively. Provider-side prompt caching is nearly free latency: OpenAI automatically reuses a matching prompt prefix and bills cached input at a 75% discount, so keep the stable parts (system prompt, tool schemas, policy text) first and byte-identical and put the volatile user turn last — a cache-stable prefix. Layer a semantic result cache on top: if a new question is close enough (by embedding similarity) to one already answered, return the stored answer and skip the model entirely.

Cut tokens. Every token is latency. Trim the system prompt, summarize or drop old context, and design tools so the agent needs fewer round-trips — each extra think-act lap is a whole model call on the clock.

Parallelize and prefetch. Fire independent tool calls and retrievals together, not in sequence. Go further with speculative prefetch: while the model is still thinking, start fetching the data the next step will probably need (the customer's recent transactions, say), so it is warm by the time it is asked for.

Here is the small-first router with streaming — the two biggest levers in one place.

# Small-model-first router that STREAMS: cheapest fast path by default, escalate only when needed.
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()                                   # reuses one pooled HTTPS connection (keep-alive) across calls

def pick_model(query, context):                     # the routing decision — the biggest latency+cost lever
    hard = context.needs_reasoning or len(query) > 600  # cheap heuristic (or a tiny classifier) for "is this hard?"
    return "gpt-4.1" if hard else "gpt-4.1-mini"    # small model first; escalate to the big one only when hard

def answer(query, context, history):
    model = pick_model(query, context)              # most turns take the fast, cheap gpt-4.1-mini path
    stream = client.responses.create(               # current OpenAI Responses API
        model=model,
        input=history + [{"role": "user", "content": query}],  # stable prefix first (history/system) → prompt-cache hit
        stream=True,                                # stream=True: get tokens as they generate, not all at the end → low TTFT
    )
    for event in stream:                            # iterate the SSE event stream from the API
        if event.type == "response.output_text.delta":  # each delta is a new chunk of the answer
            yield event.delta                       # push the chunk straight out to the browser's SSE connection
▶ Output
A balance question routes to gpt-4.1-mini and the first word reaches the browser in ~0.8s, streaming to a full answer by ~2.3s. A thorny dispute routes to gpt-4.1: slightly higher TTFT, but still streaming so it never feels stalled.

Infrastructure and RAG specifics

Infra. Keep connections pooled and alive (TLS and TCP setup is 100+ms you pay on every cold call). Deploy at the edge / in the region closest to your users so network round-trips are short. Keep a warm pool of instances so no customer eats a cold start, and autoscale on concurrency (in-flight requests), not CPU — an LLM box is busy waiting, not computing. If you self-host, vLLM gives you prefix caching (reuse the KV-cache for a shared prompt prefix — in one published test a ~10k-token prompt dropped from 4.3s to 0.6s TTFT on the repeat) and continuous batching (pack many requests through the GPU together). Continuous batching is the classic throughput-vs-latency trade-off: bigger batches serve more users per GPU but add a little wait to each one — tune it to your p95, not to your bragging rights.

RAG latency. Retrieval is often the hidden half of the clock. Tune your ANN index (approximate nearest-neighbor — trade a sliver of recall for a big speed win), pre-filter by metadata before the vector search (only this customer's documents) and post-filter after, rerank only the top-k (rerank 20, not 2,000), and cache embeddings so you never re-embed the same query or document twice.

Measuring — or you are guessing

Track p50/p95/p99 of TTFT and of total latency, and break each request into per-stage spans (edge, auth, retrieval, prefill, generation) so you can see which slice blew the budget. Load-test at your real peak concurrency, because latency under load is a different animal from latency on an idle box — and remember the trade-off runs both ways: squeeze latency and you cap throughput; chase throughput and tails grow.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the small-first router and prompt caching together cut BankAssist's spend the most — most turns never touch the big model, and cached prefixes bill at a 75% discount. Latency: optimize for p95 TTFT first (it drives perception and churn), total p95 second. Scale: warm pools plus concurrency-based autoscaling keep the tail flat through the 9 a.m. spike; a shared semantic cache means one popular answer is computed once for the whole fleet. Monitoring: one correlation ID threads the per-stage spans so a slow p99 points at the exact stage — usually retrieval or a cold model, rarely the network. Failure modes: a cache-busting prefix (a timestamp or request ID slipped into the system prompt) silently turns every call into a cache miss; watch your cache-hit rate like a vital sign. Security/compliance: never cache a semantic result across customers — key the cache by customer and entitlement, or one person's balance leaks into another's answer.

⚠ Watch out

Latency work has a floor: past a point you are shaving 20ms off a 2-second human reading speed nobody notices, while adding a draft model, a cache tier, and a router you now have to operate. Use this playbook for interactive web and chat agents where TTFT is felt. Don't over-engineer a nightly batch job (there, maximize throughput and let each request be slow), don't reach for speculative decoding expecting a TTFT win (it speeds generation, not the first token), and don't bolt on a semantic cache for highly personalized answers where almost nothing repeats — you will pay the lookup and never hit.

🧠 Remember it

Name the number, then stream first and route small. First token under a second buys you the three you need for the rest.

Building cost-efficient agents: the cost-optimization playbook

Every token, every tool call, every stored vector is on the meter. This is the whole toolbox for cutting the bill — each lever with how it works, why it helps, and a number — without making the agent dumber or less safe.

Think of your AI bill like a household utility bill. You don't cut it by turning off the fridge; you cut it by sealing the drafts, using the cheap off-peak tariff, and not heating empty rooms. An agent is the same: the savings come from many small, boring disciplines applied in the right places, not from one heroic switch. Three earlier topics in this chapter each pulled one lever on its own — model routing, caching, and the low-latency playbook; this topic is the consolidated cost view that ties them together and adds the rest.

Where the money actually goes

Before you optimize, know what you're paying for. The first surprise for most engineers: output tokens cost about 4x input tokens. On gpt-4.1 input is $2 per million tokens and output is $8 per million; on gpt-4.1-mini it's $0.40 in and $1.60 out — same 4x ratio. So a chatty, verbose agent is expensive in a way a verbose reader is not. On top of that sit reasoning (thinking) tokens on reasoning models — hidden tokens the model generates to work through a problem, billed as output even though the customer never sees them — plus per-tool and hosted-tool fees (web search, code interpreter, file search all carry their own charge), and the quieter RAG stack: embedding calls, vector-database storage and queries, and reranking.

The single most important shift is the metric. Teams instinctively watch cost per call, but a cheap call that fails and forces three retries, a re-plan, and a human handoff is not cheap. The number that matters is cost per resolved task — total spend divided by tasks actually completed correctly. A smaller model that needs two tries can cost more per resolved task than a bigger model that nails it first time. Optimize the business outcome, not the line item.

The levers, at a glance

LeverTypical savingEffortRisk
Small-model-first routing (mini → big on escalation)50–80%MediumLow–Med (mis-route hurts quality)
Provider prompt caching (cache-stable prefix)~75% off cached inputLowLow
Semantic result cache (skip the LLM on repeats)10–40%MediumMed (staleness, cross-customer leak)
Trim prompt / compact context / cap max_output_tokens10–30%LowLow
Batch API for non-urgent bulk jobs~50%LowLow (up to 24h latency)
RAG: right-size top-k, quantize vectors, cache embeddings20–60% of RAG costMediumLow–Med (recall)
Fine-tune a small model to drop few-shot examples20–50% tokens/callHighMed
Self-host at high steady volume (vLLM)Varies (crossover)HighHigh (ops burden)

Model selection and routing

This is the highest-leverage decision. Default to a small, cheap model and escalate only when the task is genuinely hard. A BankAssist chat turn reads about 2,000 input tokens and writes ~300. On gpt-4.1 that's roughly $0.0064 a turn; on gpt-4.1-mini it's about $0.0013 — five times cheaper. At 500,000 turns a month, routing 85% of them to mini drops the model bill from about $3,200 to roughly $1,050. Extend the idea to a cascade: try the cheap model, and only if a confidence check or validator is unhappy, re-run on the strong one. For a self-hosted path, distillation (training a small model to imitate a big one on your own traffic) can give near-big-model quality at mini prices. And on reasoning models, turn up reasoning effort only for the queries that actually need it — thinking tokens are billed as output, so "think hard about everything" is a quiet money leak.

Caching, token reduction, and batching

Caching is nearly free money. Provider prompt caching bills a repeated prompt prefix at a ~75% discount (cached input on mini drops from $0.40 to $0.10 per million), so keep the stable parts — system prompt, tool schemas, policy text — first and byte-identical and put the volatile user turn last. A semantic result cache goes further: if a new question is close enough to one already answered, return the stored answer and skip the model entirely. On the token side, every token is money: shorten the system prompt, summarize or drop old turns (context compaction), design tools so the agent needs fewer round-trips, ask for concise output formats, and set max_output_tokens so a runaway answer can't bill you for an essay you didn't want.

For anything not interactive — nightly document processing, backfills, bulk evals — the Batch API runs the job asynchronously within 24 hours at roughly half price. BankAssist classifies the previous night's support transcripts this way and pays about 50% less than real-time would cost.

# Submit a NON-URGENT bulk job to the Batch API — ~50% cheaper, results within 24h.
import json                                          # to write one JSON object per line (JSONL)
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()                                    # reads the API key from the environment

with open("jobs.jsonl", "w") as f:                  # one JSONL line = one independent request
    for i, text in enumerate(transcripts):          # thousands of transcripts — nobody is waiting on these
        line = {
            "custom_id": f"t-{i}",                  # lets you match each result back to its input later
            "method": "POST",
            "url": "/v1/chat/completions",          # the endpoint each line is run against
            "body": {
                "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",            # small model: bulk labeling rarely needs the big one
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Label the intent:\n{text}"}],
                "max_tokens": 20,                   # cap output — a label is short, don't pay for an essay
            },
        }
        f.write(json.dumps(line) + "\n")            # append the request as one line

up = client.files.create(file=open("jobs.jsonl", "rb"), purpose="batch")  # upload the job file
batch = client.batches.create(                      # runs off-peak at the 50%-off batch rate
    input_file_id=up.id,
    endpoint="/v1/chat/completions",
    completion_window="24h",                        # the only SLA you get: done within 24 hours
)
print(batch.status)                                 # 'validating' now → poll later for 'completed'
▶ Output
validating → the job finishes overnight and the bill is about half what the same requests would cost in real time.

RAG, self-hosting, and governing the spend

RAG cost levers: cache embeddings so you never re-embed the same text twice, and re-embed only changed documents — re-embedding BankAssist's whole policy archive nightly costs real money, while re-embedding only the ~3% that changed this week is pennies (text-embedding-3-small is just $0.02 per million tokens). Use Matryoshka or quantized vectors (shorter, lower-precision embeddings) to shrink vector-DB storage and query cost, rerank only the top-k (rerank 20 candidates, not 2,000), and right-size top-k so you don't stuff the prompt — fewer retrieved chunks means fewer input tokens on every single call.

Self-host vs API: an API charges per token with zero fixed cost — perfect until volume is huge and steady. Past a crossover point, a dedicated GPU's fixed hourly cost beats per-token pricing, if you keep it busy. That "if" is the whole game: a GPU at 10% utilization is money on fire. vLLM with continuous batching and prefix caching is how teams push utilization high enough for self-hosting to actually pay off; below steady high volume, stay on the API.

Govern the spend: set per-user and per-feature budgets with hard spend caps, route all traffic through a gateway that enforces quotas and cost controls, tag every call by feature, customer tier, and model so you can see where the money goes, build cost dashboards with alerts on anomalies, and keep a kill-switch to disable an expensive feature instantly if it misbehaves. Finally, fine-tune a small model to absorb what you currently teach with long few-shot prompts: once the behavior is in the weights, you drop those example tokens from every call — a 20–50% token cut on a high-volume path.

⚙️ In production

Cost: at BankAssist the compounding stack — small-first routing (85% to mini), prompt caching (75% off the shared policy prefix), and the Batch API for all offline work — takes the blended model bill from ~$3,200 to well under $1,000 a month without a measurable quality drop. Scale: savings compound with volume, so the routing and caching layers pay for themselves fastest on the busiest features. Monitoring: the north-star chart is cost-per-resolved-task by feature, with the prompt-cache-hit rate and the mini-vs-big routing split beside it; a cache-hit rate that quietly falls (a timestamp slipped into the prompt prefix) is a classic silent cost regression. Failure modes: over-aggressive routing that sends hard disputes to mini raises the resolved-task cost even as the per-call cost drops — watch both numbers together. Security/compliance: never key a semantic cache across customers (one person's balance must never surface in another's answer), and every spend cap and kill-switch action is logged for audit.

⚠ Watch out

Optimization has a floor and a red line. The floor: don't over-optimize cheap traffic — spending a week shaving 15% off a feature that costs $40 a month is negative ROI; chase the big, high-volume paths first. The red line: never degrade safety to save money. Dropping a fraud or identity check, skipping output validation, or routing a money-moving decision to a weaker model to save a fraction of a cent is how a bank ends up on the news — a saved cent is never worth an unsafe action. Use this playbook on your high-volume, high-spend features; don't micro-optimize low-traffic paths, and don't let any cost lever touch a compliance control.

🧠 Remember it

Route small, cache hard, batch the boring, measure cost-per-resolved-task. Output bills 4x input — so the cheapest token is the one you never generate.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking 💵 cost 🏗️ system design

Surviving a provider outage: multi-region failover & operational resilience

An earlier topic kept one running process limping along when a dependency got sick. This is the bigger emergency: a whole region — or your entire model provider — falls off the map, and the service still has to answer.

Picture a branch where it isn't one flickering lamp that fails, but the power to the entire city block. The in-process fallbacks and circuit breakers covered earlier in this chapter handle a sick dependency inside one healthy service — they degrade a capability while the service keeps breathing. This topic is a level up: the service itself, the data centre it lives in, or the model provider it calls, simply disappears. A balance query isn't slow — there is nobody home to answer it. Keeping the lights on through that is operational resilience, and for a bank it is not optional.

It isn't optional because regulators now write it into law. The EU's Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) became fully applicable on 17 January 2025, and it treats a cloud LLM vendor as an ICT third party: the bank must keep critical functions running through "severe but plausible" disruption, set recovery targets, manage third-party and concentration risk (don't bet the bank on one provider), keep a register of ICT contracts with exit strategies, and prove it all with resilience testing. "Our model provider had an outage" is not a sentence you get to say to a regulator. The design must assume the provider will fail, because one day it will.

RTO and RPO: the two numbers that drive everything

Two targets, set per function from a business-impact analysis, decide how much engineering you buy. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long a function may stay down. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much recent work or data you may lose. At BankAssist, a balance lookup might carry an RTO of a minute and a generous RPO — stale by a few seconds is fine. A money-movement instruction carries an RTO near zero and an RPO of zero: you must never lose or double a payment. DORA expects these numbers to be technically demonstrable, not aspirational — you have to show the failover actually meets them.

Active-active

Two regions both serve live traffic all the time. A region dies and the survivors just absorb its share — failover is near-instant, so the RTO is tiny. The price: you run (and pay for) double capacity, and you must keep state consistent across regions constantly.

Active-passive

One region serves; a warm standby waits. On failure you promote the standby. Cheaper, but the RTO is the promotion time, and the real danger is a standby that has quietly drifted stale or was never truly exercised — so it fails the moment you finally need it.

Failing over to a second provider, mid-incident

The move that saves you when a whole provider is down is a second provider — and the trick is to hide both behind one gateway (an OpenAI-compatible endpoint every team calls). Then a provider outage is a routing event handled in one place, not a fire every team fights alone. Two hard-won rules make it real. First, pre-provision quota on the secondary before the incident — you cannot sign up for capacity in the middle of a meltdown, and a pricier fallback model can spike your bill, so budget for it. Second, health-check the upstream provider, not just the gateway: a gateway can happily return "I'm fine" while the model behind it is unreachable, so your probe has to actually exercise a real completion.

The quiet challenge is prompt parity and quality. A second provider's model is a different brain: the same prompt can behave differently, structured-output quirks differ, and the data-handling terms differ. If you first meet those differences during the outage, your failover trades a dead service for a subtly wrong one — a worse outcome at a bank. So you keep the system prompt identical across providers, run your evaluation suite against the secondary on every change, and accept a small, measured quality dip as the honest price of staying up.

# Route every model call through ONE abstraction that can fail over to a second provider.
from openai import OpenAI                               # the official OpenAI SDK, used for both endpoints

primary   = OpenAI()                                    # primary provider — key + base_url from the environment
secondary = OpenAI(base_url="https://llm-standby.internal/v1",  # a SECOND, OpenAI-compatible provider
                   api_key=SECONDARY_KEY)               # quota provisioned AHEAD of the incident, not during it

SYSTEM = "You are BankAssist. Answer only from the given policy text."  # SAME prompt on both → prompt parity

def ask(user_msg, deadline_s=6):                        # one customer turn, with a wall-clock deadline
    for client, model in [(primary,   "gpt-4.1"),       # try the primary first...
                          (secondary, "standby-llm")]:  # ...then the secondary if the primary is down
        try:
            r = client.chat.completions.create(         # a normal chat call
                model=model,
                messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
                          {"role": "user",   "content": user_msg}],
                timeout=deadline_s,                     # fail FAST so there's time left to fail over
            )
            return r.choices[0].message.content         # first healthy provider wins
        except Exception:                               # timeout, 5xx, total provider outage...
            continue                                    # ...drop to the next provider in the list
    return "I can't answer that right now — connecting you to a banker."  # both down → degraded mode
▶ Output
Primary healthy → gpt-4.1 answers. Primary in a full outage → the same request is served by the secondary provider in about a second and the customer never notices. Both down → a safe human handoff, never a guess.

Degraded mode and keeping state alive

When even the secondary is gone, you don't show a spinner — you drop to a pre-written degraded-mode runbook. At BankAssist that means: serve cached answers to common FAQs, let customers read balances straight from core banking (a plain lookup needs no model), freeze anything that requires generation, and route everything else to a human queue with an honest "our assistant is briefly unavailable." The runbook is written and rehearsed before the incident, because 3 a.m. is the worst time to invent a plan. And remember state: if your agent uses durable checkpoints (covered earlier), those checkpoints must be replicated across regions — a standby that starts blind, with no memory of in-flight tasks, isn't a failover, it's a fresh outage.

⚙️ In production

Cost & scale: active-active roughly doubles steady-state spend but buys a near-zero RTO; active-passive is cheaper but only as good as its last untested drill — pick per function from the RTO/RPO, not by taste. Latency: a short primary timeout is what buys the failover its time budget, so set it tight enough that trying the secondary still fits the customer's deadline. Failure modes: the silent killers are a stale/undersized standby, a secondary with no pre-provisioned quota, and a gateway health check that passes while the model behind it is dead. Monitoring: track per-provider health and the live failover rate, and alarm the instant traffic shifts to the secondary — a failover is an incident even when customers feel nothing. Security/compliance: the secondary region must enforce the identical identity, fraud, and data-residency controls, or failover becomes a compliance hole; and under DORA the whole thing must be exercised in regular game-days / chaos drills (kill the primary on purpose, confirm traffic moves) because an untested failover is a failover that doesn't work.

⚠ Watch out

The classic disaster is "we had a standby" — that nobody had tested, that had drifted stale, or whose secondary provider had no quota provisioned, so it collapsed the moment it was needed. Equally dangerous: a failover that quietly weakens a control (the backup region skips a fraud or residency check). Use multi-region, multi-provider failover for any customer-facing AI service a bank must keep running; don't treat it as "set up once" — an unrehearsed failover is worse than none, because it fails and it fooled you into thinking you were safe. And don't over-engineer a purely internal, best-effort tool to active-active; match the architecture to the function's real RTO.

🧠 Remember it

In-process fallback keeps one process limping; failover keeps the whole service alive. Two regions, two providers, one gateway — and a drill you actually run. An untested failover is just a story you tell yourself.

Capacity planning & graceful overload: SLOs, load shedding & backpressure

An earlier topic made you a polite neighbor who respects a provider's rate limits. This one asks the harder question: when a flood of real customers hits all at once, does your service bend — or does it shatter?

There is a morning every bank knows: payday. Salaries land, and a wall of people open the app at the same minute to move money, check balances, and chase a missing deposit. Traffic that sat at a gentle hum all week suddenly spikes five or ten times over. A naïve service meets that wall by trying to serve everyone — and that is exactly how it dies. Each request piles onto an overloaded queue, every response gets slower, timeouts cascade, retries pile on more load, and the whole thing spirals into a heap that serves nobody. The counter-intuitive truth of running at scale: a service that fails fast and sheds load survives; a service that tries to be a hero collapses.

SLOs and error budgets: the contract with reality

You can't protect a target you never set. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is a measurable promise — "99% of balance queries answer in under 2 seconds," "99.5% of money-movement requests succeed." The gap between that and perfection is your error budget: if the SLO is 99.9%, you are allowed to fail 0.1% of requests. That budget is a feature, not a shame. It tells you how much you can shed under pressure before you've broken your promise, and burning through it fast is a crisp, early trigger to start protecting the service rather than waiting for a full meltdown.

Plan the peak before it arrives

Capacity planning means modeling the peak, not the average: take payday's historical surge, add headroom, and load-test to it before you sign an SLA, not after a customer finds the ceiling for you. The catch specific to AI services is that you cannot simply "add more servers." Your real ceiling is the model provider's TPM and RPM limits (tokens- and requests-per-minute, which rise with your spending tier and return a 429 when crossed). Autoscaling helps for sustained growth, but it reacts in minutes (new instances, cold starts) while a payday spike hits in seconds — and no amount of scaling your own fleet moves the provider's token ceiling. So autoscaling alone can never save you from a burst. You also need the primitives that protect the service during the spike.

⚙️ Under the hood

Four primitives turn overload from a collapse into a controlled bend. Admission control: decide at the front door whether to let a request in at all — rejecting early (a fast 429 with a Retry-After) wastes far less work than letting it queue until it times out. Load shedding: when you're near the limit, deliberately drop or deflect the least important work first. Priority queues: not all requests are equal — a fraud alert outranks a balance query, which outranks a nice-to-have chat summary. Backpressure: signal upstream producers to slow down (bounded queues that stop accepting, or a "try later") instead of silently swallowing more than you can process. Rule of thumb: use backpressure for internal producers that can actually slow down; shed at the edge for the outside world that won't.

# Admission control: under overload, shed LOW-priority work so critical work still gets through.
from openai import OpenAI                               # the official OpenAI SDK
client = OpenAI()

inflight = 0                                            # how many model calls are running right now
MAX_INFLIGHT = 40                                       # our capacity ceiling — set BELOW the provider's TPM/RPM limit

PRIORITY = {"fraud_alert": 0, "money_move": 1,          # 0 = highest: a fraud alert beats...
            "balance": 2, "summary": 3}                 # ...a nice-to-have summary (shed first)

def admit(kind):                                        # the gate every request passes before any model call
    used = inflight / MAX_INFLIGHT                       # how full we are, 0.0 → 1.0
    if PRIORITY[kind] >= 3 and used > 0.7:              # once 70% full, drop summaries...
        return False                                    # ...fail FAST, don't let them crowd the queue
    if PRIORITY[kind] >= 2 and used > 0.9:              # once 90% full, drop balance checks too
        return False
    return inflight < MAX_INFLIGHT                       # P0/P1 (fraud, money) admitted until we're truly full

def handle(kind, prompt):                               # entry point for one request of a given kind
    global inflight
    if not admit(kind):                                 # rejected at the door...
        return {"retry_after": 2}                        # ...tell the caller to come back — backpressure, not a hang
    inflight += 1                                        # take a capacity slot
    try:
        r = client.chat.completions.create(             # the real work, only for admitted requests
            model="gpt-4.1-mini", timeout=6,            # cheap model + fast timeout for routine turns
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
        return r.choices[0].message.content
    finally:
        inflight -= 1                                   # always release the slot, success or failure
▶ Output
At a payday surge, fraud_alert and money_move keep going through; summary requests get {"retry_after": 2} and are dropped. The service bends — critical money work survives, the nice-to-haves wait.

Note the shape of the failure. A shed request isn't a crash — it's a fast, honest "not now, try in 2 seconds." That Retry-After is backpressure made polite: it tells the caller to slow down instead of hammering a service that's already underwater. And the ceiling (MAX_INFLIGHT) sits deliberately below the provider's hard rate limit, so you shed your way, gracefully, before the provider sheds for you with raw 429s.

⚙️ In production

Cost & scale: shedding caps spend under a spike — you never pay for work you drop — and it keeps you inside the provider's TPM/RPM ceiling that no autoscaler can raise. Latency: a fast reject is the point; a rejected request returns in milliseconds instead of timing out after seconds, which is what stops the death spiral. Failure modes: the collapse pattern is unbounded queues plus retries — requests wait past their own deadline, then clients retry, multiplying load; bounded queues with admission control break the loop. Monitoring: watch the SLO and error-budget burn rate, the shed rate by priority class, and queue depth — rising shedding of high-priority work is a page, rising shedding of summaries is business as usual. Security/compliance: shedding must respect priority, never safety — you may drop a summary, but a fraud check or a money-movement guardrail is never skipped to save capacity; log every shed decision so an auditor can see what was dropped and why.

⚠ Watch out

The fatal mistake is an unbounded queue: it feels generous ("we'll get to everyone") but it just lets latency climb until every request times out and the client retries, doubling the flood — the death spiral. Equally wrong is shedding by accident instead of by design: if you don't choose what to drop, the provider's raw 429s will drop things for you, at random, including fraud alerts. Use admission control, priority queues, and load shedding on any shared, customer-facing AI service that can be hit by a burst; don't shed or deprioritize safety-critical work to protect throughput, and don't lean on autoscaling for second-scale spikes — it reacts too slowly and can't lift the provider's token ceiling anyway.

🧠 Remember it

Under overload, bend don't break: shed the nice-to-haves, keep the money moving, and fail fast with a "try again in 2s." A hero that serves everyone serves no one — a bounded queue and a priority lane beat an infinite queue every time.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking 🧱 resilience 🏗️ system design

Evaluation & Production — LLMOps & Deployment

Building a clever agent is one thing; shipping it, versioning it, scaling it, and keeping it healthy for years in a bank is another job entirely — this chapter is the engineering machinery around the model, told as plainly as the rest.

What LLMOps is, and how it differs from classic MLOps

LLMOps is the set of habits and tools for shipping and running LLM and agent systems — the factory around the model, not the model itself.

Imagine two different bakeries. In the first, the baker grows the wheat, mills the flour, and bakes the bread — they own every step. In the second, the baker buys ready-made flour from a supplier and focuses entirely on the recipe, the oven settings, and serving customers fast. Classic MLOps is the first bakery: you train your own model from your own data, so most of your work is about data pipelines, training runs, and model weights. LLMOps is usually the second bakery: the "flour" (a frontier model like Claude or GPT) is bought through an API, and your real craft is the prompt, the retrieved context, the tools, and the evaluation that proves it behaves.

MLOps stands for Machine Learning Operations — the discipline of reliably training, deploying, and monitoring machine-learning models. LLMOps is the same spirit applied to large language models and agents, but the centre of gravity moves. You rarely touch model weights; instead your versioned "artifacts" become prompts, system instructions, retrieval indexes, tool definitions, and eval suites.

Classic MLOps centres on…

Training data and feature pipelines, the training run, model weights, retraining on drift, and metrics like accuracy or AUC. The model is yours; reproducing a training run is the hard problem.

LLMOps centres on…

Prompts and context, retrieval quality, tool wiring, token cost and latency, non-deterministic behaviour, guardrails, and eval-based quality. The model is often rented; proving behaviour is the hard problem.

Going deeper — the three things that make LLMOps genuinely different

  • Non-determinism. A classic model gives the same output for the same input. An LLM can answer differently each call. So "it passed once" means nothing — you evaluate over many cases and watch distributions, not single runs.
  • Quality is judged, not measured. There's no single accuracy number for "was this overdraft explanation correct and polite?" You lean on golden-set tests, LLM-as-judge scoring, and human review — the eval suite is your test suite.
  • The expensive resource is tokens, not GPUs. Your running cost is dollars per million tokens and seconds of latency per request, so cost and speed monitoring sit right next to correctness.

In production

In a bank, LLMOps is also where model governance lives. A regulator following SR 11-7 (the US guidance on managing model risk) will ask: which prompt and model version produced this customer answer last March, who approved it, what did it score on your eval set, and can you reproduce it? LLMOps is the paper trail that answers all of that. If you can't name the exact prompt + model + index version behind an answer, you don't have an LLMOps practice yet — you have a demo.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist works beautifully on a developer's laptop. Then a customer complains about a wrong wire-transfer fee. The team scrambles: which prompt was live? Was it the new model rollout? Did someone re-index the fee schedule? With no LLMOps, nobody can say. With it, they open the trace, see "prompt v12, claude model X, index 2026-03-04, eval score 0.94," reproduce it in seconds, and fix the one chunk that was stale. Same code — the difference is the whole lifecycle was recorded.

⚙️ In production

Treat LLMOps as a governed system from day one, and budget with real numbers. A mid-size BankAssist deployment serving ~50,000 answers/day at ~700 tokens each on a gpt-4.1-class model runs roughly $150–400/day in tokens — the single biggest line item, dwarfing the few dollars/day of compute that serves it. Latency is dominated by the model call (p50 ~1–2s, p95 ~3–5s for a grounded RAG answer), so your SLOs live and die on the provider, not your Python. Scale is about concurrency against the model API — requests-per-minute and tokens-per-minute quotas — not a GPU fleet. The failure modes that actually page you: a provider outage or a 429 rate-limit storm, a silent quality regression after an innocent prompt edit, and a cost spike from a runaway agent loop. So monitoring watches three families at once — service health (error rate, p95), spend (cost/answer, tokens/min vs quota), and quality (sampled faithfulness). For compliance, bind every answer to a reproducible record — prompt + model + index version + eval score — and keep PII out of logs: that record is the SR 11-7 evidence an auditor opens first.

When to lean on LLMOps — and when not. Use the full discipline — versioned prompts, eval gates, cost and quality monitoring — the moment an agent touches real customers or real money. You do not need the classic-MLOps machinery (feature stores, retraining schedulers, GPU training clusters) unless you are actually training or fine-tuning your own weights; for an API-based agent that is effort spent in the wrong place.

⚠ Watch out

Don't copy a classic-MLOps checklist wholesale. Spending weeks on a feature store and retraining schedule for a system that calls an API and reads a prompt is effort in the wrong place. Put the energy where LLMOps actually bites: prompt/version control, evals, cost, and guardrails.

🧠 Remember it

MLOps versions the weights; LLMOps versions the words — prompts, context, tools, and evals around a model you often rent.

Experiment tracking: never lose a good run again

An experiment tracker is a lab notebook that writes itself — every prompt, setting, score, and cost logged automatically so you can compare and reproduce.

Early on, every team does the same sad thing: they tweak a prompt, eyeball a few answers, think "that's better!", tweak again, and a week later cannot remember which version was good. Experiment tracking ends that. Each time you run your pipeline, you log the inputs (prompt text, model name, temperature, retrieval settings), the outputs, and the metrics (eval scores, token cost, latency). Later you sort the table by score and see exactly what won.

The two tools you'll hear named most are MLflow (open-source, self-hostable, strong on the full model lifecycle) and Weights & Biases (hosted, with Weave as its LLM-tracing layer). Both now auto-capture LLM calls: one line of setup and every request to OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain and friends is recorded for you.

# Track a BankAssist prompt experiment with MLflow 3 (open-source).
import mlflow                                  # the tracking + GenAI library
from anthropic import Anthropic               # official Anthropic client (Messages API)

mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://mlflow.internal:5000")  # point at the bank's private tracking server
mlflow.set_experiment("bankassist-overdraft-faq")       # group related runs under one named experiment
mlflow.anthropic.autolog()                    # auto-capture every Claude call: prompt, response, tokens, latency

client = Anthropic()                          # reads the API key from the environment
SYSTEM = "You are BankAssist. Answer only from the provided policy text."  # the prompt we're testing

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="overdraft-v12"):   # one tracked run = one experiment attempt
    mlflow.log_param("model", "claude-opus-5-5")   # record which model, so we can compare models later
    mlflow.log_param("temperature", 0.2)           # record the setting that shapes randomness
    msg = client.messages.create(                  # the actual LLM call (autolog records it automatically)
        model="claude-opus-5-5",                   # current model id under test
        max_tokens=400,                            # cap output length (controls cost + latency)
        system=SYSTEM,                             # the prompt variant we want to score
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the overdraft fee?"}],  # a test question
    )
    mlflow.log_metric("eval_faithfulness", 0.94)   # store the quality score from your judge/eval step
    mlflow.log_metric("cost_usd", 0.0031)          # store the dollar cost so cheap+good runs stand out
▶ Output
Logged run 'overdraft-v12' → faithfulness 0.94 · cost $0.0031 · 712 tokens · 1.2s
Compare at http://mlflow.internal:5000/#/experiments/3

Now "which prompt was best?" is a sort, not a memory test. The Weights & Biases equivalent is just as short — import weave; weave.init("bankassist") auto-patches your model SDK, and every call plus any @weave.op()-decorated function shows up as a traced, comparable run with online evaluation on live traffic.

⚙️ Under the hood

A tracker stores three things per run: params (inputs you chose), metrics (numbers you measured), and artifacts (files you produced — the full prompt, the dataset, a chart). The magic of autolog is that it hooks into the model client library, so it sees every request and response without you wiring each one by hand. That's also why it captures token counts and latency "for free" — they're in the API response.

In production

Tracking isn't only for the lab. Teams log a sample of production runs too, so a dashboard shows live faithfulness, cost per answer, and p95 latency trending over time. One serious caveat for banks: a default MLflow tracking server ships with no authentication, and 2026 brought a run of advisories about missing authorization on its endpoints. Never expose it to the open internet — put it behind your VPC, SSO, and a reverse proxy, exactly like any other internal system that holds customer-derived data.

Going deeper — what to actually log, and how much

Three tuning decisions separate a useful tracker from an expensive one. Sampling: in the lab you log every run, but in production you log a sample — 1–5% of traffic is plenty to trend quality and cost without flooding the store. Cardinality: params you'll group by (model, prompt version, intent) are cheap; dumping every retrieved chunk as a param is not — put large blobs in artifacts, keep params small and queryable. What's a metric vs an artifact: numbers you'll sort and chart (faithfulness, cost_usd, latency) are metrics; the full prompt, the dataset, a confusion chart are artifacts. MLflow stores metrics/params in a backend store (SQLite for a laptop, Postgres for a team) and artifacts in object storage (S3/GCS/Azure Blob), so the two scale independently. Autolog's overhead is near-zero because logging is batched on a background thread — your request latency barely moves (typically <5ms added).

⚙️ In production

Cost & scale: the tracker itself is cheap — a small Postgres plus an object-store bucket — but it grows without discipline. At 50,000 answers/day, logging 100% of runs with full prompts can add tens of GB/month of artifacts; sample at 2–5% and set a retention policy (e.g. 90 days hot, then archive) to keep it bounded. Latency: autolog is async, so it adds negligible time to each answer; the risk is a slow or down tracking server blocking a naive synchronous log_metric — always fire-and-forget and never let telemetry sit on the request path. Failure modes: a flaky tracking server dropping runs (you lose the audit trail, not the answer), and param-cardinality blowups slowing the UI. Security/compliance for a bank: a default MLflow tracking server ships with no authentication and drew a run of 2025–2026 advisories for missing authorization on its REST endpoints — never expose it to the internet; put it behind the VPC, SSO, and a reverse proxy, encrypt the artifact bucket, and redact PII before it is logged. The experiment store holds customer-derived data and inherits every control that data already has.

When to use it — and when not. Use a tracker the instant you are comparing more than a couple of prompt or model variants, or shipping anything customers see — you need the sortable, reproducible record. Skip the heavy self-hosted server for a one-off throwaway script on your laptop; local file-based MLflow or a notebook table is enough until a second person needs to see the results.

⚠ Watch out

Prompts and traces can contain customer PII (names, account numbers). Treat your tracking store as sensitive data: redact or tokenize PII before logging, lock down access, and set retention limits. A convenient "log everything" habit becomes a compliance breach the day an auditor finds account numbers sitting in plain text in your experiment history.

🧠 Remember it

If you can't sort your experiments by score, you're not experimenting — you're guessing. One line of autolog turns guessing into a sortable table.

Prompt & model registry: versioning prompts and models as artifacts

A registry is the shared shelf where approved prompts and models live with version numbers and friendly labels, so code asks for "the champion" instead of hard-coding a specific version.

Tracking records every run you tried. A registry is the next step: it's where you promote the winners and give them names the rest of the system can trust. Think of it like software releases — you don't tell every service "use commit a1b2c3"; you tag a release "v2.3" and point things at it. A registry does that for prompts and models.

Two registries matter in LLMOps. A model registry holds model versions with lifecycle labels — in modern MLflow these are aliases like @champion and @challenger (the old fixed "stages" such as Staging/Production are deprecated in favour of flexible aliases and tags). A prompt registry does the same for prompt text: each edit is a new version with a commit message, and you can roll back instantly if a "better" prompt turns out worse.

# Register a prompt as a versioned artifact, then an approved model alias.
import mlflow                                        # MLflow GenAI registry API

prompt = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(              # save this prompt text as a tracked, versioned artifact
    name="bankassist-overdraft",                   # stable name the app will look up by
    template="Answer ONLY from this policy:\n{{context}}\nQ: {{question}}",  # the prompt, with fill-in slots
    commit_message="Tighten grounding: forbid outside knowledge",           # why this version exists (audit trail)
)
print(prompt.name, "v" + str(prompt.version))      # confirm the new version number it got

client = mlflow.MlflowClient()                      # handle for registry operations
client.set_prompt_alias(                            # give the good version a friendly, movable label
    "bankassist-overdraft", alias="production",     # apps request 'production', not a frozen number
    version=prompt.version,                          # point the label at the version we just approved
)

# In the running app, load by ALIAS so a promotion needs no code change:
live = mlflow.genai.load_prompt("prompts:/bankassist-overdraft@production")  # fetch whatever 'production' points to now
filled = live.format(context="Overdraft fee: $35.", question="What is the fee?")  # fill the slots for this request
▶ Output
bankassist-overdraft v12
alias 'production' → v12 (was v11) · rollback = move alias back to v11
⚙️ Under the hood

Why aliases beat hard-coded versions: the label is a layer of indirection. Your app binds to @champion at startup (or per request). Promoting v12 means pointing that one label at v12; rolling back means pointing it at v11. No code change, no redeploy, no scramble — the fastest "undo" you can have in production.

In production

In a regulated bank, the registry is also your approval gate. Moving a prompt or model to @champion is a change event: it should require a reviewer's sign-off (maker-checker), carry the eval scores that justified it, and leave an immutable record of who approved what and when. That's not bureaucracy for its own sake — it's exactly the evidence SR 11-7 model-risk reviews and internal audit will ask to see.

Going deeper — aliases, immutability, and the rollback math

Two design choices make a registry trustworthy. First, versions are immutable: each registered prompt or model version is a frozen snapshot with an auto-incrementing number and a commit message, so "what exactly was v11?" always has one answer. Second, aliases are movable pointers — @champion, @challenger, @shadow — that you re-point without touching the frozen versions. (Modern MLflow deprecated the old fixed stages like Staging/Production precisely because a handful of rigid buckets couldn't express champion/challenger, canary, or per-region rollouts; flexible aliases + tags can.) The rollback math is the payoff: a bad promotion is undone in one API call that moves @champion from v12 back to v11 — seconds, no rebuild, no redeploy, no scramble. Promotion across environments is the same move: point the target environment's alias at the version that already passed in the source environment, so the exact bytes you tested are the bytes that go live.

⚙️ In production

Cost/latency/scale: the registry sits off the hot path — apps resolve an alias to a version at startup or on a cache TTL (say every 60s), not on every request, so it adds no per-answer latency and trivial load. Cache the resolved version and treat the registry as a control plane, not a runtime dependency on the critical path. Failure modes: the registry being briefly unreachable (serve the last-cached version, alert, don't hard-fail customers); and an alias pointed at a version that was never eval-gated (the dangerous one). Monitoring: emit which prompt/model version served each answer as a trace attribute, so a quality dip can be tied to the exact promotion that caused it. Security/compliance for a bank: moving an alias to @champion is a change event — require maker-checker sign-off, attach the eval scores that justified it, and keep an immutable who-approved-what-when record. That log is exactly what an SR 11-7 model-risk review and internal audit ask to see. Lock write access to the registry to a small approver group; everyone else can read.

When to use it — and when not. Use a registry the moment more than one environment or more than one person depends on "the approved prompt/model" — it buys you governed promotion and one-move rollback. For a solo prototype with a single hard-coded prompt you are still iterating on, it is premature; a Git-committed prompt file is enough until you need approvals and instant rollback.

⚠ Watch out

A prompt is code. If "fixing the fee wording" means someone edits a string in production with no version, no review, and no eval, you've bypassed every control you built. Treat prompt edits like code deploys: versioned, reviewed, eval-gated, reversible.

🧠 Remember it

Ship labels, not numbers. Point your app at @champion; promotion and rollback become a one-line label move, not a redeploy.

🛒 The internal AI marketplace

Once a bank has dozens of teams building agents, a self-service catalog (an internal AI marketplace) becomes the shop window over everything above. It's one governed place where teams discover and reuse approved agents, prompts, models, tools, and datasets instead of each rebuilding them — or worse, wiring in an unvetted model on the side. Every listing carries its owner, its eval scores, typical cost per call, a data-sensitivity tag, and its approval status, so a team can judge fitness before adopting. This is pure reuse, governance, and cost control at once: fewer duplicate builds, only vetted components in production, and spend you can see. It builds directly on the pieces already covered — the registry supplies the versioned, approved artifacts; the gateway enforces access and quotas; the eval suite supplies the scores on each card. At BankAssist, the fraud team needs document extraction and simply adopts the KYC team's approved extraction agent straight from the catalog — eval-passed, PII-tagged, costed — instead of building and re-certifying their own.

Data & model versioning: DVC and DagsHub

Git is brilliant for code and hopeless for gigabytes — so DVC teaches Git to track big files by pointer, and DagsHub hosts the whole picture in one place.

Your RAG system doesn't just depend on code. It depends on data: the corpus of policy PDFs you ingested, the chunked-and-cleaned dataset, the embeddings, the golden eval set, and sometimes a fine-tuned model file. When an answer goes wrong, "which version of the policy corpus was indexed?" is as important as "which prompt?" But Git chokes on large binary files — commit a 2 GB index a few times and your repo is unusable.

DVC (Data Version Control) solves this elegantly. It stores the big file in cheap remote storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) and commits only a tiny pointer file to Git. So Git still versions everything, but it's tracking a 100-byte hash, not the 2 GB blob. DagsHub is "GitHub for ML": it hosts your Git repo, your DVC remote storage (100 GB free per repo), and an MLflow tracking server together, so code, data, experiments, and models all live and diff in one place.

# Version the BankAssist policy corpus and embeddings with DVC.
dvc init                                   # turn this Git repo into a DVC project (one-time)
dvc remote add -d storage s3://bankassist-dvc/store   # set the default big-file remote (versioned data lives here)

dvc add data/policy_corpus/               # tell DVC to track this folder; it writes a small .dvc pointer
git add data/policy_corpus.dvc .gitignore # commit the POINTER to Git, not the gigabytes
git commit -m "corpus 2026-03-04: new wire-transfer fee schedule"  # Git now records exactly which data this is
dvc push                                   # upload the actual big files to S3 remote

# Months later, reproduce the exact state behind a customer answer:
git checkout corpus-2026-03-04            # restore the code + pointers from that moment
dvc pull                                   # download the matching big files from the remote
▶ Output
Added data/policy_corpus/ (1,284 files, 2.1 GB) → tracked by data/policy_corpus.dvc
Pushed 2.1 GB to s3://bankassist-dvc/store · Git repo grew by 0.1 KB

Read that last line again: Git grew by a tenth of a kilobyte while versioning 2.1 GB of policy documents. That's the whole trick — Git holds the pointer, the remote holds the bytes, and the two stay in lockstep through ordinary git checkout + dvc pull.

DVC also captures pipelines. A dvc.yaml file lists stages (parse → chunk → embed) with their inputs and outputs, and a dvc.lock file records the exact hashes that produced the current index. If no input changed, DVC skips re-running a stage — reproducibility and a cache in one file.

🏦 Picture this

Audit asks BankAssist's team to prove what the assistant "knew" on March 4th, when it quoted a wire fee. The team runs git checkout corpus-2026-03-04 && dvc pull, rebuilds that exact index, and reproduces the answer byte-for-byte — prompt v12, model X, corpus from that day. Without data versioning, the honest answer would have been "we think it was roughly that version" — which does not survive a regulator.

⚙️ Under the hood

DVC identifies files by content hash (like Git's objects). Two commits that reference the same unchanged dataset point at the same stored blob — no duplication. The remote is just object storage, so your security team controls it with the same bucket policies, encryption, and access logs they already use. Nothing exotic to govern.

Data catalogs & governance: DataHub and Atlan

DVC answers "which version of the data was this?" A data catalog answers the sibling questions a bank's governance team actually asks: "where did this data come from, who owns it, what's in it, who's allowed to see it, and what downstream things break if it changes?" That is lineage (the map of what-feeds-what), ownership, classification (tagging a field as PII or confidential), and audit — and it matters doubly for an LLM, because a RAG answer is only as trustworthy as the corpus behind it.

Two names lead here. DataHub (open-source, born at LinkedIn, now backed by Acryl/DataHub) is an extensible metadata graph: it ingests metadata from your warehouses, lakes, pipelines and BI tools, draws column-level lineage, and exposes it through a UI and a programmatic API. You self-host it, so a bank keeps all metadata inside its own perimeter. Atlan is the commercial, managed "active metadata" platform — catalog, lineage, policy workflows, PII/classification, and collaboration in one place, with governance workflows (approvals, access requests) built for data+AI teams (Gartner named it a Leader in its 2025–2026 governance Magic Quadrants). Rule of thumb: DataHub for engineering-led teams that want open-source control; Atlan for a managed, governance-and-collaboration-first platform with less ops burden.

# Register lineage for the BankAssist corpus in DataHub (open-source catalog).
from datahub.emitter.rest_emitter import DatahubRestEmitter          # client that POSTs metadata to the DataHub server
from datahub.emitter.mcp import MetadataChangeProposalWrapper        # wraps one metadata change to emit
from datahub.metadata.schema_classes import (                        # typed lineage aspect classes
    UpstreamLineageClass, UpstreamClass, DatasetLineageTypeClass,
)
from datahub.emitter.mce_builder import make_dataset_urn             # builds a stable dataset id (a URN)

emitter = DatahubRestEmitter("https://datahub.internal:8080")        # point at the bank's private DataHub

corpus = make_dataset_urn("s3", "bankassist/policy_corpus")          # the raw policy-docs dataset (the source)
index  = make_dataset_urn("vectorstore", "bankassist/faq_index")     # the vector index built from that corpus

lineage = UpstreamLineageClass(upstreams=[                           # declare "the index was built FROM the corpus"
    UpstreamClass(dataset=corpus, type=DatasetLineageTypeClass.TRANSFORMED),  # edge type = a transform step
])
emitter.emit(MetadataChangeProposalWrapper(entityUrn=index, aspect=lineage))  # send the lineage fact to the catalog
▶ Output
Emitted lineage: s3:bankassist/policy_corpus → vectorstore:bankassist/faq_index (TRANSFORMED)
DataHub UI now shows the index's upstreams, owner, and PII tags · searchable by any reviewer

Now a governance reviewer can open the faq_index in the catalog and see, in one graph, that it was built from the policy corpus, who owns it, which fields are tagged PII, and everything downstream that would break if the corpus changed. Atlan's equivalent is its pyatlan SDK plus auto-captured lineage from connected sources — same picture, managed for you.

⚙️ In production

Cost/scale: DVC's remote is just object storage — pennies per GB-month — and dedupes by content hash, so two commits referencing the same unchanged 2 GB corpus store it once. A catalog (DataHub self-hosted) adds a small always-on service (metadata store + search), sized to your metadata volume, not your data volume. Latency: both are off the answer path — dvc pull and lineage queries happen in pipelines and reviews, never per customer request. Failure modes: a drifted DVC pointer (Git says one hash, the remote has another — re-push to heal), and stale lineage if emission isn't wired into the pipeline (fix by emitting lineage as a pipeline step, not by hand). Monitoring: alert if a nightly dvc push or a lineage-emit step fails, so the audit trail never silently goes dark. Security/compliance for a bank: the DVC remote now holds customer-derived documents, so it inherits data-residency (region-locked bucket), encryption-at-rest, access logging and retention rules; the catalog becomes your evidence for data governance — PII classification, access policy, and the lineage that proves, under SR 11-7 and privacy regulation, exactly which data produced a given answer and who was allowed to touch it.

When to use which — and when not. Use DVC whenever a wrong answer makes "which data version was indexed?" a real question — that's any production RAG system. Add a catalog (DataHub or Atlan) once several datasets, teams, or regulators need shared lineage, ownership and PII governance. You do not need a full catalog for a single-corpus prototype — DVC plus a README is enough until governance, discovery, or audit across many assets becomes the pain.

⚠ Watch out

Your DVC remote now holds customer-derived documents. It inherits every data-residency and encryption rule your bank applies to that data — region-locked bucket, encryption at rest, access logging, retention. "It's just a cache" is how sensitive data quietly leaks into an ungoverned store.

🧠 Remember it

DVC = Git for the heavy stuff: commit the pointer, push the bytes. If you can't rebuild last March's index on demand, you can't audit last March's answer.

Pipeline orchestration: Airflow, Dagster, and Prefect

An orchestrator is the reliable scheduler that runs your multi-step jobs on time, in order, retries the flaky parts, and tells you when something breaks.

Your RAG index isn't built once and forgotten. Documents change, so you re-ingest: fetch new PDFs, parse them, chunk, embed, upsert into the vector store, then run a smoke-test eval. That's a chain of steps that must run in the right order, on a schedule (say nightly), with retries if a step hiccups, and an alert if it fails. Running that by hand, or with a lonely cron job and crossed fingers, breaks the moment step 3 fails silently and you serve a half-built index all day.

An orchestrator runs these pipelines properly. The three you'll meet are Apache Airflow (the long-standing default, huge ecosystem; Airflow 3 added asset-aware scheduling, and Airflow 2 is approaching end-of-life — verify the date), Dagster (asset-centric — you declare the data assets you want and it figures out the steps), and Prefect (lightest-weight, pure-Python @flow/@task decorators). All three give you the same essentials: a dependency graph, scheduling, retries, and a monitoring UI.

# Nightly BankAssist re-indexing pipeline with Prefect 3 (Python-native).
from prefect import flow, task             # flow = whole pipeline; task = one retryable step

@task(retries=3, retry_delay_seconds=30)   # if fetching flakes, retry 3x before failing the run
def fetch_docs() -> list[str]:             # step 1: pull new/changed policy docs
    return load_changed_policies()         # returns the list of documents to re-ingest

@task                                       # step 2 depends on step 1's output
def chunk_and_embed(docs: list[str]) -> int:  # parse, chunk, embed into vectors
    return upsert_to_vector_store(docs)     # write vectors in; return how many chunks

@task                                       # step 3: guard quality before the index goes live
def smoke_eval() -> float:                  # run a tiny golden-set eval on the fresh index
    score = run_golden_set()                # measure retrieval quality right now
    if score < 0.90:                        # if the new index is worse than our bar...
        raise ValueError(f"eval {score} below 0.90 — holding rollout")  # ...fail loudly, don't publish a bad index
    return score

@flow(name="bankassist-reindex")            # the pipeline Prefect schedules and monitors
def reindex():                              # orchestrates the steps in dependency order
    docs = fetch_docs()                     # run step 1
    n = chunk_and_embed(docs)               # step 2 waits for step 1 automatically
    score = smoke_eval()                    # step 3 gates the result
    print(f"indexed {n} chunks · eval {score}")  # summary for the run log

if __name__ == "__main__":                  # local run; in prod you'd schedule it nightly
    reindex()
▶ Output
fetch_docs ✓ (41 docs) → chunk_and_embed ✓ (1,902 chunks) → smoke_eval ✓ (0.93)
indexed 1902 chunks · eval 0.93 · run SUCCEEDED

The quiet hero here is smoke_eval: because it raises on a bad score, the orchestrator marks the run failed and the stale-but-good index keeps serving. The pipeline refuses to publish a worse index — automation that protects quality instead of blindly shipping.

Reach for Airflow / Dagster when…

You have many pipelines, a team, and need a battle-tested UI, backfills, and a big connector ecosystem. Airflow is the safe enterprise default; Dagster shines for data-asset-heavy, dbt-style platforms where you think in terms of tables and datasets.

Reach for Prefect when…

You want the lightest path from "a Python script" to "a scheduled, retrying, observable pipeline" without much infrastructure. Great for a small LLMOps team standing up ingestion and eval jobs quickly.

In production

Orchestrators give you three things that matter at a bank: idempotency (a re-run shouldn't double-insert chunks — key your upserts so re-running is safe), observability (every run's status, logs, and duration in one UI for audit), and alerting (page someone when the nightly re-index fails, before customers notice stale answers). Schedule the heavy work off-peak, and always gate the publish step on an eval so a bad ingest can't silently degrade production.

Going deeper — tasks vs assets, and the 2026 landscape

The big mental split is task-centric vs asset-centric. Airflow historically describes steps ("run fetch, then embed, then eval"); Airflow 3.0 (April 2025) added first-class assets with an @asset decorator and asset-aware scheduling, and Airflow 2 is heading toward end-of-life (verify the exact date before you pin a version). Dagster is asset-first by design — you declare the data asset you want ("the faq_index") and it derives the steps and re-materializes only what's stale. Prefect 3 stays the lightest: plain @flow/@task Python with dynamic, eventful workflows and minimal infra. Tuning knobs that matter: set retries with backoff only on genuinely transient steps (a flaky fetch, yes; a failing eval, no — that's a real signal); cap concurrency so a re-index doesn't exhaust your embedding-API rate limit; and make every write idempotent (keyed upserts) so a retried run can't double-insert chunks.

⚙️ In production

Cost/scale: the orchestrator itself is cheap (a scheduler + a small metadata DB); the spend lives in what the pipeline does — re-embedding a 2 GB corpus might be tens of thousands of embedding calls, so schedule heavy re-indexing off-peak and only on changed documents, not the whole corpus nightly. Latency: these are batch jobs off the customer path, measured in minutes, so the SLO is "finished before the business day," not milliseconds. Failure modes that bite a bank: a step failing silently and serving a half-built index all day; a non-idempotent re-run doubling chunks; and a backfill accidentally hammering the vector store. Monitoring: every run's status, duration and logs in one UI (an audit record), plus an alert on failure that pages on-call before customers notice stale answers — a run that merely "didn't start" is as dangerous as one that errored, so alert on missed schedules too. Security/compliance: the pipeline reads customer-derived documents and holds credentials to the vector store and model APIs — keep secrets in a vault (not in the DAG), run workers in the bank's network, and gate the publish step on an eval so a bad ingest can never silently reach production.

When to use it — and when not. Use an orchestrator the moment a job has more than one step, must run on a schedule, or needs retries and alerting — i.e. any real re-indexing or eval pipeline. Don't reach for Airflow's full weight for a single nightly script with no dependencies; a cron job plus an alert (or Prefect's lightweight flow) is enough until you have several interdependent pipelines and a team watching them.

⚠ Watch out

The classic failure is a pipeline that fails silently: step 3 errors, nobody's alerted, and BankAssist quotes last month's fees for a week. Non-negotiables: make steps idempotent, fail loudly, alert on failure, and never let a run publish an index it didn't eval.

🧠 Remember it

An orchestrator is a reliable robot assistant: runs your steps in order, retries the flaky ones, refuses to ship a bad result, and pages you when it can't cope.

Packaging & scaling: Docker, Kubernetes, Kubeflow, SageMaker

Four tools, four jobs: Docker packs your app into a box, Kubernetes runs many boxes reliably, Kubeflow adds ML pipelines on top, and SageMaker is AWS's managed "do it for me" version.

Your agent works on your laptop. How does it run the same way on a server, and keep running for thousands of customers at 9am on payday? That's packaging and scaling, and it's a ladder of four tools — each one picking up where the last leaves off.

Docker — put the app in a box

A container bundles your code and everything it needs (Python version, libraries, system packages) into one portable image. "Works on my machine" dies here: the image that passed tests is byte-for-byte the image that runs in production.

# Dockerfile — a reproducible box for the BankAssist API.
FROM python:3.12-slim                       # pin the exact base image so builds are reproducible
WORKDIR /app                                # all following commands run in this folder
COPY requirements.txt .                     # copy deps first so Docker caches this layer
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt  # install pinned libraries into the image
COPY . .                                    # copy the app code into the image
EXPOSE 8000                                 # document the port the API serves on
CMD ["uvicorn", "app:api", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]  # how to start the service
▶ Output
Successfully built image bankassist:1.4.0 (312 MB) · identical in dev, staging, prod
✅ Tip

That uvicorn app:api line is serving a plain FastAPI app — the usual way to wrap a BankAssist agent as a REST endpoint. If your app is a LangChain chain, LangServe can auto-generate that FastAPI/REST layer — routes, request/response schemas, and a built-in playground — straight from a runnable in a few lines. One honest caveat: LangServe has been deprecated since late 2024 and now only takes bug fixes, so for new work LangChain points you at LangGraph Platform or a hand-written FastAPI app. Treat it as a quick wrapper for simple chains, not a foundation to build on.

Kubernetes — run many boxes, reliably

Kubernetes (often "K8s") runs your containers across a fleet of machines. You declare "I want 5 copies of BankAssist, each with this much memory," and K8s keeps that true — restarting crashed copies, spreading them across machines, and autoscaling up when traffic spikes and down when it's quiet.

# k8s deployment: keep N copies of BankAssist healthy and load-balanced.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment                            # a Deployment manages a set of identical pods
metadata:
  name: bankassist
spec:
  replicas: 5                               # run 5 copies for capacity + redundancy
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: bankassist:1.4.0           # the exact Docker image we built and tested
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }  # guaranteed resources per copy (for scheduling)
            limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "1Gi" }     # ceiling so one copy can't starve the node
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8000 }      # don't send traffic until the copy is truly ready
▶ Output
deployment.apps/bankassist created · 5/5 pods Ready · traffic balanced across nodes

Kubeflow & SageMaker — the ML-aware layers

Kubeflow runs on top of Kubernetes and adds ML-specific pieces: Kubeflow Pipelines (its DAG engine for training and ingestion workflows) and KServe for model serving with autoscaling and canary rollouts — all portable across any K8s cluster, including on-prem. Amazon SageMaker AI is the opposite philosophy: AWS manages the hard parts for you. Managed training jobs, one-call model endpoints with auto-scaling and shadow testing, and (via operators) the option to drive it from Kubernetes if you prefer. You trade portability and control for speed and far less ops burden.

⚙️ The classic SageMaker surface

Beyond hosting a model, Amazon SageMaker AI is a whole predictive-ML platform, and the AWS certification exams expect you to recognise its parts: JumpStart (a catalogue of pre-trained and foundation models you deploy in a click), Feature Store (a governed, reusable home for model features), Data Wrangler (visual data prep and cleaning), Clarify (bias detection and explainability reports), Model Monitor (watches a live endpoint for data and prediction drift), and SageMaker Pipelines (CI/CD-style ML workflows). These belong to the classic machine-learning world that sits around the GenAI stack rather than inside it. When a bank reaches for these: when it trains or hosts its own models — a fraud-scoring model, a churn predictor, or a fine-tuned open-weight LLM — and needs bias, drift, and lineage evidence for model-risk review, not just an API call to a frontier model.

In production

For most banking agent services — which call a model API and do light orchestration — plain Docker on Kubernetes is the sweet spot: standard, auditable, and something your platform team already runs. Reach for Kubeflow or SageMaker when you're actually training or hosting your own models (an on-prem open-weight model, say) and want managed pipelines and GPU-backed serving. Don't over-build: a dependency on Kubernetes expertise you may not have will cost more than it saves.

Going deeper — what actually scales an agent service

Here's the counter-intuitive part for LLM services: your pods are mostly waiting on the model API, not burning CPU. So the right autoscaling signal is usually concurrent in-flight requests (or queue depth), not CPU%, and the real ceiling is the provider's tokens-per-minute quota, not your node count — adding pods past that quota just produces more 429s. Practical knobs: set requests/limits modestly (an I/O-bound agent needs ~0.25–0.5 vCPU and 256–512 MB, not a whole core), use a readiness probe so traffic only hits warmed pods, keep a liveness/graceful-shutdown so in-flight answers finish on a rollout, and image-slim (a python:3.12-slim base + multi-stage build keeps images ~300 MB and pulls fast). For cost, a small fixed baseline of replicas plus burst autoscaling beats a large always-on fleet.

⚙️ In production

Cost: for an API-calling agent the container fleet is a rounding error next to tokens — a handful of 0.5 vCPU pods (a few dollars/day) front a model bill in the hundreds; don't over-provision compute to chase a cost that lives at the provider. Latency: K8s adds negligible overhead; your p95 is the model call, so autoscale for concurrency and keep a warm pool to avoid cold-start spikes during payday peaks. Scale/failure modes: the ones that page you are provider rate-limits (shed load or queue, don't thrash), a bad image rollout (use rolling updates + readiness probes + instant rollback to the previous image tag), and a pod OOM-killed by an unbounded response (set memory limits). Monitoring: pod health and restarts, plus the app's own cost/latency/quality metrics. Security/compliance for a bank: pin exact base-image digests, scan images for CVEs in CI, run as non-root, pull secrets from a vault (never bake keys into the image), enforce network policies so the agent pod can reach only the model API and vector store, and keep everything in an approved region. Kubeflow/SageMaker inherit these same controls and add GPU-backed serving when you host your own weights.

When to climb each rung — and when not. Use Docker always (reproducibility is free). Use Kubernetes when you genuinely run multiple services, need autoscaling and self-healing, and have (or can rent) the platform skills. Reach for Kubeflow/SageMaker only when you are actually training or hosting your own models and want managed ML pipelines or GPU serving. Do not stand up a K8s cluster for a single modest API that a managed container service (Cloud Run, ECS/Fargate, App Runner) would run with a fraction of the ops burden.

⚠ Watch out
