Kubernetes is powerful and genuinely complex. Adopting it for a single modest API is a common and expensive mis-step — you inherit a steep operational burden for capacity you don't need. Match the tool to the real traffic and team, not to the architecture diagram you wish you had.

🧠 Remember it

Box it (Docker) → run many (K8s) → add ML (Kubeflow) → or let AWS do it (SageMaker). Climb only as far as your traffic and team need.

CI/CD for AI: promoting through dev, staging, and prod with eval gates and canary

CI/CD is the automated assembly line that takes a change from "a developer edited a prompt" to "it's safely live," stopping it at every gate it can't pass.

CI/CD means Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery: every change is automatically built, tested, and promoted through environments. For ordinary software the tests are unit tests. For an AI system the headline test is different and vital — an eval gate: run the candidate prompt/model against your golden set and block the release if quality, cost, or safety regress. Because LLMs are non-deterministic, "a human clicked around and it seemed fine" is not a gate. A scored eval over many cases is.

Changes flow through three environments. Dev (the developer's sandbox), staging (a production-like rehearsal with real-ish data), and prod (live customers). You promote only when each gate passes, and the riskiest step — going fully live — is softened with a canary: send a small slice of real traffic (say 5%) to the new version first, watch the metrics, and only then roll it out to everyone.

# .github/workflows/promote.yml — GitHub Actions CI/CD with an eval gate.
name: bankassist-promote
on:
  pull_request: { branches: [main] }        # run checks on every proposed change
jobs:
  eval-gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5            # get the candidate code + prompt version
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.12" }     # match our runtime for a faithful test
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt  # install deps to run the eval
      - run: python -m pytest tests/unit      # fast correctness checks first
      - name: Run golden-set eval             # THE gate: score the candidate on real cases
        run: python evals/run.py --suite golden --fail-under 0.90  # exit non-zero if quality < 0.90
      - name: Block on cost regression        # guard the bill, not just quality
        run: python evals/check_cost.py --max-usd-per-100 0.50     # fail if 100 answers would cost > $0.50
# A failing step exits non-zero → the PR cannot merge → nothing ships unproven.
▶ Output
unit ✓ · golden-set eval 0.93 ≥ 0.90 ✓ · cost $0.41/100 ≤ $0.50 ✓ → PR mergeable
(on failure: ✗ eval 0.86 < 0.90 → merge blocked)

In production

Promotion in a bank is both automated and governed. The eval gate gives objective evidence; a human reviewer still signs off on the move to @champion (maker-checker). During canary, watch the real signals — faithfulness on sampled traffic, error rate, latency, cost, and escalation rate — and wire an automatic rollback: if the canary's metrics breach a threshold, the pipeline moves the alias back to the previous version with no human in the loop. Fast, reversible, recorded.

Going deeper — tuning the eval gate so it's trusted, not gamed

A gate is only useful if it's both strict enough to catch regressions and stable enough to trust. Three tuning realities: (1) because the system is non-deterministic, run each golden case a few times and gate on the aggregate (e.g. mean faithfulness ≥ 0.90 across 50 cases × 3 reps), not a single pass, or a flaky answer will randomly block or sneak through. (2) Gate on three axes, not one — quality and cost ($/100 answers) and safety (no PII leak, no forbidden tool) — since a prompt can get "smarter" by getting more expensive or less safe. (3) Keep an eval budget: running 150 LLM-judged cases per PR costs real money (cents to low dollars per run), so sample for fast feedback on every PR and run the full suite before promotion. The canary then catches what the lab can't — distribution shift in real questions — so watch it for a bounded window (say 30–60 min or N requests) before full rollout.

⚙️ In production

Cost/latency of the pipeline: the eval gate adds minutes and a few dollars to each promotion — cheap insurance against a bad prompt reaching customers. Scale: run eval cases concurrently (bounded) so a 150-case suite finishes in a couple of minutes, not an hour. Failure modes: a green unit suite hiding a quality/safety regression (that's what the eval gate is for), a flaky gate from too-small a sample (raise N and reps), and a canary with no automatic rollback (a bad version bleeds onto real customers until a human notices). Monitoring during canary: watch sampled faithfulness, error rate, p95 latency, cost/answer and escalation rate on the 5% slice; wire an automatic rollback that moves the alias back if any breaches threshold — fast, reversible, recorded. Security/compliance for a bank: promotion is automated and governed — the eval scores are the objective evidence, a human still signs off on the move to @champion (maker-checker), and the whole run (what was tested, the scores, who approved) is kept as the immutable change record SR 11-7 and audit expect. Eval tools must hit sandboxes, never real money.

When to use it — and when not. Use an eval-gated CI/CD pipeline for anything customer-facing: it's the only thing standing between a well-meaning prompt edit and a production incident. For a pure research spike with no users, a manual eval run is fine — but the day a second person can ship a change, put the gate in, because "someone clicked around and it seemed fine" is not a control.

⚠ Watch out

A green unit-test suite proves the code runs; it says nothing about whether answers are correct and safe. The LLM-specific risk is a quality or safety regression that compiles perfectly. The eval gate — not the unit tests — is what stands between a bad prompt and your customers. Treat it as the real gate, and keep the golden set honest and growing.

🧠 Remember it

No eval, no promote. Gate on quality + cost + safety, canary the rollout, and keep rollback one label-move away.

Managed agent runtimes: Bedrock AgentCore, Vertex Agent Engine, LangGraph Platform

A managed agent runtime is a hosting service purpose-built for agents — it handles sessions, memory, scaling, and identity so you don't rebuild that plumbing yourself.

An agent is harder to host than a plain web API. It's often long-running (a task can take minutes), stateful (it remembers a conversation), needs per-user memory, must call tools with the right identity and permissions, and has to scale while keeping each user's session straight. You can build all that on Docker + Kubernetes. Or you can use a managed agent runtime that provides these as ready-made primitives. Three serious options have matured by 2026:

  • AWS Bedrock AgentCore (GA since late 2025) — a set of primitives: Runtime (secure serverless execution, up to long-running sessions), Memory (short-term session + long-term cross-session), Identity (who the agent acts as, and what it may touch), Gateway (turn APIs into agent tools), plus Observability and Evaluations. Framework-agnostic — it'll host a LangGraph or Strands agent alike. Natural fit if the bank is on AWS.
  • Google Vertex AI Agent Engine (renamed Agent Runtime in 2026) — a managed runtime with Sessions for conversation history and a Memory Bank for long-term per-user memory. You write the agent (ADK, LangGraph, LangChain, LlamaIndex, or custom), wrap it, deploy, and call it with streaming. Natural fit on Google Cloud.
  • LangGraph Platform / LangSmith Deployment — purpose-built for long-running, stateful LangGraph agents. One command builds a container and deploys it with Postgres and Redis provisioned for you (for checkpoints and state), tightly integrated with LangSmith tracing/evals. Offers managed-cloud, hybrid (control plane hosted, data plane in your VPC), and fully self-hosted options — the last two matter a lot to banks.
# Deploy a BankAssist agent to Vertex AI Agent Engine (managed runtime).
from vertexai import agent_engines          # Vertex managed-agent deployment API
from vertexai.preview.reasoning_engines import AdkApp  # wrapper that makes an ADK agent deployable
from bankassist.agent import root_agent     # our already-built agent (tools, prompt, model)

app = AdkApp(agent=root_agent, enable_tracing=True)  # wrap it; tracing on for observability

remote = agent_engines.create(              # deploy to the managed runtime (scaling handled for us)
    app,                                    # the wrapped agent to host
    requirements=["google-cloud-aiplatform[adk,agent_engines]"],  # deps baked into the hosted image
    display_name="bankassist-prod",         # name it so we can find it in the console
)

reply = remote.stream_query(                # call the deployed agent; stream tokens back
    user_id="cust-8842",                    # ties this turn to the user's session + memory
    message="Did my March wire fee get waived?",  # the customer's question
)
▶ Output
Deployed: projects/bankassist/.../reasoningEngines/6610... · sessions + memory managed
stream: "Yes — a one-time courtesy waiver was applied on Mar 4 (see §4.2)…"

Notice how little infrastructure code that is. No load balancer, no session store, no autoscaler — the runtime supplies sessions, memory, and scaling. Your code is the agent; the platform is the plumbing. The LangGraph equivalent is a single langgraph deploy that builds the image and wires up Postgres + Redis for you.

Use a managed runtime when…

You want sessions, memory, identity, and scaling without building them; you're already on that cloud; and you value speed-to-prod. It collapses weeks of platform work into a deploy call.

Build it yourself (Docker/K8s) when…

You need full control, strict data residency the managed option can't meet, portability across clouds, or you're avoiding lock-in. A LangGraph hybrid/self-hosted deploy is a middle path: managed control, your-VPC data.

In production

For a bank, the deciding questions are rarely about features — they're about data residency, identity, and auditability. Where does session and memory data physically live, and is that region allowed? Can the runtime's Identity layer enforce that the agent acts with least privilege and can't become a confused deputy? Does it emit traces your audit and SR 11-7 processes can consume? This is exactly why LangGraph's in-your-VPC option and AgentCore's Identity primitive get banking attention: they answer the governance questions, not just the scaling ones.

Going deeper — what you're really renting, and the billing shape

A managed runtime sells you four primitives you'd otherwise build: sessions (per-conversation state), memory (short-term within a session, long-term across sessions), identity (who the agent acts as and what it may touch), and scale (serverless execution for long, bursty tasks). The billing shape is usually consumption-based, which is unusually friendly for agents: AWS Bedrock AgentCore (GA October 2025; its Policy and Evaluations components reached GA in 2026) meters Runtime per second and, crucially, charges nothing for I/O-wait and idle time — so an agent that spends 20s waiting on a tool isn't billed for the wait. AgentCore's Identity adds no extra charge when used through Runtime or Gateway; Memory and Gateway are billed per-thousand events/calls. The tuning levers are mostly architectural: keep memory writes deliberate (long-term memory is storage you pay for and must govern), scope identity to least privilege, and keep your agent logic decoupled from the host SDK so a price or residency change doesn't trap you.

⚙️ In production

Cost: consumption pricing means a low-traffic BankAssist agent can cost cents/day in runtime on top of its token bill, scaling linearly with use — no idle fleet. Watch two line items that surprise teams: long-term memory storage (per-event) and inter-service network transfer (standard rates apply). Latency: the runtime adds little; your p95 is still the model plus tool calls, though cold starts on a cold session can add a beat — keep sessions warm for hot customers. Scale: the platform handles concurrency and session routing, which is the weeks of plumbing you're buying. Failure modes: provider/region outage (have a fallback or degraded mode), a confused-deputy escalation if Identity is loose, and lock-in friction when names/APIs shift (Vertex "Agent Engine → Agent Runtime," LangGraph "Platform → LangSmith Deployment"). Security/compliance for a bank — the deciding questions: where do session and memory data physically live (is the region allowed)? can Identity enforce least privilege so the agent can't become a confused deputy? does it emit traces your audit and SR 11-7 processes can consume? This is exactly why LangGraph's in-your-VPC (hybrid/self-hosted) option and AgentCore's Identity primitive get banking attention — they answer governance, not just scaling.

When to use it — and when not. Use a managed runtime when you want sessions, memory, identity and scale without building them, you're already on that cloud, and speed-to-prod matters — it collapses weeks of platform work into a deploy call. Build it yourself on Docker/K8s (or a LangGraph self-hosted/hybrid deploy) when you need strict data residency the managed option can't meet, cross-cloud portability, or you're deliberately avoiding lock-in. Don't adopt one just because it's new: if your agent is a simple stateless request/response, a plain container is simpler and cheaper.

⚠ Watch out

Managed runtimes are moving fast — names and APIs are shifting (Vertex's "Agent Engine → Agent Runtime," LangGraph Platform's "→ LangSmith Deployment"). Pin SDK versions, read the current docs before you wire anything load-bearing, and keep your agent logic decoupled from the host so you can move if pricing or residency forces it. Lock-in is the quiet cost of convenience.

🧠 Remember it

A managed runtime rents you sessions, memory, identity, and scale. Ask first: where does the data live, and who does the agent act as? — not how fast is it?

The UI and demo layer: Gradio, Streamlit, and Hugging Face Spaces

Before a banking AI feature ships, people need to try it — and Gradio, Streamlit, and Spaces turn your Python into a shareable web app in minutes, not sprints.

A pipeline nobody can click is a hard sell. Product managers, compliance reviewers, and pilot users need a real interface to poke at. Writing a full React front-end for a throwaway demo is wasted effort. Gradio and Streamlit are Python libraries that generate a web UI straight from your functions, and Hugging Face Spaces hosts either one with a free URL you can share.

Gradio — fastest chat/ML demo

A few lines give you a working chatbot with streaming via ChatInterface. Every Gradio app is also an API by default, and on Spaces it can use free ZeroGPU for model inference. The go-to for "let people chat with the agent."

Streamlit — richer dashboards

More layout control, widgets, and charts — better when you're building an internal tool or dashboard (eval results, cost trends, a reviewer console) rather than a bare chat. Has built-in auth support.

# A shareable BankAssist chat demo in ~10 lines with Gradio.
import gradio as gr                          # the UI library
from bankassist.agent import answer          # our function: question (+ history) -> reply

def respond(message, history):               # Gradio calls this on every user turn
    for partial in answer(message, history): # our agent yields the reply token-by-token
        yield partial                        # stream each chunk so the UI types live

demo = gr.ChatInterface(                      # ready-made chat UI with streaming + history
    fn=respond,                              # the function that produces answers
    title="BankAssist (pilot)",              # header shown to testers
    description="Internal pilot — do not enter real customer data.",  # a visible safety notice
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    demo.launch(auth=("pilot", "secret"))    # basic gate so only invited testers get in
▶ Output
Running on local URL: http://127.0.0.1:7860 · share it, or push to a private HF Space

In production

Here's the line that keeps you out of trouble: these are for demos, pilots, and internal tools — not the customer-facing production front-end. The real BankAssist widget in online banking is a hardened web app behind the bank's auth, WAF, and audit logging. Gradio/Streamlit are the fast track to validate an idea and gather feedback, then you build the production surface properly. A public Hugging Face Space is great for an open demo and completely wrong for anything touching real accounts.

Hugging Face tooling: Tasks, the Inference SDK, and private Spaces/registries

Spaces host the UI, but Hugging Face is also three things a bank's AI team uses behind the demo. First, HF Tasks — a plain-English catalog of what models do (text-generation, summarization, text-classification, zero-shot, embeddings, ASR) with the inputs/outputs and example models for each. It's the fastest way to answer "is there an open model for this job, and what shape are its inputs?" before you commit. Second, the Inference SDK — the InferenceClient in huggingface_hub — a single client that calls hosted models through Inference Providers with an OpenAI-compatible surface, so you can A/B an open model against your default gpt-4.1 with almost no code change. Third, private model registries and Spaces — repos and Spaces can be private or gated, access-controlled by token and org, which is the only mode a bank should use.

# Call an open model through Hugging Face's InferenceClient (OpenAI-compatible).
from huggingface_hub import InferenceClient      # official HF client; pip install huggingface_hub (v0.28+)

client = InferenceClient(                         # one client, many hosted providers
    provider="auto",                              # "auto" = first available provider for this model
    api_key="hf_...",                             # your HF token; calls are billed to your HF account
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(            # same shape as the OpenAI chat API — easy to swap
    model="meta-llama/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct",    # a model id ON THE HUB (not the provider's own id)
    messages=[                                     # standard chat messages
        {"role": "system", "content": "Answer only from the policy text provided."},  # grounding
        {"role": "user", "content": "Summarise the overdraft clause in one line."},   # the task
    ],
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)            # read the reply exactly like the OpenAI client
▶ Output
"Overdraft fee is $35 per item, capped at one charge per day." · model via HF Inference Providers
(swap model=… to A/B an open model against gpt-4.1 with no other code change)

For a bank, the point isn't the public playground — it's that the same client can point at a model you host yourself (Text Generation Inference, or an Inference Endpoint in your own region) and that private/gated repos keep weights and datasets inside your governance perimeter. HF Tasks helps you pick the right open model; the SDK lets you trial it; private Spaces/registries keep the trial compliant.

⚙️ In production

Cost/latency: Gradio/Streamlit demos are tiny (a single small container, a few dollars/month on a private Space or internal host); the cost is the model behind them. The InferenceClient is billed per token to your HF account on shared providers, or by the hour for a dedicated Inference Endpoint — pick dedicated when you need fixed latency (p95) and data isolation, shared for cheap experiments. Scale: these UIs are for a handful of pilot users, not thousands of customers — don't load-test a Gradio app as if it were the product. Failure modes: a pilot quietly pointed at production data; a public Space leaking a token or transcript; an open model that's smaller/weaker than the demo implied. Monitoring: even a pilot should log who used it and what they asked (for the flywheel), minus PII. Security/compliance for a bank: keep every pilot on synthetic or masked data, behind SSO/VPN, clearly labelled "not production"; use private/gated HF repos and Spaces only, rotate tokens, and for anything touching real weights or data prefer self-hosted TGI or a region-locked Inference Endpoint over shared public inference.

When to use it — and when not. Use Gradio/Streamlit + a private Space to validate an idea, gather feedback, and let compliance click around — fast, cheap, disposable. Use HF Tasks + the Inference SDK to scout and trial open models. Do not use any of these as the customer-facing production surface for real accounts: that is a hardened app behind the bank's auth, WAF, DLP and audit logging. The demo is the test drive, not the car you sell.

⚠ Watch out

The dangerous shortcut: a demo that "works great," so someone quietly points it at production data and real customers. A pilot Gradio app on a public Space has none of a bank's controls — no proper authentication, no DLP, no residency guarantees, no audit trail. Keep pilots on synthetic or masked data, behind the VPN, clearly labelled "not production." The warning banner in the code above isn't decoration.

🧠 Remember it

Gradio/Streamlit = the test drive, not the car you sell. Perfect to prove the idea; never the production cockpit for real accounts.

Monitoring in production and the data flywheel

Shipping is the start, not the finish — monitoring tells you it's healthy right now, and the data flywheel turns everyday production into next month's improvement.

Once BankAssist is live, two jobs never stop. First, monitoring: watching the health signals so you catch trouble before customers do. Second, closing the data flywheel: feeding what happens in production back into your evals and training so the system gets better the more it's used.

Monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana

The standard open-source pair: Prometheus collects numbers (it "scrapes" metrics your app exposes and stores them over time), and Grafana draws them as dashboards and fires alerts. For an LLM system you watch the usual service metrics and the AI-specific ones: request rate, error rate, p95 latency, tokens and cost per answer, cache hit rate, and sampled quality (faithfulness on a slice of live traffic), plus guardrail trips and escalation rate.

# Expose BankAssist metrics for Prometheus to scrape.
from prometheus_client import Counter, Histogram, start_http_server  # metric types + exposer

ANSWERS   = Counter("ba_answers_total", "Answers served", ["outcome"])  # count answers, split by outcome
LATENCY   = Histogram("ba_latency_seconds", "End-to-end latency")        # distribution → gives us p95/p99
COST_USD  = Counter("ba_cost_usd_total", "Cumulative token cost in USD")  # running dollar spend

start_http_server(9100)                     # serve /metrics on :9100 for Prometheus to read

def handle(question):                        # wraps one customer request
    with LATENCY.time():                     # time the whole handling automatically
        reply, cost, ok = run_agent(question)  # do the work; get reply, its cost, success flag
    COST_USD.inc(cost)                        # add this answer's cost to the running total
    ANSWERS.labels(outcome="ok" if ok else "error").inc()  # tally success vs failure for the error-rate panel
    return reply
▶ Output
Serving /metrics on :9100 · Grafana alert: p95 latency > 4s for 5m → page on-call
panel: cost/answer $0.004 · error rate 0.3% · faithfulness(sampled) 0.93

The data flywheel

This is the part that compounds. Every day, production generates gold: questions customers actually ask, thumbs-up/down, human corrections, and escalations to a live agent (each escalation is a case the AI couldn't handle). The flywheel captures those signals, turns the failures into new eval cases, and uses them to improve prompts or fine-tune — then you redeploy, and the loop spins again, a little better each turn.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist keeps escalating one kind of question: "why was I charged two overdraft fees in one day?" Grafana shows the spike in escalations for that intent. The flywheel kicks in: those real transcripts are curated, the hardest ten become new golden-set cases, the team adds a retrieval source for the daily-fee-cap policy, the eval score on that intent jumps from 0.6 to 0.95, and the new version canaries out. A month later that escalation line is flat. The product got smarter because it was used, not because someone guessed.

⚙️ Under the hood

The flywheel only works if feedback is captured with context. Store each production interaction with its trace id, the prompt + model + index versions, the retrieved chunks, and the user signal. Then a thumbs-down is traceable to an exact, reproducible failure you can turn into a test. Feedback without that context is just noise you can't act on.

In production

In a bank, the flywheel runs on rails. Transcripts used for improvement must be PII-handled (masked or consented) before they become training or eval data. Promoting a failure into the golden set and shipping a fine-tune both go through the same governed CI/CD gates and sign-offs as any other change. Done right, this loop is also your best evidence for regulators that the model is monitored and continuously validated — the living core of an SR 11-7 ongoing-monitoring program.

Product analytics for LLMs: PostHog

Prometheus/Grafana watch the system; PostHog watches the product and the user. It's a product-analytics platform (events, funnels, session replay, feature flags, A/B experiments) with an LLM analytics layer bolted on: it captures each generation as an event with the model, token counts, cost and latency, tied to a user. Because the LLM data sits next to the rest of your product data, you can answer questions the infra dashboards can't: which intents customers actually ask, where they drop off, whether a 👎 correlates with a particular prompt version, and — via feature flags — roll a new prompt to 5% of users and measure the funnel effect before full release. Its tradeoff is honest: PostHog's view is event-shaped, great for product trends and cheap (a generous free tier — on the order of 100k LLM events/month with ~30-day retention), but shallower than a span-tree tracer like LangSmith for deep step-by-step debugging. Many teams run both.

# Capture each BankAssist generation as a product-analytics event with PostHog.
from posthog.ai.openai import OpenAI            # PostHog's drop-in instrumented OpenAI wrapper

client = OpenAI(                                 # same OpenAI client surface you already use
    api_key="sk-...",                           # your OpenAI key
    posthog_client=posthog,                     # hands PostHog the generations to record
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(          # normal call; PostHog logs it automatically
    model="gpt-4.1",                            # current model id
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Why two overdraft fees today?"}],  # the question
    posthog_distinct_id="cust-8842",            # tie this generation to the user (for funnels/retention)
    posthog_properties={"intent": "overdraft", "prompt_version": "v12"},  # props to break down + filter by
)
▶ Output
PostHog event '$ai_generation' · user cust-8842 · intent=overdraft · 712 tok · $0.0031 · 1.2s
dashboard: cost by intent · 👎 rate by prompt_version · funnel: asked → answered → escalated

For a bank, that intent and prompt_version breakdown is gold: you see which topics cost the most, which prompt version customers rate worst, and whether a feature-flagged rollout improved the escalation funnel — product evidence that complements the per-answer trace. Keep distinct_id a pseudonymous customer key, never a raw account number, and self-host PostHog or use its EU region if residency demands it.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the monitoring stack is cheap relative to tokens — Prometheus/Grafana are a small always-on pair; PostHog's LLM analytics runs free to ~100k events/month then usage-based. The expensive mistake is sampled LLM-judge quality scoring: judging every answer can cost as much as answering, so score a slice (e.g. 5–10%). Latency: metric emission is async and sub-millisecond; never let a down metrics/analytics endpoint block an answer. Scale: at 50,000 answers/day you're emitting a few metric samples per request — trivial for Prometheus; cardinality (too many label values) is the real scaling risk, so keep labels like intent bounded. Failure modes: watching only uptime while faithfulness quietly rots; alert fatigue from tight thresholds; and PII riding into the analytics store. Monitoring the right things: service health (error rate, p95), spend (cost/answer, tokens/min), and a sampled quality metric — the last is the one most teams forget. Security/compliance for a bank: treat every store (metrics, analytics, transcripts) as PII-bearing — mask before logging, region-lock, set retention; transcripts used for the flywheel must be masked or consented before they become eval/training data, and promotions through the flywheel go through the same governed gates as any change (your living SR 11-7 ongoing-monitoring evidence).

When to use what — and when not. Use Prometheus/Grafana for system health and SLOs; add PostHog when you want product-level insight (intents, funnels, feature-flagged prompt rollouts, user-tied 👍/👎). Use a span-tree tracer when you need to debug how one answer was built. Don't rely on product analytics alone for deep per-step debugging, and don't rely on infra metrics alone to tell you answers are correct — you need both a health signal and a quality signal.

⚠ Watch out

Two silent killers. First, monitoring only system health, not answer quality — latency can be perfect while faithfulness quietly rots; watch a sampled quality metric, not just uptime. Second, feeding raw production data into training without PII controls or governance — the fastest way to turn a helpful flywheel into a compliance incident. Mask, consent, and gate.

🧠 Remember it

Monitor the gauges, spin the flywheel: every escalation is a free eval case. Watch quality, not just uptime — and never let raw PII ride the loop.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

LangSmith tracing: an X-ray of every agent run

LangSmith tracing records the full, nested story of each request — every retrieval, model call, and tool step — so you can open any answer and see exactly how it was produced.

When a plain web service misbehaves, you read a log line. When an agent misbehaves, a log line is useless: the answer came from a chain of steps — fetch policy, call the model, call a tool, call the model again — and you need to see the whole tree, with the inputs and outputs of each step. LangSmith is a hosted platform (by the LangChain team) built for exactly this. Its first job is tracing: it captures each run as a trace — a tree of runs (also called spans) where child steps nest under their parent — and shows you token counts, latency, cost, and the exact prompt at every node.

The lovely part is how little you add to your code. You decorate a function with @traceable, and wrap your model client once. From then on, every call is recorded, nested correctly, and grouped into a project — a named folder of traces, usually one per app or environment (say bankassist-prod vs bankassist-staging).

# Trace a BankAssist answer to LangSmith — one decorator, full visibility.
import os                                          # read config from the environment
from langsmith import traceable                    # decorator that records a function as a run in the trace tree
from langsmith.wrappers import wrap_openai         # auto-traces every call made through an OpenAI client
from openai import OpenAI                           # the OpenAI client BankAssist already uses

os.environ["LANGSMITH_TRACING"] = "true"           # turn tracing on (unset = zero overhead, nothing sent)
os.environ["LANGSMITH_API_KEY"] = os.environ["LS_KEY"]   # auth to your LangSmith workspace
os.environ["LANGSMITH_PROJECT"] = "bankassist-prod"      # the project = folder these traces land in

client = wrap_openai(OpenAI())                      # wrapped client: prompt, tokens, latency captured automatically

@traceable(run_type="retriever")                   # tag this as a retrieval step (shown as such in the tree)
def fetch_policy(question: str) -> str:            # step 1: find the relevant policy text
    return search_index(question)                  # your existing vector search; its I/O is logged

@traceable(run_type="chain")                       # the parent run that ties the whole answer together
def answer(question: str) -> str:                  # children below nest under this run
    context = fetch_policy(question)               # child run #1 — the retriever above
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(         # child run #2 — the LLM call, auto-traced
        model="gpt-4.1",                           # current model id
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": f"Answer only from:\n{context}"},  # grounded prompt
            {"role": "user", "content": question},
        ],
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.content         # the text we return (and that LangSmith records)

answer(                                             # run it; the trace shows both children under 'answer'
    "What is the overdraft fee?",
    langsmith_extra={"metadata": {"thread_id": "cust-8842-sess-01"}},  # group multi-turn runs into one conversation
)
▶ Output
Trace 'answer' → project bankassist-prod · 2 child runs (retriever · llm)
712 tokens · 1.2s · cost $0.0031 · thread cust-8842-sess-01 · open in LangSmith UI

That thread_id in the metadata is the other everyday tracing tool: a thread stitches many separate traces into one conversation. A customer's five back-and-forth questions become five traces grouped under one thread, so you can read the whole chat as the customer experienced it — not five disconnected runs. (Any string works as the id; the LangSmith docs suggest a uuid7, which sorts by time.)

⚙️ Under the hood

Tracing is background and non-blocking: the SDK batches runs and ships them to LangSmith on a worker thread, so your request latency barely moves. @traceable works for any Python function (not just LangChain code), and wrap_openai patches the client so model I/O, token usage, and cost arrive without extra wiring. Prefer @traceable over the older RunTree object — it's the current, de-emphasizes-the-boilerplate path. If your bank standardises on OpenTelemetry, set LANGSMITH_OTEL_ENABLED=true and the same traces flow over OTel.

In production

For a bank, a trace is an audit artefact. When a customer disputes an answer, you open its trace and see the exact prompt, the retrieved chunks, the model id, the tokens, and the latency — the reproducible record SR 11-7 ongoing-monitoring reviews expect. Scope projects per environment, add metadata (customer segment, intent, prompt version) so you can filter and search traces later, and treat the trace store like any PII system: redact account numbers before they're logged, lock access, and set retention — LangSmith's base retention is short (14 days) with a longer extended tier, so decide retention deliberately rather than by default.

⚙️ In production

Cost/latency: tracing is near-free on the request path — the SDK batches runs and ships them on a background worker, so your p95 barely moves (typically <5ms). The cost is storage and plan tier, not compute: at 50,000 answers/day with 2–3 child runs each you generate ~100k–150k runs/day, so pick a sampling rate and retention deliberately. Scale: sample in high-traffic prod (trace 100% in staging, a slice in prod) and the pipeline keeps up; the failure mode is an unsampled flood plus long retention quietly running up the bill. Failure modes: trace export silently failing (you keep serving answers but lose the audit trail — alert on export errors), and metadata attached only to the parent run so per-thread token totals come out wrong. Monitoring: traces are the raw material for your dashboards and online evals, so treat the trace pipeline as a monitored dependency. Security/compliance for a bank: a trace is an audit artefact — the reproducible record (exact prompt, retrieved chunks, model id, tokens, latency) that an SR 11-7 ongoing-monitoring review and a customer dispute both need. So redact account numbers before they're logged, scope projects per environment, lock access, and set retention on purpose — LangSmith's base retention is short (14 days) with a longer extended tier, so decide rather than drift. If the bank standardises on OpenTelemetry, set LANGSMITH_OTEL_ENABLED=true and the same traces flow over OTel into your existing stack.

When to use it — and when not. Trace every agent that does more than one step, especially anything customer-facing — a single log line can't explain a chain of retrieval, model and tool calls, and you'll need the record for audit. For a trivial one-shot prompt with no tools you can skip it, but the moment behaviour is a tree, tracing is the cheapest debugging and compliance insurance you can buy.

⚠ Watch out

Thread and metadata must be attached to every run, including nested child runs — if only the parent carries the thread_id, your conversation grouping and per-thread token totals come out wrong. And never let raw prompts containing customer PII land in traces unmasked; a convenient "trace everything" switch becomes a compliance finding the day an auditor spots an account number in plain text.

🧠 Remember it

A trace is the X-ray, a thread is the chart. One shows how a single answer was built; the other shows the whole conversation. @traceable + one wrapped client gives you both.

Offline evaluation with LangSmith: datasets, evaluate(), and experiments

Offline evaluation runs a fixed set of test questions through your agent and scores the answers automatically, so "is the new version better?" becomes a number, not an opinion.

You tightened a prompt. Is it actually better, or does it just feel better on the three examples you happened to try? Because an LLM can answer differently each time, eyeballing a few cases proves nothing. Offline evaluation fixes this: you keep a dataset of example questions (with the right answers where you have them), run your agent over all of them, and score every output with evaluators. The whole run is saved as an experiment you can compare against yesterday's. "Offline" means it runs on a curated set in the lab — not on live customer traffic.

Three LangSmith pieces make this concrete. A dataset holds examples (each an inputs dict and an optional reference_outputs — the expected answer); datasets are versioned (every edit is a new version you can pin with as_of=) and can be sliced into splits (e.g. regression, edge-cases). The evaluate() function (and its async twin aevaluate()) runs a target function over the data with a list of evaluators. An evaluator is just a function with a fixed signature: it receives inputs, outputs, and reference_outputs and returns a score.

# Score a BankAssist version against a golden dataset in LangSmith.
from langsmith import evaluate                      # runs a target over a dataset with evaluators
from openevals.llm import create_llm_as_judge       # prebuilt LLM-as-judge evaluator factory
from openevals.prompts import CORRECTNESS_PROMPT     # a ready-made grading rubric for 'is it correct?'

# --- the thing under test: one example's inputs -> your app's output ---
def bankassist(inputs: dict) -> dict:              # 'inputs' is one example's input dict
    return {"answer": run_agent(inputs["question"])}  # call the real agent; return its answer

# --- a custom evaluator: three dicts in, one score out ---
def grounded(inputs: dict, outputs: dict, reference_outputs: dict) -> dict:  # the fixed signature
    hit = reference_outputs["answer"].lower() in outputs["answer"].lower()   # did we include the key fact?
    return {"key": "grounded", "score": float(hit)}  # name the metric + its 0/1 score

correctness = create_llm_as_judge(                  # a second, LLM-graded evaluator
    prompt=CORRECTNESS_PROMPT,                      # the rubric that defines 'correct'
    feedback_key="correctness",                     # what this score is called in the UI
)

results = evaluate(                                  # run every example through target + evaluators
    bankassist,                                     # the target function above
    data="bankassist-golden-v3",                    # the dataset (by name) to test against
    evaluators=[grounded, correctness],             # score each result two ways
    experiment_prefix="overdraft-prompt-v12",       # names this experiment so we can compare it
    max_concurrency=8,                              # run 8 examples in parallel (much faster)
    num_repetitions=3,                             # repeat each 3x to see non-deterministic variance
)
▶ Output
Experiment 'overdraft-prompt-v12:a1b2' · 50 examples × 3 reps
grounded 0.96 · correctness 0.94 · p50 1.1s · $0.0030/ex · Comparison View ready

Open the experiment in LangSmith and you get a table of every example, its output, and its scores — click any row to jump into that run's full trace. Line two experiments up in the Comparison View and it highlights, example by example, where v12 beat v11 and where it regressed — the single most useful screen for deciding whether to promote a change.

⚙️ Under the hood — evaluating the path, not just the answer

For agents, a right-looking final answer can hide a wrong path (it called a tool it shouldn't, or skipped a required check). The agentevals package scores the trajectory — the ordered list of tool calls — against a reference. create_trajectory_match_evaluator(mode=...) offers four strictness levels: strict (same tools, same order), unordered (same tools, any order), superset (made at least the required calls), and subset (made no calls beyond the allowed set). For BankAssist, a subset check is gold: it fails any run that called a tool it had no business touching.

In production

Two practices make bank evals trustworthy. First, mock side effects: an eval must never fire a real refund, transfer, or account change — point tools at a sandbox so running the suite a thousand times moves no money. Second, pin the dataset version (as_of=) in every CI run so a result is reproducible months later when audit asks "what did v12 score, and against which test set?" This is what turns the eval-gate idea into an evidenced control: an objective score, on a named dataset version, saved as an immutable experiment.

⚙️ In production

Cost: an offline run's cost is dominated by the model calls — your agent's call per example plus any LLM-as-judge call. A 50-example suite × 3 repetitions × (1 agent + 1 judge) ≈ 300 model calls, a few cents to low dollars per run; a 500-example nightly suite with judges can reach tens of dollars, so keep a fast PR subset and a fuller nightly/promotion suite. Latency: run with max_concurrency (e.g. 8) so a 50-case suite finishes in a couple of minutes instead of serial crawl. Scale: datasets grow from production failures — budget for them to 10× over a year and keep splits (regression, edge-cases) so you can run the relevant slice. Failure modes: a non-deterministic flake passing on a single run (use num_repetitions and read the spread), a judge that drifts (spot-check against human labels), and — the dangerous one for a bank — an eval that fires a real side effect. Security/compliance: mock side effects so running the suite a thousand times moves no money (point tools at a sandbox), and pin the dataset version (as_of=) in every CI run so a score is reproducible months later when audit asks "what did v12 score, against which test set?" That named-version, immutable experiment is what turns the eval gate into an evidenced SR 11-7 control.

When to use it — and when not. Run offline eval before every promotion and in CI on every PR — it's how "feels better" becomes a comparable number and how regressions are caught before customers. It's less useful for a brand-new capability with no golden data yet; there, start by hand-curating a dozen cases (even a tiny set beats vibes) and grow it from real failures. Offline eval checks a fixed set in the lab; it does not tell you how live traffic is doing — pair it with online evaluation for that.

⚠ Watch out

A stale golden set gives false confidence — it keeps proving you're good at last year's questions. Grow it continuously from real production failures (that's what the annotation and online-eval loops feed). And don't trust a single run of a non-deterministic system: use num_repetitions and read the spread, not just the average, or a flaky answer will slip through a one-shot pass.

🧠 Remember it

Dataset in, experiment out. evaluate() turns "feels better" into a scored, versioned, comparable number — and agentevals checks the path, not only the answer.

Prompt management with the Prompt Hub: versioned prompts as governed artifacts

The Prompt Hub stores each prompt like source code — every save is a commit, and movable tags like production let your app load "the approved one" without a redeploy.

In most teams the prompt is the least-governed, most-powerful line of code in the whole system. Someone edits a string, the behaviour of the entire agent changes, and there's no version, no review, no record. LangSmith's Prompt Hub (prompt management) treats prompts the way Git treats code. Each time you save a prompt you create an immutable commit identified by a hash. You attach movable tags (labels) to commits — so your running app asks for my-prompt:production and gets whatever commit that tag currently points at. Promoting a new prompt, or rolling back a bad one, is just moving the tag.

You can edit and test prompts in the Playground — a browser console where non-engineers (a compliance officer, a product manager) can tweak wording, swap the model or parameters, and run the prompt over a whole dataset to see the effect before anything ships. From code, you push a new version and pull by name, commit hash, or tag.

# Version a BankAssist prompt in the Prompt Hub, then load it by tag.
from langsmith import Client                        # client for prompts, datasets, feedback
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate  # the template object we store

client = Client()                                   # reads LANGSMITH_API_KEY from the environment

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate([                        # build the prompt with a fill-in slot
    ("system", "Answer ONLY from this policy:\n{context}"),  # grounding instruction
    ("user", "{question}"),                          # the slot filled per request
])

client.push_prompt(                                 # save it — creates a new immutable commit (a hash)
    "bankassist-overdraft",                         # stable name the app looks it up by
    object=prompt,                                   # the template version to store
    tags=["reviewed"],                              # attach a movable label to this commit
)

# In the running app, pull by TAG so a promotion needs no code change:
live = client.pull_prompt("bankassist-overdraft:production")  # fetch whatever 'production' points at now
filled = live.invoke({                              # fill the slots for this request
    "context": "Overdraft fee: $35.",
    "question": "What is the fee?",
})
▶ Output
Pushed bankassist-overdraft @ commit 7f3a9c2 (tag: reviewed)
Pulled 'production' → commit 6b1e… · promote = move tag to 7f3a9c2 · rollback = move it back

Notice the names staging and production are reserved tags in LangSmith for environment promotion — exactly the two gates a change should pass through. Pulling name:7f3a9c2 pins an exact commit forever; pulling name:production follows the label. Your app code never changes when you promote.

In production

For a bank this is prompt governance, and it answers questions auditors actually ask: who changed the overdraft prompt, when, why, and who approved moving it to production? The commit history is the paper trail; the reviewed → staging → production tag flow is a maker-checker gate. Pair it with the eval workflow: a commit earns the production tag only after it clears the golden-set experiment, so every live prompt has a score behind it. Keep secrets and customer data out of prompt text — a prompt in the Hub is shared across your workspace.

⚙️ In production

Cost/latency: the Hub is a control plane, not a per-request dependency — pull_prompt fetches a prompt over the network, so cache the resolved commit (refresh on a short TTL, say 60s) rather than pulling on every answer; a naive per-request pull adds a round-trip to your p95 and a hard dependency on the Hub being up. Scale: with caching, load on the Hub is negligible regardless of traffic. Failure modes: the Hub briefly unreachable (serve the last-cached commit, alert, don't hard-fail customers); pulling a floating bare name so a Playground edit silently changes live behaviour; and secrets or customer data pasted into prompt text (a prompt is shared across the workspace). Monitoring: record which prompt commit served each answer as trace metadata, so a quality dip ties back to the exact promotion. Security/compliance for a bank — this is prompt governance: the commit history answers "who changed the overdraft prompt, when, why, and who approved production?"; the reviewed → staging → production tag flow is a maker-checker gate; and pairing it with the eval workflow means a commit earns production only after it clears the golden-set experiment, so every live word has a reviewer and a score behind it. Lock who can move the production tag to a small approver group.

When to use it — and when not. Use a prompt registry/Hub the moment a prompt reaches customers or more than one person edits it — you need commits, tags, review and instant rollback. It also lets non-engineers (compliance, product) safely tune wording in the Playground behind the gate. For a solo prototype you're still shaping, a Git-committed prompt file is enough; add the Hub when approvals, environment promotion, and audit become real needs.

⚠ Watch out

The anti-pattern is pulling a floating version (the bare name, always-latest) in production: someone edits the prompt in the Playground and your live behaviour changes with no deploy, no review, no eval. Always pull by a tag you control (:production) or a pinned commit hash — never the bare name — so a change can't reach customers until the tag is deliberately moved.

🧠 Remember it

A prompt is code: commit it, tag it, pull the tag. Promotion and rollback become a label move, and every live word has a reviewer and a score behind it.

Dashboards & alerts: from "we emit metrics" to "we get paged"

LangSmith dashboards chart your agent's health from its own traces, and alerts page the on-call the moment cost, errors, latency, or answer quality cross a line.

Tracing records what happened; dashboards turn that stream of traces into the handful of charts a team watches all day, and alerts make sure someone is told when a chart goes bad — without a human staring at it. Because LangSmith already has every trace, you don't instrument anything extra: the metrics are computed from the runs you're already sending.

Dashboards come in two flavours — prebuilt (an out-of-the-box project view) and custom (charts you define). The metrics that matter for an LLM system: request/run count, error rate, latency (p50/p99 and time-to-first-token), tokens and cost, and feedback scores (your sampled quality signal). You can group by tag, metadata, or run name — so one chart becomes "p99 latency per intent" or "cost per customer segment" — and render as line, bar, KPI, or table.

Alert on…Typical BankAssist ruleWhy it matters
Error rateerrors > 2% over 15 mina broken tool or model outage
Latencyp99 > 4s over 5 mincustomers feel the app stall
Feedback scoreavg correctness < 0.90quality is quietly regressing
Run countdrops to ~0traffic stopped — the app is down
Cost / token usagespend spikes vs baselinea runaway loop or prompt bloat

When an alert fires, it reaches your team through a channel: a native Slack integration (on LangSmith Cloud), PagerDuty (via its Events API v2, so it raises a real incident and respects on-call rotation), or a generic webhook you can wire to Microsoft Teams, email, or your own endpoint. Alerts are scoped per project, so bankassist-prod and bankassist-staging page different people.

# The JSON a LangSmith alert POSTs to your webhook when it fires.
{
  "alert_name": "faithfulness-drop",         # the alert you configured on the project
  "project": "bankassist-prod",              # which tracing project tripped
  "metric": "feedback.correctness",          # the metric being watched
  "condition": "avg < 0.90 over 15m",        # threshold + window that was breached
  "observed": 0.84,                           # the value that tripped the alert
  "dashboard_url": "https://smith.langchain.com/o/…/dashboards/…"  # deep link to investigate
}
▶ Output
PagerDuty incident #4821 raised (severity: high) → on-call paged
Slack #bankassist-oncall: "⚠ faithfulness-drop in bankassist-prod · 0.84 < 0.90 · investigate →"

In production

This closes the operational loop for an SR 11-7 ongoing-monitoring program: you're not just able to inspect the model, you're told automatically when it drifts. The highest-value alert is on a quality signal (sampled correctness / feedback), not just uptime — latency can be perfect while answers quietly rot. Route quality and availability alerts to the right owners (model-risk vs platform on-call), set windows wide enough to avoid flapping, and keep the dashboard deep-link in the alert so the responder lands on the evidence, not a blank console.

⚙️ In production

Cost/latency: dashboards and alerts add nothing to the answer path — they're computed from traces you already send, so there's no extra instrumentation and no per-request overhead. The only "cost" is getting thresholds right. Scale: group-by on bounded dimensions (intent, prompt version, segment) scales fine; high-cardinality group-bys (per customer id) are the thing that makes a dashboard crawl — aggregate instead. Failure modes that matter at a bank: alert fatigue (too-tight thresholds page at 3am over noise until the channel is muted — tune windows and thresholds against real baselines, e.g. p99 > 4s for 5 min, not a single spike); a silent page that never arrives (test the alert path end-to-end, including the "run count drops to ~0 = app is down" alert); and watching only health, never quality. Routing: send quality alerts (sampled correctness) to model-risk owners and availability alerts to platform on-call, via Slack for awareness and PagerDuty (Events API v2) for a real, rotation-respecting incident; keep the dashboard deep-link in the payload so the responder lands on evidence, not a blank console. Security/compliance: this is the automated half of SR 11-7 ongoing monitoring — you're not just able to inspect the model, you're told when it drifts; scope alerts per environment (prod vs staging page different people) and keep PII out of alert payloads.

When to use it — and when not. Wire dashboards and alerts for anything live with real users — the highest-value alert is on a quality signal, not just uptime. You don't need a paging rotation for an internal pilot nobody depends on; a weekly glance at the dashboard is fine there. But the day customers rely on the agent, "someone will notice" is not a monitoring strategy — an alert turns "a chart went red" into "the on-call's phone buzzed."

⚠ Watch out

Two failure modes. Alert fatigue: thresholds set too tight page the team at 3am over noise until everyone mutes the channel — tune windows and thresholds against real baselines. And watching only health, not quality: a green latency/error dashboard tells you the plumbing works, not that the answers are right. Always include a sampled quality metric, or you'll be the last to know the model regressed.

🧠 Remember it

Chart the gauges, wire the siren. Dashboards show health and quality; an alert turns "a chart went red" into "the on-call's phone buzzed." Page on quality, not just uptime.

Annotation queues & human feedback: turning judgement into golden data

An annotation queue is a review inbox where experts grade real agent runs against a rubric, and their verdicts flow straight back into feedback scores and the golden dataset.

Some questions a machine can't score well: was this overdraft explanation correct, complete, and appropriately empathetic for a customer in distress? For those you need a human — but "a human looks at some outputs" has to become a repeatable pipeline, not an occasional favour. LangSmith's annotation queues are that pipeline. You route runs into a named queue; reviewers open it, see each run with a rubric (the exact feedback keys and options to fill in), score them one by one with a progress bar, and their scores are saved as feedback on those runs.

Feedback doesn't only come from reviewers. Your product can attach an end user's 👍/👎 to the exact run that produced the answer with one call — and for browser code that shouldn't hold an API key, LangSmith issues presigned feedback tokens so the page can submit a rating safely.

# Capture an end-user rating, then open a human review queue with a rubric.
from langsmith import Client
client = Client()

# 1) A customer taps 👎 — attach that signal to the exact run that answered them:
client.create_feedback(
    run_id="run-9f12ab",                        # the specific traced answer being rated
    key="user_thumbs",                          # the name of this feedback metric
    score=0,                                     # 0 = thumbs-down, 1 = thumbs-up
    comment="Quoted the wrong wire fee",        # optional free text from the user
)

# 2) Create a review queue so experts grade flagged runs consistently:
queue = client.create_annotation_queue(
    name="overdraft-review",                     # where reviewers find runs to grade
    description="Grade grounding + tone on flagged overdraft answers",  # the review's purpose
)
# Reviewers score each run against the rubric; verdicts save as feedback,
# and 'Add to Dataset' turns a reviewed run into a new golden example.
▶ Output
Feedback 'user_thumbs'=0 attached to run-9f12ab
Queue 'overdraft-review' created · 12 runs waiting → reviewed → 4 added to golden set

Two queue styles cover different needs. A single-run queue grades one run at a time against the rubric — good for "is this answer acceptable?" A pairwise annotation queue shows two runs side by side (say, the current prompt vs a candidate) and the reviewer picks A better / B better / Equal — far easier and more reliable for humans than assigning absolute numbers, and perfect for deciding between two model or prompt versions. During review, an expert can also write an assertion — the acceptance criterion for that case — which becomes the expected output when the run is added to a dataset.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist gets a cluster of 👎 on wire-transfer answers. An automation routes those exact runs into the overdraft-review queue. A payments specialist grades ten of them against a rubric (grounded? correct fee? right tone?), writes the correct expected answer as an assertion on the worst three, and clicks "Add to Dataset." Those three become new golden examples. Next week's prompt change is scored against them automatically — the same failure can never ship twice. The reviewers spent twenty minutes; the control is permanent.

In production

This is the human-in-the-loop evaluation pipeline — distinct from the HITL approval gate that pauses a live transaction for sign-off. For a bank it does two governance jobs at once: it provides documented human oversight of model quality (reviewers, rubrics, timestamps — exactly what SR 11-7 expects), and it manufactures the golden data that keeps evals honest. Mask PII before runs enter a queue, and record who reviewed what: the annotation history is itself an audit artefact.

⚙️ In production

Cost: the expensive resource here is human time, not compute — a reviewer grades perhaps 20–40 runs/hour, so you cannot review everything. Route only the runs worth a human's attention: 👎'd answers, low online-judge scores, and a small random sample for calibration. Latency: this is an asynchronous loop (hours to days), deliberately off the customer path — it manufactures future test cases, it doesn't gate a live answer (that's the separate HITL approval gate that pauses a transaction). Scale: use pairwise queues (A better / B better / Equal) where you can — humans are far more consistent and faster at "which is better?" than at absolute 1–5 scores. Failure modes: a vague rubric producing inconsistent scores you can't trust; a queue that fills faster than reviewers drain it (prioritise and cap intake); and feedback collected but never fed back into the dataset (wasted effort). Monitoring: track queue depth, inter-reviewer agreement, and how many reviewed runs actually become golden examples. Security/compliance for a bank: mask PII before runs enter a queue, and record who reviewed what and when — the annotation history is itself an audit artefact and provides the documented human oversight of model quality (reviewers, rubrics, timestamps) that SR 11-7 expects.

When to use it — and when not. Use annotation queues for the judgement calls a machine grades poorly — tone, empathy, completeness, "is this acceptable for a distressed customer?" — and to manufacture golden data from real failures. You don't need a queue for things an automated check settles cleanly (exact-match facts, schema validity, forbidden-tool checks); spend scarce reviewer time on the genuinely subjective, and let evaluators handle the rest.

⚠ Watch out

A rubric that's vague ("rate quality 1-5") produces inconsistent scores you can't trust — different reviewers mean different things by "3." Define concrete feedback keys with clear options, and prefer pairwise comparisons when you can: humans are far more reliable at "which is better?" than at absolute scores. And collecting feedback you never feed back into the dataset is wasted effort — close the loop or don't bother.

🧠 Remember it

A thumbs-down is a future test case. Route it to a queue, grade it against a rubric, add it to the golden set — and the same mistake can't ship twice.

Online evaluators & automations: grading live traffic as it happens

Online evaluation scores a sample of real production traces in real time — no reference answers needed — and automation rules act on what it finds, routing weak runs to humans or datasets.

Offline evaluation asks "how good is this version on our test set?" Online evaluation asks the harder, live question: "how good are the answers we're giving customers right now?" There's no reference answer for a brand-new customer question, so online evaluators use reference-free judges — an LLM-as-judge scoring faithfulness ("does the answer stick to the retrieved policy?") or tone on each sampled run as it flows through production.

These judges are wired up with automations (also called run rules). A rule is three parts: a filter (which runs it watches), a sampling rate (what fraction to act on — crucial, because judging every run with an LLM would double your bill), and an action. Actions include running an online evaluator, adding the run to an annotation queue (human review), adding it to a dataset, or firing a webhook. You can chain them — judge every sampled run, and only when the score is low, send that run on for human review — and set a spend limit per evaluator so online grading can't run away with cost.

# An automation rule (shown as its configuration): sample, judge, route failures.
rule = {
    "name": "live-faithfulness",                # what this rule is called in the project
    "project": "bankassist-prod",               # the tracing project it watches
    "filter": "eq(run_type, 'chain')",          # only top-level answer runs (not every child step)
    "sampling_rate": 0.1,                        # score just 10% of them — a decimal 0-1, controls cost
    "evaluator": "faithfulness-judge",          # LLM-as-judge; needs NO reference answer (reference-free)
    "on_low_score": {                            # chained action: fires only when the judge scores low
        "when": "score < 0.8",                  # the threshold that counts as a weak answer
        "action": "add_to_annotation_queue",    # send weak answers to humans for review
        "queue": "overdraft-review",            # the queue they land in
    },
    "spend_limit_usd_per_day": 25,              # cap the judge's daily cost so it can't run away
}
# Saved on the project, this now runs continuously over newly sampled production runs
# (and can backfill over historical traces too).
▶ Output
Rule 'live-faithfulness' active · scoring ~10% of bankassist-prod chains
last hour: 180 runs sampled · avg faithfulness 0.93 · 6 low scores → sent to overdraft-review

In production

Online evaluation is the engine of continuous validation — the part of SR 11-7 that says a model must be monitored in use, not just blessed once before launch. It gives you a live quality number you can alert on, and it feeds the flywheel automatically: low-scoring live runs become review items become golden examples become the next eval gate. Tune the sampling rate to balance signal against cost, keep an LLM judge honest by occasionally checking it against human labels (judges drift and have biases), and keep spend limits on so a traffic spike can't turn your monitoring into your biggest bill.

⚙️ In production

Cost — the headline risk: an online judge is itself an LLM call, so grading 100% of traffic can cost as much as serving it. Sample (e.g. 10%) and set a hard spend limit per evaluator (say $25/day) so a traffic spike can't turn your monitoring into your biggest bill. At 50,000 answers/day, a 10% sample is ~5,000 judge calls/day — a few dollars, bounded. Latency: run judges asynchronously on sampled traces after the answer is returned, never inline — the customer must never wait on the grader. Scale: tune the sampling rate to the signal you need; more traffic means you can sample a smaller fraction and still trend reliably. Failure modes: trusting a drifting judge as ground truth (it's a model with biases — recalibrate against human labels periodically), alerting on single scores instead of trends (noisy), and an unbounded judge quietly outspending the agent. Monitoring/compliance for a bank: online eval is the engine of continuous validation — the SR 11-7 requirement that a model be monitored in use, not blessed once. Chain it: judge the sample, trend live faithfulness on the dashboard, alert on the trend, and route low-scoring runs to a human queue and then the golden set — so production failures automatically become the next eval gate. Keep PII masked before runs reach the judge, and keep the whole loop governed.

When to use it — and when not. Use online evaluation once you have live traffic and need a real-time quality number — it catches the distribution shift and new questions that an offline golden set never saw, with no reference answer required. It's overkill before you have meaningful traffic (offline eval on a golden set is enough there), and it should complement, not replace, offline eval and human review — a reference-free judge is a strong signal, not a verdict.

⚠ Watch out

Don't blindly trust the online judge or treat it as ground truth — an LLM grader is itself a model with biases, so validate it against human reviews periodically and alert on trends, not single scores. And set the sampling rate and spend limit deliberately: judging 100% of traffic with an LLM can quietly cost more than the agent it's watching.

🧠 Remember it

Sample, judge, route. Online eval grades live answers with no reference, trends quality on the dashboard, and chains the failures straight to a human — monitoring that improves the product, not just watches it.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking 🔭 LangSmith

Migrating and upgrading the generation model safely

A rented model is like electricity from the grid: one day the utility upgrades the generator — or retires the old line entirely — and if you haven't planned for it, your lights flicker at the worst moment.

Here is a fact of life when you build on a hosted model: you do not own it, and it will not stay still. Providers publish a deprecation notice (the model still works, but the clock is ticking), then a shutdown date (calls start failing). On top of that, even a model that stays available can quietly change behaviour as the provider tunes it. So "swap the model" is not a one-line edit you do in a panic the week before a shutdown — it is a repeatable procedure you rehearse, because at a bank the thing you are changing is the voice that answers customers about their money. (Re-embedding and re-indexing when you change the embedding model is a separate job covered elsewhere; this topic is strictly about the generation model that writes the answer.)

Start with two boring documents that save you every time. A model inventory lists every place a model id appears — which service, which prompt, which environment, which model, pinned to which exact dated version. And a deprecation calendar tracks, per model, its announced deprecation and shutdown dates from the provider's deprecations page, so a retirement never surprises you. The golden rule underneath both: pin the exact dated version (for example gpt-4.1-2025-04-14), never a floating alias like gpt-4.1. A floating alias can shift under you with no code change and no warning; a pinned version changes only when you decide to change it.

The heart of the procedure is shadow (or replay) evaluation. You take your golden set — the curated, labelled questions you trust — and run both the outgoing model and the candidate over the exact same inputs, then diff the scores answer by answer. This catches the silent regressions that a quick eyeball never would: a new model that is more accurate on average but suddenly refuses a legitimate overdraft question, or drops the formal tone your compliance team signed off on.

# Shadow-replay: run the RETIRING model and the CANDIDATE on the SAME golden inputs, then diff.
from openai import OpenAI                       # official OpenAI client
client = OpenAI()                               # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

OLD = "gpt-4.1-2025-04-14"                      # the retiring model — PINNED to a dated version, never a floating alias
NEW = "gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14"                 # the candidate replacement, also pinned
SYSTEM = "You are BankAssist. Answer only from the provided policy text."  # identical prompt = a fair diff

def answer(model, question):                    # one grounded generation call
    r = client.responses.create(model=model, instructions=SYSTEM, input=question)  # swap ONLY the model id
    return r.output_text                        # the text a customer would actually see

golden = load_golden_set()                      # your curated, labelled test questions
regressions = []                                # cases where the new model scores worse
for case in golden:                             # replay every case through both models
    old_score = judge(case, answer(OLD, case.q))   # score the retiring model's answer
    new_score = judge(case, answer(NEW, case.q))   # score the candidate on the SAME input
    if new_score + 0.03 < old_score:            # small tolerance; flag real drops only
        regressions.append((case.id, old_score, new_score))  # collect what got worse

print(f"{len(regressions)} regressions of {len(golden)} cases — review before any rollout")  # gate the migration
▶ Output
7 regressions of 300 cases — review before any rollout
worst: case fee-wire-intl · tone dropped 0.92→0.71 (candidate sounds casual) · compliance phrasing missing

Notice what the diff surfaced: the candidate is cheaper, but it got more casual and dropped a required compliance phrase. That is the whole point — you learn this on your laptop, not from a customer complaint. The fix is usually prompt re-tuning: each model generation reacts differently to the same instructions, so the prompt that was perfect for the old model may need its tone and grounding rules re-stated for the new one. Re-tune, then re-run the replay until the regressions are gone or explained.

Going deeper — canary, rollback, and A/B on live traffic

Passing offline eval earns a candidate a cautious trip to production, not a full switch. You canary: route a tiny slice of live traffic (1%, then 5%, then 25%) to the new model while 99% stays on the proven one, and wire an automatic rollback — if live quality, error rate, or cost crosses a threshold, the system re-points to the old model on its own, without waiting for a human at 2am. Because your prompts and models live behind movable aliases (the registry pattern this chapter already covered), rollback is a one-line label move in seconds, not a redeploy. For the subtler "is new actually better?" question, run an A/B test: split live traffic, let both models answer real customers, and compare resolution rate, escalation rate, and faithfulness over a few days until the result is statistically real, not noise.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist runs on a model the provider announces will shut down in 90 days. The team opens the deprecation calendar (no surprise — it was tracked), pins a candidate, and replays the golden set: average quality is fine, but the diff flags that the candidate answers wire-transfer questions in a chattier tone and skips a regulator-required disclaimer. They re-tune the prompt to re-impose the formal voice and the disclaimer, replay until clean, then canary at 1% with an auto-rollback on faithfulness. Two quiet weeks and an A/B later, they promote — and because every step was recorded with eval scores, the model-risk committee signs off in one meeting. Customers never notice the engine was changed.

⚙️ In production

Cost/scale: the migration itself costs real tokens — a shadow replay runs your golden set through two models, and an A/B doubles judge calls on sampled live traffic — so budget it as a project line and sample live grading rather than scoring 100%. Latency: replay and A/B grading run off the customer path (async, on sampled traces); the only user-facing latency change is the new model's own speed, which you measure during canary (a cheaper model can be faster and slightly worse — the diff tells you the trade). Failure modes that actually bite a bank: a floating alias silently upgrading behaviour with no eval; a shutdown date arriving with no migration done (calls start failing); a candidate that wins on average but regresses on the few high-stakes, compliance-sensitive intents; and prompt drift because the new model needed re-tuning nobody did. Monitoring: stamp every answer with the exact model version that served it, so a quality dip ties to the migration that caused it, and alert on the deprecation calendar itself (e.g. 60 days before any shutdown). Compliance/governance: a model swap is a change event under SR 11-7 model-risk guidance — it needs maker-checker sign-off, the replay and A/B evidence attached, a communicated note on any intended behaviour change, and a reproducible record of which version answered which customer. The rollback plan is part of the sign-off, not an afterthought.

When to run the full procedure — and when not. Use the whole pipeline — inventory, pin, replay, re-tune, canary, A/B, sign-off — whenever the model change touches real customers or real money, which in a bank is nearly always. You can skip the canary and A/B for a purely internal, low-stakes tool where a bad answer costs nothing and you can roll back by hand; there, an offline replay plus a pinned version is enough. What you should never skip, even for a trivial change, is pinning the version and recording the swap — an unpinned, unrecorded model change is the one that bites you in an audit.

⚠ Watch out

The classic disaster is "it's just a newer model, ship it." A higher average score can hide a regression exactly where it hurts most — tone, refusals, or a compliance phrase on your highest-stakes intents. Never swap a generation model straight into production on vibes: replay the golden set, re-tune the prompt, canary with auto-rollback, and keep the old version one label-move away.

🧠 Remember it

Pin it, replay it, canary it. You rent the model, so you can't stop it changing — but you can diff old-vs-new on your golden set and keep the old one one click away.

FinOps for AI: cost attribution, chargeback & unit economics

A bank will not run a system it cannot bill back — so the question is never just "what did the AI cost?" but "which business unit, resolving which customer query, spent that money?"

Imagine the whole bank shares one electricity meter. The bill arrives, it is large, and nobody can say whether the mortgage team or the cards team ran up the cost — so nobody feels responsible, and the bill only grows. An AI platform without cost attribution is exactly that shared meter. FinOps (the discipline of bringing financial accountability to variable cloud and AI spend) fixes it by answering two questions for every dollar: who spent it and on what unit of business value. (This topic is about attributing and understanding spend; the levers for cutting it — caching, routing to cheaper models, prompt compression — live in the reliability chapter, so we only point at them here.)

The first idea to internalise is unit economics. Cost per API call is almost useless as a business metric — a "cheap" call that takes three retries and two tool loops to resolve one customer can cost more than one clean expensive call. So you measure cost against a unit of business work: cost per conversation, or better, cost per resolved customer query. Tokens are just the intermediate denominator on the way there. "$0.018 per resolved query, down from $0.025 last quarter" is a number a finance partner can actually reason about; "3.2 million tokens" is not.

To get there, you must tag every call. Each model request should carry who made it (team, tenant, business unit, customer segment) and what it was for (feature, environment, conversation id). This is the part the FinOps Foundation's token-economics work flags as the core challenge: model providers do not natively enforce your tagging structure, so you attach it yourself and ship a cost event to your own store.

# Tag every model call with who/what, capture token usage, and price it — the raw material for chargeback.
from openai import OpenAI                        # official OpenAI client
client = OpenAI()                               # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

# $ per input/output token — keep this in config and check it against the current price card.
PRICE = {"gpt-4.1": (2.00/1_000_000, 8.00/1_000_000)}  # (input_rate, output_rate)

def ask(question, *, team, tenant, feature, conv_id):   # every call must declare who + what
    r = client.responses.create(                # the grounded generation call
