Most banking phone traffic (balances, branch hours, "did my salary land?") is perfectly happy on the cascade; pay the premium only where it earns its keep.

Architecture~Latency (time-to-first-audio)~Relative cost / minEffort to runWhen to use
Speech-native RealtimeLowest (~0.5–0.8 s)Highest (audio tokens, ~several ¢/min)Low (one API)Warmth-critical or emotional turns; small premium flows
Streamed managed cascadeLow (~0.6–1.0 s)Low (text brain + ~sub-¢ STT + ¢-level TTS)Medium (framework wires it)Most phone traffic; the sensible default
Self-hosted cascadeLow–medium (depends on your GPUs)Near-zero per minute (you pay for hardware)High (you run STT/LLM/TTS + ops)High, steady volume where GPU rent beats per-minute fees
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's phone line used to run every call on gpt-realtime and the audio-token bill was brutal. The team switched the high-volume lines — balances, branch hours, card activation — to a streamed Pipecat cascade: Deepgram for ears, gpt-4.1-mini for the brain, Cartesia for the mouth, with the greeting and the recording disclosure pre-rendered to files. First audio still lands in well under a second, and the per-minute cost dropped by more than half. The one flow they kept on Realtime is the complaints line, where a warm, instant voice genuinely calms upset customers.

⚙️ In production

Measure the thing you're actually trading: chart p95 time-to-first-audio and cost-per-call side by side, per flow, so a "cheaper" change that quietly adds 400 ms gets caught. A cascade's blessing is that every line item is separately tunable — swap a pricier TTS for a cheaper one, downgrade the brain for simple intents, raise your semantic-cache hit rate — and each shows up cleanly in its own metric. Watch the cache hit rate and the small-vs-large model split; a drifting split (more turns escalating to gpt-4.1) is a cost leak worth an alert. Keep per-stage timeouts with a defined fallback (DTMF or a human) so one slow vendor can't freeze a call. For a bank, the cascade's readable text middle is a compliance gift: log the transcript at each hop, redact PII before storage, never persist raw card-number audio, and capture recording consent in the opening seconds. If you self-host, right-size GPUs to your concurrent call peak, not your daily total, and keep vLLM's prefix cache warm so the first caller after a quiet spell isn't punished.

⚠ Watch out

Chasing the cheapest possible stack can quietly wreck the call. A bargain STT that mishears account numbers, or a TTS with an awkward rhythm, costs you in retries, failed containment, and annoyed customers — far more than the few cents you saved. And a cascade has more moving parts than one Realtime model: three vendors, three failure modes, three latency budgets to keep in line. When not to use the cascade: for genuinely warmth-critical or emotionally delicate turns, the extra ~100–200 ms and the flatter, text-routed voice can be the wrong trade — pay for Realtime there. And never buy cheapness by dropping the read-back on money-moving actions; a confirmed transfer is always worth the extra turn.

🧠 Remember it

Realtime bills you for audio; a streamed cascade keeps the middle as cheap text. Stream between the parts, speak on the first clause, cache what repeats, route easy turns to a small model — and you get almost the Realtime feel for a fraction of the Realtime price.

Intelligent Document Processing: straight-through field extraction

Not every banking AI reads a knowledge base to chat. A huge, quiet workload is simply reading a form and typing what it says into a system — millions of times, with no human touching most of them.

Picture the back office of any bank. Somewhere there is a room — physical or virtual — where people open scanned KYC forms, loan applications, bank statements, cheques, and supplier invoices, and copy the details into the core system by hand. Name here, date of birth there, IBAN into that box. It is slow, it is expensive, and a tired human on form nine hundred makes mistakes. Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) is the use-case that automates this: it extracts structured fields from high volumes of documents and processes them automatically, so a person only ever sees the handful that genuinely need judgement.

This is not retrieval or RAG. Nobody is asking a question. The job is narrow and mechanical: given a document, produce a clean, validated record — {name, dob, iban, amount, …} — and either post it straight through or hand it to a reviewer. The individual building blocks here — vision models that read images, OCR and table parsing, confidence estimation, and the maker-checker review pattern — are each covered in their own topics; this lesson is about assembling them into one production IDP pipeline.

The pipeline, stage by stage

Every IDP system is the same five moves. Ingest: a scan, photo, or PDF arrives (from a branch scanner, a mobile upload, or an email inbox) and gets normalised — deskewed, split into pages, and given a unique ID for the audit trail. Classify: a quick model tags what kind of document this is, because a cheque and a loan application need different field schemas. Extract: a vision-capable model reads the page and fills a strict schema — this is the heart of it. Validate: deterministic rules check the extracted values. Confidence-gate: each field carries a score, and the gate decides auto-accept or human review.

Per-field confidence: the number that runs everything

The gate only works if each field comes with an honest confidence. Two techniques are common in 2025. The rigorous one is logprobs: the model emits a probability for every token it writes, so you find the tokens that spell a field's value and average their probabilities — a value the model was sure of scores near 1.0, a guessed one scores low. Open-source libraries now do exactly this against OpenAI structured outputs, scoring only the value tokens and skipping the JSON punctuation. The simpler one is model-reported (verbalized) confidence: you add a confidence field to the schema and ask the model to rate itself 0–1. It is easier to wire but less calibrated, so logprobs are preferred where the money is real. Either way, remember what the number is: a probability estimate, not a verified accuracy — which is why you still calibrate the threshold on labelled data and keep deterministic validation underneath it.

# BankAssist KYC capture: extract fields WITH a per-field confidence, then gate each one.
from openai import OpenAI          # official OpenAI SDK (v1+)
import json                        # to parse the returned JSON record
client = OpenAI()                  # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

field = {"type": "object",                        # every field returns its value AND a 0-1 confidence
         "properties": {"value": {"type": "string"},
                        "confidence": {"type": "number"}},
         "required": ["value", "confidence"], "additionalProperties": False}

schema = {"type": "object",                        # the exact record we want back — no stray keys
          "properties": {"full_name": field, "date_of_birth": field, "iban": field},
          "required": ["full_name", "date_of_birth", "iban"],
          "additionalProperties": False}

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                          # vision-capable, cheap default for high-volume IDP
    response_format={"type": "json_schema",        # Structured Outputs guarantees the shape
        "json_schema": {"name": "kyc", "schema": schema, "strict": True}},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text": "Extract each KYC field and rate your confidence 0-1."},
        {"type": "image_url",                      # the scanned form, inlined as base64
         "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64," + form_b64}},
    ]}],
)

doc = json.loads(resp.choices[0].message.content)  # {"full_name": {"value":.., "confidence":..}, ...}
THRESHOLD = 0.95                                    # auto-accept only above this; tune on labelled data

review = [name for name, f in doc.items()          # any weak OR rule-failing field is flagged
          if f["confidence"] < THRESHOLD or not valid(name, f["value"])]  # valid() = checksum/format rules

if review:                                          # one bad field sends the WHOLE doc to a human
    route_to_review_queue(doc, flagged=review)      # maker-checker: a person fixes just the flagged fields
else:
    post_to_core_banking(doc)                       # straight-through: no human ever touched it
▶ Output
full_name 0.99 ✓ · date_of_birth 0.97 ✓ · iban 0.83 ✗ (failed mod-97 checksum) → routed to review, flagged: [iban]. The other two were perfect, but one weak field holds the record back.

Validation rules: the cheap safety net under the model

Confidence tells you what the model believes; validation tells you what is provably wrong, for free. These are deterministic checks you run on every extracted record: format checks (does the date parse? is the IBAN the right length and country shape?), checksums (IBAN mod-97, card Luhn, many national ID digits), and cross-field rules (do the line items sum to the invoice total? is the applicant at least 18 from the date of birth?). A field can be high-confidence and invalid — the model confidently misread a smudged digit — so a failed rule always forces review no matter the score. Validation is the governor that stops a confident mistake from flowing straight through.

Everything that scores above the threshold and passes every rule is auto-accepted; everything else lands in the human-in-the-loop review queue. A good queue shows the reviewer the original image beside the extracted fields, highlights only the flagged ones, and lets them fix a value in seconds — so the human spends their attention where it matters instead of re-typing the whole form. Their corrections are gold: they become the labelled data you use to re-calibrate thresholds and measure true accuracy.

The one metric that matters: STP rate

The headline number for any IDP system is its straight-through-processing (STP) rate — the share of documents auto-accepted with no human touch, at an agreed quality bar. That caveat is everything: a 99% STP rate is worthless if it waves bad records through. In practice, LLM/agentic extraction pushes STP into roughly the 85–95% band for clean, standard document types, where older OCR-template systems sat nearer 60–80%. The biggest lever on STP is not raw model accuracy but the confidence threshold and routing: a well-calibrated score lets you lower the threshold and auto-accept more without dropping below your error budget. Alongside STP, track throughput (docs/hour), cost per document (a gpt-4.1-mini extraction is fractions of a cent; reserve gpt-4.1 for the hard document types), and the review queue's size and turnaround.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's onboarding team used to key every KYC packet by hand — passport page, proof of address, the signed form — taking a reviewer about seven minutes each. They wrapped the five stages above around gpt-4.1-mini vision, with IBAN mod-97, a date-parse check, and an "18+" cross-field rule under a 0.95 gate. Now 9 in 10 packets post straight to the core system in seconds; the reviewer sees only the blurry scans and the odd handwritten field, with just those boxes highlighted. Average handling time fell from seven minutes to about forty seconds on the ones a human still sees, and onboarding that took two days now clears same-day.

⚙️ In production

Treat the threshold as a dial you own, not a constant: set it per field and per document type (an IBAN gate can be stricter than a free-text address gate), and re-calibrate monthly against the corrections flowing out of the review queue — document mixes drift. Watch for confidence drift and a quietly rising review rate, which usually means a new form layout or a worse scanner upstream; alert on it. Right-size the model to the document: route easy, native-PDF forms to gpt-4.1-mini and escalate only genuinely messy scans to gpt-4.1, so cost tracks difficulty. On compliance — this is a bank — every document needs a full audit trail: the source image hash, the model and prompt version, the raw extraction, each confidence, which rules fired, and who approved any correction, all immutable. Handle the PII in these forms under least-privilege access, encrypt at rest, redact where you can, and honour retention limits (delete when the regulatory clock runs out; don't hoard raw images forever). Batch overnight volumes to smooth throughput, and keep a dead-letter path for documents the pipeline can't classify at all.

⚠ Watch out

The classic trap is trusting a high confidence as if it were correctness. Verbalized confidence especially can be cheerfully overconfident, and even logprobs are only calibrated if you've checked them against labelled truth — an uncalibrated 0.97 is just a vibe. Always keep deterministic validation underneath, and never let confidence alone clear a money-moving or identity-critical field. When NOT to use straight-through IDP: for low-volume, high-stakes, or highly variable documents — a one-off complex legal agreement, a bespoke corporate loan file — the engineering and calibration cost outweighs the saving, and a human should simply read it. IDP earns its keep on volume with structure: many documents, similar shapes, clear fields. If every document is a snowflake, you're building a pipeline to process one of each.

🧠 Remember it

Extract → validate → gate. The model reads, the rules catch what's provably wrong, and the confidence gate decides who touches it. Your score is the valve and STP is the scoreboard — but only ever at a quality bar you can defend.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Platforms & APIs — OpenAI Platform Essentials

A friendly tour of the OpenAI platform plumbing that every banking AI project leans on — which API to call, which tools to host, how to teach a model new behaviour, and how to run big jobs cheaply and safely without surprising your finance team or your regulator.

Chat Completions vs the Responses API: two front doors to the same model

Both let you talk to the model. One remembers nothing between calls; the other can hold the conversation and run tools for you.

Imagine two tellers at BankAssist's head office. The first teller has no memory at all: every time you walk up, you must re-tell her the whole story from scratch — who you are, what you asked a minute ago, everything. She's fast, simple, and famously reliable, and she's been doing the job for years. The second teller keeps a little file open for your visit. You can say "carry on from where we were," and she already has the thread. She can also walk to the back office, look something up, and come back with the answer — all on one request.

That is the difference between the two ways to call an OpenAI model today:

  • Chat Completions (client.chat.completions.create) — the long-standing, stateless endpoint. You hold the conversation history and resend it every time. It returns a choices array. Still fully supported and used everywhere.
  • The Responses API (client.responses.create) — the newer primitive and the recommended default for new projects. It takes input + instructions, can remember the conversation for you, can call hosted tools in a single built-in loop, and returns a typed output array of items.
🏦 Picture this

A customer tells BankAssist, "I lost my debit card." BankAssist replies, "I can block it — which account?" The customer says, "the joint one." With Chat Completions, your code must resend both earlier turns on that second call, or the model has no idea what "the joint one" refers to. With the Responses API, you can just pass the new message plus a pointer to the previous reply, and the platform stitches the thread together for you.

In plain terms — what each call looks like

Here is the stateless teller. Notice that we own the list of messages.

# Chat Completions: stateless. We carry the whole history ourselves.
from openai import OpenAI               # the official OpenAI Python client
client = OpenAI()                       # reads OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment

history = [                             # WE keep this list and resend it every turn
    {"role": "system", "content": "You are BankAssist, a careful bank helper."},  # standing instructions
    {"role": "user", "content": "I lost my debit card."},                          # the customer's message
]

resp = client.chat.completions.create(  # the classic stateless endpoint
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",               # a current, inexpensive general model
    messages=history,                   # the full conversation so far — nothing is remembered server-side
)
reply = resp.choices[0].message.content # answers live under choices[0].message
history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": reply})  # we must append the reply ourselves to keep the thread
print(reply)                            # show the model's answer
▶ Output
I can block that card right away so no one can use it. Which account is the card linked to?

Now the same idea with the Responses API. The key move is previous_response_id: instead of resending the history, you hand the platform a receipt for the last reply, and it continues from there.

# Responses API: the platform can hold the thread for us.
first = client.responses.create(        # the recommended default endpoint for new work
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",               # same model family, different front door
    instructions="You are BankAssist, a careful bank helper.",  # system-style guidance goes in its own field
    input="I lost my debit card.",      # the user's turn — a plain string is fine
)
print(first.output_text)                # output_text is a helper that pulls the final text out of the output array

second = client.responses.create(       # the follow-up turn
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    previous_response_id=first.id,      # THE key line: chain to the earlier reply; no need to resend history
    input="the joint one",              # the platform already knows what "the joint one" refers to
)
print(second.output_text)               # the model resolves the reference using the remembered thread
▶ Output
I can block that card right away so no one can use it. Which account is the card linked to? Done — I've blocked the debit card on your joint account. A replacement will arrive in 5–7 business days.

Going deeper — three ways the Responses API holds state

"Remembering the conversation" is not one feature but three, and picking the right one matters in a bank where data retention is audited:

  1. previous_response_id — the simplest. Each reply has an id; pass it on the next call and OpenAI chains the context. One gotcha: your top-level instructions are not carried forward automatically, so resend them each turn if you need them.
  2. Pass the prior items back yourself — take the output items from the last response and include them in the next input. More code, but you control exactly what's kept, which is handy when you must trim or redact sensitive turns.
  3. The Conversations API — a persistent conversation object you create once and attach each turn to. Think of it as a named folder the platform keeps on the server. "Conversations + Responses" is what reached feature parity with the old Assistants API.
⚙️ Under the hood — why the Responses API exists

It's not just "Chat Completions with memory." The Responses API was built for the agent era, so it bundles things that used to be your job: a single request can call several tools in a built-in loop (search, then calculate, then answer) instead of you hand-rolling that loop; it has better prompt-cache utilization (cheaper, faster repeat calls); and it supports encrypted reasoning items so a reasoning model's private thinking can be carried between turns without you storing it. By default responses are stored server-side (store: true); set store: false to keep nothing — important when a dataset must not linger.

In production — migration and the API being retired

One fact you must not miss: the Assistants API has been shut down — its final sunset was 26 August 2026 — in favour of the Responses API; always confirm the current status in OpenAI's deprecations docs. Any tutorial that teaches "threads, assistants, and runs" is teaching a sunsetting API. The replacement is Responses + Conversations. If you inherit a BankAssist codebase built on Assistants, migrating is mandatory, not optional:

  • An assistant (its instructions + tools) becomes parameters you pass to responses.create, or a reusable config in your own code.
  • A thread becomes a Conversation object (or you chain with previous_response_id).
  • A run becomes a single responses.create call — the tool loop that a "run" used to manage is now built in.

For brand-new work, reach for the Responses API. Keep Chat Completions when you have a mountain of existing code that works, when you need a dead-simple stateless call, or when a library you depend on only speaks Chat Completions. Both talk to the same models; the choice is about the shape of your integration, not the quality of the answer.

⚙️ In production
  • Cost — the Responses API does not make long threads cheaper. previous_response_id re-bills every earlier token as input on each turn, exactly as resending history would. For BankAssist's long support chats, summarise or trim old turns or the per-conversation bill creeps up.
  • Latency — one responses.create can hide several model turns (think → call tool → answer), so its wall-clock time is the sum of those hops. Stream the output so the customer sees words appear while the tool loop finishes behind the scenes.
  • Scale — stored responses have a limited life (commonly a 30-day window); for threads that must outlive that, attach turns to a durable Conversation object instead of chaining receipts.
  • Failure modes — a stale or never-stored previous_response_id returns a 404; your top-level instructions silently do not chain. Handle both — fall back to resending state and always re-send the system guidance.
  • Monitoring — log the response.id chain per conversation so an auditor can reconstruct exactly what BankAssist said and when; track input vs output tokens per turn to catch runaway history.
  • Security / compliance — responses are stored server-side by default (store: true). A bank under zero-data-retention must set store: false (and carry encrypted reasoning for reasoning models) so no customer turn lingers on the platform.

When to use it / when NOT: reach for the Responses API on all new BankAssist work and anything agentic (tools, reasoning, server-held threads). Stay on Chat Completions for a large existing stateless codebase, a dead-simple one-shot call, or a dependency that only speaks Chat Completions. Never start new work on the retired Assistants API.

⚠ Watch out

Don't confuse three OpenAI things that sound alike: the Responses API (the platform endpoint you call), the Agents SDK (a separate orchestration library that uses Responses under the hood), and the old Assistants API (being retired). Writing new code against Assistants in 2026 is building on a foundation that's on its way out.

🧠 Remember it

Chat Completions = you are the memory. Responses = the platform can be the memory. Assistants is retired — Responses + Conversations took its chair.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Hosted tools vs tools you build: convenience against control

The platform can run some tools for you on its own servers — or you can write the tool yourself and keep every byte of data inside your bank.

When an AI "uses a tool," it means the model decides it needs to do something — search the web, read a file, run a calculation — and emits a request to do it. The question is: who actually runs that tool? You have two choices, and in a bank the choice is often about data boundaries more than code.

Hosted (built-in) tools

OpenAI runs them on its infrastructure. You just switch them on in your request. Examples: web search, file search (over files you upload to the platform), code interpreter (a sandbox that runs Python), image generation, computer use, and remote MCP servers. Convenience: you write almost nothing.

Self-built (function) tools

You describe a function to the model; when it "calls" the tool, the model only returns the request — your own code runs it, on your own servers, against your own systems. Control: the data never leaves your walls, and you decide exactly what happens.

🏦 Picture this

A customer asks BankAssist two things in one breath: "What are today's mortgage rates in the news, and what's the balance on my current account?" The first half is fine for a hosted web search tool — it's public information. The second half must never go to a hosted tool: a customer's live balance lives in the core banking system, behind the bank's firewall, under audit. That's a self-built function tool that calls an internal API and returns only what the model is allowed to see.

In plain terms — the data boundary

This is the whole decision in one picture. A hosted tool means your request (and whatever it needs — the files, the query) is processed on OpenAI's side. A self-built tool means the model asks, but your code answers, so sensitive data stays home.

Here's a self-built function tool on the Responses API. The model never touches the balance system directly — it only emits a call, and your code decides what to run and what to hand back.

# A self-built tool: the model requests it, but OUR code runs it inside the bank.
tools = [{                                 # describe the tool so the model knows it exists
    "type": "function",                    # a function tool = your code, not a hosted one
    "name": "get_balance",                 # the name the model will call
    "description": "Get the live balance for one of the signed-in user's accounts.",  # helps the model choose it correctly
    "parameters": {                        # JSON Schema for the arguments the model must supply
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"account": {"type": "string", "enum": ["current", "savings", "joint"]}},  # constrain to known accounts
        "required": ["account"],
    },
}]

resp = client.responses.create(            # ask the model, offering the tool
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    input="What's the balance on my current account?",  # the user's question
    tools=tools,                           # make the tool available this turn
)
# The model does NOT get the balance. It returns a function call we must fulfil:
for item in resp.output:                   # walk the typed output items
    if item.type == "function_call":       # found the model's request to use our tool
        args = item.arguments              # JSON string, e.g. {"account": "current"}
        balance = core_banking_lookup(args)  # OUR code hits the internal system — data stays inside the bank
        # ...then send the result back as a function_call_output on the next responses.create call.
⚙️ Under the hood — file search is a managed RAG you don't maintain

The hosted file search tool is essentially a retrieval system OpenAI runs for you: you upload documents to a vector store on the platform, and the model searches them at answer time. That's convenient — no chunking, embedding, or vector database to run. The trade-off is the boundary: those documents now live on OpenAI's servers. For BankAssist's public product brochures that's often fine; for confidential credit-risk memos a bank usually prefers its own retrieval pipeline behind the firewall, feeding the model through a self-built tool. Convenience versus control, again.

In production — the rules banks actually apply

  • Classify the data first. Public → hosted tools are fair game. Confidential or regulated (PII, balances, KYC) → self-built tools so it never crosses the boundary.
  • Hosted tools add latency and cost you don't control — a web search round-trip or a code-interpreter sandbox spin-up takes real time. Budget for it.
  • Treat hosted-tool output as untrusted. A web search can return a page containing hidden "ignore your rules" instructions (prompt injection). Never let a tool result silently drive a money-moving action without your own checks.
  • Self-built tools are where you enforce authorization. The model asking for "the joint account" doesn't mean this user is allowed to see it — your code must verify that, every time.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — hosted tools carry their own charges on top of tokens (a web-search call, a code-interpreter container-session, file-search storage plus per-query fees). Self-built tools cost you nothing extra at OpenAI — you pay for the internal infrastructure you already run.
  • Latency — a hosted web round-trip adds roughly 1–3 seconds and a code-interpreter sandbox needs seconds to spin up; a self-built tool is as fast as your own API. Budget the hop into your p95 (the 95th-percentile latency — the near-worst-case wait a real customer feels).
  • Scale — hosted tools scale within OpenAI's quotas (and have their own limits); self-built tools scale with your core-banking capacity, so load-test the internal API behind get_balance before launch.
  • Failure modes — hosted tools can time out or return partial results; a retrieved web page may carry a hidden "ignore your rules" prompt-injection. Treat every hosted-tool result as untrusted and never let it drive a money move unchecked.
  • Monitoring — log each tool call with its name, arguments, latency and outcome. Alert on tool error rate and on any self-built tool that returns data the signed-in user was not authorised to see.
  • Security / compliance — the self-built handler is where you enforce authorization on every call — the model asking for "the joint account" is not proof this user may see it. PII, balances and KYC data stay behind the firewall, reached only through self-built tools.

When to use it / when NOT: use hosted tools for public, low-sensitivity work (search public rates, retrieve public brochures, crunch a CSV) where speed-to-build wins. Use self-built tools whenever the data is confidential or regulated, whenever an authorization check is needed, or whenever the action moves money — never hand customer PII to a hosted tool for convenience.

⚠ Watch out

The convenience of hosted tools can quietly become a compliance problem. "We'll just upload all our policy PDFs to file search" is easy — until someone realises confidential documents left the bank's control. Decide the data boundary before you pick the tool, not after.

🧠 Remember it

Hosted = convenience, your data visits OpenAI. Self-built = control, your data stays home. Public facts can travel; customer money cannot.

🏭 production 🔒 security 🏦 banking

Fine-tuning: SFT, DPO, RFT, and vision — teaching behaviour, not facts

Fine-tuning sends the model to school to change how it acts. It is the wrong tool for fresh facts — that's RAG's job.

Before anything else, hold this line firmly: fine-tuning changes behaviour; RAG supplies facts. If BankAssist keeps replying in a chatty, casual tone when the bank needs a formal one, that's behaviour — fine-tune it. If BankAssist doesn't know last Tuesday's new wire fee, that's a fact — retrieve it. Teams waste weeks (and real money) trying to fine-tune their way to current fees, then the fees change and they're stale again. Don't cross the wires.

💡 Key idea

Fine-tuning bakes a skill, style, or format into the model's weights so you don't have to spell it out in every prompt. It makes the model reliably do a thing — not know a new thing.

OpenAI's platform offers four fine-tuning methods. They differ mainly in what shape of training data you feed them:

1. SFT — Supervised Fine-Tuning (the default)

You show the model many examples of "when the input looks like this, answer like this." It learns to imitate your examples. Data shape: a JSONL file where each line is a full example conversation.

# SFT data: each line = one ideal conversation. The model learns to copy this style.
{"messages": [
  {"role": "system", "content": "You are BankAssist. Reply formally, cite the policy section."},  # the behaviour we want baked in
  {"role": "user", "content": "can i overdraft?"},                                  # a realistic messy user input
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "Yes. Per Deposit Agreement §4.2, an overdraft item fee of $35 applies; one courtesy waiver is available per 12 months."}  # the gold answer, in the exact tone/format we want
]}

Give it dozens to a few hundred clean examples and the model starts answering in that formal, cite-the-section style without you repeating the instruction every time. SFT is where you start.

2. DPO — Direct Preference Optimization (teach taste with pairs)

Sometimes you can't write the one perfect answer, but you can say "this reply is better than that one." DPO learns from pairs: a preferred answer and a rejected one for the same prompt. It nudges the model toward the kind you like and away from the kind you don't.

# DPO data: for one input, a preferred answer and a non-preferred one.
{"input": {"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is my money safe here?"}]},  # the prompt
 "preferred_output":     [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Yes — deposits are protected up to the insured limit. Here's exactly what's covered..."}],  # calm, specific, compliant — the style we reward
 "non_preferred_output": [{"role": "assistant", "content": "Totally safe, don't worry about it!"}]}  # vague over-promising — the style we push away from

A common recipe: run SFT first to get the model roughly right, then DPO to polish its judgment on the subtle "which of these two is better" calls.

3. RFT — Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (learn from a grader)

When "good" is checkable but not writable — the answer is right or wrong, passes a rule or doesn't — you can let the model try, get scored, and improve. You supply a grader (a reward function or model that scores each attempt), and the model is trained to earn higher scores. RFT is for complex, reasoning-heavy tasks and runs on OpenAI's o-series reasoning models.

# RFT: you provide tasks + a grader. The model is rewarded for getting them right.
# Example task: classify a transaction dispute into the correct regulatory category.
{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Charge I never made, $420, merchant abroad."}],  # the task input
 "reference_answer": "unauthorized_transaction"}   # the grader checks the model's label against this and rewards a match

Think of SFT as "copy these answers," DPO as "prefer this over that," and RFT as "here's a scorekeeper — go earn points." RFT shines where there's a clear notion of correct that a grader can measure.

4. Vision fine-tuning (teach it to read your images)

This is SFT extended so your examples can include images alongside text. BankAssist might learn to read a specific cheque layout, flag a particular forged-signature pattern, or extract fields from the bank's own ID-document format. Data shape is SFT's, with image URLs or base64 images inside the user message.

⚙️ Under the hood — what each method actually does to the weights

All four methods work the same deep down: they nudge the model's weights (its millions of internal dials) a little at a time, over several passes through your data — each pass is called an epoch. What changes is the signal that steers each nudge. SFT shows the model your gold answer and shifts the weights to make those exact words more likely next time — plain imitation. DPO feeds a pair and shifts the weights to raise the odds of the preferred answer and lower the odds of the rejected one, so it learns your taste without you ever writing a number. RFT lets the model try, runs your grader to turn each attempt into a reward score, and uses reinforcement learning to push the weights toward higher-scoring behaviour — try, score, adjust, repeat. Vision is just SFT with images added to the input, so the same imitation step also tunes how the model reads a picture. In every case you are not bolting on a fact store — you are reshaping reflexes already baked into the weights. That is exactly why it changes behaviour and cannot reliably add fresh facts.

In production — the honest costs and traps

  • Data quality is everything. A few hundred clean, consistent examples beat thousands of sloppy ones. One contradictory example teaches the model to be inconsistent.
  • It's a snapshot, not a subscription. A fine-tuned model is frozen at training time. New product, new tone, new rule → you retrain. Budget for the retraining treadmill.
  • You own a custom model now. That means versioning, evaluation before rollout, and a rollback plan — a bank can't quietly ship a model that starts refusing valid requests.
  • Availability shifts. Which base models accept which fine-tuning method changes over time, and OpenAI has signalled parts of the fine-tuning program are winding down. Always confirm the current supported models and methods in the platform docs before you plan a project around them.
  • Start cheaper. Before fine-tuning, try a better prompt, few-shot examples, or RAG. Fine-tune only when you've proven prompting alone can't get the behaviour reliable.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — you pay to train (per token in the training file, often multiplied by epochs) and a premium to run the custom model at inference. Weigh that against the alternative: a well-prompted base model with cached few-shot examples is sometimes cheaper overall.
  • Latency — a fine-tuned small model (e.g. a tuned gpt-4.1-mini) can actually be faster and cheaper at inference than stuffing a huge few-shot prompt into a big model every call — the behaviour is baked in, so the prompt shrinks.
  • Scale — you now own a versioned asset. Every retrain needs an eval gate, a canary rollout, and a one-click rollback before BankAssist serves it to customers.
  • Failure modes — catastrophic forgetting (it gets worse at things you didn't train), silent drift as the world changes, and stale behaviour frozen at training time. One contradictory training example teaches inconsistency.
  • Monitoring — run the full eval suite before rollout, then watch live refusal rate, tone adherence and task accuracy; a tuned model that starts refusing valid requests must trip an alert.
  • Security / compliance — training data is governed data — scrub PII, honour consent, keep a model card and lineage for the audit trail. Important: OpenAI is winding down self-serve fine-tuning (new training jobs are slated to end in early 2027 and tunable base models are being retired on a rolling schedule), so confirm current method and model support before planning a project.

When to use it / when NOT: fine-tune when you have proven that prompting, few-shot and RAG cannot make a behaviour, style or format reliable, and you have dozens-to-hundreds of clean examples. Do NOT fine-tune to add facts (that is RAG), to chase a moving target like a fee schedule, or before you have exhausted cheaper prompt fixes.

⚠ Watch out

The classic expensive mistake: fine-tuning to inject knowledge. Teams train a model on the fee schedule, fees change next month, and the model confidently quotes the old numbers — with no way to cite a source. Facts belong in RAG, where you edit one document and the next answer is current. Behaviour belongs in fine-tuning.

🧠 Remember it

SFT = copy. DPO = prefer. RFT = score. Vision = see. And over it all: fine-tune behaviour, RAG the facts.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

The Batch API: big, patient jobs at about half price

When you have a mountain of requests and no customer waiting, batch them — pay roughly 50% less and get results within 24 hours.

Not every AI job is a live chat. Sometimes BankAssist's team needs to embed every document in the archive, or re-score last month's 200,000 chat transcripts for quality. Doing that one live request at a time is slow and costs full price. The Batch API is built exactly for this: you hand OpenAI a big file of requests, go home, and collect the finished results later — at about 50% lower cost, with a turnaround window of up to 24 hours.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist is launching semantic search over 80,000 archived policy and FAQ pages. Every chunk needs an embedding. Doing it live would hammer the rate limits and cost full freight. Instead the team writes all 80,000 embedding requests into one file, submits it as a batch on Friday evening, and by Saturday morning the whole vector store is built — for roughly half the price, with no customer ever waiting on it.

In plain terms — the shape of a batch

A batch is a JSONL file (one JSON object per line). Each line is one request, tagged with a custom_id you choose. That ID is vital: results come back in no guaranteed order, so the custom_id is how you match each answer to the question that produced it.

# Step 1: write a JSONL file — one line per request, each with a unique custom_id.
# requests.jsonl
{"custom_id": "chunk-0001", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/embeddings", "body": {"model": "text-embedding-3-small", "input": "Overdraft item fee: $35..."}}
{"custom_id": "chunk-0002", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/embeddings", "body": {"model": "text-embedding-3-small", "input": "Wire transfer fee: $25..."}}
# ...80,000 lines like this. custom_id is yours; it must be unique in the file.

# Step 2: upload the file, create the batch, then poll until it's done.
f = client.files.create(                 # upload the JSONL as a batch-input file
    file=open("requests.jsonl", "rb"),
    purpose="batch",                     # tells the platform this file is for batching
)
batch = client.batches.create(           # kick off the batch job
    input_file_id=f.id,                  # point at the uploaded file
    endpoint="/v1/embeddings",           # which API every line targets (one endpoint per batch)
    completion_window="24h",             # the window you accept — the source of the discount
)
print(batch.id, batch.status)            # e.g. "batch_abc123 validating" — now wait and poll

done = client.batches.retrieve(batch.id) # check later; status moves to "completed"
results = client.files.content(done.output_file_id)  # download the results JSONL once finished
# Each result line carries its custom_id — THAT is how you line answers back up with inputs.
⚙️ Under the hood — why it's cheaper

The discount isn't magic; it's a trade. By accepting a 24-hour window instead of an instant reply, you let OpenAI schedule your work when its systems have spare capacity, smoothing out the peaks. You give up speed and buy back cost. Batch also has its own, separate rate limits, so a big batch won't eat into the live quota your customer-facing BankAssist depends on — a genuinely useful isolation in production.

In production — where batch fits a bank

  • Great for: bulk embedding (building or rebuilding a vector store), offline evaluation ("re-grade 200k transcripts against our new quality rubric"), overnight classification, data enrichment, synthetic data generation.
  • Not for: anything a customer is waiting on. If there's a spinner, use a live call.
  • Keep custom_id meaningful and unique (e.g. the document+chunk id). Out-of-order results with duplicate or vague ids become a painful reconciliation bug.
  • Handle partial failure. Some lines in a batch can fail while others succeed; the results file reports per-line errors. Plan to retry just the failures, not the whole job.
  • Mind the per-batch limits (number of requests and file size) and split very large jobs into several batches.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — the headline win: roughly 50% off both input and output tokens versus the same requests sent live. For BankAssist's 80,000-chunk embedding job that is real money saved on a task no customer sees.
  • Latency — the deal is a completion window of up to 24 hours (often faster). Never put a batch anywhere a user is watching a spinner — it is for offline work only.
  • Scale — batch has its own separate rate limits and per-batch caps (file size and request-count limits, plus per-model enqueued-token ceilings), so a huge overnight run won't starve the live quota your customer-facing BankAssist depends on. Split very large jobs across several batches.
  • Failure modes — individual lines can fail while others succeed, and a batch that exceeds its window returns whatever finished plus an error file. Design to retry only the failed custom_ids, not the whole job.
  • Monitoring — poll status and read request_counts (total / completed / failed); reconcile every result against its custom_id so nothing is silently dropped.
  • Security / compliance — both the input and output files live on the platform until you remove them. For regulated data, delete them after you have collected results, and keep an index of which batch processed which records for audit.

When to use it / when NOT: batch bulk embedding, overnight classification, offline re-grading of transcripts, data enrichment and synthetic-data jobs. Do NOT batch anything interactive, time-critical, or that a customer is waiting on — use a live call there.

⚠ Watch out

A batch is not fire-and-forget. If you submit it and never poll, or you reuse a vague custom_id like "row" across lines, you get back a pile of out-of-order results you cannot reliably match to their inputs — a silent data-corruption bug. Always use a unique, meaningful custom_id (e.g. doc42-chunk-0007) and always reconcile every line.

🧠 Remember it

No one's waiting? Batch it. Half the cost, up to a day's wait, and custom_id is the name tag that reunites each answer with its question.

🏭 production 💰 cost 🏦 banking

The Moderation API: a free safety net on the way in and out

A free classifier that flags unsafe content — run it on what the user sends and on what the model replies.

A bank assistant lives in a regulated, reputation-sensitive world. You don't want a customer typing something abusive and getting a model that plays along, and you really don't want the model itself producing something harmful under your bank's name. The Moderation API is a purpose-built safety classifier that scores text (and images) against categories of harm — hate, harassment, violence, self-harm, sexual content, and more. Best of all for a budget: it's free and doesn't count against your usual usage quota, so there's no cost excuse to skip it.

🏦 Picture this

Late at night, a distressed customer types a message to BankAssist hinting at self-harm. A naive bot would plough on about overdraft fees. With a moderation check on the input, BankAssist instead recognises the flag, stops the normal flow, and switches to a pre-approved, compassionate response with a helpline — exactly the handling the bank's safety team signed off. The moderation call cost nothing and may have mattered more than any feature in the product.

In plain terms — screen both directions

Think of moderation as two doormen: one checks people coming in (the user's message) and one checks what goes out (the model's reply). Input screening catches abusive or distressing prompts before you act on them. Output screening is your last line of defence against the model saying something it shouldn't — especially valuable just after you've added retrieval or tools that can pull in unpredictable text.

# Moderate the USER'S message before doing anything with it.
mod = client.moderations.create(         # the free safety classifier endpoint
    model="omni-moderation-latest",      # current multimodal moderation model (text + images)
    input="user's message text here",     # what we want checked
)
result = mod.results[0]                   # one result per input

if result.flagged:                       # True if ANY category crossed the model's threshold
    categories = result.categories       # booleans per category: hate, harassment, self_harm, violence, ...
    scores = result.category_scores      # 0–1 confidence per category — use these for YOUR own thresholds
    handle_unsafe(categories, scores)    # route to a safe flow instead of the normal answer
else:
    answer = normal_bankassist_reply()   # safe to proceed
⚙️ Under the hood — flagged, categories, and your own thresholds

Each result gives you three things: flagged (a single yes/no using OpenAI's default thresholds), categories (a yes/no per harm type), and category_scores (a 0-to-1 confidence per type). The scores are the pro tool. A bank might decide to block only above a high score but log and review anything above a lower one — tuning its own thresholds per category instead of relying on the single default flagged flag. Lower your threshold and you catch more but annoy more innocent users (false positives); raise it and you miss more (false negatives). That dial is a policy decision, made with your risk team.

In production — moderation as a pipeline stage, not an afterthought

  • Wrap every turn. Moderate input before processing and output before sending. In a RAG system, also consider screening retrieved text — a poisoned document is untrusted input too.
  • It's fast and free, so there's no cost argument against running it — but it does add a network round-trip; account for the latency.
  • Log flags for audit. In banking, "we detected and safely handled it" is a story you may need to tell a regulator. Keep the evidence.
  • Moderation is not your only guardrail. It catches broad harm categories; it won't catch "gave wrong financial advice" or "leaked another customer's data." Pair it with business rules, authorization checks, and human escalation.
  • Have a safe fallback ready. When something is flagged, the model shouldn't improvise. Route to pre-approved responses or a human.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — the Moderation API is free and does not draw on your usual usage quota, so there is no budget excuse to skip it on either direction.
  • Latency — it still adds a network round-trip (typically ~100–300 ms). Run the input check as a pre-gate, and where speed matters fire the output check in parallel with streaming so it rarely shows up on the critical path.
  • Scale — free does not mean limitless: the endpoint has its own rate limits. At high volume, batch where you can and handle its 429s like any other call.
  • Failure modes — if the moderation call itself errors or times out, fail safe — block or route to a cautious canned reply rather than letting unscreened content through.
  • Monitoring — log flagged, the per-category category_scores and the hashed user id (not the raw content where avoidable). A rising flag count on one user is an early abuse signal.
  • Security / compliance — for a bank, "we detected and safely handled it" is a story you may have to tell a regulator — keep the evidence. Tune per-category thresholds with your risk team, and remember moderation is one guard, not the whole guardrail stack.

When to use it / when NOT: wrap every single turn — moderate input before acting and output before sending, and screen retrieved text in a RAG flow. Do NOT lean on it to catch wrong financial advice, PII leaks or authorization errors; those need business rules and human escalation, not a harm classifier.

⚠ Watch out

Don't treat a passing moderation check as "this answer is correct and compliant." Moderation only says "this isn't in a harm category." A perfectly polite, non-flagged reply can still quote the wrong fee or overstep into regulated advice. Safety and accuracy are different problems with different guards.

🧠 Remember it

Two doormen, no cover charge: check what comes in and what goes out. It's free — run it both ways, every turn.

🏭 production 🔒 safety 🏦 banking

Embeddings, rate limits, and surviving the 429

Embeddings turn text into meaning-vectors — the fuel for search and RAG. And whatever you call, rate limits decide how fast you're allowed to go.

An embedding is a list of numbers that captures the meaning of a piece of text, so a computer can measure how close two texts are in meaning. It's the quiet engine under semantic search, RAG retrieval, clustering, and recommendations. The current workhorses are text-embedding-3-small (fast, cheap, 1536 numbers per text by default) and text-embedding-3-large (more accurate, 3072 numbers, costlier). A neat trick on both: the dimensions parameter lets you ask for shorter vectors, trading a little accuracy for less storage and faster search.

# Turn a banking chunk into a meaning-vector, and ask for a shorter vector to save space.
resp = client.embeddings.create(         # the embeddings endpoint
    model="text-embedding-3-small",      # current, inexpensive embedding model
    input="Overdraft item fee: $35; one courtesy waiver per 12 months.",  # one chunk of a document
    dimensions=512,                      # optional: shorten from 1536 → 512 to cut storage & speed up search
)
vector = resp.data[0].embedding          # the list of numbers we store in the vector DB

batch_resp = client.embeddings.create(   # embed MANY texts in one call — far more efficient than one-by-one
    model="text-embedding-3-small",
    input=["chunk one text", "chunk two text", "chunk three text"],  # a list → results come back in the same order
)
print(len(batch_resp.data))              # 3 — one embedding per input, order preserved
▶ Output
3
✅ Tip

Always embed the query with the same model you used for the documents. Vectors from two different models live in different "meaning spaces" and their distances are meaningless together — a subtle bug that quietly wrecks retrieval quality.

Going deeper — rate limits, tiers, and why you'll meet the 429

OpenAI caps how fast you can call, mainly as RPM (requests per minute) and TPM (tokens per minute). Your caps depend on your usage tier — new accounts start low (Tier 1) and climb (Tier 2, 3, …) automatically as your trusted payment history grows. Cross a cap and the API replies with HTTP 429 — "Too Many Requests." This isn't a bug; it's the platform asking you to slow down. The professional response is exponential backoff with jitter: wait a bit and retry, and if it fails again wait longer, adding a little randomness so a fleet of clients doesn't all retry in lockstep.

# Retry a 429 with exponential backoff + jitter. Simple, and it saves you in production.
import time, random                       # time for sleeping, random for jitter
from openai import RateLimitError         # the exception raised on an HTTP 429

def embed_with_backoff(text, tries=6):    # try up to 6 times before giving up
    for attempt in range(tries):          # attempt = 0, 1, 2, ...
        try:
            return client.embeddings.create(          # the call that may be rate-limited
                model="text-embedding-3-small", input=text)
        except RateLimitError:            # only retry the "too many requests" case
            if attempt == tries - 1:      # out of attempts?
                raise                     # give up and let the caller handle it
            wait = (2 ** attempt) + random.random()   # 1s, 2s, 4s... (+ up to 1s jitter so clients don't sync up)
            time.sleep(wait)              # pause before trying again

The one subtlety worth stating plainly: we only retry on RateLimitError (a 429). A different error — a bad request, an auth failure — should not be retried, because waiting won't fix it; you'd just hammer a request that can never succeed.

⚙️ Under the hood — don't just retry; avoid the limit

Backoff is the cure, but prevention is cheaper. Three habits keep BankAssist under its caps: batch your inputs (send many texts in one embeddings call instead of one per request — fewer requests, same work); use the Batch API for huge offline jobs (it has separate limits and won't starve your live traffic); and smooth your sending rate (a client-side queue that paces calls beats bursting and bouncing off 429s all day). The official SDK already retries transient errors a few times for you — but a bank should still own its backoff and monitoring rather than trust defaults blindly.

In production — the operational checklist

  • Expect 429s at scale and handle them everywhere you call the API — embeddings, chat, moderation alike. A single un-guarded call can take down a whole ingestion run.
  • Request a tier increase ahead of a launch, not during the incident. Tiers climb with usage history, so plan the ramp.
  • Cap total retries and set timeouts. Infinite backoff turns a rate-limit blip into a hung system.
  • Monitor your headroom. Track how close you run to your RPM/TPM caps and alert before you hit them, so you scale the tier or the pacing in advance.
  • Re-embedding is expensive and rate-limited. If you ever change embedding models, you must re-embed your entire corpus — plan that as a batch job, not a live scramble.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — per-call embeddings are cheap (fractions of a cent per 1K tokens), but re-embedding an entire corpus is the big-ticket item. The way to control cost is to embed in big batched calls and run full re-embeds through the Batch API at ~50% off.
  • Latency — one call that embeds a list of 100 chunks is far faster and cheaper than 100 calls. Batch your inputs and pace a client-side queue rather than bursting into 429s.
  • Scale — your ceiling is RPM and TPM, set by your usage tier; new accounts start at Tier 1 and climb with payment history. Request a tier bump before a launch, not during the incident.
  • Failure modes — 429 storms during ingestion; a single un-guarded call can take down a whole run. Retry only retryable errors (429s, transient 5xx), cap total retries, and set timeouts so backoff never hangs the system.
  • Monitoring — track headroom against your RPM/TPM caps and alert before you hit them; watch retry counts as a leading indicator of pacing problems.
  • Security / compliance — pin the embedding model version — changing it forces a full, rate-limited re-embed of everything, because vectors from two models aren't comparable. For customer data, keep the vectors in a bank-controlled store, not a third-party one.

When to use it / when NOT: use text-embedding-3-small as the default workhorse, stepping up to -3-large only when retrieval quality measurably needs it, and shorten with dimensions to save storage. Use exponential backoff on 429s — but do NOT retry 400/401 errors; waiting never fixes a bad request or a bad key.

⚠ Watch out

Retrying every error with backoff is a trap. A 429 says "wait" — retry it. A 400 (bad request) or 401 (bad key) says "this will never work" — retrying just floods the API and can itself trip rate limits. Retry the retryable; fail fast on the rest.

🧠 Remember it

Same model in and out for embeddings. And when you see 429, don't panic — back off, double, jitter, retry. Prevent with batching; survive with backoff.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 💰 cost

Inside the Responses API: items, call_id, and the three ways to remember

A Responses reply isn't one blob of text — it's a little stack of typed cards. Learn to read the cards and you understand everything the model did.

When you call the Responses API, the answer doesn't come back as a single string. It comes back as an array of typed items — think of a short stack of index cards, each with a type on the top corner. One card might say "here's my message to the user." Another might say "I want to call a tool." A reasoning model slips in a card that says "here's my private thinking." Your code's job is to flip through the cards and handle each by its type. Once you see a reply this way, the whole API stops feeling mysterious.

🏦 Picture this

A BankAssist customer asks, "Did my salary land, and what's the mortgage rate in today's news?" The model thinks for a moment, decides it needs the live balance, and asks the web for the rate. The reply you get back isn't a sentence — it's a stack: a reasoning card (its private plan), a function_call card ("run get_balance"), and a web_search_call card. Only after your code answers the function call does a final message card with the human reply appear. Reading the stack is how you follow what happened.

In plain terms — the common item types

Every item has a type. These are the ones you meet daily:

  • message — the model's text for the user. Its content holds output_text parts (and sometimes a refusal part, when the model declines the request).
  • reasoning — a reasoning model's internal thinking. Usually opaque; you carry it, you don't read it.
  • function_call — "please run this tool." Carries a name, an arguments JSON string, and a call_id.
  • function_call_output — your card: the tool's result, tagged with the same call_id so the model knows which request it answers.

The call_id is the quiet hero. It is the string that links a request to its answer. When the model emits a function_call with call_id: "call_x9", you must send back a function_call_output with call_id: "call_x9". Get it wrong and the model can't tell which tool result belongs to which request — especially when it called three tools at once.

# Read the stack of items by type, then answer the tool call using its call_id.
resp = client.responses.create(            # the recommended endpoint for new work
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                  # model names move fast — confirm the current one in the docs
    input="Did my salary land this week?",  # the user's turn
    tools=[get_balance_tool],              # a self-built function tool we defined elsewhere
)

tool_outputs = []                          # we'll collect our answers here
for item in resp.output:                   # flip through the stack of typed cards
    if item.type == "function_call":       # the model wants us to run a tool
        result = run_tool(item.name, item.arguments)  # OUR code runs it inside the bank
        tool_outputs.append({              # build the matching answer card
            "type": "function_call_output",  # the item type the model expects back
            "call_id": item.call_id,       # SAME call_id — this is what links answer to request
            "output": result,              # the tool result as a string
        })

follow_up = client.responses.create(       # send the tool results back so the model can finish
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",
    previous_response_id=resp.id,          # chain to the turn that asked for the tools
    input=tool_outputs,                    # our function_call_output cards go in as the new input
)
print(follow_up.output_text)               # now the final message card is ready
▶ Output
Yes — your salary of $2,480 landed on Tuesday into your current account.

Going deeper — three ways to hold the thread, and what each costs you

"Remembering the conversation" has three concrete mechanisms, and in a bank the difference is about retention and billing, not just convenience:

MechanismWho stores itWatch out for
previous_response_idOpenAI, server-sideYour top-level instructions do not carry forward — resend them. And every prior token is still re-billed as input each turn.
Manual replay (pass prior output items back in input)You, in your own appMost control — you can trim or redact turns. For reasoning models you must replay all items, including the opaque reasoning cards, or the model loses its train of thought.
Conversations APIOpenAI, as a durable objectA named folder on the server you attach each turn to. Its items are not subject to the 30-day response TTL (time-to-live — the window after which a stored response is auto-deleted) — good for long-running cases.
⚙️ Under the hood — store, retention, and zero-data-retention

By default the Responses API sets store: true: your response is kept server-side (commonly a 30-day retention window) so previous_response_id can find it later. Set store: false and nothing lingers — essential when a dataset must not be retained. But there's a catch for reasoning models: if you don't store, the private reasoning items vanish too, which hurts quality across a tool loop. The fix is encrypted reasoning items — ask for reasoning.encrypted_content in the include field, and the model hands you its thinking as an encrypted blob you replay on the next turn. You keep the benefit of reasoning while storing nothing in the clear. This is the standard pattern for zero-data-retention (ZDR) banking setups. Exact retention periods and ZDR terms change — verify them against your OpenAI data-retention agreement.

In production — the things that bite

  • instructions don't chain. With previous_response_id, resend your system guidance every turn or BankAssist quietly forgets it's a formal bank assistant.
  • Chaining still bills the whole history. Server-side memory saves you code, not tokens — prior turns are re-charged as input each call. Long threads get expensive; trim or summarize.
  • Match every call_id exactly. With parallel tool calls, a mismatched id is a maddening bug where the model "ignores" a result it actually never received correctly.
  • For reasoning models, replay everything. If you hold history yourself, keep the reasoning items too — dropping them is like erasing someone's notes mid-thought.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — chaining with previous_response_id saves code, not tokens — every prior turn is re-billed as input each call. Long BankAssist cases get expensive; trim, summarise, or drop stale items you control.
  • Latency — when the model needs several tools, emit the function_call_output cards for parallel calls together in one follow-up input rather than one round-trip per tool — fewer hops, lower latency.
  • Scale — for cases that outlive the ~30-day response TTL (a dispute that runs for weeks), attach turns to a durable Conversation object whose items aren't subject to that TTL.
  • Failure modes — a mismatched call_id makes the model "ignore" a result it never correctly received; dropping the opaque reasoning items on a reasoning model erases its train of thought; an expired previous_response_id 404s.
  • Monitoring — log the item type stream and every call_id pairing per turn, so a failed tool loop is debuggable and an auditor can see exactly which tool answered which request.
  • Security / compliance — default store: true keeps responses server-side; a zero-data-retention bank sets store: false and replays reasoning.encrypted_content so reasoning survives the tool loop with nothing stored in the clear.

When to use it / when NOT: pick previous_response_id for simple chained turns, manual replay when you must trim or redact (and to carry reasoning under ZDR), and a Conversation for durable, long-running cases. Do NOT rely on chaining to carry your instructions — resend them — and do NOT blindly json.loads a message without first checking its content parts.

⚠ Watch out

APIs move fast — verify in the docs. Retention windows, the exact include fields, and which models emit reasoning items all shift between releases. Treat the field names here as the shape to look for, and confirm the current spelling on the platform before you ship.

🧠 Remember it

A reply is a stack of cards; call_id is the string tying question to answer. And memory comes in three sizes: a receipt (previous_response_id), your own notebook (manual replay), or a filing cabinet (Conversations).

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

The hosted-tools catalog: a toolbox OpenAI runs for you

Five tools you switch on instead of building: search the web, search your files, run code, make images, and reach out to remote MCP servers.

A self-built function tool means your code runs the work. A hosted (built-in) tool flips that: you just name it in your request and OpenAI runs it on its own servers, folding the result back into the same response. It's the difference between owning a workshop and renting one by the hour. For a bank, each of these is a judgement call about convenience versus the data boundary — but knowing the catalog means you reach for the right one instead of rebuilding it.

💡 Key idea

Hosted tools turn multi-step plumbing (search, retrieve, execute, cite) into a single responses.create call. You trade some control and visibility for a lot less code.

The five you'll actually use

🔎 Web search

The model searches the live web and answers with clickable url_citation annotations. You can fence it in with filters.allowed_domains or blocked_domains (a capped list each), hint a user_location, and trade depth for cost with search_context_size (low / medium / high).

📁 File search

Hosted RAG: you upload documents into a vector store, then point the tool at it with vector_store_ids. OpenAI chunks, embeds, and retrieves for you; answers come with file_citation annotations. Tune with max_num_results and metadata filters.

🐍 Code interpreter

A sandboxed Python environment the model can write and run code in — maths, CSV crunching, chart-making — then read its own output back. Great for "calculate" tasks where a language model alone is shaky.

🖼️ Image generation

The model can generate images inline via the image_generation tool (the same capability the Images API exposes), returning the picture as base64. Useful for mock statements, marketing visuals, or diagrams.

And the fifth: remote MCP connectors. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for exposing tools over a network. Point the Responses API at a remote MCP server and the model can use its tools without you writing any glue — handy for connecting BankAssist to an internal service or a vetted vendor. Because it reaches outside, it supports an approval step (require_approval) so a human or a rule can gate sensitive calls.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's help centre has 2,000 public FAQ and policy pages. Rather than stand up its own vector database for the public content, the team uploads those pages to a hosted vector store and switches on file search. Now "What's the daily ATM withdrawal limit?" is answered straight from the bank's own documents, with a citation the customer can click — and the team wrote almost no retrieval code.

# Two hosted tools in ONE request: search the bank's uploaded docs, and the public web.
resp = client.responses.create(            # one call does retrieval + search + answer
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                  # verify the current model name in the docs
    input="What's our ATM withdrawal limit, and are rates in the news today?",
    tools=[
        {                                  # hosted RAG over our own uploaded documents
            "type": "file_search",         # the file-search hosted tool
            "vector_store_ids": ["vs_bankassist_faq"],  # the vector store we filled earlier
            "max_num_results": 4,          # cap how many chunks it pulls in
        },
        {                                  # hosted live web search, fenced to trusted domains
            "type": "web_search",          # the web-search hosted tool
            "filters": {"allowed_domains": ["ft.com", "bankofengland.co.uk"]},  # only cite sources we trust
            "search_context_size": "low",  # keep it cheap and fast for a quick fact
        },
    ],
)
print(resp.output_text)                    # the answer, stitched from both tools
# Citations live as annotations on the message item: url_citation (web) and file_citation (files).
▶ Output
Your ATM withdrawal limit is $500 per day [1]. On rates, the Bank of England held the base rate at its last meeting [2].

In production — the catalog meets the bank's rules

  • Classify before you connect. File search over public brochures is fine; confidential memos usually stay behind the firewall in your own retrieval pipeline fed through a self-built tool.
  • Fence web search. Use allowed_domains so answers cite sources your compliance team trusts, and treat every returned page as untrusted (prompt-injection risk).
  • Gate MCP. A remote connector reaches outside your walls — require approval on anything that can move money or read PII, and pin to vetted servers only.
  • Budget the hidden latency and cost. A web round-trip or a code-interpreter spin-up takes real time, and each hosted tool has its own billing. Measure it.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — each hosted tool bills on its own meter on top of tokens: web search by call (and by search_context_size), file search by vector-store storage plus per-query fees, code interpreter by container time, image generation per image. A chatty tool loop can quietly dominate a bill.
  • Latency — a web round-trip or a code-interpreter spin-up adds real seconds; measure each tool's contribution to p95 and cap max_num_results / search_context_size for quick facts.
  • Scale — hosted vector stores have size and file-count limits; plan how BankAssist's growing FAQ corpus is chunked and refreshed, and when a self-run pipeline becomes the better fit.
  • Failure modes — prompt injection hidden in a fetched web page or uploaded file, a remote MCP server that is slow or down, and stale citations. Treat all tool output as untrusted and degrade gracefully when a tool fails.
  • Monitoring — track per-tool call counts, error rates and latency, and the share of answers that actually carry url_citation / file_citation annotations — missing citations are a quality red flag.
  • Security / compliance — fence web search with allowed_domains to sources compliance trusts; gate remote MCP with require_approval on anything that moves money or reads PII, and pin to vetted servers only; classify documents before uploading to a hosted vector store.

When to use it / when NOT: switch on hosted tools to ship fast over public, low-sensitivity data — file search over public brochures, fenced web search for public rates, code interpreter for maths. Do NOT point hosted file search at confidential memos or wire an un-approved MCP connector into a money-moving flow; keep that behind the firewall in a self-built pipeline.

⚠ Watch out

APIs move fast — verify in the docs. The exact tool names, config fields, per-tool pricing, and which models support which hosted tool all change between releases. Confirm the current catalog on the platform before wiring a tool into a customer flow.

🧠 Remember it

Rent, don't build: search the web, search your files, run code, make images, reach an MCP server — five tools you switch on, not write. Public data can use them freely; customer data needs a second thought.

🏭 production 🔒 security 🏦 banking

The Evals API and the grader family: scoring answers at scale

An eval is an exam for your AI. The grader is the marking scheme — and OpenAI gives you four kinds, from a simple string match to an LLM that judges quality.

Before you trust BankAssist with real customers, you need a way to ask, "Is it actually right?" — not by eyeballing ten replies, but by running hundreds of test cases and scoring them automatically. That's what an eval is: a dataset of inputs with expected outcomes, plus one or more graders (marking schemes) that each output is run through. The Evals API lets you define this once and run it against any model, so when a new model appears you re-run the same exam and compare scores instead of guessing.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist must classify every incoming dispute into the right regulatory category. The team builds a dataset of 500 past disputes with the known-correct label on each. A grader checks the model's label against the known one. Now any prompt tweak or model upgrade is a number: "94% correct, up from 91%." No more "it feels better." That number is what the risk committee signs off on.

In plain terms — the two pieces

An eval has a dataset (the questions and their expected answers, often a JSONL file) and testing criteria (one or more graders). You template values from each row with {{ item.* }} for the dataset fields and {{ sample.output_text }} for what the model produced. The graders are the interesting part — here is the family:

GraderWhat it doesReach for it when…
string_checkExact/contains match: eq, ne, like, ilike. Returns 0 or 1.The answer is a label or exact token — "is it exactly unauthorized_transaction?"
text_similarityFuzzy closeness to a reference: fuzzy, bleu, gleu, meteor, cosine, rouge. Passes at a pass_threshold.The answer is free text that should be close to a model answer, not identical.
score model (LLM-as-judge)Another model reads the output and scores it in a range, with reasoning steps and a pass_threshold."Good" is a judgement call — tone, helpfulness, compliance — that only a reader can assess.
pythonYour own sandboxed grade(sample, item) function returns a score.Correctness needs real logic — parse JSON, check a number is within range, verify a calculation.
# Define an eval: a dataset schema plus two testing criteria (graders).
eval_obj = client.evals.create(            # create the reusable eval definition
    name="dispute-classification",         # a human-friendly name
    data_source_config={                   # describes the shape of each dataset row
        "type": "custom",
        "item_schema": {                   # each row has an input and a known-correct label
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {"dispute": {"type": "string"}, "label": {"type": "string"}},
        },
        "include_sample_schema": True,      # lets criteria reference the model's own output
    },
    testing_criteria=[
        {                                  # grader 1: is the label EXACTLY right?
            "type": "string_check",        # deterministic 0/1 grader
            "name": "exact_label",
            "input": "{{ sample.output_text }}",  # what the model produced
            "operation": "eq",             # must equal...
            "reference": "{{ item.label }}",     # ...the known-correct label from the row
        },
        {                                  # grader 2: an LLM judges whether the explanation is sound
            "type": "score_model",         # LLM-as-judge grader
            "name": "reasoning_quality",
            "model": "gpt-4.1-mini",       # the judge model (confirm current name in docs)
            "pass_threshold": 0.7,         # score at/above this counts as a pass
        },
    ],
)
print(eval_obj.id)                          # now run it against a model + dataset and read result_counts
▶ Output
eval_8f2a...
⚙️ Under the hood — graders are shared with fine-tuning

The same grader family powers reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT): the grader that scores an eval is the grader that rewards the model during RFT training. So the effort you spend writing a solid python or score-model grader pays off twice — once for measuring and once for teaching. A practical tip: combine graders. Use string_check for the hard-correctness part (right label) and a score_model judge for the soft part (was the explanation clear and compliant), then weight them.

In production — evals as a gate, not a vanity metric

  • Make it a release gate. No prompt or model change ships to BankAssist until the eval score clears a bar. "Feels better" is not a control a regulator accepts.
  • Hold out a test set. Keep some cases the model and the prompt-tuner never see, so a good score means generalization, not memorization.
  • Watch the LLM judge. A score-model grader is itself a model — it can be inconsistent or biased. Spot-check its marks against human review periodically.
  • Version everything. Dataset version, grader version, model version. When a score moves, you must know which one changed.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — string_check and python graders are essentially free compute; a score_model (LLM-as-judge) grader runs a whole model per row, so a 500-case run is 500 extra model calls. Reserve the judge for the parts only a reader can assess.
