  • Latency — evals are offline and batchable, so latency rarely matters — but a big judge-based run takes time; schedule it, don't block a deploy on a synchronous eval.
  • Scale — keep a held-out test set the prompt-tuner never sees, and version the dataset, the graders and the model together so a moving score is traceable to one change.
  • Failure modes — the LLM judge is itself a model — it drifts and can be biased or gameable; a prompt can overfit to the eval and still fail in the wild. Combine a hard grader (right label) with a soft one (clear, compliant explanation) and weight them.
  • Monitoring — track the score over time as a release metric and spot-check the judge's marks against human review periodically.
  • Security / compliance — the eval is the control the risk committee signs off on — "94%, up from 91%" is defensible where "feels better" is not. Note: OpenAI's hosted Evals went read-only around 31 October 2026 and the tooling is being wound down, so build your own harness; the concepts here (datasets, testing criteria, the four grader kinds) are durable.

When to use it / when NOT: make an eval the release gate for every prompt or model change to BankAssist, and reuse the same graders to reward an RFT run. Do NOT ship on vibes, and do NOT trust a single LLM-judge score without a hard grader and periodic human calibration beside it.

⚠ Watch out

APIs move fast — verify in the docs. OpenAI has signalled that its hosted Evals and grader tooling is being wound down in favour of newer dataset workflows. The concepts here — datasets, testing criteria, and the four grader kinds — are durable and worth knowing for interviews and for building your own harness, but confirm the current hosted offering before you depend on it.

🧠 Remember it

Four marking schemes: match it (string_check), is it close (text_similarity), judge it (score model), run code on it (python). An eval turns "feels better" into a number you can defend.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Reasoning controls: paying for thinking, on purpose

Reasoning models think before they answer. You control how hard they think — and that thinking is billed, even though you can't read it.

Some models "think" privately before replying — they work through the problem step by step, then hand you the conclusion. That hidden thinking is written as reasoning tokens, and here's the part that surprises people: those tokens are billed like output tokens and they take up room in the context window, even though the API never shows them to you. So reasoning isn't free, and "more thinking" isn't always better. The job is to spend thinking where it pays and save it where it doesn't.

💡 Key idea

Reasoning effort is a dial, not a switch. Turn it up for a knotty problem, down for a lookup. You're trading money and latency for depth of thought.

In plain terms — the effort dial

The main control is reasoning.effort. Lower effort means fewer reasoning tokens — faster and cheaper, but shallower. Higher effort means the model thinks longer — slower and pricier, but better on hard problems. The exact level names vary by model family (you'll see values like minimal, low, medium, high, and sometimes a "none" that switches reasoning off), so check the model reference rather than hard-coding a level you assume exists.

# A reasoning model: control how hard it thinks, and read what the thinking cost.
resp = client.responses.create(            # Responses API carries reasoning cleanly
    model="o4-mini",                       # a reasoning model — confirm the current name in the docs
    input="A customer overpaid their loan by $312.40 across 3 payments. "
          "Explain how to apply the refund under our policy.",  # a genuinely multi-step task
    reasoning={"effort": "high"},          # think hard — this is worth the extra tokens
    max_output_tokens=2000,                # caps reasoning + visible output TOGETHER (see note)
)
print(resp.output_text)                    # the visible answer

usage = resp.usage                         # the receipt for the call
print(usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens)  # hidden thinking you still paid for
▶ Output
Apply the $312.40 as a credit to the principal, effective the date of the final overpayment... 734
⚠ Watch out

max_output_tokens caps reasoning and the visible answer together. Set it too low on a high-effort call and the model spends the whole budget thinking, leaving nothing for the reply — you get back status: "incomplete" and an empty or truncated answer. Give reasoning room to breathe.

Going deeper — summaries and encrypted thinking

You can't read the raw reasoning, but you can ask for a summary of it with reasoning.summary (values like auto or concise) — a readable gloss of how the model got there, useful for debugging or for showing a supervisor why BankAssist reached a decision. Separately, when you run stateless or under zero-data-retention, the model's reasoning normally can't persist across a tool loop. The fix is encrypted reasoning items: request reasoning.encrypted_content in include, get the thinking back as an encrypted blob, and replay it on the next turn. The model picks up its own train of thought without anything being stored in the clear.

⚙️ Under the hood — effort is a cost lever

Most BankAssist traffic — "what's my balance," "where's the nearest branch" — needs little or no reasoning; running those at high effort burns money for no gain. Reserve high effort for the genuinely hard cases: a tangled dispute, a multi-step eligibility check, a reconciliation. A good production pattern is to route by difficulty: a cheap classifier (or a simple rule) decides whether a query is "easy" or "hard," and only the hard ones go to a reasoning model at higher effort. That one decision can cut a reasoning bill dramatically.

In production — the honest checklist

  • Watch reasoning_tokens in usage. It's the line item that quietly dominates a reasoning bill. Track it per request type.
  • Give max_output_tokens headroom on high-effort calls, or you'll pay for thinking and get a truncated answer.
  • Carry reasoning items across tool loops (stored, or encrypted-and-replayed) so the model doesn't lose its place mid-task.
  • Summaries for the audit trail. A reasoning summary can be the "why" you show a reviewer — but it's a gloss, not a verbatim log.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — reasoning tokens are billed as output and can be the single largest line on the bill — high effort can use many times the tokens of minimal for the same question. Route by difficulty so only genuinely hard cases pay for deep thinking.
  • Latency — effort trades directly against speed: higher effort means a longer think before the first visible token. For interactive BankAssist turns, prefer lower effort and stream; save high effort for background or clearly complex tasks.
  • Scale — put a cheap classifier or a simple rule in front: "balance / branch lookup" goes to a plain model, "tangled dispute / eligibility check" goes to a reasoning model at higher effort. That one routing decision can slash the reasoning bill.
  • Failure modes — set max_output_tokens too low on a high-effort call and the model spends the whole budget thinking, returning status: "incomplete" with an empty or truncated answer. Give the visible reply headroom.
  • Monitoring — track reasoning_tokens from usage.output_tokens_details per request type; it is the metric that quietly dominates a reasoning spend.
  • Security / compliance — you cannot read the raw thinking, but a reasoning.summary gives an auditable "why" for a supervisor; under ZDR, replay reasoning.encrypted_content so reasoning survives a tool loop without being stored in the clear.

When to use it / when NOT: turn effort up for multi-step reasoning — disputes, reconciliations, eligibility logic — where correctness pays for the extra tokens. Turn it down (or use a non-reasoning model) for lookups, chit-chat and simple extraction, where high effort burns money for no gain.

⚠ Watch out

APIs move fast — verify in the docs. Which effort levels exist, which models are reasoning models, and the exact include and reasoning.* fields all shift between releases. Don't hard-code an effort level you haven't confirmed the current model accepts.

🧠 Remember it

Thinking is invisible but not free — reasoning tokens are billed and fill the context. Turn the effort dial up for hard problems, down for lookups, and always leave room for the actual answer.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 💰 cost

Structured Outputs: guaranteeing the JSON actually fits your schema

Asking nicely for JSON gets you usually-valid JSON. Strict Structured Outputs gets you JSON that provably matches your schema — every time.

When BankAssist extracts data — "pull the amount, the account, and the category from this dispute" — you need the result as clean JSON your code can parse without flinching. There are two ways to get JSON from the model, and they are not the same. JSON mode promises the output is valid JSON — but says nothing about its shape; fields can be missing, renamed, or the wrong type. Structured Outputs with strict: true promises the output matches your exact JSON Schema — the right fields, the right types, every time. For anything that feeds downstream code, strict is the one you want.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist reads 10,000 dispute emails overnight and writes each as a row: amount, account type, category. With JSON mode, a few hundred come back with amount as a string, or a missing category, and the overnight job crashes at 3 a.m. With strict Structured Outputs, every single row has exactly the three fields in the right types — the job runs clean, because the model was constrained to the schema, not merely asked to follow it.

In plain terms — the strict-mode rules

To use strict: true, your schema must play by a few rules (the model enforces them, so your schema must satisfy them or the request is rejected):

  • additionalProperties: false on every object — no surprise extra fields.
  • Every property listed in required — all of them, no exceptions.
  • "Optional" is done with a null type — since everything must be required, an optional field becomes a union like ["string", "null"].
  • Only a subset of JSON Schema is supported — stick to the documented keywords.
# Strict Structured Outputs on the Responses API: the model MUST return this shape.
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "amount":  {"type": "number"},                       # a real number, not "$312.40" as text
        "account": {"type": "string", "enum": ["current", "savings", "joint"]},  # constrained choices
        "category": {"type": ["string", "null"]},            # "optional" = allow null, since all keys are required
    },
    "required": ["amount", "account", "category"],            # strict mode: EVERY property must be listed
    "additionalProperties": False,                            # strict mode: no extra fields allowed
}

resp = client.responses.create(            # Responses API uses text.format for the schema
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                  # confirm the current model name in the docs
    input="Dispute: I was charged $312.40 on my current account, no idea what for.",
    text={"format": {                      # text.format is where Structured Outputs lives on Responses
        "type": "json_schema",
        "name": "dispute",
        "schema": schema,
        "strict": True,                    # THE switch: guarantee the output matches the schema
    }},
)

msg = resp.output[0]                        # the message item
if msg.content[0].type == "refusal":       # ALWAYS check for a refusal before parsing
    print("Refused:", msg.content[0].refusal)   # safety refusals come back as a refusal part, not your JSON
else:
    data = json.loads(resp.output_text)    # safe to parse — it provably fits the schema
    print(data["amount"], data["account"]) # use the fields with confidence
▶ Output
312.4 current
⚠ Watch out

Strict mode guarantees the shape, not that the model will answer at all. A model can still refuse on safety grounds — and a refusal comes back as a refusal content part, not as your JSON. If you blindly json.loads the output without checking for a refusal first, your parser throws on perfectly correct behaviour. Check for the refusal part every time.

⚙️ Under the hood — constrained decoding and the first-call tax

Strict mode works by constrained decoding: the platform compiles your schema into a grammar and only lets the model emit tokens that keep the output valid. That's why the guarantee is real rather than best-effort. One practical cost: the first request with a new schema pays a small latency tax while that grammar is compiled; later requests with the same schema reuse it and are fast. So keep your schemas stable and reused, not regenerated per call. The same strict: true idea also applies to function/tool schemas — the model's tool arguments can be constrained to fit exactly.

In production — when to use which

  • Feeding code or a database? Strict Structured Outputs. The guarantee is the whole point.
  • Just want "some JSON" for a human to glance at? JSON mode is lighter, but you'll still parse defensively.
  • Always handle the refusal branch in a bank — a safety refusal is correct behaviour, not an error to crash on.
  • Reuse schemas to dodge the first-call compile tax at scale, and keep them within the supported JSON-Schema subset.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — strict Structured Outputs adds no meaningful token cost; the only overhead is a one-time grammar compile. The savings are downstream — far fewer failed overnight jobs and defensive re-parses.
  • Latency — the first request with a new schema pays a small latency tax while its grammar is compiled; later calls reuse it and are fast. Keep schemas stable and reused, never regenerated per call.
  • Scale — at BankAssist's 10,000-emails-a-night scale, a stable, reused schema means the grammar is warm and every row comes back in the exact shape the loader expects.
  • Failure modes — a safety refusal arrives as a refusal content part, not your JSON — parse blindly and you crash on correct behaviour. An unsupported JSON-Schema keyword gets the whole request rejected up front.
  • Monitoring — parse errors on strict output should sit at essentially zero — alert if they rise (it usually means a schema drifted). Track the refusal rate as its own signal.
  • Security / compliance — for anything that feeds a ledger, a database or a downstream decision, strict output is the integrity guarantee an auditor wants; the same strict: true idea constrains tool-call arguments too.

When to use it / when NOT: use strict Structured Outputs whenever the output feeds code, a schema or a database — the guarantee is the whole point. Plain JSON mode is fine for throwaway JSON a human will glance at, but still parse it defensively; and always handle the refusal branch in a bank.

✅ Tip

If you are not on the OpenAI platform, two open-source libraries give you the same "always-valid JSON" guarantee. Instructor wraps your client and validates the reply into a Pydantic model (a typed Python data class), automatically retrying the call when a parse fails. Outlines constrains decoding to a schema, a regex, or a grammar, so the model simply cannot emit an invalid token in the first place. Same goal as strict Structured Outputs — validate-and-retry versus constrain-as-you-go — just different plumbing.

🧠 Remember it

JSON mode = valid JSON. Structured Outputs = valid and the right shape. The strict rules: no extra fields, everything required, optional means "or null" — and check for a refusal before you parse.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Function calling, the advanced controls: strict schemas, tool_choice, and grammar tools

Basic function calling just works. The advanced controls decide which tool runs, whether its arguments are guaranteed valid, and how to keep your prompt cache from shattering.

Once BankAssist has a handful of tools — check balance, block card, open dispute, look up a branch — new questions appear. How do I force the model to use a tool (or forbid it)? How do I guarantee the arguments are valid so my code never crashes on a malformed call? How do I restrict which tools are available this turn without paying to rebuild my prompt cache? These are the production controls, and they're the difference between a demo and a system that holds up under real traffic.

1. Strict tool schemas — valid arguments, guaranteed

Just like Structured Outputs, you can set strict: true on a function tool so the model's arguments provably match your schema (same rules: additionalProperties: false, every property required, optional via a null union). This kills a whole class of bugs where the model calls block_card with a missing account field and your handler throws.

# A strict function tool: the arguments are GUARANTEED to fit the schema.
block_card = {
    "type": "function",
    "name": "block_card",
    "description": "Block a debit or credit card on one of the user's accounts.",  # write it so an intern could call it right
    "parameters": {
        "type": "object",
        "properties": {"account": {"type": "string", "enum": ["current", "savings", "joint"]}},
        "required": ["account"],           # strict: list every property
        "additionalProperties": False,     # strict: no stray fields
    },
    "strict": True,                        # guarantee the arguments match — no malformed calls
}

2. tool_choice and allowed_tools — steering without breaking the cache

tool_choice decides whether and which tool the model may call this turn:

  • "auto" — the model decides (the default).
  • "required" — it must call some tool (good when you know an action is needed).
  • a named choice — force this specific tool.
  • "none" — forbid tools; answer in words only.

Now the subtle, money-saving one. Imagine you have 30 tools but want to offer only 3 on a given turn. The naive move — send a shorter tools list — changes the prompt prefix and throws away your prompt cache, because tool definitions sit near the front of the prompt. Instead, keep the full tools list stable and use allowed_tools to restrict the callable subset. You narrow what the model may pick without editing the cached prefix — so the cache keeps paying off.

# Keep the full tools list stable; restrict THIS turn with allowed_tools to preserve the cache.
resp = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                  # confirm the current model name in the docs
    input="Please block my card.",
    tools=all_30_tools,                    # the SAME big list every turn — stable prefix = cache hits
    tool_choice={                          # restrict the choosable subset without editing the list
        "type": "allowed_tools",
        "mode": "auto",                    # model may pick from the allowed set (or "required" to force one)
        "tools": [{"type": "function", "name": "block_card"},
                  {"type": "function", "name": "get_balance"}],  # only these two are callable this turn
    },
)
⚙️ Under the hood — custom and grammar-constrained tools

Most tools take JSON arguments, but some don't fit JSON neatly — a tool that wants a snippet of SQL, a shell command, or a specific code dialect. Custom (freeform) tools let the model return a plain-text input instead of a JSON object. To keep that free text valid, you can attach a context-free grammar (using a lark or regex definition) so the model can only produce strings the grammar allows — e.g. only well-formed, read-only SQL. It's constrained decoding again, but shaping free text instead of JSON. Powerful for a bank that wants the model to emit, say, a safe query language without risking a malformed or dangerous command.

In production — the controls that matter at scale

  • Turn on strict for tools that touch money. A guaranteed-valid block_card argument is one less 3 a.m. incident.
  • Prefer allowed_tools over editing the list when you have many tools — it preserves the prompt cache and keeps per-turn cost down.
  • Tool definitions cost tokens. Every tool you offer is text in the prompt; a huge toolset is expensive on every call. Keep the catalog lean, or load tools by context.
  • Write descriptions for "the intern." The model picks tools from their descriptions — vague ones cause wrong calls. Say exactly when to use each, and when not to.
  • Carry reasoning items back with tool outputs on reasoning models, or the model forgets why it called the tool.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — every tool definition is text in the prompt, billed on every call. A 30-tool catalog is a fixed tax per request; keep the list lean or load tools by context — and prefer allowed_tools over trimming the list so you don't shatter the prompt cache.
  • Latency — strict tools add only a tiny first-call grammar-compile tax; the bigger latency lever is cache hits, which editing the tools list destroys.
  • Scale — as BankAssist grows past a handful of tools, keep the full tools list stable every turn (stable prefix = cache hits) and narrow the choosable set per turn with allowed_tools.
  • Failure modes — without strict, the model can call block_card with a missing account and your handler throws; editing the tools list mid-session silently cache-busts and spikes cost. A vague tool description causes wrong tool picks.
  • Monitoring — track per-tool call counts and argument-validation error rates, plus the cache hit-rate — a sudden drop usually means someone reordered or regenerated the tool defs.
  • Security / compliance — turn on strict for every money-touching tool, enforce authorization inside the handler (the model's request is never proof of permission), and grammar-constrain freeform tools so, e.g., only read-only SQL can be emitted.

When to use it / when NOT: use strict schemas for any consequential tool, tool_choice to force or forbid tools when you know an action is (or isn't) needed, and allowed_tools to narrow a large catalog without reprinting it. Do NOT shorten the tools list to restrict choices, and do NOT ship vague descriptions — the model picks tools from them.

⚠ Watch out

APIs move fast — verify in the docs. The exact spelling of tool_choice / allowed_tools, how custom and grammar tools are declared, and which models support them change between releases. Confirm the current form before you build a large toolset around it.

🧠 Remember it

strict = valid arguments, tool_choice = whether/which, allowed_tools = narrow the menu without reprinting it. Keep the tools list stable and the cache keeps paying.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 💰 cost

Prompt caching: paying full price once, then a discount for the repeats

If the start of your prompt is the same every call, the platform can remember its work on that part — and charge you a fraction to reuse it.

BankAssist's prompt has a big, unchanging head: a long system instruction, the bank's policies, the tool definitions. Only the customer's actual question changes at the end. Re-processing that identical head on every single call is wasteful — and you'd be paying for it every time. Prompt caching fixes this: the platform saves the work it did on a repeated prefix and, on the next call that starts the same way, reuses it at a steep discount. You do almost nothing to turn it on; you do a fair bit to keep it working.

💡 Key idea

Caching works on a prefix, not on scattered text. The longest run of tokens from the very start that matches a previous call is what gets reused. Change anything near the front and the match breaks.

In plain terms — how the reuse happens

Under the hood, a model turns your prompt into internal state (the attention "KV" cache — the key/value numbers it builds while reading each token) as it reads it. Caching stores that state for a prefix and, on a matching call, loads it instead of recomputing. Two facts shape everything you do with it:

  • There's a minimum. Caching kicks in only once the prefix is long enough — commonly around 1,024 tokens on current models. Short prompts simply report zero cached tokens.
  • It's longest-matching-prefix. The platform finds the longest run from the start that matches. So the order of your prompt is the whole game: static content first, dynamic content last.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's prompt is a 3,000-token head (system rules + policy excerpts + 20 tool definitions) followed by the customer's 40-token question. Put that way — static head, dynamic tail — nearly every call reuses the 3,000-token prefix for a fraction of the price, and only the little tail is fresh work. Now flip it: paste the customer's question before the policies. Every call has a different start, nothing matches, and the cache never fires. Same tokens, wildly different bill.

# Caching is automatic — your job is to ORDER the prompt so the prefix repeats.
resp = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                  # confirm the current model name in the docs
    instructions=BANK_SYSTEM_RULES,        # STATIC and first — the big reusable head
    input=[
        {"role": "developer", "content": BANK_POLICY_EXCERPTS},  # STATIC — keep it stable, keep it early
        {"role": "user", "content": customer_question},          # DYNAMIC — the only part that changes, put it LAST
    ],
    tools=all_tools,                       # STATIC — stable tool defs near the front help the prefix match
    prompt_cache_key="bankassist-support", # routes similar calls together to improve hit-rate
)

cached = resp.usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens  # Responses API reports cached input tokens here (Chat Completions uses usage.prompt_tokens_details)
print(f"reused {cached} tokens from cache")  # monitor this — it's your hit-rate signal
▶ Output
reused 3008 tokens from cache
⚙️ Under the hood — the economics and the knobs

A cache read is billed at a steep discount versus fresh input (on the order of one-tenth the input price — treat the exact figure as something to confirm, since it moves). Some setups let you extend how long a prefix stays warm, trading a small write surcharge for a longer time-to-live. Two knobs worth knowing: prompt_cache_key routes similar requests to the same cache for better hit-rates and cleaner accounting (keep each key+prefix under roughly 15 requests/minute so you don't thrash it), and the cached_tokens field in usage is how you monitor whether caching is actually working. If that number is near zero on prompts you expected to reuse, something near the front is changing.

In production — keeping the hit-rate high

  • Static first, dynamic last — the single most important habit. Rules, policies, tool defs up front; the user's turn at the end.
  • Keep tool definitions stable. Reordering or regenerating them changes the prefix and silently kills the cache.
  • Beware compaction and summarization. When your memory layer rewrites or truncates earlier turns, the prefix changes and reuse resets — a sneaky cause of a cost spike.
  • Monitor cached_tokens as a metric. Alert if the hit-rate drops; it usually means someone moved dynamic content toward the front.
  • Don't put per-user secrets in the shared prefix expecting them to cache — and never let caching logic leak one customer's data into another's prompt.
⚙️ In production
  • Cost — a cache read is billed at a steep discount versus fresh input (commonly in the range of one-half to one-tenth of input price, depending on the model family). For BankAssist's 3,000-token static head reused on nearly every call, that is most of the input bill turned into a fraction.
  • Latency — a cache hit doesn't just cut cost — it cuts time-to-first-token, because the platform loads saved state instead of re-reading the prefix. Static-first ordering makes BankAssist feel snappier, not just cheaper.
  • Scale — caching needs a long-enough prefix (commonly ~1,024 tokens before it engages). Keep each prompt_cache_key + prefix under roughly 15 requests/minute so you don't thrash the cache.
  • Failure modes — any change near the front of the prompt — reordered tool defs, a regenerated system block, memory compaction that rewrites earlier turns — breaks the match and silently resets reuse, showing up as a sudden cost spike.
  • Monitoring — treat cached_tokens (on the Responses API: usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens) as a first-class metric and alert if the hit-rate drops on prompts you expect to reuse.
  • Security / compliance — never place per-user secrets or one customer's data in a shared prefix expecting it to cache — and make sure cache routing can never leak one customer's context into another's prompt.

When to use it / when NOT: lean on prompt caching whenever a large, stable head (system rules, policies, tool defs) repeats across calls — order it static-first, dynamic-last, and keep tool defs stable. It does nothing for short prompts below the threshold or for prompts whose front changes every call, so don't design around it there.

⚠ Watch out

APIs move fast — verify in the docs. The exact minimum-token threshold, the read discount and any write surcharge, the TTL options, and the usage field names all vary by model and change over time. Use the shapes here to reason about cost, but confirm the current numbers on the platform before you forecast a bill.

🧠 Remember it

Same start = cheap repeat. Put the unchanging stuff first, the question last, keep tool defs stable, and watch cached_tokens to know it's working.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 💰 cost

Staying compliant on the platform — moderation, safety identifiers & abuse monitoring

Shipping on a model provider is a shared-responsibility deal: they watch the platform, you watch your traffic.

When you build on the OpenAI platform, you are not only buying model calls — you are agreeing to a usage policy and inheriting some safety machinery you are expected to use. Skip it and two things happen: harmful content slips through to your customers, and the provider's automated abuse systems can throttle or suspend your whole account because of a few bad actors. Both are avoidable with a couple of cheap habits on every request.

🏦 Picture this

A handful of users start pasting abusive and policy-breaking prompts into BankAssist's chat. Without safeguards, the provider sees the stream of violations coming from one API key and flags the account — now every customer is affected. With a moderation gate and per-user safety identifiers in place, the bad content is blocked up front and the provider can see the abuse is isolated to a few hashed user IDs, not the business.

1. The moderation gate

OpenAI's Moderation API (the omni-moderation model) is free and classifies text/images across categories like harassment, hate, self-harm, sexual, and violence. The pattern: screen the user's input before you send it to the model, and optionally screen the model's output before you show it. It is a filter you run; it does not replace your own policy, but it catches the obvious cases cheaply.

from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI()                                   # reads your API key from the environment

def is_safe(text: str) -> bool:
    r = client.moderations.create(                  # the free moderation endpoint
        model="omni-moderation-latest",             # current multimodal moderation model
        input=text,                                 # the user message (or model output) to screen
    )
    return not r.results[0].flagged                 # flagged=True means it tripped a category

user_msg = "How do I dispute a fraudulent charge?"
if not is_safe(user_msg):                            # pre-flight gate BEFORE the expensive model call
    reply = "I can't help with that request."       # refuse/redirect without hitting the model
else:
    reply = "..."                                    # proceed to your normal BankAssist call
▶ Output

A benign banking question passes the gate; a policy-breaking one is blocked before it ever reaches the model — saving tokens and keeping your logs clean.

2. Safety identifiers — protect the account, not just the request

Send a stable, unique per-end-user value in the safety_identifier parameter on each call (this is the current replacement for the older user field). It lets the provider detect and act on abuse at the level of one user — rate-limiting or flagging a single bad identifier — instead of penalising your entire account. Crucially, it must not contain real personal data: hash your internal customer ID so the value is stable but anonymous.

import hashlib

def safety_id(customer_id: str) -> str:
    salt = "bankassist-v1"                           # a fixed app secret so IDs can't be reversed by guessing
    return hashlib.sha256((salt + customer_id).encode()).hexdigest()  # stable, anonymous per-user token

resp = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",                            # your normal model
    input=user_msg,                                  # the (already moderation-passed) user message
    safety_identifier=safety_id("CUST-88213"),       # hashed ID — NEVER the raw email or customer number
)
▶ Output

Every request now carries a consistent, non-identifying fingerprint for that customer. Abuse from one fingerprint stays contained to that fingerprint.

⚠ Watch out

Never put raw PII in safety_identifier — no emails, no account numbers, no names. Hash a stable internal ID with an app-side salt. Sending venkatesh@example.com here would leak a customer identity to a parameter that exists purely for abuse-tracking.

3. Automated abuse monitoring & shared responsibility

The provider runs its own automated monitoring against its usage policies. Sending safety identifiers is how you cooperate with it: it turns "this account is misbehaving" into "this one hashed user is misbehaving," which protects your other customers. Prompt injection and jailbreak attempts are the other half of the deal — the platform helps, but screening inputs, constraining tool permissions, and checking outputs remain your job.

⚙️ In production
  • Make it a wrapper — one function that moderates input, attaches safety_identifier, calls the model, and moderates output. No call bypasses it.
  • Log moderation outcomes — store category scores and the hashed ID (not the raw content where you can avoid it) for audit and for spotting abuse trends.
  • Fail safe — if the moderation call errors, default to blocking or to a cautious canned reply, not to passing content through.
  • Review flagged traffic — a rising count on one safety identifier is your early warning before the provider ever acts.

When to use it / when NOT: apply the moderate-in, hashed-safety_identifier, moderate-out wrapper on every production call that serves real end users. Do NOT skip the safety identifier on customer traffic (it is what keeps one bad actor from getting your whole account throttled), and do NOT ever put raw PII in it.

🧠 Remember it

Moderate in, hash your user, moderate out. The hashed ID is a name tag for abuse-tracking — stable enough to spot a repeat offender, anonymous enough to never leak who they are.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🔐 compliance

Platforms & APIs — Cloud: AWS, Azure & Google

Almost no bank builds its AI from bare metal up. It picks a cloud — Amazon, Microsoft, or Google — and builds on the managed AI stack that cloud already runs for it. This chapter is a calm, honest tour of all three, and of the one decision under all of them: let the cloud manage it, or build it yourself.

Why banks build on a cloud's managed AI stack

A managed platform is the cloud running the plumbing — models, scaling, logging, safety — so your team spends its time on the banking logic, not the servers.

Imagine two teams at BankAssist asked to ship a customer-support assistant. Team A rents raw servers, downloads an open model, wires up a vector database, writes its own scaling, its own logging, its own content filters, its own key rotation. Team B opens the AWS console, calls a model that is already running, points a managed service at its policy PDFs, switches on a safety filter, and ships in a week. Both can work. But Team B borrowed a kitchen that was already built; Team A built the kitchen first.

A managed cloud AI platform is that pre-built kitchen. The cloud provider hosts the large language models, keeps them patched and scaled, and wraps them in services for retrieval, agents, safety, identity, and monitoring. You call an API; they run the hard parts.

In plain terms

Three things push banks toward managed platforms, and all three are about trust and paperwork, not just convenience:

  • Compliance and contracts. A bank cannot send customer data to just any service. The big clouds offer signed agreements, audited certifications (think SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS), and — crucially — a promise in writing that your prompts and documents are not used to train the shared model. That paperwork is often the real reason a platform gets chosen.
  • Data residency. Regulators often say customer data must stay inside a country or region. Managed platforms let you pin a model and its data to a specific region (say, Frankfurt for EU customers), so nothing crosses a border it shouldn't.
  • Less infrastructure to own. GPUs are scarce and expensive. Scaling a model to Monday-morning traffic, patching it, keeping it up at 3am — that is a full-time job the cloud already does. You rent the result.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's risk committee asks one question before any AI project: "If an auditor calls, can we show where the data went and prove the model didn't learn from it?" With a managed platform, the answer is a signed enterprise agreement, a region setting, and an audit log. With a hand-rolled stack, the answer is "we'll write that up" — months of work. That single conversation is why most regulated banks start managed.

The honest tradeoffs

Managed is not free of cost or lock-in. You pay a premium over raw compute, you move at the vendor's pace, and your code leans on that vendor's service shapes — moving to another cloud later is real work. This chapter weighs all of it properly — the platform tours and a managed-versus-self-built decision table do the real accounting. For now, hold the big idea: managed trades some control and money for speed, compliance, and a smaller operational burden.

⚙️ In production

What a managed stack actually costs and breaks when real traffic hits it, in bank terms:

  • Cost shape. You pay per token (a few dollars per million input tokens, more for output) plus per-service fees — vector storage, safety checks, agent runtime seconds. The premium over raw GPU is typically modest for small-to-medium volume and only starts to hurt at huge, steady scale. A useful rule of thumb BankAssist uses: below a few million requests a month, the managed premium is cheaper than one extra ML-ops engineer; above that, model the break-even carefully.
  • Latency. A managed call adds network hops you don't control — auth, safety filter, retrieval, generation. Budget 300–900 ms for a plain grounded answer and stream tokens so the customer feels instant speed while the full answer forms.
  • Scale & failure modes. Shared capacity means you can be throttled by other tenants (HTTP 429); plan retry-with-backoff and a fallback region. A regional outage at the vendor becomes your outage unless you've designed a second region or model.
  • Monitoring. Watch tokens-per-request (not just request count), p95 latency, throttle rate, safety-block rate, and cost-per-conversation. These four catch almost every production surprise before finance or compliance does.
  • Security/compliance for a bank. Pin the region, sign the enterprise agreement that excludes your data from training, turn on audit logging from day one, and encrypt with keys you can revoke. The platform's certifications (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS) are inherited — but only for the parts the vendor runs.
⚠ Watch out

"Managed" does not mean "safe by default." The cloud secures the platform; you still own what you put in it — your prompts, your access rules, your data boundaries. This split is called the shared responsibility model, and misreading it (assuming the vendor guards your data for you) is how banks leak customer records on a perfectly secure platform.

When to use managed: you need to ship to a regulated deadline, your team is small, compliance paperwork matters, and you want the newest models the week they land. When NOT to: a regulator demands a full air-gap (data never leaves your own data centre), or you run enormous constant volume with the ML-ops team to own GPUs cheaply — then self-host that workload instead.

🧠 Remember it

Managed = rent the kitchen, cook your own dish. They run the stove; the recipe and the ingredients are still on you.

AWS Bedrock: foundation models, Knowledge Bases, Agents & Guardrails

Amazon Bedrock is one door to many models, plus managed building blocks for RAG, agents, and safety — all behind AWS's compliance and region controls.

Start with the simplest idea. Amazon Bedrock is a single API in front of many foundation models from different makers — Anthropic's Claude, Amazon's own Nova and Titan families, Meta's Llama, Cohere, Mistral, and more. You don't host any of them; AWS does. You pick a model by its ID and call it. Switching from one model to another is often a one-line change, which is the whole appeal: no GPUs, no model downloads, and your data stays inside your AWS account's boundary.

Here is the plainest possible call — ask a model a banking question through Bedrock:

# Call a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock — no servers, no model download.
import boto3                                   # the AWS SDK for Python; your door to every AWS service
import json                                    # Bedrock takes and returns JSON request bodies

client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="eu-central-1")  # region pins data to Frankfurt (EU residency)

resp = client.converse(                        # converse() is the unified chat API that works across model makers
    modelId="anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0",  # pick the model by ID; swap this string to change models
    messages=[{"role": "user",                 # one turn of conversation from the customer
               "content": [{"text": "What is BankAssist's overdraft fee?"}]}],  # the actual question
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 300, "temperature": 0.2},  # cap length; low temperature = steady, factual tone
)
print(resp["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"])  # pull the model's reply text out of the response
▶ Output
I don't have your account-specific fee schedule here. For BankAssist's current overdraft fee, please check the Deposit Account Agreement…

Notice the answer is honest but useless on its own — the model has no access to BankAssist's documents. That is exactly the gap the next three services fill.

Knowledge Bases — managed RAG

Bedrock Knowledge Bases is RAG you don't have to build. RAG means "retrieve the right documents, then let the model answer from them." Normally you'd wire up chunking, an embedding model, and a vector database yourself. A Knowledge Base does all of that for you: you point it at a data source — an S3 bucket of PDFs, SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive, OneDrive, or a web crawl — and it ingests, chunks, embeds, and stores everything in managed vector storage, keeping it synced as documents change. For the embedding step it defaults to Amazon's own Titan Text Embeddings (the AWS-native embedding model, now at V2), though Cohere and other embedding models are on the menu too. For the vector store you can pick managed options including Amazon S3 Vectors — vector storage built natively into Amazon S3 (generally available since late 2025) that trades a little query speed for a large cut in storage cost on big, infrequently-queried corpora. At query time it does hybrid search (meaning + keywords) and can re-rank results, then hands the passages to the model. AWS also offers a fully managed version — Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base — where even the vector store is run for you, alongside a "custom" option for teams that want to bring their own vector database. Names and availability here move quickly, so verify on the AWS docs.

Bedrock Agents — tool use & actions

A model that can only talk is limited. Bedrock Agents lets the model do things: you define action groups (functions the agent may call, such as "look up account balance" or "open a dispute"), attach a Knowledge Base for facts, and the agent decides when to call which. It plans, calls your APIs, reads the results, and composes an answer. Note a shift happening in 2026: AWS now steers new agent work toward the newer AgentCore stack, with the original agents sometimes called "Agents Classic." Treat classic Bedrock Agents as the simple, built-in option and AgentCore as the heavier production one.

Guardrails — managed safety

Bedrock Guardrails is a configurable safety layer you place around any model. You switch on policies — denied topics (e.g. "never give investment advice"), content filters (hate, violence, sexual, self-harm), sensitive-information filters that detect and redact PII like account numbers, word filters for profanity or competitor names, and contextual grounding checks that flag when an answer drifts from the retrieved source (a hallucination catch). It inspects both the user's input and the model's output, and it works across any model on Bedrock — even image content.

⚙️ Under the hood

The quiet superpower of Bedrock is model portability behind one contract. Because the converse API is shared, your prompt, your Guardrail, and your Knowledge Base don't care whether the model underneath is Claude or Nova. When a newer, cheaper, or faster model lands, you change one ID and re-run your evaluations. That decoupling — app logic on one side, model choice on the other — is what makes a managed platform worth the premium for a bank that must swap models as the market moves.

✅ Tip — build the workflow visually with Bedrock Flows

When the steps are fixed — "check the question, retrieve from the Knowledge Base, call a Lambda, then answer" — you don't have to hand-write the orchestration. Amazon Bedrock Flows is a drag-and-drop canvas where you link prompts, Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails, and Lambda functions into one workflow, with condition branches and loops, then version it and call it from an API. Use Flows for a clear, visual pipeline a whole team (including non-coders) can read and audit; write code instead when the control flow is dynamic, heavily conditional, or needs logic a visual graph would make awkward.

In production

At real traffic, a few things decide whether this holds up:

  • Cost. You pay per token (input and output), plus storage and queries for the Knowledge Base, plus a per-text-unit charge for Guardrails. A chatty agent that re-reads a big Knowledge Base on every turn gets expensive fast — watch token volume, not just request count. For steady high load, Bedrock offers provisioned throughput (reserved capacity) instead of pay-per-call.
  • Latency. Each hop — guardrail, retrieval, tool call, generation — adds milliseconds. Multi-step agents feel slower than a plain call. Stream the answer to the customer so it feels fast, and keep retrieval tight.
  • Compliance. Pin the region for data residency, use an AWS enterprise agreement that excludes your data from training, log every call through CloudTrail, and encrypt with your own KMS keys. Guardrails give you an auditable "we blocked X" record — gold for a regulator.
  • Failure modes. Models get throttled under load (plan retries with backoff), a region can have an outage (have a fallback model/region), and the contextual grounding check can be too strict or too loose (tune its threshold against real transcripts).
✅ Tip

Turn on Guardrails from day one, even in the prototype. It is far easier to loosen a safety policy you can see working than to bolt one on after a compliance review finds the gap.

⚙️ In production

Numbers and failure modes a BankAssist team should hold in its head before go-live on Bedrock:

  • Cost, concretely. Generation is billed per input and output token; a Knowledge Base adds a per-query retrieval charge plus the embedding and vector-storage cost of ingestion; Guardrails bill per "text unit" (roughly 1,000 characters) on both the input and output check. The sneaky line item is a chatty agent that stuffs large retrieved passages into every turn — input tokens, not request count, drive the bill. For steady high load, buy provisioned throughput (reserved capacity) so latency stays flat and cost becomes predictable.
  • Latency budget. Each hop adds up: input guardrail (~tens of ms), retrieval (~50–200 ms), model generation (hundreds of ms to seconds), output guardrail. A single grounded answer is usually under a second; a multi-step agent can be several. Stream the reply and keep retrieval tight (fewer, better chunks).
  • Scale & failure modes. Under bursts the model throttles — wrap every converse call in retry-with-exponential-backoff and jitter. Have a fallback model ID and a fallback region ready, because a region can have a bad day. The contextual grounding check can be tuned too strict (blocks good answers) or too loose (lets hallucinations through) — calibrate its threshold against real transcripts, not a guess.
  • Monitoring & compliance. Log every call through CloudTrail, meter tokens and Guardrail blocks in CloudWatch, encrypt with your own KMS keys, and keep the Guardrail block records — "we refused to give investment advice, here's the log" is exactly the evidence a regulator wants. Pin the region (e.g. eu-central-1) for data residency.
⚠ Watch out

Don't let an agent silently re-ingest or re-scan a large Knowledge Base on every turn — it quietly multiplies your token and retrieval bill and your latency. Cache retrievals within a conversation and retrieve only when the question actually needs fresh facts.

When to use Bedrock's built-in pieces: you want one API across model makers, managed RAG, and safety without running infrastructure — the common case. When NOT to: you need a deeply custom retrieval pipeline or a self-hosted open-weight model fine-tuned on private data — then bring your own vector store and serving, or self-host, and use Bedrock only for the hosted frontier model.

✅ Tip — when you'd rather not build at all: Amazon Q

Bedrock is for building your own assistant; sometimes AWS has already built one for you. Amazon Q Developer is a coding assistant in the IDE and AWS console — it writes, explains, and tests code and helps BankAssist's own engineers ship and troubleshoot faster. Amazon Q Business is a ready-made enterprise RAG assistant: connect it to SharePoint, Confluence, S3, and internal wikis, and staff ask plain-English questions over that knowledge with permission-aware, cited answers — a fast way to give the operations team a grounded helper without writing a retrieval pipeline at all.

🧠 Remember it

Bedrock = one door, four rooms: models to think, Knowledge Bases to recall, Agents to act, Guardrails to behave.

AWS Bedrock AgentCore: running agents in production

AgentCore is the set of managed services for operating real agents — secure runtime, memory, identity, tool gateways, observability, and evaluation — so the hard parts of "agent in production" are handled for you.

Building an agent that works in a demo is easy. Running one safely for thousands of customers — isolating each session, remembering the right things, logging in to downstream systems on the user's behalf, exposing tools without leaking them, watching it for drift — is the hard 90%. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (generally available since late 2025) is AWS's answer: a modular set of services, each solving one of those production problems. You can use any one of them on its own, and they work with agents built in any framework.

The six pieces, in plain words

  • Runtime — a serverless place to run your agent, with each user session isolated from every other (so one customer's conversation can never bleed into another's). It scales to zero when idle and uses snapshotting to keep cold starts fast. This is the "where does my agent actually execute" answer.
  • Memory — managed short-term memory (this conversation) and long-term memory (facts worth keeping across sessions, like "this customer prefers email"). You get expiry controls and namespaces so memories stay separated per user. No Redis cluster to run yourself.
  • Identity — lets an agent act as a user against other systems using proper OAuth, including a consent step where the customer approves access. This is how an agent calls the payments API on Mrs. Khan's behalf without you hard-coding a god-mode credential.
  • Gateway — turns your existing APIs, Lambda functions, and even AWS Step Functions into tools the agent can call, exposed through the open Model Context Protocol (MCP). It supports OpenAPI definitions too, so a REST API you already have becomes an agent tool with little glue code.
  • Observability — traces, metrics, and spans for every agent step, built on OpenTelemetry and surfaced in CloudWatch. When an agent gives a wrong answer, you can replay exactly which tool it called and what it saw.
  • Evaluations (evaluators) — managed "LLM-as-a-judge" scoring of your agent's behaviour: run a batch of test cases, or score live traffic online, across named quality dimensions. This is how you prove the agent is still behaving after a model swap.
⚙️ Under the hood — the Strands Agents SDK

AgentCore runs your agent, but something has to be the agent. AWS's open-source Strands Agents SDK is the common choice: you write the agent's logic in a few lines of Python (a model, a system prompt, a list of tools), and Strands handles the reason-act loop. It has built-in integration with AgentCore Runtime, so the same agent you test on your laptop deploys to the managed runtime with almost no change. AgentCore is framework-agnostic, though — LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents, and others run on it too; Strands is just the one that fits like a glove.

Here is a tiny Strands agent, then the two commands that put it on AgentCore Runtime:

# A minimal BankAssist agent with one tool, written with the Strands SDK.
from strands import Agent, tool               # Agent = the reason-act loop; tool = marks a function the agent may call
from strands.models import BedrockModel       # use a foundation model hosted on Amazon Bedrock

@tool                                         # this decorator exposes the function to the agent as a callable tool
def get_overdraft_fee(account_type: str) -> str:  # a real banking action the agent can invoke
    """Return the overdraft fee for an account type."""  # the docstring tells the model when to use this tool
    return "Overdraft item fee: $35; one courtesy waiver per 12 months."  # would call a live API in reality

agent = Agent(                                # assemble the agent
    model=BedrockModel(model_id="anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0"),  # the brain, served by Bedrock
    system_prompt="You are BankAssist. Use tools for facts; never guess fees.",  # its standing instructions
    tools=[get_overdraft_fee],                # the tools it is allowed to use
)

result = agent("What's the overdraft fee on a checking account?")  # run one turn locally to test
print(result.message)                         # see the grounded answer before deploying
▶ Output
The overdraft item fee is $35, with one courtesy waiver available per 12 months.
# Deploy the exact same agent to a managed, serverless runtime — two commands.
agentcore configure --entrypoint agent.py    # creates a config: how to package and run this agent
agentcore launch                              # packages the code, deploys it, returns a secure HTTPS endpoint
▶ Output
✓ Agent deployed to AgentCore Runtime · endpoint: https://…agentcore…/invoke

A deploy pattern: Lambda + API Gateway in front

A common, cheap way to expose a small agent to your web and mobile apps is to put a thin AWS Lambda function behind Amazon API Gateway. API Gateway gives you a public HTTPS URL, authentication, rate limiting, and request validation; the Lambda holds the short bit of code that invokes your agent; the agent (on AgentCore Runtime, or even inside the Lambda for very light use) does the thinking. This keeps your front door managed and your agent logic small.

✅ Tip — the serverless glue around an agent

Most of the plumbing between an agent and the bank's systems is ordinary AWS serverless building blocks, so you pay only when they run: AWS Lambda for the short functions an agent calls (look up a balance, open a dispute) and for thin request handlers; Amazon SQS for queues that absorb bursts and hand slow work — document ingestion, batch scoring — to background workers without dropping it; and Aurora Serverless for a Postgres/MySQL database that scales capacity up and down on demand, handy for conversation state, audit records, or a pgvector store that shouldn't run a full-size instance around the clock.

In production

AgentCore exists precisely because production is where agents fall over. The services map to the usual failures: Runtime session isolation stops cross-customer leaks; Memory expiry stops stale or ballooning context (and runaway storage cost); Identity stops the "confused deputy" problem where an agent uses one customer's token to touch another's data; Gateway rate limits stop a looping agent from hammering your core banking API; Observability turns "it gave a weird answer" into a replayable trace; Evaluations catch quality regressions the day you change a model. The costs to watch are the usual agent ones — tokens per step, tool-call fan-out, and memory storage — plus the per-service charges, which are consumption-based. Load-test the whole chain, because latency is cumulative across every hop.

⚠ Watch out

AgentCore is powerful and therefore easy to over-adopt. If your "agent" is really a single retrieval-and-answer call, you do not need session runtimes, memory stores, and identity brokering — plain Bedrock plus a Knowledge Base is simpler and cheaper. Reach for AgentCore when the agent genuinely acts over multiple steps, holds state, and touches protected systems.

When to use: a multi-step, stateful agent that logs into downstream banking systems on the customer's behalf and must be isolated, audited, and evaluated. When NOT to: a stateless Q&A bot, or a quick internal tool — the per-service machinery is overhead you won't use.

⚙️ In production

AgentCore reached general availability in October 2025, and its billing is pure consumption-based — no upfront commitment, and each service (Runtime, Memory, Identity, Gateway, Observability, Evaluations) is priced independently so you only pay for what you switch on. For a BankAssist deployment that matters in concrete ways:

  • Cost drivers. Runtime bills for active compute (vCPU- and memory-seconds while your agent is actually working — I/O wait and idle are not charged, and it scales to zero when quiet). Memory bills for stored short- and long-term records. Identity is not charged separately when used through Runtime or Gateway. Observability flows through CloudWatch pricing. Layered on top is the model's own token cost, which is usually the largest line — so the biggest lever is fewer, tighter steps, not shaving service fees.
  • Latency. Snapshotting keeps cold starts fast, but every tool hop through Gateway and every memory read adds milliseconds; a multi-step dispute investigation can run several seconds end to end. Load-test the whole chain, because latency is cumulative across all six services.
  • Failure modes mapped to services. Runtime isolation stops cross-customer session bleed; Memory expiry stops stale context and runaway storage cost; Identity stops the "confused deputy" (one customer's token touching another's data); Gateway rate limits stop a looping agent from hammering the core banking API; Observability turns "it gave a weird answer" into a replayable trace; Evaluations catch quality regressions the day you swap a model.
  • Monitoring & compliance. Observability is built on OpenTelemetry and surfaced in CloudWatch — trace every step, alert on tool-error rate and step-count blowups, and keep the traces as the audit record. Pin the region and run everything inside your AWS account boundary.
🧠 Remember it

AgentCore in one breath: Runtime runs it, Memory recalls it, Identity logs it in, Gateway hands it tools, Observability watches it, Evaluations grade it.

Azure OpenAI Service: deployments & content filters

Azure OpenAI gives you OpenAI's models inside Microsoft's enterprise cloud, where you deploy a model as your own private endpoint and a safety filter rides along automatically.

Many banks are Microsoft shops — their identity, email, and data already live in Azure. For them, the natural way to use OpenAI's models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, the o-series reasoning models, and newer ones as they land) is the Azure OpenAI Service: the same models, but served from inside Azure, under Azure's compliance, networking, and regional controls, with a contractual promise that your data is not used to train the shared models.

Deployments — the key idea

In Azure you don't just call a global model name. You create a deployment: you take a base model (say GPT-4o), give it a name you choose (say bankassist-gpt4o), pick a region, and pick a capacity type. That deployment is your private endpoint for that model. Why bother? Because the deployment is where region (data residency), capacity (throughput), version pinning, and the attached content filter all live. You call your deployment name, not a global model, so you control exactly which version and region answer each request.

# Call your own Azure OpenAI deployment — note you call the deployment name, not the raw model.
from openai import AzureOpenAI                 # the official OpenAI client, configured for Azure

client = AzureOpenAI(                          # build a client pointed at your Azure resource
    azure_endpoint="https://bankassist.openai.azure.com/",  # your private resource URL (region + tenant bound)
    api_version="2024-10-21",                 # pin the API version so behaviour doesn't shift under you
    azure_ad_token_provider=get_token,        # use Entra ID (Azure AD) identity, not a static key — safer for banks
)

resp = client.chat.completions.create(        # the standard chat call
    model="bankassist-gpt4o",                 # this is the DEPLOYMENT name you created, not "gpt-4.1"
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise our refund policy in one line."}],  # the task
    temperature=0.2,                          # keep it steady and factual for banking copy
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)        # the model's reply
▶ Output
Refunds are issued to the original payment method within 5–7 business days of approval.

Content filters — safety that rides along

Every Azure OpenAI deployment has a content filter attached. By default it screens both the prompt and the response across four categories — hate, sexual, violence, and self-harm — each at low/medium/high severity, and can also catch jailbreak attempts and (optionally) protected material. When something trips the filter, the request is blocked and the API returns a 400 error describing which rule fired, so your app can handle it gracefully. You can create custom filter configurations (tighter or looser per category) at the resource level and attach them to specific deployments — for example, a stricter filter on the public customer bot than on an internal analyst tool.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist runs two deployments off the same GPT-4o model: bankassist-public with a strict filter and a short token cap for the customer chatbot, and bankassist-analyst with a looser filter and higher throughput for the internal fraud team. Same model, two personalities and two safety postures — all set at the deployment level, no code difference beyond the name.

✅ Tip — RAG with no glue: "On Your Data"

Azure OpenAI has a built-in RAG shortcut called On Your Data: point a deployment at an Azure AI Search index (or Blob storage), and the service retrieves the relevant chunks and grounds the answer for you — with citations — inside a single chat call, no custom retrieval code to wire up. It's the quickest way to get a grounded BankAssist answer over your own documents; when you outgrow it (multi-hop questions, agentic retrieval, fine-grained control), you graduate to the fuller knowledge services in Microsoft Foundry.

In production

Three things matter at scale. Capacity: a deployment is either pay-as-you-go (token-metered, with per-minute quotas) or Provisioned Throughput Units (PTUs) — reserved capacity that gives steady latency for heavy, predictable load; busy banks often mix them. Identity and network: use Microsoft Entra ID instead of API keys, lock the endpoint behind a private network (Private Link), and the whole thing stays inside your Azure tenant. Filter tuning and abuse monitoring: the default filter can be too blunt for banking language ("this charge is killing me" is not violence), so test it on real transcripts and request custom thresholds; note that Azure also runs abuse monitoring, which you can scope for sensitive data under the right agreement. Watch for 429 throttling under bursts and add retry-with-backoff.

⚙️ In production

Running a deployment for real BankAssist traffic comes down to five levers:

  • Capacity & cost. Pay-as-you-go is token-metered with a per-minute TPM/RPM (tokens- and requests-per-minute) quota; heavy, predictable load is cheaper and steadier on PTUs (reserved capacity) covered by a one-year Reservation for the discount. Non-urgent work (summarising yesterday's calls, classifying a backlog) belongs on a Batch deployment at roughly half price. Busy banks run all three off the same model family.
  • Latency. Pay-go latency drifts with shared demand; a PTU deployment holds a flat p95 because the capacity is yours. For the customer bot, that predictability is worth the reservation.
  • Throttling & resilience. Expect 429s under spikes — retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and consider spillover from a full PTU to a Standard deployment so a spike degrades gracefully instead of failing.
  • Monitoring. Stream request and token metrics to Azure Monitor; alert on throttle rate, filter-block rate, p95 latency, and tokens-per-conversation. Diagnostic logs are also your audit trail.
  • Security/compliance. Authenticate with Entra ID managed identity (not keys), put the endpoint behind Private Link with public access off, choose the region for residency, and keep the "not used for training" DPA (Data Processing Addendum — the data-handling contract) clause on file.
⚠ Watch out

Do not confuse the region you deployed in with where your request is processed. A low-cost global deployment type can process a customer's message in any Azure region on earth even though the resource "lives" in the EU — a residency trap set entirely by the deployment type you choose. Pick the deployment type deliberately for anything touching customer PII.

When to use Azure OpenAI deployments: you're a Microsoft shop, your identity and data already live in Azure, and you want OpenAI's models under Azure's compliance, networking, and no-training contract. When NOT to: you need a model Azure doesn't host, or deep weight-level fine-tuning on private data — reach for an open-weight model you host, or the wider Foundry model catalog.

⚙️ Under the hood — where Azure OpenAI sits now

Azure OpenAI is increasingly presented as part of a bigger umbrella, Microsoft Foundry (recently renamed from Azure AI Foundry, with the names still overlapping across docs in 2026). Foundry adds a model catalog beyond OpenAI (Llama, Mistral, and others) plus agent and knowledge services. For a plain "call a model" need, Azure OpenAI deployments are still the direct path; Foundry is the wider platform around them.

🧠 Remember it

On Azure you don't call a model, you call a deployment — model + region + filter, wrapped in a name you own.

Microsoft Foundry: Foundry IQ, the Agent Framework, MCP, OpenAPI & A2A

Foundry is Microsoft's full agent platform — managed knowledge over Azure AI Search, a unified framework for building and orchestrating agents, and open protocols so agents can use tools and talk to each other.

Once a bank needs more than "call a model," Microsoft points it at Microsoft Foundry (the platform formerly, and still often, called Azure AI Foundry). Think of it as Azure's counterpart to AWS's Bedrock-plus-AgentCore: models, managed RAG, an agent framework, and the plumbing to run agents in an enterprise. Three parts matter most.

Foundry IQ — managed knowledge over Azure AI Search

Foundry IQ is Microsoft's managed knowledge layer, built on top of Azure AI Search (Azure's search-and-vector engine). You create knowledge bases that point at your data sources, and Foundry IQ handles the retrieval — including agentic retrieval, where a hard question is broken into several sub-queries, searched, and the results merged (multi-hop), rather than a single one-shot lookup. It is the "give my agent trustworthy, cited facts" service, and because it rides on Azure AI Search, it inherits that engine's security trimming — so a user only ever retrieves documents they're allowed to see. That last point is huge in banking, where a retail customer and a private-wealth manager must never see each other's documents.

The Microsoft Agent Framework (with Magentic)

The Microsoft Agent Framework (version 1.0, 2026) is the open-source SDK for building agents, and it is the merger of Microsoft's two earlier efforts: Semantic Kernel (its enterprise plumbing — state, type safety, telemetry) and AutoGen (its multi-agent orchestration research). You write agents once, in .NET or Python, and get both lineages in one supported package.

Its headline multi-agent pattern is Magentic (from Microsoft's "Magentic-One" research). In the Magentic pattern, a manager agent is given an open-ended goal, builds a running "task ledger" (a plan it updates as it learns), and delegates steps to specialist agents, re-planning when something fails. It's built for messy, open problems where you can't script the steps in advance. Alongside it sit simpler patterns: sequential (a fixed pipeline), group chat (agents discuss), and handoff (one agent passes control to another).

Tools and talking: MCP, OpenAPI, and A2A

An agent is only as useful as what it can touch and who it can call. Foundry leans on open standards for both:

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) — a standard way to plug tools into an agent. Point the agent at an MCP server and its tools appear, no custom integration per tool. The same standard AWS's AgentCore Gateway speaks, which is the point of a standard.
  • OpenAPI tools — hand the agent an OpenAPI spec (the standard description of a REST API, which most banks already have for their internal services) and each endpoint becomes a callable tool. Your existing "get balance" API becomes an agent action with no new code.
  • A2A (Agent-to-Agent) — a protocol for agents to discover and call other agents, even ones built on a different platform or by a different team. One agent publishes a "card" describing what it can do; another finds it and delegates to it. This is how BankAssist's support agent could call the fraud team's separately-owned agent without either side knowing the other's internals.
# A tiny agent in the Microsoft Agent Framework that uses an MCP tool server (Python).
from agent_framework import ChatAgent         # the unified agent type (successor to Semantic Kernel + AutoGen)
from agent_framework.azure import AzureOpenAIChatClient  # talk to your Azure OpenAI deployment
from agent_framework import MCPStreamableHTTPTool        # attach tools exposed by an MCP server

tools = MCPStreamableHTTPTool(                 # connect to a running MCP server...
    name="banking-tools",                     # a label for this tool group
    url="https://tools.bankassist.internal/mcp",  # ...where your account/dispute tools live
)

agent = ChatAgent(                             # build the agent
    chat_client=AzureOpenAIChatClient(deployment_name="bankassist-gpt4o"),  # the model, via your deployment
    instructions="You are BankAssist. Use the banking tools for anything account-specific.",  # standing rules
    tools=tools,                              # the MCP tools it may call
)

reply = await agent.run("Open a dispute for the $35 overdraft fee on my checking account.")  # one task
print(reply.text)                             # the agent plans, calls the dispute tool, and confirms
▶ Output
I've opened dispute #D-20481 for the $35 overdraft fee on your checking account. You'll get an update within 5 business days.

In production

Foundry's selling point for a bank is governance by inheritance: agents run inside your Azure tenant, under Entra ID identity, with Azure's networking, logging, and compliance already wrapped around them, and Foundry IQ's security-trimmed retrieval means an agent can't surface a document the user couldn't open. The costs and failure modes mirror any agent platform — token spend climbs with multi-agent chatter (Magentic can fan out fast, so cap steps and set budgets), retrieval must be tuned so agentic multi-hop doesn't balloon latency, and multi-agent and A2A setups widen the attack surface (a called agent is untrusted input — validate what comes back). Observability is built on OpenTelemetry, so you can trace every agent and sub-agent step.

⚠ Watch out

Magentic looks magical in a demo and is tempting everywhere. But an open-ended, self-re-planning manager is harder to predict, harder to cost, and harder to audit than a fixed sequential pipeline. In a regulated flow where the steps are known — KYC, then risk check, then decision — use the sequential pattern. Save Magentic for genuinely open investigations where the path can't be scripted.

When to use Foundry's agent stack: you need multi-agent orchestration, security-trimmed RAG, and tool/agent interop (MCP, OpenAPI, A2A) governed inside your Azure tenant. When NOT to: a single grounded Q&A call — a plain Azure OpenAI deployment plus one search index is simpler and cheaper than standing up the whole platform.

⚙️ In production

Foundry's pitch to a bank is governance by inheritance — agents run inside your tenant under Entra ID, with Azure networking, logging, and compliance already wrapped around them, and Foundry IQ's security-trimmed retrieval means an agent literally cannot surface a document the user couldn't open. What that costs and how it breaks at scale:

  • Cost. Three stacked meters: model tokens, agentic-retrieval queries (Foundry IQ over Azure AI Search — a search tier you provision), and agent runtime. Multi-agent chatter is the budget killer: a Magentic manager delegating to three specialists can multiply token spend several-fold per request. Cap steps, set per-conversation budgets, and prefer the simplest pattern that solves the task.
  • Latency. Agentic (multi-hop) retrieval breaks a hard question into sub-queries — more accurate but slower; tune how many hops you allow so p95 stays acceptable for a live chat.
  • Failure modes & attack surface. Multi-agent and A2A widen the attack surface — a called agent's reply is untrusted input, so validate what comes back and never let one agent's output silently trigger a privileged action. An uncapped Magentic manager can loop and burn tokens; set step and cost limits.
  • Monitoring & compliance. Observability is built on OpenTelemetry, so you can trace every agent and sub-agent step and keep it as the audit record. Pair it with Azure's Evaluation SDK to prove behaviour after a model swap. Security trimming must be verified per data source — test that a retail persona genuinely cannot retrieve a private-wealth document.
🧠 Remember it

Foundry = IQ remembers, the Agent Framework thinks, Magentic manages, and MCP / OpenAPI / A2A connect — tools in, other agents across.

Google Vertex AI: Agent Builder, Agent Engine & the ADK

Google's stack mirrors the others — an open kit to build agents, a managed runtime to host them, and a builder console to assemble them — all around the Gemini models.

The third big cloud, Google, offers the same shape through Vertex AI, its umbrella for machine learning and generative AI. Google's agent pieces rhyme with AWS's and Azure's — the names differ, but the ideas repeat. Around the Gemini model family sit three layers worth knowing.

  • ADK (Agent Development Kit) — Google's open-source framework for writing agents in code (Python, Java, and more). You define a model, instructions, and tools, and the ADK runs the loop. It's the counterpart to AWS's Strands SDK and Microsoft's Agent Framework. You build and test locally, then deploy elsewhere.
  • Agent Engine — the managed, serverless runtime that hosts your agent in production, handling scaling, sessions, memory, and monitoring so you don't run servers. Crucially it is framework-agnostic: it can host agents built with ADK, LangGraph, CrewAI, or others — the parallel to AWS's AgentCore Runtime.
  • Agent Builder — the higher-level console and services for assembling agents and grounding them in your data (including grounding on Google Search and on your own Vertex AI Search indexes), aimed at getting an agent up without wiring every piece by hand.

Here is the shape in code: a tiny BankAssist agent written with the ADK, then the one call that deploys it to the managed runtime. Tools are just plain Python functions — the ADK exposes them to the model automatically.

# A minimal BankAssist agent with the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK).
from google.adk.agents import Agent          # Agent = the reason-act loop around a Gemini model

def get_branch_hours(city: str) -> dict:      # a plain function becomes a tool automatically
    """Return opening hours for the branch in a city."""  # docstring tells the model when to call it
    return {"city": city, "hours": "Mon-Fri 9:00-17:00"}  # would hit a live API in reality

root_agent = Agent(                           # assemble the agent
    name="bankassist_branch",                 # a stable name used by the runtime and logs
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",                 # the Gemini model that does the thinking
    instruction="You are BankAssist. Use tools for branch facts; never guess hours.",  # standing rules
    tools=[get_branch_hours],                 # the tools it is allowed to call
)

# Deploy the same agent to the managed runtime (Agent Engine) — no servers to run.
import vertexai                               # the Vertex AI SDK
from vertexai import agent_engines           # the managed agent runtime API

vertexai.init(                                # pin project AND region for data residency
    project="bankassist-prod",               # your Google Cloud project
    location="europe-west4",                  # keep EU customers' data in an EU region
    staging_bucket="gs://bankassist-agents",  # where the packaged agent is staged
)
remote = agent_engines.create(               # package + deploy; returns a managed, scalable endpoint
    agent_engine=root_agent,                 # the ADK agent from above — same code, now hosted
    requirements=["google-cloud-aiplatform[adk,agent_engines]"],  # deps baked into the deployment
)
