The same models, wrapped in the enterprise controls a regulated bank needs to pass an audit.

Picking Azure OpenAI over the raw OpenAI platform is rarely about the model — it is the same family of models. It is about everything around the model: who can call it, where the data sits, how you prove it to a regulator, and how you avoid being caught out when a model version is retired. For a bank, those wrappers are the whole point.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist runs a credit-decision assistant that must be explainable and auditable. The team pins it to a specific model version, routes every call over a private network with no public endpoint, uses a managed identity instead of a shared key, and keeps a dated Transparency Note on file. When Azure announces that version will retire, they get a notice, test the successor in staging, and migrate before the deadline — no surprise outage, no audit finding.

1. Model lifecycle & retirements

Azure publishes each model as dated versions that move through preview → GA (generally available) → deprecation → retirement. When you create a deployment you choose how it tracks versions: pin to a specific version (it never changes under you), or let it auto-update to the default. Azure posts retirement dates in advance; once a version retires, deployments on it stop working.

💡 Key idea

A bank pins. Auto-update is convenient for a prototype, but a regulated workload must not have its behaviour change silently — you pin a version, test every candidate upgrade, and migrate on a schedule you control, ahead of the retirement date.

# Create a deployment PINNED to a specific model version and set to never auto-update.
az cognitiveservices account deployment create \
  --name bankassist-openai \                       # the Azure OpenAI resource
  --resource-group rg-bankassist \                 # its resource group
  --deployment-name bankassist-credit \            # your deployment name (what the app calls)
  --model-name gpt-4.1 \                            # the base model family
  --model-version "2025-04-14" \                    # PIN an exact dated version — behaviour won't shift under you
  --model-format OpenAI \                           # the model provider format
  --sku-name ProvisionedManaged \                   # regional provisioned: single-region residency + steady latency
  --sku-capacity 50 \                               # reserved PTU capacity for predictable throughput
  --version-upgrade-option NoAutoUpgrade            # never auto-migrate; YOU choose when to move versions
▶ Output
Deployment 'bankassist-credit' created · model gpt-4.1 v2025-04-14 · upgrade: NoAutoUpgrade · sku: ProvisionedManaged

2. Your data stays yours

Microsoft's commitment for Azure OpenAI is that your prompts and completions are not used to train the underlying models, and are not shared with other customers or with OpenAI for that purpose. You also choose the region your deployment runs in, which supports data-residency rules (e.g. keeping an EU bank's traffic in EU regions).

3. Content filtering & abuse monitoring

Azure applies configurable content filters across categories (hate, sexual, violence, self-harm) at several severity levels, on both input and output. Separately, Azure stores prompts briefly for abuse monitoring by default — and, importantly for banks, you can apply for modified abuse monitoring so that sensitive data is not stored and is not subject to human review, which is often a precondition for handling regulated customer data.

4. The security baseline & enterprise controls

  • Private networking — put the resource behind Private Link / a VNet so it has no public endpoint; traffic never crosses the internet.
  • Managed Identity, not keys — authenticate with Entra ID managed identities so no API key is minted, copied, or leaked.
  • Customer-managed keys — encrypt stored data with keys you control in Key Vault.
  • RBAC — least-privilege roles for who can deploy, call, and administer.
  • Diagnostic logging — stream usage and request logs to Azure Monitor for audit and anomaly detection.
⚠ Watch out

The single most common leak is a hard-coded API key in a repo or config. On Azure the fix is structural: turn key auth off, use Managed Identity, and keep the endpoint private. A key that is never issued cannot be stolen.

When to pin + wrap in the full baseline: any production, customer-facing, or regulated workload (credit decisions, PII) — pin the version, hide the endpoint, drop the key, keep the logs. When auto-update and keys are acceptable: only a throwaway prototype on synthetic data that no real customer touches and that never feeds a decision.

5. Transparency Notes & Responsible AI

Microsoft publishes Transparency Notes describing a service's intended uses, capabilities, and limitations. For governance you pair the relevant Transparency Note with your own documented use case — it feeds straight into model risk management and the kind of model cards a regulator expects.

⚙️ In production — a go-live checklist
  • ☐ Deployment pinned to a specific model version; retirement date tracked in your calendar.
  • ☐ Private Link / VNet; public network access disabled.
  • ☐ Managed Identity for auth; key auth disabled; secrets (if any) in Key Vault.
  • ☐ Content filters configured to policy; modified abuse monitoring approved if handling regulated PII.
  • ☐ Region chosen for data residency; "data not used for training" commitment recorded.
  • ☐ Diagnostic logs to Azure Monitor; RBAC least-privilege; Transparency Note on file with your use-case doc.
🧠 Remember it

Pin the model, hide the endpoint, drop the key, keep the receipts. That sentence is most of an Azure OpenAI audit.

Fine-Tuning & Model Adaptation

RAG lends a model the right pages to read; fine-tuning actually re-wires how the model thinks and speaks. This chapter takes you from "fine-tuning exists" all the way to training a small open model on one GPU, aligning it to your bank's voice, and serving it in production — in plain words, with real, current code.

Fine-tune vs RAG vs prompt: a crisp decision framework

The one rule that saves teams months: RAG changes what the model knows, fine-tuning changes how it behaves, and prompting changes what you ask for right now.

Imagine a new hire at BankAssist. There are three ways to get better work out of them. You can hand them the right file before they answer a customer (that's RAG). You can send them on a two-week training course so they internalise the bank's tone, forms, and procedures (that's fine-tuning). Or you can just give them clearer instructions for this one task — "reply in two sentences, formal tone" (that's prompting). Same person, three very different levers.

These are not rivals. Mature banking systems use all three at once. The skill is knowing which lever a given problem actually needs — because reaching for the wrong one is how teams burn a quarter solving the wrong thing.

The core distinction, in one line each

  • Prompting — you shape behaviour with words in the context window. Cheapest, fastest, zero training. Try this first, always.
  • RAG — you inject facts at answer time by retrieving documents. For knowledge that is large, private, or changes often.
  • Fine-tuning — you bake behaviour into the model's weights with examples. For a consistent style, format, or skill the model keeps getting wrong.

How to actually choose

Work down this list and stop at the first lever that fits:

  1. Can a better prompt fix it? Clearer instructions, a few examples (few-shot), a stricter output spec. If yes, you're done — no pipeline to maintain.
  2. Is the gap missing knowledge? If the model needs facts it was never trained on — your fee schedule, a customer's history, a new regulation — that's RAG. You cannot train facts in reliably, and the day you finish training, the facts change.
  3. Is the gap a stubborn behaviour? If the model, even with a great prompt and good context, keeps answering in the wrong tone, botching your JSON schema, or misclassifying complaint types — that's a behaviour the weights need to learn. Fine-tune.
Symptom at BankAssistLeverWhy
"It quotes last year's overdraft fee."RAGA fact that changes — retrieve the current schedule.
"It's too chatty; we need two formal sentences."PromptOne instruction usually fixes tone for a single task.
"Across 10k tickets it still won't hold our house style or always emit valid JSON."Fine-tuneA consistent behaviour at scale belongs in the weights.
"It doesn't understand our internal acronyms when searching."Fine-tune (the embedding model)Domain jargon retrieval is a behaviour of the retriever.
"It needs both today's policy AND our precise tone."RAG + fine-tuneFacts from RAG, voice from training. They stack.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's team had two complaints. First, customers got stale interest rates — they fixed that with RAG, re-indexing the rate sheet nightly. Second, the assistant's replies sounded like a generic chatbot, not their warm-but-formal brand, and it kept wrapping answers in markdown the mobile app couldn't render. They tried prompting ("reply in plain text, formal tone") and it worked 80% of the time — but 1-in-5 slips is a brand problem at a million messages a month. So they fine-tuned a small model on 8,000 of their own gold replies. Rates: RAG. Voice and format: fine-tuning. Exactly the right tool in each hand.

Going deeper — the three levers are a cost ladder

Read the order prompt → RAG → fine-tune as a ladder of standing cost, and climb only as far as you must. A prompt change is free and ships in minutes — you edit a string. RAG adds a permanent bill: an embedding model, a vector store, an ingestion pipeline, and a few hundred milliseconds of retrieval on every call, but it buys you fresh facts with citations. Fine-tuning adds a one-time training cost (GPU hours, data labour) plus the ongoing weight of owning a model artifact — versioning, evals, re-approval on every base upgrade — in exchange for behaviour no prompt can hold at scale. The magnitudes are worlds apart: a prompt tweak is an afternoon; a solid RAG stack is weeks of engineering and real monthly infra; a single LoRA run is an overnight job but drags a governance tail behind it for the model's whole life. Reaching for a higher rung than the problem needs is the most common and most expensive mistake in applied LLM work.

They also compose, and in production they usually do. BankAssist's live stack is all three at once: a tight system prompt sets the task, RAG injects today's rate sheet and the caller's account context, and a fine-tune holds the warm-but-formal voice and the strict plain-text format. Each lever owns the job it is best at — and when something regresses, you know which one to inspect.

⚙️ In production

At a bank the choice is also an operational one, not only a quality one. Cost & latency: prompting adds only tokens; RAG adds a retrieval hop (budget 50–300 ms and a vector-DB bill); a served fine-tune adds nothing per request if merged, or a few percent if you hot-swap adapters. Scale: prompts and RAG scale by spending more on the same hosted model; a fine-tune means you now operate a model (GPUs, autoscaling, a serving stack). Failure modes differ by lever — a prompt regresses when someone edits it, RAG fails silently when retrieval returns the wrong chunk, a fine-tune fails when the base is upgraded underneath it. Monitoring: log which levers touched each answer so a bad reply is attributable to the prompt, the retrieved context, or the weights. Security/compliance: a hosted prompt-only system is the lightest audit; a fine-tune is the heaviest (training-data lineage, model-risk sign-off under SR 11-7), so don't take on that burden for a problem a prompt solves.

⚠ Watch out

The classic expensive mistake: fine-tuning to inject facts. Teams train a model on their product catalogue, ship it, and a week later the catalogue changes — now the model is confidently stale and can't cite a source. Facts want RAG. Never bake volatile knowledge into weights.

When to use fine-tuning: a behaviour, style, format, or skill the model keeps getting wrong even with a strong prompt and good context, across thousands of cases. When NOT: when the gap is missing or changing facts (use RAG), or when one clear instruction fixes it (just prompt) — training there is slower, costlier, and quickly stale.

💡 Key idea

Fine-tuning teaches how to answer, not what's true today. If you can fix it with a sentence, prompt. If it's a fact, retrieve. If it's a behaviour that survives thousands of examples, train.

🧠 Remember it

Prompt it, retrieve it, or train it — in that order. RAG = knowledge, fine-tune = behaviour, prompt = right now.

Full fine-tuning vs PEFT: the cost problem that parameter-efficient tuning solves

Full fine-tuning rewrites every weight in the model — accurate, but ruinously heavy. PEFT freezes the giant model and trains a tiny add-on instead, getting ~99% of the benefit at ~1% of the cost.

A language model is a huge pile of numbers called weights — an 8-billion-parameter model has 8 billion of them. Fine-tuning means continuing to train the model on your examples so those numbers shift toward the behaviour you want.

Full fine-tuning: update everything

The straightforward approach updates all the weights. It works, and for the deepest behaviour changes it's the gold standard. But the bill is brutal, and the reason is memory, not just time.

To train a weight, your GPU must hold far more than the weight itself. For each parameter, standard training keeps the weight, its gradient, and two optimizer values (the Adam optimizer's running averages) — and if you train in full 32-bit precision, that's roughly 16 bytes per parameter. For an 8B model that's about 128 GB just for the training state, before you've stored a single activation. No single consumer GPU comes close; you're renting a cluster of 80 GB data-centre cards.

⚙️ Under the hood — where the memory goes

Rough full-fine-tune memory per parameter in mixed precision: weights (2 bytes) + gradients (2 bytes) + optimizer state (8 bytes for Adam's two moments in fp32) + a master fp32 copy of the weights (4 bytes) ≈ 16 bytes. Multiply by 8 billion and you get ~128 GB — and you still haven't counted activations, which grow with batch size and sequence length. This is why "just fine-tune it" quietly means "spin up 2–4 A100/H100 GPUs."

PEFT: freeze the giant, train a sliver

PEFT stands for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning. The insight is simple and powerful: you don't need to move all 8 billion weights to teach a new behaviour. Instead, freeze the entire pretrained model (so none of its weights change and none need gradients or optimizer state) and add a small set of new, trainable weights — often well under 1% of the total. You train only those. The frozen model keeps everything it already knew; the little add-on learns your task.

Because only the sliver is trainable, you only pay memory for the sliver's gradients and optimizer state. Suddenly the same 8B model fine-tunes on a single GPU.

In production

At a bank, PEFT isn't just cheaper — it changes the whole operating model, and in ways auditors love:

  • Cost and access. A single GPU (even a rented 24–48 GB card) can tune a 7–8B model with PEFT. A whole team can experiment in parallel instead of queuing for a cluster.
  • Tiny, portable artifacts. A full fine-tune produces a new multi-gigabyte model you must store and ship. A PEFT adapter is typically a few megabytes to a few hundred — one base model, many small adapters. You can version, diff, and roll back an adapter like a config file.
  • Governance. The base model is unchanged and auditable; your change is isolated in a small, reviewable adapter. For model-risk governance (think SR 11-7), "here is exactly what we changed, it's 40 MB, here's the training data lineage" is a far easier story than "we retrained all 8 billion weights."
  • Serving. You can host one base model in memory and hot-swap many adapters on top — a fraud-triage adapter, a complaints adapter, a collections adapter — without loading three full models. (This is adapter hot-swapping at serving time.)
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's platform team priced two paths to the same complaint-summarisation model. Full fine-tuning an 8B model meant renting a 4×A100 node for the run, producing a fresh 16 GB checkpoint to store, scan, and ship through change control — and repeating all of it for the next use case. PEFT meant one 48 GB GPU overnight, a 40 MB adapter, and a base model that never changed. They ran five experiments in parallel on five cheap cards instead of queuing for the cluster, and compliance reviewed a 40 MB diff instead of a new eight-billion-weight brain. Same quality on the task; a tenth of the cost and a tenth of the governance friction.

Going deeper — when full fine-tuning still earns its keep

PEFT's "~99% of the benefit at ~1% of the cost" holds for adaptation — nudging tone, format, a classification, a domain's phrasing. It starts to lag in three situations worth naming. First, teaching a genuinely new capability the base barely saw — a new human language, a novel reasoning skill — where you need to move many weights, not a thin correction. Second, very large, diverse datasets (hundreds of thousands to millions of examples): with that much signal, full fine-tuning's extra capacity converts into measurably better quality. Third, continued pretraining on a big corpus of in-domain text, which is a full-weight job by nature. Modern PEFT variants narrow even these gaps: use_rslora=True rescales the adapter (alpha/√r instead of alpha/r) so higher ranks actually pay off, and use_dora=True (DoRA) splits each update into a magnitude and a direction for close-to-full-tune quality at a small extra cost. The honest rule of thumb: start with PEFT; escalate to full fine-tuning only when a careful eval says the adapter has hit a ceiling.

⚙️ In production

Cost: PEFT turns a multi-GPU cluster job into a single-GPU one and a multi-gigabyte artifact into a few-megabyte one — cheaper to train, store, and move. Latency & scale: a merged PEFT model serves exactly like the base (zero overhead); kept separate, one base in memory backs many adapters, so a bank's business lines share one GPU footprint instead of one model each. Failure modes: an adapter silently mismatches if served on a different or differently-quantized base — pin the pair. Monitoring: track trainable-parameter count and adapter size as a sanity check; a suddenly huge adapter means a mis-set target or rank. Security/compliance: the auditable story is far cleaner — "the base is unchanged and vendor-signed; our change is this 40 MB, reviewable adapter with this data lineage" is exactly what model-risk governance (SR 11-7) wants, versus "we retrained all 8 billion weights."

⚠ Watch out

PEFT is not strictly worse than full fine-tuning — for most adaptation tasks it matches it closely. But when you're teaching a genuinely new capability or domain language the base model barely saw (a new human language, a highly specialised reasoning skill), full fine-tuning or continued pretraining can pull ahead. PEFT adapts; it doesn't teach from scratch.

When to use PEFT: almost always — any task-adaptation, style, format, or classification fine-tune, especially on one GPU or under strict data-residency rules. When NOT (prefer full fine-tuning / continued pretraining): teaching a brand-new capability or language, training on very large diverse corpora, or when a rigorous eval shows the adapter has plateaued below your bar.

🧠 Remember it

Freeze the whale, train the remora. PEFT keeps the giant model still and rides a tiny trainable add-on — ~1% of the weights, a fraction of the GPUs.

LoRA: how low-rank adapters actually work

LoRA is the most popular PEFT method. The trick: a big weight change can be squeezed into two skinny matrices, so you train a few million numbers instead of a few billion.

LoRA means Low-Rank Adaptation. To feel it, forget matrices for a second. Suppose a weight is a giant 1000×1000 grid — a million numbers. Fine-tuning wants to add a correction to that grid. The surprising, well-tested observation is that the useful part of that correction is "low-rank" — it has far less real information than a million numbers, so it can be rebuilt from two thin strips.

The simple intuition

Think of the correction as a 1000×1000 picture that happens to be very smooth and repetitive. You don't need to store every pixel; you can describe it with a short recipe. LoRA stores the recipe, not the picture. Two small matrices multiplied together reconstruct the big correction on the fly — and those two small matrices have a tiny fraction of the numbers.

The math, lightly

Call the original frozen weight W (say 1000×1000 = 1,000,000 numbers). Normally fine-tuning learns a change ΔW of the same size. LoRA instead writes that change as the product of two skinny matrices:

ΔW = B × A, where A is r × 1000 and B is 1000 × r.

Here r is the rank — a small number you choose, like 8 or 16. With r = 8, matrix A has 8×1000 = 8,000 numbers and B has 1000×8 = 8,000 numbers: 16,000 trainable numbers instead of 1,000,000 — about 1.6%. At inference, the model computes its normal output and simply adds the LoRA correction: output = W·x + (B·A)·x. The frozen W never moves; only A and B learn.

The dials you'll actually turn

  • Rank r — how much capacity the adapter has. Higher r learns more complex changes but trains more numbers and risks overfitting. 8–16 is a great starting range; 32–64 for harder tasks.
  • Alpha (lora_alpha) — a scaling factor on the correction. The effective strength is roughly alpha / r. A common recipe is alpha = 2 × r (e.g. r=16, alpha=32).
  • Target modules — which weight matrices get adapters. You can target just the attention projections, or (as QLoRA recommends) all linear layers, which usually gives the best results.
  • Dropout — a little regularisation on the adapter to fight overfitting on small datasets.

Here's a real, current LoRA config with the modern PEFT library:

# Define a LoRA adapter config with Hugging Face PEFT (current API).
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model   # LoraConfig describes the adapter; get_peft_model attaches it
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM  # loader for a decoder LLM (the base we'll adapt)

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-8B")  # load the frozen base model once

lora = LoraConfig(                     # all the dials for the adapter live here
    r=16,                              # rank: adapter capacity — 16 is a solid default
    lora_alpha=32,                     # scaling; alpha=2*r is a common, stable choice
    target_modules="all-linear",       # adapt every linear layer — usually best quality
    lora_dropout=0.05,                 # light dropout guards against overfitting small data
    bias="none",                       # don't train bias terms — keeps the adapter tiny
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",             # tells PEFT this is a text-generation model
)

model = get_peft_model(base, lora)     # freeze base, inject trainable A/B matrices
model.print_trainable_parameters()     # sanity check: how little are we actually training?
▶ Output
trainable params: 20,971,520 || all params: 8,211,603,456 || trainable%: 0.2554

Read that output slowly: we're training 21 million numbers out of 8.2 billion — about a quarter of one percent. That's the whole LoRA promise on one line.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist wants a model that always structures a complaint summary into exactly five fields. A full fine-tune would need a cluster and produce a new 16 GB model. With LoRA at r=16, the trainable part is ~21M parameters, training runs overnight on one GPU, and the shippable artifact — the adapter — is about 40 MB. The compliance team reviews a 40 MB diff, not a new 8-billion-weight brain.

Going deeper — the dials behind the dials

Two refinements change how rank behaves. rsLoRA (use_rslora=True) swaps LoRA's scaling from alpha/r to alpha/√r; the plain formula quietly shrinks the effective update as you raise rank, so high ranks underperform — rsLoRA fixes that, letting r=64 or 128 actually pay off on harder tasks. DoRA (use_dora=True) decomposes each weight update into a magnitude and a direction and learns them separately, closing much of the remaining gap to full fine-tuning for a small compute surcharge. On target modules, the research-backed default is "all linear layers" (attention and the MLP projections); adapting only the attention q/v projections trains fewer parameters but usually leaves quality on the table. On alpha, remember the effective strength is roughly alpha/r — if you change r, keep the ratio in mind rather than copying an old alpha blindly. And one subtlety that bites at serving time: you can merge the learned B·A back into W for zero-overhead inference, but merging into a 4-bit-quantized base can shift numerics slightly, so always evaluate after a merge.

⚙️ In production

Cost & artifact size: at r=16 on an 8B model you train ~21M of ~8.2B parameters (~0.26%) and ship a ~40 MB adapter — cheap to train overnight on one GPU and trivial to store, diff, and roll back. Latency: unmerged, the extra B·A matmul adds a small per-token cost; merged, there is none — pick per use case. Scale: because adapters are tiny, one base in memory can back many of them (fraud, tone, collections) instead of a full model each. Failure modes: too-high rank on a small dataset overfits; an alpha/rank mismatch makes the adapter either inert or overpowering; a merge into a quantized base can drift. Monitoring: always print trainable_parameters before a run and log rank/alpha/target-modules with the checkpoint. Compliance: the adapter is your change — version it with its base hash and training data so an auditor can reproduce exactly what shipped.

⚠ Watch out

Cranking rank to "be safe" backfires on small datasets — a high-rank adapter has enough capacity to memorise your few thousand examples and generalise worse. Start low (r=8–16), measure, and raise only if the eval says you're under-fitting. More rank is not more quality.

When to use LoRA: the default for almost every banking fine-tune where the base runs comfortably in 16-bit on your GPU and you want portable, swappable, auditable adapters. When NOT: if the base won't fit in memory at 16-bit, reach for QLoRA; if you're teaching a wholly new capability on huge data, consider full fine-tuning.

🧠 Remember it

Two skinny matrices, one big idea. LoRA rebuilds a huge weight update from B·A — train ~1%, add it on top, leave the base frozen.

QLoRA: fitting a big model onto one small GPU

QLoRA squeezes the frozen base model down to 4-bit so it fits in memory, then trains ordinary LoRA adapters on top — letting you fine-tune a model that would never otherwise load on a single card.

LoRA solved the training memory (you only optimise a sliver). But there's a second bill: the frozen base model still has to live in GPU memory so you can run it forward. An 8B model in 16-bit is ~16 GB; a 70B model is ~140 GB. Even frozen, the big ones don't fit on one GPU. QLoRA — Quantized LoRA — attacks exactly that.

The core idea

Quantization means storing each weight with fewer bits. Instead of 16 bits per number, QLoRA stores the frozen base in a clever 4-bit format. That's a ~4× shrink: the 8B base drops from ~16 GB to ~5 GB, and a 70B model becomes something a single 48 GB card can hold. The base is only being read during training (it's frozen), so the small precision loss barely matters. The LoRA adapters you actually train stay in full precision, so learning quality holds up.

Three ingredients make it work without wrecking accuracy:

  • NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat) — a 4-bit number format designed for the bell-curve spread of neural-net weights, so it loses less information than naive 4-bit rounding.
  • Double quantization — it even quantizes the little scaling constants that quantization itself needs, squeezing out extra megabytes.
  • bfloat16 compute — when a weight is actually used in a calculation, it's temporarily expanded back to 16-bit, so the math stays stable. Storage is 4-bit; arithmetic is 16-bit.

In code, QLoRA is "LoRA, plus a quantization config when you load the base." The current libraries make it clean:

# QLoRA = load the base in 4-bit (bitsandbytes), then attach LoRA.
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig  # BitsAndBytesConfig holds the 4-bit settings
from peft import LoraConfig, prepare_model_for_kbit_training, get_peft_model

bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(                       # the recipe for 4-bit loading
    load_in_4bit=True,                          # store base weights in 4 bits, not 16
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",                  # NF4 format — best for neural-net weight spreads
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,             # quantize the scaling constants too — extra memory saved
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,      # do the actual math in 16-bit for stability
)

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(    # load an 8B model that now needs only ~5 GB
    "Qwen/Qwen3-8B",
    quantization_config=bnb,                    # apply the 4-bit recipe at load time
    device_map="auto",                          # place the model on the available GPU automatically
)
base = prepare_model_for_kbit_training(base)    # small fixes so a quantized model can train cleanly

lora = LoraConfig(                              # same LoRA dials as before
    r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear",
    lora_dropout=0.05, bias="none", task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)
model = get_peft_model(base, lora)              # 4-bit frozen base + trainable 16-bit adapters = QLoRA
▶ Output
Loading checkpoint shards: 100% ... | 4-bit base ~5.1 GB on cuda:0

In production

QLoRA is how a bank with modest hardware — or strict on-prem rules — fine-tunes at all. A regulator may forbid sending customer data to a hosted training API, so training must happen inside the bank's own VPC. QLoRA puts a capable 8–13B tune within reach of a single rented or owned 24–48 GB GPU, keeping data in-house. The trade-off is honest: training is a bit slower than pure 16-bit LoRA (there's dequantize overhead on every forward pass), and for the very highest quality on a task the base struggles with, plain LoRA or full tuning on bigger hardware can edge it out. For 95% of banking adaptation work, QLoRA is the pragmatic default.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's risk team was told, flatly, that customer transcripts could never leave the bank's own VPC — no hosted training API, full stop. Their only in-house GPU was a single 48 GB card, and a 16-bit 13B base wouldn't even load for training. With QLoRA they quantized the frozen base to 4-bit (~8 GB), trained full-precision LoRA adapters on top, and ran the whole fraud-triage fine-tune overnight inside the VPC. Nothing sensitive crossed the network boundary, and the artifact that came out — a small adapter — went straight into change control.

Going deeper — what you trade for the memory

QLoRA's savings are real but not free. Every forward pass has to dequantize 4-bit weights back to bfloat16 to do the math, so training runs roughly 20–40% slower than pure 16-bit LoRA on the same card — you're spending time to buy memory. Quality stays close to 16-bit LoRA for most adaptation tasks thanks to three design choices: NF4, a 4-bit format shaped to the bell-curve spread of neural weights; double quantization, which quantizes the quantization constants themselves to claw back a few hundred more megabytes; and bf16 compute, so only storage is lossy, not the arithmetic. The rough memory math: an 8B base drops from ~16 GB to ~5 GB, a 13B from ~26 GB to ~8 GB, a 70B from ~140 GB to ~46 GB — which is exactly what turns a single 48 GB card into a 70B-tuning machine. For the very highest quality on a task the base struggles with, plain 16-bit LoRA or full fine-tuning on bigger hardware can still edge QLoRA out; for ~95% of banking adaptation, QLoRA is the pragmatic default.

⚙️ In production

Cost: QLoRA is often the difference between "rent one GPU" and "rent a cluster" — the headline reason banks can fine-tune at all on owned hardware. Latency: this is a training-time technique; for serving you typically merge or serve the adapter on a normally-loaded base, so request latency is unaffected. Scale: it unlocks bigger bases (13B–70B) on modest cards, but the slower step time means budget more wall-clock for large runs. Failure modes: the headline pitfall is the train-vs-serve numerics mismatch — train on a 4-bit base, then merge into 16-bit, and behaviour can drift. Monitoring: confirm the 4-bit base actually loaded small (watch the VRAM report) and re-run your eval after any merge. Security/compliance: QLoRA is what keeps regulated training on-prem — no customer data leaves the bank's VPC, frequently a hard legal requirement rather than a preference.

⚠ Watch out

Quantization affects the frozen base you train against. If you later serve the merged model in full 16-bit, there can be a small mismatch between training-time and serving-time numerics. The clean habit: keep the adapter separate and serve it on the same-precision base you trained on, or evaluate carefully after any merge.

When to use QLoRA: when the base won't fit in 16-bit on your GPU, or when strict data-residency rules force training onto limited in-house hardware. When NOT: when the base already fits comfortably in 16-bit and you want maximum speed/quality — plain LoRA is faster; and avoid training on a 4-bit base if you plan to serve a 16-bit merge without re-evaluating.

🧠 Remember it

Shrink to fit, then adapt. QLoRA = 4-bit frozen base (so it loads) + full-precision LoRA (so it learns). One GPU, one big model.

SFT with TRL: instruction tuning and the data format that drives it

Supervised fine-tuning just shows the model thousands of "here's the input, here's the ideal reply" pairs until the ideal reply becomes its habit. The TRL library makes it a handful of lines.

SFT is Supervised Fine-Tuning — the workhorse. "Supervised" means every training example has a known right answer. You hand the model a prompt and the exact response you wish it had given, and training nudges its weights to make that response more likely next time. Do this across a good dataset and the model generalises the pattern.

When the examples are instructions-and-answers — "summarise this complaint" → a perfect summary — SFT is also called instruction tuning: you're teaching a base model to follow instructions and hold a conversation in your style.

The data format is the whole game

Modern SFT expects your data in one of a few clean shapes. For a chat assistant, the conversational prompt-completion format is the sweet spot — a list of messages with roles. TRL automatically applies the model's chat template and, by default, computes the training loss only on the assistant's reply, so the model learns to produce answers, not to parrot the user's question.

# One SFT training example in the conversational prompt-completion format.
example = {
  "prompt": [                                      # what the model sees — the loss is NOT computed here
    {"role": "system",
     "content": "You are BankAssist. Reply in two formal sentences, plain text."},  # bakes in house style
    {"role": "user",
     "content": "Why was I charged $35?"},         # a real customer-style question
  ],
  "completion": [                                    # the ideal reply — loss IS computed here, so the model learns it
    {"role": "assistant",
     "content": "That $35 is the overdraft item fee applied when a payment "
                "posts against insufficient funds. One courtesy waiver is "
                "available every 12 months on request."},
  ],
}

You collect thousands of these (gathering that data well is a task of its own), save them as a dataset, and train. Here is the full, current TRL loop with LoRA — this is production-shaped, not a toy:

# Supervised fine-tune a chat model on BankAssist replies, with LoRA, using TRL.
from datasets import load_dataset                 # loads your JSONL/HF dataset of prompt-completion pairs
from trl import SFTTrainer, SFTConfig            # SFTTrainer runs SFT; SFTConfig holds the settings
from peft import LoraConfig                       # so we train adapters, not the whole model

train_ds = load_dataset("json",                   # read our own exported examples ...
    data_files="bankassist_sft.jsonl", split="train")  # ... one JSON object per line

args = SFTConfig(                                  # training configuration
    output_dir="bankassist-tone-lora",            # where checkpoints + the adapter are saved
    num_train_epochs=3,                           # passes over the data — small data wants a few
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,                # examples per step (raise if GPU memory allows)
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,                # simulate a larger batch without more memory
    learning_rate=2e-4,                           # higher LR is normal for LoRA (only adapters learn)
    max_length=1024,                              # cap token length so batches fit
    assistant_only_loss=True,                     # learn ONLY from assistant turns, not user text
    bf16=True,                                     # 16-bit training — faster, less memory
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(                              # wire model + data + config + adapter together
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-8B",                        # base model to adapt (a string = TRL loads it)
    args=args,                                     # the settings above
    train_dataset=train_ds,                        # our labelled examples
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32,   # attach LoRA → this is a PEFT fine-tune
        target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
)
trainer.train()                                   # run it; the adapter lands in output_dir
trainer.save_model()                              # save the final adapter for serving
▶ Output
{'loss': 1.42, 'epoch': 1.0} ... {'loss': 0.61, 'epoch': 3.0} Model saved to bankassist-tone-lora/

Falling loss means the model is getting better at reproducing your ideal replies. (Falling loss alone is not proof it got better overall — you still need to evaluate on held-out tasks.) To do QLoRA instead, you'd add the 4-bit BitsAndBytesConfig (the quantization recipe shown earlier) via SFTConfig(model_init_kwargs=...) or by passing a pre-quantized model — same trainer, 4-bit base.

⚙️ Under the hood — why "assistant-only loss" matters

If you train on the full text (user + assistant), the model spends capacity learning to predict the customer's words too — which is useless and dilutes the signal. assistant_only_loss=True masks everything except the assistant's reply, so every gradient pushes toward "give this answer." For prompt-completion data, TRL does the equivalent by default via completion-only loss. It's a small flag with a big effect on sample efficiency.

In production

Three things decide whether an SFT run is worth shipping: data quality (a few thousand clean, on-brand examples beat a hundred thousand noisy ones), held-out evaluation (always keep a test set the model never trains on), and reproducibility (pin the base model version, dataset version, and config — for model governance you must be able to recreate exactly what you shipped). Track runs with a tool like Weights & Biases or Trackio so every experiment is logged. And budget for iteration: your first dataset will have mistakes you only notice when the model faithfully copies them.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's first SFT run looked perfect — loss fell beautifully — but the model kept ending replies with "Best, the Support Team," a signature baked into 1,200 of their mined email examples. The model had faithfully learned an artifact nobody wanted. They stripped the signatures, re-ran on 8,000 cleaned pairs with assistant_only_loss on, and the tic vanished. The lesson stuck: the training run was the easy part; the hour spent reading the data by hand was the one that mattered.

Going deeper — the knobs that decide SFT quality

Four settings do most of the work. Epochs: small datasets (a few thousand examples) usually want 1–3 passes; more and the model memorises rather than generalises — watch held-out loss, not training loss. Learning rate: LoRA tolerates a higher LR (1e-4 to 2e-4) because only the adapters move; a full fine-tune needs a far gentler 1e-5 to 2e-5. Sequence length (max_length): cap it to the shortest value that holds your real prompts and replies — longer costs memory quadratically in attention, and over-length examples are truncated from the right, silently dropping the end of your ideal answer. Loss masking: assistant_only_loss=True (on conversational data whose chat template emits a {% generation %} mask) spends every gradient on the reply, not on re-predicting the customer's words — a big win in sample efficiency. One more lever for throughput: packing concatenates short examples to fill each sequence, cutting wasted padding and speeding training on datasets of many short tickets.

⚙️ In production

Cost: a few-thousand-example LoRA SFT is an overnight single-GPU job; the expensive, recurring cost is building and curating the data, not the compute. Latency/scale: SFT changes the weights, not the serving path — a merged model serves at base speed. Failure modes: the model faithfully copies every defect in the data (template artifacts, a mis-stated fee, inconsistent tone) and falling loss hides it, so loss is never your ship signal. Monitoring: track runs in Weights & Biases or Trackio and gate releases on a held-out eval, not on loss curves. Reproducibility/compliance: pin the base-model version, dataset version, and config so you can recreate exactly what you shipped — in a regulated shop an un-reproducible fine-tune is not shippable. Security: scrub PII before data enters the pipeline; a model can memorise and later emit a rare training string, and a real customer's details surfacing in an answer is a reportable breach.

⚠ Watch out

Garbage in, garbage amplified. SFT is a mirror — if 3% of your examples use the wrong tone, misstate a fee, or leak a template artifact, the model learns that too, confidently. Clean and spot-check your data by hand before you ever hit train(). Data review is the highest-leverage hour in the whole pipeline.

When to use SFT: to teach a consistent behaviour, format, voice, or skill you can demonstrate with thousands of clean (prompt, ideal-reply) pairs. When NOT: when you only have a handful of examples (prompt instead), when the gap is facts (use RAG), or before you've cleaned the data — SFT amplifies whatever you feed it.

🧠 Remember it

Show, don't tell — a thousand times. SFT = pairs of (prompt, ideal reply); the model learns to make the ideal reply its reflex. Loss on the answer only.

Preference & alignment tuning: RLHF, RLAIF, and DPO

SFT teaches one good answer per prompt. Preference tuning goes further: it shows the model two answers and says "this one is better than that one" — teaching taste, not just correctness.

SFT has a ceiling. It can only imitate the single answer you wrote. But "good" is often comparative — reply A is warmer, safer, better-grounded than reply B, even though both are acceptable. Teaching that preference is called alignment or preference tuning, and it's what turns a competent model into one that reliably matches human judgement about quality, safety, and tone.

RLHF — the original recipe

RLHF is Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. It runs in three stages. First, you do SFT to get a decent starting model. Second, humans look at many pairs of answers and mark which is better; you train a separate reward model to predict those human judgements — essentially a model that scores any answer. Third, you use reinforcement learning (an algorithm called PPO) to update the main model so it produces answers the reward model scores highly, while a leash keeps it from drifting too far from the original. It works brilliantly — it's how the first great chat models were aligned — but it's a lot of moving parts: a reward model to train and maintain, an unstable RL loop, and three or four models in memory at once.

RLAIF — swap the humans for an AI judge

RLAIF is Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback. It's the same shape as RLHF, but instead of thousands of human labels, a strong "judge" model does the preference labelling, guided by a written constitution — a set of principles like "prefer the answer that cites a policy" or "prefer the answer that refuses to reveal account data." It's far cheaper and faster to scale than human labelling, and surprisingly competitive. The catch: your alignment is only as good as the judge and its principles — bias or blind spots in the judge flow straight into your model.

DPO — skip the reward model entirely

DPO is Direct Preference Optimization, and it's why preference tuning is now within reach of ordinary teams. DPO proved you can learn from "chosen vs rejected" pairs directly, with a simple classification-style loss — no separate reward model, no RL loop. You just need a dataset of (prompt, chosen answer, rejected answer) triples. The training nudges the model to make the chosen answer more likely and the rejected one less likely, relative to where it started. Concretely, for each pair the loss measures two things — how much more likely your model makes the chosen answer than a frozen copy of itself (the reference model), and the same for the rejected answer — then shifts the weights to widen that gap in the chosen answer's favour. No reward model scores anything; the frozen reference is the only yardstick, and the beta dial sets how hard the model is allowed to pull away from it. Same goal as RLHF, a fraction of the machinery — which is exactly why it has become the default.

RLHF / RLAIF

Trains a reward model, then optimises with RL. Powerful and flexible (RLAIF scales the labelling with an AI judge), but heavy: multiple models, an unstable loop, careful tuning. Reach for it when you need fine-grained reward shaping or ongoing online feedback.

DPO

Learns directly from preference pairs with a simple loss. No reward model, no RL, stable, runs with LoRA on one GPU. The practical default for most teams who just have "A is better than B" data.

DPO in current TRL is almost identical to SFT — the difference is the dataset shape (prompt, chosen, rejected) and the beta dial:

# Align a model with DPO on BankAssist preference pairs (current TRL API).
from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import DPOTrainer, DPOConfig             # DPOTrainer runs DPO; DPOConfig holds its settings
from peft import LoraConfig

pref_ds = load_dataset("json",                    # each row: prompt + a chosen reply + a rejected reply
    data_files="bankassist_prefs.jsonl", split="train")

args = DPOConfig(                                  # DPO-specific config
    output_dir="bankassist-aligned",              # where the aligned adapter is saved
    beta=0.1,                                      # leash strength: higher = stay closer to the start model
    learning_rate=1e-5,                           # DPO uses a smaller LR than SFT — it's a gentle nudge
    num_train_epochs=1,                           # preference tuning usually needs only a pass or two
    bf16=True,
)

trainer = DPOTrainer(                              # no separate reward model needed — that's the point
    model="bankassist-tone-lora",                 # start from the SFT'd model (align AFTER instruction tuning)
    args=args,
    train_dataset=pref_ds,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32,   # align with LoRA too — cheap and reversible
        target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
)
trainer.train()                                   # nudges chosen up, rejected down, vs the frozen reference
▶ Output
{'loss': 0.69, 'rewards/accuracies': 0.52, ...} {'loss': 0.31, 'rewards/accuracies': 0.88, ...}

Watch rewards/accuracies climb toward 1.0 — that's the share of pairs where the model now correctly prefers the chosen answer. The beta dial is the safety leash: too low and the model drifts and degrades; too high and it barely learns. 0.1 is a sensible start.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's SFT model was fluent but occasionally too casual and once offered to "waive any fee, just ask!" — a compliance no-go. The team gathered pairs: for each prompt, the chosen reply was the measured, policy-correct one; the rejected reply was the over-promising or too-casual one. One DPO pass later, the model reliably preferred the compliant phrasing — without anyone writing a reward model or babysitting an RL loop.

Going deeper — the beta dial and the DPO family

DPO's one critical knob is beta, the leash to the frozen reference model. Low beta (say 0.05) lets the model move far toward your preferences but risks drifting into degenerate or off-distribution text; high beta (0.3+) keeps it safely close but barely learns. Start around 0.1 and tune by watching rewards/accuracies (the share of pairs ranked correctly, which should climb toward 1.0) alongside a quality eval — high accuracy with falling general quality means beta is too low. DPO also spawned a useful family you'll meet in TRL: ORPO folds preference learning into SFT in a single stage, so you skip the separate alignment pass entirely; KTO learns from unpaired thumbs-up / thumbs-down labels, far cheaper to collect than matched pairs; IPO changes the loss to resist overfitting on easy pairs; and SimPO drops the reference model to save memory. RLHF/RLAIF with PPO still wins when you need fine-grained reward shaping or a continuous online-feedback loop, but for "here are chosen-vs-rejected pairs," DPO and its relatives are the pragmatic default.

⚙️ In production

Cost: DPO is dramatically cheaper to operate than RLHF — no reward model to train and maintain, no unstable RL loop, and it runs with LoRA on one GPU. RLHF keeps three-to-four models in memory and demands careful tuning; take that on only if you truly need it. Data cost: the real expense is collecting comparable preference pairs (or thumbs-up/down for KTO) — plan the labelling pipeline. Latency/scale: alignment changes weights, not serving, so there's no inference-time cost. Failure modes: too-low beta causes reward-hacking and verbose or degenerate output; non-comparable pairs (chosen and rejected on different topics) teach noise; aligning a raw base aligns gibberish. Monitoring: watch rewards/accuracies and reward margins during training, and a safety/tone eval after. Compliance: for a bank, record the constitution or rubric behind any RLAIF-style AI labels, and keep a human in the loop for high-stakes refusal and compliance behaviours — an auto-judge's blind spots flow straight into the model.

⚠ Watch out

Align after you instruction-tune, not instead of it. DPO sharpens preferences on top of a model that already answers well; run it on a raw base and you'll align gibberish. And keep your preference pairs genuinely comparable — the chosen and rejected should answer the same prompt, differing in quality, not topic.

When to use preference tuning: after SFT, when "good" is comparative — safer, warmer, more policy-correct phrasing — and you have (or can judge) chosen-vs-rejected pairs; DPO/ORPO/KTO for most teams. When NOT: before you have a competent SFT model, when a single ideal answer per prompt already captures what you want (plain SFT is enough), or without a reward model and online loop you can actually maintain (don't reach for PPO-based RLHF).

🧠 Remember it

SFT teaches an answer; DPO teaches taste. RLHF/RLAIF get there via a reward model + RL; DPO skips both and learns straight from "chosen beats rejected."

Data prep: building the dataset, synthetic data, and distillation

A fine-tune is only as good as its data. The real work isn't the training run — it's assembling a few thousand clean, on-brand, correctly-labelled examples. Here's how banks actually get them.

You now know how to train. But where do the thousands of (prompt, ideal reply) pairs come from? This is where most of the effort — and most of the quality — lives. There are three honest sources, usually blended.

1. Mine your own history

Banks sit on gold: past support tickets, resolved complaints, chat transcripts, approved email replies. These are real customer questions with human-approved answers — the best possible training data because they already match your voice and your rules. The work is curation: pick the good resolutions, strip personal data, and reshape them into the prompt-completion format.

2. Generate synthetic data

Real logs run out, and some scenarios are rare (a specific fraud pattern, an edge-case dispute). Synthetic data generation uses a strong LLM to manufacture training examples — plausible customer questions and ideal answers you'd struggle to collect naturally. You seed it with your policies and a few real examples, then ask for many variations.

# Generate synthetic SFT examples with a strong model (any frontier LLM works).
from openai import OpenAI                          # using the OpenAI client here; the pattern is provider-agnostic
import json
client = OpenAI()                                  # reads the API key from the environment

policy = "Overdraft item fee: $35; one courtesy waiver per 12 months on request."  # ground truth to anchor answers

resp = client.chat.completions.create(             # ask the model to invent realistic Q/A pairs
    model="gpt-4.1",                               # a current, capable generation model
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content":
        f"Using ONLY this policy: '{policy}', write 5 realistic customer "
        f"questions and ideal 2-sentence formal answers as JSON "
        f"[{{'q':..., 'a':...}}]. Do not invent facts beyond the policy."}],  # the anti-hallucination guardrail
)
pairs = json.loads(resp.choices[0].message.content)  # parse into usable Q/A pairs to add to the dataset
▶ Output
[{"q": "Can my overdraft fee be removed?", "a": "A courtesy waiver of the $35 overdraft item fee is available once every 12 months on request. ..."}, ...]

3. Distillation — teacher → student

Distillation is a focused kind of synthetic data: you use a big, expensive teacher model to produce high-quality answers, then fine-tune a small, cheap student model to imitate them. You're "distilling" the teacher's skill on your task into a model you can run for pennies. The teacher answers 10,000 of your prompts; the student trains on those answers; now your small in-house model performs like the frontier model on that narrow slice — at a tiny fraction of the cost and fully on-prem.

In production

Data prep at a bank carries compliance weight, not just engineering weight:

  • PII first. Strip or synthesise names, account numbers, and balances before data touches a training pipeline. A model can memorise and later regurgitate rare training strings — a real customer's details leaking in an answer is a breach. Synthetic data shines here: it's realistic without being real.
  • Check the teacher's licence. Some frontier providers restrict using their outputs to train competing models. Read the terms before you distil — this is a legal question, not just a technical one.
  • Quality filter the synthetic set. LLM-generated data can be subtly wrong or repetitive. Run it through validation (does it respect the policy? is it de-duplicated? does a second model or a human rate it as good?) before training on it.
  • Keep lineage. Record where every example came from (mined / synthetic / distilled), which teacher and prompt produced it, and who approved it. Governance will ask.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist needed training data for a rare dispute type that appeared in only 40 real tickets — nowhere near enough. They seeded a strong model with those 40 real examples plus the exact policy text and generated 2,000 synthetic variations, then ran every one through a validator that checked it quoted the fee correctly and matched the house tone, and had a human spot-check a 5% sample. Of 2,000, about 1,600 passed. Blended with the 40 real tickets, that gave a clean, on-policy dataset for a scenario they could never have mined enough of — and every example carried a tag saying whether it was mined or synthetic.

Going deeper — how much data, and how clean

Quantity matters less than people expect; quality matters more. For a focused behaviour or format fine-tune, a few thousand clean, on-brand examples routinely beat a hundred thousand noisy ones — the model mirrors whatever it sees, so noise is actively harmful, not just wasted. Three curation steps repay themselves many times over. Deduplicate: near-duplicate examples let the model memorise instead of generalise and quietly skew the distribution. Balance: make sure rare but important cases (a specific fraud pattern, a refusal) are represented, or the model learns they don't matter. Validate synthetic output: LLM-generated data is often subtly wrong or repetitive, so filter it — does it respect the policy? is it unique? would a second model or a human rate it as good? On distillation specifically, the student is capped at the teacher's quality and inherits its biases, and training a model only on another model's output, round after round, causes "model collapse" where diversity drains away — which is exactly why you anchor to real policy text and salt in genuine human examples.

⚙️ In production

Security/PII first: strip or synthesise names, account numbers, and balances before data touches the pipeline — a model can memorise and later regurgitate a rare training string, and a real customer's details leaking in an answer is a breach. Synthetic data shines here: realistic without being real. Legal: check the teacher model's licence before distilling — some providers forbid using their outputs to train competing models; this is a legal question, not just technical. Cost: generation is cheap per example but the quality-filter and human-review steps are the real spend — budget for them. Failure modes: un-filtered synthetic data injects repetition and subtle factual drift; un-deduplicated data causes memorisation. Monitoring/lineage: record where every example came from (mined / synthetic / distilled), which teacher and prompt produced it, and who approved it — governance will ask you to prove the provenance of the data behind a shipped model.

⚠ Watch out

Synthetic data inherits the generator's mistakes and blind spots. If you train only on a teacher's answers, you cap the student at the teacher's quality and its biases — and repeated self-training can cause "model collapse," where variety quietly drains away. Always anchor synthetic data to real policies and salt in genuine human examples.

When to use synthetic/distilled data: to fill rare or sensitive scenarios you can't mine enough of, and to pour a frontier teacher's skill into a small in-house student — always anchored to real policy and blended with human examples. When NOT: as your only source (you'll cap quality at the teacher and risk collapse), when the teacher's licence forbids it, or before you've built the validation and PII-scrubbing steps.

🧠 Remember it

Mine it, make it, or distil it. Real logs are gold, synthetic fills the gaps, distillation pours a big teacher's skill into a small student. Scrub PII before any of it trains.

Fine-tuning embedding models for domain jargon

The highest-ROI fine-tune in banking often isn't the chat model at all — it's the little embedding model behind your search, taught to understand your acronyms and products.

Remember how RAG works: an embedding model turns text into a vector (a list of numbers capturing meaning) so that similar meanings sit close together, and search finds the nearest chunks. Off-the-shelf embedding models are trained on the open web — so they have a weak grasp of your internal jargon. To a generic model, "Reg E," "RDC," and "the courtesy pay program" are near-gibberish; it can't tell they're closely related to a customer asking about "disputing a mobile check deposit error." Retrieval misses, and the whole RAG answer is wrong — no matter how good your chat model is.

The idea: teach "these mean the same thing"

Fine-tuning an embedding model is contrastive learning: you show it pairs of texts that should be close (an anchor and a positive) and it reshapes its vector space to pull them together — and implicitly pushes unrelated texts apart. Feed it pairs like ("can I reverse a mobile deposit?", "Remote Deposit Capture (RDC) dispute procedure") and it learns that your customers' plain language maps to your internal document language.

The clever part: with the standard loss, you don't even need to label negatives. MultipleNegativesRankingLoss treats the other positives in the same batch as negatives automatically — so a dataset of just (question, right-passage) pairs is enough.

# Fine-tune an embedding model on BankAssist query→passage pairs.
from datasets import load_dataset
from sentence_transformers import (                # the standard library for embedding models
    SentenceTransformer, SentenceTransformerTrainer, SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments)
from sentence_transformers.losses import MultipleNegativesRankingLoss

model = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5")  # a strong general base embedding model to adapt

train_ds = load_dataset("json",                   # rows with an 'anchor' (customer question) ...
    data_files="bank_pairs.jsonl", split="train") # ... and a 'positive' (the correct internal passage)

loss = MultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model)        # in-batch negatives: other rows act as wrong answers

args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(       # training settings
    output_dir="bank-embeddings",                 # where the tuned embedding model is saved
    num_train_epochs=2,                           # a couple of passes is usually plenty
    per_device_train_batch_size=32,               # BIGGER batch = more in-batch negatives = better
    learning_rate=2e-5,                           # gentle LR — we're nudging, not rebuilding
)

trainer = SentenceTransformerTrainer(             # wire model + data + loss together
    model=model, args=args, train_dataset=train_ds, loss=loss)
trainer.train()                                   # reshape the vector space around bank jargon
model.save_pretrained("bank-embeddings")          # save it to plug into your RAG retriever
▶ Output
{'loss': 0.84, 'epoch': 1.0} ... {'loss': 0.19, 'epoch': 2.0} Saved to bank-embeddings/
⚙️ Under the hood — why batch size matters here

With in-batch negatives, each anchor is contrasted against every other positive in the batch. A batch of 32 gives each question 31 "hard-ish" wrong answers to push away from; a batch of 128 gives 127. More negatives sharpen the signal, so for embedding fine-tuning you generally want the largest batch your GPU allows — the opposite instinct from chat fine-tuning, where tiny batches are fine. Mining true hard negatives (plausible-but-wrong passages) and adding them explicitly pushes quality even further.

In production

Why this is often the best first fine-tune a bank does: it's cheap (embedding models are small — millions, not billions, of parameters — and train in minutes), safe (it improves retrieval, never generates customer-facing text, so it can't hallucinate a fee), and high-leverage (better retrieval lifts the quality ceiling of your entire RAG system at once). The catch you must plan for: if you retrain the embedding model, you must re-embed and re-index your whole document store — old vectors from the generic model and new vectors from the tuned model live in different coordinate systems and can't be compared. Schedule that re-index, and version your index alongside the embedding model so a query always hits vectors built by the same model.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's RAG kept missing when customers used plain language for internal terms — "reverse a mobile deposit" never retrieved the "Remote Deposit Capture (RDC) dispute" procedure, so the answer was wrong no matter how good the chat model was. They built ~6,000 (customer-phrasing → correct-passage) pairs from resolved tickets, fine-tuned a small BGE embedding model for a few minutes on one GPU with in-batch negatives, and recall@5 on a held-out query set jumped from 0.71 to 0.93. One cheap, safe tune lifted the quality ceiling of the entire assistant — then they re-indexed the whole document store so every vector came from the new model.

Going deeper — hard negatives and measuring the lift

In-batch negatives (where every other positive in the batch acts as a wrong answer) get you a long way for free, which is why bigger batches help so much here — 128 gives each query 127 contrasts, 32 gives only 31. The next quality step is hard negatives: passages that look plausible but are wrong (a different fee's policy, a neighbouring product), mined by running your current retriever and grabbing high-ranked incorrect hits. Adding a few explicit hard negatives per query teaches the sharp distinctions that in-batch randoms miss. Measure the result with retrieval metrics, not loss — recall@k (did the right passage make the top k?) and NDCG (is it ranked near the top?) on a held-out query set, compared against the off-the-shelf base. Two design choices to pin down early: the embedding dimension (it fixes your vector-store schema) and whether the base supports Matryoshka truncation (letting you shorten vectors later to trade a little accuracy for a lot of storage and speed).

⚙️ In production

Cost: embedding models are small (millions, not billions, of parameters), so this is often the cheapest fine-tune a bank can do — minutes on one GPU. Safety: it's also the safest customer-facing-adjacent tune, because a retriever ranks text, it never generates it — a better embedding can't hallucinate a fee. Leverage: retrieval quality is the ceiling of the whole RAG system, so lifting it improves every downstream answer at once. The big operational cost — re-indexing: a retrained embedding model lives in a new vector space, so you must re-embed and re-index your entire document store; for millions of chunks that's a real batch job to schedule, with compute and a cutover plan. Failure mode: mixing vectors from two models in one index returns nonsense silently. Monitoring/compliance: version the index alongside the embedding model so a query always hits vectors built by the same model, and keep the pairs dataset for reproducibility.

⚠ Watch out

Never mix embeddings from two different models in one index. A query embedded by the tuned model, searched against chunks embedded by the old one, returns nonsense — distances across different vector spaces are meaningless. Re-index everything on every embedding-model change, no exceptions.

When to fine-tune embeddings: when retrieval misses because off-the-shelf models don't grasp your acronyms, products, or customers' plain-language phrasing — usually the highest-ROI first fine-tune in a bank. When NOT: when retrieval is already strong (fix the chat model or prompts instead), or when you can't afford to re-index the whole store after — never ship a new embedding model against an old index.

🧠 Remember it

Teach the retriever your slang. Fine-tuning embeddings on (question → right passage) pairs lifts the ceiling of all of RAG — cheap, safe, high ROI. Re-index after.

Fine-tuning encoder & seq2seq models (BERT, T5)

Not every fine-tune is a chatty LLM. Sometimes the right tool is a tiny model that doesn't write at all — it reads a sentence and stamps a label, or rewrites one short text into another. That's where BERT and T5 shine.

So far every model in this chapter has been a decoder — a generative LLM that writes free text one token at a time. But two older, smaller families are still the best tool for whole classes of banking jobs, and they fine-tune beautifully on modest hardware.

An encoder model (the BERT family) reads a whole sentence at once and turns it into a rich understanding of the text — but it never generates. You bolt a tiny classification head on top and it outputs a label: "this ticket is a dispute," "this message is angry," "this token is an account number." A seq2seq model (an encoder-decoder, like T5) does both: it reads an input and generates a transformed output — great for "rewrite this messy complaint into one clean sentence" or "turn this request into a structured field." Think of it this way: an encoder is a judge that gives a verdict, a decoder is a writer that drafts prose, and seq2seq is a translator that turns one text into another.

The workflow: Hugging Face Trainer, not TRL

Generative SFT used TRL's SFTTrainer. Encoder and seq2seq fine-tuning use the plain Hugging Face Trainer instead, with a different model loader for each shape: AutoModelForSequenceClassification for whole-sentence classification (intent, sentiment, complaint type), AutoModelForTokenClassification for per-word tagging (a PII tagger that marks every account number and name), and AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM (with Seq2SeqTrainer) for text-to-text. Because these models are small — BERT-base is ~110M parameters, not 8B — you usually full fine-tune them directly on one modest GPU, no LoRA or quantization needed.

Here's a complete, current intent classifier for BankAssist — the router that decides which flow a message belongs to:

# Fine-tune a small BERT encoder as a fast BankAssist intent classifier.
from datasets import load_dataset                     # loads our labelled (text, label) rows
from transformers import (AutoTokenizer,              # turns text into the token IDs the model reads
    AutoModelForSequenceClassification,               # BERT body + a fresh classification head on top
    TrainingArguments, Trainer, DataCollatorWithPadding)  # the training loop + per-batch padding

labels = ["balance", "card_lost", "dispute", "loan", "other"]  # our fixed set of intent classes
ds = load_dataset("json", data_files="bank_intents.jsonl")     # rows: {"text": ..., "label": 0..4}

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")   # the tokenizer that MATCHES this base
def encode(b): return tok(b["text"], truncation=True)     # truncate over-long text to BERT's 512-token limit
ds = ds.map(encode, batched=True)                         # pre-tokenize the whole dataset once

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(  # load BERT ...
    "bert-base-uncased", num_labels=len(labels))            # ... with a new head sized to our 5 classes

args = TrainingArguments(                            # training settings
    output_dir="bank-intent-bert",                  # where checkpoints are saved
    num_train_epochs=3,                             # a few passes is plenty for a small classifier
    per_device_train_batch_size=16,                 # encoders are tiny, so batches can be large
    learning_rate=2e-5,                             # gentle LR is the standard for BERT fine-tuning
    eval_strategy="epoch",                          # score the held-out set after every epoch
)

trainer = Trainer(                                   # wire model + data + config together
    model=model, args=args,
    train_dataset=ds["train"], eval_dataset=ds["test"],
    processing_class=tok,                           # current API — replaces the old `tokenizer=` arg
    data_collator=DataCollatorWithPadding(tok),     # pad each batch to its longest row, not a fixed max
)
trainer.train()                                     # full fine-tune the whole 110M-param model — no LoRA
▶ Output
{'eval_loss': 0.21, 'eval_accuracy': 0.96, 'epoch': 3.0}

For a PII tagger, the shape barely changes: swap in AutoModelForTokenClassification and give it a label per token (e.g. O, ACCOUNT, NAME) so the model marks exactly which words to redact. For a seq2seq job — say, normalising a rambling complaint into one structured line — you switch to the text-to-text loader and trainer:

# Seq2seq (T5): read a messy complaint, generate a clean one-line summary.
from transformers import (AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM,     # T5 = an encoder-decoder that GENERATES text
    Seq2SeqTrainer, Seq2SeqTrainingArguments, DataCollatorForSeq2Seq)  # the seq2seq variants of the loop

model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained("t5-small")  # a small text-in/text-out base to adapt
collator = DataCollatorForSeq2Seq(tok, model=model)       # pads inputs AND target labels together
# Seq2SeqTrainingArguments adds predict_with_generate=True so eval actually decodes text;
# then Seq2SeqTrainer(model, args, ..., data_collator=collator).train() — same rhythm as above.

How this differs from generative SFT

Encoder / seq2seq (Trainer)

Small models (100M–many fewer than 1B), so you full fine-tune on one GPU — no LoRA, no 4-bit. A classifier outputs a label with a probability, not prose, so it can't hallucinate a fee. Inference is milliseconds, often even on CPU, and the output is deterministic and easy to audit. Loss is cross-entropy on the label (or on the generated tokens for T5).

Generative LLM SFT (TRL)

Billions of parameters, so you reach for LoRA/QLoRA to tune at all. The output is open-ended text that must be checked for correctness and safety. Latency is higher, cost per call larger, and behaviour is harder to pin down. Loss is next-token prediction over the assistant's reply.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist needed to route every incoming message to the right flow — balance, lost card, dispute, loan — before spending money on an LLM. Early on they asked a big generative model "which intent is this?" — it worked, but cost real tokens and sometimes replied with a sentence instead of a clean label. They fine-tuned bert-base-uncased on 12,000 labelled tickets instead. The result: a 110 MB model that classifies in ~8 ms on a CPU at 96% accuracy, returns a proper probability so low-confidence messages fall to an "other" bucket for a human, and never once invents an answer. The expensive LLM now runs only after the cheap, auditable router has decided it's needed.

⚙️ In production

Cost: these models are tiny — full fine-tuning is minutes-to-hours on one modest GPU, and serving is so cheap that a classifier often runs happily on CPU, making it the ideal high-volume front-door (routing, triage, guardrails) before any costly LLM call. Latency: single-digit milliseconds per classification versus hundreds for a generative reply. Scale: one small GPU (or a CPU box) handles enormous throughput, so these are perfect for scoring every message, not just some. Failure modes: a classifier always returns one of its known classes — it cannot say "I don't know" unless you add an explicit other/abstain class and a confidence threshold; class imbalance quietly biases it toward common labels; and label drift (new complaint types appearing) degrades it silently. Monitoring: track per-class precision/recall and the share of low-confidence predictions, not just overall accuracy. Security/compliance: deterministic, auditable outputs are a governance gift — a PII tagger that flags account numbers for redaction, or a router whose every decision carries a probability, is far easier to sign off than a free-text generator.

⚠ Watch out

A classifier can't abstain on its own. Feed a trained 5-class intent model something it's never seen and it will still confidently pick one of its five labels — so always add an other class and a confidence threshold that routes uncertain inputs to a human. Two more traps: you must tokenize at serving time with the exact same tokenizer you trained with, and classic BERT caps at 512 tokens — a long complaint gets silently truncated, so check your inputs fit (or chunk them).

One-line note: vision models (ViT, for image classification) and speech models (ASR for speech-to-text, TTS for text-to-speech) fine-tune with this very same Trainer pattern — you just swap the loader (e.g. AutoModelForImageClassification) and the processor. For a text-first banking assistant they're rarely needed, so they're out of scope here.

When to fine-tune an encoder/seq2seq model: whenever the job is to decide (intent, sentiment, complaint type, PII tagging) or to transform one short text into another at high volume and low latency — these beat an LLM on cost, speed, and auditability. When NOT: when the task genuinely needs open-ended generation, reasoning, or conversation — that's a decoder LLM's job.

🧠 Remember it

Encoders decide, decoders write, seq2seq transforms. For labels and tags, fine-tune a tiny BERT with the plain Trainer — full fine-tune, milliseconds, no hallucinations.

Evaluating a fine-tune: did it actually help? (and catastrophic forgetting)

Falling training loss is not success. The only honest question is "is the model better on tasks it will really face — without having gotten worse at everything else?"

Training will always report a lovely falling loss, because the model is memorising your examples. That tells you nothing about whether it generalises, and nothing about what it may have broken. Real evaluation is where fine-tuning projects are won or lost.

Rule one: a held-out test set

Split your data before training: most for training, a slice the model never sees for testing. After training, measure performance on that held-out set. If it's good on data it trained on but poor on the held-out set, it overfit — it memorised instead of learning. This split is non-negotiable.

Rule two: measure what you actually care about

Pick task-shaped metrics, not just loss. For a classifier, accuracy and F1. For structured output, the percent of replies that are valid JSON with the right fields. For tone and helpfulness, an LLM-as-judge (a strong model scoring replies against a rubric) or human review on a sample. Always compare three contenders on the same test set: the base model, the base model with a good prompt (your real baseline), and your fine-tune. If the fine-tune doesn't beat a well-prompted base, it wasn't worth the pipeline.

A word on the classic NLP metrics

Courses and papers love three old-school text scores. Know what each means — and why, for an open-ended assistant, they're only side-dials.

MetricWhat it measuresUse it forIts limit
PerplexityHow "surprised" the model is by held-out text — the exponential of the average loss; lower means it predicts the words better.Tracking language-modelling quality while training; comparing models on the same corpus.Says nothing about task correctness — a fluent, confident, wrong answer can still score beautifully.
BLEUN-gram precision overlap against a reference — how much of the model's wording appears in the "right" answer.Translation and other constrained generation with one expected wording.Brittle for open-ended replies; it punishes perfectly valid paraphrases and synonyms.
ROUGERecall-oriented overlap against a reference — how much of the reference the output manages to cover.Summarisation, where covering the key points is the job.Still surface word-matching; it misses meaning and paraphrase just like BLEU.

For BankAssist's open-ended answers these overlap metrics are weak proxies — a correct reply can be worded a hundred ways — so this chapter leans instead on the task metrics above, an LLM-as-judge, and a held-out golden set.

Rule three: watch for catastrophic forgetting

Catastrophic forgetting is the sneaky failure: in learning your narrow task, the model forgets general abilities it used to have.
