You train it to classify complaints beautifully, and discover it now writes worse summaries, drops its multilingual skill, or ignores safety guardrails. Because your task-specific eval looks great, you won't notice unless you deliberately test the old skills too.

How to fight forgetting: train gently (fewer epochs, lower learning rate — PEFT/LoRA already helps because the base stays frozen), mix in some general examples alongside your task data so the model rehearses old skills, and keep a general-skills regression suite you run after every fine-tune.

# A minimal "did it help AND did it break anything?" check.
from datasets import load_dataset

held_out = load_dataset("json", data_files="bank_test.jsonl", split="train")  # task test set — never trained on
regression = load_dataset("json", data_files="general_skills.jsonl", split="train")  # old-skills guard set

def score(model, ds):                              # run the model over a dataset, return a quality score
    return sum(judge(model.generate(x["prompt"]), x["reference"]) for x in ds) / len(ds)  # avg rubric score

print("task  — base:", score(base, held_out),      # baseline on the task we're improving
      "tuned:", score(tuned, held_out))            # want this HIGHER than base
print("general — base:", score(base, regression),  # baseline on unrelated general skills
      "tuned:", score(tuned, regression))          # want this NOT lower — else it forgot
▶ Output
task — base: 0.61 tuned: 0.89 # fine-tune clearly helped the target task general — base: 0.83 tuned: 0.81 # barely moved — no catastrophic forgetting ✅

In production — the toolchain

The ecosystem you'll actually reach for: Hugging Face Transformers + PEFT + TRL for the training itself; Unsloth for 2× faster, lower-memory LoRA/QLoRA runs (a drop-in that's great for single-GPU work); and Axolotl for config-driven training where a whole run is described in one YAML file — ideal for reproducible, reviewable bank pipelines. For evaluation, lean on a held-out set plus an LLM-judge harness, and track every run (base version, data version, config, scores) in an experiment tracker so model governance can trace exactly what you shipped and why it was approved. A fine-tune without a logged, reproducible eval is not shippable in a regulated shop.

# Unsloth: the same LoRA idea, tuned for speed and low memory (current API).
from unsloth import FastLanguageModel             # Unsloth's optimized model loader
model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(  # loads base + tokenizer together
    model_name="unsloth/Qwen3-8B-bnb-4bit",       # a pre-quantized 4-bit base = fast load, low VRAM
    max_seq_length=2048,                          # cap sequence length to bound memory
    load_in_4bit=True,                            # QLoRA-style 4-bit base
)
model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(          # attach LoRA adapters, Unsloth-accelerated
    model, r=16, lora_alpha=32,                   # same rank/alpha dials you already know
    target_modules=["q_proj","k_proj","v_proj","o_proj",  # which matrices get adapters ...
                    "gate_proj","up_proj","down_proj"],   # ... attention + MLP projections
    use_gradient_checkpointing="unsloth",         # Unsloth's memory-saving checkpointing mode
)
# from here you hand `model` to TRL's SFTTrainer exactly as before.
▶ Output
==((====))== Unsloth: Fast Qwen3 patching. Loaded in 4-bit. ~5.0 GB VRAM.
🏦 Picture this

BankAssist's complaint-classifier fine-tune scored a gorgeous 0.89 on its task — ship it, surely. Their regression suite said otherwise: the same model's general-summarisation score had slipped from 0.83 to 0.74, and one safety probe that used to refuse a wire-fraud how-to now answered it. Catastrophic forgetting had traded a narrow win for two real losses, one of them an incident waiting to happen. They retrained with fewer epochs, a lower learning rate, and 15% general-skills examples mixed in; the task score held at 0.87, general stayed at 0.82, and the safety probe refused again. Only then did it ship.

Going deeper — the three-way comparison and judge discipline

The single most informative eval is a three-way one on the same held-out set: the raw base, the base with a good prompt (your real baseline), and your fine-tune. Skipping the middle contender is how teams ship a pipeline that a well-written prompt would have beaten for free. Pick metrics shaped like the task: accuracy and F1 for a classifier, percent-valid-JSON-with-right-fields for structured output, and an LLM-as-judge (a strong model scoring against a written rubric) or human review for tone and helpfulness. Judges need discipline of their own: pin the judge model and the rubric, watch for position bias (judges favour the first answer — randomise order) and length bias (they favour longer replies), and calibrate the judge against human labels on a sample so you trust its scores. For catastrophic forgetting, keep a standing regression suite of old general skills and safety/refusal cases, and run it after every tune — LoRA already helps because the base stays frozen, and mixing a slice of general examples into training rehearses the old skills.

⚙️ In production

Gate on eval, never on loss: falling training loss only means the model memorised your examples — releases are gated on a held-out task eval plus a regression suite, not on the loss curve. Cost: an LLM-judge harness costs real API tokens per run; budget it and cache judgements. Failure modes: overfitting (great on train, poor on held-out), catastrophic forgetting (task up, general skills down), and — most dangerous — a silent safety regression the task eval can't see. Monitoring: track every run's base version, data version, config, and all three scores in an experiment tracker; in production, keep sampling live answers against the rubric to catch drift after deploy. Toolchain: Transformers + PEFT + TRL to train, Unsloth for 2× faster low-memory LoRA/QLoRA, Axolotl for config-driven YAML runs. Compliance: a fine-tune without a logged, reproducible eval is not shippable in a regulated shop — governance must trace exactly what shipped and why it was approved; in banking a capability regression is a bug, a safety regression is a reportable incident.

⚠ Watch out

The most dangerous fine-tune is one that aced its task eval and silently lost a safety behaviour — a model that used to refuse "tell me how to commit wire fraud" but, after tuning, now helps. Always include safety and refusal cases in your regression suite. In banking, a capability regression is a bug; a safety regression is an incident.

When to trust a fine-tune: when it beats a well-prompted base on a held-out set and your regression suite shows no general-skill or safety loss — then ship. When NOT: when it only beats the raw base (a prompt may be enough), when you only measured the target task (you can't see what broke), or when the run isn't reproducible — don't ship what you can't recreate.

🧠 Remember it

Beat a good prompt, break nothing. Judge a fine-tune on a held-out set vs a well-prompted base — and keep a regression suite so you'd catch what it forgot.

Serving a fine-tuned model: adapter swapping at scale

The payoff of LoRA shows up at serving time: host one base model in memory and hot-swap many tiny adapters on top — many specialised models for the price of one.

You've trained an adapter. Now customers need answers. There are two ways to ship a LoRA fine-tune, and the choice shapes your whole serving architecture.

Option A — merge the adapter into the base

You can merge the LoRA correction permanently back into the base weights, producing a single standalone model with zero adapter overhead at inference. It's the simplest thing to serve — just another model — and the fastest per request, because there's no extra adapter math.

# Merge a LoRA adapter into the base to get one standalone model.
from peft import AutoPeftModelForCausalLM          # loads a base + its trained adapter together

model = AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(  # reload base + adapter from the training output
    "bankassist-tone-lora")
merged = model.merge_and_unload()                  # fold B·A into W → a plain model, adapter gone
merged.save_pretrained("bankassist-merged")        # save the fused model for normal serving
▶ Output
Saved merged model to bankassist-merged/ (serve like any base model)

The downside: you're back to one big model per behaviour. Three fine-tunes (tone, fraud-triage, collections) means three full models to store and load — losing LoRA's lightness.

Option B — serve the base + hot-swap adapters

The powerful pattern. A modern inference server (like vLLM) loads the base model once and keeps many small adapters alongside it. Each request names which adapter it wants, and the server applies that adapter's correction on the fly. One 5 GB base in memory can back dozens of 40 MB adapters — dozens of specialised models, one base's worth of GPU.

# Serve a base model with multiple hot-swappable LoRA adapters via vLLM.
# Start the server: --enable-lora turns on adapter support.
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-8B \                         # the single base model, loaded once
  --enable-lora \                                 # allow LoRA adapters to be attached
  --max-loras 4 \                                 # how many adapters can be active at once
  --max-lora-rank 16 \                            # must be >= the rank your adapters trained at
  --lora-modules tone=./bankassist-tone-lora \    # register a named adapter at startup ...
                 fraud=./bankassist-fraud-lora    # ... and another; name it per request

# A request just names the adapter it wants in the "model" field.
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "tone",                            # route THIS request through the "tone" adapter
       "messages": [{"role": "user",
                     "content": "Why was I charged $35?"}]}'   # same base, tone-specialised reply
▶ Output
{"choices":[{"message":{"role":"assistant","content":"That $35 is the overdraft item fee ... One courtesy waiver is available every 12 months on request."}}]}

In production

Adapter swapping is a serious cost and governance win for banks:

  • Cost. One GPU backs many business lines. You don't pay for three idle models when traffic is uneven; the shared base absorbs it.
  • Safe, fast rollout. A new adapter is a ~40 MB file. You can canary it to 5% of traffic, compare metrics, and roll back by pointing requests at the old adapter name — no multi-gigabyte redeploy. (With runtime adapter loading enabled, you can even register new adapters without restarting the server.)
  • Governance. Each adapter is independently versioned, approved, and audited. "Which model answered this 2026 complaint?" resolves to "base vX + adapter tone-v7," both pinned and logged.

The trade-offs to weigh: a tiny per-token overhead versus a merged model (usually worth it), a rank ceiling (--max-lora-rank must cover your biggest adapter), and the operational discipline of pinning base + adapter versions together so an answer is always reproducible. When a single behaviour dominates all your traffic and latency is sacred, merge; when you serve many behaviours or iterate fast, swap.

🏦 Picture this

BankAssist ran three fine-tunes — tone, fraud-triage, collections — and nearly deployed three separate 8B models: three GPUs, three idle-capacity bills. Instead they put one base on a vLLM server with --enable-lora and registered all three 40 MB adapters beside it. Each request names its adapter in the model field; one ~5 GB base in memory now serves all three business lines on a single card. When they shipped a new tone adapter, they canaried it to 5% of traffic by routing those requests to tone-v8, compared metrics for a day, and promoted it — no multi-gigabyte redeploy, and rollback was just pointing requests back at tone-v7.

Going deeper — batching, ranks, and runtime loading

Modern servers don't just hold many adapters; they can serve different adapters in the same batch, applying each request's B·A correction while sharing the base's heavy matmuls — so multi-adapter throughput stays close to single-model throughput, with only a small per-token overhead versus a merged model. Two settings govern the setup: --max-loras caps how many adapters can be active at once (and thus GPU memory for adapter weights), while --max-lora-rank must be at least the highest rank you trained — set it too low and you get a dimension mismatch, a crash or silent truncation, not graceful degradation. For fast iteration, runtime loading (gated by VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING=1, with adapters added via a load endpoint) lets you register a new adapter without restarting the server. The merge-vs-swap decision is the real architectural fork: merge when one behaviour dominates all traffic and every millisecond counts (zero adapter overhead, but you're back to a full model per behaviour); swap when you serve many behaviours or iterate fast (one base's footprint, instant rollout and rollback).

⚙️ In production

Cost: one GPU backs many business lines — you don't pay for three idle models when traffic is uneven; the shared base absorbs it. Latency/throughput: a merged model has zero adapter overhead; hot-swapping adds a small per-token cost but keeps batched throughput near single-model levels — measure both under real load and pick per use case. Scale & rollout: a new adapter is a ~40 MB file, so you can canary to 5% and roll back by name, no gigabyte redeploy; with runtime loading you add adapters without a restart. Failure modes: an adapter on the wrong or differently-quantized base degrades silently (not a clean error); --max-lora-rank below an adapter's rank crashes or truncates. Monitoring: log the exact base hash + adapter version that produced every answer. Compliance: "which model answered this 2026 complaint?" must resolve to "base vX + adapter tone-v7," both pinned, logged, independently approved, and reproducible — pin base and adapter versions together.

⚠ Watch out

Adapters are only valid on the exact base they were trained against. Serve a "tone" adapter trained on Qwen3-8B on top of a different base — or a differently-quantized one — and you'll get subtly degraded, hard-to-debug output rather than a clean error. Pin and record the base-model version with every adapter, and re-validate after any base upgrade.

When to swap adapters: when you serve several behaviours, iterate quickly, or want cheap canaries and instant rollback — one base, many 40 MB adapters, one GPU. When to merge instead: when a single behaviour dominates all traffic and latency is sacred. When NOT to serve an adapter at all: on any base other than the exact one it trained against — re-validate after every base upgrade.

🧠 Remember it

One engine, many hats. Merge when a single behaviour rules; swap adapters when you serve many — one base, dozens of 40 MB personalities, one GPU's footprint.

🎯 interview 🏭 production 🏦 banking

Interview Prep — Questions from Basic to Advanced

A current (2025–2026) question bank for RAG and agentic-AI engineering roles, graded Basic → Intermediate → Advanced. Each answer is a complete answer you could actually teach: a crisp reply first, then the why, a concrete BankAssist example, the trade-off that decides it, and the extra line a strong candidate adds — then the banking system-design prompts to rehearse.

LLM Fundamentals

BasicQ. What is a large language model, in one sentence?
A. A neural network trained on massive text to predict the next token given the preceding ones — answering, summarizing and coding all emerge from that one objective. Why it matters: it is a probabilistic text-continuation engine, not a database, so it can be fluent and wrong at the same time. BankAssist: when a customer asks "why was I charged twice?", the model is not looking up the truth — it is predicting a plausible reply, which is exactly why we ground it on the real transaction record first. Trade-off: fluency is free, correctness is not. Strong answer adds: because it predicts rather than retrieves, accuracy is something you engineer around it (retrieval, tools, validation), not something it guarantees.
BasicQ. What is a token, and why do you pay per token?
A. A token is a sub-word unit (roughly ¾ of a word in English) produced by the tokenizer; models read and write only in tokens. You pay per input + output token because GPU compute scales with tokens processed. BankAssist: pasting a 12-page terms-and-conditions PDF into every prompt can be ~15k tokens a call — multiply by a million calls a month and that one habit is most of the bill. Trade-off: more context can help accuracy but each token costs money and latency. Strong answer adds: rule of thumb ~4 characters/token, and non-English or code tokenizes worse, so a Hindi or JSON-heavy workload costs more tokens for the same meaning.
BasicQ. What is the context window?
A. The maximum number of tokens the model can attend to at once — prompt plus completion combined. Exceed it and the earliest content is truncated or dropped, so facts silently disappear. BankAssist: in a long support chat, if we keep appending the whole history, the customer's original issue can scroll out of the window and the agent "forgets" why they called. Trade-off: bigger windows cost more and suffer "lost in the middle" — facts buried in the center get less attention than those at the start or end. Strong answer adds: a large window is a budget, not a filing cabinet; curate what goes in rather than dumping everything.
BasicQ. What do temperature and top-p do?
A. Temperature rescales the probability distribution — low (0–0.3) is focused and repeatable, high (0.8+) is diverse and creative; top-p (nucleus) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability ≥ p and samples from those. Why: both control how much randomness enters sampling. BankAssist: for "what's my balance?" we run temperature ~0 so the format and numbers are stable; for drafting three marketing variations we raise it. Trade-off: creativity vs reliability. Strong answer adds: tune one, leave the other at default — stacking both makes behavior hard to reason about, and note some reasoning models ignore these knobs entirely.
BasicQ. Why isn't temperature 0 fully deterministic?
A. Temperature 0 makes sampling greedy — it always picks the single most likely token. The catch: GPUs add up numbers in slightly different orders from one run to the next (floating-point math isn't perfectly associative), and tricks like dynamic batching and expert routing nudge those sums. When two tokens are almost tied, that tiny wobble can flip which one wins. Why it matters: "set temp 0 for reproducibility" is a half-truth. BankAssist: a compliance test that asserts byte-identical output across runs will flake intermittently and erode trust in the test suite. Trade-off: you can get close to reproducible with a fixed seed and pinned infrastructure, but providers rarely guarantee it. Strong answer adds: test for semantic equivalence or schema-validity, not exact string match.
IntermediateQ. Reasoning models vs standard models — when do you use each?
A. Reasoning models (o-series / extended-thinking models) spend extra "thinking" tokens on an internal chain before answering, lifting math, planning and multi-step logic; standard models (gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini) answer directly, cheaper and faster. Why: you are trading latency and cost for depth. BankAssist: use gpt-4.1-mini to classify an incoming message's intent and extract the account number; escalate to a reasoning model only for a genuinely hard dispute-resolution flow with many conditional steps. Trade-off: a reasoning model on a simple extraction just burns tokens and adds seconds. Strong answer adds: route by difficulty — most traffic is easy, so defaulting everything to the expensive model is the most common cost mistake.
IntermediateQ. How do you get reliable JSON out of a model?
A. Use a native structured-output / JSON-schema mode or tool-calling path that constrains decoding to your schema, rather than asking politely in the prompt — then validate against the schema on receipt and retry on failure. Why: constrained decoding makes malformed JSON impossible at the token level, where prose instructions only make it unlikely. BankAssist: the intent classifier returns {intent, account_id, confidence} every time, so downstream routing code never crashes on a stray apology or a markdown code fence. Trade-off: schemas add a little rigidity and setup. Strong answer adds: still validate even with constrained output — the shape is guaranteed, the values (a hallucinated account number) are not.
IntermediateQ. What are logprobs and what are they good for?
A. Logprobs are the model's per-token log-probabilities — how sure it was of each token it chose. They let you estimate confidence, build a classifier from one forward pass, flag low-confidence spans for review, and compare candidate completions. BankAssist: on an automated loan-document extraction, a low logprob on the extracted income figure routes that one field to a human checker instead of auto-approving. Trade-off: they signal the model's certainty, not factual truth — a model can be confidently wrong. Strong answer adds: calibrate the threshold against labeled data; raw logprobs are not probabilities of correctness until you map them.
IntermediateQ. What is in-context learning?
A. The model's ability to learn a task from examples placed in the prompt (zero/one/few-shot) with no weight update — the forward pass simply conditions on the demonstrations. Why: it lets you "teach" a new task instantly and cheaply. BankAssist: to make the model classify transactions into our internal category codes, we drop five labeled examples in the prompt rather than fine-tuning a model. Trade-off: it is instant but limited by context size, costs tokens every call, and does not persist across calls. Strong answer adds: when the same examples are sent on every request, move them behind prompt caching so you pay for them once.
IntermediateQ. Open-weight vs closed-weight models — trade-offs?
A. Open-weight (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, gpt-oss) give self-hosting, data residency, fine-tuning control and no per-token fee; closed (GPT, Claude, Gemini) give frontier capability and zero ops but send data to an API and lock you to a vendor. Why it matters especially in banking: data residency and auditability can be non-negotiable. BankAssist: we might self-host an open-weight model inside our VPC for anything touching raw customer PII, and use a closed frontier model for internal, de-identified analytics. Trade-off: self-hosting shifts cost from per-token fees to GPUs, MLOps and lower peak capability. Strong answer adds: frame it as build-vs-buy for inference, driven by data classification, not by benchmark scores alone.
AdvancedQ. Explain self-attention and the role of Q, K, V.
A. Each token is turned into three vectors: a Query (what this token is looking for), a Key (what it offers to others) and a Value (what it actually carries). Attention compares every token's Query to all the Keys to get a match score (a scaled dot-product); softmax turns those scores into weights that add up to 1; each token then takes a weighted blend of the Values — so every position pulls in context from the whole sentence. Multi-head attention runs this several times in parallel, each "head" in its own subspace, so the model can track different kinds of relationships at once. BankAssist: in "transfer $500 from savings to checking", attention is how "$500" binds to "transfer" and "savings" binds to "from" rather than "to". Trade-off: complexity is O(L²) in sequence length, which is why long contexts get expensive fast. Strong answer adds: that quadratic cost is the root reason for the whole long-context optimization industry (FlashAttention, GQA, sparse attention).
AdvancedQ. What is a KV cache, and why does it dominate long-context serving cost?
A. During autoregressive decoding, the Keys and Values of past tokens are cached so each new token doesn't recompute them. Why it dominates: the cache grows linearly with sequence length × layers × heads and is unique per request, so at long context and high concurrency, memory bandwidth — not matmul — becomes the bottleneck. BankAssist: a 100k-token policy document stuffed into context means a huge per-request cache, so we can batch far fewer concurrent chats on the same GPU. Trade-off: throughput collapses even though the GPU's compute sits idle. Strong answer adds: GQA/MQA, KV quantization (INT8) and paged attention shrink it — and prompt caching reuses a shared prefix's KV across requests.
AdvancedQ. What is Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and why is it popular?
A. MoE replaces dense feed-forward layers with many "expert" sub-networks plus a gating router that activates only the top-k experts per token. Why it's popular: it decouples total parameters (capacity) from active parameters (compute), so a model can be huge yet cheap per token. BankAssist: it's why a very capable model can serve our chat traffic at a price that makes per-customer automation viable. Trade-off: experts must be load-balanced and routing can be unstable, and the full model still has to fit in GPU memory even though only a slice runs. Strong answer adds: active-vs-total parameter count is the number to quote when reasoning about MoE cost and memory, not just "parameters".
AdvancedQ. How do models handle long context — positional encodings and RoPE?
A. Transformers are order-agnostic, so position is injected via positional encodings; modern LLMs use Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), which rotate Q/K by position so attention depends on relative distance. Context is pushed past the trained length with RoPE scaling (NTK/YaRN). BankAssist: this is why a model advertised at 128k tokens can still "work" on a slightly longer document — but the answer quality in the middle quietly degrades. Trade-off: attention still weakens with distance ("lost in the middle"), so a bigger window is not a guarantee of recall. Strong answer adds: put the most important context (the question, key clauses) at the start or end, and test recall at your real document lengths rather than trusting the advertised max.
AdvancedQ. Walk through pretraining → alignment (SFT, RLHF, DPO).
A. Pretraining learns next-token prediction on web-scale text (raw capability); SFT (supervised fine-tuning) teaches instruction-following from curated input→output pairs; alignment via RLHF (reward model + PPO) or the simpler DPO (direct preference optimization on chosen/rejected pairs) shapes behavior toward human preferences and safety. In one line: pretraining gives knowledge, alignment gives usefulness and manners. BankAssist: alignment is why the model politely refuses to help someone socially-engineer another customer's account instead of cheerfully complying. Trade-off: heavy alignment can cause over-refusal (an "alignment tax") on legitimate edge cases. Strong answer adds: DPO is now the common choice over full RLHF because it skips training a separate reward model while getting similar preference-following.

Prompting

BasicQ. What goes in a system prompt vs a user prompt?
A. The system prompt holds the stable frame — persona, rules, output format, guardrails and durable few-shot examples; the user prompt holds the per-turn request. Why: models weight system instructions higher and it keeps the fixed scaffolding separate from variable input. BankAssist: "You are BankAssist. Never reveal another customer's data. Answer only from the provided context." lives in the system prompt; "What was my last transaction?" is the user turn. Trade-off: higher priority is not ironclad protection — a cleverly injected instruction can still override it. Strong answer adds: keeping the system prompt stable across turns also lets you prompt-cache it, cutting cost and latency.
BasicQ. Zero-shot vs one-shot vs few-shot?
A. Zero-shot asks for the task with no examples, one-shot gives one demonstration, few-shot gives several. Why: examples pin down format and edge-case handling that instructions alone leave ambiguous. BankAssist: zero-shot handles "summarize this statement"; but to force our exact dispute-category labels we show three labeled examples so the model copies the schema. Trade-off: every example spends context tokens on every call. Strong answer adds: start zero-shot, add examples only where failures cluster, and pick diverse examples that cover the hard cases rather than three near-duplicates.
BasicQ. What is Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting?
A. Asking the model to show intermediate reasoning before the final answer ("think step by step"), which improves multi-step tasks by giving it room to work. Why: the generated reasoning tokens become context the final answer conditions on. BankAssist: for a fee-dispute decision with several conditions, letting the model reason first catches cases a snap answer would get wrong. Trade-off: it costs tokens and latency, and you usually don't want to show that reasoning to the customer. Strong answer adds: keep the reasoning in a separate field/tags, parse only the final answer, and skip CoT entirely on reasoning models that already think internally.
IntermediateQ. How do you reduce hallucination through prompting alone?
A. Ground the model with retrieved context and instruct it to answer only from that context, cite the source, and say "I don't know" when the context is insufficient; lower temperature and ask for quotes. Why: an explicit "refuse if unsupported" instruction plus citations makes unsupported claims visible and gives the model permission to decline. BankAssist: "Using only the policy text below, answer and quote the clause; if it's not covered, say you'll connect a specialist." beats an open-ended answer that invents a refund window. Trade-off: prompting alone reduces but never eliminates hallucination — it's a mitigation, not a guarantee. Strong answer adds: back it with a deterministic check (verify the cited clause actually exists in the retrieved text) rather than trusting the model's self-report.
IntermediateQ. When is CoT a bad idea in production?
A. When latency and cost matter and the task is simple — classification, extraction, routing — CoT wastes tokens and can even introduce rationalized errors. Why: for a one-step task the reasoning adds no accuracy but adds seconds and spend, and sometimes the model "reasons itself" into a wrong answer. BankAssist: intent classification at scale runs tens of millions of times — adding a reasoning preamble there would blow the latency budget for zero benefit. Trade-off: use it only where a measured accuracy gain justifies the token spend. Strong answer adds: on reasoning models, bolting on "think step by step" is redundant and can degrade quality.
IntermediateQ. What is prompt chaining, and why decompose a prompt?
A. Splitting a complex task into a sequence of focused prompts (extract → transform → format), each with one narrow job. Why: each step is simpler, individually testable, cacheable, and you can insert validation between steps. BankAssist: loan-doc processing chains extract-fields → validate-against-rules → generate-decision-letter, so a bad extraction is caught before it taints the letter. Trade-off: more calls means more latency and more orchestration. Strong answer adds: chaining also lets you right-size each step — a cheap model for extraction, a stronger one only for the final judgment.
IntermediateQ. What is self-consistency and when is it worth the cost?
A. Self-consistency samples the same prompt several times at non-zero temperature and takes the majority answer, smoothing out one-off reasoning slips. Why: averaging several independent attempts beats a single sample on hard reasoning. BankAssist: for a tricky eligibility calculation that feeds a human reviewer, three samples that agree give a higher-confidence recommendation than one. Trade-off: it costs N× the tokens and latency, so it's only for high-stakes, low-volume decisions — never for every chat turn. Strong answer adds: use agreement rate as a confidence signal — when the samples disagree, that's a strong cue to escalate to a human.
AdvancedQ. Few-shot example selection — static vs dynamic?
A. Static examples are fixed in the prompt; dynamic selection retrieves the most similar examples to the current input from a pool (k-NN over embeddings). Why dynamic helps: on diverse inputs, examples close to the query teach the model the right pattern for that case. BankAssist: a dispute about a foreign-transaction fee pulls in prior foreign-fee examples, while an overdraft dispute pulls overdraft examples. Trade-off: dynamic adds a retrieval step and can bias toward frequent cases or leak labels. Strong answer adds: balance relevance with diversity so you don't retrieve three near-identical examples and starve the rare edge cases.
AdvancedQ. How do you make prompts robust and maintainable at scale?
A. Treat prompts as code: version them in source control, template them with typed variables, separate instructions from data with delimiters, and gate every change behind an eval suite so regressions can't ship. Why: a one-word prompt tweak can quietly tank accuracy across millions of calls. BankAssist: changing the refusal wording goes through a PR, runs against the golden set, and is rolled back automatically if faithfulness drops. Trade-off: this discipline is upfront work that teams skip until the first silent regression burns them. Strong answer adds: this is where DSPy-style compilation replaces hand-tuning — you optimize prompts against a metric instead of guessing.
AdvancedQ. What is meta-prompting / using a model to improve its own prompts?
A. Meta-prompting uses an LLM to critique and rewrite prompts (or generate examples) against observed failures, instead of a human hand-editing wording. Why: it systematizes the slow trial-and-error loop and can surface instructions a human wouldn't phrase. BankAssist: we feed a batch of misrouted chats to a "prompt-fixer" model that proposes a sharper routing instruction, which we then A/B against the golden set. Trade-off: the model can over-fit to the examples you showed it and produce a longer, costlier prompt. Strong answer adds: always validate the machine-written prompt on a held-out eval set before trusting it — treat it as a candidate, not a verdict.

Embeddings & Vector Search

BasicQ. What is an embedding?
A. A fixed-length vector that encodes the meaning of text (or image/audio) so semantically similar items land near each other in vector space. Why it's useful: once meaning is geometry, "find similar" becomes "find nearby", powering retrieval, clustering, classification and dedup. BankAssist: "I can't log in" and "password reset not working" embed to nearby vectors, so both match the same help article even though they share no keywords. Trade-off: embeddings capture topical similarity, which isn't always the relevance you want. Strong answer adds: similar meaning → small distance; the whole stack rests on that one geometric fact.
BasicQ. Cosine vs dot product vs Euclidean — when to use which?
A. Cosine measures angle (direction) and ignores magnitude; dot product rewards both alignment and magnitude; Euclidean measures straight-line distance. Why it matters: for normalized vectors cosine and dot product rank identically, and most text-embedding models are trained and tuned for cosine. BankAssist: our FAQ search normalizes vectors and uses cosine, so a short query and a long article compare on meaning, not length. Trade-off: pick the metric the embedding model was trained on — mismatching it quietly degrades recall. Strong answer adds: if vectors are normalized at ingest, dot product is cheapest and equals cosine, so many production stores default to it.
BasicQ. What is a vector database and why "approximate" search?
A. A store that indexes embeddings for fast nearest-neighbor search plus metadata filtering. Why approximate: exact search scans every vector (O(n)), which at millions of vectors is too slow, so Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes trade a tiny bit of recall for massive speed-ups. BankAssist: searching 10M policy chunks per chat turn is only feasible because ANN returns the top matches in milliseconds. Trade-off: you accept that it may occasionally miss a true top-k result. Strong answer adds: measure recall@k on your own data — the "little" recall loss is workload-dependent and can be large with aggressive settings.
IntermediateQ. Dense vs sparse vs multi-vector embeddings?
A. Dense (one vector per chunk) captures semantics; sparse (BM25/SPLADE) captures exact terms and rare tokens; multi-vector (ColBERT) keeps one vector per token for fine-grained late-interaction matching. Why mix them: each covers the others' blind spot. BankAssist: dense finds the right policy by meaning, but only sparse reliably matches an exact error code like "ERR-4012" or a specific policy number. Trade-off: hybrid adds a second index and a fusion step; multi-vector is far more accurate but much heavier on storage. Strong answer adds: hybrid dense+sparse is the production default precisely because banking queries mix natural language with exact identifiers.
IntermediateQ. Explain the HNSW index and its key parameters.
A. Hierarchical Navigable Small World builds a multi-layer proximity graph; search starts at a sparse top layer and greedily hops down to dense lower layers near the query. Key knobs: M (neighbors per node) and efConstruction/efSearch, which trade recall against latency and memory. BankAssist: we raise efSearch for a compliance search where missing a relevant doc is unacceptable, and lower it for low-stakes FAQ lookups to save latency. Trade-off: higher ef = better recall but slower queries and more RAM. Strong answer adds: HNSW gives top recall/latency but is RAM-hungry, which is why billion-scale often moves to IVF-PQ.
IntermediateQ. What is the "same-model rule"?
A. You must embed queries and documents with the same model and version — vectors from different models live in incompatible spaces and their distances are meaningless. Why it bites: nothing errors out, the results just quietly get worse. BankAssist: if we "upgrade" the embedding model but only re-embed new documents, old policy chunks become unreachable and customers get wrong answers with no error in the logs. Trade-off: changing the embedding model means re-indexing the entire corpus — a real cost at 10M docs. Strong answer adds: plan embedding upgrades as blue/green re-index with versioned collections, never an in-place swap.
IntermediateQ. What are Matryoshka embeddings and quantization used for?
A. Matryoshka embeddings let you truncate a vector to fewer dimensions with graceful quality loss; quantization (scalar INT8, or product quantization into sub-vector codes) compresses vectors ~4–32×. Why: both cut the memory and search cost that dominate at scale. BankAssist: dropping from 1536 to 512 dims across 10M chunks slashes RAM and query time, and we measured the recall hit was acceptable for FAQ search. Trade-off: every compression trades some recall — it's workload-specific. Strong answer adds: measure recall per use case before shipping; the acceptable loss for FAQ search may be unacceptable for a compliance search.
AdvancedQ. IVF vs HNSW vs PQ — how do you choose at a billion vectors?
A. IVF partitions space into clusters and searches only the nearest few (cheap memory, needs training and nprobe tuning); HNSW gives top recall/latency but high RAM; PQ compresses vectors for memory and is often combined as IVF-PQ for billion-scale. Why: at a billion vectors, RAM and cost usually dominate the decision. BankAssist: a bank-wide archive of a billion document chunks likely lands on IVF-PQ to fit memory budgets, while a hot 5M-chunk FAQ stays on in-memory HNSW. Trade-off: you're picking a corner of the recall/latency/RAM/cost box. Strong answer adds: always quote measured recall at your target latency — index choice is meaningless without the recall number on your data.
AdvancedQ. How does metadata filtering interact with ANN, and when does exact search win?
A. Pre-filtering narrows candidates before the ANN search but can break the graph's connectivity (you prune the very nodes the walk needs); post-filtering is simpler but may return too few results after filtering. Why it's a top pitfall: filtered recall can silently collapse. BankAssist: "show only this customer's documents" is so selective that a brute-force exact scan of their few thousand chunks is faster and more accurate than ANN. Trade-off: pre- vs post-filter is a recall-vs-simplicity choice. Strong answer adds: when a filter shrinks candidates to thousands, skip ANN entirely and scan exactly.
AdvancedQ. How do you keep a vector index fresh with constant updates?
A. Support incremental upserts and soft-deletes, batch heavy re-indexing off-peak, and use versioned collections for zero-downtime upgrades (blue/green). Why: HNSW tolerates inserts but degrades with heavy deletes, so periodic compaction/rebuild is needed. BankAssist: a policy changes daily — we upsert the new chunk and soft-delete the old so customers never get yesterday's refund rule, and compact weekly. Trade-off: separating the write path from the serving index adds plumbing but prevents update churn from hurting query latency. Strong answer adds: track index staleness as a monitored metric — stale answers are a correctness bug, not just an ops detail.

RAG — Ingestion, Chunking, Retrieval, Eval, Production

BasicQ. What is RAG and what problem does it solve?
A. Retrieval-Augmented Generation fetches relevant documents at query time and injects them into the prompt so the model answers from current, private, authoritative data. Why: it fixes stale knowledge, hallucination, lack of private data and the need for citations — an "open-book exam" for the LLM. BankAssist: the model knows nothing about our fee schedule, so we retrieve the current policy and have it answer from that, with a citation the customer can trust. Trade-off: answer quality is now capped by retrieval quality — garbage in, garbage out. Strong answer adds: RAG injects facts, not behavior; it won't teach a new output format or skill — that's fine-tuning's job.
BasicQ. Describe the two RAG flows.
A. Offline (ingestion): load → clean → parse → chunk → embed → index. Online (query): embed query → retrieve top-k → (rerank) → assemble context → generate with citations. Why distinguish them: the offline pipeline quietly sets the ceiling on online quality. BankAssist: if ingestion mangles a policy table, no amount of clever prompting at query time recovers the lost rows. Trade-off: ingestion is unglamorous but it's where most RAG quality is won or lost. Strong answer adds: version the ingestion pipeline too — a change to chunking is as impactful as a change to the model.
BasicQ. What are chunk_size and chunk_overlap?
A. Chunk size is how much text per retrievable unit; overlap repeats a tail of one chunk at the start of the next so facts spanning a boundary aren't lost. Why tune them: too large dilutes relevance and wastes context, too small fragments meaning. BankAssist: a fee rule split mid-sentence across two chunks returns half an answer — overlap keeps the whole rule retrievable. Trade-off: more overlap means more storage and some duplicate retrieval. Strong answer adds: count in tokens, not characters, and respect document structure (don't cut through a table) rather than slicing blindly.
IntermediateQ. Name chunking strategies and how you'd choose.
A. Fixed-size, recursive (split on structural separators), token-aware, semantic (cut where meaning shifts) and structure-aware (markdown/tables/code). Why it's the lever it is: poor chunking is the #1 cause of production RAG failures. BankAssist: recursive for general policy prose, structure-aware for the fee tables so rows stay intact, semantic when a doc jumps between unrelated topics. Trade-off: smarter chunking costs more compute at ingest and is harder to debug. Strong answer adds: choose by document type, not by a single global setting — a bank's corpus is heterogeneous and one chunker rarely fits all.
IntermediateQ. What is hybrid search and why Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)?
A. Hybrid runs dense (semantic) and sparse (BM25/keyword) retrieval together, catching both meaning and exact terms; RRF merges the two ranked lists by rank position rather than raw scores. Why RRF: dense and sparse scores live on incompatible scales, so fusing by rank sidesteps the normalization problem. BankAssist: "dispute a charge" is a semantic match, but "charge on card ending 4012" needs the exact token — hybrid catches both. Trade-off: two indexes and a fusion step add complexity and latency. Strong answer adds: RRF is the robust default, but tune the per-retriever weight when one source is clearly stronger for your corpus.
IntermediateQ. What is reranking and why a cross-encoder?
A. A reranker re-scores the top-N retrieved candidates with a model that reads the query and document together (a cross-encoder), producing far more accurate relevance than the bi-encoder used for fast first-stage retrieval. Why two stages: retrieve broadly and cheaply, then rerank a small pool expensively but accurately. BankAssist: first-stage pulls 50 policy chunks, the reranker promotes the one that actually answers the customer's exact question to the top. Trade-off: the cross-encoder adds latency and cost per candidate, so you rerank 50, not 5000. Strong answer adds: reranking often buys more accuracy per dollar than upgrading the generator model.
IntermediateQ. How do you evaluate a RAG system?
A. Grade retrieval and generation separately. Retrieval: context precision/recall, hit rate, MRR/NDCG. Generation: faithfulness (grounded?), answer relevancy, answer correctness. The "RAG Triad" — context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance — boxes in hallucination. Why separate: a bad answer could be bad retrieval or bad generation, and you must know which to fix. BankAssist: if faithfulness is high but answers are wrong, the bug is retrieval, not the model. Trade-off: good eval needs a maintained golden set, which is real ongoing work. Strong answer adds: back offline metrics with online signals (deflection, thumbs, escalation) as the ground truth.
IntermediateQ. Query transformation techniques — name a few.
A. Query rewriting (fix a vague/conversational query), multi-query / RAG-Fusion (generate variants and fuse results), HyDE (embed a hypothetical answer), step-back prompting (ask a broader question first) and decomposition (split a complex query into sub-queries). Why: they bridge the gap between how users ask and how documents are written. BankAssist: "it got declined again" gets rewritten into "credit card transaction decline reasons" before retrieval, so it actually matches the docs. Trade-off: each transform adds an LLM call and latency. Strong answer adds: apply them adaptively — only rewrite when the raw query retrieves poorly, not on every turn.
AdvancedQ. Contextual retrieval, parent-document, and sentence-window — what problem do they solve?
A. The core tension: small chunks retrieve precisely but lack context for generation. Parent-document retrieves small but returns the parent; sentence-window returns neighbors around the hit; contextual retrieval prepends an LLM-generated summary of the chunk's place in the doc before embedding. Why: all three decouple the retrieval unit from the generation unit. BankAssist: we match a precise clause but hand the model the whole section so it answers in context instead of quoting a fragment. Trade-off: contextual retrieval costs an LLM call per chunk at ingest. Strong answer adds: retrieve small, generate large — the unit you search on need not be the unit you read from.
AdvancedQ. What is Agentic RAG and how does it differ from naive RAG?
A. Retrieval becomes a decision, not a reflex: the agent decides whether to retrieve, which source/tool, how to reformulate, and whether results are good enough or need another loop. Variants: Self-RAG (reflect on retrieve/quality), Corrective RAG (grade docs, fall back to web), Adaptive RAG (route by question difficulty). Why: real questions vary wildly in what they need. BankAssist: "what's my balance?" skips retrieval and calls an API; "explain this fee vs the new policy" retrieves and may loop to refine. Trade-off: more accurate but higher latency, cost and complexity. Strong answer adds: only pay for the loop when the question warrants it — route easy queries down the cheap path.
AdvancedQ. What is GraphRAG and when is it worth it?
A. GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph (entities + relations) from the corpus and retrieves over it, enabling multi-hop "how is X connected to Y?" and global-summary questions that flat vector search can't answer. Why: vector search finds similar passages, not relationships across them. BankAssist: "which accounts are linked to this flagged counterparty?" is a graph traversal, not a similarity lookup — ideal for fraud rings. Trade-off: building and maintaining the graph is costly and complex. Strong answer adds: reserve it for genuinely relational, linked domains (counterparties, org structures); for ordinary FAQ it's over-engineering.
AdvancedQ. Design a RAG eval that catches regressions before release.
A. Maintain a versioned golden set (questions + reference answers + expected source chunks), compute retrieval and generation metrics per release, and gate CI on thresholds (e.g. faithfulness ≥ target). Why: without a gate, a "small" prompt or chunking change silently regresses quality in production. BankAssist: a chunking tweak that quietly drops fee-table recall is caught by the CI gate before customers ever see a wrong fee. Trade-off: curating and refreshing the golden set is ongoing effort. Strong answer adds: include adversarial and no-answer cases, use LLM-as-judge with a calibrated rubric, and track online metrics as the real ground truth.
AdvancedQ. How do you enforce access control in RAG over 10M permissioned docs?
A. Attach ACL metadata (owner, roles, classification) at ingestion and filter retrieval by the caller's entitlements — never retrieve what the user can't see, because if it reaches the context the LLM will leak it. Why: the model has no concept of permissions; security must happen before generation. BankAssist: a teller's query must never surface a document only a compliance officer may read, even as a "source". Trade-off: pre-filtering at the index is safest but complicates the ANN search; per-tenant/per-role partitions add ops overhead. Strong answer adds: treat it as a permissions problem with search attached, and test with an adversarial "can user A retrieve user B's data?" suite.
AdvancedQ. RAG vs long-context vs fine-tuning — decide.
A. RAG for large/changing/private knowledge needing citations and freshness; long-context when a handful of documents fit the window and you don't want an index; fine-tuning to change behavior/format/style or deep domain skill, not to inject facts. Why: they solve different problems and compose. BankAssist: RAG for the fee schedule (changes weekly), long-context for one 40-page contract in a single session, fine-tuning to lock the model into our exact letter format. Trade-off: fine-tuning facts in means re-training every time they change — expensive and stale-prone. Strong answer adds: default order prompt → RAG → fine-tune, and note RAFT fine-tunes a model to use retrieved context and ignore distractors.

Agents — Loop, Tools, Reasoning, Memory

BasicQ. What makes software "agentic"?
A. An LLM that, in a loop, decides its own actions to reach a goal — using tools, observing results, and continuing until done. The four parts: a model (brain), tools (hands), memory (state) and an orchestration loop. Why it's different: the model controls the control flow, not a fixed script. BankAssist: a dispute agent decides on its own to first fetch the transaction, then check the merchant, then draft a resolution — the order isn't hard-coded. Trade-off: that autonomy is powerful but less predictable and harder to bound. Strong answer adds: the hallmark is dynamic control flow — if the steps are fixed, it's a workflow, not an agent.
BasicQ. Agent vs RAG vs fixed workflow — when use an agent?
A. A fixed workflow wins when the steps are known and stable (cheaper, predictable); RAG answers knowledge questions; an agent earns its keep only when the path is dynamic — unknown number/order of steps, tool choice depending on intermediate results. Why: autonomy you don't need is just added cost and risk. BankAssist: "reset my password" is a fixed 3-step flow; "investigate this suspicious transaction" genuinely needs an agent. Trade-off: agents add latency, cost and failure modes. Strong answer adds: prefer the most constrained option that solves the problem — reach for an agent last, not first.
BasicQ. What is a tool / function call?
A. A tool is a function you expose to the model via a name, description and JSON-Schema of parameters; the model emits a structured request to call it, your code executes it and returns the result as an observation. Why this design: the model never runs code — it asks, your runtime acts, so you keep control. BankAssist: get_balance(account_id) is a tool; the model requests it, our backend runs the real query, and the number comes back as an observation. Trade-off: every tool is new attack surface and must be authorized. Strong answer adds: the tool's description is effectively part of the prompt — vague descriptions cause mis-routing.
BasicQ. What is the ReAct pattern?
A. Reason + Act: the agent interleaves a Thought (reasoning), an Action (tool call) and an Observation (result), looping until it can answer. Why it helps: explicit reasoning curbs blind tool-spamming and makes the trace debuggable. BankAssist: Thought "I need the transaction" → Action get_transaction → Observation "$500 to MerchantX" → Thought "now check if disputed" → ... Trade-off: it leans on the model's reasoning, context grows fast on long tasks, and it can loop. Strong answer adds: always pair ReAct with a hard iteration cap and loop detection so a confused agent can't spin forever.
IntermediateQ. How should tools return errors?
A. Return failures to the model as structured data (an error message/status), not by throwing — so the agent can read what went wrong and self-correct or try another path. Why: an exception kills the loop; a readable error lets the agent recover. BankAssist: returning "invalid account format, expected 10 digits" lets the agent re-ask the customer instead of crashing the chat. Trade-off: you must still cap retries so it doesn't loop on an unrecoverable error. Strong answer adds: make errors actionable and pair with retries/backoff for transient failures plus a loop cap for permanent ones.
IntermediateQ. How do you write tool names and descriptions the model follows?
A. Use clear, verb-based names and descriptions written for the model as the reader: what it does, when to use it, what each argument means and its units; keep schemas tight with enums and required fields. Why: ambiguous or overlapping tools cause mis-routing — the description is the prompt. BankAssist: splitting a vague "account_tool" into get_balance and block_card with crisp descriptions stops the model calling the wrong one. Trade-off: very fine-grained tools mean more of them to maintain and present. Strong answer adds: if the model keeps mis-calling, fix the description before touching the prompt — it's usually the cheaper fix.
IntermediateQ. Parallel tool calls — when and what's the rule?
A. When several tool calls are independent (no call needs another's output), the model can request them in parallel to cut latency. The rule: never parallelize calls with data dependencies. Why: a dependent call needs the earlier result, and concurrent writes race. BankAssist: fetching balance, recent transactions and card status at once is safe and fast; "transfer then check new balance" must be sequential. Trade-off: parallel writes risk race conditions and double-execution. Strong answer adds: keep parallelism to reads — serialize anything that mutates state.
IntermediateQ. Short-term vs long-term agent memory.
A. Short-term is the context window — the agent's working RAM for the current task. Long-term persists across sessions in external stores: episodic (past events), semantic (facts) and procedural (how-to/skills). Why split them: the window is small and costly, so durable knowledge lives outside and is pulled in on demand. BankAssist: short-term holds this chat; long-term remembers the customer prefers SMS alerts and disputed a fee last month. Trade-off: carrying everything bloats context and cost. Strong answer adds: long-term recall is just RAG over the agent's own history — retrieve only what's relevant now, don't replay the whole transcript.
IntermediateQ. Function calling vs tool use — distinction?
A. Function calling is the specific API mechanism by which a model emits structured arguments mapping to a function; tool use is the broader pattern of selecting and invoking external capabilities (hosted tools, code execution, MCP). In one line: function calling is one implementation of tool use. Why it matters: interviewers use the terms loosely and want to see you know the levels. BankAssist: our agent uses function calling for in-house APIs and MCP for shared enterprise tools — both are "tool use". Trade-off: none conceptually; it's a vocabulary precision check. Strong answer adds: name MCP and code-execution as tool-use forms that aren't classic function calling.
AdvancedQ. What is context engineering and why does it matter more than prompt engineering now?
A. Curating exactly what occupies the context window each turn — system prompt, tools, retrieved facts, memory and pruned history — so the model has the right information and nothing distracting. Why it now dominates: performance degrades with irrelevant or overflowing context ("lost in the middle"), and context is a scarce, costly budget. BankAssist: a long agent run that keeps every tool result will bury the customer's actual question under stale observations and start answering the wrong thing. Trade-off: curation logic is extra engineering. Strong answer adds: prompt engineering is wording one message; context engineering is managing the whole window over a multi-step run.
AdvancedQ. Techniques to manage a long-running agent's context budget.
A. Compaction/summarization of old turns, tool-result pruning (drop or truncate stale observations), retrieving memory on demand instead of carrying it, and context isolation via sub-agents that each get a clean window and return only a summary. Why: otherwise context grows until it overflows or degrades. BankAssist: a fraud investigation summarizes completed lookups into a short findings note and drops the raw API dumps, keeping the window focused. Trade-off: summarization can lose a detail you later need. Strong answer adds: checkpoint state so you can pause/resume, and keep the compaction prompt itself under eval so it doesn't silently drop key facts.
AdvancedQ. Compare CoT, ReAct, Plan-and-Execute, Tree-of-Thoughts, and Reflexion.
A. CoT: linear reasoning, no tools. ReAct: interleave reason/act/observe. Plan-and-Execute: plan the whole route first, then execute (fewer LLM calls, less adaptive). Tree-of-Thoughts: branch, evaluate, keep the best (expensive search). Reflexion: act, self-critique, retry with the lesson in memory. Why know all five: each trades adaptivity against cost. BankAssist: Plan-and-Execute suits a predictable onboarding checklist; ReAct suits an open-ended investigation. Trade-off: Tree-of-Thoughts can explode cost for marginal gain. Strong answer adds: pick by how much the task needs to adapt mid-run versus how tight the cost/latency budget is.
AdvancedQ. How do you stop an agent from running away?
A. Hard budgets: max iterations, max tokens, max tool calls, wall-clock timeout and a spend cap; plus loop detection (repeated identical actions), a required stop/finish tool, and human-in-the-loop gates on costly or irreversible actions. Why: an LLM in a loop can burn money or take damaging actions with no natural stop. BankAssist: an agent stuck re-querying a failing API hits the iteration cap and escalates to a human instead of spinning for an hour. Trade-off: tight caps can cut off a legitimately long task. Strong answer adds: default to stopping and escalating over guessing — in banking, a safe halt beats a confident wrong action.
AdvancedQ. How do you handle a timeout on an ambiguous write?
A. If a write tool times out, you don't know whether it committed — so never retry blindly. Make writes idempotent with a client-supplied idempotency key so a safe retry can't double-execute; otherwise verify state before retrying. Why: a blind retry on a money movement can double-charge a customer. BankAssist: a transfer that times out is retried with the same idempotency key, so the backend recognizes and dedupes it — the customer is charged once. Trade-off: idempotency keys add plumbing on every write path. Strong answer adds: for truly non-idempotent actions, escalate to a human rather than guess.
IntermediateQ. RAG vs Agents vs Agentic RAG — when do you reach for each?
A. RAG is a fixed retrieve-then-generate pipeline — one hop, no decisions — ideal when the task is "answer from our knowledge." Agents add a think-act loop with tools and the freedom to plan multi-step actions — needed when the task requires doing (call APIs, take actions), not just answering. Agentic RAG is the middle ground: an agent that treats retrieval as one of its tools, so it can decide whether to search, rewrite the query, search multiple sources, and iterate until the context is good enough. Why pick deliberately: every step of autonomy you add buys capability but costs latency, cost, and new failure modes. BankAssist: "what's the overdraft policy?" is plain RAG; "dispute this charge and refund me" is an agent; "research my mortgage options across these docs and summarize" suits agentic RAG, which re-queries until it has the right clauses. Trade-off: a fixed pipeline is predictable and cheap; an agentic loop is flexible but needs budgets, guardrails, and tracing. Strong answer adds: default to the least autonomy that solves the task — reach for agentic RAG only when single-shot retrieval demonstrably misses, not by default.

Multi-Agent Architectures

BasicQ. When do you need multiple agents instead of one?
A. When a single agent's context/tooling gets overloaded, when distinct specialties benefit from focused prompts and tools, or when sub-tasks can run in parallel. Why caution: multi-agent is not automatically better — a bad split adds cost, latency and coordination bugs. BankAssist: fraud investigation splits cleanly into data-gathering, link-analysis and case-writing specialists; a simple balance query does not. Trade-off: every added agent multiplies tokens and introduces handoff failure modes. Strong answer adds: start with one agent and split only on evidence that one is genuinely overloaded.
BasicQ. Name the main multi-agent topologies.
A. Sequential pipeline (prompt chaining), router/handoff (send to the right specialist), parallel (sectioning or voting), orchestrator-worker (a lead delegates to workers), planner-generator-evaluator, and hierarchies/DAGs; debate/group-chat has many agents converge on one answer. Why know them: naming the pattern signals you've thought about structure, not just "spawn agents". BankAssist: a router sends billing vs fraud vs lending questions to different specialists. Trade-off: richer topologies add coordination cost. Strong answer adds: map the topology to the task shape — routing for triage, orchestrator-worker for decompose-and-synthesize, voting for high-stakes calls.
IntermediateQ. Explain the orchestrator-worker (supervisor) pattern and its bottleneck.
A. A lead agent decomposes the task, delegates sub-tasks to specialized workers, and synthesizes their outputs. Why it's popular: it's flexible and parallelizable. The bottleneck: the orchestrator is a single decision point — every branch waits on it and its judgment caps overall quality. BankAssist: the fraud lead farms out transaction, device and graph lookups in parallel, then writes the case — but if the lead triages wrong, the whole investigation points the wrong way. Trade-off: parallelism vs a central point of failure. Strong answer adds: keep the orchestrator's prompt and tools lean, and eval it separately — it's the quality ceiling.
IntermediateQ. How should an agent handoff work?
A. The receiving agent should validate it can handle the request and reject with a reason if not, so the orchestrator can reroute; the handoff payload should be crisp — a summary, sources, confidence notes and open questions, not the whole raw transcript. Why: clean handoffs prevent context bloat and silent error propagation. BankAssist: the triage agent hands the fraud specialist "likely card-skimming, 3 suspect transactions, confidence 0.7", not the entire chat log. Trade-off: summarizing risks dropping a detail the next agent needs. Strong answer adds: schema-validate the handoff payload so a malformed delegation is caught at the boundary.
IntermediateQ. Sectioning vs voting in parallel agents?
A. Sectioning splits a task into independent parts done concurrently then merged (speed + context isolation); voting runs the same task multiple times/ways and aggregates (majority or judge) to raise reliability on hard calls. Why distinguish: one cuts latency, the other cuts error. BankAssist: sectioning fetches device, geo and transaction data in parallel; voting runs the final fraud/no-fraud call three times and takes the consensus. Trade-off: voting costs N× tokens for the same task. Strong answer adds: reserve voting for the one decision that really matters, not for every step.
IntermediateQ. How do agents share state — chat history vs a blackboard?
A. Agents can coordinate by passing messages (replayed chat history) or by reading/writing a shared external store (a "blackboard"). Why the blackboard often wins: grounding shared state in a durable store stops drift and context bloat from replaying long transcripts. BankAssist: the fraud workers write findings into a shared case object that the case-writer reads, instead of each re-sending the full conversation. Trade-off: messages are simpler to wire up but bloat the context as transcripts grow; a blackboard scales but needs concurrency control — rules for who writes what, and when. Strong answer adds: use the store as the source of truth and keep inter-agent messages to short summaries.
AdvancedQ. The multi-agent trade-off: quality vs cost vs latency.
A. More agents can raise quality (specialization, review, voting) but multiply token spend, add coordination latency, and create new failure modes (error propagation, context drift). Why it's the key senior point: a sprawling crew often loses to one well-engineered agent. BankAssist: a 6-agent chat that costs 6× and adds seconds may not beat a single agent with good tools and tight context for a routine query. Trade-off: specialization gains must exceed coordination cost. Strong answer adds: justify each agent with a measured quality gain — if you can't name the metric it improves, cut it.
AdvancedQ. How do you make a multi-agent system reliable?
A. Checkpoint state so a crashed run resumes; on a failing or low-quality agent, retry with a different agent, fall back, or escalate to a human; add conflict resolution for disagreeing agents (judge/voting); cap global budget across the whole system; and trace every inter-agent message. Why: failure compounds across agents, so each boundary needs a safety net. BankAssist: if the graph-analysis agent errors mid-investigation, the orchestrator resumes from the last checkpoint rather than re-running every lookup. Trade-off: all this resilience is real engineering. Strong answer adds: a global budget is essential — per-agent caps alone don't stop the system as a whole from runaway spend.
AdvancedQ. How do you prevent error propagation and context drift across agents?
A. Validate each agent's output against a schema/spec before passing it on, keep handoffs to summaries (not raw context), isolate each agent's working context, and add an evaluator/critic step in the loop. Why: an unchecked wrong output becomes the next agent's trusted input and compounds silently. BankAssist: a mis-extracted transaction amount, validated at the handoff, is caught before it drives a wrong fraud score. Trade-off: validation and critics add calls and latency. Strong answer adds: ground shared state in an external store rather than replayed chat, so drift can't accumulate turn over turn.
AdvancedQ. In-process sub-agents vs networked agents (A2A) — how do you choose?
A. In-process sub-agents run inside one service, sharing memory and deployment — simple, fast, fully under your control. Networked agents over a protocol like A2A are separate services (often owned by other teams or vendors) that discover and delegate to each other. Why it matters: the boundary changes your security, versioning and failure model. BankAssist: the fraud workers are in-process; delegating to the bank's separate KYC agent (a different team's service) goes over A2A with its own auth. Trade-off: networked agents add latency, trust boundaries and operational coupling. Strong answer adds: keep things in-process until an organizational or ownership boundary forces a protocol — don't distribute for its own sake.

Frameworks — LangChain / LangGraph / etc.

BasicQ. What does an agent framework buy you, and what's the tax?
A. It provides prebuilt loops, tool/memory abstractions, integrations, streaming and observability — faster to start. The tax: abstraction hides control flow, adds dependencies and version churn, and can make debugging harder. Why it matters: frameworks move fast and breaking changes are common. BankAssist: a framework gets our first agent running in a day, but when it mis-routes we have to dig through its internals to see why. Trade-off: speed-to-start vs transparency. Strong answer adds: for a simple, well-understood loop a plain provider SDK is often clearer than any framework.
BasicQ. LangChain vs LangGraph — how do they relate?
A. LangChain supplies components and high-level agent helpers (models, retrievers, tools, composition); LangGraph is the lower-level orchestration runtime where you model the agent as a stateful graph of nodes and edges. Why both: they're complementary — LangGraph runs beneath for complex, stateful, multi-actor flows. BankAssist: we use LangChain's retrievers for RAG and LangGraph to orchestrate a fraud investigation with loops and branches. Trade-off: two layers to learn. Strong answer adds: current LangChain exposes create_agent as the modern helper — avoid the deprecated initialize_agent/AgentExecutor in new code.
IntermediateQ. In LangGraph, what are state, nodes, edges, and conditional edges?
A. State is a shared typed object threaded through the graph (updated via reducers); nodes are functions that read/write state and do work; edges define the next node; conditional edges branch based on state, enabling loops, routing and cycles a linear chain can't express. Why graphs: real agents need branches and loops, not a straight line. BankAssist: a conditional edge routes "needs human approval" to a review node and everything else straight to execution. Trade-off: more expressive but more to reason about than a simple chain. Strong answer adds: reducers are how concurrent nodes merge updates without clobbering each other's state.
IntermediateQ. Checkpointer vs store in LangGraph?
A. A checkpointer persists the full graph state per thread at every step, enabling pause/resume, time-travel, human-in-the-loop and multi-turn memory; a store holds cross-thread, long-term memory (facts shared across conversations). In one line: checkpointer = this run's state, store = durable knowledge. Why both: one resumes a task, the other remembers across tasks. BankAssist: the checkpointer lets a paused approval resume exactly where it stopped; the store remembers the customer's alert preferences across sessions. Trade-off: durable persistence adds infrastructure. Strong answer adds: the checkpointer is also what makes human-in-the-loop clean — you pause, a human acts, you resume from the same state.
IntermediateQ. Pick a framework for: typed outputs, document-heavy RAG, graph orchestration, role-play crew.
A. Pydantic AI for typed/validated outputs; LlamaIndex for document/RAG-centric apps; LangGraph for complex stateful orchestration; CrewAI for role-playing multi-agent crews. Why name-match: each is strongest at a different shape of problem. BankAssist: Pydantic AI guarantees our decision object validates; LlamaIndex powers policy RAG; LangGraph runs the fraud investigation. Trade-off: mixing several frameworks adds surface area. Strong answer adds: also know OpenAI Agents SDK / Google ADK for provider-native agents, DSPy to optimize prompts, and Haystack for explicit inspectable pipelines.
IntermediateQ. What are handoffs in the OpenAI Agents SDK?
A. A handoff is a first-class primitive where one agent transfers control to another by exposing the target agent as a tool the model can call; the SDK also provides guardrails, sessions and tracing around the loop. Why it's clean: routing between specialists becomes a normal tool call the model decides on, with the framework handling the transfer. BankAssist: a triage agent hands off to a "disputes" agent via a handoff tool when it detects a chargeback intent. Trade-off: it's provider-native, so it couples you to that ecosystem. Strong answer adds: handoffs are the SDK's answer to the router/handoff topology — useful, but keep the business logic outside the framework so you can port it.
AdvancedQ. When would you use no framework at all?
A. When the workflow is a simple, well-understood loop — a direct provider SDK with your own control flow gives maximum transparency, minimal dependencies and the easiest debugging/eval. Why: you own every line, so there's no hidden control flow to fight. BankAssist: a fixed "classify → retrieve → answer" flow is cleaner as 50 lines of our own code than wrapped in a framework. Trade-off: you re-implement persistence, retries and observability yourself if you later need them. Strong answer adds: frameworks pay off when you need their orchestration, persistence, integrations or observability — not before.
AdvancedQ. What is DSPy and why is it different?
A. DSPy treats prompts as parameters to optimize, not strings to hand-tune: you declare signatures (input→output) and modules, then an optimizer compiles few-shot examples/instructions against a metric and training set. Why it's different: it replaces manual prompt tweaking with compilation. BankAssist: instead of hand-crafting the dispute-classifier prompt, we define the signature and let DSPy optimize it against our labeled set. Trade-off: it needs a metric and training data, which is upfront setup. Strong answer adds: it makes prompts portable across models — recompile when you switch models instead of re-tuning strings by hand.
AdvancedQ. How do you avoid framework lock-in?
A. Keep business logic, tool implementations and prompts outside framework-specific classes; wrap the model/provider behind your own interface; store prompts and eval sets independently. Why: frameworks churn and sometimes die — your domain logic shouldn't die with them. BankAssist: our dispute-resolution rules live in plain Python the framework merely calls, so swapping LangGraph for something else is a glue change, not a rewrite. Trade-off: the wrapper layer is a little extra code. Strong answer adds: use the framework for orchestration glue, not as the home of your domain logic.

MCP, A2A & Protocols

BasicQ. What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)?
A. An open standard (introduced by Anthropic in late 2024) that lets an AI app connect to tools and data through one uniform interface instead of bespoke integrations — "one plug instead of a tangle of wires." Why: it standardizes how an agent discovers and calls external capabilities. BankAssist: our agent reaches the CRM, the knowledge base and the ticketing system through MCP servers rather than three hand-written integrations. Trade-off: you run and secure the protocol layer. Strong answer adds: MCP is for agent-to-tool/data; it's one side of a larger protocol family that also covers agent-to-agent and agent-to-UI.
BasicQ. What are MCP's roles and primitives?
A. Roles: host (the app), client (the connector inside the host) and server (exposes capabilities). Primitives: tools (actions the model can call), resources (data/content it can read) and prompts (reusable templates). Why the split: it cleanly separates who hosts the model from who exposes the capability. BankAssist: the chat app is the host, its MCP client talks to a "transactions" server exposing a get_transactions tool and account resources. Trade-off: more moving parts than a direct function call. Strong answer adds: one host's client can speak to many servers, which is what makes capabilities composable across teams.
BasicQ. How does an MCP client talk to a server (transports)?
A. MCP messages are JSON-RPC carried over a transport — stdio for a local server (a subprocess on the same machine) or HTTP (streamable HTTP / SSE) for a remote one. Why it matters: the transport decides the trust and deployment model. BankAssist: a local PDF-parsing server runs over stdio inside our VPC, while a shared enterprise "customer-data" server is reached over authenticated HTTP. Trade-off: remote servers add network latency and a bigger attack surface than local ones. Strong answer adds: remote/HTTP servers need real auth and TLS — a networked MCP server is a service, with all the security that implies.
IntermediateQ. MCP vs A2A — what's the difference?
A. MCP is vertical: agent-to-tool/data (how an agent calls a capability). A2A (Agent-to-Agent) is horizontal: agent-to-agent (how peer agents discover, delegate and collaborate). Why both: a real system uses each for its direction. BankAssist: an orchestrator delegates to a KYC agent over A2A, while each specialist reaches its own tools via MCP. Trade-off: adopting both means two protocol layers to operate. Strong answer adds: A2A was donated by Google to the Linux Foundation in 2025 (now the Agent2Agent Protocol Project, v1.0, 150+ orgs) — naming its neutral governance signals you track the ecosystem.
IntermediateQ. Why standardize with MCP instead of custom tool integrations?
A. Custom integrations are N×M (every app × every tool); MCP makes it N+M — build a server once and any MCP client uses it, add a client once and it reaches every server. Why it compounds: you get reuse, a shared security model and an ecosystem. BankAssist: the "transactions" MCP server we build for the chat agent is instantly reusable by the fraud agent and the internal analytics tool. Trade-off: you pay for the protocol layer and its upkeep. Strong answer adds: the win is organizational — teams share capabilities instead of each re-integrating the same systems.
IntermediateQ. How does an agent discover and safely consume MCP tools at runtime?
